questions.q: Which two cell types make up nervous tissue?
options: Neuroglia and chondrocytes
Neurons and adipocytes
Neurons and fibroblasts
Neurons and neuroglia
questions.why: Nervous tissue has two kinds of cells. Neurons are the signaling cells that carry electrical impulses, with a cell body and long processes. Neuroglia, or glial cells, are smaller supporting cells that protect, nourish, and insulate the neurons, and they far outnumber them.
notes: Chondrocytes are cartilage cells sitting in lacunae. Neuroglia are half right, but the signaling cells of nervous tissue are neurons, not chondrocytes.
Adipocytes are fat-storing cells of adipose connective tissue. Neurons are half right, but adipocytes do not belong in nervous tissue.
Fibroblasts are the cells that build connective tissue fibers and matrix. Neurons are half right, but fibroblasts belong to connective tissue, not nervous tissue.
Correct. Nervous tissue is neurons plus neuroglia.
questions.answerText: Neurons and neuroglia

questions.q: Nervous tissue and the epidermis of the skin both arise from which germ layer?
options: Mesoderm
Both mesoderm and endoderm
Ectoderm
Endoderm
questions.why: The ectoderm is the outermost of the three germ layers. It gives rise to the epidermis of the skin and to all nervous tissue, because the brain and spinal cord develop from a tube of ectoderm called the neural tube. This shared origin links the outer skin and the nervous system in development.
notes: The mesoderm forms muscle, bone, cartilage, blood, and most connective tissue. It would be the answer for the connective tissue of the dermis, but not for the epidermis or nervous tissue.
Neither the mesoderm nor the endoderm forms nervous tissue or the epidermis. Students choose this when they are unsure and hedge across layers.
Correct. Both come from the ectoderm.
The endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts. Pick it for a question about the inner lining of the gut or airways.
questions.answerText: Ectoderm

questions.q: Which chain correctly links a germ layer to a tissue it forms and then to a location of that tissue?
options: Ectoderm forms nervous tissue, found in the brain
Mesoderm forms the epidermis, found in the skin
Endoderm forms nervous tissue, found in the brain
Ectoderm forms bone, found in the skeleton
questions.why: The ectoderm, the outer germ layer, forms all nervous tissue, and the brain is made of nervous tissue, so this chain links correctly at every step. Checking each link separately is how to catch the errors in the other chains. The ectoderm also forms the epidermis, the mesoderm forms bone and most connective tissue, and the endoderm forms the linings of the gut and airways.
notes: Correct. Ectoderm forms nervous tissue, which builds the brain.
The epidermis comes from the ectoderm, not the mesoderm. The mesoderm would be correct for the dermis or for bone.
The endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts, not nervous tissue. The second and third links are right, but the chain starts from the wrong layer.
Bone develops from the mesoderm, not the ectoderm. The chain would be correct if it started with the mesoderm.
questions.answerText: Ectoderm forms nervous tissue, found in the brain

questions.q: A nervous tissue slide shows a large cell body with a prominent nucleus and several long processes branching from it, surrounded by many small nuclei. What is the large cell?
options: A fibroblast
A neuroglial cell
A multipolar neuron
A smooth muscle cell
questions.why: A large cell body with a prominent nucleus and several long processes extending from it is a multipolar neuron, the most common type of neuron. Its processes are many dendrites and a single axon. The many small nuclei scattered around it belong to neuroglia, the smaller supporting cells that far outnumber neurons.
notes: A fibroblast is a connective tissue cell with an elongated nucleus that builds fibers. It does not have a large cell body with long branching processes.
Neuroglia are the small cells whose nuclei surround the neuron on this slide. They support and protect neurons and are much smaller than a neuron's cell body.
Correct. A large cell body with many processes is a multipolar neuron.
A smooth muscle cell is spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus and no branching processes. It is the answer for a slide of a hollow organ wall.
questions.answerText: A multipolar neuron

questions.q: Which part of a neuron receives incoming signals from other cells?
options: The axon
The axon hillock
The synaptic bulb
The dendrites
questions.why: Dendrites are the short, branched, tree-like processes that extend from the cell body. Their job is to receive incoming signals and carry them toward the cell body. A multipolar neuron has many dendrites but only one axon, which is how you tell them apart on a slide.
notes: The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body toward other cells. Pick it if the question asked which process sends the signal out.
The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region where the cell body joins the axon. Pick it if the question asked where the axon begins.
The synaptic bulb is the swollen tip at the end of an axon terminal, where the signal is passed to the next cell. It sends signals rather than receiving them.
Correct. Dendrites receive incoming signals.
questions.answerText: The dendrites

questions.q: Which part of a neuron carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body toward other cells?
options: The cell body
The nucleolus
The axon
The dendrite
questions.why: The axon is the single long process of a neuron. It carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body, and at its far end it branches into axon terminals that contact the next cell. A neuron can have many dendrites, but it has only one axon.
notes: The cell body holds the nucleus and is the neuron's metabolic center. It is where the axon starts, not the process that carries the impulse away.
The nucleolus is a small dark spot inside the nucleus, visible in the cell body on a neuron slide. It is not a process and does not carry impulses.
Correct. The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body.
Dendrites carry signals toward the cell body, the opposite direction. Pick them if the question asked which processes receive incoming signals.
questions.answerText: The axon

questions.q: Which part of a neuron contains the nucleus and serves as the cell's metabolic center?
options: The dendrites
The cell body
The synaptic bulb
The axon
questions.why: The cell body, also called the soma, holds the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm, so it is where the neuron makes its proteins and keeps itself alive. On a multipolar neuron slide it is the large central part of the cell, often with a clearly visible nucleus and a dark nucleolus inside.
notes: Dendrites are branched processes that receive signals. They extend from the cell body but do not hold the nucleus.
Correct. The cell body holds the nucleus and is the neuron's metabolic center.
The synaptic bulb is the swollen tip of an axon terminal that passes the signal to the next cell. It is far from the nucleus.
The axon is the single long process that carries impulses away. It contains no nucleus.
questions.answerText: The cell body

questions.q: On a neuron, what is the synaptic bulb?
options: The swollen tip at the end of an axon terminal
A short, branched process that receives signals
The cone-shaped region where the axon begins
A gap in the myelin sheath along the axon
questions.why: At its far end, the axon splits into fine branches called axon terminals, and each one ends in a small swelling, the synaptic bulb (also called the synaptic end bulb). The bulb holds the machinery that passes the signal to the next cell. It is one of the three nerve tissue structures listed for the Module 1 lab.
notes: Correct. The synaptic bulb is the swollen tip of an axon terminal.
A short, branched process that receives signals is a dendrite. Pick it if the question asked what brings signals toward the cell body.
The cone-shaped region where the axon begins is the axon hillock, at the junction with the cell body. Pick it if the question asked where the axon starts.
A gap in the myelin sheath is a node of Ranvier. Pick it for a question about a myelinated axon in a nerve.
questions.answerText: The swollen tip at the end of an axon terminal

questions.q: Where in the body is nervous tissue found?
options: The walls of the intestines and bladder
The tendons and ligaments
The heart wall and blood vessels
The brain, spinal cord, and nerves
questions.why: Nervous tissue is made of neurons and neuroglia, and its job is to detect changes and carry electrical signals. It is found in the brain and spinal cord, which make up the central nervous system, and in the nerves that branch out to the rest of the body.
notes: The walls of the intestines and bladder are mainly smooth muscle, lined by epithelium. Pick smooth muscle for that location.
Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue. Pick them for a slide of parallel collagen bundles.
The heart wall is cardiac muscle, and blood vessel walls are mostly smooth muscle and connective tissue. Nerves reach these organs, but the walls themselves are not nervous tissue.
Correct. Nervous tissue makes up the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
questions.answerText: The brain, spinal cord, and nerves

questions.q: On a nervous tissue slide, one large neuron with long processes is surrounded by many small, dark nuclei that have no visible processes. What are the small nuclei?
options: Synaptic bulbs
Dendrites
Neuroglia
Smooth muscle cells
questions.why: Neuroglia are the supporting cells of nervous tissue. They are much smaller and far more numerous than neurons, so on a slide they appear as many small, dark nuclei scattered around the large neuron cell bodies. Telling neurons from neuroglia under the microscope is a listed lab skill.
notes: Synaptic bulbs are swellings at the tips of axon terminals. They are parts of a neuron, not separate cells with nuclei.
Dendrites are processes of the neuron itself and do not have their own nuclei. Pick them if the question asked about the branches coming off the cell body.
Correct. The many small nuclei around the neuron belong to neuroglia.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped muscle cells in the walls of hollow organs. They are not found scattered among neurons in nervous tissue.
questions.answerText: Neuroglia

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares neurons with neuroglia?
options: Neuroglia carry impulses, while neurons only support and protect
Neurons and neuroglia are the same size and both carry impulses
Neuroglia are smaller and more numerous, and only neuroglia can divide
Neurons are smaller and more numerous, and only neurons can divide
questions.why: Neurons are the excitable cells that receive and transmit nerve impulses, and mature neurons cannot divide. Neuroglia are the support cells that nourish, support, and protect neurons. They are smaller and far more numerous, and they keep the ability to divide.
notes: This swaps the two roles. Neurons carry impulses, while neuroglia support and protect them.
Neurons are generally much larger than neuroglia, and carrying impulses is the job of neurons, not glia.
Correct. Neuroglia are smaller, more numerous, and still able to divide.
This reverses the two cells. Neurons are the larger cells, and mature neurons cannot divide.
questions.answerText: Neuroglia are smaller and more numerous, and only neuroglia can divide

questions.q: A glioma is a brain tumor that arises from glial cells. Why do tumors like this arise from glia rather than from mature neurons?
options: Glial cells can still divide, while mature neurons cannot
Glial cells are larger than neurons, so they have more room to grow
Neurons are protected by intercalated discs that stop growth
Neurons are found only in nerves, not inside the brain
questions.why: A tumor is a mass of cells dividing out of control, so it can only arise from cells that are still able to divide. Mature neurons have lost that ability, but neuroglia keep it. That is why tumors of brain tissue come from glial cells rather than from mature neurons.
notes: Correct. Tumors come from dividing cells, and glia can divide while mature neurons cannot.
Glial cells are smaller than neurons, not larger. Size is not what lets a cell form a tumor anyway.
Intercalated discs are junctions between cardiac muscle cells, not structures in nervous tissue.
Neurons are found throughout the brain and spinal cord as well as in ganglia. Their cell bodies are plentiful inside the brain.
questions.answerText: Glial cells can still divide, while mature neurons cannot

questions.q: The trachea has an epithelial lining, rings of hyaline cartilage in its wall, and nervous tissue in the nerves that reach it. Which set matches each tissue to its germ layer?
options: Lining from ectoderm, cartilage from mesoderm, nervous tissue from endoderm.
Lining from mesoderm, cartilage from endoderm, nervous tissue from ectoderm.
Lining from endoderm, cartilage from ectoderm, nervous tissue from mesoderm.
Lining from endoderm, cartilage from mesoderm, nervous tissue from ectoderm.
questions.why: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract. Mesoderm forms cartilage along with bone, muscle, and blood. Ectoderm forms all nervous tissue. The trachea shows all three germ layers in one organ.
notes: The lining and nervous tissue are swapped. The respiratory lining comes from endoderm, and nervous tissue comes from ectoderm.
Cartilage comes from mesoderm, not endoderm, and the airway lining comes from endoderm. Only the nerves are matched correctly here.
The lining is right, but cartilage comes from mesoderm and nervous tissue from ectoderm. Those two are swapped.
Correct. Airway lining is endodermal, cartilage is mesodermal, and nervous tissue is ectodermal.
questions.answerText: Lining from endoderm, cartilage from mesoderm, nervous tissue from ectoderm.

questions.q: On a multipolar neuron slide, a student finds the one spot where a single long process leaves the cell body. Which part of the neuron is that spot, and which process does it lead into?
options: The synaptic bulb, leading into a dendrite.
The axon hillock, leading into the axon.
The axon hillock, leading into a dendrite.
The nucleolus, leading into the axon.
questions.why: A multipolar neuron has many dendrites and only one axon. The axon leaves the cell body at a region called the axon hillock. Finding the hillock tells you which process is the axon, the one that carries the impulse away from the cell body.
notes: The synaptic bulb is at the far end of the axon, not where a process leaves the cell body. Dendrites are the branching processes that receive signals.
Correct. The axon hillock is where the single axon leaves the cell body.
The hillock is right, but it leads into the axon. Dendrites are the many branching processes that receive signals and carry them toward the cell body.
The nucleolus is the dark spot inside the nucleus, in the middle of the cell body. It does not form part of any process.
questions.answerText: The axon hillock, leading into the axon.

questions.q: A student views a large neuron cell body with a nucleus that contains one dark dot, surrounded by many small, separate nuclei. She labels the dark dot a glial cell inside the neuron. What is the dark dot, and what are the glia?
options: The dot is the axon hillock; the glia are the branching dendrites.
The dot is a glial cell; the small nuclei around it are other neurons.
The dot is the nucleolus; the glia are the small nuclei around the neuron.
The dot is the synaptic bulb; the glia are the nucleoli of the neuron.
questions.why: A neuron's large nucleus holds a dark nucleolus, both structures to identify on the multipolar neuron slide. Neuroglia are the supporting cells of nervous tissue, and on a slide they appear as many small nuclei scattered around the neurons. Glia sit beside neurons, not inside them.
notes: The axon hillock is at the base of the axon, outside the nucleus. Dendrites are parts of the neuron, not glial cells.
Glia do not sit inside a neuron's nucleus. The small, numerous nuclei around the large cell are the neuroglia.
Correct. The dark dot is the nucleolus, and the many small nuclei around the neuron are neuroglia.
The synaptic bulb is at the end of the axon, far from the nucleus. Nucleoli are part of nuclei, not separate glial cells.
questions.answerText: The dot is the nucleolus; the glia are the small nuclei around the neuron.

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which two structures make up the central nervous system?
options: The brain and the spinal cord
The nerves and the ganglia
The neurons and the neuroglia
The brain and the cranial nerves
questions.why: The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain, which sits in the cranial cavity, and the spinal cord, which runs in the vertebral canal. Together they process incoming information and issue commands, so the CNS is the control center of the nervous system. Everything outside these two organs, including the nerves, ganglia, and sensory receptors, belongs to the peripheral nervous system.
notes: Correct. The brain and the spinal cord together form the CNS.
Nerves (bundles of axons) and ganglia (clusters of cell bodies) sit outside the brain and spinal cord. Choose them for a question asking what makes up the peripheral nervous system.
Neurons and neuroglia are the two cell types of nervous tissue, and they are found in both the CNS and the PNS. Pick them if the question asked which cells make up nervous tissue.

The brain is part of the CNS, but the cranial nerves are bundles of axons that leave the brain and run outside it, so they belong to the PNS. This pairing would fit a question about the brain and the 12 pairs of nerves attached to it.
questions.answerText: The brain and the spinal cord

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which part of a neuron contains the nucleus?
options: The axon
The dendrite
The axon terminal
The cell body
questions.why: The cell body, also called the soma or perikaryon, holds the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm, which makes it the metabolic center of the neuron. Its Nissl bodies (clusters of rough ER and ribosomes) make the proteins the whole cell needs, including those used far out in the axon. The processes that extend from the cell body, the dendrites and the axon, do not hold the nucleus.
notes: The axon is the single long process that carries the impulse away from the cell body toward other cells. It would be the answer for a question about which part conducts the signal away.
Dendrites are the short, branched processes that receive incoming signals and carry them toward the cell body. Pick the dendrite for a question about the receiving part of a neuron.
Axon terminals are the fine branches at the far end of the axon that contact the target cell. They would be right for a question about where the neuron hands its signal to the next cell.
Correct. The cell body holds the nucleus and is the metabolic center of the neuron.
questions.answerText: The cell body

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which glial cell forms the myelin sheath around axons in the central nervous system?
options: The Schwann cell
The microglia
The oligodendrocyte
The astrocyte
questions.why: Oligodendrocytes are CNS glial cells whose processes wrap around axons to form the myelin sheath, a fatty covering that insulates the axon and speeds the impulse. One oligodendrocyte can send processes to several axons at once, myelinating a segment of each. In the PNS the same job belongs to a different cell, the Schwann cell, so the location of the axon decides the answer.
notes: Schwann cells also form myelin, but only around axons in the peripheral nervous system. Pick the Schwann cell when the question places the axon in a peripheral nerve.
Microglia are the small phagocytic glia of the CNS that clear away debris and microbes. They would be the answer for a question about the defense cells of the brain and spinal cord.
Correct. Oligodendrocytes make the myelin in the brain and spinal cord.

Astrocytes are star-shaped CNS glia that support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier; they do not make myelin. Choose the astrocyte for a question about the blood-brain barrier or structural support.
questions.answerText: The oligodendrocyte

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What are the regular gaps in the myelin sheath along an axon called?
options: The axon hillocks
The axon terminals
The nodes of Ranvier
The synaptic clefts
questions.why: Myelin is laid down in segments, and the short, bare stretches of axon between the segments are the nodes of Ranvier. The impulse jumps from one node to the next, a pattern called saltatory conduction, which is why myelinated axons conduct much faster than unmyelinated ones. Each segment between two nodes is wrapped by one Schwann cell in the PNS or by one process of an oligodendrocyte in the CNS.
notes: The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region where the axon leaves the cell body, at the very start of the axon. It would be the answer for a question about where the axon joins the cell body.
Axon terminals are the fine branches at the far end of the axon. Choose them for a question about where the neuron contacts its target cell.
Correct. The nodes of Ranvier are the bare gaps between myelin segments.
A synaptic cleft is a gap too, but it is the space between two cells at a chemical synapse, not a gap in the myelin. Pick it for a question about the space that neurotransmitter crosses.
questions.answerText: The nodes of Ranvier

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which glial cell forms the myelin sheath around axons in the peripheral nervous system?
options: The Schwann cell
The satellite cell
The oligodendrocyte
The ependymal cell
questions.why: Schwann cells are the myelin-forming glia of the PNS. Each Schwann cell wraps one segment of one axon, and its outer layer, which holds its nucleus and cytoplasm, forms the neurolemma. That neurolemma guides a cut axon as it regrows, which is why peripheral nerves can regenerate while CNS tracts usually cannot.
notes: Correct. Schwann cells myelinate axons in peripheral nerves.
Satellite cells are the other PNS glia, but they surround neuron cell bodies inside ganglia instead of wrapping axons. Pick them for a question about the support cells in a ganglion.
Oligodendrocytes form myelin too, but only in the CNS. Choose the oligodendrocyte when the axon is in the brain or spinal cord.

Ependymal cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord and help produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid. They would be right for a question about the lining of the CNS cavities.
questions.answerText: The Schwann cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the single long process of a neuron that carries the impulse away from the cell body?
options: The axon hillock
The myelin sheath
The axon
The dendrite
questions.why: The axon is the single long process of a neuron, and it carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands. It begins at the axon hillock and ends in branching axon terminals. A typical neuron has many dendrites bringing signals in but only one axon sending the signal out.
notes: The axon hillock is the cone-shaped spot on the cell body where the axon starts; it is the beginning of the axon, not the whole process. Choose it for a question about where the cell body joins the axon.

The myelin sheath is a fatty wrapping made by glial cells around many axons, so it is not a process of the neuron itself. It would be right for a question about what insulates the axon and speeds the impulse.
Correct. The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body.
Dendrites are short, branched processes that carry signals toward the cell body, the opposite direction. Pick the dendrite for a question about the receiving processes of a neuron.
questions.answerText: The axon

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which glial cell acts as the defense cell of the central nervous system?
options: The satellite cell
The microglia
The ependymal cell
The astrocyte
questions.why: Microglia are small phagocytic glial cells of the CNS. Phagocytic means they engulf and digest material, so they remove dead cells, debris, and microbes from the brain and spinal cord. Of the four CNS glia, they are the only ones whose main job is defense; the others support neurons, make myelin, or line the fluid-filled cavities.
notes: Satellite cells are PNS glia that surround neuron cell bodies inside ganglia, so they are not even in the CNS. They would be right for a question about support cells in a peripheral ganglion.
Correct. Microglia engulf debris and microbes in the CNS.
Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and help produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid. Choose them for a question about the lining of the CNS cavities.

Astrocytes are star-shaped CNS glia that support neurons, help form the blood-brain barrier, and maintain the chemical environment around neurons. Pick the astrocyte for a question about the blood-brain barrier.
questions.answerText: The microglia

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the tiny gap between the two cells at a chemical synapse called?
options: The node of Ranvier
The axon hillock
The synaptic vesicle
The synaptic cleft
questions.why: At a chemical synapse the sending and receiving cells do not touch. The narrow space between them is the synaptic cleft, and the neurotransmitter released by the sending cell diffuses across this gap to reach the receiving cell. That is why the signal crosses a chemical synapse as a chemical message rather than through direct contact.
notes: A node of Ranvier is a gap in the myelin sheath along an axon, not a gap between two cells. It would be right for a question about where the impulse jumps during saltatory conduction.
The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region where the axon leaves the cell body. Choose it for a question about where the axon begins.
Synaptic vesicles are tiny sacs inside the sending axon terminal that store neurotransmitter before it is released. Pick the vesicle for a question about where neurotransmitter is stored.
Correct. The synaptic cleft is the gap the neurotransmitter crosses.
questions.answerText: The synaptic cleft

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which structural class of neuron has many dendrites and one axon and is the most common type?
options: The multipolar neuron
The unipolar neuron
The sensory neuron
The bipolar neuron
questions.why: Multipolar neurons have many dendrites and one axon, and they are the most common structural class. Almost all neurons in the brain and spinal cord are multipolar, including motor neurons and interneurons. The structural classes are named for how many processes leave the cell body: many for multipolar, two for bipolar, and one for unipolar.
notes: Correct. Multipolar neurons have many dendrites and one axon.
A unipolar neuron has a single fused process that leaves the cell body, and it is the typical shape of a sensory neuron. Choose it for a question about the shape of most sensory neurons.

Sensory neuron is a functional name for a neuron that carries signals toward the CNS, not a structural class. Most sensory neurons are unipolar, so they do not have many dendrites. Pick it for a question about direction of signaling.
A bipolar neuron has just one dendrite and one axon and is found in the retina, the inner ear, and the olfactory area. Pick it for a question about neurons in the special sense organs.
questions.answerText: The multipolar neuron

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the cone-shaped region of the cell body where the axon begins called?
options: The node of Ranvier
The synaptic end bulb
The axon terminal
The axon hillock
questions.why: The axon hillock is the cone-shaped part of the cell body that narrows into the start of the axon. It marks the boundary between the cell body, which receives and processes input, and the axon, which carries the impulse away. On a slide it is the tapered point where the single axon leaves the soma.
notes: A node of Ranvier is a bare gap in the myelin sheath further along the axon. Pick it for a question about the gaps where the impulse jumps.
Synaptic end bulbs are the swellings at the tips of the axon terminals that hold the synaptic vesicles. Choose them for a question about the signal-sending end of the neuron.
Axon terminals are the fine branches at the far end of the axon, the opposite end from the hillock. They would be right for a question about where the neuron contacts its target.
Correct. The axon hillock is where the cell body narrows into the axon.
questions.answerText: The axon hillock

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What are the two cell types that make up nervous tissue?
options: Sensory cells and motor cells
Astrocytes and Schwann cells
Neurons and neuroglia
Axons and dendrites
questions.why: Nervous tissue is built from two cell types. Neurons are the excitable cells that receive, conduct, and transmit nerve impulses, and neuroglia (glial cells) are the smaller, very numerous support cells that nourish, insulate, and protect them. Unlike neurons, glial cells can still divide.
notes: Sensory and motor neurons are functional classes of neurons, so both are neurons and the support cells are missing. This would fit a question about neurons that carry signals toward and away from the CNS.

Astrocytes and Schwann cells are both glial cells, one from the CNS and one from the PNS, so the neurons are missing. Choose this pair for a question asking for one CNS glial cell and one PNS glial cell.
Correct. Nervous tissue is built from neurons and their support cells, the neuroglia.
Axons and dendrites are processes of a single neuron, not separate cell types. Pick them for a question about the two kinds of processes that extend from the cell body.
questions.answerText: Neurons and neuroglia

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the small sac in the axon terminal that stores neurotransmitter called?
options: The Nissl body
The synaptic cleft
The synaptic end bulb
The synaptic vesicle
questions.why: Synaptic vesicles are tiny membrane sacs packed inside the synaptic end bulbs at the tips of the axon terminals. Each vesicle stores neurotransmitter, the chemical messenger, until a signal arrives and the vesicles release it into the synaptic cleft. Only the sending side of a synapse holds these vesicles.
notes: Nissl bodies are clusters of rough ER and ribosomes in the cell body that make proteins. They would be right for a question about the site of protein synthesis in a neuron.
The synaptic cleft is the gap between the two cells that the neurotransmitter crosses after release, not a sac that stores it. Pick it for a question about the space between the cells.

The synaptic end bulb is the swelling at the tip of an axon terminal that contains the vesicles; it is the container, not the sac itself. Choose it for a question about the swelling that holds the signal-sending machinery.
Correct. Synaptic vesicles store neurotransmitter until it is released.
questions.answerText: The synaptic vesicle

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The sensory division of the peripheral nervous system is also known by which name?
options: The afferent division
The autonomic division
The somatic division
The efferent division
questions.why: Afferent means carrying toward, so the afferent (sensory) division carries signals from sensory receptors toward the CNS. Its partner, the efferent (motor) division, carries commands away from the CNS to the muscles and glands. Afferent signals arrive at the CNS, and efferent signals exit it.
notes: Correct. Afferent means carrying toward, and the sensory division carries signals toward the CNS.
The autonomic nervous system is a subdivision of the motor division that controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. Choose it for a question about involuntary motor commands.
The somatic nervous system is a subdivision of the motor division that carries voluntary commands to skeletal muscle. It would be right for a question about the nerves that move skeletal muscle.
The efferent division is the motor division, which carries commands away from the CNS to muscles and glands. Pick it for a question asking for the other name of the motor division.
questions.answerText: The afferent division

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which subdivision of the motor division carries voluntary commands to skeletal muscle?
options: The somatic nervous system
The enteric nervous system
The sensory (afferent) division
The autonomic nervous system
questions.why: The motor (efferent) division of the PNS is split by the kind of effector it controls. The somatic nervous system is the voluntary branch, and its motor neurons carry commands from the CNS directly to skeletal muscle. The autonomic nervous system, by contrast, controls effectors that work without conscious control.
notes: Correct. The somatic nervous system is the voluntary branch that drives skeletal muscle.
The enteric nervous system is the network of neurons in the wall of the GI tract that can work on its own. Choose it for a question about the nervous system of the gut.
The sensory division carries signals toward the CNS from receptors, so it does not carry commands at all. It would be right for a question about input from receptors.
The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary branch, carrying commands to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. Pick it for a question about heart rate or gland secretion.
questions.answerText: The somatic nervous system

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which subdivision of the motor division carries involuntary commands to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands?
options: The sensory (afferent) division
The central nervous system
The autonomic nervous system
The somatic nervous system
questions.why: The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary branch of the motor division of the PNS. Its motor neurons carry commands to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, the effectors that work without conscious control. It has two divisions, the sympathetic division for fight or flight and the parasympathetic division for rest and digest, and many organs receive both.
notes: The sensory division carries input from receptors toward the CNS rather than commands out to effectors. Choose it for a question about signals arriving at the CNS.
The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, where commands are issued, but it is not a subdivision of the motor division of the PNS. It would be right for a question about where information is integrated.
Correct. The autonomic nervous system runs the effectors we do not consciously control.
The somatic nervous system is the voluntary branch of the motor division, carrying commands to skeletal muscle. Pick it for a question about moving a limb on purpose.
questions.answerText: The autonomic nervous system

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Nerves and ganglia have one feature in common. Which statement describes it?
options: Both are bundles of axons
Both are clusters of cell bodies
Both lie inside the CNS
Both lie outside the CNS
questions.why: Nerves and ganglia are the two main structures of the peripheral nervous system, which includes every neural structure outside the brain and spinal cord. A nerve is a bundle of axons and a ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies, so they differ in what they contain but share their location outside the CNS. Inside the CNS, the matching structures are called tracts and nuclei.
notes: Only a nerve is a bundle of axons; a ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies. This statement would fit a comparison of a nerve and a tract, which are both bundles of axons.
Only a ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies; a nerve is a bundle of axons. This statement would fit a comparison of a ganglion and a nucleus.
This is the reverse of the truth. The structures that lie inside the CNS are tracts and nuclei, so pick this statement for a question about those two.
Correct. Nerves and ganglia are both structures of the peripheral nervous system.
questions.answerText: Both lie outside the CNS

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which glial cell helps form the blood-brain barrier?
options: The astrocyte
The oligodendrocyte
The ependymal cell
The microglia
questions.why: Astrocytes are star-shaped glial cells of the CNS. Their processes wrap around the capillaries of the brain and help form the blood-brain barrier, which limits what can pass from the blood into brain tissue. They also give structural support, guide the growth of neurons, and keep the chemical environment around neurons stable.
notes: Correct. Astrocytes help form the blood-brain barrier.
Oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheaths around axons in the CNS. Pick the oligodendrocyte for a question about CNS myelin.
Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and help produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid. They would be right for a question about the lining of the CNS cavities.
Microglia are the small phagocytic glia that clear debris and microbes from the CNS. Choose them for a question about the defense cells of the brain.
questions.answerText: The astrocyte

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which glial cell lines the cavities of the brain and spinal cord and helps circulate cerebrospinal fluid?
options: The ependymal cell
The astrocyte
The oligodendrocyte
The microglia
questions.why: Ependymal cells are CNS glia that line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. They help produce cerebrospinal fluid and help move it through those spaces. Their position as the lining of the fluid-filled cavities is what sets them apart from the other three CNS glia.
notes: Correct. Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal.
Astrocytes are star-shaped CNS glia that support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier, but they do not line the cavities. Pick the astrocyte for a question about the blood-brain barrier.
Oligodendrocytes wrap CNS axons in myelin. They would be the answer for a question about which cell myelinates axons in the brain or spinal cord.
Microglia are phagocytic CNS glia that remove debris and microbes. Choose them for a question about defense in the brain and spinal cord.
questions.answerText: The ependymal cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which glial cell surrounds and supports the neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia?
options: The oligodendrocyte
The satellite cell
The astrocyte
The Schwann cell
questions.why: Satellite cells are PNS glia that form a layer around each neuron cell body inside a ganglion, such as a posterior root ganglion. They support those cell bodies in the same way that astrocytes support neurons in the CNS. The PNS has only two kinds of glia: satellite cells around cell bodies and Schwann cells around axons.
notes: Oligodendrocytes form myelin around CNS axons. They would be right for a question about myelin in the brain or spinal cord.
Correct. Satellite cells surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia.
Astrocytes are the main support cells around neurons in the CNS, not in peripheral ganglia. Choose the astrocyte for a question about support or the blood-brain barrier in the brain.
Schwann cells are also PNS glia, but they wrap axons in myelin rather than surrounding cell bodies. Pick the Schwann cell for a question about myelin in a peripheral nerve.
questions.answerText: The satellite cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An interneuron lies entirely within which division of the nervous system?
options: The autonomic nervous system
The somatic nervous system
The central nervous system
The peripheral nervous system
questions.why: Interneurons, also called association neurons, lie entirely within the brain and spinal cord. They connect sensory neurons to motor neurons and link neurons to each other, so they carry out much of the processing the CNS performs. Sensory and motor neurons, by contrast, have long processes that extend out into the PNS.
notes: The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary motor branch of the PNS that runs to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. It would be right for a question about control of the viscera.
The somatic nervous system is the voluntary motor branch of the PNS that runs to skeletal muscle. Choose it for a question about the motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle.
Correct. Interneurons lie entirely within the brain and spinal cord.

The PNS holds the nerves, ganglia, and receptors outside the brain and spinal cord. Sensory and motor neurons have processes that run in the PNS, so pick it for a question about where those long processes travel.
questions.answerText: The central nervous system

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: By function, which type of neuron carries signals from receptors toward the central nervous system?
options: The sensory neuron
The interneuron
The motor neuron
The multipolar neuron
questions.why: Neurons are classified by function according to the direction they carry signals relative to the CNS. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry input from receptors toward the CNS, and most of them are unipolar in shape. Motor neurons carry commands away from the CNS, and interneurons connect the two inside the CNS.
notes: Correct. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry input toward the CNS.
Interneurons stay entirely within the CNS and connect sensory neurons to motor neurons. Choose the interneuron for a question about the neurons that link input to output inside the brain or cord.
Motor (efferent) neurons carry commands in the opposite direction, away from the CNS to muscles and glands. Pick the motor neuron for a question about signals leaving the CNS.
Multipolar is a structural class based on shape, not on the direction a neuron carries signals. It would be right for a question about a neuron with many dendrites and one axon.
questions.answerText: The sensory neuron

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Neurons are sorted into multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar types according to which feature?
options: The direction in which they carry signals
The type of glial cell that supports them
Whether their axon has a myelin sheath
How many processes leave the cell body
questions.why: The structural classification of neurons is based on shape, specifically how many processes leave the cell body. Multipolar neurons have many (several dendrites and one axon), bipolar neurons have two (one dendrite and one axon), and unipolar neurons have a single process that then splits. The other way to classify neurons is functional, by the direction they carry signals.
notes: Direction is the basis of the functional classification, which gives sensory, motor, and interneurons. Pick this feature for a question about how those three functional classes are defined.
Glial cells differ between the CNS and the PNS, but neurons are not named for the glia around them. This would fit a question about the difference between Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes.
Myelin divides axons into myelinated and unmyelinated, which affects conduction speed but not the structural class. Choose this feature for a question about what makes white matter white.
Correct. The structural classes count the processes extending from the cell body.
questions.answerText: How many processes leave the cell body

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a motor neuron and which structure?
options: Another neuron's dendrite
A skeletal muscle fiber
A secretory gland cell
A supporting glial cell
questions.why: A synapse is any site where a neuron communicates with another neuron, a muscle cell, or a gland. The neuromuscular junction is the specific synapse where the axon terminal of a somatic motor neuron meets a skeletal muscle fiber. The neurotransmitter released there crosses the cleft and triggers the muscle fiber to contract.
notes: A synapse between two neurons is a neuron-to-neuron synapse, such as an axodendritic or axosomatic synapse. Pick this for a question about where an axon meets a dendrite or cell body.
Correct. The neuromuscular junction links a motor neuron to a skeletal muscle fiber.

Neurons do synapse with gland cells, for example in autonomic pathways, but that synapse is not called the neuromuscular junction. Choose a gland cell for a question about autonomic effectors that secrete.
Glial cells support neurons but are not the target of motor commands. This would fit a question about the cells that wrap axons or surround cell bodies.
questions.answerText: A skeletal muscle fiber

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Within a neuron, which structures receive signals and carry them toward the cell body?
options: The axon terminals
The axon hillock
The axon
The dendrites
questions.why: Dendrites are the short, branched, tree-like processes of a neuron, and they are its main receiving surface. Signals from other neurons arrive at synapses on the dendrites and travel toward the cell body. From there the signal can continue to the axon hillock and out along the axon.
notes: Axon terminals are the branches at the end of the axon that pass the signal on to the next cell. Choose them for a question about where a neuron hands off its signal.
The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region where the axon leaves the cell body. It would be right for a question about where the axon begins.
The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body, the opposite direction. Pick the axon for a question about the outgoing process.
Correct. Dendrites are the receiving processes of the neuron.
questions.answerText: The dendrites

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The motor division of the peripheral nervous system is also known by which name?
options: The efferent division
The autonomic division
The somatic division
The afferent division
questions.why: Efferent means carrying away, so the efferent (motor) division carries commands from the CNS out to the effectors, the muscles and glands. It includes the somatic nervous system for skeletal muscle, the autonomic nervous system for smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, and the enteric nervous system in the wall of the digestive tract. Its counterpart is the afferent (sensory) division, which carries input toward the CNS.
notes: Correct. Efferent means carrying away, and the motor division carries commands away from the CNS.

The autonomic nervous system is one part of the motor division, the involuntary part that reaches smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. It is a subdivision, not another name for the whole division.
The somatic nervous system is one part of the motor division, the voluntary part that reaches skeletal muscle, not another name for the whole division.
The afferent division is the sensory division, which carries signals toward the CNS, the opposite direction. Pick it for the other name of the sensory division.
questions.answerText: The efferent division

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The cell body of a neuron is also known by which single-word term?
options: The axolemma
The axoplasm
The soma
The neurolemma
questions.why: Soma means body, so soma is the one-word name for the cell body of a neuron; perikaryon is another name for the same part. The soma holds the nucleus and the Nissl bodies and is the metabolic center of the neuron. The look-alike terms axoplasm, axolemma, and neurolemma all describe the axon or its wrapping instead.
notes: The axolemma is the plasma membrane that surrounds the axon. Choose it for a question about the membrane of the axon.
Axoplasm is the cytoplasm inside the axon, not the cell body. Pick it for a question about the fluid contents of the axon.
Correct. Soma means body, and it is another name for the cell body.

The neurolemma is the outer layer of a Schwann cell wrapped around a peripheral axon, so it is part of a glial cell, not the neuron. It would be right for a question about what guides a cut peripheral axon as it regrows.
questions.answerText: The soma

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Pyramidal cells of the cerebral cortex and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum share which structural feature?
options: Both are glial support cells
Both are multipolar neurons
Both are unipolar neurons
Both are bipolar neurons
questions.why: Pyramidal cells in the cerebral cortex and Purkinje cells in the cerebellum are two named examples of multipolar neurons, each with many dendrites and one axon. They have distinctive shapes, which is why they are given their own names, but structurally they still fall in the multipolar class. Multipolar neurons are the most common type in the brain and spinal cord.
notes: Glial cells are the support cells of nervous tissue, such as astrocytes and Schwann cells. Pyramidal and Purkinje cells are neurons, so pick glial cells only for a question about support cells.
Correct. Pyramidal and Purkinje cells are both distinctive multipolar neurons.
Unipolar neurons have a single process and are the typical shape of sensory neurons. Choose unipolar for a question about the shape of most sensory neurons.
Bipolar neurons have one dendrite and one axon and are found in the retina, the inner ear, and the olfactory area. Pick bipolar for a question about neurons in the special sense organs.
questions.answerText: Both are multipolar neurons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A neuron has a single short process that leaves the cell body and then divides in two, and most sensory neurons have this shape. Which structural class is it?
options: A multipolar neuron
A motor neuron
A unipolar neuron
A bipolar neuron
questions.why: A unipolar neuron has only one process leaving the cell body, and that single process splits into two branches, one running toward the periphery and one toward the CNS. This shape is typical of sensory neurons, whose cell bodies sit in ganglia such as the posterior root ganglion. The structural class depends only on how many processes leave the cell body.
notes: A multipolar neuron has many dendrites and one axon. Choose it for a question about motor neurons or interneurons.

Motor neuron is a functional name for a neuron that carries commands away from the CNS, not a shape class, and motor neurons are multipolar. It would be right for a question about direction of signaling.
Correct. A unipolar neuron has a single process leaving the cell body.
A bipolar neuron has two separate processes, one dendrite and one axon, leaving opposite ends of the cell body. Pick it for a question about neurons in the retina or inner ear.
questions.answerText: A unipolar neuron

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A glial cell in the spinal cord sends out several processes, and each one wraps a segment of a different axon in myelin. Which glial cell is it?
options: An ependymal cell
An astrocyte
A Schwann cell
An oligodendrocyte
questions.why: Oligodendrocytes are the myelin-forming cells of the CNS, and each one has a few long processes. Each process wraps a segment of a different axon, so one oligodendrocyte myelinates parts of several axons. A Schwann cell in the PNS is different: it myelinates one segment of a single axon.
notes: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and the central canal of the cord and help circulate cerebrospinal fluid. They would be right for a question about the lining of the central canal.

Astrocytes are star-shaped CNS glia with many processes, but those processes support neurons and wrap capillaries rather than forming myelin. Choose the astrocyte for a question about the blood-brain barrier.
A Schwann cell wraps just one segment of one axon, and it works only in the PNS. Pick it for a question about myelin in a peripheral nerve.
Correct. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of several CNS axons.
questions.answerText: An oligodendrocyte

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which pair names the two types of glial cells found in the peripheral nervous system?
options: Astrocytes and microglia
Satellite cells and ependymal cells
Schwann cells and satellite cells
Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes
questions.why: The PNS has two kinds of glia. Schwann cells wrap peripheral axons in myelin and form the neurolemma, and satellite cells surround and support the neuron cell bodies inside ganglia. The other four glial types, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells, are found in the CNS.
notes: Astrocytes and microglia are both CNS glia, so neither belongs in the PNS. Pick this pair for a question asking for the CNS glia that support neurons and defend the tissue.
Satellite cells are PNS glia, but ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal of the CNS. Pick ependymal cells for a question about the lining of the ventricles.
Correct. These are the only two glial cells of the PNS.
These are the two myelin-forming cells, but the oligodendrocyte works in the CNS. Choose this pair for a question asking which cells make myelin in the PNS and CNS.
questions.answerText: Schwann cells and satellite cells

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: On a neuron model, you point to the fine branches at the far end of the axon that pass the signal to the next cell. Which part are you pointing to?
options: The dendrites
The cell body
The axon hillock
The axon terminals
questions.why: The axon ends by splitting into fine branches called axon terminals, and each terminal ends in a synaptic end bulb that contacts the next cell. These terminals are where the neuron hands its signal off to another neuron, a muscle cell, or a gland. Dendrites look branched too, but they are at the receiving end, clustered around the cell body.
notes: Dendrites are also branched, but they sit on the cell body and receive signals rather than pass them on. Pick the dendrites for a question about the receiving branches of a neuron.
The cell body holds the nucleus and is the metabolic center of the neuron. It would be right for a question about the part that contains the nucleus and Nissl bodies.
The axon hillock is at the start of the axon, where it leaves the cell body, not at the far end. Choose it for a question about where the axon begins.
Correct. Axon terminals are the end branches that contact the target cell.
questions.answerText: The axon terminals

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The axon hillock forms the junction between which two parts of a neuron?
options: Two neighboring myelin segments
The cell body and the axon
The dendrites and the cell body
The axon and its terminals
questions.why: The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region of the cell body that tapers into the beginning of the axon. It is the boundary between the receiving and processing part of the neuron, the cell body, and the conducting part, the axon. Each neuron has one axon, so it has one axon hillock.
notes: The bare gap between two myelin segments is a node of Ranvier. Choose this for a question about where the impulse jumps during saltatory conduction.
Correct. The axon hillock is where the cell body narrows into the axon.
Dendrites join the cell body directly, with no cone-shaped region between them. This pairing would fit a question about where incoming signals travel after a dendrite receives them.
The axon ends by branching into axon terminals at its far end, which is the opposite end from the hillock. Pick this pairing for a question about how the axon ends.
questions.answerText: The cell body and the axon

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A neuron in the retina has one dendrite and one axon. Which structural class is it?
options: A unipolar neuron
A multipolar neuron
A Purkinje cell
A bipolar neuron
questions.why: Bipolar neurons have exactly two processes, one dendrite and one axon, leaving opposite sides of the cell body. They are rare and found in special sense organs: the retina of the eye, the inner ear, and the olfactory area. The structural class is set by how many processes leave the cell body, so two processes means bipolar.
notes: A unipolar neuron has a single process leaving the cell body, and it is the typical shape of a sensory neuron. Pick unipolar for a question about the shape of most sensory neurons.
A multipolar neuron has many dendrites and one axon and is the most common type in the brain and spinal cord. Choose it for a question about motor neurons or interneurons.
A Purkinje cell is a distinctive multipolar neuron of the cerebellum with a large, branching tree of dendrites. It would be right for a question naming a special neuron of the cerebellum.
Correct. Bipolar neurons have one dendrite and one axon.
questions.answerText: A bipolar neuron

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A synapse is a site where a neuron passes its signal to another cell. Which list gives the kinds of cells a neuron can synapse with?
options: A glial cell, blood cell, or skin cell
A muscle cell, bone cell, or fat cell
A neuron, muscle cell, or gland cell
Only the dendrite of another neuron
questions.why: A synapse is the junction where a neuron communicates with another cell. The target can be another neuron, a muscle cell, or a gland cell, which is why muscles and glands are grouped together as the effectors of the nervous system. The synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber has its own name, the neuromuscular junction.
notes: This list misses all three main targets. A neuron synapses with another neuron, a muscle cell, or a gland cell. Glial cells are the support cells around neurons, and blood cells and skin cells are not on that list.

Muscle cells are real synaptic targets, but this list swaps bone cells and fat cells in for the other two targets, neurons and gland cells. It would only be right if the question asked about muscle alone.
Correct. Neurons synapse with other neurons and with the effectors, muscles and glands.
Dendrites are common targets, but axons also end on cell bodies, on other axons, and on muscle and gland cells. This would fit a question about an axodendritic synapse specifically.
questions.answerText: A neuron, muscle cell, or gland cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: At a synapse, which term names the neuron that sends the signal across the cleft?
options: The afferent neuron
The presynaptic neuron
The postsynaptic neuron
The efferent neuron
questions.why: At a synapse, pre means before and post means after, measured from the synaptic cleft. The presynaptic neuron is the sender, and its synaptic end bulbs release neurotransmitter into the cleft. The postsynaptic cell, which may be a neuron, muscle cell, or gland cell, receives that neurotransmitter on the far side.
notes: Afferent describes a neuron that carries signals toward the CNS, which is a functional class, not a position at a synapse. Choose it for a question about sensory neurons.
Correct. Pre means before, so the presynaptic neuron sits before the cleft and sends the signal.
The postsynaptic neuron is on the receiving side of the cleft, after the gap. Pick it for a question about the cell that receives the neurotransmitter.
Efferent describes a neuron that carries commands away from the CNS, another functional class. It would be right for a question about motor neurons.
questions.answerText: The presynaptic neuron

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: After a small stroke, glial cells in the damaged brain tissue engulf the dead cells and debris. Which glial cells are doing this?
options: Oligodendrocytes
Astrocytes
Microglia
Ependymal cells
questions.why: Microglia are small phagocytic glial cells of the CNS, meaning they engulf and digest material. When brain tissue is damaged, as in a stroke, they move in and remove dead cells, debris, and any microbes. This makes them the defense and cleanup crew of the brain and spinal cord.
notes: Oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheaths around CNS axons. Choose them for a question about myelin loss in the brain, as in multiple sclerosis.

Astrocytes support neurons, help form the blood-brain barrier, and keep the chemical environment stable, but engulfing debris is not their main role. Pick them for a question about the blood-brain barrier.
Correct. Microglia are the phagocytic cleanup and defense cells of the CNS.
Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and help circulate cerebrospinal fluid. They would be right for a question about the lining of the brain cavities.
questions.answerText: Microglia

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Trace the path a signal takes through one neuron, from where it is received to where it is handed off. Which order is correct?
options: Dendrites, cell body, axon hillock, axon, axon terminals
Axon terminals, axon, axon hillock, cell body, dendrites
Dendrites, axon, cell body, axon hillock, axon terminals
Axon, dendrites, cell body, axon hillock, axon terminals
questions.why: Signals arrive at the dendrites, the receiving processes, and travel toward the cell body. From the cell body the signal reaches the axon hillock, where the axon begins, then runs along the axon to the axon terminals, which pass it to the next cell. The direction is always dendrites in and axon out.
notes: Correct. The signal is received, passes through the cell body, and leaves along the axon.
This is the correct path run backward, from the sending end to the receiving end. It would fit a question that asked for the order from the axon terminals back to the dendrites.

This sends the signal into the axon before the cell body, but the axon begins at the hillock on the far side of the cell body. Students who choose this often forget that the hillock is where the axon starts.
This starts at the axon, but the axon is the outgoing process, not where signals arrive. Students who choose this mix up the axon, which sends, with the dendrites, which receive.
questions.answerText: Dendrites, cell body, axon hillock, axon, axon terminals

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Each choice pairs a glial cell with its location and its job. Which pairing is fully correct?
options: The oligodendrocyte is a CNS glial cell that myelinates CNS axons
The satellite cell is a CNS glial cell that lines brain cavities
The Schwann cell is a CNS glial cell that myelinates CNS axons
The astrocyte is a PNS glial cell that supports ganglion cell bodies
questions.why: Each glial cell belongs to one division and has one main job. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes form myelin, astrocytes support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier, microglia defend, and ependymal cells line the cavities. In the PNS, Schwann cells form myelin and satellite cells surround cell bodies in ganglia.
notes: Correct. Oligodendrocytes are CNS glia, and they form the myelin in the brain and spinal cord.
Satellite cells are PNS glia that surround cell bodies in ganglia, and the cells that line brain cavities are ependymal cells. Pick satellite cells for a question about support in a ganglion.
The Schwann cell does make myelin, but it works in the PNS, not the CNS. This pairing would be correct if it said the Schwann cell is a PNS glial cell that myelinates PNS axons.

Astrocytes are CNS glia that support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier; the cells around ganglion cell bodies are satellite cells. Choose astrocytes for a question about the blood-brain barrier.
questions.answerText: The oligodendrocyte is a CNS glial cell that myelinates CNS axons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: You touch a hot pan and pull your hand away. Which sequence lists the three functions of the nervous system in the order they happen?
options: Sensory, integrative, motor
Integrative, sensory, motor
Motor, sensory, integrative
Sensory, motor, integrative
questions.why: The nervous system handles every task in three steps. In the sensory function, receptors detect a change, here the heat, and send input toward the CNS. In the integrative function, the CNS analyzes the input and decides on a response, and in the motor function, commands go out to the effectors, here the arm muscles that pull the hand away.
notes: Correct. The stimulus is detected, the CNS processes it, and the muscles respond.
This has the CNS processing information before any sensory input has arrived, which cannot happen. The integrative step always needs incoming information to work on.
This puts the response first, before anything has been detected or processed. Students pick it when they focus on the movement and forget that the heat had to be sensed first.
This sends the response out before the CNS has decided on it. Integration has to come between sensing and responding, because the CNS decides what the response will be.
questions.answerText: Sensory, integrative, motor

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: At a chemical synapse, which sequence lists the structures in order from the sending neuron to the receiving cell?
options: Synaptic cleft, synaptic vesicles, postsynaptic cell
Synaptic vesicles, synaptic cleft, postsynaptic cell
Postsynaptic cell, synaptic cleft, synaptic vesicles
Synaptic vesicles, postsynaptic cell, synaptic cleft
questions.why: The sending neuron stores neurotransmitter in synaptic vesicles inside its synaptic end bulbs. When a signal arrives, the vesicles release the neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, the narrow gap between the cells. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and reaches the postsynaptic cell on the other side.
notes: This puts the cleft before the vesicles, but the vesicles sit inside the sending terminal, so the neurotransmitter starts there before it enters the cleft.
Correct. Neurotransmitter leaves the vesicles, crosses the cleft, and reaches the postsynaptic cell.
This is the correct order run backward, from the receiving cell to the sender. It would fit a question that asked for the order from the receiving side back to the sending side.
This has the neurotransmitter reach the receiving cell before crossing the gap. The cleft lies between the two cells, so it must be crossed first.
questions.answerText: Synaptic vesicles, synaptic cleft, postsynaptic cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Each choice gives the direction that each functional class of neuron carries signals relative to the CNS. Which set is fully correct?
options: Sensory toward the CNS, motor away from the CNS, interneuron within the CNS
Sensory within the CNS, motor toward the CNS, interneuron away from the CNS
Sensory away from the CNS, motor toward the CNS, interneuron within the CNS
Sensory toward the CNS, motor within the CNS, interneuron away from the CNS
questions.why: Neurons are classified by function according to the direction they carry signals. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry input from receptors toward the CNS, motor (efferent) neurons carry commands away from the CNS to effectors, and interneurons connect the two entirely within the CNS. Remembering that interneurons never leave the CNS rules out most wrong sets quickly.
notes: Correct. Sensory neurons bring input in, motor neurons send commands out, and interneurons connect them inside the CNS.
This places the sensory neuron inside the CNS and sends the interneuron out of it, but interneurons are the only class that stays entirely within the CNS.
This swaps the sensory and motor directions. Sensory input has to travel toward the CNS to be processed, and motor commands travel away to reach the effectors.
The sensory direction is right, but motor neurons must leave the CNS to reach muscles and glands, and interneurons never leave it.
questions.answerText: Sensory toward the CNS, motor away from the CNS, interneuron within the CNS

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which set correctly matches each of the four CNS glial cells to its main job?
options: Astrocyte defends; oligodendrocyte lines cavities; microglia forms myelin; ependymal cell supports neurons
Astrocyte lines cavities; oligodendrocyte supports neurons; microglia forms myelin; ependymal cell defends
Astrocyte forms myelin; oligodendrocyte defends; microglia lines cavities; ependymal cell supports neurons
Astrocyte supports neurons; oligodendrocyte forms myelin; microglia defends; ependymal cell lines cavities
questions.why: The CNS has four kinds of glia, each with a main job. Astrocytes support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier, oligodendrocytes form the myelin around CNS axons, microglia are phagocytes that clear debris and microbes, and ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and help circulate cerebrospinal fluid. Anchoring one pairing, such as oligodendrocytes with myelin, makes it easier to sort the rest.
notes: This gives microglia the myelin job, but microglia are small phagocytic cells that clear debris. Myelin in the CNS is made by oligodendrocytes.
This gives the lining of the cavities to astrocytes, but the cells lining the ventricles and central canal are ependymal cells.
Every job here is shifted one cell over. Myelin in the CNS comes from oligodendrocytes, not astrocytes, so this set fails from its first pairing.
Correct. Each CNS glial cell is matched to its main job.
questions.answerText: Astrocyte supports neurons; oligodendrocyte forms myelin; microglia defends; ependymal cell lines cavities

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: You decide to raise your arm. Which path does this voluntary motor command follow through the divisions of the nervous system?
options: CNS, sensory division of the PNS, somatic nervous system, skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle, somatic nervous system, motor division of the PNS, CNS
CNS, motor division of the PNS, somatic nervous system, skeletal muscle
CNS, motor division of the PNS, autonomic nervous system, skeletal muscle
questions.why: A voluntary command starts in the CNS, which decides on the response. It leaves through the motor (efferent) division of the PNS and specifically through the somatic nervous system, the voluntary branch whose motor neurons reach skeletal muscle. The skeletal muscle is the effector that carries out the movement.
notes: The sensory division carries input toward the CNS, so it cannot carry a command out to a muscle. Pick the sensory division for a question about signals arriving from receptors.
This is the correct path run backward, from the muscle to the CNS. Commands travel outward from the CNS, so the CNS must come first.
Correct. A voluntary command leaves the CNS through the somatic part of the motor division.

The autonomic nervous system carries involuntary commands to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, not to skeletal muscle. Choose it for a question about an involuntary response such as a change in heart rate.
questions.answerText: CNS, motor division of the PNS, somatic nervous system, skeletal muscle

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The sensory receptors in the skin belong to which division of the nervous system?
options: The central nervous system
The peripheral nervous system
The motor (efferent) division
The autonomic nervous system
questions.why: The peripheral nervous system includes every neural structure outside the brain and spinal cord: the nerves, the ganglia, and the sensory receptors. Receptors in the skin detect changes such as touch and temperature and start signals that sensory neurons carry toward the CNS. They feed the sensory (afferent) side of the PNS.
notes: The CNS is only the brain and spinal cord, where sensory input is processed. Pick the CNS for a question about where the input from receptors is analyzed.
Correct. Sensory receptors lie outside the brain and spinal cord, so they are part of the PNS.
The motor division carries commands away from the CNS to effectors, while receptors feed the sensory side. It would be right for a question about signals leaving the CNS.

The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary motor branch to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, so it carries commands out rather than receiving stimuli. Choose it for a question about control of the viscera.
questions.answerText: The peripheral nervous system

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: How many pairs of cranial nerves and spinal nerves does the body have?
options: 10 pairs of cranial nerves and 33 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 33 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
31 pairs of cranial nerves and 12 pairs of spinal nerves
questions.why: The nerves of the PNS come in pairs, one on each side. Twelve pairs of cranial nerves leave the brain, and 31 pairs of spinal nerves leave the spinal cord: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. These nerves are bundles of axons that carry signals between the CNS and the rest of the body.
notes: Neither number is right. There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, not 10, and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The 33 comes from the count of vertebrae before the sacral and coccygeal ones fuse, which is a different number.
The cranial count is right, but there are 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The 33 is a mix-up with the count of vertebrae before fusion.
Correct. There are 12 cranial pairs and 31 spinal pairs.
This swaps the two numbers. The 12 pairs belong to the cranial nerves that attach to the brain, and the 31 pairs belong to the spinal nerves that attach to the spinal cord.
questions.answerText: 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Nissl bodies, clusters of rough ER and ribosomes, are found in which part of a neuron?
options: The synaptic end bulbs
The cell body
The axon
The axon hillock
questions.why: Nissl bodies are clusters of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes in the cell body, and they are where the neuron makes its proteins. Their presence is one reason the cell body is called the metabolic center of the neuron. The axon depends on proteins made in the cell body, which is why an axon cut off from its cell body dies.
notes: Synaptic end bulbs are the swellings at the tips of the axon terminals that hold the synaptic vesicles. They would be right for a question about where neurotransmitter is stored.
Correct. Nissl bodies sit in the cell body, the metabolic center of the neuron.
The axon carries the impulse away and depends on the cell body for its proteins because it does not make them in bulk. Choose it for a question about the long outgoing process.
The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region where the axon begins, right next to the cell body, but it lacks Nissl bodies. Pick it for a question about where the axon joins the cell body.
questions.answerText: The cell body

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the plasma membrane of the axon called?
options: The axolemma
The axoplasm
The sarcolemma
The neurolemma
questions.why: Lemma means husk or covering, and the axolemma is the plasma membrane that surrounds the axon. The cytoplasm inside it is the axoplasm. The neurolemma sounds similar but belongs to the Schwann cell, a glial cell wrapped around the axon, not to the neuron.
notes: Correct. The axolemma is the plasma membrane of the axon.
Axoplasm is the cytoplasm inside the axon, the contents rather than the membrane. Pick it for a question about the fluid inside the axon.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of a muscle fiber, not of a neuron. It would be right for a question about the membrane surrounding a skeletal muscle cell.
The neurolemma is the outer layer of a Schwann cell, which wraps around a peripheral axon from the outside. Choose it for a question about what guides a cut peripheral axon as it regrows.
questions.answerText: The axolemma

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is a bundle of axons within the central nervous system called?
options: A tract
A nucleus
A ganglion
A nerve
questions.why: The same kind of structure gets a different name depending on whether it is in the CNS or the PNS. A bundle of axons inside the brain or spinal cord is a tract, and the matching bundle in the PNS is a nerve. Tracts make up much of the white matter, since their axons are usually myelinated.
notes: Correct. A bundle of axons inside the CNS is a tract.
A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies in the CNS, not a bundle of axons. Choose it for a question about a group of cell bodies inside the brain or cord.
A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies in the PNS. It would be right for a question about cell bodies grouped outside the CNS.
A nerve is also a bundle of axons, but it lies in the PNS. Pick nerve when the bundle is outside the brain and spinal cord.
questions.answerText: A tract

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is a cluster of neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system called?
options: A nucleus
A nerve
A tract
A ganglion
questions.why: A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS. A good example is the posterior root ganglion beside the spinal cord, which holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons. Inside the CNS the matching cluster of cell bodies is called a nucleus.
notes: A nucleus is also a cluster of neuron cell bodies, but it lies inside the CNS. Pick nucleus when the cluster is in the brain or spinal cord.
A nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS. It would be right for a question about a cable of axons running out to the body.
A tract is a bundle of axons inside the CNS, not a cluster of cell bodies. Choose it for a question about axon bundles in the brain or cord.
Correct. A cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion.
questions.answerText: A ganglion

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares how Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes myelinate axons?
