options: One Schwann cell wraps many axons; one oligodendrocyte wraps just one axon segment
Both cells wrap exactly one segment of one axon, but in different divisions
Schwann cells myelinate CNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate PNS axons
One Schwann cell wraps one axon segment; one oligodendrocyte wraps many axons
questions.why: Both cells make myelin, but they do it differently. A Schwann cell, in the PNS, wraps a single segment of one axon and leaves its outer layer, the neurolemma, on the outside. An oligodendrocyte, in the CNS, sends out several processes that each wrap a segment of a different axon, and it leaves no neurolemma.
notes: This reverses the two cells. Students who choose it often picture the Schwann cell as the larger cell, but it is the oligodendrocyte that sends processes to many axons.
The difference in division is real, Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS, but only the Schwann cell is limited to one axon segment.
This swaps their locations. Schwann cells work in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS.
Correct. A Schwann cell serves one segment of one axon, while an oligodendrocyte reaches several axons.
questions.answerText: One Schwann cell wraps one axon segment; one oligodendrocyte wraps many axons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: During saltatory conduction along a myelinated axon, the impulse jumps between which structures?
options: The axon terminals
The Nissl bodies
The synaptic clefts
The nodes of Ranvier
questions.why: Saltatory comes from a word meaning to leap. On a myelinated axon the impulse leaps from one node of Ranvier, a bare gap in the myelin, to the next, skipping the insulated stretches in between. That is why myelinated axons conduct impulses much faster than unmyelinated ones.
notes: Axon terminals are the end branches of the axon that contact the next cell. They would be right for a question about where the signal is handed off.
Nissl bodies are clusters of rough ER and ribosomes in the cell body that make proteins. Choose them for a question about protein synthesis in a neuron.
Synaptic clefts are the gaps between two cells at a synapse, at the end of the axon rather than along it. Pick them for a question about the space that neurotransmitter crosses.
Correct. The impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next.
questions.answerText: The nodes of Ranvier

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Motor neurons and interneurons share which structural class?
options: Motor is unipolar; interneuron is bipolar
Both are unipolar
Both are multipolar
Both are bipolar
questions.why: Functional class and structural class are separate ways of naming a neuron, but they line up in a pattern. Motor neurons and interneurons are both multipolar, with many dendrites and one axon, while most sensory neurons are unipolar. Multipolar is the most common structural class in the brain and spinal cord for this reason.
notes: Neither half is right, since both of these functional classes are multipolar. This mix-up comes from linking the functional names to the wrong shapes.
Unipolar is the typical shape of sensory neurons, not motor neurons or interneurons. Pick unipolar for a question about the shape of most sensory neurons.
Correct. Motor neurons and interneurons both have many dendrites and one axon.
Bipolar neurons have one dendrite and one axon and are found in the retina, inner ear, and olfactory area. Choose bipolar for a question about special sense organs.
questions.answerText: Both are multipolar

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which pairing of a functional class of neuron with its typical structural class is correct?
options: Motor neuron, bipolar
Interneuron, unipolar
Motor neuron, unipolar
Sensory neuron, unipolar
questions.why: The two ways of classifying neurons, by function and by shape, line up in a predictable way. Most sensory (afferent) neurons are unipolar, with a single process leaving the cell body that splits into two branches. Motor neurons and interneurons are both multipolar.
notes: Motor neurons are multipolar, with many dendrites and one axon. Bipolar neurons are the rare type found in the retina, inner ear, and olfactory area.
Interneurons are multipolar, like motor neurons. Unipolar is the shape linked to sensory neurons, so pick unipolar for a question about them.
Motor neurons are multipolar, not unipolar. Students choose this when they remember that unipolar belongs to one functional class but forget which one.
Correct. Most sensory neurons are unipolar.
questions.answerText: Sensory neuron, unipolar

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which pigment harmlessly builds up in neurons with age?
options: Nissl substance
Myelin
Melanin
Lipofuscin
questions.why: Lipofuscin is a harmless pigment that builds up inside the cell bodies of neurons as a person ages. Neurons are long-lived cells that do not divide, so this pigment gradually collects in them over the years. It is a sign of age, not of disease.
notes: Nissl substance (Nissl bodies) is clusters of rough ER and ribosomes in the cell body where proteins are made. It would be right for a question about the site of protein synthesis.
Myelin is a fatty wrapping made by glial cells around axons, not a pigment that builds up with age. Choose it for a question about what insulates axons.
Melanin is the pigment made by melanocytes in the epidermis that colors the skin and hair. Pick it for a question about skin color or protection from UV light.
Correct. Lipofuscin is the harmless pigment that collects in aging neurons.
questions.answerText: Lipofuscin

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A cluster of neuron cell bodies sits deep inside the brain. What is this cluster called?
options: A ganglion
A nerve
A nucleus
A tract
questions.why: In nervous tissue, a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS is called a nucleus, and the matching cluster outside the CNS is called a ganglion. Because this cluster sits inside the brain, it is a nucleus. This use of nucleus is different from the nucleus of a single cell, which is the organelle that holds its DNA.
notes: A ganglion is also a cluster of neuron cell bodies, but it lies outside the CNS. Pick ganglion when the cluster sits in the PNS, such as beside the spinal cord on a posterior root.
A nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS. It would be right for a question about a cable of axons running out to the body.
Correct. A cluster of cell bodies inside the CNS is a nucleus.
A tract is a bundle of axons inside the CNS, not a cluster of cell bodies. Choose it for a question about axon bundles running through the brain or cord.
questions.answerText: A nucleus

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Interneurons are also known by which other name?
options: Bipolar neurons
Association neurons
Efferent neurons
Afferent neurons
questions.why: Interneurons are also called association neurons because they associate, or connect, other neurons. They lie entirely within the brain and spinal cord, linking sensory neurons to motor neurons and to each other. Structurally they are multipolar.
notes: Bipolar is a structural class (one dendrite and one axon) found in special sense organs, not a functional name. It would be right for a question about neurons in the retina.
Correct. Interneurons are also called association neurons because they link other neurons together.
Efferent neurons are motor neurons that carry commands away from the CNS. Choose efferent for a question asking for the other name of motor neurons.
Afferent neurons are sensory neurons that carry signals toward the CNS. Pick afferent for a question asking for the other name of sensory neurons.
questions.answerText: Association neurons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A brain tumor is far more likely to arise from glial cells than from neurons. Which property of neurons explains this?
options: Neurons cannot divide
Neurons lack a nucleus
Neurons have no cell membrane
Neurons divide faster than glia
questions.why: A tumor is a mass of cells that keep dividing, so it can only arise from cells that are able to divide. Mature neurons generally do not divide, but glial cells still can. That is why most tumors of nervous tissue come from glia. A tumor of glial cells is a glioma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor.
notes: Correct. A tumor needs dividing cells, and mature neurons do not divide.
Neurons do have a nucleus, which sits in the cell body. Students choose this when they mix up not dividing with having no nucleus, as with mature red blood cells.
Neurons have a plasma membrane, and the part around the axon is called the axolemma. This choice comes from a misunderstanding of what a neuron is built from.
This is the reverse of the truth. If neurons divided faster, they would be the more likely source of a tumor, not the less likely one.
questions.answerText: Neurons cannot divide

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the neurolemma?
options: The outer layer of a Schwann cell
The plasma membrane that surrounds the axon
The gap between myelin segments
The cytoplasm inside the axon
questions.why: When a Schwann cell wraps an axon, the layers of its membrane form the myelin sheath, and its outer layer, which holds the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm, is left on the outside as the neurolemma. The neurolemma forms a tube that guides a cut peripheral axon as it regrows. Oligodendrocytes in the CNS do not leave a neurolemma, which is one reason CNS tracts rarely regrow.
notes: Correct. The neurolemma is the outer layer of the Schwann cell, holding its nucleus and cytoplasm.
The plasma membrane of the axon is the axolemma, which belongs to the neuron itself. Pick axolemma for a question about the axon membrane.
A gap between myelin segments is a node of Ranvier. Choose it for a question about where the impulse jumps in saltatory conduction.
The cytoplasm inside the axon is the axoplasm. It would be right for a question about the contents of the axon.
questions.answerText: The outer layer of a Schwann cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An axon ends on a dendrite of another neuron. What type of synapse is this?
options: An axosomatic synapse
An axodendritic synapse
An axoaxonic synapse
A neuromuscular junction
questions.why: Synapses between neurons are named for the two parts that meet, always starting with the axon of the sending neuron. An axon ending on a dendrite is axodendritic, on a cell body is axosomatic, and on another axon is axoaxonic. Dendrites are the most common receiving site because they are the receiving processes of the neuron.
notes: An axosomatic synapse is an axon ending on the cell body (soma) of another neuron. Pick it when the axon contacts a cell body.
Correct. Axo plus dendritic names an axon ending on a dendrite.
An axoaxonic synapse is an axon ending on another axon. Choose it when both sides of the synapse are axons.
A neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber, not between two neurons. It would be right for a question about where a nerve meets muscle.
questions.answerText: An axodendritic synapse

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which part of the nervous system is a network of neurons in the wall of the GI tract that can work on its own?
options: The central nervous system
The enteric nervous system
The sensory (afferent) division
The somatic nervous system
questions.why: The enteric nervous system, sometimes called the brain of the gut, is a network of neurons in the wall of the GI tract. It controls the smooth muscle and glands of the gut and can operate on its own, even without input from the brain. It is one of the divisions of the motor side of the PNS, alongside the somatic and autonomic systems.
notes: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, not a network in the wall of the gut. Choose it for a question about where most information is processed.
Correct. The enteric nervous system is the gut's own network of neurons.
The sensory division carries input from receptors all over the body toward the CNS. It would be right for a question about signals traveling into the brain and cord.
The somatic nervous system is the voluntary motor branch that carries commands to skeletal muscle. Pick it for a question about voluntary movement.
questions.answerText: The enteric nervous system

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An axon ends on the cell body of another neuron. What type of synapse is this?
options: An axoaxonic synapse
A neuromuscular junction
An axosomatic synapse
An axodendritic synapse
questions.why: Synapses between neurons are named for the parts that meet, starting with the axon of the sending neuron. The cell body is also called the soma, so an axon ending on a cell body forms an axosomatic synapse. The other two types are axodendritic, ending on a dendrite, and axoaxonic, ending on another axon.
notes: An axoaxonic synapse is an axon ending on another axon. Choose it when both sides of the synapse are axons.
A neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber. It would be right for a question about where a nerve meets a muscle.
Correct. Soma means cell body, so an axon ending on a cell body forms an axosomatic synapse.
An axodendritic synapse is an axon ending on a dendrite, the most common arrangement. Pick it when the axon contacts a dendrite.
questions.answerText: An axosomatic synapse

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: On a myelinated axon, the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next. What is this type of conduction called?
options: Saltatory conduction
Continuous conduction
Decussation
Convergence
questions.why: Saltatory comes from a word meaning to leap. Myelin insulates the axon, so on a myelinated axon the impulse leaps from one node of Ranvier, a bare gap in the myelin, to the next. This skipping is why myelinated axons conduct much faster than unmyelinated ones.
notes: Correct. Saltatory conduction is the jumping pattern seen on myelinated axons.
Continuous conduction is the slower, step-by-step spread along an unmyelinated axon, which has no nodes to jump between. Pick it for a question about axons without myelin.
Decussation is the crossing of a pathway to the opposite side of the CNS. Choose it for a question about why one side of the brain serves the other side of the body.
Convergence is a circuit pattern in which many neurons feed onto one neuron. It would be right for a question about how neurons are wired in a neuronal pool.
questions.answerText: Saltatory conduction

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which distinctive multipolar neuron is found in the cerebellum?
options: The pyramidal cell
The Purkinje cell
The bipolar neuron
The unipolar neuron
questions.why: Purkinje cells are large multipolar neurons with an elaborate, fan-shaped tree of dendrites, and they are found in the cortex of the cerebellum. They are given their own name because of that distinctive shape, but structurally they are still multipolar. Their partner name to remember is the pyramidal cell, the distinctive multipolar neuron of the cerebral cortex.
notes: Pyramidal cells are also distinctive multipolar neurons, but they are found in the cerebral cortex. Pick the pyramidal cell for a question about the cerebral cortex.
Correct. Purkinje cells are the distinctive multipolar neurons of the cerebellum.
Bipolar neurons have one dendrite and one axon and are found in the retina, inner ear, and olfactory area. Choose bipolar for a question about special sense organs.
Unipolar neurons have a single process and are the typical shape of sensory neurons. It would be right for a question about the shape of most sensory neurons.
questions.answerText: The Purkinje cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A patient has a slow-growing mass of dividing cells in the brain. Which cell type most likely gave rise to it?
options: A multipolar neuron
A glial cell
An interneuron
A sensory neuron
questions.why: A tumor is a mass of dividing cells, so it must start from a cell type that can still divide. Mature neurons generally do not divide, but glial cells can. A tumor of glial cells is a glioma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor.
notes: Multipolar neurons are the most common neurons in the brain, but mature neurons cannot divide, so they rarely form tumors. Pick multipolar for a question about the shape of motor neurons and interneurons.
Correct. Glial cells can still divide, so most brain tumors start from glia.
Interneurons connect sensory and motor neurons inside the CNS, but as neurons they cannot divide. It would be right for a question about the neurons that link input to output.
Sensory neurons carry signals toward the CNS, and like all mature neurons they cannot divide. Choose it for a question about input from receptors.
questions.answerText: A glial cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An infant's nerve impulses travel more slowly than an adult's. Which structural difference best explains this?
options: The infant has less myelination
The infant's neurons lack dendrites
The infant's neurons lack nuclei
The infant has fewer neurons
questions.why: Myelin insulates axons and lets the impulse jump from node to node, which makes conduction much faster. Myelination is not complete at birth; it increases from birth to maturity. With less myelin, an infant's nerve conduction is slower than an adult's.
notes: Correct. Myelination increases from birth to maturity, so infant axons conduct more slowly.
Infant neurons have dendrites, and dendrites receive signals rather than set the speed of conduction along the axon. Pick dendrites for a question about where a neuron receives input.
Every neuron has a nucleus in its cell body, at any age. This choice comes from mixing up neurons with cells such as mature red blood cells that lose their nucleus.
Neurons cannot divide, so a person does not add large numbers of new neurons after birth. A smaller neuron count would not explain slower conduction along each axon anyway.
questions.answerText: The infant has less myelination

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A surgeon repairing a severed nerve in the forearm lines up the cut ends so the axons can regrow. Which feature of the PNS makes this regrowth possible?
options: The neurolemma of Schwann cells
The end-feet of astrocytes
The phagocytic action of microglia
The myelin of the oligodendrocytes
questions.why: In the PNS, each Schwann cell leaves its outer layer, the neurolemma, wrapped around the axon. After a cut, the neurolemma forms a tube that guides the regrowing axon back toward its target. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes leave no neurolemma, which is why a cut nerve in the arm can regrow but a cut tract in the cord usually cannot.
notes: Correct. The neurolemma forms a guiding tube for the regrowing axon.
Astrocytes are CNS glia whose end-feet wrap capillaries and help form the blood-brain barrier. They would be right for a question about the blood-brain barrier.
Microglia are CNS cleanup cells, not part of peripheral nerves. Choose them for a question about clearing debris after a brain injury.
Oligodendrocytes are CNS cells and are not found in a forearm nerve, and they leave no neurolemma. Pick them for a question about why a cut tract in the spinal cord usually cannot regrow.
questions.answerText: The neurolemma of Schwann cells

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A cluster of neuron cell bodies sits just outside the spinal cord on a posterior root. Which term names it?
options: A tract
A nucleus
A nerve
A ganglion
questions.why: A cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion. The cluster described here is the posterior (dorsal) root ganglion, which holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons for that segment of the cord. Inside the CNS, the same kind of cluster would be called a nucleus.
notes: A tract is a bundle of axons inside the CNS. Choose it for a question about the axon bundles in the white matter of the cord.
A nucleus is also a cluster of cell bodies, but it lies inside the CNS. Pick nucleus if the cluster were within the gray matter of the cord or brain.
A nerve is a bundle of axons outside the CNS, not a cluster of cell bodies. It would be right for a question about the spinal nerve formed where the roots join.
Correct. A cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion.
questions.answerText: A ganglion

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system strips a covering from CNS axons and signals slow or fail. Which structure is being lost?
options: The dendrites
The cell body
The myelin sheath
The synaptic vesicles
questions.why: The myelin sheath is a lipid-rich covering that insulates axons and lets the impulse jump from node to node. In multiple sclerosis, the immune system destroys the myelin around CNS axons, the myelin made by oligodendrocytes. Without it, signals along those axons slow down or fail.
notes: Dendrites are the branched receiving processes of a neuron, not a covering. Choose them for a question about where a neuron receives signals.
The cell body holds the nucleus and is the metabolic center, but it is not a covering around the axon. Pick it for a question about where Nissl bodies are found.
Correct. Multiple sclerosis destroys the myelin around CNS axons.
Synaptic vesicles are sacs of neurotransmitter inside the axon terminals. They would be right for a question about where neurotransmitter is stored.
questions.answerText: The myelin sheath

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A typical neuron has many dendrites but only one axon. Which statement best explains how this shape fits its job?
options: Dendrites gather input from many cells; the axon sends one output
Dendrites and the axon both gather input from many other cells
Dendrites make the proteins; the axon stores the neurotransmitter
Dendrites send output to many cells; the axon gathers the input
questions.why: Dendrites are the receiving processes of the neuron, and having many of them gives a large surface for synapses from many other cells. The neuron combines this input and, if it fires, sends a single impulse out along its one axon. The axon can then branch at its end into many axon terminals, so that one output can still reach several target cells.
notes: Correct. Many dendrites collect input, and one axon carries the result away.
Only the dendrites are a receiving surface. The axon carries the impulse away from the cell body toward other cells.

This gives the dendrites and the axon the wrong jobs. Proteins are made mainly at the Nissl bodies of the cell body, and neurotransmitter is stored in vesicles in the synaptic end bulbs at the axon terminals, not along the axon.
This reverses the jobs. Dendrites receive signals and carry them toward the cell body, while the axon carries the impulse away.
questions.answerText: Dendrites gather input from many cells; the axon sends one output

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Why does a myelin sheath make an axon conduct impulses faster?
options: Myelin shortens the axon, so the impulse has less distance to go
The impulse jumps from node to node, skipping the insulated parts
The nodes of Ranvier release neurotransmitter along the axon
Myelin carries the impulse itself, so the axon membrane is bypassed
questions.why: Myelin is a multilayered, lipid-rich covering that insulates the axon. Because of that insulation, the impulse does not spread step by step along the covered stretches. Instead it jumps from one node of Ranvier, a bare gap in the myelin, to the next. This saltatory conduction is much faster than conduction along an unmyelinated axon.
notes: Myelin wraps around the axon without changing its length. The gain in speed comes from the jumping pattern, not from a shorter path.
Correct. Myelin insulates the axon, so the impulse leaps between the nodes of Ranvier.
Neurotransmitter is released only at the axon terminals, at synapses. The nodes are simply bare gaps in the myelin that the impulse jumps between.
Myelin is an insulating wrap made by glial cells; it does not carry the impulse. The impulse still travels on the axon membrane, just only at the nodes.
questions.answerText: The impulse jumps from node to node, skipping the insulated parts

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: At a chemical synapse the two cells do not touch. How does the signal get from one cell to the next?
options: The two cell membranes fuse so the impulse passes directly
Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft
A strip of myelin bridges the gap between the two cells
The impulse jumps across the cleft as it does between nodes
questions.why: At a chemical synapse there is no direct contact between the cells. When the impulse reaches the axon terminal, synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. The neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the cleft and reach the receiving cell, carrying the signal to it as a chemical message.
notes: At a chemical synapse the membranes stay separate, with the synaptic cleft between them. Students choose this when they picture the two cells as joined.
Correct. The signal crosses the gap as a chemical message.
Myelin wraps axons to insulate them and does not cross from one cell to another. Pick myelin for a question about what speeds conduction along an axon.
Jumping from node to node happens along a myelinated axon, not across a synapse. At a chemical synapse the impulse itself stops at the terminal and a chemical carries the message over.
questions.answerText: Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Mature neurons cannot divide. Why does this make damage to the brain or spinal cord especially serious?
options: The remaining neurons divide quickly to fill in the damaged area
Lost neurons are not replaced, so lost function may not return
Schwann cells move into the brain and guide new tracts to grow
Glial cells turn into new neurons and take over the lost function
questions.why: Mature neurons cannot divide, so when neurons in the brain or spinal cord die, there are no new neurons to take their place. In addition, CNS axons regrow very poorly because oligodendrocytes leave no neurolemma to guide them. Together these facts mean that a brain or spinal cord injury often causes lasting loss of function.
notes: This contradicts the starting fact, since mature neurons do not divide. Dividing is something glial cells can do, not neurons.
Correct. Because neurons do not divide, neurons lost to injury are not replaced.
Schwann cells are PNS glia and do not repair CNS tracts. They would be right for a question about how a cut peripheral nerve regrows.
Glial cells can divide, but they do not take over the work of lost neurons. After a CNS injury, astrocytes fill the damaged area with scar tissue instead.
questions.answerText: Lost neurons are not replaced, so lost function may not return

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Glial cells do not carry nerve impulses. Which statement best describes why they are still essential?
options: They replace dead neurons by dividing into new neurons
They support, nourish, insulate, and protect neurons
They carry nerve impulses from one neuron to the next
They store the neurotransmitter used at every synapse
questions.why: Neuroglia are the support cells of nervous tissue, and they make up about half the volume of the CNS. Each type has a job that keeps neurons working: astrocytes support neurons and maintain their environment, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells form myelin, microglia clear debris, ependymal cells line the cavities, and satellite cells surround cell bodies in ganglia. Without them, neurons could not function or survive.
notes: Glial cells can divide, but they do not replace lost neurons. After a CNS injury, astrocytes fill the damaged area with scar tissue instead.
Correct. Glia keep neurons supported, supplied, insulated, and protected.
This contradicts the question, since glia do not carry impulses. Neurons carry impulses, and synapses pass them from cell to cell.
Neurotransmitter is stored in synaptic vesicles inside the synaptic end bulbs of neurons, not in glial cells. Pick vesicles for a question about neurotransmitter storage.
questions.answerText: They support, nourish, insulate, and protect neurons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The cell body of a neuron is packed with Nissl bodies, clusters of rough ER and ribosomes. Why does a neuron need so much protein-making machinery there?
options: The proteins are stored in the cell body as an energy reserve
The proteins are used to build new neurons when the cell divides
Nissl bodies make the myelin that wraps the length of the axon
The whole neuron, even a long axon, relies on cell body proteins
questions.why: Nissl bodies are where the neuron makes its proteins, and most of them sit in the cell body, the metabolic center of the neuron. Those proteins must supply the dendrites and an axon that can be very long, so the cell body keeps making them throughout the life of the neuron. This dependence is why the part of an axon cut off from its cell body dies.
notes: Nissl bodies are protein factories, not storage depots for fuel. This choice mixes up making proteins with storing energy.
Mature neurons cannot divide, so the proteins are not used for division. They maintain the existing cell throughout its long life.
Myelin is made by glial cells, oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS, not by the neuron. Pick those cells for a question about where myelin comes from.
Correct. The cell body makes the proteins that the rest of the neuron depends on.
questions.answerText: The whole neuron, even a long axon, relies on cell body proteins

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A nerve in the forearm is cut cleanly. Which part of each cut axon dies?
options: The part beyond the cut, away from the cell body
The part still attached to the cell body
Only the cell body, while the whole axon survives
Neither part, because an axon can live on its own
questions.why: The cell body is the life support of the neuron because its Nissl bodies make the proteins that the axon needs. When an axon is cut, the part beyond the cut is separated from that supply and dies. The part still attached to the cell body survives, and in the PNS it can regrow along the tube formed by the neurolemma.
notes: Correct. The part cut off from the cell body loses its protein supply and dies.

The part still connected to the cell body keeps receiving proteins, so it survives and is the part that can regrow. Students choose this when they forget that the cell body is the life support of the axon.
The cell body is the part most likely to survive a cut far out in the forearm, because it is still intact. The axon depends on the cell body, not the other way around.
An axon cannot make enough of its own proteins and depends on the cell body for them. Once separated, the distant part cannot survive.
questions.answerText: The part beyond the cut, away from the cell body

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Gray matter is made mostly of which neural components?
options: Myelinated axons running together in tracts
Cerebrospinal fluid and ependymal cells
Connective tissue sheaths around blood vessels
Cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons
questions.why: Gray matter is nervous tissue made mostly of neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons, along with neuroglia. Because it lacks much myelin, it looks gray. It forms the outer cortex of the brain and the inner core of the spinal cord.
notes: Myelinated axons in tracts make up white matter, and the fatty myelin is what gives it a white color. Pick this for a question about white matter.
Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles and central canal, which are lined by ependymal cells. This would fit a question about the fluid-filled spaces of the CNS.
Connective tissue sheaths wrap nerves and vessels, but they are not what gray matter is made of. Choose connective tissue for a question about the coverings of a peripheral nerve.
Correct. Gray matter is where the cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers are.
questions.answerText: Cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: White matter is made mostly of which structures?
options: Dendrites and their synapses on cell bodies
Clusters of neuron cell bodies
Myelinated axons running in bundles
Unmyelinated fibers and glial nuclei
questions.why: White matter is nervous tissue made mostly of myelinated axons running together in bundles, the tracts of the CNS. The myelin around these axons is fatty, and that lipid is what gives the tissue its white color. It lies beneath the cortex in the brain and forms the outer part of the spinal cord.
notes: Dendrites and synapses are concentrated in gray matter, where the cell bodies are. Choose them for a question about where neurons receive input.
Clusters of cell bodies are found in gray matter, as nuclei inside the CNS. Pick this for a question about what makes up gray matter.
Correct. White matter is bundles of myelinated axons.
Unmyelinated fibers belong to gray matter, since they lack the white myelin. This would fit a question about why gray matter looks gray.
questions.answerText: Myelinated axons running in bundles

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which pair of terms both name bundles of axons?
options: Nucleus and ganglion
Nerve and ganglion
Tract and nucleus
Tract and nerve
questions.why: The nervous system uses four terms that sort into two pairs. A bundle of axons is a tract in the CNS and a nerve in the PNS, while a cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus in the CNS and a ganglion in the PNS. Deciding first whether the structure is axons or cell bodies, and then whether it is inside or outside the CNS, leads to the right term.
notes: Nucleus and ganglion both name clusters of neuron cell bodies, one in the CNS and one in the PNS. Pick this pair for a question about clusters of cell bodies.
Nerve and ganglion are the two PNS terms, but a ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies. This pair would fit a question asking which terms are used outside the CNS.
Tract and nucleus are the two CNS terms, but a nucleus is a cluster of cell bodies, not a bundle of axons. Choose this pair for a question asking which terms are used inside the CNS.
Correct. A tract is a bundle of axons in the CNS, and a nerve is one in the PNS.
questions.answerText: Tract and nerve

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is a bundle of axons in the peripheral nervous system called?
options: A nucleus
A tract
A ganglion
A nerve
questions.why: A nerve is a bundle of axons outside the CNS, wrapped in connective tissue. The body has 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. Inside the brain and spinal cord, a bundle of axons is called a tract instead.
notes: A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS. Choose it for a question about a group of cell bodies in the brain.
A tract is also a bundle of axons, but it lies inside the CNS. Pick tract when the bundle runs within the brain or spinal cord.
A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies in the PNS. It would be right for a question about the cell bodies grouped on a posterior root.
Correct. A bundle of axons in the PNS is a nerve.
questions.answerText: A nerve

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: When the term nucleus names a structure in the brain, what does it mean?
options: A cluster of neuron cell bodies in the PNS
The organelle that holds a single cell's DNA
A bundle of myelinated axons in the CNS
A cluster of neuron cell bodies in the CNS
questions.why: In the nervous system, nucleus has a second meaning besides the organelle in a single cell. A nucleus here is a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS, such as a cranial nerve nucleus in the brainstem or the basal nuclei deep in the cerebrum. The matching cluster outside the CNS is a ganglion.
notes: A cluster of cell bodies in the PNS is a ganglion. Pick this for a question asking what a ganglion is.
This is the meaning of nucleus in cell biology, the control center of one cell. It would be right for a cell question, not for a named structure made of many neurons.
A bundle of axons in the CNS is a tract. Choose this for a question asking what a tract is.
Correct. In this sense a nucleus is a group of cell bodies inside the CNS.
questions.answerText: A cluster of neuron cell bodies in the CNS

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which pair of terms both name clusters of neuron cell bodies?
options: Nucleus and tract
Ganglion and nerve
Tract and nerve
Nucleus and ganglion
questions.why: A cluster of neuron cell bodies has two names depending on where it is: a nucleus inside the CNS and a ganglion in the PNS. Their axon-bundle counterparts are the tract in the CNS and the nerve in the PNS. Decide cell bodies or axons first, then inside or outside the CNS.
notes: Nucleus and tract are the two CNS terms, but a tract is a bundle of axons. Choose this pair for a question asking which terms are used inside the CNS.
Ganglion and nerve are the two PNS terms, but a nerve is a bundle of axons. This pair would fit a question asking which terms are used outside the CNS.
Tract and nerve both name bundles of axons, one in the CNS and one in the PNS. Pick this pair for a question about bundles of axons.
Correct. A nucleus is a cluster of cell bodies in the CNS, and a ganglion is one in the PNS.
questions.answerText: Nucleus and ganglion

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is a neuronal pool?
options: A cluster of sensory cell bodies outside the cord
A fluid-filled cavity inside the brain, lined by glia
A group of linked CNS neurons that work together
A bundle of myelinated axons in a peripheral nerve
questions.why: Neurons rarely act alone. A neuronal pool is a functional group of interconnected neurons in the CNS that processes information together, and the way the pool is wired, such as convergence or divergence, shapes how a signal is handled. The term describes how neurons work as a team rather than naming a single anatomical part.
notes: A cluster of sensory cell bodies outside the cord is a posterior root ganglion. This would be right for a question about where sensory neuron cell bodies sit.
A fluid-filled cavity lined by ependymal cells is a ventricle, which holds cerebrospinal fluid. Pick this for a question about the ventricles.
Correct. A neuronal pool is a functional group of linked neurons in the CNS.
A bundle of axons in the PNS is a nerve, a structural term rather than a working group. Choose this for a question asking what a nerve is.
questions.answerText: A group of linked CNS neurons that work together

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The corpus callosum is a broad band of myelinated axons linking the two cerebral hemispheres. Which tissue type is it?
options: A nucleus
A ganglion
Gray matter
White matter
questions.why: White matter is made of myelinated axons running together in bundles, and the lipid-rich myelin gives it its white color. The corpus callosum is a large band of white matter that carries axons between the right and left cerebral hemispheres. In the cerebrum, white matter lies beneath the gray cortex.
notes: A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS, which would be gray, not a band of axons. It would be right for a question about a group of cell bodies deep in the brain.
A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS. Choose it for a question about cell bodies grouped beside the spinal cord.
Gray matter is made of cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons, such as the cerebral cortex. Pick it for a question about the outer layer of the cerebrum.
Correct. A band of myelinated axons is white matter.
questions.answerText: White matter

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Many neurons feed their signals onto a single target neuron. What is this circuit pattern called?
options: Divergence
Serial processing
Convergence
Parallel processing
questions.why: Convergence comes from a word meaning to come together. In a converging circuit, signals from many neurons funnel onto one target neuron, which then combines them into a single response. Its mirror image is divergence, in which one neuron spreads its signal to many.
notes: Divergence is the opposite pattern, in which one neuron spreads its signal out to many. Pick it when a single neuron sends to many targets.
Serial processing is a signal passing along a single straight chain of neurons, as in a reflex arc. Choose it for a one-after-another chain.
Correct. Many inputs coming together onto one neuron is convergence.
Parallel processing is a signal sent along several pathways at the same time. It would be right for a question about one signal traveling several routes at once.
questions.answerText: Convergence

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: One neuron spreads its signal outward to many other neurons. What is this circuit pattern called?
options: Serial processing
Convergence
Integration
Divergence
questions.why: Divergence comes from a word meaning to branch apart. In a diverging circuit, one neuron passes its signal to many others, so a single input can affect many targets. Its mirror image is convergence, in which many neurons feed onto one.
notes: Serial processing passes a signal along a single straight chain of neurons, one after another. Choose it for a reflex arc.
Convergence is the reverse, with many neurons feeding onto one. Pick it when many inputs funnel onto a single neuron.

Integration is the combining of incoming signals so that a neuron produces a single response, not the spreading of a signal. It would be right for a question about what a neuron does with many inputs.
Correct. One neuron sending to many is divergence.
questions.answerText: Divergence

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A signal passes along a single straight chain of neurons, one after another, as in a reflex arc. What is this circuit pattern called?
options: Convergence
Divergence
Parallel processing
Serial processing
questions.why: In serial processing, a signal passes from one neuron to the next along a single chain, like links in a line. A reflex arc is the classic example: receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, and effector in a fixed sequence. Parallel processing, by contrast, sends the signal along several pathways at once.
notes: Convergence is many neurons feeding onto one. It would be right for many inputs funneling onto a single neuron.
Divergence is one neuron spreading its signal to many. Choose it for a single neuron branching to many targets.
Parallel processing sends a signal along several pathways at the same time. Pick it when the signal splits into separate routes at once.
Correct. A single chain of neurons in a row is serial processing.
questions.answerText: Serial processing

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An axon ends on the axon of another neuron. What type of synapse is this?
options: An axosomatic synapse
A neuromuscular junction
An axoaxonic synapse
An axodendritic synapse
questions.why: Synapses between neurons are named for the parts that meet, starting with the axon of the sending neuron. When the receiving part is another axon, the synapse is axoaxonic. The other two neuron-to-neuron types are axodendritic, ending on a dendrite, and axosomatic, ending on a cell body.
notes: An axosomatic synapse is an axon ending on a cell body (soma). Choose it when the receiving part is the cell body.
A neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber, not between two neurons. It would be right for a question about where a nerve meets muscle.
Correct. An axon ending on another axon forms an axoaxonic synapse.
An axodendritic synapse is an axon ending on a dendrite, the most common type. Pick it when the receiving part is a dendrite.
questions.answerText: An axoaxonic synapse

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What are the chemical messengers that carry a signal across the synaptic cleft called?
options: Synaptic vesicles
Hormones
Neurofibrils
Neurotransmitters
questions.why: Neurotransmitters are the chemical messengers of a chemical synapse. They are stored in synaptic vesicles, released into the synaptic cleft when a signal arrives, and diffuse across the gap to reach the receiving cell. Their action is local to the synapse, unlike hormones, which travel in the blood.
notes: Synaptic vesicles are the sacs that store neurotransmitter, not the messengers themselves. Choose them for a question about where neurotransmitter is held before release.
Hormones are chemical messengers too, but they are released by endocrine glands into the blood and travel throughout the body. Pick hormones for a question about endocrine signaling.
Neurofibrils are cytoskeletal fibers that give the neuron its shape and support. They would be right for a question about the internal support of a neuron.
Correct. Neurotransmitters carry the signal across the cleft.
questions.answerText: Neurotransmitters

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares convergence and divergence?
options: Both describe a pathway crossing over to the opposite side of the brain and cord
Both describe a signal passed along one straight chain of neurons
Convergence spreads one neuron to many; divergence funnels many onto one
Convergence funnels many neurons onto one; divergence spreads one to many
questions.why: Convergence and divergence are mirror-image circuit patterns in a neuronal pool. In convergence, signals from many neurons funnel onto one target neuron, and in divergence, one neuron spreads its signal out to many. The word roots help: converge means to come together, and diverge means to branch apart.
notes: Crossing to the opposite side is decussation, which concerns pathways rather than circuit wiring. Choose this for a question about why one side of the brain serves the other side of the body.
A single straight chain of neurons is serial processing, a different pattern. Pick this description for a question about serial processing in a reflex arc.
This swaps the two definitions. Converge means to come together, so convergence is the pattern in which many inputs meet on one neuron.
Correct. The two patterns are mirror images of each other.
questions.answerText: Convergence funnels many neurons onto one; divergence spreads one to many

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A single sensory neuron entering the spinal cord branches and passes its signal to many interneurons at several levels of the cord. Which circuit pattern is this?
options: Decussation
Serial processing
Convergence
Divergence
questions.why: In a diverging circuit, one presynaptic neuron branches and synapses on many postsynaptic neurons. Here a single sensory neuron branches inside the cord and reaches many interneurons at different levels, so one input reaches many targets. Convergence is the reverse, with many neurons feeding onto one.
notes: Decussation is a pathway crossing to the opposite side of the CNS, not a branching pattern. It would be right for a question about why the left brain serves the right body.
Serial processing is a single straight chain of neurons, one after another, with no branching. Choose it for a simple chain like the reflex arc.
Convergence is the reverse, with many neurons feeding onto one. Pick it if many sensory neurons all fed onto a single interneuron.
Correct. One neuron passing its signal to many neurons is divergence.
questions.answerText: Divergence

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A signal is sent along several separate pathways at the same time instead of down one chain. Which pattern is this?
options: Serial processing
Decussation
Parallel processing
Convergence
questions.why: In parallel processing, a signal travels along several pathways at the same time, so different parts of the CNS can handle the same information at once. Serial processing, by contrast, uses a single chain, as in a reflex arc.
notes: Serial processing is the opposite arrangement, a single chain of neurons one after another. Pick it for a reflex arc.
Decussation is the crossing of a pathway to the opposite side of the CNS. It would be right for a question about why each side of the brain serves the opposite side of the body.
Correct. Sending a signal along several pathways at once is parallel processing.
Convergence is many neurons feeding onto one, a funneling pattern rather than several routes at once. Choose it when many inputs meet on a single neuron.
questions.answerText: Parallel processing

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The cortex of the cerebellum is made mostly of neuron cell bodies and dendrites. Which tissue type is it?
options: Gray matter
White matter
A peripheral nerve
A ganglion
questions.why: Gray matter is made of neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons. In the brain, including the cerebellum, gray matter forms the outer cortex and white matter lies beneath it. The spinal cord is arranged the other way around, with gray matter inside.
notes: Correct. Cell bodies and dendrites make gray matter.
White matter is made of myelinated axons running in bundles, and it lies beneath the cortex. Pick it for a question about the tissue under the cerebellar cortex.
A peripheral nerve is a bundle of axons outside the CNS, not part of the cerebellum. Choose it for a question about bundles of axons in the PNS.
A ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS, while the cerebellum is part of the brain. It would be right for a question about cell bodies grouped beside the spinal cord.
questions.answerText: Gray matter

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: At a synapse, which structure is the receiving membrane that the signal reaches after crossing the gap?
options: The postsynaptic membrane
The presynaptic terminal
The synaptic vesicle
The synaptic cleft
questions.why: A synapse has a sending side, a gap, and a receiving side. Neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic terminal, crosses the synaptic cleft, and reaches the postsynaptic membrane, the membrane of the receiving cell. Post means after, so the postsynaptic membrane is the structure after the gap.
notes: Correct. The postsynaptic membrane is on the receiving side of the cleft.
The presynaptic terminal is on the sending side, before the cleft. Pick it for a question about the structure that releases neurotransmitter.
Synaptic vesicles are sacs inside the presynaptic terminal that store neurotransmitter. It would be right for a question about where neurotransmitter is held before release.
The synaptic cleft is the gap itself, between the two cells. Choose it for a question about the space that neurotransmitter crosses.
questions.answerText: The postsynaptic membrane

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Inside the CNS, which pair of terms names a bundle of axons and a cluster of cell bodies?
options: Tract for the axon bundle, nucleus for the cell-body cluster
Tract for the axon bundle, ganglion for the cell-body cluster
Nerve for the axon bundle, nucleus for the cell-body cluster
Nerve for the axon bundle, ganglion for the cell-body cluster
questions.why: The same structures take different names inside and outside the CNS. Inside the brain and spinal cord, a bundle of axons is a tract and a cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus. Outside the CNS, they are a nerve and a ganglion.
notes: Correct. Tract and nucleus are the CNS terms.
Tract is right, but a ganglion lies outside the CNS. This mixes one CNS term with one PNS term.
Nucleus is right, but a nerve lies outside the CNS. This mixes one PNS term with one CNS term.
Nerve and ganglion are the matching terms for the PNS. Pick this pair when both structures lie outside the brain and spinal cord.
questions.answerText: Tract for the axon bundle, nucleus for the cell-body cluster

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares where gray and white matter sit in the brain and in the spinal cord?
options: Both have white matter on the outside and gray matter on the inside
The brain has gray outside and white inside; the cord is the reverse
Both have gray matter on the outside and white matter on the inside
The brain has white outside and gray inside; the cord is the reverse
questions.why: Gray matter (cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons) and white matter (myelinated axons) swap positions between the two CNS organs. In the brain, gray matter forms the outer cortex with white matter beneath it. In the spinal cord, gray matter forms the butterfly-shaped core and white matter surrounds it.
notes: This is true for the cord but not the brain. Students choose it when they apply the cord pattern to the whole CNS.
Correct. The two organs have opposite arrangements.
This is true for the brain but not the cord. Students choose it when they apply the brain pattern to the whole CNS.
This swaps the two organs. The brain has an outer cortex of gray matter, and the cord has its gray matter in the inner core.
questions.answerText: The brain has gray outside and white inside; the cord is the reverse

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Why does white matter look white?
options: It is packed with neuron cell bodies
Its axons are wrapped in fatty myelin
It is filled with cerebrospinal fluid
It contains no blood vessels at all
questions.why: White matter is made of myelinated axons, and myelin is a multilayered covering rich in lipid. That fatty material is what makes the tissue look white. Gray matter has few myelinated axons and many cell bodies, so it looks gray instead.
notes: Neuron cell bodies are concentrated in gray matter, and they give it the gray look. Pick this for a question about what makes gray matter gray.
Correct. The lipid in myelin gives white matter its color.
Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles and central canal, not the white matter. Choose it for a question about the fluid-filled spaces of the CNS.
White matter does have blood vessels, and having none would not make tissue white. This choice confuses color with blood supply.
questions.answerText: Its axons are wrapped in fatty myelin

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the combining of all the incoming signals so that a neuron produces a single response called?
options: Decussation
Divergence
Integration
Serial processing
questions.why: A neuron can receive signals from many other neurons at once. Integration is the combining of all those incoming signals so that the neuron produces a single response, such as firing or not firing. The same idea, on a larger scale, is the integrative function of the CNS, which analyzes input and decides on a response.
notes: Decussation is the crossing of a pathway to the opposite side of the CNS. Pick it for a question about why each side of the brain serves the opposite side of the body.
Divergence is a circuit pattern in which one neuron spreads its signal to many. Choose it for a question about one neuron reaching many targets.
Correct. Integration is the combining of incoming signals into one response.
Serial processing is a signal passing along a single straight chain of neurons. It would be right for a question about the chain of a reflex arc.
questions.answerText: Integration

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A brain MRI shows damage in the band of myelinated axons just beneath the cerebral cortex. Which tissue is damaged?
options: Gray matter
A ganglion
White matter
The pia mater
questions.why: In the brain, gray matter forms the outer cortex and white matter lies beneath it. White matter is made of myelinated axons running in bundles, and the myelin gives it its color. Damage to the band of myelinated axons under the cortex is therefore damage to white matter, the kind of change a radiologist looks for on a scan.
notes: Gray matter is the cortex itself, made of cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons. Pick it if the damage were in the outer layer of the cerebrum.
A ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS, not inside the brain. Choose it for a question about cell bodies grouped beside the spinal cord.
Correct. Myelinated axons beneath the cortex form the white matter.
The pia mater is the thin innermost membrane on the surface of the brain, outside the cortex rather than beneath it. It would be right for a question about the membrane that clings to the brain.
questions.answerText: White matter

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A signal needs to reach several brain regions at the same time so they can work on it at once. Which processing pattern does this?
options: Convergence
Serial processing
Parallel processing
Decussation
questions.why: In parallel processing, a signal travels along several pathways at the same time. That lets several brain regions receive and work on the same information at once instead of one after another. Serial processing, by contrast, passes the signal down a single chain, as in a reflex arc.
notes: Convergence funnels many neurons onto one, the opposite of spreading a signal out. Choose it when many inputs meet on a single neuron.
Serial processing passes the signal along one chain, one neuron after another, so regions would receive it in turn rather than at once. Pick it for a reflex arc.
Correct. Parallel processing sends a signal along several pathways at the same time.
Decussation is a pathway crossing to the opposite side of the CNS. It would be right for a question about why each side of the brain serves the opposite side of the body.
questions.answerText: Parallel processing

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: In a neuronal pool, many sensory neurons all feed their signals onto a single output neuron. Which circuit pattern is this?
options: Serial processing
Decussation
Divergence
Convergence
questions.why: In a converging circuit, signals from many neurons come together onto one target neuron. That single neuron then combines, or integrates, all the input into one response. Convergence lets the CNS combine information from many sources before acting.
notes: Serial processing is a single straight chain of neurons with no funneling. Choose it for the simple chain of a reflex arc.

Decussation is a pathway crossing to the opposite side of the CNS, not a wiring pattern within a pool. It would be right for a question about why one side of the brain serves the other side of the body.
Divergence is the reverse, one neuron spreading its signal to many. Pick it if a single sensory neuron sent its signal to many output neurons.
Correct. Many neurons feeding onto one is convergence.
questions.answerText: Convergence

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A ball flies toward you. Your eyes detect it, your brain judges its path and decides to duck, and your muscles move you. Which function is the judging and deciding step, and where does it happen?
options: Sensory, in the receptors
Integrative, in the PNS
Integrative, in the CNS
Motor, in the muscles
questions.why: The nervous system handles every task in three steps. In the sensory function, receptors detect a change, in the integrative function, the CNS analyzes the input and decides on a response, and in the motor function, commands go out to the effectors. Judging the path of the ball and deciding to duck is the integrative step, which takes place in the CNS.
notes: The sensory function is the first step, when the eyes detect the ball. Pick it for the detecting step, not the deciding step.
Integrative is the right function, but it happens in the brain and spinal cord, not in the PNS. The PNS only carries signals to and from the CNS.
Correct. The CNS analyzes the input and decides on the response.
The motor function is the last step, when commands reach the muscles and you duck. Choose it for the responding step.
questions.answerText: Integrative, in the CNS

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Signals cross a chemical synapse in only one direction, from the sending cell to the receiving cell. Which structural fact explains this?
options: Only the sending terminal holds vesicles of neurotransmitter
Myelin covers the receiving side and blocks any return signal
The receiving cell is always a muscle fiber that cannot signal
Only the receiving cell has a membrane facing the cleft
questions.why: At a chemical synapse, only the presynaptic terminal contains synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitter. When a signal arrives, those vesicles release the neurotransmitter, which crosses the cleft to the postsynaptic membrane. The receiving side has no vesicles to send a message back, so the signal can only travel from the sending cell to the receiving cell.
notes: Correct. Only the presynaptic side can release neurotransmitter.
Myelin wraps axons along their length, not the receiving side of a synapse. Pick myelin for a question about what speeds conduction along an axon.

The receiving cell is often another neuron or a gland cell, not always a muscle fiber, and many receiving neurons go on to signal other cells. The one-way flow comes from where the vesicles are, not from the type of receiving cell.

Both cells have a membrane facing the cleft, the presynaptic membrane on one side and the postsynaptic membrane on the other. The difference lies in what each side holds, not in whether it has a membrane.
questions.answerText: Only the sending terminal holds vesicles of neurotransmitter

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which swellings at the tips of the axon terminals hold the synaptic vesicles?
options: The synaptic end bulbs
The axon hillocks
The Nissl bodies
The nodes of Ranvier
questions.why: Each axon terminal ends in a small swelling called a synaptic end bulb, which holds the signal-sending machinery of the neuron. Inside the end bulbs are the synaptic vesicles, tiny sacs that store neurotransmitter. When a signal arrives, the vesicles release their neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.
notes: Correct. Synaptic end bulbs are the swellings that hold the vesicles.
The axon hillock is the cone-shaped region where the axon starts, at the opposite end from the terminals. Choose it for a question about where the axon leaves the cell body.
Nissl bodies are clusters of rough ER and ribosomes in the cell body that make proteins. They would be right for a question about protein synthesis in a neuron.
Nodes of Ranvier are bare gaps in the myelin along the length of the axon, not swellings at its tips. Pick them for a question about where the impulse jumps.
questions.answerText: The synaptic end bulbs

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The central nervous system consists of which two structures?
options: The brain and the cranial nerves
The brain and the spinal cord
The cerebrum and the cerebellum
The spinal cord and the spinal nerves
questions.why: The central nervous system (CNS) is made of the brain and the spinal cord, the two organs that integrate information and send out commands. The brain sits in the cranial cavity and the cord runs down the vertebral canal. Everything outside them, including the cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and ganglia, belongs to the peripheral nervous system (PNS), which carries signals to and from the CNS.
notes: The brain belongs to the CNS, but the cranial nerves are part of the PNS because they leave the brain and travel out to the head, neck, and viscera. Students pick this when they assume any nerve attached to the brain counts as central.
Correct. The brain and the spinal cord together make up the CNS.

The cerebrum and cerebellum are two regions of the brain, so this pair leaves out the diencephalon, the brainstem, and the whole spinal cord. Pick them if the question asked for the largest and second largest parts of the brain.

The spinal cord belongs to the CNS, but the spinal nerves branch off it and belong to the PNS. A spinal nerve would be the answer if the question asked which structure carries mixed sensory and motor axons out through an intervertebral foramen.
questions.answerText: The brain and the spinal cord

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: In the central nervous system, a cluster of neuron cell bodies is called what?
options: A tract
A nucleus
A nerve
A ganglion
questions.why: The nervous system uses different names for the same kind of structure depending on whether it is in the CNS or the PNS. A cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus in the CNS and a ganglion in the PNS. A bundle of axons is a tract in the CNS and a nerve in the PNS.
notes: A tract is a bundle of axons in the CNS, such as an ascending tract in the spinal cord. It would be the answer if the question asked about a bundle of axons rather than cell bodies.
Correct. A cluster of cell bodies in the CNS is a nucleus.
A nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS, such as a spinal nerve. Pick it if the question asked what a bundle of axons is called outside the CNS.
A ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system, such as the dorsal root ganglion. Pick it if the question asked about the PNS.
questions.answerText: A nucleus

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is a cluster of neuron cell bodies located in the peripheral nervous system called?
options: A fascicle
A plexus
A ganglion
A nucleus
questions.why: A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies that lies outside the central nervous system. Examples include the dorsal root ganglia beside the spinal cord and the autonomic ganglia. The matching cluster inside the brain or spinal cord has a different name, a nucleus, so the location decides which term to use.
notes: A fascicle is a bundle of axons inside a nerve, wrapped by perineurium. It is made of nerve fibers, not cell bodies.
A plexus is a network where nerves join and regroup, such as the brachial plexus. Pick it for a branching network of nerves rather than a cluster of cell bodies.
Correct. A cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion.
A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the central nervous system, such as a cranial nerve nucleus in the brainstem. Pick it if the cluster were in the brain or spinal cord.
questions.answerText: A ganglion

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which structures make up the peripheral nervous system?
options: The nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord
The brain and spinal cord with their coverings
The brainstem, cerebellum, and cranial nerve nuclei
The tracts and nuclei found inside the brain and spinal cord
questions.why: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) includes all neural structures outside the brain and spinal cord: the cranial and spinal nerves, the ganglia, the sensory receptors, and the motor endings. Its job is to carry sensory input from receptors into the central nervous system (CNS) and carry motor commands back out to muscles and glands. The brain and spinal cord themselves make up the CNS.
notes: Correct. Everything neural outside the brain and spinal cord belongs to the PNS.
The brain and spinal cord, with their meninges, make up the central nervous system. Pick this for the CNS.
The brainstem and cerebellum are parts of the brain, so they belong to the CNS. The cranial nerve nuclei sit inside the brainstem too, even though the nerves that leave them are peripheral.
Tracts and nuclei are the CNS names for bundles of axons and clusters of cell bodies. Their PNS counterparts are nerves and ganglia, so pick tracts and nuclei for the inside of the brain and cord.
questions.answerText: The nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A cordlike organ of the peripheral nervous system bundles many axons together inside connective tissue wrappings. What is it called?
options: A nerve
A nucleus
A tract
A ganglion
questions.why: A nerve is a cordlike organ of the peripheral nervous system made of many axons bundled together and wrapped in three layers of connective tissue. Some of its axons are myelinated and some are not. The CNS counterpart, a bundle of axons inside the brain or spinal cord, is called a tract.
notes: Correct. A wrapped bundle of peripheral axons is a nerve.
A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS. Pick it for a group of cell bodies in the brainstem or cord.
A tract is a bundle of axons inside the brain or spinal cord, and it lacks the connective tissue wrappings of a nerve. Pick it for a bundle of axons in the CNS.
A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS, not a bundle of axons. Pick it for a swelling such as the dorsal root ganglion.
questions.answerText: A nerve

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The dorsal root ganglion and the posterior gray horn of the cord both contain clusters of neuron cell bodies. Why is only the dorsal root ganglion called a ganglion?
options: It holds myelinated axons, and nuclei hold only unmyelinated axons
It holds sensory neurons, and only sensory clusters are called ganglia
It is larger, and only clusters above a certain size are called ganglia
It lies outside the CNS, and clusters inside the CNS are called nuclei
questions.why: The name for a cluster of neuron cell bodies depends on where it is. Inside the brain or spinal cord a cluster is a nucleus, and outside the CNS it is a ganglion. The dorsal root ganglion sits on the dorsal root just outside the cord, so it is a ganglion even though it lies right next to the CNS.
notes: Myelinated versus unmyelinated axons is the difference between white and gray matter, not between ganglia and nuclei. Pick it for a question about white matter.
Autonomic ganglia hold motor neurons, so ganglia are not limited to sensory neurons. The type of neuron does not decide the name.
Size has nothing to do with the name. A tiny cluster outside the CNS is still a ganglion, and a large one inside the brain is still a nucleus.
Correct. Location decides the name: ganglion outside the CNS, nucleus inside it.
questions.answerText: It lies outside the CNS, and clusters inside the CNS are called nuclei

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: How are gray matter and white matter arranged in the brain?
options: Gray matter outside, white matter inside
White matter outside, gray matter inside
Gray matter only in the brainstem and cerebellum
Gray and white matter evenly mixed throughout
questions.why: Gray matter is made of neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated fibers, while white matter is made of myelinated axons, and the fatty myelin is what makes it look white. In the brain, the gray matter forms an outer layer (the cortex), and the white matter lies beneath it, carrying signals between areas. The spinal cord has the reverse arrangement, so it helps to name the organ before naming the layer.
notes: Correct. The cerebral cortex is an outer layer of gray matter over a core of white matter.
This is the arrangement in the spinal cord, where a butterfly of gray matter sits at the core and white matter wraps around it. Pick it if the question asked about a cross section of the spinal cord.

Gray matter is not limited to the brainstem and cerebellum. The cerebrum has a whole outer layer of gray matter, the cerebral cortex, along with deep gray masses such as the basal nuclei. This choice comes from forgetting that the cortex itself is gray matter.
The two are not randomly mixed. Gray matter collects where cell bodies gather (the cortex and deep nuclei), and white matter forms organized bundles of axons, so each sits in predictable places.
questions.answerText: Gray matter outside, white matter inside

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What are the two main divisions of the nervous system?
options: The sensory and motor divisions
The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
The central and peripheral nervous systems
The somatic and autonomic nervous systems
questions.why: The nervous system is first split by location. The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord, which process information and issue commands. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is every neural structure outside them, including the 12 pairs of cranial nerves, the 31 pairs of spinal nerves, the ganglia, and the sensory receptors. Every other split you learn in this unit is a subdivision inside one of these two.
notes: Sensory and motor describe the direction signals travel within the PNS, input toward the CNS and output away from it. Choose this pair if the question asked how the PNS is divided by the direction its neurons carry signals.

The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions are the two halves of the autonomic nervous system, two levels further down. They would be the answer for a question about fight or flight versus rest and digest.
Correct. The CNS and PNS are the top-level split, based on whether a structure lies inside or outside the brain and spinal cord.

The somatic and autonomic systems are subdivisions of the motor side of the PNS, sorted by the effector they control. Pick them if the question asked how the PNS motor division splits into voluntary and involuntary parts.
questions.answerText: The central and peripheral nervous systems

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which organs make up the central nervous system?
options: The brain, cord, and all ganglia
The spinal cord and spinal nerves
The brain and cranial nerves
The brain and spinal cord
questions.why: The CNS is made of just two organs: the brain in the cranial cavity and the spinal cord in the vertebral canal. Together they receive sensory input, process it, and send out commands. Anything neural that lies outside these two organs, such as nerves, ganglia, and sensory receptors, belongs to the peripheral nervous system.
notes: Ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS, so they are peripheral by definition. A cluster of cell bodies inside the CNS is called a nucleus instead.
Spinal nerves branch off the cord and exit the vertebral canal, so they belong to the PNS even though the cord itself is CNS. Students pick this when they assume anything named spinal is central.
Cranial nerves attach to the brain, but they leave it to reach the head and body, so they are part of the PNS. This pairing comes from assuming that anything attached to the brain must be central.
Correct. The brain and spinal cord are the only two organs of the CNS.
questions.answerText: The brain and spinal cord

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What are the three functions of the nervous system, in the order they happen during a response?
options: Sensory, motor, and integrative
Sensory, protective, and secretory
Sensory, integrative, and motor
Integrative, sensory, and motor
questions.why: The nervous system handles every task in the same three steps. Sensory function comes first: receptors detect a change inside or outside the body and send that input toward the CNS. Integrative function is the CNS analyzing the input, storing it, and deciding on a response. Motor function comes last, when the CNS sends commands out to the effectors, the muscles and glands that carry out the response.
notes: These are the right three functions, but motor output cannot happen before the CNS has processed the input and decided on a response. Students pick it when they remember the names but not the sequence.

Protection and secretion are not among the three nervous system functions. Glands do secrete, but they are effectors that receive motor commands, and the CNS is protected by bone, meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid rather than by its own function.
Correct. Input comes in, the CNS processes it, and a response goes out.
These are the right three functions, but integration cannot come first because the CNS has nothing to analyze until sensory input arrives. This order mixes up the sequence.
questions.answerText: Sensory, integrative, and motor

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which list names the three basic parts of every neuron?
options: Axon hillock, axon, and synapse
Cell body, dendrites, and axon
Cell body, axon, and Schwann cell
Dendrites, axon, and myelin sheath
questions.why: Every neuron has a cell body, also called the soma, which holds the nucleus and is the metabolic center of the cell. Branched dendrites receive incoming signals, and a single axon carries the impulse away toward other cells. Features such as myelin are added by other cells, and a synapse forms where a neuron meets its target, so neither is one of the three basic parts.
notes: The axon hillock is only the cone-shaped region where the cell body joins the axon, and a synapse is a junction between two cells rather than part of one neuron. This list mixes a small region and a junction in with one true part.
Correct. The cell body, dendrites, and axon are the three parts every neuron has.
A Schwann cell is a PNS glial cell that wraps an axon in myelin, not a part of the neuron itself. It would be the answer if the question asked which cell myelinates a peripheral axon.
The myelin sheath is not part of every neuron. It is a fatty wrapping laid around some axons by glial cells, so pick it if the question asked what insulates an axon and speeds the impulse.
questions.answerText: Cell body, dendrites, and axon

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the main job of the dendrites of a neuron?
options: They receive incoming signals
