They carry the impulse to other cells
They insulate the axon
They make proteins for the neuron
questions.why: Dendrites are the short, branched, tree-like processes of a neuron. Their many branches give the neuron a large surface for receiving signals from other cells, and they pass that incoming information toward the cell body. A neuron usually has many dendrites but only one axon.
notes: Correct. Dendrites are the receiving branches of the neuron.
Carrying the impulse away toward other cells is the job of the axon, the single long process of the neuron. Pick this if the question asked what the axon does.
Insulating the axon is the job of the myelin sheath, made by Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS. Choose this if the question asked what myelin does.
Protein synthesis is centered in the cell body, at the Nissl bodies. Some Nissl bodies reach into the dendrites, but the main job of the dendrites is receiving signals.
questions.answerText: They receive incoming signals

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the job of the axon of a neuron?
options: It holds the nucleus and makes the cell's proteins
It receives incoming signals from other neurons
It carries the impulse away to other cells
It speeds the impulse by insulating the axon
questions.why: The axon is the single long process of a neuron, and it conducts the nerve impulse away from the cell body. At its far end it branches into axon terminals, which contact the next neuron, a muscle cell, or a gland. Because the axon depends on the cell body for its proteins, it cannot survive if it is cut off from the cell body.
notes: Holding the nucleus and making proteins describes the cell body, the metabolic center of the neuron. It would be the answer for a question about the soma.
Receiving incoming signals is the job of the dendrites, the branched processes of the neuron. Pick this if the question asked what dendrites do.
Correct. The axon is the outgoing process that carries the impulse away.
Insulating the axon and speeding the impulse is the job of the myelin sheath, a wrapping laid around the axon by glial cells. Choose this if the question asked what myelin does.
questions.answerText: It carries the impulse away to other cells

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the axon hillock?
options: The gaps in the myelin sheath spaced along the axon
The swelling on a spinal root that holds sensory cell bodies
The fine branching ends of the axon that contact the target cell
The cone-shaped region joining the cell body to the axon
questions.why: The axon hillock is the cone-shaped part of the cell body that narrows down into the axon. It marks where the cell body ends and the axon begins, so it is the landmark for finding the start of the axon on a neuron model or slide. A hillock is a small hill, which describes its tapered, mound-like shape.
notes: The gaps in the myelin sheath are the nodes of Ranvier. They would be the answer if the question asked where the impulse jumps along a myelinated axon.
A swelling on a spinal root that holds sensory cell bodies is the posterior (dorsal) root ganglion. Choose it for a question about where sensory neuron cell bodies sit outside the cord.
The fine branches at the far end of the axon are the axon terminals, which contact the target cell. Pick them if the question asked where the axon meets the next cell.
Correct. The axon hillock is where the cell body tapers into the axon.
questions.answerText: The cone-shaped region joining the cell body to the axon

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An injury cuts through an axon partway along its length. Why does the part of the axon beyond the cut die?
options: It loses the cell body that supplies its proteins
It loses the synapse that makes its proteins
It loses the myelin sheath that supplies its nutrients
It loses the dendrites that supply its energy
questions.why: The cell body is the neuron's metabolic center. Its Nissl bodies, clusters of rough ER and ribosomes, make the proteins the whole neuron needs, and microtubules carry those materials down the axon. Once part of the axon is separated from the cell body, it no longer receives these supplies and it degenerates. This is why the location of a nerve injury, near or far from the cell body, helps predict whether the neuron survives.
notes: Correct. The axon depends on the cell body for its proteins, so the separated piece dies.
A synapse is a junction where the axon passes its signal to another cell, and it does not make proteins. The synapse would be the answer if the question asked where neurotransmitter is released.
The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds the impulse, but it is not the axon's supply line. Pick myelin if the question asked what is lost in multiple sclerosis.
Dendrites receive incoming signals; they do not supply the axon with energy or materials. This choice comes from thinking of the dendrites as the neuron's control center instead of the cell body.
questions.answerText: It loses the cell body that supplies its proteins

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which list gives the three structural classes of neurons, named for their shape?
options: Sensory, motor, and interneurons
Pyramidal, Purkinje, and bipolar
Multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar
Astrocytes, microglia, and Schwann cells
questions.why: Structural classification counts the processes leaving the cell body. A multipolar neuron has many dendrites and one axon, a bipolar neuron has one dendrite and one axon, and a unipolar neuron has a single fused process. The names come from the number of poles, or processes, the cell body has.
notes: Sensory, motor, and interneurons are the functional classes, sorted by the direction a neuron carries its signal. Pick this list if the question asked how neurons are classified by function.

Pyramidal and Purkinje cells are named examples of multipolar neurons, found in the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum. They would be the answer if the question asked for distinctive multipolar neurons, not the three shape classes.
Correct. Multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar are the three shape classes.
Astrocytes, microglia, and Schwann cells are neuroglia, the support cells of nervous tissue, not neurons. Choose this list for a question about glial cells.
questions.answerText: Multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which structural type of neuron is the most common, found throughout the brain and spinal cord and as the motor neurons?
options: Unipolar neuron
Bipolar neuron
Sensory (afferent) neuron
Multipolar neuron
questions.why: Multipolar neurons have many dendrites and one axon, and they are the most common type in the body. Most neurons of the brain and spinal cord are multipolar, including the interneurons that link sensory and motor neurons, and every motor neuron that carries commands out to muscles and glands is multipolar. The pyramidal cells of the cerebral cortex and the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum are well-known examples.
notes: Unipolar neurons have a single fused process and are the typical shape of a sensory neuron. They would be the answer if the question asked for the shape of the neurons that carry input toward the CNS.
Bipolar neurons have one dendrite and one axon and are rare, found only in the retina, the inner ear, and the olfactory area. Pick bipolar if the question asked which neurons are found in the retina.

Sensory (afferent) is a functional class, not a structural shape, and sensory neurons carry input toward the CNS rather than serving as motor neurons. Choose it if the question asked how a neuron carrying input from the skin is classified by function.
Correct. Multipolar neurons are the most common type and include all motor neurons.
questions.answerText: Multipolar neuron

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which structural shape is typical of a sensory neuron?
options: Multipolar
Unipolar
Bipolar
Pyramidal
questions.why: Most sensory (afferent) neurons are unipolar: a single fused process leaves the cell body and then splits, with one branch running out to the receptor and the other running into the CNS. The cell bodies of these neurons sit in ganglia outside the CNS, such as the posterior root ganglia of the spinal nerves.
notes: Multipolar neurons have many dendrites and one axon. They are the shape of motor neurons and interneurons, so pick multipolar if the question asked about a neuron that carries commands to a muscle.
Correct. Unipolar is the typical shape of a sensory neuron.

Bipolar neurons are sensory too, but only in a few special sense organs: the retina, the inner ear, and the olfactory area. Pick bipolar if the question asked about the neurons of the retina, not the typical sensory neuron.
Pyramidal cells are a distinctive multipolar neuron of the cerebral cortex, not a sensory shape. They would be the answer for a question about named neurons of the cerebral cortex.
questions.answerText: Unipolar

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which list gives the three functional classes of neurons?
options: Somatic, autonomic, and enteric
Sensory, integrative, and motor
Sensory, motor, and interneurons
Multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar
questions.why: Functional classification sorts neurons by the direction they carry a signal relative to the CNS. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry input toward the CNS, motor (efferent) neurons carry commands away from it to muscles and glands, and interneurons, also called association neurons, sit within the CNS and connect sensory neurons to motor neurons.
notes: Somatic, autonomic, and enteric are divisions of the motor side of the nervous system, not classes of individual neurons. They would be the answer for a question about the motor divisions of the PNS.

Sensory, integrative, and motor are the three functions of the nervous system, not the names of neuron classes. The middle class of neuron is called the interneuron, even though integration is the work it does.
Correct. Sensory, motor, and interneurons are the three functional classes.
Multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar are the structural classes, sorted by shape. Pick this list if the question asked how neurons are classified by the number of processes.
questions.answerText: Sensory, motor, and interneurons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A neuron carries input from a skin receptor toward the spinal cord, and a single process leaves its cell body. How is it classified by structure and by function?
options: Structurally bipolar; functionally sensory
Structurally unipolar; functionally sensory
Structurally multipolar; functionally interneuron
Structurally unipolar; functionally motor
questions.why: Neurons are classified two ways. By structure, a neuron with a single process leaving its cell body is unipolar. By function, a neuron that carries input from a receptor toward the CNS is sensory, or afferent. This pairing is the usual one, because most sensory neurons are unipolar.
notes: Bipolar neurons have two processes, one dendrite and one axon, and are found only in the retina, inner ear, and olfactory area. This would fit a neuron in the retina, not one with a single process carrying touch from the skin.
Correct. A single process makes it unipolar, and carrying input toward the CNS makes it sensory.

Multipolar interneurons lie entirely within the CNS and link sensory to motor neurons. This would be the answer for a neuron inside the spinal cord gray matter that connects the incoming and outgoing neurons of a reflex.
The shape is right, but a motor (efferent) neuron carries commands away from the CNS, and motor neurons are multipolar. Pick motor if the neuron carried a command from the cord out to a muscle.
questions.answerText: Structurally unipolar; functionally sensory

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes neuroglia compared with neurons?
options: They are larger than neurons and far fewer in number
They are support cells that, like neurons, cannot divide
They support neurons and, unlike neurons, can still divide
They are signaling cells that carry impulses like neurons do
questions.why: Neuroglia, or glial cells, are the support cells of nervous tissue. They nourish, support, and protect neurons and make up about half the volume of the CNS. They are smaller than neurons and very numerous, and unlike neurons they keep the ability to divide. That ability is why most tumors of nervous tissue arise from glia rather than from neurons.
notes: Glia are smaller than neurons, not larger, and they are very numerous, making up about half the volume of the CNS. This statement gets the size backward.
Glia are support cells, but they can still divide. Only neurons have lost that ability, which is the main contrast between the two cell types.
Correct. Glia are support cells, and they can still divide while neurons cannot.
Carrying nerve impulses is the job of neurons, the excitable signaling cells. Glia support and protect neurons rather than sending the signals themselves.
questions.answerText: They support neurons and, unlike neurons, can still divide

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which cells form the myelin sheath in the CNS, and which form it in the PNS?
options: Ependymal cells in the CNS; Schwann cells in the PNS
Oligodendrocytes in the CNS; Schwann cells in the PNS
Astrocytes in the CNS; satellite cells in the PNS
Schwann cells in the CNS; oligodendrocytes in the PNS
questions.why: Myelin is made by a different glial cell on each side of the nervous system. In the CNS, an oligodendrocyte sends out a few long processes and myelinates a segment of each of several axons. In the PNS, a Schwann cell wraps one segment of one axon and leaves an outer layer called the neurolemma, which helps a damaged peripheral axon regrow.
notes: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and help make cerebrospinal fluid; they do not make myelin. Pick ependymal cells for a question about the lining of the ventricles.
Correct. Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons and Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons.

Astrocytes support CNS neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier, and satellite cells surround neuron cell bodies in PNS ganglia. This pair would be the answer if the question asked which glia support neurons without making myelin.
This swaps the two cells. Schwann cells work only in the PNS and oligodendrocytes only in the CNS, so the locations are reversed.
questions.answerText: Oligodendrocytes in the CNS; Schwann cells in the PNS

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which glial cells are the small phagocytes of the CNS that remove debris and microbes?
options: Satellite cells
Ependymal cells
Microglia
Astrocytes
questions.why: Microglia are small phagocytic cells of the CNS, meaning they engulf and digest material. They clear away debris from dead and damaged cells and engulf microbes. They are the CNS's own immune defense.
notes: Satellite cells are PNS glia that surround and support neuron cell bodies inside ganglia. Choose them if the question asked which glia sit around the cell bodies in a posterior root ganglion.

Ependymal cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the cord and help produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid. They would be the answer for a question about the lining of the ventricles.
Correct. Microglia are the phagocytes of the CNS.

Astrocytes are star-shaped glia that support neurons, help form the blood-brain barrier, guide neuron growth, and keep the chemical environment stable. Pick astrocytes for a question about the blood-brain barrier.
questions.answerText: Microglia

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which description matches the astrocytes?
options: Engulf debris and microbes, acting as the small phagocytes of the CNS
Line the ventricles and central canal and help produce cerebrospinal fluid
Support neurons, help form the blood-brain barrier, guide growth
Wrap myelin around segments of several CNS axons at the same time
questions.why: Astrocytes are star-shaped glial cells and the most numerous glia of the CNS. They hold neurons in place, help form the blood-brain barrier, guide growing neurons in the embryo, and keep the chemical environment around neurons stable. Their name comes from astro, meaning star, for their many radiating processes.
notes: Engulfing debris and microbes is the job of the microglia, the phagocytes of the CNS. Choose this if the question asked which glia clean up after an injury or infection.
Lining the ventricles and central canal and helping make cerebrospinal fluid is the job of the ependymal cells. This would be the answer for a question about the cells that line the brain's cavities.
Correct. Support, the blood-brain barrier, and guiding neuron growth are astrocyte jobs.
Wrapping myelin around several CNS axons at once is the job of the oligodendrocytes. Pick this if the question asked which cell myelinates axons in the brain and cord.
questions.answerText: Support neurons, help form the blood-brain barrier, guide growth

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Tumors of nervous tissue almost never arise from neurons. Which cells do they usually come from, and why?
options: Glial cells, because they can still divide
Schwann cells, because they myelinate brain axons
Glial cells, because they are larger than neurons
Glial cells, because they lack a nucleus
questions.why: A tumor is a mass of cells dividing out of control, so it can only arise from cells that still divide. Neurons have lost that ability, but neuroglia keep it throughout life. That is why tumors of nervous tissue usually come from glial cells. A tumor of glial cells is called a glioma, and it is a common type of brain tumor.
notes: Correct. Glia keep the ability to divide, so they are the usual source of these tumors.
Schwann cells are PNS glia; the cells that myelinate axons in the brain are oligodendrocytes. Pick Schwann cells if the question asked which glia myelinate a peripheral nerve in the arm.
The cell type is right, but the reason is wrong. Glia are actually smaller than neurons, and size has nothing to do with forming a tumor; the ability to divide is what matters.
Glial cells do have a nucleus, and a cell without one could not divide at all. This reason confuses glia with mature red blood cells, which are the cells that lack a nucleus.
questions.answerText: Glial cells, because they can still divide

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Inside the CNS, what is a cluster of neuron cell bodies called, and what is a bundle of axons called?
options: A ganglion and a tract
A ganglion and a nerve
A nucleus and a tract
A nucleus and a nerve
questions.why: The same two kinds of structure get different names depending on whether they are inside or outside the CNS. Inside the brain and spinal cord, a cluster of neuron cell bodies is a nucleus and a bundle of axons is a tract. Outside the CNS, the matching terms are ganglion and nerve. Note that this kind of nucleus is a group of cells, not the nucleus inside a single cell.
notes: A tract is correct for a CNS bundle of axons, but a ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS. This mixes one CNS term with one PNS term.
A ganglion and a nerve are the PNS terms for a cluster of cell bodies and a bundle of axons. Pick this pair if the question asked about structures outside the brain and spinal cord.
Correct. Nucleus and tract are the CNS terms.
A nucleus is correct for a CNS cluster of cell bodies, but a nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS. This mixes one CNS term with one PNS term.
questions.answerText: A nucleus and a tract

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: In the PNS, what is a cluster of neuron cell bodies called, and what is a bundle of axons called?
options: A nucleus and a tract
A nucleus and a nerve
A ganglion and a tract
A ganglion and a nerve
questions.why: Outside the brain and spinal cord, a cluster of neuron cell bodies is called a ganglion, and a bundle of axons wrapped in connective tissue is called a nerve. A posterior root ganglion and the sciatic nerve are examples. Inside the CNS, the same two structures are called a nucleus and a tract.
notes: A nucleus and a tract are the CNS terms for a cluster of cell bodies and a bundle of axons. Pick this pair if the question asked about structures inside the brain or spinal cord.
A nerve is correct for a PNS bundle of axons, but a nucleus is a cluster of cell bodies inside the CNS. This mixes one CNS term with one PNS term.
A ganglion is correct for a PNS cluster of cell bodies, but a tract is a bundle of axons inside the CNS. This mixes one PNS term with one CNS term.
Correct. Ganglion and nerve are the PNS terms.
questions.answerText: A ganglion and a nerve

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is white matter made of?
options: Unmyelinated axons and dendrites
Neuron cell bodies
Myelinated axons
Neuroglia and blood vessels
questions.why: White matter is nervous tissue made of myelinated axons. Myelin is a fatty wrapping of lipid and protein, and that fat gives these regions their pale, glossy look. White matter is where signals travel over distance, and in the CNS its axons run in bundles called tracts.
notes: Unmyelinated axons and dendrites lack the fatty myelin wrapping, so they are found in gray matter, not white. They would be part of the answer for a question about gray matter.
Neuron cell bodies are the main part of gray matter, the tissue where signals are processed. Pick cell bodies if the question asked what gray matter is made of.
Correct. Myelinated axons make up white matter.
Neuroglia and blood vessels are present throughout nervous tissue, but they are not what defines white matter. This choice comes from forgetting that the white color comes from myelin.
questions.answerText: Myelinated axons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which description fits gray matter?
options: Cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons
Bundles of myelinated axons wrapped by Schwann cells
Connective tissue that wraps fascicles of nerve axons
Myelinated axons running in long bundles called tracts
questions.why: Gray matter is made of neuron cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons, and neuroglia. Because it lacks the fatty myelin that makes white matter pale, it looks gray. Gray matter is where synapses happen and information is processed, such as the cerebral cortex and the inner core of the spinal cord.
notes: Correct. Cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons make up gray matter, along with neuroglia.
Myelinated axons wrapped by Schwann cells are found in peripheral nerves, not in gray matter. This would fit a question about the axons inside a PNS nerve.
Connective tissue around fascicles of axons is the perineurium of a peripheral nerve. Choose this if the question asked which nerve wrapping surrounds each fascicle.
Myelinated axons running in tracts make up white matter, the tissue that carries signals over distance. Pick this if the question asked what white matter is made of.
questions.answerText: Cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: On a spinal cord model, a swelling on the posterior root just outside the cord holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons. Which general term fits this structure?
options: A ganglion
A nucleus
A nerve
A tract
questions.why: Two questions sort these four terms: is the structure a cluster of cell bodies or a bundle of axons, and is it inside the CNS or outside it? This swelling holds cell bodies and sits outside the cord, so it is a ganglion, the posterior (dorsal) root ganglion. A cluster of cell bodies inside the CNS would be a nucleus.
notes: Correct. A cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion.
A nucleus is also a cluster of cell bodies, but it lies inside the brain or spinal cord. Pick nucleus if the cell bodies were within the CNS, such as the motor nuclei in the anterior horn.
A nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS, such as the spinal nerve formed just beyond this swelling. Choose it for a bundle of axons outside the CNS.
A tract is a bundle of axons inside the CNS, such as the ascending and descending tracts in the white matter of the cord. It would be the answer for a bundle of axons, not a cluster of cell bodies.
questions.answerText: A ganglion

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: In the cerebrum, where is the gray matter of the cerebral cortex located relative to the white matter?
options: Inside, surrounded by the white matter
Only in front of the white matter
Outside, covering the white matter
Mixed evenly through the white matter
questions.why: The cerebral cortex is a thin outer layer of gray matter, rich in neuron cell bodies, that covers the cerebrum. Beneath it lies the white matter, made of myelinated axons that link the cortex to other regions. This arrangement is the reverse of the spinal cord, so always name the organ before naming where each layer sits.
notes: Gray matter inside with white matter around it is the arrangement of the spinal cord. Pick this if the question asked about a cord cross-section.
The cortex covers the whole surface of the cerebrum, not just the front. This mix-up may come from the frontal lobe, which is only one region of the cortex.
Correct. The gray cortex covers the white matter of the cerebrum.
The cortex is a distinct outer layer, not gray matter scattered evenly through the white. This choice comes from not separating the cortex from the white matter beneath it.
questions.answerText: Outside, covering the white matter

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the arrangement of gray and white matter in the brain and in the spinal cord?
options: Brain: gray outside, white inside. Cord: white outside, gray inside
Brain: white outside, gray inside. Cord: gray outside, white inside
In both the brain and the spinal cord, gray sits outside and white inside
In both the brain and the spinal cord, white sits outside and gray inside
questions.why: Gray matter is where the cell bodies are, and white matter is where the myelinated axons run. In the cerebrum, the gray cortex lies on the outside over the white matter. In the spinal cord the pattern flips: a butterfly-shaped gray core is surrounded by white columns of tracts. Because the two swap positions, name the organ first, then the layer.
notes: Correct. The brain has gray outside, and the cord has gray inside.
This statement reverses both organs. The cerebral cortex is gray and on the outside of the brain, and the cord's gray matter is the inner butterfly.
This is true of the brain only. The cord reverses the pattern, with gray matter in the core and white matter outside.
This is true of the spinal cord only. The cerebrum has its gray cortex on the outside.
questions.answerText: Brain: gray outside, white inside. Cord: white outside, gray inside

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is a synapse?
options: A gap in the myelin sheath where the impulse jumps ahead
The connective tissue wrapping around an axon
The site where a neuron communicates with another cell
The cone-shaped region of the cell body where the axon begins
questions.why: A synapse is the junction where a neuron passes its signal to another cell: another neuron, a muscle cell, or a gland. At a chemical synapse the two cells do not touch. The sending cell releases neurotransmitter, which crosses a narrow gap to reach the receiving cell. Synapses are named for what the axon ends on, such as axodendritic (onto a dendrite) or axosomatic (onto a cell body).
notes: A gap in the myelin sheath is a node of Ranvier. Pick it if the question asked where the impulse jumps along a myelinated axon.
The connective tissue wrapping around an individual axon in a nerve is the endoneurium. Choose it if the question asked for the innermost nerve wrapping.
Correct. A synapse is where a neuron passes its signal to another cell.
The cone-shaped region where the axon begins is the axon hillock. It would be the answer for a question about where the cell body joins the axon.
questions.answerText: The site where a neuron communicates with another cell

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the synaptic cleft?
options: The sac that stores neurotransmitter in the end bulb
The narrow gap neurotransmitter crosses between cells
The bare gap between two segments of myelin along an axon
The swelling at the tip of an axon terminal that sends the signal
questions.why: At a chemical synapse, the sending and receiving cells do not touch. The synaptic cleft is the narrow gap between them. Neurotransmitter released from the sending cell diffuses across the cleft to reach the receiving cell, which is how the signal crosses from one cell to the next.
notes: The sacs that store neurotransmitter are the synaptic vesicles, found inside the end bulbs. Pick them if the question asked where neurotransmitter is stored.
Correct. The synaptic cleft is the gap the neurotransmitter crosses.
The bare gap between segments of myelin is a node of Ranvier. That is a gap along a single axon, not a gap between two cells.
The swelling at the tip of an axon terminal is a synaptic end bulb. Choose it if the question asked which structure holds the vesicles and sends the signal.
questions.answerText: The narrow gap neurotransmitter crosses between cells

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What do synaptic vesicles store, and where are they found?
options: Myelin, inside the Schwann cells wrapped around the axon
Cerebrospinal fluid, inside the ependymal cells of the ventricles
Neurotransmitter, inside the dendrites of the receiving neuron
Neurotransmitter, in the synaptic end bulbs of the axon
questions.why: Synaptic vesicles are tiny sacs inside the synaptic end bulbs, the swellings at the tips of the axon terminals. They store neurotransmitter, the chemical messenger. When an impulse reaches the end bulb, the vesicles release their neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, and it crosses to the next cell. The vesicles are on the sending side of the synapse.
notes: Myelin is a wrapping of lipid and protein laid down around the axon by Schwann cells, not stored in vesicles. Pick Schwann cells if the question asked which cells myelinate PNS axons.

Cerebrospinal fluid is produced with the help of ependymal cells and the choroid plexus, but it fills the ventricles rather than being stored in vesicles. Choose ependymal cells for a question about the lining of the ventricles.
The contents are right, but the location is wrong. Dendrites are on the receiving side of the synapse, while vesicles sit in the sending axon's end bulbs.
Correct. Synaptic vesicles store neurotransmitter in the end bulbs.
questions.answerText: Neurotransmitter, in the synaptic end bulbs of the axon

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What is the myelin sheath, and what does it do?
options: A connective tissue layer that bundles axons into a fascicle
A fluid-filled sac that stores neurotransmitter at the terminal
A fatty wrapping that insulates the axon and speeds the impulse
A protein coat that slows the impulse to protect the axon
questions.why: The myelin sheath is a multilayered covering of lipid and protein wrapped around an axon by glial cells: Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS. It insulates the axon and makes the impulse travel much faster, because the impulse jumps from one gap in the myelin to the next. In multiple sclerosis, CNS myelin is stripped away and signals slow or fail.
notes: The connective tissue layer around each fascicle is the perineurium. Pick it if the question asked which wrapping bundles axons into fascicles.
A sac that stores neurotransmitter is a synaptic vesicle. It would be the answer if the question asked where neurotransmitter is kept before release.
Correct. Myelin is a fatty wrapping that insulates the axon and speeds the impulse.
Myelin speeds the impulse rather than slowing it, and it is mostly lipid, not a simple protein coat. Students pick this when they think of myelin only as protection.
questions.answerText: A fatty wrapping that insulates the axon and speeds the impulse

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: What are the nodes of Ranvier?
options: Clusters of rough ER in the cell body
Swellings at the end of the axon terminals
Knots of interneurons in the gray matter
Gaps in the myelin sheath along the axon
questions.why: The myelin sheath is not continuous. It is laid down in segments, and the short bare gaps between segments are the nodes of Ranvier. On a myelinated axon the impulse jumps from node to node, called saltatory conduction, which is much faster than traveling along an unmyelinated axon.
notes: Clusters of rough ER and ribosomes in the cell body are the Nissl bodies, where proteins are made. Pick them if the question asked about protein synthesis in a neuron.
The swellings at the ends of the axon terminals are the synaptic end bulbs. They would be the answer if the question asked where synaptic vesicles are found.
A cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS is a nucleus, not a node. Choose nucleus if the question asked about a group of cell bodies in the brain or cord.
Correct. The nodes of Ranvier are the gaps between segments of myelin.
questions.answerText: Gaps in the myelin sheath along the axon

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Why can a cut nerve in the arm often regrow, while a cut tract in the spinal cord usually cannot?
options: Oligodendrocytes leave a neurolemma that guides regrowth; Schwann cells do not
Schwann cells leave a neurolemma that guides regrowth; oligodendrocytes do not
Neurons in the PNS can divide to replace the cut cells; CNS neurons cannot
PNS axons lack myelin, so they regrow faster than myelinated CNS axons
questions.why: In the PNS, each Schwann cell wraps one segment of one axon and leaves an outer layer called the neurolemma. After a cut, the neurolemma forms a regeneration tube that guides the regrowing axon back toward its target. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes leave no neurolemma, they release substances that block regrowth, and astrocytes fill the area with scar tissue, so regrowth is very limited.
notes: This swaps the two cells. The neurolemma belongs to Schwann cells in the PNS, and oligodendrocytes in the CNS do not have one.
Correct. The Schwann cell's neurolemma guides PNS axons as they regrow.
Neurons cannot divide in either the PNS or the CNS. A peripheral nerve recovers when the surviving neuron regrows its axon, not when new neurons are made.
Many PNS axons are myelinated, and the arm's nerves contain plenty of them. The difference in regrowth comes from the neurolemma, not from whether the axon has myelin.
questions.answerText: Schwann cells leave a neurolemma that guides regrowth; oligodendrocytes do not

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares convergence and divergence in a neuronal pool?
options: Convergence: one straight chain. Divergence: several paths at the same time
Convergence: many neurons feed onto one. Divergence: one neuron spreads to many
Convergence: one neuron spreads to many. Divergence: many neurons feed onto one
Convergence: pathways cross sides. Divergence: pathways stay on one side
questions.why: A neuronal pool is a group of interconnected neurons in the CNS that process information together, and the wiring pattern shapes how a signal is handled. In convergence, many neurons send their signals onto a single neuron, so one cell can combine input from many sources. In divergence, one neuron sends its signal out to many neurons, so a single input can spread widely. Converge means come together, and diverge means spread apart.
notes: A single straight chain is serial processing, and several paths at once is parallel processing. Pick these terms if the question asked about serial versus parallel processing.
Correct. Convergence is many onto one, and divergence is one onto many.
This swaps the two terms. Converge means come together, so convergence is many onto one, and divergence is one out to many.

Crossing to the opposite side is called decussation, which is why each half of the brain serves the opposite half of the body. This would be the answer for a question about why a stroke affects the opposite side.
questions.answerText: Convergence: many neurons feed onto one. Divergence: one neuron spreads to many

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An injury cuts only the motor fibers that run to the heart, smooth muscle, and glands, while skeletal muscle still works. Which motor division is damaged, and is it part of the CNS or the PNS?
options: The somatic nervous system, part of the PNS
The enteric nervous system, part of the CNS
The autonomic nervous system, part of the PNS
The autonomic nervous system, part of the CNS
questions.why: The motor side of the PNS is split by the effector it controls. The somatic nervous system runs skeletal muscle, while the autonomic nervous system runs smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. Both are motor divisions of the peripheral nervous system, which carries commands away from the CNS.
notes: The somatic system controls skeletal muscle, which still works here. It is the autonomic system that runs the heart, smooth muscle, and glands.
The enteric system is a network in the wall of the digestive tract, and it sits outside the brain and cord. It is not the division for the heart and all glands.
Correct. Motor fibers to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands belong to the autonomic nervous system, a motor division of the PNS.
The division is right, but the CNS is only the brain and spinal cord. The autonomic motor division is part of the PNS.
questions.answerText: The autonomic nervous system, part of the PNS

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A network of neurons in the wall of a section of intestine keeps the gut's smooth muscle moving even after its links to the brain and spinal cord are cut. Which division is this, and which division normally connects to it and adjusts it?
options: The autonomic nervous system, adjusted by the enteric nervous system
The enteric nervous system, adjusted by the autonomic nervous system
The enteric nervous system, adjusted by the somatic nervous system
The somatic nervous system, adjusted by the autonomic nervous system
questions.why: The enteric nervous system is a network of roughly 100 million neurons in the wall of the digestive tract. It controls the gut's smooth muscle and glands and can run on its own. The autonomic nervous system connects to it and adjusts it, which is why some textbooks count it as part of the ANS.
notes: This reverses the relationship. The network in the gut wall is the enteric system, and the ANS adjusts it.
Correct. The enteric nervous system runs the gut wall on its own, and the autonomic nervous system connects to it and adjusts it.
The division is right, but the somatic system controls skeletal muscle. The ANS is the one that connects to the enteric system.
The somatic system sends voluntary commands to skeletal muscle. It does not run the smooth muscle in the gut wall.
questions.answerText: The enteric nervous system, adjusted by the autonomic nervous system

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: On a neuron slide, one process leaves the cell body from a pale cone with no dark granules, while the others leave from cytoplasm dotted with dark granules. Which process is the axon, and how do you know?
options: The one from the pale cone, because the axon hillock lacks Nissl bodies
One from the dotted cytoplasm, because Nissl bodies mark the axon
The one from the pale cone, because the hillock is packed with Nissl bodies
The most branched one, because the axon is the most branched process
questions.why: Nissl bodies are clusters of rough ER and ribosomes that stain dark, and they appear in the cell body and the dendrites. The axon hillock, where the cell body narrows into the axon, has none, so it stains paler. That pale cone is how you find the axon on a slide and tell it apart from the dendrites.
notes: Correct. The axon hillock has no Nissl bodies, so the pale cone marks where the axon begins.
Nissl bodies appear in the cell body and dendrites, not at the start of the axon. A process leaving from dotted cytoplasm is a dendrite.
The process is right, but the reason is backward. The hillock is pale because it has no Nissl bodies.
Dendrites are the short, heavily branched processes. The axon is a single long process that branches mainly at its far end, into axon terminals.
questions.answerText: The one from the pale cone, because the axon hillock lacks Nissl bodies

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A neuron's axon is cut just past the axon hillock. Signals arriving at the dendrites can still reach which part, and where will impulses no longer arrive?
options: They reach neither the cell body nor the axon terminals
They still reach the axon terminals, but not the cell body
They still reach the cell body, and the dendrites carry them on to the terminals
They still reach the cell body, but impulses no longer reach the axon terminals
questions.why: A signal travels through a neuron in one direction. Dendrites receive it and carry it toward the cell body, the impulse starts at the trigger zone where the hillock meets the axon, and the axon carries it away to the axon terminals. A cut just past the hillock leaves the dendrites and cell body connected but separates them from the far end of the axon and its terminals.
notes: The dendrites and cell body are on the same side of the cut, so signals still reach the cell body.
Dendrites carry signals toward the cell body, which is still connected to them. The cut is between the cell body and the terminals, so the terminals are what lose the signal.
Dendrites carry signals toward the cell body, not out to the axon terminals. Only the axon carries the impulse away to the terminals.
Correct. Dendrites still deliver signals to the cell body, but the cut axon cannot carry impulses out to the terminals.
questions.answerText: They still reach the cell body, but impulses no longer reach the axon terminals

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: On a model, an axon from neuron A ends on the long single process of neuron B, close to where that process branches into B's own terminals. What type of synapse is this, and which neuron is postsynaptic?
options: Axodendritic, with neuron B postsynaptic
Axoaxonic, with neuron A postsynaptic
Axoaxonic, with neuron B postsynaptic
Axosomatic, with neuron A postsynaptic
questions.why: A neuron's long single process that branches into terminals at its far end is its axon. Synapse names start with axo for the sending axon and end with the part it lands on, so an axon ending on another axon is axoaxonic. The cell that receives the signal is the postsynaptic cell, which here is neuron B.
notes: Neuron B is postsynaptic, but its long single process that ends in terminals is an axon, not a dendrite. Dendrites are short and heavily branched.
The type is right, but neuron A is the one sending the signal, so it is presynaptic. The receiving neuron is B.
Correct. The long single process that ends in terminals is B's axon, so this is an axoaxonic synapse with B receiving.
An axosomatic synapse ends on a cell body, not on the long process. Neuron A is also the sender, not the receiver.
questions.answerText: Axoaxonic, with neuron B postsynaptic

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: An electron micrograph shows two cells that do not touch, separated by a gap of about 30 nanometers, with tiny sacs on one side only. What kind of synapse is this, and how does the signal cross the gap?
options: A chemical synapse, with neurotransmitter diffusing across the cleft
An electrical synapse, with gap junctions joining the cells
An electrical synapse, with neurotransmitter diffusing across the cleft
A chemical synapse, with ions passing through gap junctions
questions.why: At a chemical synapse the two cells do not touch. They are separated by the synaptic cleft, only about 20 to 50 nanometers wide, and synaptic vesicles on the presynaptic side store neurotransmitter. The neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across the cleft to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
notes: Correct. A gap of about 20 to 50 nanometers with vesicles on one side is a chemical synapse, and neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft.
An electrical synapse joins two cells directly through gap junctions, so the cells are connected. Here the cells do not touch and vesicles are present.
Neurotransmitter crossing a cleft is how a chemical synapse works. An electrical synapse has no cleft to cross, because gap junctions connect the cells.
The synapse type is right, but gap junctions belong to electrical synapses. At a chemical synapse the signal crosses as neurotransmitter.
questions.answerText: A chemical synapse, with neurotransmitter diffusing across the cleft

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: A slide taken from a swelling on a peripheral nerve shows neuron cell bodies, each surrounded by small satellite cells. What is this structure, and what would the same kind of cluster be called inside the brainstem?
options: A nucleus, which inside the CNS would be called a ganglion
A ganglion, which inside the CNS would be called a tract
A tract, which inside the CNS would be called a nerve
A ganglion, which inside the CNS would be called a nucleus
questions.why: First decide whether you are looking at cell bodies or axons, then whether you are inside the CNS or outside it. A cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS, with satellite cells around them, is a ganglion. The same kind of cluster inside the CNS, such as a cranial nerve nucleus in the brainstem, is called a nucleus.
notes: This reverses the rule. A nucleus is the CNS cluster of cell bodies, and a ganglion is the PNS cluster.
Ganglion is right, but a tract is a bundle of axons in the CNS. The CNS cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus.
Tracts and nerves are bundles of axons, not clusters of cell bodies. A nerve is also the PNS term, not the CNS term.
Correct. A cluster of cell bodies in the PNS is a ganglion, and the same kind of cluster inside the CNS is a nucleus.
questions.answerText: A ganglion, which inside the CNS would be called a nucleus

questions.topic: Nervous system organization and nervous tissue
questions.q: The basal ganglia sit deep in the cerebrum. A student says their name proves they are part of the PNS. Why is the student wrong, and which term fits them better?
options: They sit in the CNS, so nerves is the better term
They sit in the CNS, so basal nuclei is the better term
They are bundles of axons, so tracts is the better term
They are in the PNS, so basal ganglia is correct
questions.why: By the naming rule, a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS is a nucleus, and one in the PNS is a ganglion. The basal ganglia are clusters of cell bodies deep in the cerebrum, which is part of the CNS. Basal ganglia is an older name that breaks the rule, so many texts use basal nuclei instead.
notes: They are in the CNS, but a nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS. A cluster of cell bodies in the CNS is a nucleus.
Correct. Cell body clusters inside the CNS are nuclei, so basal nuclei fits, and basal ganglia is an older name that breaks the rule.
The basal nuclei are masses of gray matter, clusters of cell bodies, not bundles of axons. Tracts make up the white matter.
The cerebrum is part of the brain, which is CNS. The name ganglia here is an older exception, not proof of a PNS location.
questions.answerText: They sit in the CNS, so basal nuclei is the better term

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: What are the four major regions of the brain?
options: The midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata, and hypothalamus
The frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes
The cortex, ventricles, gyri, and sulci
The cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem, and cerebellum
questions.why: The brain is divided into four major regions. The cerebrum is the large upper region for conscious thought and voluntary movement, the diencephalon sits deep beneath it, the brainstem is the stalk that connects to the spinal cord, and the cerebellum sits behind the brainstem and coordinates movement. Every other named brain part, such as a lobe, the thalamus, or the pons, is a subdivision of one of these four.
notes: This list mixes regions. The midbrain, pons, and medulla are the three parts of the brainstem, and the hypothalamus belongs to the diencephalon. The midbrain, pons, and medulla alone would answer a question about the regions of the brainstem.

These are four of the five lobes of the cerebrum, so they divide only one region of the brain. Pick this list if the question asked for the surface lobes of a cerebral hemisphere that are named for the skull bones above them.
These are features of the brain rather than regions. The cortex is the outer gray matter, gyri and sulci are its ridges and grooves, and the ventricles are fluid-filled chambers inside the brain.
Correct. The cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem, and cerebellum are the four major regions.
questions.answerText: The cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem, and cerebellum

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which is the largest part of the brain?
options: The cerebellum
The diencephalon
The cerebrum
The brainstem
questions.why: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and is the seat of conscious thought, sensation, and voluntary movement. It is made of the right and left cerebral hemispheres, joined by the corpus callosum. Its surface is folded into gyri and sulci so that more cortex fits inside the skull.
notes: The cerebellum is the second largest part of the brain, sitting behind the brainstem below the occipital lobes. It would be the answer if the question asked which region coordinates movement, posture, and balance.
The diencephalon is a small region tucked deep between the cerebrum and the brainstem. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus.
Correct. The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain.
The brainstem is the narrow stalk that connects the higher brain to the spinal cord. It would be the answer if the question asked which region is made of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.
questions.answerText: The cerebrum

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: What is the cerebral cortex?
options: The broad band of white matter joining the hemispheres
The fluid-filled chambers inside the cerebrum
The thin outer layer of gray matter on the cerebrum
The deep masses of gray matter within the cerebrum
questions.why: The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of gray matter that covers the cerebrum, only about 2 to 4 mm thick. Gray matter is made of neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated fibers, so the cortex is where most of the cerebrum's neurons actually sit. Its folds, the gyri and sulci, greatly increase the amount of cortex that fits in the skull.
notes: This describes the corpus callosum, a band of white matter (myelinated axons) that connects the right and left hemispheres. Pick it if the question asked which structure lets the two hemispheres communicate.
This describes the ventricles, the fluid-filled chambers where cerebrospinal fluid is made. Pick it if the question asked where the choroid plexus is found.
Correct. The cortex is the thin outer gray matter layer of the cerebrum.
This describes the basal nuclei (basal ganglia), clusters of gray matter buried within the cerebral white matter that help regulate movement. They are deep, not on the surface.
questions.answerText: The thin outer layer of gray matter on the cerebrum

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: The raised folds on the surface of the cerebral cortex are called what?
options: Gyri
Sulci
Fissures
Ventricles
questions.why: The cerebral cortex is folded into raised ridges called gyri (singular gyrus), with grooves between them. Folding lets a large sheet of cortex fit inside the skull. Named gyri, such as the precentral gyrus, serve as landmarks for functional areas.
notes: Correct. Gyri are the raised folds of the cortex.

Sulci are the shallow grooves that lie between the gyri, the dips rather than the ridges. Pick sulci if the question asked about the grooves, such as the central sulcus between the frontal and parietal lobes.
Fissures are the deepest grooves on the brain, which divide major regions, such as the longitudinal fissure between the hemispheres. They would be the answer for a question about the deepest grooves.
Ventricles are fluid-filled chambers deep inside the brain, not surface features. Pick them if the question asked where cerebrospinal fluid is produced.
questions.answerText: Gyri

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: What is the corpus callosum?
options: The white matter band joining the two hemispheres
The tapered inferior end of the spinal cord
The sensory relay station deep in the diencephalon
The outer layer of gray matter on the cerebrum
questions.why: The corpus callosum is a broad band of white matter, meaning bundles of myelinated axons, that connects the right and left cerebral hemispheres. It is the largest set of commissural fibers, the class of fibers that link matching areas in the two hemispheres. It lies at the bottom of the longitudinal fissure.
notes: Correct. The corpus callosum is the white matter band that joins the hemispheres.
This describes the conus medullaris, the cone-shaped end of the spinal cord near the L1 to L2 disc. It would be the answer for a question about where the cord ends.
This describes the thalamus, the paired gray matter masses of the diencephalon that relay sensory signals to the cortex.
This describes the cerebral cortex, which is gray matter on the surface of the cerebrum. Pick it if the question asked which layer holds most of the cerebrum's neuron cell bodies.
questions.answerText: The white matter band joining the two hemispheres

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: The precentral gyrus lies at the rear of which lobe of the cerebrum?
options: The parietal lobe
The occipital lobe
The temporal lobe
The frontal lobe
questions.why: The precentral gyrus is the ridge just in front of the central sulcus, which makes it the most posterior gyrus of the frontal lobe. It holds the primary motor cortex, which initiates voluntary movement. The name tells you its position: pre means in front of, and central refers to the central sulcus.
notes: The parietal lobe lies just behind the central sulcus, and its front edge is the postcentral gyrus, home of the primary somatosensory cortex. Pick the parietal lobe if the question asked about the postcentral gyrus.
The occipital lobe is at the back of the cerebrum and processes vision. It would be the answer if the question asked where the primary visual cortex is found.
The temporal lobe lies on the lower side of the cerebrum, below the lateral sulcus. Pick it if the question asked where the primary auditory cortex is located.
Correct. The precentral gyrus forms the back edge of the frontal lobe.
questions.answerText: The frontal lobe

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which lobe of the cerebrum sits at the very back and is dedicated to processing vision?
options: The parietal lobe
The temporal lobe
The frontal lobe
The occipital lobe
questions.why: The occipital lobe forms the back of each cerebral hemisphere, beneath the occipital bone, and handles visual processing. The primary visual cortex lies at the calcarine sulcus on its medial surface. Damage to this lobe causes loss of vision even when the eyes themselves are healthy.
notes: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus and handles touch and body sensation. Pick it if the question asked where the postcentral gyrus is found.
The temporal lobe lies on the lower side of the cerebrum and handles hearing and memory. It would be the answer for a question about the primary auditory cortex.
The frontal lobe is at the front of the cerebrum and handles voluntary movement, planning, and speech production. Pick it if the question asked where the primary motor cortex or Broca area sits.
Correct. The occipital lobe is at the back and processes vision.
questions.answerText: The occipital lobe

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which cerebral lobe lies on the lower side of the cerebrum and is associated with hearing and memory?
options: The insula
The parietal lobe
The temporal lobe
The occipital lobe
questions.why: The temporal lobe sits on the lower side of each hemisphere, below the lateral sulcus and beneath the temporal bone. It holds the primary auditory cortex, much of the language comprehension area (Wernicke area), and structures used for memory. Its position near the ear helps students remember its role in hearing.
notes: The insula is buried deep within the lateral sulcus rather than lying on the lower outer surface, and it handles taste and visceral sensation. Pick it if the question asked which lobe cannot be seen from the outside.
The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, above the temporal lobe, and handles touch and spatial orientation. Pick it if the question asked which lobe holds the primary somatosensory cortex.
Correct. The temporal lobe handles hearing and memory.
The occipital lobe is at the back of the cerebrum and processes vision. It would be the answer for a question about the primary visual cortex.
questions.answerText: The temporal lobe

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which cerebral lobe is buried deep within the lateral sulcus rather than lying on the outer surface?
options: The temporal lobe
The insula
The parietal lobe
The frontal lobe
questions.why: Each cerebral hemisphere has five lobes. Four of them lie on the surface, but the fifth, the insula, is hidden deep within the lateral sulcus and covered by the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. The insula is involved in taste, visceral sensation, and emotion.
notes: The temporal lobe forms the lower side of the cerebrum and is visible from outside, below the lateral sulcus. It would be the answer if the question asked which lobe handles hearing.
Correct. The insula is the lobe hidden in the lateral sulcus.
The parietal lobe lies on the surface behind the central sulcus. Pick it if the question asked which lobe handles touch and body sensation.
The frontal lobe forms the front of the cerebrum and is visible on the surface. It would be the answer for a question about the lobe holding the primary motor cortex.
questions.answerText: The insula

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: The basal nuclei (basal ganglia) are deep masses of which type of matter, and within which brain region?
options: Gray matter, deep within the cerebrum
White matter, deep within the cerebrum
White matter, within the brainstem
Gray matter, within the cerebellum
questions.why: The basal nuclei, also called the basal ganglia or cerebral nuclei, are clusters of neuron cell bodies buried within the white matter of the cerebrum, which makes them gray matter. They include the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. They help start and regulate movement and suppress unwanted movement.
notes: Correct. The basal nuclei are gray matter deep in the cerebrum.

The region is right, but the basal nuclei are clusters of cell bodies, which makes them gray matter. The white matter around them is made of myelinated axons, such as the internal capsule, which runs beside the basal nuclei.

This misses on both counts. The brainstem does contain white matter tracts, but the basal nuclei are gray matter and lie in the cerebrum. Pick white matter in the brainstem if the question asked where the descending motor tracts pass through on their way to the cord.

The cerebellum does have deep gray matter nuclei, such as the dentate nucleus, but those are the deep cerebellar nuclei, not the basal nuclei. Pick this if the question asked about nuclei buried in the arbor vitae.
questions.answerText: Gray matter, deep within the cerebrum

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: The longitudinal fissure is best classified as which kind of surface feature?
options: A fissure, the deepest type of groove
A gyrus, a raised fold of cortex
A sulcus, a shallow groove
A ventricle, a fluid-filled chamber
questions.why: The cerebral surface has ridges (gyri), shallow grooves (sulci), and the deepest grooves (fissures), which divide major regions of the brain. The longitudinal fissure is a fissure that separates the right and left cerebral hemispheres. The falx cerebri, a fold of dura mater, dips down into it.
notes: Correct. The longitudinal fissure is one of the deepest grooves.
A gyrus is a raised ridge of cortex, such as the precentral gyrus, not a groove. Pick a gyrus if the question asked about the folds between the grooves.
A sulcus is a shallow groove between gyri, such as the central sulcus. It would be the answer for a groove that separates lobes rather than whole hemispheres.
A ventricle is a fluid-filled chamber inside the brain, not a surface feature. Pick it if the question asked about spaces that hold cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.answerText: A fissure, the deepest type of groove

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Four of the five cerebral lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital) are named for what?
options: The skull bone lying over each one
The cranial nerve passing through each one
The artery that supplies each one
The ventricle each one surrounds
questions.why: The frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes each lie under the cranial bone of the same name, so the bone tells you the lobe. The fifth lobe, the insula, is the exception, because it is hidden deep in the lateral sulcus and no bone lies directly over it. Using the skull as a map is a quick way to locate each lobe on a model.
notes: Correct. Each surface lobe takes the name of the cranial bone above it.

Cranial nerves are numbered in the order they leave the brain, from front to back, and are named for their job or their path. No cerebral lobe is named after a cranial nerve, so this choice mixes up brain naming with nerve naming. Pick cranial nerves for a question about the twelve pairs of nerves attached to the brain.

The lobes are not named for their arteries. The cerebral arteries are named for their position (anterior, middle, and posterior), and each one supplies more than one lobe. For example, the posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe and the underside of the temporal lobe.

The lateral ventricles do extend into several lobes, but the lobes are not named for them. Students sometimes connect the two because the ventricle horns reach into the frontal, occipital, and temporal lobes.
questions.answerText: The skull bone lying over each one

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which deep groove separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum?
options: The central sulcus
The lateral sulcus
The transverse fissure
The longitudinal fissure
questions.why: Fissures are the deepest grooves on the brain and divide major regions. The transverse fissure runs horizontally between the underside of the occipital lobes and the top of the cerebellum, separating the cerebrum from the cerebellum. The tentorium cerebelli, a fold of dura mater, extends into this fissure.
notes: The central sulcus is a groove that separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe, with the precentral gyrus in front and the postcentral gyrus behind. It would be the answer for a question about the boundary between motor and somatosensory cortex.
The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes, and the insula lies hidden in it. Pick it if the question asked where the insula is found.
Correct. The transverse fissure separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum.
The longitudinal fissure runs front to back down the midline and separates the right and left cerebral hemispheres. Pick it if the question asked what divides the two hemispheres.
questions.answerText: The transverse fissure

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: The corpus callosum is the largest example of which class of cerebral white matter fibers?
options: Projection fibers
Ascending tract fibers
Commissural fibers
Association fibers
questions.why: Cerebral white matter is sorted into three classes of fibers by where they begin and end. Commissural fibers connect matching areas of the two hemispheres, and the corpus callosum is the largest commissure. The word commissure means a joining across the midline.
notes: Projection fibers connect the cortex with lower brain regions and the spinal cord, and the internal capsule is the major example. They would be the answer if the question asked about fibers running up and down rather than across.

Ascending tracts carry sensory signals up the spinal cord and brainstem toward the brain. They are not one of the three classes of cerebral fibers, so a student who confuses cord tracts with cerebral fibers picks this.
Correct. The corpus callosum is made of commissural fibers.
Association fibers connect gyri within the same hemisphere, such as the arcuate fasciculus linking Broca and Wernicke areas. Pick this class if the question asked about fibers that stay on one side.
questions.answerText: Commissural fibers

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which cerebral lobe lies just behind the central sulcus and processes touch and other body sensations?
options: The frontal lobe
The occipital lobe
The parietal lobe
The temporal lobe
questions.why: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, under the parietal bone. Its front edge is the postcentral gyrus, which holds the primary somatosensory cortex, the area that receives conscious touch, pressure, and body position. The parietal lobe also contributes to spatial orientation.
notes: The frontal lobe lies in front of the central sulcus, not behind it, and holds the primary motor cortex. Pick it if the question asked which lobe initiates voluntary movement.
The occipital lobe is at the back of the cerebrum and processes vision. It would be the answer if the question asked where the primary visual cortex sits.
Correct. The parietal lobe processes body sensation.
The temporal lobe is on the lower side of the cerebrum, below the lateral sulcus, and handles hearing and memory. Pick it for a question about the primary auditory cortex.
questions.answerText: The parietal lobe

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares gray matter and white matter in the cerebrum?
options: Gray matter is cell bodies on the outside; white matter is myelinated axons inside
Gray matter and white matter are both cell bodies, differing only in color
Gray matter is cell bodies on the inside; white matter is myelinated axons outside
Gray matter is myelinated axons on the outside; white matter is cell bodies inside
questions.why: Gray matter is made of neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated fibers, while white matter is bundles of myelinated axons whose fatty myelin gives them a pale color. In the cerebrum the gray matter forms the outer cortex and the white matter lies beneath it, with islands of deep gray matter (the basal nuclei) buried inside. The spinal cord has the reverse arrangement.
notes: Correct. In the cerebrum, gray matter is the outer cortex of cell bodies and white matter is the inner myelinated axons.
White matter is axons, not cell bodies, and the color difference comes from myelin. A student who thinks the two differ only in shade picks this.
This is the layout of the spinal cord, where gray matter forms the inner butterfly and white matter lies outside. Pick it if the question asked about a cross-section of the cord.
This swaps the makeup of the two tissues. Myelin is what makes white matter white, so myelinated axons cannot be gray matter.
questions.answerText: Gray matter is cell bodies on the outside; white matter is myelinated axons inside

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Moving down the central axis of the brain from the cerebrum to the spinal cord, which sequence of regions is correct?
options: Cerebrum, brainstem, diencephalon, spinal cord
Cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem, spinal cord
Cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem, spinal cord
Cerebellum, diencephalon, brainstem, spinal cord
questions.why: The cerebrum sits on top, and the diencephalon lies deep beneath it in the center of the brain. Below the diencephalon, the brainstem runs downward as the midbrain, pons, and medulla, and the medulla continues as the spinal cord. The cerebellum is off this central axis, attached to the back of the brainstem.
notes: This places the brainstem above the diencephalon. The diencephalon connects the cerebrum to the brainstem, so it comes before the brainstem when moving down.
Correct. Cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem, then spinal cord.

The cerebellum is attached to the back of the brainstem, not stacked between the cerebrum and brainstem. A student who orders the regions by how they look from the side, rather than along the central axis, picks this.
This starts at the cerebellum, which sits behind the brainstem rather than on top of the central axis. Pick the cerebellum if the question asked which region lies behind the brainstem.
questions.answerText: Cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem, spinal cord

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Moving inward from the surface of a cerebral hemisphere, which sequence of tissues is correct?
options: Cerebral cortex, cerebral white matter, basal nuclei
Basal nuclei, cerebral white matter, cerebral cortex
Cerebral cortex, basal nuclei, cerebral white matter
Cerebral white matter, cerebral cortex, basal nuclei
questions.why: The cerebral cortex is the thin layer of gray matter on the surface of the cerebrum. Beneath it lies the cerebral white matter, the myelinated axons that connect cortical areas with each other and with lower regions. The basal nuclei are masses of gray matter buried deep within that white matter, so they are the deepest of the three.
notes: Correct. Cortex, then white matter, then the basal nuclei.
This is the correct sequence read from deep to superficial. Pick it only if the question asked for the order moving outward from the center.
The basal nuclei are buried within the white matter, not sandwiched between the cortex and the white matter. Pick this only if the basal nuclei lay directly under the cortex, which they do not.
White matter is not on the surface of the cerebrum; it lies beneath the cortex. This order matches the spinal cord, where white matter is outside, which is a common mix-up.
questions.answerText: Cerebral cortex, cerebral white matter, basal nuclei

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?
options: The central sulcus
The lateral sulcus
The parieto-occipital sulcus
The longitudinal fissure
questions.why: The central sulcus runs across the top of each hemisphere and separates the frontal lobe in front from the parietal lobe behind. The precentral gyrus, with the primary motor cortex, lies just in front of it, and the postcentral gyrus, with the primary somatosensory cortex, lies just behind it. That makes it a key landmark between movement and sensation areas.
notes: Correct. The central sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes.
The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes, and the insula lies hidden within it. Pick it if the question asked what sets off the temporal lobe.
The parieto-occipital sulcus separates the parietal lobe from the occipital lobe. It would be the answer if the question asked about the boundary in front of the occipital lobe.
The longitudinal fissure separates the right and left cerebral hemispheres, not two lobes of the same hemisphere. Pick it if the question asked what divides the cerebrum into halves.
questions.answerText: The central sulcus

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Four lobes of each cerebral hemisphere are named for the cranial bones above them. Which fifth lobe lies hidden deep within the lateral sulcus?
options: The cingulate gyrus
The insula
The hippocampus
The temporal lobe
questions.why: The frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes each take their name from the skull bone that covers them. The insula is the fifth lobe, and it is folded out of sight deep in the lateral sulcus, so you only see it when the temporal lobe is pulled away. The insula handles taste, visceral sensation, and emotion.
notes: The cingulate gyrus is a limbic gyrus that arches above the corpus callosum on the medial surface of each hemisphere. It would be the answer for a question about the limbic gyrus involved in expressing emotion.
Correct. The insula is the hidden fifth lobe, buried deep in the lateral sulcus.
The hippocampus is a limbic structure tucked into the medial temporal lobe, not a lobe of its own. Pick it if the question asks which structure is essential for forming new long-term memories.

The temporal lobe forms the lower border of the lateral sulcus, but it is one of the four bone-named lobes and sits on the surface. Choose it for a question about hearing, language comprehension, or memory.
questions.answerText: The insula

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which cerebral lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
options: The temporal lobe
The frontal lobe
The parietal lobe
The occipital lobe
questions.why: The occipital lobe forms the back of each cerebral hemisphere, and its primary visual cortex sits along the calcarine sulcus. This area receives the raw visual signals relayed from the eyes, and the visual association area around it turns those signals into recognized faces and objects. Damage here causes loss of vision even when the eyes themselves are healthy.
notes: The temporal lobe on the lower side of the cerebrum handles hearing, language comprehension, and memory. It would be the answer for the primary auditory cortex.

The frontal lobe at the front of the cerebrum handles voluntary movement, speech production at Broca's area, judgment, and personality. Pick it for a question about the primary motor cortex or the prefrontal cortex.
The parietal lobe sits behind the central sulcus and receives touch, pressure, and body position at the postcentral gyrus. Choose it for a question about the primary somatosensory cortex.
Correct. The primary visual cortex lies in the occipital lobe at the back of the cerebrum.
questions.answerText: The occipital lobe

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: The primary motor cortex lies along the precentral gyrus. Which cerebral lobe is this gyrus part of?
options: The frontal lobe
The occipital lobe
The temporal lobe
The parietal lobe
questions.why: The precentral gyrus is the ridge just in front of the central sulcus, and everything in front of that sulcus belongs to the frontal lobe. The primary motor cortex on this gyrus sends the commands that start voluntary movement. The name helps you place it, since pre means before, so the precentral gyrus sits before (anterior to) the central sulcus.
notes: Correct. The precentral gyrus is the most posterior ridge of the frontal lobe and holds the primary motor cortex.
The occipital lobe at the back of the cerebrum processes vision. It would be the answer for a question about the primary visual cortex.
The temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus and handles hearing, language comprehension, and memory. Choose it for a question about the primary auditory cortex.
The parietal lobe begins just behind the central sulcus, and its first ridge is the postcentral gyrus. Pick it if the question asks where the primary somatosensory cortex lies.
questions.answerText: The frontal lobe

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: What are the raised ridges of the folded cerebral cortex called?
options: Sulci
Folia
Gyri
Fissures
questions.why: The cerebral cortex is folded so that more of it fits inside the skull. Each raised ridge of the fold is a gyrus (plural gyri), and the grooves between them are sulci. Named gyri, such as the precentral and postcentral gyri, mark the locations of specific functional areas.
notes: Sulci are the shallow grooves that run between the gyri, the low points of the folds rather than the ridges. Pick sulci if the question asks for the grooves, as in the central sulcus.
Folia are the fine, leaf-like folds on the surface of the cerebellum, not the cerebrum. Choose folia if the question asks about the surface folds of the cerebellum.
Correct. The raised ridges of the cerebral cortex are gyri.
Fissures are the deepest grooves, which divide major regions of the brain, such as the longitudinal fissure between the hemispheres. They would be the answer for a question about the deepest grooves.
questions.answerText: Gyri

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which deep groove separates the left and right cerebral hemispheres?
options: The transverse fissure
The longitudinal fissure
The central sulcus
The lateral sulcus
questions.why: The longitudinal fissure runs front to back along the midline and splits the cerebrum into right and left hemispheres. A fold of dura called the falx cerebri dips down into it. At the bottom of the fissure, the corpus callosum bridges the two hemispheres so they can still share information.
notes: The transverse fissure is the horizontal groove that separates the cerebrum above from the cerebellum below. It would be the answer for a question about the boundary between those two regions.
