Correct. The myelencephalon becomes the medulla, and its cavity is the lower fourth ventricle, which continues into the central canal.
The metencephalon becomes the pons and cerebellum, and its cavity is the upper part of the fourth ventricle. The medulla comes from the vesicle behind it.
questions.answerText: Myelencephalon, the lower part of the fourth ventricle

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: On the side of a brain specimen, you find the deepest groove first. Then you find a groove that runs without a break from the top of the hemisphere almost down to that deep groove. Which gyrus lies just behind this second groove, and which lobe is it in?
options: The postcentral gyrus, in the frontal lobe
The insula, in the lateral sulcus
The precentral gyrus, in the frontal lobe
The postcentral gyrus, in the parietal lobe
questions.why: The deepest groove on the side is the lateral sulcus. The central sulcus usually runs without a break from the top of the hemisphere almost down to it, with a long gyrus on each side. Post means after, so the postcentral gyrus is just behind the central sulcus, at the front of the parietal lobe.
notes: The gyrus name is right, but the central sulcus separates the frontal lobe in front from the parietal lobe behind. The postcentral gyrus is in the parietal lobe.
The insula is the fifth lobe, hidden deep in the lateral sulcus. It is not a gyrus behind the central sulcus on the surface.
The precentral gyrus is the one just in front of the central sulcus, at the back of the frontal lobe. The question asks for the gyrus behind it.
Correct. The unbroken groove is the central sulcus, and the gyrus just behind it is the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe.
questions.answerText: The postcentral gyrus, in the parietal lobe

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: To see the insula on a brain specimen, which lobe do you gently pull away, and from which lobes?
options: The frontal lobe, away from the parietal lobe
The temporal lobe, away from frontal and parietal
One hemisphere, away from the other
The occipital lobe, away from the cerebellum
questions.why: The insula is the fifth lobe, hidden deep inside the lateral sulcus. The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above, and those three lobes cover the insula. Gently pulling the temporal lobe away from the frontal and parietal lobes opens the sulcus so you can look in.
notes: The frontal and parietal lobes are separated by the central sulcus, which does not hide a lobe. The insula is under the lateral sulcus.
Correct. The insula lies deep in the lateral sulcus, so you pull the temporal lobe down away from the frontal and parietal lobes above.
Pulling the hemispheres apart opens the longitudinal fissure, which shows the corpus callosum at its floor. The insula is on the side of each hemisphere.
The occipital lobe and cerebellum are separated by the transverse fissure at the back of the brain. Opening that fissure does not reach the insula.
questions.answerText: The temporal lobe, away from frontal and parietal

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: On a horizontal section, a white band bent into a V points toward the midline. The caudate nucleus and thalamus lie on its inner side, and a lens-shaped gray mass lies on its outer side. What is the band, and which class of fibers runs in it?
options: The internal capsule, made of projection fibers
The internal capsule, made of association fibers
The corpus callosum, made of commissural fibers
The arcuate fasciculus, made of projection fibers
questions.why: Projection fibers connect the cortex with the lower brain and spinal cord. Below the cortex they fan out as the corona radiata, then gather into one compact band, the internal capsule. On a horizontal section it is a V-shaped white band with the caudate nucleus and thalamus on its medial side and the lentiform nucleus on its lateral side.
notes: Correct. The V-shaped band between the caudate and thalamus inside and the lentiform nucleus outside is the internal capsule, a band of projection fibers.
The band is right, but association fibers stay within one hemisphere, linking gyri and lobes. The internal capsule carries projection fibers to and from the brainstem and cord.

The corpus callosum is the largest commissural bundle, the arched band above the diencephalon on a midsagittal section. It crosses the midline instead of running between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus.
The arcuate fasciculus is a long association tract that links Broca's area and Wernicke's area. It is not the V-shaped band beside the thalamus.
questions.answerText: The internal capsule, made of projection fibers

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: On a coronal section, a lens-shaped gray mass lies lateral to the internal capsule, with a darker outer part and a paler inner part. Which part touches the internal capsule, and what is it called?
options: The darker outer part, the putamen
The darker outer part, the globus pallidus
The paler inner part, the globus pallidus
The paler inner part, the caudate nucleus
questions.why: The lens-shaped mass lateral to the internal capsule is the lentiform nucleus, made of the putamen and the globus pallidus. The putamen is the outer, darker part. The globus pallidus is the inner, paler part, and it sits between the putamen and the internal capsule. Pallidus means pale.
notes: The putamen is the darker part, but it is the outer, lateral part of the lentiform nucleus. The globus pallidus lies between it and the internal capsule.
The globus pallidus is the paler part, not the darker one, and it is the inner part. The darker outer part is the putamen.
Correct. The globus pallidus is the paler, medial part of the lentiform nucleus, lying between the putamen and the internal capsule.
The caudate nucleus is not part of the lentiform nucleus. It lies on the medial side of the internal capsule, bulging into the lateral ventricle.
questions.answerText: The paler inner part, the globus pallidus

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: On a coronal section, a gray mass bulges into the lateral wall of the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle. Which nucleus is this, and which nucleus does it pair with to form the striatum?
options: The head of the caudate nucleus, paired with the globus pallidus
The thalamus, paired with the hypothalamus
The putamen, paired with the globus pallidus
The head of the caudate nucleus, paired with the putamen
questions.why: The caudate nucleus is long and curved, and its large head bulges into the lateral wall of the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle. The caudate nucleus and the putamen together are called the striatum. Bands of gray matter cross the internal capsule between them and give the area its striped look.
notes: The nucleus is right, but the globus pallidus pairs with the putamen to form the lentiform nucleus. The striatum is the caudate with the putamen.
The thalamus and hypothalamus are parts of the diencephalon around the third ventricle. The mass in the wall of the anterior horn is the caudate head.
The putamen and globus pallidus form the lentiform nucleus, which lies lateral to the internal capsule. Neither bulges into the lateral ventricle.
Correct. The head of the caudate bulges into the anterior horn, and the caudate with the putamen forms the striatum.
questions.answerText: The head of the caudate nucleus, paired with the putamen

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: Which sequence traces the limbic ring from above the corpus callosum down into the temporal lobe?
options: Cingulate gyrus, uncus, parahippocampal gyrus
Parahippocampal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, uncus
Uncus, cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus
Cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, uncus
questions.why: The cingulate gyrus arches just above the corpus callosum on the medial surface. It curves around the back of the corpus callosum and continues down into the temporal lobe as the parahippocampal gyrus. The front end of the parahippocampal gyrus hooks back on itself to form the uncus, completing the C-shaped ring.
notes: The uncus is the hooked front end of the parahippocampal gyrus, so it comes last, at the end of that gyrus.
The parahippocampal gyrus is in the temporal lobe, so it comes after the cingulate gyrus, not before it.
The uncus is in the temporal lobe at the end of the ring, not above the corpus callosum where the ring starts.
Correct. The cingulate gyrus curves behind the corpus callosum into the parahippocampal gyrus, whose front end hooks back as the uncus.
questions.answerText: Cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, uncus

questions.topic: Cerebrum: lobes, cortex areas and deep structures
questions.q: In a dissection, you follow the fornix backward from the mammillary bodies, under the corpus callosum and along the lower edge of the septum pellucidum. Which structure will it lead you to, and where does that structure sit?
options: The cingulate gyrus, above the corpus callosum
The amygdala, deep to the uncus in the temporal lobe
The hippocampus, in the floor of the inferior horn
The hippocampus, in the roof of the third ventricle
questions.why: The fornix is an arching band of white matter that carries the output of the hippocampus. It runs forward under the corpus callosum along the lower edge of the septum pellucidum and ends at the mammillary bodies. Traced backward, it leads to the hippocampus, a curved ridge rolled into the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle in the medial temporal lobe.
notes: The cingulate gyrus arches above the corpus callosum on the medial surface. The fornix runs below the corpus callosum and leads to the hippocampus.
The amygdala is an almond-shaped nucleus in front of the hippocampus, deep to the uncus. The fornix carries the output of the hippocampus, not the amygdala.
Correct. The fornix carries hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies, so following it back leads to the hippocampus in the floor of the inferior horn.

The structure is right, but the hippocampus sits in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, in the temporal lobe. The back of the roof of the third ventricle is formed by the epithalamus.
questions.answerText: The hippocampus, in the floor of the inferior horn

questions.q: Which structure of the diencephalon serves as the relay station that sorts incoming sensory information and forwards it to the cortex?
options: The hypothalamus
The thalamus
The epithalamus
The pineal gland
questions.why: The thalamus is a pair of oval gray matter masses that makes up about 80 percent of the diencephalon. Its nuclei receive incoming sensory signals and relay each type on to the correct area of the cerebral cortex. That is why it is called the main sensory relay station of the brain.
notes: The hypothalamus sits below the thalamus and is the master control center for homeostasis, regulating body temperature, hunger, thirst, and the pituitary gland. Pick it for a question about homeostasis rather than sensory relay.
Correct. The thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex.
The epithalamus is the small posterior part of the diencephalon. It would be the answer if the question asked which part of the diencephalon contains the pineal gland.
The pineal gland is the endocrine gland of the epithalamus that secretes melatonin. Pick it if the question asked which brain structure produces melatonin.
questions.answerText: The thalamus

questions.q: Which part of the diencephalon contains the pineal gland?
options: The epithalamus
The third ventricle
The hypothalamus
The thalamus
questions.why: The diencephalon has three parts: the thalamus, the hypothalamus, and the epithalamus. The epithalamus is the small posterior part, and it contains the pineal gland, an endocrine gland that secretes melatonin. The prefix epi means upon, a reminder that it sits on the back of the thalamus.
notes: Correct. The pineal gland is part of the epithalamus.
The third ventricle is the fluid-filled cavity enclosed by the diencephalon, not one of its tissue parts. Pick it if the question asked which ventricle lies in the diencephalon.
The hypothalamus lies below the thalamus and controls homeostasis and the pituitary gland. It would be the answer if the question asked which part of the diencephalon connects to the pituitary.
The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon and relays sensory information to the cortex. Pick it if the question asked which structure is the main sensory relay station.
questions.answerText: The epithalamus

questions.q: What are the three regions of the brainstem?
options: The thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus
The cerebrum, diencephalon, and cerebellum
The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata
The frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes
questions.why: The brainstem is the stalk that connects the cerebrum, diencephalon, and cerebellum to the spinal cord. From top to bottom it is made of the midbrain, the pons, and the medulla oblongata. Every ascending and descending tract passes through it, and it holds the nuclei of most cranial nerves.
notes: These are the three parts of the diencephalon, the region just above the brainstem. They would be the answer if the question asked about the parts of the diencephalon.
These are three of the four major brain regions, each separate from the brainstem. Pick them if the question asked which regions sit above or behind the brainstem.
Correct. The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata make up the brainstem.
These are lobes of the cerebrum, the outer part of the brain. Pick a list of lobes if the question asked about subdivisions of a cerebral hemisphere.
questions.answerText: The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata

questions.q: Which region of the brainstem is the most inferior, joining the spinal cord?
options: The diencephalon
The pons
The medulla oblongata
The midbrain
questions.why: The medulla oblongata is the lowest region of the brainstem and merges with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. It contains the pyramids and the vital centers that control heart rate, breathing rhythm, and blood vessel diameter. Because of those centers, injury to the medulla is quickly life-threatening.
notes: The diencephalon sits above the brainstem and is a separate major brain region. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the thalamus and hypothalamus.
The pons is the rounded middle region of the brainstem, a bridge to the cerebellum. It would be the answer if the question asked which region lies between the midbrain and the medulla.
Correct. The medulla oblongata is the lowest brainstem region and is continuous with the cord.
The midbrain is the most superior region of the brainstem, surrounding the cerebral aqueduct. Pick it if the question asked which brainstem region is highest or which one holds the colliculi.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: Which brain structure sits behind the brainstem and coordinates movement, posture, and balance?
options: The cerebellum
The thalamus
The pons
The cerebrum
questions.why: The cerebellum is the second largest part of the brain. It sits in the posterior cranial fossa, behind the brainstem and below the occipital lobes, and is attached to the brainstem by three pairs of cerebellar peduncles. It coordinates movement, posture, and balance so that motion is smooth and accurate.
notes: Correct. The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem and coordinates movement.
The thalamus is in the diencephalon, deep in the center of the brain. Pick it if the question asked which structure relays sensory information to the cortex.

The pons is part of the brainstem itself, in front of the cerebellum, and it relays motor information to the cerebellum through the middle cerebellar peduncles. Pick it for a question about the bridge between the cerebellum and the rest of the brainstem.
The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and sits above the other regions. It would be the answer if the question asked which region initiates voluntary movement and conscious thought.
questions.answerText: The cerebellum

questions.q: The thalamus and hypothalamus are both structures of which major brain region?
options: The diencephalon
The cerebrum
The cerebellum
The brainstem
questions.why: The diencephalon is the deep central region between the cerebrum and the brainstem. It has three parts: the thalamus, the hypothalamus, and the epithalamus, and it surrounds the third ventricle. The thalamus is its largest part, and the hypothalamus lies just below the thalamus.
notes: Correct. The thalamus and hypothalamus are parts of the diencephalon.
The cerebrum is the large outer region with the cortex, cerebral white matter, and basal nuclei. Pick it if the question asked which region contains the lobes.
The cerebellum is a separate region behind the brainstem that coordinates movement. Pick it if the question asked which region contains the vermis and arbor vitae.
The brainstem is made of the midbrain, pons, and medulla, below the diencephalon. It would be the answer if the question asked which region holds the vital centers of the medulla.
questions.answerText: The diencephalon

questions.q: Where is the midbrain located within the brainstem, relative to the pons and medulla?
options: It is the most superior part
It is the lowest part, joining the cord
It lies behind the pons and medulla
It is the middle, rounded part
questions.why: The midbrain, also called the mesencephalon, is the short, most superior region of the brainstem, just below the diencephalon. It surrounds the cerebral aqueduct and contains the colliculi, the cerebral peduncles, and the substantia nigra. Below it come the pons and then the medulla oblongata.
notes: Correct. The midbrain is the highest region of the brainstem.
The lowest region, continuous with the spinal cord, is the medulla oblongata. This position would be the answer if the question asked about the medulla.
The structure lying behind the brainstem is the cerebellum, which is not part of the brainstem at all. Pick this position for a question about the cerebellum.
The middle, rounded region of the brainstem is the pons, whose name means bridge. Pick this position if the question asked where the pons sits.
questions.answerText: It is the most superior part

questions.q: The pons is the middle region of the brainstem. Which two regions sit immediately above and below it?
options: The medulla above and the midbrain below
The cerebrum above and the spinal cord below
The midbrain above and the medulla below
The diencephalon above and the cerebellum below
questions.why: From top to bottom, the brainstem runs midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata. The pons sits between the midbrain above and the medulla below, and it also forms a bridge to the cerebellum behind it. Its pontine nuclei relay motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum.
notes: This reverses the brainstem order. The midbrain is the highest brainstem region and the medulla is the lowest, so a student who flips the sequence picks this.

The cerebrum and spinal cord are at the far ends of the central axis, separated from the pons by the diencephalon and midbrain above and the medulla below. This would only fit a question about the ends of the whole brain-to-cord axis.
Correct. The midbrain lies above the pons and the medulla lies below it.

The diencephalon sits above the midbrain, not directly on the pons, and the cerebellum lies behind the pons rather than below it. This pairing mixes up neighboring regions that are not part of the brainstem.
questions.answerText: The midbrain above and the medulla below

questions.q: Which brain region lies deep between the cerebrum and the brainstem and contains the main sensory relay station and the homeostasis control center?
options: The cerebellum
The corpus callosum
The diencephalon
The medulla oblongata
questions.why: The diencephalon is the deep central region that links the cerebral hemispheres to the brainstem. It contains the thalamus, which relays sensory signals to the cortex, the hypothalamus, which controls homeostasis, and the epithalamus with the pineal gland. It surrounds the third ventricle.
notes: The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem, not between the cerebrum and brainstem, and coordinates movement. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the arbor vitae and vermis.

The corpus callosum is a band of white matter connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, not a brain region with relay or control centers. Pick it if the question asked what joins the right and left hemispheres.
Correct. The diencephalon holds the thalamus and hypothalamus.

The medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem and holds the vital cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centers. It would be the answer for a question about the centers that control heartbeat and breathing.
questions.answerText: The diencephalon

questions.q: Which small endocrine gland is housed within the epithalamus?
options: The hypothalamus
The pineal gland
The thalamus
The pituitary gland
questions.why: The epithalamus is the small posterior part of the diencephalon, and its best-known structure is the pineal gland. The pineal gland is an endocrine gland that secretes melatonin, which helps set sleep-wake rhythms. It sits in the midline at the back of the third ventricle.
notes: The hypothalamus is a separate part of the diencephalon below the thalamus and is the homeostasis control center. Pick it for a question about the link between the nervous and endocrine systems.
Correct. The pineal gland is the endocrine gland of the epithalamus.
The thalamus is the large paired relay station of the diencephalon, not a gland. Pick it if the question asked which structure forms about 80 percent of the diencephalon.

The pituitary gland hangs below the hypothalamus, attached by a stalk, rather than sitting in the epithalamus. It would be the answer if the question asked which endocrine gland the hypothalamus controls directly.
questions.answerText: The pineal gland

questions.q: Which part of the diencephalon links the nervous system with the endocrine system and is the main control center for homeostasis?
options: The thalamus
The epithalamus
The pineal gland
The hypothalamus
questions.why: The hypothalamus lies below the thalamus and is the master control center for homeostasis. It controls the autonomic nervous system, regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, and sleep-wake rhythms, and directs endocrine function through the pituitary gland. That pituitary connection is why it is called the link between the nervous and endocrine systems.
notes: The thalamus is the sensory relay station that forwards signals to the cortex. Pick it if the question asked which structure sorts incoming sensory information.
The epithalamus is the small posterior part of the diencephalon containing the pineal gland. It would be the answer if the question asked which part of the diencephalon houses the pineal gland.
The pineal gland is an endocrine gland that secretes melatonin, but it does not control the pituitary or overall homeostasis. Pick it for a question about the source of melatonin.
Correct. The hypothalamus is the homeostasis center and the nervous-endocrine link.
questions.answerText: The hypothalamus

questions.q: Which list orders the three regions of the brainstem from superior to inferior?
options: Midbrain, medulla oblongata, pons
Medulla oblongata, pons, midbrain
Midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata
Pons, midbrain, medulla oblongata
questions.why: The brainstem runs from the midbrain at the top, just below the diencephalon, through the rounded pons in the middle, to the medulla oblongata at the bottom, which merges with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. The cranial nerve nuclei follow the same order, with III and IV in the midbrain, V through VIII in the pons, and IX, X, and XII in the medulla.
notes: This swaps the pons and medulla. The medulla is the lowest region and is continuous with the spinal cord, so it cannot sit above the pons.
This is the right sequence read in the wrong direction, from inferior to superior. Pick it only if the question asked for the order starting at the spinal cord.
Correct. Midbrain, pons, then medulla oblongata.
This puts the pons above the midbrain. The midbrain is the highest region, directly below the diencephalon, so the pons belongs second.
questions.answerText: Midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata

questions.q: The third ventricle is the midline cavity enclosed by which brain region?
options: The cerebellum
The midbrain
The cerebrum
The diencephalon
questions.why: The diencephalon surrounds the third ventricle. The right and left thalami form its upper side walls, and the hypothalamus forms its floor and lower walls, with the massa intermedia crossing the ventricle in most brains. In front the third ventricle opens into each lateral ventricle through an interventricular foramen, and behind it drains into the cerebral aqueduct.
notes: The cerebellum lies over the roof of the fourth ventricle, not around the third. Pick it if the question asked which region lies behind the fourth ventricle.
The midbrain surrounds the cerebral aqueduct, the narrow channel that carries CSF from the third to the fourth ventricle. It would be the answer for a question about the aqueduct.
The cerebrum encloses the lateral ventricles, one in each hemisphere. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the lateral ventricles.
Correct. The diencephalon encloses the third ventricle.
questions.answerText: The diencephalon

questions.q: Match each condition to the structure it involves: Parkinson disease, hydrocephalus, and spinal cord injury. Which set is correct?
options: Parkinson disease, ventricles; hydrocephalus, substantia nigra; spinal cord injury, cord tracts
Parkinson disease, substantia nigra; hydrocephalus, ventricles; spinal cord injury, cord tracts
Parkinson disease, cord tracts; hydrocephalus, ventricles; spinal cord injury, substantia nigra
Parkinson disease, substantia nigra; hydrocephalus, cord tracts; spinal cord injury, ventricles
questions.why: Parkinson disease comes from loss of the substantia nigra, a darkly pigmented nucleus in the midbrain that works with the basal nuclei to regulate movement. Hydrocephalus is a buildup of cerebrospinal fluid that enlarges the ventricles. A spinal cord injury interrupts the ascending and descending tracts, so function is lost below the injury.
notes: This swaps Parkinson disease and hydrocephalus. The ventricles hold CSF and enlarge in hydrocephalus, while Parkinson disease involves a movement-regulating nucleus.
Correct. Substantia nigra, ventricles, and cord tracts, in that order.
This swaps Parkinson disease and spinal cord injury. The substantia nigra is in the midbrain, not the cord, and loss of cord tracts is the injury itself.
This swaps hydrocephalus and spinal cord injury. Hydrocephalus is a fluid problem in the ventricles, and spinal cord injury damages tracts, not ventricles.
questions.answerText: Parkinson disease, substantia nigra; hydrocephalus, ventricles; spinal cord injury, cord tracts

questions.q: Which region of the brainstem surrounds the cerebral aqueduct?
options: The pons
The midbrain
The medulla oblongata
The diencephalon
questions.why: The midbrain, or mesencephalon, is the short upper region of the brainstem, and the cerebral aqueduct runs through its center. The aqueduct carries CSF from the third ventricle down to the fourth. The roof of the midbrain behind the aqueduct is the tectum, with its four colliculi.
notes: The pons lies in front of the fourth ventricle, below the aqueduct. Pick it if the question asked which brainstem region lies in front of the fourth ventricle.
Correct. The cerebral aqueduct runs through the midbrain.

The medulla oblongata is the lowest brainstem region, with the lower fourth ventricle behind it and the central canal continuing below. It would be the answer for the region continuous with the spinal cord.
The diencephalon surrounds the third ventricle, above the midbrain, and it is not part of the brainstem. Pick it if the question asked which region encloses the third ventricle.
questions.answerText: The midbrain

questions.q: The massa intermedia (interthalamic adhesion) is a bridge that joins which two structures?
options: The right and left cerebellar hemispheres
The third and fourth ventricles
The right and left thalami
The right and left cerebral hemispheres
questions.why: The thalami are paired oval masses of gray matter that form the side walls of the third ventricle. In most brains they touch across the middle of the ventricle at a small bridge called the massa intermedia, or interthalamic adhesion. Inter means between, so the name says it lies between the two thalami.
notes: The right and left cerebellar hemispheres are joined by the vermis, the narrow midline band of the cerebellum. It would be the answer for a question about the cerebellum's midline.
The third and fourth ventricles are connected by the cerebral aqueduct, a channel through the midbrain. Pick the aqueduct if the question asked how CSF passes between those ventricles.
Correct. The massa intermedia joins the two thalami.
The right and left cerebral hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum, a large band of commissural fibers. Pick that structure if the question asked what connects the hemispheres.
questions.answerText: The right and left thalami

questions.q: Which three structures make up the diencephalon?
options: The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata
The thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus
The cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem
The caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus
questions.why: The diencephalon is the deep brain region that sits between the cerebrum and the brainstem and surrounds the third ventricle. It has three parts: the thalamus, the large sensory relay that makes up about 80 percent of it, the hypothalamus below it, which is the control center for homeostasis, and the small epithalamus at the back, which holds the pineal gland.
notes: These three regions make up the brainstem, which lies below the diencephalon and connects it to the spinal cord. Pick them if the question asks which structures form the brainstem.
Correct. The thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus together form the diencephalon around the third ventricle.
These are three of the four major parts of the brain, and the diencephalon is the fourth. Choose this set if the question asks for the major brain regions other than the diencephalon.
These are basal ganglia, deep gray matter masses buried in the cerebral white matter that help regulate movement. They would be the answer for a question about the core basal ganglia components.
questions.answerText: The thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus

questions.q: Which part of the diencephalon is the main sensory relay station to the cerebral cortex?
options: The thalamus
The substantia nigra
The hypothalamus
The epithalamus
questions.why: The thalamus is a pair of oval gray matter masses that makes up about 80 percent of the diencephalon. Nearly all sensory signals heading for the cortex stop at a thalamic nucleus first, where they are sorted and passed on to the correct cortical area. That is why the thalamus is called the gateway or relay station to the cortex.
notes: Correct. The thalamus relays sensory input to the cerebral cortex.
The substantia nigra is a darkly pigmented nucleus of the midbrain, not the diencephalon, and it helps regulate movement with the basal ganglia. Choose it for a question about Parkinson disease.

The hypothalamus lies below the thalamus and is the master control center for homeostasis, including body temperature, hunger, thirst, and the autonomic nervous system. Pick it for a question about homeostatic control.
The epithalamus is the small posterior part of the diencephalon, and it holds the pineal gland. It would be the answer for a question about where melatonin is made.
questions.answerText: The thalamus

questions.q: Which endocrine gland of the epithalamus secretes melatonin?
options: The pineal gland
The pituitary gland
The hypothalamus
The habenular nuclei
questions.why: The epithalamus is the small posterior roof of the diencephalon, and its endocrine gland is the pineal gland. The pineal gland secretes melatonin, a hormone tied to the sleep and wake cycle. It is a small midline structure, so it is easy to find on a sagittal section of the brain just above the midbrain.
notes: Correct. The pineal gland is the endocrine gland of the epithalamus and secretes melatonin.

The pituitary gland hangs below the hypothalamus on a stalk and sits in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, not in the epithalamus. Pick it for a question about the gland controlled by the hypothalamus.

The hypothalamus is a separate part of the diencephalon below the thalamus that controls homeostasis and the pituitary. It would be the answer for a question about the control center for body temperature or thirst.

The habenular nuclei are also part of the epithalamus, but they are clusters of neurons, not a gland, and they do not secrete melatonin. Choose them if the question asks about the other named structure of the epithalamus.
questions.answerText: The pineal gland

questions.q: What is the branching, tree-like pattern of white matter inside the cerebellum called?
options: The internal capsule
The folia
The corpus callosum
The arbor vitae
questions.why: When the cerebellum is cut in a sagittal section, its inner white matter branches out like the limbs of a tree under the outer gray cortex. This pattern is called the arbor vitae, which means tree of life. It carries signals into and out of the cerebellar cortex.
notes: The internal capsule is a band of projection fibers in the cerebrum that carries traffic between the cortex and the brainstem and spinal cord. It would be the answer for the major projection pathway beside the basal ganglia.
The folia are the fine, leaf-like folds on the outer surface of the cerebellum, made of cerebellar cortex. Choose them if the question asks about the surface folds rather than the inner white matter.
The corpus callosum is the large band of commissural white matter joining the two cerebral hemispheres. Pick it for a question about the tract that connects the left and right cerebrum.
Correct. The arbor vitae is the tree-like white matter inside the cerebellum.
questions.answerText: The arbor vitae

questions.q: A patient can move every limb but cannot coordinate movement, keep posture, or balance well. Which brain region is most likely affected?
options: The thalamus
The cerebellum
The hypothalamus
The cerebrum
questions.why: The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem in the posterior cranial fossa and coordinates movement, posture, and balance. It compares the movement that was commanded with what the body is actually doing and smooths out the difference. When it is damaged, a person can still move, but movements become clumsy and balance is poor.
notes: The thalamus is the main sensory relay of the diencephalon. It would be the answer for a question about sensory signals being sorted and passed on to the cortex.
Correct. The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture, and balance.
The hypothalamus controls homeostasis, such as body temperature, hunger, and thirst. Choose it for a problem with temperature regulation, not coordination.
The cerebrum, through the primary motor cortex, starts voluntary movement. Damage there causes weakness or paralysis, so pick it if the patient could not move a limb at all.
questions.answerText: The cerebellum

questions.q: An imaging study finds a lesion in the adult structure that develops from the mesencephalon. Which region is this?
options: The midbrain
The cerebrum
The pons
The medulla oblongata
questions.why: The mesencephalon is the one primary brain vesicle that does not divide again, and it matures into the midbrain and the cerebral aqueduct running through it. The midbrain is the most superior region of the brainstem. Its name and the vesicle's name match, since mesencephalon means middle brain.
notes: Correct. The mesencephalon matures into the midbrain.
The cerebrum develops from the telencephalon, the most anterior secondary vesicle. Pick it if the lesion were in a structure from the telencephalon.
The pons develops from the metencephalon, along with the cerebellum. It would be the answer for a lesion in a metencephalon structure.
The medulla oblongata develops from the myelencephalon, the most posterior vesicle. Choose it for a lesion in a myelencephalon structure.
questions.answerText: The midbrain

questions.q: Damage to the cerebellum causes clumsy, poorly coordinated movement rather than paralysis. Which statement explains this?
options: The cerebellum smooths and coordinates movements other regions start
The cerebellum relays sensory signals on to the cerebral cortex
The cerebellum sends the commands that start voluntary movement
The cerebellum holds the motor neurons that connect to skeletal muscle
questions.why: Voluntary movement is started by the primary motor cortex, and the signals reach muscles through motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord. The cerebellum works alongside this pathway, comparing the intended movement with what the body is actually doing and correcting the difference. Without it, the person can still move, but movements become jerky and balance suffers.
notes: Correct. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement rather than starting it, so its loss causes clumsiness, not paralysis.
Relaying sensory signals to the cortex is the job of the thalamus in the diencephalon. Choose it for a question about the main sensory relay station.
Starting voluntary movement is the job of the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus. Damage there causes weakness or paralysis, so pick this for a question about that cortex.

Motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle sit in the anterior gray horn of the spinal cord and in cranial nerve nuclei of the brainstem. Their loss would cause paralysis, so pick this idea for a question about the anterior horn.
questions.answerText: The cerebellum smooths and coordinates movements other regions start

questions.q: A small injury to the cerebral cortex is rarely fatal, but an injury of similar size in the medulla oblongata often is. What explains the difference?
options: It holds the hippocampus, which stores every long-term memory
It holds the primary motor cortex that starts all voluntary movement
It holds the centers that run heartbeat, breathing, and blood pressure
It produces nearly all of the cerebrospinal fluid that cushions the brain
questions.why: The medulla oblongata contains the cardiac center, the respiratory center, and the vasomotor center. These centers adjust the heartbeat, set the basic rhythm of breathing, and control blood vessel diameter, so they keep the body alive moment to moment. Losing a patch of cortex can cause a serious deficit, but losing these centers can stop breathing and circulation.
notes: The hippocampus sits in the medial temporal lobe, not the medulla, and it forms new long-term memories rather than storing every memory. Damage to it causes memory loss, which is not immediately fatal.
The primary motor cortex is in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, not the medulla. Damage there causes weakness, so pick it for a question about one-sided paralysis after a cortical stroke.
Correct. The medulla's cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centers make injury there immediately life-threatening.
Cerebrospinal fluid is made by the choroid plexus in the ventricles, not by the medulla itself. Choose the choroid plexus for a question about where CSF is made.
questions.answerText: It holds the centers that run heartbeat, breathing, and blood pressure

questions.q: Which three regions make up the brainstem?
options: The caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus
The cerebrum, cerebellum, and diencephalon
The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata
The thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus
questions.why: The brainstem is the stalk that connects the cerebrum, diencephalon, and cerebellum to the spinal cord. From top to bottom it is made of the midbrain, the pons, and the medulla oblongata. Every ascending and descending tract passes through it, and it holds the nuclei of cranial nerves III through X and XII.
notes: These are core basal ganglia buried deep in the cerebrum. They would be the answer for a question about the deep gray matter masses that regulate movement.
These are the other three major parts of the brain. Choose them if the question asks which major regions are not part of the brainstem.
Correct. The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata form the brainstem.
These three parts form the diencephalon, which sits above the brainstem around the third ventricle. Pick them if the question asks about the diencephalon.
questions.answerText: The midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata

questions.q: Which region is the most superior part of the brainstem?
options: The cerebellum
The medulla oblongata
The pons
The midbrain
questions.why: The brainstem runs from the midbrain at the top, through the pons in the middle, to the medulla oblongata at the bottom. The midbrain, also called the mesencephalon, is short and sits just below the diencephalon. The cerebral aqueduct runs through it.
notes: The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem and attaches to it by the cerebellar peduncles, but it is not part of the brainstem. Choose it for a question about coordination of movement.
The medulla oblongata is the most inferior region of the brainstem and merges into the spinal cord. It would be the answer for the lowest region.
The pons is the rounded middle region of the brainstem. Pick it if the question asks for the middle region.
Correct. The midbrain is the most superior region of the brainstem.
questions.answerText: The midbrain

questions.q: Which region is the most inferior part of the brainstem?
options: The pons
The midbrain
The medulla oblongata
The tectum
questions.why: The medulla oblongata is the lowest region of the brainstem. It is continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. It holds the pyramids and the vital centers for heart rate, breathing, and blood vessel diameter.
notes: The pons is the middle region of the brainstem, between the midbrain and the medulla. It would be the answer for the middle region.
The midbrain is the most superior region of the brainstem, just below the diencephalon. Pick it if the question asks for the highest region.
Correct. The medulla oblongata is the most inferior region of the brainstem.
The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, made of the four colliculi, so it sits near the top of the brainstem. Choose it for a question about the colliculi.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: What is the roof of the midbrain, made of four rounded bumps, called?
options: The pyramids
The vermis
The cerebral peduncles
The tectum
questions.why: Tectum means roof. It forms the posterior surface of the midbrain and is made of four rounded bumps called colliculi, an upper pair and a lower pair. The superior colliculi serve visual reflexes and the inferior colliculi serve auditory reflexes.
notes: The pyramids are a pair of ridges on the front of the medulla formed by the descending corticospinal tracts. Pick them for a question about the front surface of the medulla.
The vermis is the narrow midline band connecting the two cerebellar hemispheres. It would be the answer for a question about the middle of the cerebellum.
The cerebral peduncles are the paired stalks on the front of the midbrain that carry descending motor tracts. Choose them if the question asks about the front of the midbrain rather than its roof.
Correct. The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, made of the four colliculi.
questions.answerText: The tectum

questions.q: The superior colliculi of the midbrain are centers for which kind of reflex?
options: Visual reflexes
Withdrawal reflexes
Auditory reflexes
Respiratory reflexes
questions.why: The superior colliculi are the upper pair of bumps on the roof of the midbrain. They are reflex centers that turn the eyes and head toward something seen, such as a sudden movement. They are not where you become aware of the sight; that happens in the occipital cortex.
notes: Correct. The superior colliculi are visual reflex centers.
Withdrawal reflexes, such as pulling a hand off a hot stove, are spinal reflexes handled in the gray matter of the spinal cord. It would be the answer for a question about the reflex arc.
Auditory reflexes, such as turning toward a sound, are handled by the inferior colliculi, the lower pair. Pick this if the question asks about the inferior colliculi.
The respiratory center that sets breathing rhythm is in the medulla oblongata. Choose this for a question about the medullary vital centers.
questions.answerText: Visual reflexes

questions.q: The inferior colliculi of the midbrain are centers for which kind of reflex?
options: Cough reflexes
Auditory reflexes
Stretch reflexes
Visual reflexes
questions.why: The inferior colliculi are the lower pair of bumps on the tectum, the roof of the midbrain. They serve auditory reflexes, such as turning the head toward a sudden sound. A handy way to keep the pairs straight is upper for eyes, lower for ears.
notes: The cough reflex is coordinated in the medulla oblongata, which also handles swallowing and vomiting. It would be the answer for a question about protective airway reflexes.
Correct. The inferior colliculi are auditory reflex centers.
Stretch reflexes, such as the knee-jerk, are spinal reflexes completed in the spinal cord. Choose this for a question about a reflex arc through the cord.
Visual reflexes are handled by the superior colliculi, the upper pair. Pick this if the question asks about the superior colliculi.
questions.answerText: Auditory reflexes

questions.q: Which brainstem region has a name that means bridge?
options: The midbrain
The tectum
The pons
The medulla oblongata
questions.why: Pons is Latin for bridge. This rounded middle region of the brainstem bridges the medulla, the midbrain, and the cerebellum. Its pontine nuclei relay motor information from the cerebral cortex across to the cerebellum through the middle cerebellar peduncles.
notes: The midbrain, or mesencephalon, means middle brain. Pick it for a question about the most superior region of the brainstem.
Tectum means roof, and it is the roof of the midbrain. Choose it for a question about the four colliculi.
Correct. Pons means bridge.
The medulla oblongata means oblong marrow, and it is the lowest brainstem region. It would be the answer for a question about the region continuous with the spinal cord.
questions.answerText: The pons

questions.q: What is the pair of ridges on the front of the medulla, formed by the descending corticospinal tracts, called?
options: The pontine nuclei
The colliculi
The cerebral peduncles
The pyramids
questions.why: The pyramids are two raised ridges on the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata. They are formed by the corticospinal tracts, the motor fibers running from the cerebral cortex down to the spinal cord. At the lower end of the medulla, most of these fibers cross to the other side at the decussation of the pyramids.
notes: The pontine nuclei are gray matter clusters in the pons that relay motor information to the cerebellum. Choose them for a question about that relay.
The colliculi are the four bumps on the roof of the midbrain that serve visual and auditory reflexes. Pick them for a question about the tectum.

The cerebral peduncles are stalks on the front of the midbrain that also carry descending motor tracts. They would be the answer if the question asked about the front of the midbrain instead of the medulla.
Correct. The pyramids are the corticospinal ridges on the front of the medulla.
questions.answerText: The pyramids

questions.q: In which brainstem region do most corticospinal fibers cross to the opposite side?
options: The midbrain
The medulla oblongata
The cerebellum
The pons
questions.why: The corticospinal tracts form the pyramids on the front of the medulla. Near the lower end of the medulla, most of these fibers cross the midline at the decussation of the pyramids. This crossing is why each cerebral hemisphere controls movement on the opposite side of the body.
notes: The midbrain carries the corticospinal fibers in its cerebral peduncles, but they have not crossed yet. Pick the midbrain for a question about the cerebral peduncles.
Correct. Most corticospinal fibers cross at the decussation of the pyramids in the medulla.
The cerebellum is not part of the brainstem and does not carry the corticospinal tracts. It would be the answer for a question about coordinating movement.
The pons carries the corticospinal fibers downward but does not host the crossover. Choose it for a question about the pontine nuclei relaying motor signals to the cerebellum.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: Which center in the medulla oblongata sets the basic rhythm of breathing?
options: The cardiac center
The respiratory center
The pontine nuclei
The vasomotor center
questions.why: The medulla oblongata holds three vital centers. The respiratory center sets the basic rhythm of breathing, so breathing continues automatically even during sleep. The cardiac and vasomotor centers sit nearby and handle the heart and blood vessels.
notes: The cardiac center adjusts the rate and force of the heartbeat. Pick it for a question about medullary control of the heart.
Correct. The respiratory center of the medulla sets the basic breathing rhythm.
The pontine nuclei are gray matter clusters in the pons that relay motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum. They would be the answer for a question about that relay.
The vasomotor center adjusts the diameter of blood vessels and so blood pressure. Choose it for a question about blood vessel diameter.
questions.answerText: The respiratory center

questions.q: Which center in the medulla oblongata adjusts the diameter of blood vessels?
options: The pontine nuclei
The vasomotor center
The cardiac center
The respiratory center
questions.why: The vasomotor center of the medulla controls how wide or narrow blood vessels are. Narrowing vessels raises blood pressure and widening them lowers it, so this center helps regulate blood pressure. The word vasomotor literally means vessel mover.
notes: The pontine nuclei are in the pons and relay motor signals to the cerebellum. Choose them for a question about cortex-to-cerebellum relay.
Correct. The vasomotor center adjusts blood vessel diameter.
The cardiac center adjusts the rate and force of the heartbeat. Pick it if the question asks about heart rate rather than vessel diameter.
The respiratory center sets the basic rhythm of breathing. It would be the answer for a question about breathing rhythm.
questions.answerText: The vasomotor center

questions.q: What is the network of gray matter neurons spread through the core of the entire brainstem called?
options: The reticular formation
The tectum
The substantia nigra
The pontine nuclei
questions.why: The reticular formation is not a single nucleus. It is a net of gray matter cell bodies woven through the white matter of the midbrain, pons, and medulla. Its ascending part, the reticular activating system, keeps the cortex awake, and its descending part helps set resting muscle tone.
notes: Correct. The reticular formation is the network of neurons running through the core of the brainstem.
The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, made of the four colliculi. Pick it for a question about the visual and auditory reflex centers.
The substantia nigra is a single, darkly pigmented nucleus of the midbrain that helps regulate movement. Choose it for a question about Parkinson disease.
The pontine nuclei are clusters of gray matter limited to the pons that relay motor signals to the cerebellum. They would be the answer for that relay.
questions.answerText: The reticular formation

questions.q: Which darkly pigmented midbrain nucleus helps regulate movement along with the basal ganglia?
options: The superior colliculi
The pontine nuclei
The substantia nigra
The cardiac center
questions.why: Substantia nigra means black substance, named for the dark pigment in its neurons. This midbrain nucleus is grouped with the basal ganglia by function and helps start and smooth movement. Its loss is the basis of Parkinson disease.
notes: The superior colliculi are bumps on the roof of the midbrain that serve visual reflexes. Choose them for a question about turning the eyes toward a sight.
The pontine nuclei lie in the pons and relay motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum. Pick them for a question about that relay.
Correct. The substantia nigra is the darkly pigmented midbrain nucleus that works with the basal ganglia.
The cardiac center is in the medulla oblongata and adjusts the heartbeat. It would be the answer for a question about medullary control of heart rate.
questions.answerText: The substantia nigra

questions.q: What is the ascending part of the reticular formation that keeps the cerebral cortex awake and alert called?
options: The superior colliculi
The reticular activating system
The substantia nigra
The vasomotor center
questions.why: The reticular activating system, or RAS, is the ascending part of the reticular formation. It sends a constant stream of signals up to the cortex that keeps it awake, alert, and attentive, and it filters out unimportant stimuli. When the RAS is turned down, the result is sleep, and severe damage to it can cause coma.
notes: The superior colliculi are visual reflex centers on the roof of the midbrain. They would be the answer for a question about turning toward a sight.
Correct. The reticular activating system is the ascending arousal system of the reticular formation.
The substantia nigra is a pigmented midbrain nucleus that helps regulate movement. Choose it for a question about Parkinson disease.
The vasomotor center is a medullary center that adjusts blood vessel diameter. Pick it for a question about blood pressure control.
questions.answerText: The reticular activating system

questions.q: The brainstem holds the nuclei for which cranial nerves?
options: Cranial nerves III through X and XII
All twelve cranial nerves
Cranial nerves I through VI
Cranial nerves IX, X, and XII only
questions.why: Cranial nerves I and II connect to the forebrain, so they have no brainstem nucleus. The midbrain holds the nuclei of III and IV, the pons holds V through VIII, and the medulla holds IX, X, and XII, with the VIII nuclei sitting at the junction of the pons and medulla. The nucleus of XI sits just below the brainstem, in the upper cervical spinal cord.
notes: Correct. The nuclei of III through X and XII sit in the brainstem, and the XI nucleus sits just below it in the upper cervical cord.
This forgets that CN I and CN II connect to the forebrain, so they have no brainstem nucleus, and that the CN XI nucleus sits in the upper cervical cord.
This set includes CN I and II, which connect to the forebrain, and leaves out VII through X and XII, which do have brainstem nuclei.
These are the nerves with nuclei in the medulla, but the midbrain and pons also hold nuclei, for III through VIII. Pick this set if the question asked about the medulla alone.
questions.answerText: Cranial nerves III through X and XII

questions.q: The nuclei for the oculomotor nerve (CN III) and the trochlear nerve (CN IV) lie in which brainstem region?
options: The midbrain
The pons
The cerebellum
The medulla oblongata
questions.why: Cranial nerve nuclei are stacked in the brainstem in roughly the same order as the nerve numbers, from top to bottom. The midbrain, the highest region, holds the nuclei for CN III and CN IV. Below it, the pons holds V through VIII, and the medulla holds IX, X, and XII.
notes: Correct. The oculomotor and trochlear nuclei sit in the midbrain.
The pons holds the nuclei for CN V, VI, VII, and VIII. Pick it if the question asks about the trigeminal, abducens, or facial nerve nuclei.
The cerebellum is not part of the brainstem and holds no cranial nerve nuclei. Choose it for a question about coordinating movement.
The medulla oblongata holds the nuclei for CN IX, X, and XII, lower in the brainstem than III and IV. It would be the answer for the glossopharyngeal, vagus, or hypoglossal nuclei.
questions.answerText: The midbrain

questions.q: An injury to the medulla oblongata leaves a patient unable to regulate heart rate and breathing. Which centers were damaged?
options: The pontine nuclei
The cardiac and respiratory centers
The cerebral peduncles
The superior and inferior colliculi
questions.why: The medulla oblongata holds three vital centers. The cardiac center adjusts the rate and force of the heartbeat, and the respiratory center sets the basic rhythm of breathing. The vasomotor center beside them controls blood vessel diameter, which is why injury to the medulla is so dangerous.
notes: The pontine nuclei lie in the pons and relay motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum. Choose them for a question about that relay.
Correct. The cardiac and respiratory centers of the medulla control the heartbeat and breathing.
The cerebral peduncles are stalks on the front of the midbrain that carry descending motor tracts. They would be the answer for a question about the front of the midbrain.
The colliculi are the visual and auditory reflex centers on the roof of the midbrain. Pick them for a question about turning toward a sight or sound.
questions.answerText: The cardiac and respiratory centers

questions.q: Which structures relay motor information from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum?
options: The substantia nigra
The colliculi
The pontine nuclei
The pyramids
questions.why: The pontine nuclei are clusters of gray matter in the pons. They receive motor information from the cerebral cortex and pass it to the cerebellum through the thick middle cerebellar peduncles. This lets the cerebellum compare what the cortex intends with what the body is doing.
notes: The substantia nigra is a pigmented midbrain nucleus that works with the basal ganglia to regulate movement. It would be the answer for a question about Parkinson disease.
The colliculi are reflex centers on the roof of the midbrain for vision and hearing. Choose them for a question about the tectum.
Correct. The pontine nuclei relay motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum.
The pyramids are ridges on the front of the medulla formed by the corticospinal tracts heading to the spinal cord, not the cerebellum. Pick them for a question about the front of the medulla.
questions.answerText: The pontine nuclei

questions.q: A stroke in the right cerebral hemisphere weakens the left side of the body. Which brainstem feature explains this crossover?
options: The reticular activating system
The internal capsule
The corpus callosum
The decussation of the pyramids
questions.why: The corticospinal motor fibers run down from the cortex and form the pyramids on the front of the medulla. At the lower medulla, most of them cross to the opposite side at the decussation of the pyramids. By the time they reach the spinal cord they serve the opposite side of the body, so right-sided brain damage weakens the left side.
notes: The reticular activating system is the ascending part of the reticular formation that keeps the cortex awake. Choose it for a question about consciousness or coma.

The internal capsule carries the motor fibers from the cortex toward the brainstem, but they are still on the same side there. It would be the answer for a small stroke that weakens a whole side of the body.

The corpus callosum crosses the midline, but it connects the two hemispheres to each other rather than carrying motor commands to the body. Pick it for a question about communication between hemispheres.
Correct. The decussation of the pyramids is where most motor fibers cross to the opposite side.
questions.answerText: The decussation of the pyramids

questions.q: The nuclei for cranial nerves V, VI, VII, and VIII are found mainly in which brainstem region?
options: The pons
The medulla oblongata
The midbrain
The cerebellum
questions.why: The pons holds the nuclei for the trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves. The CN VIII nuclei sit at the junction of the pons and medulla, so VIII is listed with both regions. The order follows the numbers: III and IV above in the midbrain, V through VIII in the pons, and IX, X, and XII below in the medulla.
notes: Correct. The pons holds the nuclei for CN V through VIII.
The medulla oblongata holds the nuclei for CN IX, X, and XII and shares CN VIII with the pons, so it does not hold V, VI, or VII. Choose it for the glossopharyngeal, vagus, or hypoglossal nerves.
The midbrain holds the nuclei for CN III and IV, the oculomotor and trochlear nerves. Pick it for those two nerves.
The cerebellum is behind the brainstem and holds no cranial nerve nuclei. It would be the answer for a question about coordination.
questions.answerText: The pons

questions.q: Which paired stalks on the front of the midbrain carry descending motor tracts?
options: The cerebral peduncles
The colliculi
The middle cerebellar peduncles
The pyramids
questions.why: The cerebral peduncles are two thick stalks on the anterior side of the midbrain. They carry the descending motor tracts from the cerebral cortex down toward the pons, medulla, and spinal cord. Lower down, many of these same fibers form the pyramids of the medulla.
notes: Correct. The cerebral peduncles are the motor stalks on the front of the midbrain.
The colliculi are the four bumps on the back of the midbrain that serve visual and auditory reflexes. They would be the answer for a question about the tectum.

The middle cerebellar peduncles are thick stalks that connect the pons to the cerebellum and carry input from the pontine nuclei. Choose them for a question about how the pons talks to the cerebellum.
The pyramids also carry descending corticospinal fibers, but they are ridges on the front of the medulla, not the midbrain. Pick them for a question about the medulla.
questions.answerText: The cerebral peduncles

questions.q: Which function is the reticular activating system responsible for?
options: Maintaining consciousness and arousal
Coordinating balance and posture
Producing cerebrospinal fluid
Relaying sensory signals to the cortex
questions.why: The reticular activating system, or RAS, is the ascending part of the reticular formation in the brainstem. It keeps the cortex awake, holds attention, and filters out unimportant stimuli so the brain is not overloaded. When its activity drops, a person falls asleep, and severe damage to it can cause coma.
notes: Correct. The RAS maintains consciousness and arousal.
Balance and posture are coordinated by the cerebellum. Pick this for a question about cerebellar function.
Cerebrospinal fluid is produced by the choroid plexus in the ventricles. Choose this for a question about the choroid plexus.
Relaying sensory signals to the cortex is the job of the thalamus. It would be the answer for a question about the main sensory relay station.
questions.answerText: Maintaining consciousness and arousal

questions.q: Which brainstem region is continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum?
options: The midbrain
The pons
The cerebellum
The medulla oblongata
questions.why: The medulla oblongata is the lowest region of the brainstem. At the level of the foramen magnum, the large opening in the occipital bone, it merges smoothly into the spinal cord. The fourth ventricle behind it continues downward as the central canal of the cord.
notes: The midbrain is the most superior region of the brainstem, just below the diencephalon. Pick it for a question about the top of the brainstem.
The pons is the middle region of the brainstem, above the medulla. It would be the answer for the region that bridges to the cerebellum.
The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem in the posterior cranial fossa and does not continue into the spinal cord. Choose it for a question about coordination.
Correct. The medulla oblongata merges into the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: A clinician finds the abducens nerve (CN VI) weak and looks for the lesion in the brainstem region that holds its nucleus. Which region is that?
options: The medulla oblongata
The pons
The midbrain
The cerebellum
questions.why: Each cranial nerve has a fixed nucleus, so testing the nerves one at a time helps localize a brainstem problem. The abducens nucleus sits in the pons, along with the nuclei for CN V, VII, and VIII. A weak CN VI therefore points the clinician to the pons.
notes: The medulla oblongata holds the nuclei for CN IX, X, and XII, not the abducens nucleus. It would be the answer if the weak nerve were the vagus or hypoglossal nerve.
Correct. The abducens nucleus lies in the pons.
The midbrain holds the nuclei for CN III and IV. Pick it if the weak nerve were the oculomotor or trochlear nerve.
The cerebellum is not part of the brainstem and has no cranial nerve nuclei. Choose it for a problem with coordination and balance.
questions.answerText: The pons

questions.q: A patient loses a large area of cerebral cortex but stays awake. Later, a small brainstem injury drops the patient into a coma. Which system did the brainstem injury most likely damage?
options: The basal ganglia
The vasomotor center
The reticular activating system
The cerebral peduncles
questions.why: Staying awake depends on the reticular activating system, the ascending part of the reticular formation in the brainstem. It sends a steady stream of arousing signals up to the cortex. A person can lose much of the cortex and remain awake, but damage to this small ascending network can withdraw that arousal and cause coma.
notes: The basal ganglia are deep cerebral nuclei that help start and regulate movement. Damage causes movement disorders, so pick them for a question about Parkinson-like signs.
The vasomotor center in the medulla adjusts blood vessel diameter and blood pressure. Choose it for a question about blood pressure control.
Correct. Damage to the reticular activating system can cause coma.
The cerebral peduncles carry descending motor tracts on the front of the midbrain. Damage there causes weakness, so they would be the answer for a motor problem, not loss of consciousness.
questions.answerText: The reticular activating system

questions.q: A patient develops tremor, rigid muscles, and slow movements. The cause is loss of neurons in a darkly pigmented nucleus of the midbrain. Which structure is this?
options: The superior colliculi
The substantia nigra
The respiratory center
The pontine nuclei
questions.why: Tremor, rigidity, and slow movement are the classic signs of Parkinson disease. Its basis is the loss of neurons in the substantia nigra, a dark-pigmented midbrain nucleus that works with the basal ganglia to start and smooth movement. Without it, the basal ganglia circuit cannot regulate movement normally.
notes: The superior colliculi are visual reflex centers on the roof of the midbrain. They would be the answer for a question about turning the eyes toward a flash of light.
Correct. Loss of the substantia nigra is the basis of Parkinson disease.
The respiratory center is in the medulla and sets the breathing rhythm. Choose it for a question about breathing control.
The pontine nuclei are in the pons and relay motor information to the cerebellum. Pick them for a question about the cortex-to-cerebellum relay.
questions.answerText: The substantia nigra

questions.q: An injury to one small brainstem region is immediately life-threatening because that region holds the centers for the heartbeat and breathing. Which region is it?
options: The pons
The tectum
The medulla oblongata
The midbrain
questions.why: The cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centers all sit in the medulla oblongata. They adjust the rate and force of the heartbeat, set the basic rhythm of breathing, and adjust blood vessel diameter, all without conscious effort. Damage here can stop breathing and disrupt circulation, which is why a medullary injury is so often fatal.
notes: The pons bridges to the cerebellum and holds the nuclei for CN V through VIII. It would be the answer for a weak abducens or facial nerve.
The tectum is the roof of the midbrain with the four colliculi. Choose it for a question about visual and auditory reflex centers.
Correct. The medulla oblongata holds the vital cardiac and respiratory centers.
The midbrain holds the colliculi, the cerebral peduncles, the substantia nigra, and the nuclei for CN III and IV. Pick it for a question about visual reflexes or Parkinson disease.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: A sudden bright flash makes a person turn the head and eyes toward it before they even think about it. Which midbrain structure handles this reflex?
options: The superior colliculi
The inferior colliculi
The substantia nigra
The cerebral peduncles
questions.why: The superior colliculi, the upper pair of bumps on the roof of the midbrain, are visual reflex centers. They turn the eyes and head toward something seen without any conscious decision. Becoming aware of what you are looking at happens later, in the visual cortex of the occipital lobe.
notes: Correct. The superior colliculi mediate visual reflexes.
The inferior colliculi handle auditory reflexes, turning the head toward a sudden sound. Pick them if the trigger were a loud noise instead of a flash.
The substantia nigra is a pigmented midbrain nucleus that helps regulate movement with the basal ganglia. Choose it for a question about Parkinson disease.
The cerebral peduncles carry descending motor tracts on the front of the midbrain. They would be the answer for a question about the motor stalks of the midbrain.
questions.answerText: The superior colliculi

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the tracts that pass through the brainstem?
options: No long tracts pass through; it holds only cranial nerve nuclei
Only ascending sensory tracts pass through; motor tracts bypass it
Only descending motor tracts pass through; sensory tracts bypass it
All tracts between the brain and spinal cord pass through it
questions.why: The brainstem is the stalk that connects the cerebrum, diencephalon, and cerebellum to the spinal cord. Every ascending sensory tract and every descending motor tract traveling between the brain and the body passes through it. That is why even a small brainstem lesion can interrupt many functions at once.
notes: The brainstem does hold cranial nerve nuclei, but long tracts also pass through it. This option forgets structures like the pyramids that are made of passing tracts.
Motor tracts, such as the corticospinal tracts forming the pyramids, run down through the brainstem. This option ignores the pyramids and cerebral peduncles.
Sensory tracts also pass through the brainstem on their way up to the thalamus and cortex. This option would only fit if sensation reached the brain by some other route, which it does not.
Correct. All the ascending and descending tracts between the brain and the cord run through the brainstem.
questions.answerText: All tracts between the brain and spinal cord pass through it

questions.q: Breathing continues during deep sleep and under general anesthesia even though the cerebral cortex is quiet. Which region keeps the basic breathing rhythm going?
options: The thalamus
The medulla oblongata
The primary motor cortex
The cerebellum
questions.why: The respiratory center that sets the basic rhythm of breathing lies in the medulla oblongata, below the level of conscious control. Because it works automatically, breathing goes on whether or not the cortex is active. You can override it for a short time, as when holding your breath, but the medulla takes back control.
notes: The thalamus relays sensory signals to the cortex. It would be the answer for a question about the main sensory relay station.
Correct. The respiratory center of the medulla sets the breathing rhythm automatically.
The primary motor cortex can drive voluntary breathing, such as taking a deliberate deep breath, but it is quiet in deep sleep. Pick it for a question about starting voluntary movement.
The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture, and balance. Choose it for a question about clumsy, uncoordinated movement.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: Most corticospinal fibers cross in the medulla before they enter the spinal cord. An injury damages the descending motor tracts in the left half of the cervical spinal cord. Which side of the body below the injury becomes weak?
options: The left side
Both sides equally
The right side
Neither side
questions.why: The crossing happens at the decussation of the pyramids in the lower medulla, above the spinal cord. By the time the motor fibers run down the left half of the cord, they have already crossed and serve the left side of the body. Damage to the left half of the cord therefore weakens the left side below the injury, while a lesion above the crossing, such as in the left cerebrum, weakens the right side.
notes: Correct. The fibers have already crossed in the medulla, so a left-sided cord injury weakens the left side below it.
Damage to both sides of the cord would weaken both sides. This injury involves only the left half, so only one side is affected.

Right-sided weakness would follow damage on the left above the crossing point, such as a stroke in the left motor cortex or internal capsule. This answer applies the crossover rule to a level where the fibers have already crossed.
Descending motor tracts do run through the spinal cord, so damaging them causes weakness. This option would only fit an injury that spared every tract.
questions.answerText: The left side

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the reticular formation and the reticular activating system (RAS)?
options: The reticular formation is a small part of the RAS found only in the midbrain
The RAS and the reticular formation are names for the same single nucleus
The RAS is the descending part of the reticular formation and sets resting muscle tone
The RAS is the ascending part of the reticular formation and keeps the cortex alert
questions.why: The reticular formation is a network of gray matter neurons running through the core of the midbrain, pons, and medulla. Its ascending part is the RAS, which keeps the cortex awake and filters incoming stimuli. Its descending part helps set the muscle tone of resting skeletal muscle.
notes: This reverses the relationship, since the RAS is part of the reticular formation, not the other way around. The reticular formation also runs through the whole brainstem, not just the midbrain.
The reticular formation is a spread-out network, not a single nucleus, and the RAS is only one part of it. A single named nucleus would be something like the substantia nigra.
Setting resting muscle tone is the job of the descending part of the reticular formation, not the RAS. Pick this description for a question about the descending component.
Correct. The RAS is the ascending, arousal part of the reticular formation.
questions.answerText: The RAS is the ascending part of the reticular formation and keeps the cortex alert

questions.q: A small brainstem stroke causes weakness of the arm and leg on one side plus weakness of the tongue. Why can one small brainstem lesion cause both kinds of signs?
options: The brainstem holds the primary motor cortex for both limbs and tongue
Cranial nerve nuclei sit beside the long tracts passing through it
The tongue is served by spinal nerves from the cervical enlargement
The brainstem holds the anterior gray horns for the limbs and tongue
questions.why: The brainstem is crowded. The descending motor tracts to the limbs run through it, and the cranial nerve nuclei sit right beside them. A lesion in the medulla can therefore damage both the corticospinal fibers headed for the limbs and the hypoglossal nucleus that serves the tongue.
notes: The primary motor cortex lies on the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, not in the brainstem. Pick it for a question about where voluntary movement is started.
Correct. Cranial nerve nuclei lie next to the passing long tracts, so one lesion can hit both.
The tongue is served by a cranial nerve, the hypoglossal (CN XII), not by spinal nerves. The cervical enlargement gives rise to the nerves of the upper limbs.
The anterior gray horns that drive limb muscles are in the spinal cord, not the brainstem. Choose them for a question about where somatic motor neurons for the limbs sit.
questions.answerText: Cranial nerve nuclei sit beside the long tracts passing through it

questions.q: During exercise, the heart speeds up without any conscious decision. Which center in the medulla oblongata adjusts the rate and force of the heartbeat?
options: The cardiac center
The reticular activating system
The vasomotor center
The respiratory center
questions.why: The cardiac center of the medulla adjusts how fast and how forcefully the heart beats. It works automatically, so the heart rate rises to meet demand during exercise and falls at rest without any conscious effort. Its neighbors in the medulla handle breathing rhythm and blood vessel diameter.
notes: Correct. The cardiac center adjusts the rate and force of the heartbeat.
The reticular activating system keeps the cortex awake and alert. It would be the answer for a question about arousal and consciousness.
The vasomotor center adjusts the diameter of blood vessels and so blood pressure. Pick it for a question about vessel diameter.
The respiratory center sets the basic rhythm of breathing. Choose it for a question about breathing rhythm.
questions.answerText: The cardiac center

questions.q: Which list names the three parts of the diencephalon?
options: Thalamus, hypothalamus, and cerebellum
Caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus
Thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus
Midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata
questions.why: The diencephalon is the deep region between the cerebrum and the brainstem, and it surrounds the third ventricle. It has three parts: the thalamus, which forms most of it and relays sensory signals; the hypothalamus below, which controls homeostasis; and the small epithalamus at the back, which includes the pineal gland.
notes: The thalamus and hypothalamus are correct, but the cerebellum is a separate brain part behind the brainstem. The third part of the diencephalon is the epithalamus.
These are the core nuclei of the basal nuclei (basal ganglia), deep gray matter inside the cerebrum. Choose them for a question about the deep nuclei that regulate semi-voluntary movement.
Correct. The thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus make up the diencephalon.
These are the three regions of the brainstem, which lies below the diencephalon. Pick this list if the question asked for the brainstem regions from superior to inferior.
questions.answerText: Thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus

questions.q: Which description fits the thalamus?
options: A region below it that controls hunger, thirst, and temperature
