Darkly pigmented midbrain nuclei that help regulate movement
A small posterior region that holds the pineal gland
Paired gray masses that relay sensory signals to the cortex
questions.why: The thalamus is a pair of oval gray matter masses that make up about 80 percent of the diencephalon, joined in the middle by the interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia). It is the main sensory relay station to the cortex: sensory signals stop in a thalamic nucleus before being sent on to the correct cortical area. The two thalami form the side walls of the third ventricle.
notes: This describes the hypothalamus, the master control center for homeostasis. Pick it if the question asked which structure regulates body temperature, hunger, and thirst.
This describes the substantia nigra in the midbrain, which works with the basal nuclei. Choose it for a question about the structure whose loss causes Parkinson disease.
This describes the epithalamus, the third part of the diencephalon. It would be the answer for the structure that includes the melatonin-secreting pineal gland.
Correct. The thalamus is the main sensory relay station of the diencephalon.
questions.answerText: Paired gray masses that relay sensory signals to the cortex

questions.q: Which gland is part of the epithalamus?
options: Adrenal gland
Pineal gland
Pituitary gland
Thyroid gland
questions.why: The epithalamus is the small posterior part of the diencephalon, forming part of the roof of the third ventricle. Its main structure is the pineal gland, an endocrine gland that secretes melatonin, a hormone tied to sleep-wake rhythms. The epithalamus also contains the habenular nuclei.
notes: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys in the abdomen, far from the diencephalon. They would be the answer for the glands with a cortex and medulla above each kidney.
Correct. The pineal gland is the endocrine gland of the epithalamus.
The pituitary gland hangs below the hypothalamus on a stalk and sits in the sella turcica of the sphenoid. Pick it if the question asked which gland the hypothalamus controls directly.
The thyroid gland is in the anterior neck, wrapped around the trachea below the larynx, so it is not part of the brain. Choose it for a question about the butterfly-shaped gland of the neck.
questions.answerText: Pineal gland

questions.q: Body temperature, hunger, thirst, and sleep-wake rhythms are all regulated by which structure?
options: Thalamus
Hypothalamus
Medulla oblongata
Cerebellum
questions.why: The hypothalamus, just below the thalamus, is the master control center for homeostasis, keeping the internal environment steady. It controls the autonomic nervous system, controls endocrine function through the pituitary, and regulates body temperature, hunger and thirst, and sleep-wake rhythms. It is small, but it manages many of the body's basic survival drives.
notes: The thalamus relays sensory signals to the cerebral cortex. It sits right above the hypothalamus, which makes the two easy to confuse, but it is the answer for sensory relay, not for drives like hunger and thirst.
Correct. The hypothalamus regulates these homeostatic drives.

The medulla oblongata holds the vital centers that adjust heart rate, set the breathing rhythm, and adjust blood vessel diameter, not the centers for hunger, thirst, or temperature. It would be the answer for a question about those vital centers.
The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture, and balance. Pick it if the question asked which part keeps a person steady while walking.
questions.answerText: Hypothalamus

questions.q: Which brain structure links the nervous system to the endocrine system, and how does it do it?
options: The thalamus, which relays signals to the cortex
The pineal gland, which controls the pituitary gland
The pons, which relays signals to the cerebellum
The hypothalamus, which controls the pituitary gland
questions.why: The hypothalamus is neural tissue, yet it controls the pituitary gland that hangs beneath it on a stalk, and the pituitary in turn directs many other endocrine glands. This makes the hypothalamus the bridge between the nervous system and the endocrine system. It also controls the autonomic nervous system, so it can adjust the body through both nerves and hormones.
notes: The thalamus does relay signals to the cortex, but it has no control over the pituitary. Pick it for a question about where sensory signals stop before reaching the cortex.

The pineal gland is an endocrine gland of the epithalamus that secretes melatonin, but it does not control the pituitary. It would be the answer for the gland in the diencephalon tied to sleep-wake rhythms.

The pons does relay motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum through its pontine nuclei, but that is a movement pathway, not an endocrine link. Choose it for a question about the brainstem bridge to the cerebellum.
Correct. Through its control of the pituitary, the hypothalamus connects the nervous and endocrine systems.
questions.answerText: The hypothalamus, which controls the pituitary gland

questions.q: What is the main job of the cerebellum?
options: Coordinating movement, posture, and balance
Setting the basic rhythm of breathing
Relaying sensory signals to the cerebral cortex
Producing cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles
questions.why: The cerebellum sits in the posterior cranial fossa behind the brainstem and below the occipital lobes. It does not start movement; instead it coordinates movements started by the cerebrum so they are smooth and accurate, and it maintains posture and balance. Damage to it causes clumsy, unsteady movement and poor balance.
notes: Correct. The cerebellum coordinates movement and keeps posture and balance.
The respiratory center that sets the basic rhythm of breathing is in the medulla oblongata. It would be the answer for a question about the brainstem vital centers.
Relaying sensory signals to the cortex is the job of the thalamus in the diencephalon. Pick the thalamus if the question asked for the main sensory relay station.
CSF is produced by the choroid plexus, capillary networks inside the ventricles. Choose the choroid plexus if the question asked where cerebrospinal fluid is made.
questions.answerText: Coordinating movement, posture, and balance

questions.q: What is the vermis of the cerebellum?
options: The fine, leaf-like folds of the cerebellar surface
The stalks of white matter joining it to the brainstem
The narrow midline band joining the two hemispheres
The branching white matter inside the cerebellum
questions.why: The cerebellum has two lateral hemispheres joined in the middle by a narrow strip called the vermis (the name means worm, for its segmented look). Like the hemispheres, the vermis has a folded gray matter cortex over white matter. It is a midline landmark when the cerebellum is viewed from above or behind.
notes: This describes the folia, the cerebellar version of the cerebral gyri. They would be the answer for the thin parallel ridges on the cerebellar surface.
This describes the cerebellar peduncles, three pairs of white matter stalks. Choose them for a question about how the cerebellum connects to the midbrain, pons, and medulla.
Correct. The vermis is the worm-like midline band between the cerebellar hemispheres.
This describes the arbor vitae, the tree-like white matter seen when the cerebellum is cut down the middle. Pick it if the question asked what that white matter pattern is called.
questions.answerText: The narrow midline band joining the two hemispheres

questions.q: What is the arbor vitae?
options: The network of capillaries in the ventricles that makes CSF
The tree-like pattern of white matter in the cerebellum
The midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres
The thin outer layer of gray matter on the cerebellum
questions.why: Arbor vitae means tree of life. When the cerebellum is cut along the midline, its inner white matter branches out into the folds like the limbs of a tree, with gray matter cortex covering each branch. This white matter carries signals into and out of the cerebellar cortex.
notes: This is the choroid plexus, found in the ventricles. Choose it if the question asked which structure makes cerebrospinal fluid.
Correct. The arbor vitae is the branching white matter of the cerebellum.
This is the vermis, the worm-like midline band between the hemispheres. It would be the answer for the structure joining the left and right halves of the cerebellum.
This is the cerebellar cortex, the outer gray matter that covers the folia. Pick it if the question asked where the cell bodies of the cerebellum sit at the surface.
questions.answerText: The tree-like pattern of white matter in the cerebellum

questions.q: How many pairs of cerebellar peduncles connect the cerebellum to the brainstem, and what are they called?
options: Two pairs: anterior and posterior
Three pairs: superior, middle, and inferior
Four pairs: one per brainstem region plus the cord
Three pairs: anterior, lateral, and posterior
questions.why: Three pairs of cerebellar peduncles, thick stalks of white matter, attach the cerebellum to each level of the brainstem. The superior peduncles connect to the midbrain, the middle peduncles to the pons, and the inferior peduncles to the medulla. Their names follow the brainstem regions from top to bottom.
notes: There are three pairs, not two, because each of the three brainstem regions (midbrain, pons, and medulla) has its own connection. Anterior and posterior labels do not match how the peduncles are named.
Correct. Superior, middle, and inferior peduncles connect to the midbrain, pons, and medulla.
There is no fourth pair to the spinal cord. Signals from the cord reach the cerebellum by way of the inferior peduncle at the medulla, so three pairs cover all the connections.
The count is right, but the names are not. The peduncles are named by vertical position (superior, middle, inferior), matching the midbrain, pons, and medulla they attach to.
questions.answerText: Three pairs: superior, middle, and inferior

questions.q: Which cerebellar peduncle carries mostly output from the cerebellum, and where does it connect?
options: Superior peduncle, connecting to the midbrain
Inferior peduncle, connecting to the spinal cord
Inferior peduncle, connecting to the medulla
Middle peduncle, connecting to the pons
questions.why: The superior cerebellar peduncles connect the cerebellum to the midbrain and carry mostly output, the signals the cerebellum sends out to adjust movement. The middle and inferior peduncles mainly bring information in. Remembering that most output leaves through the top pair makes the three easy to sort.
notes: Correct. The superior peduncle connects to the midbrain and carries mostly output.
No peduncle attaches directly to the spinal cord. Signals from the cord enter through the inferior peduncle at the medulla, so this choice comes from mixing up where the inferior peduncle attaches.

The inferior peduncles do connect to the medulla, but they mostly carry input from the spinal cord and the vestibular (balance) system. They would be the answer for the peduncle that brings in body position and balance signals.

The middle peduncles connect to the pons, but they carry input, the signals from the pontine nuclei that relay motor plans from the cortex. Pick them if the question asked which peduncle brings cortical information into the cerebellum.
questions.answerText: Superior peduncle, connecting to the midbrain

questions.q: Which list gives the three regions of the brainstem in order from superior to inferior?
options: Midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata
Medulla oblongata, pons, midbrain
Pons, midbrain, medulla oblongata
Thalamus, midbrain, pons
questions.why: The brainstem has three regions stacked from top to bottom. The midbrain is the short, most superior region just below the diencephalon, the pons is the rounded middle region that bulges forward, and the medulla oblongata is the most inferior region, continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
notes: Correct. Midbrain on top, pons in the middle, and medulla at the bottom.
This is the correct list in the wrong direction, from inferior to superior. Pick this order if the question asked to list the regions starting from the spinal cord.
The pons sits below the midbrain, not above it. The midbrain is the top of the brainstem, directly beneath the diencephalon.
The thalamus is part of the diencephalon, above the brainstem, and the medulla is missing from this list. It mixes the diencephalon with the brainstem.
questions.answerText: Midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes where the cranial nerve nuclei sit?
options: VII through XII are in the brainstem; III through VI are in the diencephalon
All twelve are in the brainstem, from the midbrain down to the medulla
III through X and XII are in the brainstem; XI is in the upper cervical cord
I and II are in the brainstem; the other ten are in the spinal cord
questions.why: Cranial nerves I and II connect to the forebrain, so they have no brainstem nucleus. The nuclei of III through X and XII sit in the brainstem: III and IV in the midbrain, V through VIII in the pons, and IX, X, and XII in the medulla, with the VIII nuclei at the junction of the pons and medulla. The nucleus of XI sits just below the brainstem, in the upper cervical spinal cord.
notes: The nuclei of III through VI sit in the midbrain and pons, not the diencephalon, and the XI nucleus sits in the upper cervical cord rather than the brainstem. This choice places the upper nerves one region too high.
CN I and II connect to the forebrain and have no brainstem nucleus, and the XI nucleus sits just below the brainstem in the upper cervical cord. So not all twelve sit in the brainstem.
Correct. The nuclei of III through X and XII are in the brainstem, and the XI nucleus is just below it in the upper cervical cord.
This turns the pattern upside down. CN I and II are the two nerves with no brainstem nucleus, and only the XI nucleus sits in the spinal cord.
questions.answerText: III through X and XII are in the brainstem; XI is in the upper cervical cord

questions.q: Which brainstem region is continuous with the spinal cord?
options: Midbrain
Medulla oblongata
Pons
Conus medullaris
questions.why: The medulla oblongata is the most inferior region of the brainstem. It narrows and merges into the spinal cord at the level of the foramen magnum, so there is no sharp boundary between the two. All the tracts running between the brain and the cord pass through it.
notes: The midbrain is the most superior region, connecting with the diencephalon above. It would be the answer for the brainstem region continuous with the diencephalon.
Correct. The medulla merges into the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
The pons is the middle region, above the medulla, and it bridges to the cerebellum. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the pontine nuclei.

The conus medullaris is the tapered lower end of the spinal cord near the L1 to L2 disc, not part of the brainstem. Its name sounds like medulla, which causes the mix-up; pick it for where the cord ends.
questions.answerText: Medulla oblongata

questions.q: Which tracts pass through the brainstem on their way between the brain and the spinal cord?
options: All ascending sensory and descending motor tracts
Only the commissural tracts linking the two hemispheres
Only descending motor tracts, since sensory ones bypass it
Only ascending sensory tracts, since motor ones bypass it
questions.why: The brainstem is the only connection between the higher brain and the spinal cord, so every ascending sensory tract and every descending motor tract runs through it. For example, the descending corticospinal tracts form the pyramids on the front of the medulla. This is one reason a small brainstem injury can affect sensation and movement over large parts of the body.
notes: Correct. All traffic between the brain and the cord passes through the brainstem.
Tracts linking the two hemispheres are commissural fibers, such as the corpus callosum, and they stay in the cerebrum. Pick them for a question about connecting the right and left hemispheres.
Sensory tracts cannot bypass the brainstem, because there is no other route from the cord to the thalamus and cortex. This choice gets the motor part right but leaves out half the traffic.
Motor tracts also run through the brainstem; the corticospinal fibers even form the pyramids of the medulla. This choice keeps the sensory part but leaves out the motor pathways.
questions.answerText: All ascending sensory and descending motor tracts

questions.q: A small injury to the medulla oblongata is immediately life-threatening, while a similar injury to one cerebral lobe usually is not. Why?
options: It holds the heartbeat, breathing, and blood pressure centers
It produces most of the cerebrospinal fluid that cushions the brain
It is the only brain region with its own arterial blood supply
It contains the primary motor cortex that controls every muscle
questions.why: The medulla oblongata holds three vital centers: the cardiac center adjusts the rate and force of the heartbeat, the respiratory center sets the basic rhythm of breathing, and the vasomotor center adjusts blood vessel diameter and so blood pressure. Damage there can stop breathing and disrupt circulation within minutes. A cerebral lobe has important but non-vital jobs, so damage there causes a specific loss such as vision or speech rather than death.
notes: Correct. The cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centers in the medulla keep the body alive.
CSF is produced by the choroid plexus in the ventricles, not by the medulla. Pick the choroid plexus for a question about where CSF is made.

Every brain region has an arterial supply; the medulla gets its blood from branches of the vertebral arteries, such as the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. This choice is a made-up idea, not a real feature of the medulla.
The primary motor cortex is in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, not in the brainstem. The medulla carries motor tracts down to the cord but does not start voluntary movement.
questions.answerText: It holds the heartbeat, breathing, and blood pressure centers

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the superior and inferior colliculi?
options: Superior: auditory reflexes; inferior: visual reflexes
Superior: motor tracts; inferior: sensory tracts
Superior: conscious vision; inferior: conscious hearing
Superior: visual reflexes; inferior: auditory reflexes
questions.why: The colliculi are four rounded bumps on the back of the midbrain that form its roof, the tectum. The upper pair, the superior colliculi, are reflex centers for vision, turning the eyes and head toward something seen. The lower pair, the inferior colliculi, are reflex centers for hearing, turning the head toward a sudden sound.
notes: This reverses the pairs. The upper (superior) pair serves sight and the lower (inferior) pair serves sound, so the superior colliculi handle visual reflexes.

Descending motor tracts run in the cerebral peduncles on the front of the midbrain, not in the colliculi on its back. Pick the cerebral peduncles for a question about the motor stalks of the midbrain.

The colliculi handle reflexes, not conscious perception. Conscious vision is in the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe, and conscious hearing is in the primary auditory cortex of the temporal lobe.
Correct. Upper pair for visual reflexes, lower pair for auditory reflexes.
questions.answerText: Superior: visual reflexes; inferior: auditory reflexes

questions.q: The cerebral aqueduct, which carries CSF from the third to the fourth ventricle, runs through which part of the brain?
options: Midbrain
Diencephalon
Pons
Medulla oblongata
questions.why: The cerebral aqueduct is a narrow channel running through the midbrain, the most superior region of the brainstem. The midbrain develops from the mesencephalon, and the cavity of that vesicle becomes the aqueduct. CSF flows through it from the third ventricle in the diencephalon above to the fourth ventricle behind the pons and medulla below.
notes: Correct. The cerebral aqueduct runs through the midbrain.
The diencephalon encloses the third ventricle, where the aqueduct begins. Choose it if the question asked which region surrounds the third ventricle.
The fourth ventricle, not the aqueduct, lies behind the pons. Pick the pons if the question asked which brainstem region sits in front of the fourth ventricle.
The medulla lies in front of the lower fourth ventricle and continues into the spinal cord, where the central canal runs. It would be the answer for the region continuous with the cord.
questions.answerText: Midbrain

questions.q: Which cranial nerve nuclei are located in the midbrain?
options: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII
CN IX, X, XI, and XII
CN I and CN II
CN III and CN IV
questions.why: The midbrain holds the nuclei of the oculomotor nerve (CN III) and the trochlear nerve (CN IV), both of which move the eye. The pons holds V through VIII, and the medulla holds IX, X, and XII. Moving down the brainstem, the cranial nerve numbers rise, which helps place each nucleus.
notes: CN V through VIII have their nuclei in the pons. Pick this set if the question asked which cranial nerves arise from the pons.

These nerves belong to the lowest part of the brainstem and below it. IX, X, and XII have their nuclei in the medulla, and the XI nucleus sits in the upper cervical cord, so none of them are in the midbrain.
The olfactory and optic nerves attach to the cerebrum and diencephalon, above the brainstem, so they have no brainstem nuclei.
Correct. The oculomotor and trochlear nuclei are in the midbrain.
questions.answerText: CN III and CN IV

questions.q: What does the name pons mean, and what does the pons connect?
options: Bridge; it joins medulla, midbrain, and cerebellum
Marrow; it continues down into the spinal cord
Little brain; it coordinates posture, balance, and movement
Middle brain; it surrounds the cerebral aqueduct
questions.why: Pons is Latin for bridge. The pons is the rounded middle region of the brainstem, and it bridges the medulla below, the midbrain above, and the cerebellum behind it through the thick middle cerebellar peduncles. Its pontine nuclei relay motor information from the cortex across that bridge to the cerebellum.
notes: Correct. The pons is the bridge between the medulla, the midbrain, and the cerebellum.
Medulla means marrow or inner part, and the medulla oblongata is the region that continues into the spinal cord. Choose it for the most inferior region of the brainstem.
Little brain is the meaning of cerebellum, which coordinates movement, posture, and balance. Pick it if the question asked about the part behind the brainstem.
Middle brain describes the midbrain (mesencephalon), which surrounds the cerebral aqueduct. It would be the answer for the most superior region of the brainstem.
questions.answerText: Bridge; it joins medulla, midbrain, and cerebellum

questions.q: What do the pontine nuclei relay?
options: Motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum
Hormone signals from the hypothalamus to the pituitary
Visual reflex signals from the eyes to the neck
Sensory signals from the body to the cortex
questions.why: The pontine nuclei are clusters of gray matter in the pons. They receive motor information from the cerebral cortex about planned movements and relay it through the middle cerebellar peduncles into the cerebellum. This lets the cerebellum compare what the cortex intends with what the body is actually doing.
notes: Correct. The pontine nuclei pass the cortex's motor plans on to the cerebellum.
The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland below it, linking the nervous and endocrine systems. That would be the answer for a question about how the brain controls hormone release.
Visual reflexes, such as turning the eyes and head toward a sight, are handled by the superior colliculi of the midbrain. Pick them for a question about visual reflex centers.
Relaying sensory signals to the cortex is the main job of the thalamus. Choose the thalamus if the question asked for the sensory relay station of the diencephalon.
questions.answerText: Motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum

questions.q: Which cranial nerve nuclei are located in the pons?
options: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII
CN III, IV, V, and VI
CN IX, X, XI, and XII
CN III and CN IV
questions.why: The pons holds the nuclei of the trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves. The midbrain above holds III and IV, and the medulla below holds IX, X, and XII. The vestibulocochlear nuclei sit where the pons meets the medulla, so VIII is listed with both regions.
notes: Correct. The trigeminal, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nuclei are in the pons.
This set mixes regions: III and IV belong to the midbrain, and it leaves out VII and VIII, which are in the pons. The pons group starts at V and runs through VIII.

These nerves belong below the pons. IX, X, and XII have their nuclei in the medulla, and the XI nucleus sits in the upper cervical cord. Choose this set for a question about the nerves that attach to the medulla.
CN III and IV have their nuclei in the midbrain, the region above the pons. Pick this set if the question asked about the midbrain.
questions.answerText: CN V, VI, VII, and VIII

questions.q: What forms the pyramids on the front of the medulla oblongata?
options: Descending corticospinal motor tracts
Ascending sensory tracts to the thalamus
Fibers of the middle cerebellar peduncles
Nuclei of the cardiac and respiratory centers
questions.why: The pyramids are a pair of ridges on the anterior surface of the medulla. They are formed by the corticospinal tracts, the descending motor axons that run from the primary motor cortex down to the spinal cord. Near the bottom of the medulla most of these fibers cross to the opposite side at the decussation of the pyramids.
notes: Correct. The corticospinal motor tracts form the pyramids.
Ascending sensory tracts do pass through the medulla on their way to the thalamus, but they do not form the pyramids. The pyramids are made by the descending motor tract.

The middle cerebellar peduncles are thick stalks connecting the pons to the cerebellum, at a higher level than the medulla. Choose them for a question about the bridge from the pons to the cerebellum.
The cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centers are networks of neurons deep in the medulla, not surface ridges. Pick them for a question about what makes a medullary injury life-threatening.
questions.answerText: Descending corticospinal motor tracts

questions.q: Which list names the three vital centers of the medulla oblongata?
options: Cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor
Speech, hearing, and vision
Hunger, thirst, and temperature
Visual, auditory, and vasomotor
questions.why: The medulla holds three vital centers. The cardiac center adjusts the rate and force of the heartbeat, the respiratory center sets the basic rhythm of breathing, and the vasomotor center adjusts blood vessel diameter, which controls blood pressure. Because they keep the body alive, damage to the medulla is immediately dangerous.
notes: Correct. These three centers adjust the heartbeat, set the breathing rhythm, and adjust blood vessel diameter.
Speech, hearing, and vision are handled by areas of the cerebral cortex, such as Broca's area and the primary auditory and visual cortices. They are not vital centers of the brainstem.
Hunger, thirst, and body temperature are regulated by the hypothalamus. Pick it if the question asked which structure keeps these homeostatic drives in balance.
Visual and auditory reflex centers are the superior and inferior colliculi of the midbrain. This choice includes one real medullary center but mixes in two that belong to the midbrain.
questions.answerText: Cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor

questions.q: What is the decussation of the pyramids, and what does it explain?
options: A crossing of motor fibers, so each hemisphere runs the other side
A bridge of fibers joining the two hemispheres to share memory
A split of motor fibers into the cerebellum to coordinate movement
A crossing of optic fibers, so each eye sends signals to both sides
questions.why: At the lower end of the medulla, most of the corticospinal motor fibers in the pyramids cross to the opposite side, a crossing called the decussation of the pyramids. Because of this, the left motor cortex controls muscles on the right side of the body, and the right controls the left. This is why a stroke in the right hemisphere weakens the left side of the body.
notes: Correct. The motor fibers cross in the medulla, so control is contralateral (opposite side).
The bridge joining the two hemispheres is the corpus callosum, a band of commissural fibers in the cerebrum. It would be the answer for a question about how the hemispheres share information.
Motor information reaches the cerebellum through the pontine nuclei and the middle cerebellar peduncles, not by splitting off at the pyramids. Choose the pontine nuclei for that question.
A crossing of optic nerve fibers happens at the optic chiasm, in front of the pituitary, not in the medulla. Pick the optic chiasm for a question about where visual pathways cross.
questions.answerText: A crossing of motor fibers, so each hemisphere runs the other side

questions.q: What does the reticular activating system (RAS) do?
options: Keeps the cortex awake, alert, and attentive
Relays touch and pain signals to the cortex
Coordinates posture, balance, and movement
Forms new long-term memories from experience
questions.why: The reticular formation is a net of gray matter neurons woven through the core of the brainstem. Its ascending part, the reticular activating system, keeps the cerebral cortex awake, alert, and attentive and filters out unimportant stimuli so the brain is not overloaded. When the RAS shuts down the result is sleep, and severe damage to it can cause coma.
notes: Correct. The RAS maintains consciousness and alertness.
Relaying touch and pain signals to the cortex is the job of the thalamus. Pick the thalamus for a question about the main sensory relay station.
Coordinating posture, balance, and movement is the job of the cerebellum. It would be the answer if the question asked which part keeps movement smooth and steady.
Forming new long-term memories is the job of the hippocampus in the limbic system. Choose it for a question about memory formation.
questions.answerText: Keeps the cortex awake, alert, and attentive

questions.q: What is the basilar pons?
options: The back part of the pons, which holds cranial nerve nuclei
The thick band of crosswise fibers on the front of the pons
The thick stalks that attach the pons to the cerebellum
The diamond-shaped space filled with fluid behind the pons
questions.why: The basilar pons is the front surface of the pons, a thick band of fibers that runs crosswise and curves back on each side toward the cerebellum. The pontine nuclei are scattered among these fibers. The back part of the pons is a different region, the tegmentum.
notes: The back part of the pons, with cranial nerve nuclei and part of the reticular formation, is the tegmentum.
Correct. The basilar pons is the thick band of crosswise fibers on the front of the pons.
The thick stalks that attach the side of the pons to each cerebellar hemisphere are the middle cerebellar peduncles.
The diamond-shaped space filled with cerebrospinal fluid behind the pons is the fourth ventricle.
questions.answerText: The thick band of crosswise fibers on the front of the pons

questions.q: Where are the pontine nuclei found?
options: In the medulla, below the pons
In the tegmentum of the pons
In the cerebellar hemispheres
Scattered through the basilar pons
questions.why: The pontine nuclei are clusters of gray matter scattered through the basilar pons, the front part of the pons. They receive motor information from the cerebral cortex, and their axons cross to the opposite side and enter the cerebellum.
notes: The pontine nuclei are part of the pons, as their name says. The medulla lies below the pons.
The tegmentum is the back part of the pons. It carries cranial nerve nuclei and part of the reticular formation, but the pontine nuclei sit in the front part.
The pontine nuclei send their axons into the cerebellum, but the nuclei themselves stay in the basilar pons.
Correct. The pontine nuclei are clusters of gray matter scattered through the basilar pons.
questions.answerText: Scattered through the basilar pons

questions.q: On a midsagittal model, you find the fourth ventricle, with the cerebellum over its roof. What forms its floor?
options: The front of the pons, the basilar pons
The back of the pons and upper medulla
The corpus callosum and the fornix
The thalamus and the hypothalamus
questions.why: The fourth ventricle is a diamond-shaped space filled with cerebrospinal fluid, behind the pons and upper medulla. Its floor is the back of the pons and the upper medulla, and the cerebellum lies over its roof. The cerebral aqueduct opens into it from above.
notes: The basilar pons is the front surface of the pons, facing away from the ventricle. The fourth ventricle lies behind the pons.
Correct. The floor of the fourth ventricle is the back of the pons and the upper medulla.
The corpus callosum and the fornix belong to the cerebrum, far above the brainstem. They do not border the fourth ventricle.
The thalamus and hypothalamus come from the diencephalon, whose cavity is the third ventricle, not the fourth.
questions.answerText: The back of the pons and upper medulla

questions.q: Which cranial nerve leaves the side of the pons?
options: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Abducens nerve (CN VI)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) leaves the side of the pons. The abducens (CN VI), facial (CN VII), and vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) nerves leave lower, at the pontomedullary junction where the pons meets the medulla.
notes: Correct. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) leaves the side of the pons.
The abducens nerve (CN VI) leaves at the pontomedullary junction, not the side of the pons. Pick it for a question about that junction.
The facial nerve (CN VII) leaves at the pontomedullary junction, along with CN VI and CN VIII, not from the side of the pons.
The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) leaves at the pontomedullary junction, not the side of the pons.
questions.answerText: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)

questions.q: On a brainstem model, you follow the crosswise fibers of the basilar pons around its side. Where do they lead?
options: Up into the thalamus, through the cerebral aqueduct
Down into the medulla, through the fourth ventricle
Forward to the cerebral cortex, through the fornix
Into the cerebellum, as the middle cerebellar peduncles
questions.why: The crosswise fibers of the basilar pons carry the axons of the pontine nuclei. They curve back on each side and leave the pons as the middle cerebellar peduncles, the thick stalks that enter each cerebellar hemisphere. These are the largest of the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles.
notes: The cerebral aqueduct is a fluid channel that opens into the fourth ventricle from above. It carries cerebrospinal fluid, not nerve fibers.
The fourth ventricle is a fluid-filled space behind the pons, not a pathway for fibers into the medulla.
The fornix is the white matter arch that carries hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies. It runs under the corpus callosum, far above the pons.
Correct. The crosswise fibers leave the pons as the middle cerebellar peduncles and enter the cerebellum.
questions.answerText: Into the cerebellum, as the middle cerebellar peduncles

questions.q: A stroke damages both middle cerebellar peduncles. Which flow of information is most directly cut off?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid flowing from the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle
Motor information from the cortex, relayed by the pontine nuclei to the cerebellum
Ascending signals that pass through the thalamus to keep the cortex awake
Output from the hippocampus carried forward to the mammillary bodies
questions.why: The pontine nuclei receive motor information from the cerebral cortex, and their axons cross and leave the pons as the middle cerebellar peduncles. Damage to the peduncles cuts this relay. It is the route the cerebrum uses to keep the cerebellum informed about planned movements.
notes: CSF moves from the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle, a fluid space behind the pons. The peduncles carry nerve fibers, not fluid.
Correct. The middle cerebellar peduncles carry the pontine relay of motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum.
Signals that rise through the thalamus to keep the cortex awake belong to the reticular activating system, not the middle cerebellar peduncles.
Hippocampal output travels in the fornix to the mammillary bodies, a limbic pathway that does not run through the peduncles.
questions.answerText: Motor information from the cortex, relayed by the pontine nuclei to the cerebellum

questions.q: What does the descending component of the reticular formation do?
options: Keeps the cerebral cortex awake and alert
Filters out unimportant sensory input
Helps set resting muscle tone and posture
Relays motor information to the cerebellum
questions.why: The descending component of the reticular formation sends fibers down to the spinal cord. These fibers help set the resting tone of skeletal muscles and help keep posture. It also includes the medullary centers for heart rate, breathing, and blood vessel diameter.
notes: Keeping the cortex awake and alert is the job of the ascending reticular activating system (RAS), which sends fibers up through the thalamus.
Filtering out unimportant sensory input is also a job of the ascending RAS, so the cortex is not flooded.
Correct. The descending component sends fibers to the spinal cord that help set resting muscle tone and posture.
Relaying motor information from the cortex to the cerebellum is the job of the pontine nuclei. The descending component of the reticular formation sends its fibers down to the spinal cord instead.
questions.answerText: Helps set resting muscle tone and posture

questions.q: On a cross section of the brainstem, where do you find the reticular formation?
options: In the central core, behind the large descending motor tracts
On the front surface, among the crosswise fibers of the pons
Over the roof of the fourth ventricle, under the cerebellum
On the outer surface, as a raised ridge of gray matter
questions.why: The reticular formation fills the central core of the brainstem, the tegmentum. It lies behind the large descending motor tracts and in front of the ventricle or aqueduct. It runs this way through the medulla, pons, and midbrain.
notes: Correct. The reticular formation fills the central core, behind the descending motor tracts and in front of the ventricle or aqueduct.
The crosswise fibers on the front of the pons are the basilar pons, with the pontine nuclei. The reticular formation lies deeper, in the core.
The cerebellum lies over the roof of the fourth ventricle. The reticular formation lies in front of the ventricle, in the brainstem core.
The reticular formation has no surface landmark. It is a loose net of neurons in the core, so you find it by its position in a cross section.
questions.answerText: In the central core, behind the large descending motor tracts

questions.q: Why can't you point to the reticular formation on the surface of a brainstem model?
options: It is a thin layer of white matter wrapped around the outside of the brainstem
It lies in the cerebral cortex, above the brainstem, not in the brainstem
It is a loose net of scattered neurons in the core, with no sharp borders
It is one compact nucleus hidden deep inside the cerebellum
questions.why: The reticular formation is made of small clusters of neurons scattered among bundles of white matter. Because it is spread out like a net, it has no sharp borders and no surface landmark. It fills the central core of the brainstem, so you find it by its position in a cross section.
notes: It is a net of gray matter, not white matter, and it runs through the core of the brainstem rather than around its outside.
The reticular formation runs through the brainstem, from the medulla to the midbrain. Its ascending fibers reach the cortex, but its neurons are in the brainstem.
Correct. It is a loose net of scattered neurons in the brainstem core, with no sharp borders or surface landmark.
It is not one compact nucleus, and it is not in the cerebellum. It is a loose net spread through the whole brainstem core.
questions.answerText: It is a loose net of scattered neurons in the core, with no sharp borders

questions.q: On a midsagittal section, you see a small cut oval in the middle of the thalamus, crossing a narrow midline cavity. What is the oval, and which cavity does it cross?
options: The pineal gland, crossing the cerebral aqueduct
The massa intermedia, crossing the third ventricle
A mammillary body, crossing the fourth ventricle
The massa intermedia, crossing the lateral ventricle
questions.why: The two thalami sit on either side of the third ventricle, the narrow midline cavity of the diencephalon. The massa intermedia (interthalamic adhesion) is a small bridge of gray matter that crosses the third ventricle and joins them. On a midsagittal section it appears as a small cut oval in the middle of the thalamus, though some people do not have one.
notes: The pineal gland projects backward from the roof of the third ventricle, above the midbrain. It sits at the back, not in the middle of the thalamus.
Correct. The massa intermedia is a small bridge of gray matter that crosses the third ventricle and joins the two thalami.
The mammillary bodies are small round bumps on the underside of the hypothalamus. The fourth ventricle lies behind the pons, far from the thalamus.
The oval is right, but the lateral ventricles are in the cerebral hemispheres. The midline cavity between the thalami is the third ventricle.
questions.answerText: The massa intermedia, crossing the third ventricle

questions.q: A tumor grows in the small pine-cone-shaped gland that projects backward from the roof of the third ventricle. Which part of the diencephalon holds this gland, and which part of the brainstem lies just below it?
options: The epithalamus, with the midbrain just below
The thalamus, with the cerebellum just below
The hypothalamus, with the pons just below
The epithalamus, with the medulla just below
questions.why: The epithalamus is the small, posterior, upper part of the diencephalon and forms part of the roof of the third ventricle. Its main structure is the pineal gland, which projects backward from that roof. The gland sits above the midbrain, the top region of the brainstem.
notes: Correct. The pineal gland belongs to the epithalamus and projects backward above the midbrain.
The thalamus forms the upper side walls of the third ventricle and holds the massa intermedia. The pineal gland belongs to the epithalamus, behind and above it.
The hypothalamus forms the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle, not its roof. The pons is also lower than the region just beneath the pineal gland.
The epithalamus is right, but the medulla is the lowest part of the brainstem. The midbrain lies right below the diencephalon.
questions.answerText: The epithalamus, with the midbrain just below

questions.q: On the inferior surface of the brain, you start at the optic chiasm and move backward along the midline. Which two structures do you meet next, in order, and which part of the diencephalon do they belong to?
options: The pineal gland, then the mammillary bodies, both of the thalamus
The infundibulum, then the pineal gland, both of the epithalamus
The infundibulum, then the mammillary bodies, both of the hypothalamus
The mammillary bodies, then the infundibulum, both of the hypothalamus
questions.why: Three landmarks of the hypothalamus show on the inferior surface of the brain. The optic chiasm sits at the front. Behind it is the infundibulum, the stalk that connects the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland, and behind that are the two small round mammillary bodies.
notes: The pineal gland is part of the epithalamus on the roof of the third ventricle, and the mammillary bodies are part of the hypothalamus. Neither belongs to the thalamus.
The infundibulum belongs to the hypothalamus, and the pineal gland sits on the upper back of the diencephalon. It does not show on the inferior surface.
Correct. Behind the optic chiasm come the infundibulum and then the mammillary bodies, landmarks of the hypothalamus.
These belong to the hypothalamus, but the order is reversed. The infundibulum comes right behind the chiasm, and the mammillary bodies are behind it.
questions.answerText: The infundibulum, then the mammillary bodies, both of the hypothalamus

questions.q: On a model, you follow the largest of the three thick white stalks from the cerebellum forward into the pons. Which peduncle is it, and where does most of its input come from?
options: The middle cerebellar peduncle, carrying output to the thalamus
The middle cerebellar peduncle, carrying input from the pontine nuclei
The superior cerebellar peduncle, carrying input from the pontine nuclei
The inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying input from the spinal cord
questions.why: Each pair of cerebellar peduncles joins a different part of the brainstem: superior to the midbrain, middle to the pons, and inferior to the medulla. The middle cerebellar peduncle is the largest. It carries input from the pontine nuclei, which relay signals from the cerebral cortex into the cerebellum.
notes: The peduncle is right, but it carries input to the cerebellum. Output toward the midbrain and thalamus travels in the superior peduncle.
Correct. The middle cerebellar peduncle is the largest and joins the pons, carrying input from the pontine nuclei.
The superior peduncle joins the midbrain and carries mostly output from the deep cerebellar nuclei. The stalk into the pons is the middle peduncle.
The inferior peduncle does carry input from the spinal cord, but it joins the medulla. The largest stalk into the pons is the middle peduncle.
questions.answerText: The middle cerebellar peduncle, carrying input from the pontine nuclei

questions.q: A midsagittal cut through the cerebellum shows a narrow midline strip with a branching white tree inside it and fine leaf-like folds along its edge. What is the strip, and what are the folds?
options: The vermis, with folia along its edge
The vermis, with gyri along its edge
The arbor vitae, with sulci along its edge
A cerebellar hemisphere, with folia along its edge
questions.why: The two cerebellar hemispheres are joined in the midline by a narrow strip called the vermis, so a midsagittal cut passes right through it. Inside, the white matter branches like a tree, the arbor vitae. The surface is folded into folia, thin parallel folds that are much finer than the gyri of the cerebrum.
notes: Correct. The midline strip is the vermis, the white tree is the arbor vitae, and the fine folds are folia.
The strip is right, but gyri are the larger ridges of the cerebrum. The fine leaf-like folds of the cerebellum are called folia.
The arbor vitae is the branching white tree inside the strip, not the strip itself. The folds of the cerebellar surface are folia.
The folds are folia, but the hemispheres lie to each side. A cut down the midline passes through the vermis that joins them.
questions.answerText: The vermis, with folia along its edge

questions.q: On the front of a brain model, you find the groove where the rounded bulge of the brainstem meets the tapering lowest region. What is this groove, and which cranial nerves leave along it?
options: The foramen magnum, where CN IX, X, and XII leave
The pontomedullary junction, where CN III and IV leave
The cerebral peduncle, where CN VI to VIII leave
The pontomedullary junction, where CN VI to VIII leave
questions.why: The rounded bulge is the pons, and the tapering lowest region is the medulla oblongata. The groove where they meet on the front surface is the pontomedullary junction. It is a useful landmark because three cranial nerves, VI, VII, and VIII, leave the brainstem along it.
notes: The foramen magnum is the skull opening where the medulla becomes the spinal cord. It is a bony opening, not a groove on the brainstem.
The groove is right, but CN III and IV leave the midbrain, above the pons. CN VI, VII, and VIII leave at this junction.
The cerebral peduncles are the stalks on the front of the midbrain. They are above the pons, not at its lower border.
Correct. The groove between the pons and medulla is the pontomedullary junction, where CN VI, VII, and VIII leave.
questions.answerText: The pontomedullary junction, where CN VI to VIII leave

questions.q: A lesion damages the lowest region of the brainstem, the part that becomes the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. Which region is it, and which cerebellar peduncles attach to it?
options: The pons, with the middle cerebellar peduncles
The medulla oblongata, with the inferior cerebellar peduncles
The midbrain, with the superior cerebellar peduncles
The medulla oblongata, with the middle cerebellar peduncles
questions.why: The brainstem runs midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata from top to bottom. The medulla is the lowest and becomes the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. The cerebellar peduncles attach in the same top-to-bottom order, so the inferior peduncles attach to the medulla.
notes: The pons is the middle region, and the middle peduncles do attach to it. But the pons does not continue as the spinal cord.
Correct. The medulla is continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum, and the inferior peduncles attach to it.
The midbrain is the highest region, just below the diencephalon, and the superior peduncles attach to it. It is the farthest region from the spinal cord.
The region is right, but the middle peduncles attach to the pons. The medulla gets the inferior peduncles.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata, with the inferior cerebellar peduncles

questions.q: On a cross section of the midbrain, which structures lie on the tectum, behind the cerebral aqueduct?
options: The substantia nigra and crus cerebri
The cerebral peduncles
The tegmentum and its cranial nerve nuclei
The superior and inferior colliculi
questions.why: The cerebral aqueduct is the small hole near the back of a midbrain cross section, and it orients the specimen. Everything behind it is the roof, the tectum, which carries the four rounded bumps called the corpora quadrigemina. These are the superior and inferior colliculi.
notes: These lie toward the front of the midbrain, with the substantia nigra between the crus cerebri and the tegmentum. They are well in front of the aqueduct.
The cerebral peduncles form the front of the midbrain and carry descending motor tracts. They are in front of the aqueduct, not behind it.
The tegmentum is the core of the midbrain between the aqueduct and the crura. It lies in front of the aqueduct, not on the roof.
Correct. The tectum is the roof behind the aqueduct, and it carries the four colliculi.
questions.answerText: The superior and inferior colliculi

questions.q: Which list orders the parts of the midbrain from front to back on a cross section?
options: Crus cerebri, substantia nigra, tegmentum, cerebral aqueduct, tectum
Tectum, cerebral aqueduct, tegmentum, substantia nigra, crus cerebri
Substantia nigra, crus cerebri, cerebral aqueduct, tegmentum, tectum
Crus cerebri, tegmentum, substantia nigra, tectum, cerebral aqueduct
questions.why: The most anterior part of each cerebral peduncle is the crus cerebri. Behind it lies the dark substantia nigra, then the tegmentum, the core of the midbrain. The cerebral aqueduct sits near the back, and the tectum with its colliculi forms the roof behind it.
notes: Correct. From the front, the crus cerebri comes first, then the substantia nigra, the tegmentum, the aqueduct, and the tectum at the back.
This list runs from back to front. The tectum is the roof at the back, and the crus cerebri is the most anterior part.
The crus cerebri is the most anterior part, in front of the substantia nigra. The tegmentum lies in front of the aqueduct, not behind it.
The substantia nigra lies between the crus cerebri and the tegmentum, and the tectum lies behind the aqueduct. Both are out of place here.
questions.answerText: Crus cerebri, substantia nigra, tegmentum, cerebral aqueduct, tectum

questions.q: On a midbrain specimen, a cranial nerve leaves the front surface in the gap between the two thick stalks. Which nerve is it, and what are the stalks?
options: The oculomotor nerve (CN III), between the inferior colliculi
The trochlear nerve (CN IV), between the cerebral peduncles
The oculomotor nerve (CN III), between the cerebral peduncles
The trochlear nerve (CN IV), between the superior colliculi
questions.why: The front of the midbrain is formed by the two cerebral peduncles, thick stalks that carry descending motor tracts. Two cranial nerves leave the midbrain. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) leaves the front, in the gap between the peduncles, while the trochlear nerve (CN IV) leaves the back, just below the inferior colliculi.
notes: The nerve is right, but the colliculi are on the tectum at the back. CN III leaves the front, between the cerebral peduncles.
The stalks are right, but the trochlear nerve leaves the back of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculi. The nerve between the peduncles is CN III.
Correct. CN III leaves the front of the midbrain in the gap between the two cerebral peduncles.
The trochlear nerve does leave the back, but below the inferior colliculi, not between the superior colliculi. The question describes the front surface.
questions.answerText: The oculomotor nerve (CN III), between the cerebral peduncles

questions.q: A midsagittal model shows a diamond-shaped space behind the pons with the cerebellum over its roof. If the narrow channel that opens into this space from above were blocked, which channel would it be, and which ventricle would no longer send fluid down?
options: The central canal, from the spinal cord
The cerebral aqueduct, from the third ventricle
The cerebral aqueduct, from a lateral ventricle
An interventricular foramen, from a lateral ventricle
questions.why: The diamond-shaped space behind the pons, with the cerebellum over its roof, is the fourth ventricle. The cerebral aqueduct opens into it from above. The aqueduct carries cerebrospinal fluid down through the midbrain from the third ventricle, so a blocked aqueduct would cut the fourth ventricle off from the third.
notes: The central canal runs downward from the bottom of the fourth ventricle into the spinal cord. It is below the fourth ventricle, not a channel opening into it from above.
Correct. The space is the fourth ventricle, and the cerebral aqueduct opens into it from above, carrying CSF from the third ventricle.
The channel is right, but the aqueduct drains the third ventricle. The lateral ventricles empty into the third ventricle first.
The interventricular foramina join each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle. They do not open into the fourth ventricle.
questions.answerText: The cerebral aqueduct, from the third ventricle

questions.q: A small lesion damages the back part of the pons, just in front of the fourth ventricle. Which part of the pons is this, and what does it hold?
options: The middle cerebellar peduncle, which holds the dentate nucleus
The tectum, which holds the colliculi
The basilar pons, which holds the pontine nuclei
The tegmentum, which holds cranial nerve nuclei
questions.why: The pons has a front part and a back part. The basilar pons in front is a thick band of crosswise fibers with the pontine nuclei scattered through it. The back part is the tegmentum, which carries cranial nerve nuclei and part of the reticular formation, and it forms part of the floor of the fourth ventricle.
notes: The middle peduncles are white matter stalks on the sides of the pons, and the dentate nucleus is a deep nucleus inside the cerebellum. Neither is the back part of the pons.
The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, behind the cerebral aqueduct. It is not part of the pons.
The basilar pons and its pontine nuclei are on the front surface of the pons. A lesion just in front of the fourth ventricle is in the back part.
Correct. The back part of the pons is its tegmentum, which holds cranial nerve nuclei and part of the reticular formation.
questions.answerText: The tegmentum, which holds cranial nerve nuclei

questions.q: Which two cranial nerves have no nucleus in the brainstem?
options: CN I and CN II
CN XI and CN XII
CN V and CN VIII
CN III and CN IV
questions.why: Cranial nerves I (olfactory) and II (optic) connect to the forebrain, so they have no nucleus in the brainstem. The nuclei of III through X and XII are housed in the brainstem. The nucleus of XI sits just below it, in the upper cervical spinal cord.
notes: Correct. The olfactory (I) and optic (II) nerves connect to the forebrain, so they have no brainstem nucleus.

The CN XII nucleus is in the medulla, so this pair does not fit. CN XI has its nucleus just below the brainstem, but the two nerves with no brainstem nucleus at all are the ones that connect to the forebrain.
CN V is assigned to the pons, and CN VIII has its nuclei at the junction of the pons and medulla. Both are in the brainstem.
The nuclei of CN III and IV are in the midbrain, the top region of the brainstem.
questions.answerText: CN I and CN II

questions.q: Where does the motor nucleus of the accessory nerve (CN XI) sit?
options: In the pons of the brainstem
In the upper cervical spinal cord
In the midbrain of the brainstem
In the medulla oblongata of the brainstem
questions.why: Most cranial nerve nuclei from III to XII sit in the brainstem, but the accessory nerve is the exception. Its motor nucleus is in the upper cervical spinal cord, just below the medulla. Its rootlets rise through the foramen magnum and then leave the skull with the vagus nerve, which is why it is grouped with the medulla in the 2-2-4-4 rule.
notes: The pons holds the nuclei of CN V, VI, VII, and VIII. CN XI is much lower.
Correct. The CN XI motor nucleus sits in the upper cervical cord, just below the brainstem.
The midbrain holds the nuclei of CN III and IV, the highest of the brainstem nuclei. CN XI is at the opposite end.
CN XI is grouped with the medulla in the 2-2-4-4 rule, but its motor nucleus actually sits below the medulla in the upper cervical cord.
questions.answerText: In the upper cervical spinal cord

questions.q: Which brainstem region houses the nuclei of cranial nerves IX, X, and XII?
options: The upper cervical spinal cord
The midbrain
The medulla oblongata
The pons
questions.why: The cranial nerve nuclei line up from top to bottom in the same order as the nerve numbers. The midbrain holds III and IV, and the pons holds V through VIII. The medulla, the lowest region, holds IX, X, and XII.
notes: The upper cervical cord holds the motor nucleus of CN XI. The nuclei of IX, X, and XII are in the medulla above it.
The midbrain holds only III and IV, the first of the brainstem nuclei.
Correct. The medulla holds the nuclei of IX, X, and XII.
The pons holds the nuclei of V, VI, VII, and VIII, which come before IX in number and sit higher.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: On a brainstem model, a thin cranial nerve leaves the back surface, just below the inferior colliculi. Which nerve is it, and which region holds its nucleus?
options: The oculomotor nerve (CN III), with its nucleus in the midbrain
The abducens nerve (CN VI), with its nucleus in the pons
The trochlear nerve (CN IV), with its nucleus in the pons
The trochlear nerve (CN IV), with its nucleus in the midbrain
questions.why: The inferior colliculi are bumps on the tectum, the roof of the midbrain. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) leaves the back of the midbrain just below them. A nerve usually leaves near the level of its nucleus, and the midbrain holds the nuclei of III and IV.
notes: CN III's nucleus is in the midbrain, but CN III leaves the front of the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles, not the back.
CN VI leaves the front of the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, near the midline. It does not leave the back below the colliculi.
The nerve is right, but its nucleus is in the midbrain, at the same level where it leaves. The pons holds V through VIII.
Correct. CN IV leaves the back of the midbrain just below the inferior colliculi, and its nucleus is in the midbrain.
questions.answerText: The trochlear nerve (CN IV), with its nucleus in the midbrain

questions.q: A lesion cuts only the reticular formation fibers that run down to the spinal cord. Which component is cut, and what is most affected?
options: The descending component, with alertness and attention affected
The descending component, with resting muscle tone and posture affected
The ascending reticular activating system, with alertness affected
The ascending reticular activating system, with muscle tone and posture affected
questions.why: The reticular formation has two components that run in opposite directions. The ascending reticular activating system (RAS) sends fibers up through the thalamus to the cortex and keeps it awake and alert. The descending component sends fibers down to the spinal cord and helps set the resting tone of skeletal muscles and keep posture.
notes: The component is right, but alertness and attention depend on the ascending RAS. The descending fibers set muscle tone and posture.
Correct. Fibers running down to the cord belong to the descending component, which helps set resting muscle tone and posture.
This pairing is true of the RAS, but the RAS runs up to the cortex. The question describes fibers that run down to the spinal cord.
The RAS sends fibers up through the thalamus to the cortex, not down to the cord. Muscle tone and posture belong to the descending component.
questions.answerText: The descending component, with resting muscle tone and posture affected

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: What are the ventricles of the brain?
options: The fluid-filled chambers within the brain
The dural folds that partition the cranium
The raised folds of the cerebral cortex
The deep gray matter masses of the cerebrum
questions.why: The ventricles are connected, fluid-filled chambers deep within the brain, lined by ependymal cells. Cerebrospinal fluid is made in them by the choroid plexus. There are four: two lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, and the fourth ventricle.
notes: Correct. The ventricles are the fluid-filled chambers inside the brain.

These are the dural reflections, such as the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, which are folds of dura mater. Pick them if the question asked what separates the hemispheres or the cerebrum from the cerebellum.
These are the gyri, the ridges of the folded cortex. Pick gyri if the question asked about the raised folds on the surface of the cerebrum.
These are the basal nuclei (basal ganglia), gray matter masses buried in the cerebral white matter that help regulate movement. They would be the answer for a question about deep gray matter.
questions.answerText: The fluid-filled chambers within the brain

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Which ventricle is the fluid-filled cavity located within the diencephalon?
options: The fourth ventricle
The third ventricle
A lateral ventricle
The central canal
questions.why: The third ventricle is the narrow, midline cavity enclosed by the diencephalon, with the thalamus forming its side walls. It receives CSF from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina and sends it on through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle. Like the other ventricles, it contains choroid plexus.
notes: The fourth ventricle lies between the brainstem (pons and upper medulla) and the cerebellum. It would be the answer if the question asked which ventricle sits in front of the cerebellum.
Correct. The third ventricle lies within the diencephalon.
The lateral ventricles are paired, one in each cerebral hemisphere. Pick a lateral ventricle if the question asked which ventricle lies within the cerebrum.
The central canal is the CSF channel running the length of the spinal cord. Pick it if the question asked which space is continuous with the fourth ventricle inside the cord.
questions.answerText: The third ventricle

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Which meningeal layer is the outermost of the three?
options: The choroid plexus
The arachnoid mater
The dura mater
The pia mater
questions.why: The dura mater is the outermost meninx, a tough membrane of dense connective tissue. Around the brain it has two layers, an outer periosteal layer against the skull and an inner meningeal layer. Its name means tough mother, which fits its role as the strong outer covering.
notes: The choroid plexus is a network of capillaries in the ventricles that produces CSF, not a meningeal layer. Pick it if the question asked where cerebrospinal fluid is made.
The arachnoid mater is the middle meninx, a delicate, lace-like membrane. Pick it if the question asked which layer forms the arachnoid granulations.
Correct. The dura mater is the outermost meninx.

The pia mater is the innermost meninx, a thin vascular membrane that clings to the surface of the brain and cord. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer follows every gyrus and sulcus.
questions.answerText: The dura mater

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Which meningeal layer lies directly against the surface of the brain and spinal cord?
options: The ependymal lining
The pia mater
The dura mater
The arachnoid mater
questions.why: The pia mater is the innermost meninx, a thin membrane rich in blood vessels that clings directly to the brain and spinal cord and dips into every sulcus. Its name means tender mother. Around the cord it also forms the denticulate ligaments and the filum terminale, which anchor the cord in place.
notes: The ependymal lining is the layer of glial cells that lines the inside of the ventricles and central canal, not the outer surface. Pick ependymal cells if the question asked what lines the fluid-filled cavities inside the CNS.
Correct. The pia mater clings directly to the brain and cord.
The dura mater is the tough outermost layer, lying against the skull or vertebral canal rather than the brain. Pick it if the question asked which layer forms the dural venous sinuses.

The arachnoid mater is the delicate middle layer, separated from the brain by the CSF-filled subarachnoid space. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer lies between the dura and pia.
questions.answerText: The pia mater

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: How many meningeal membranes wrap the brain and spinal cord?
options: Three
Two
Four
Five
questions.why: Three connective tissue membranes, the meninges, wrap the brain and spinal cord. From outside in they are the dura mater, the arachnoid mater, and the pia mater. The same three layers continue from the cranium down through the vertebral canal.
notes: Correct. There are three meninges.
Two is the number of layers in the cranial dura (periosteal and meningeal), not the number of meninges. Students who count the dura's layers instead of the membranes pick this.
Four would add a layer that does not exist. A student who counts the CSF-filled subarachnoid space or the periosteum as a membrane may land on four.
Five has no basis in the meninges. It can come from mixing the meningeal layers with the spaces between them.
questions.answerText: Three

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: What is the name of the middle meningeal layer, a delicate, web-like membrane?
options: The arachnoid mater
The dura mater
The dural sinus
The pia mater
questions.why: The arachnoid mater is the middle meninx, a delicate membrane whose fine, web-like strands cross the subarachnoid space below it. Its name comes from the Greek word for spider, because of that web-like look. It also forms the arachnoid granulations, where CSF is returned to the blood.
notes: Correct. The arachnoid mater is the web-like middle layer.
The dura mater is the tough outermost layer, not the delicate middle one. Pick it if the question asked which meninx is built of dense connective tissue.
A dural sinus is a venous channel formed where the two layers of the cranial dura separate, not a meningeal layer. Pick it if the question asked where venous blood from the brain collects.
The pia mater is the thin innermost layer that clings to the brain surface. It would be the answer for a question about the meninx that follows every sulcus.
questions.answerText: The arachnoid mater

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Which meningeal space contains cerebrospinal fluid around the brain and spinal cord?
options: The epidural space
The subdural space
The subarachnoid space
The dural venous sinuses
questions.why: The subarachnoid space lies between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, and it is filled with cerebrospinal fluid that bathes the whole surface of the brain and cord. Below the end of the cord, this space widens into the lumbar cistern. That is why a lumbar puncture targets the subarachnoid space to sample CSF.
notes: The epidural space lies between the spinal dura and the vertebral bone and holds fat and veins, not CSF. It would be the answer if the question asked where an epidural injection is placed.
The subdural space lies between the dura and the arachnoid and is only a potential space with a thin film of fluid. Pick it if the question asked where a subdural hematoma collects.
Correct. CSF around the brain and cord is in the subarachnoid space.
The dural venous sinuses carry venous blood, and they receive CSF only after it is reabsorbed at the arachnoid granulations. Pick them if the question asked where CSF ends up after reabsorption.
questions.answerText: The subarachnoid space

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Where is the choroid plexus located?
options: Along the central canal of the cord
Within the dura mater
In the subarachnoid space
In the ventricles of the brain
questions.why: The choroid plexus is a network of capillaries wrapped in ependymal cells, found in the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles. It produces cerebrospinal fluid, which is why CSF is said to be made in the ventricles. From there the fluid circulates out into the subarachnoid space.
notes: The central canal is lined by ependymal cells and holds CSF, but it does not contain choroid plexus. Pick it for a question about the CSF channel continuous with the fourth ventricle.
The dura mater contains the dural venous sinuses, which drain venous blood, not the choroid plexus. It would be the answer if the question asked where the superior sagittal sinus is found.
The subarachnoid space holds CSF after it leaves the ventricles, but no choroid plexus lies there. Pick it if the question asked where CSF bathes the outer surface of the brain.
Correct. The choroid plexus sits in the ventricles.
questions.answerText: In the ventricles of the brain

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: How many lateral ventricles are there in the brain?
options: Three
Four
Two
One
questions.why: The lateral ventricles are paired, with one inside each cerebral hemisphere. Each connects to the single third ventricle through an interventricular foramen. Together with the third and fourth ventricles, they make four ventricles in all.
notes: Three is the number of ventricles a student gets by counting both lateral ventricles plus only one of the unpaired ventricles. The lateral ventricles alone number two.
Four is the total number of ventricles in the brain (two lateral, the third, and the fourth). Pick four if the question asked how many ventricles the brain has altogether.
Correct. There are two lateral ventricles.
One would describe the third or fourth ventricle, each of which is a single midline chamber. The lateral ventricles are paired because there are two hemispheres.
questions.answerText: Two

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Which structure runs the length of the spinal cord and is continuous above with the fourth ventricle?
options: The central canal
The subarachnoid space
The cerebral aqueduct
The interventricular foramen
questions.why: The central canal is a narrow channel in the center of the spinal cord, lined by ependymal cells and filled with cerebrospinal fluid. At its upper end it opens into the fourth ventricle. Some of the CSF in the system passes into it, but most leaves the fourth ventricle through the apertures into the subarachnoid space.
notes: Correct. The central canal runs through the cord and joins the fourth ventricle.

The subarachnoid space surrounds the outside of the cord, between the arachnoid and pia, rather than running through its center. Pick it if the question asked where CSF bathes the surface of the cord.
The cerebral aqueduct is the channel through the midbrain that connects the third ventricle to the fourth. Pick it if the question asked what links those two ventricles.
The interventricular foramen connects a lateral ventricle to the third ventricle. It would be the answer for the first opening CSF passes through after leaving a lateral ventricle.
questions.answerText: The central canal

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Which space around the spinal cord is the site of an epidural injection?
options: The subarachnoid space
The subdural space
The central canal
The epidural space
questions.why: The epidural space lies between the spinal dura mater and the bone of the vertebral canal, and it is filled with fat and veins. Anesthetic injected there bathes the spinal nerve roots without the needle entering the dura. The prefix epi means upon, so the space sits on the outside of the dura.
notes: The subarachnoid space lies deeper, between the arachnoid and pia, and holds CSF. It would be the answer if the question asked where a lumbar puncture draws fluid.
The subdural space lies between the dura and the arachnoid and is only a potential space. Pick it if the question asked where a subdural hematoma collects.
The central canal is the CSF channel inside the spinal cord itself, which no injection targets. Pick it if the question asked which channel is continuous with the fourth ventricle.
Correct. An epidural injection goes into the epidural space.
questions.answerText: The epidural space

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: What clear fluid fills the ventricles and the subarachnoid space?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid
Venous blood
Synovial fluid
Lymph
questions.why: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a clear, watery fluid that fills the ventricles, the central canal, and the subarachnoid space around the brain and cord. It floats the brain so it does not crush its own base, cushions the CNS against blows, and keeps a stable chemical environment around the neurons. It is made by the choroid plexus and reabsorbed at the arachnoid granulations.
notes: Correct. Cerebrospinal fluid fills the ventricles and subarachnoid space.
Venous blood from the brain drains into the dural venous sinuses, not the ventricles or subarachnoid space. Pick it if the question asked what the superior sagittal sinus carries.
Synovial fluid lubricates the joint cavity of a synovial joint. Pick it if the question asked what fills the space inside a knee or shoulder joint.
Lymph is fluid carried in lymphatic vessels and filtered by lymph nodes. It would be the answer for a question about the fluid in the thoracic duct.
questions.answerText: Cerebrospinal fluid

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: CSF enters the cerebral aqueduct from which ventricle?
options: The central canal
The third ventricle
A lateral ventricle
The fourth ventricle
questions.why: The cerebral aqueduct is the narrow channel through the midbrain that carries CSF from the third ventricle down to the fourth ventricle. The third ventricle sits in the diencephalon, just above the midbrain. Because the aqueduct is so narrow, it is one of the points where a blockage can back up CSF.
notes: The central canal is in the spinal cord and connects to the fourth ventricle, far below the aqueduct's starting point. Pick it for a question about the CSF channel inside the cord.
Correct. The third ventricle drains into the cerebral aqueduct.

A lateral ventricle sends its CSF into the third ventricle through an interventricular foramen, not directly into the aqueduct. Pick it if the question asked where CSF flow through the ventricles begins.
The fourth ventricle receives CSF from the aqueduct rather than sending fluid into it. It would be the answer if the question asked where the cerebral aqueduct empties.
questions.answerText: The third ventricle

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: The cranial dura mater has two layers. Where they separate, they form channels that collect venous blood from the brain. What are these channels called?
options: The interventricular foramina
The dural venous sinuses
The arachnoid granulations
The subdural spaces
questions.why: The two layers of the cranial dura, the periosteal and meningeal layers, are fused except where they part to form the dural venous sinuses. These channels collect venous blood from the brain and CSF returned by the arachnoid granulations. The main route runs from the superior sagittal sinus to the confluence of sinuses, through the transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and out the internal jugular veins.
notes: The interventricular foramina are openings that connect each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle. They would be the answer for a question about CSF flow between ventricles.
Correct. The dural venous sinuses form between the two dural layers.
Arachnoid granulations are projections of the arachnoid mater that push into the dural sinuses and return CSF to the blood. Pick them if the question asked where CSF is reabsorbed.
The subdural space lies between the dura and the arachnoid, below the dura, rather than between the dura's own two layers. Pick it if the question asked where a subdural hematoma collects.
questions.answerText: The dural venous sinuses

questions.topic: Meninges, ventricles, CSF and brain blood supply
questions.q: Cerebrospinal fluid is returned to the venous blood through projections of which meningeal layer?
options: The dura mater
The pia mater
The ependymal lining
The arachnoid mater
questions.why: The arachnoid mater sends small projections called arachnoid granulations up through the dura into the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal sinus.
