Correct. The patellar reflex is a spinal reflex, processed in the gray matter of the cord.
questions.answerText: In the spinal cord

questions.q: Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the thigh muscle. Which reflex arc component detects this stretch?
options: The integration center
The motor neuron
The receptor
The effector
questions.why: The receptor is the first component of a reflex arc; it detects the stimulus and triggers a signal in the sensory neuron. In the patellar reflex, the stimulus is the stretch of the thigh muscle caused by tapping its tendon, and receptors in that muscle detect it. The same muscle then serves as the effector when it contracts.
notes: The integration center is the synapse in the spinal cord where the signal is processed, not where the stretch is detected. Choose it for a question about where the signal is processed.
The motor neuron carries the command from the cord back to the muscle. It would be right for a question about the component just before the effector.
Correct. The receptor detects the stretch and starts the signal.
The effector is the muscle that contracts at the end of the arc. The thigh muscle is the effector in this reflex, but the structure that senses the stretch is the receptor within it.
questions.answerText: The receptor

questions.q: A spinal pathway crosses from one side of the CNS to the other, so the right side of the brain serves the left side of the body. Which term names this crossing?
options: Decussation
Integration
Divergence
Convergence
questions.why: Decussation is the crossing of a pathway from one side of the CNS to the other. Because most sensory and motor pathways decussate, each half of the brain senses and controls the opposite half of the body. This crossing explains why damage to one side of the brain affects the opposite side of the body.
notes: Correct. Decussation is the crossing of a pathway to the opposite side.
Integration is the combining of incoming signals so a neuron produces a single response. It would be right for a question about what happens when many signals reach one neuron.
Divergence is a circuit pattern in which one neuron spreads its signal to many. Choose it for a question about one neuron reaching many targets.
Convergence is a circuit pattern in which many neurons feed onto one. Pick it for a question about many inputs meeting on a single neuron.
questions.answerText: Decussation

questions.q: Which sequence places the five components of a reflex arc in order from stimulus to response?
options: Sensory neuron, receptor, integration center, effector, motor neuron
Receptor, motor neuron, integration center, sensory neuron, effector
Receptor, sensory neuron, motor neuron, integration center, effector
Receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector
questions.why: Every reflex arc runs the same five components in order. The receptor detects the stimulus, the sensory neuron carries the signal to the CNS, the integration center processes it, the motor neuron carries the command out, and the effector, a muscle or gland, carries out the response. The order follows the three functions of the nervous system: sensory input, integration, and motor output.
notes: This puts the sensory neuron before the receptor and the effector before the motor neuron. Nothing can travel until the receptor detects the stimulus, and the effector can only act after the motor neuron delivers the command.
This swaps the sensory and motor neurons. The sensory neuron must carry the signal into the CNS before the motor neuron can carry a command out.
This skips straight from the sensory neuron to the motor neuron, then processes the signal afterward. Processing in the CNS has to happen before a command goes out.
Correct. The signal is detected, carried in, processed, carried out, and acted on.
questions.answerText: Receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector

questions.q: In a withdrawal reflex, which sequence traces the signal from the structure that detects the stimulus to the synapses where it is processed?
options: Receptor, sensory neuron, integration center
Effector, motor neuron, integration center
Receptor, integration center, sensory neuron
Sensory neuron, receptor, integration center
questions.why: The first half of a reflex arc brings information in. The receptor in the skin detects the painful stimulus, the sensory neuron carries the signal into the spinal cord, and the integration center, here a set of synapses with interneurons in the cord, processes it. The second half then sends the command out through the motor neuron to the effector.
notes: Correct. These are the first three components of the arc, in order.
These are the last three components run backward. This sequence would fit a question that asked for the output half of the arc in reverse.
This processes the signal before it has been carried into the CNS. The sensory neuron is the link that brings the signal to the integration center.
This puts the sensory neuron before the receptor, but the sensory neuron has nothing to carry until the receptor detects the stimulus.
questions.answerText: Receptor, sensory neuron, integration center

questions.q: In a withdrawal reflex, the signal has just been processed in the spinal cord. Which sequence completes the arc from that point?
options: Integration center, sensory neuron, effector
Integration center, motor neuron, receptor
Integration center, motor neuron, effector
Integration center, effector, motor neuron
questions.why: The second half of a reflex arc sends the response out. From the integration center in the spinal cord, a motor neuron carries the command out through the anterior root to the effector. In a withdrawal reflex, the effector is the set of muscles that pull the limb away from the painful stimulus.
notes: The sensory neuron brings the signal into the cord earlier in the arc. Commands leave the cord on a motor neuron.
The receptor is the first component of the arc, where the stimulus was detected, not the last. The command goes to the effector, the muscle that pulls the hand away.
Correct. The command leaves the cord on a motor neuron and reaches the muscle.
This has the muscle respond before the motor neuron has delivered the command. The motor neuron must come before the effector.
questions.answerText: Integration center, motor neuron, effector

questions.q: Classify three reflexes: the patellar reflex by its effector, the stretch reflex by its number of synapses, and the blink reflex by whether it is inborn. Which set of labels is correct?
options: Patellar is somatic, stretch is polysynaptic, blink is innate
Patellar is somatic, stretch is monosynaptic, blink is learned
Patellar is somatic, stretch is monosynaptic, blink is innate
Patellar is autonomic, stretch is monosynaptic, blink is innate
questions.why: Reflexes are classified in three separate ways. By effector, the patellar reflex is somatic because it acts on skeletal muscle. By synapse count, the stretch reflex is monosynaptic, and by origin, the blink reflex is innate because it is present from birth.
notes: The stretch reflex has a single synapse, so it is monosynaptic. Polysynaptic would fit the withdrawal reflex, which uses interneurons.
The first two labels are right, but the blink reflex is present at birth, so it is innate. Learned would fit catching a suddenly dropped object.
Correct. Each reflex is labeled by the right basis.
The patellar reflex acts on skeletal muscle in the thigh, so it is somatic. Autonomic would fit the pupillary light reflex, which acts on smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: Patellar is somatic, stretch is monosynaptic, blink is innate

questions.q: Which order runs from the smallest structure to the largest: a single axon, a tract, and a white column of the spinal cord?
options: White column, tract, axon
Axon, white column, tract
Tract, axon, white column
Axon, tract, white column
questions.why: The white matter of the spinal cord is organized in levels. A single axon is the smallest unit, many axons with a common origin and destination form a tract, and several tracts together make up a white column. The cord has anterior, posterior, and lateral white columns.
notes: This is the correct order run from largest to smallest. It would fit a question that asked for the order from the largest structure down.
This puts the column inside the tract, but it is the other way around: each white column holds several tracts.
This places the tract below a single axon, but a tract is a bundle of many axons, so it must be larger.
Correct. Axons group into tracts, and tracts group into columns.
questions.answerText: Axon, tract, white column

questions.q: The anterior horn of the spinal cord holds clusters of motor neuron cell bodies. Because these clusters lie inside the CNS, what are they called?
options: Ganglia
Nuclei
Tracts
Nerves
questions.why: The gray matter of the spinal cord is shaped into horns, and the anterior horn holds the somatic motor nuclei that drive skeletal muscle. A cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS is called a nucleus, so these clusters are nuclei. The axons of these motor neurons leave the cord through the anterior root.
notes: Ganglia are clusters of cell bodies outside the CNS, such as the posterior root ganglion. Pick ganglia when the cluster lies in the PNS.
Correct. Clusters of cell bodies inside the CNS are nuclei.
Tracts are bundles of axons in the CNS, found in the white columns rather than the gray horns. Choose tracts for a question about the white matter of the cord.
Nerves are bundles of axons outside the CNS. They would be right for a question about the spinal nerves leaving the vertebral canal.
questions.answerText: Nuclei

questions.q: In a reflex arc, which component carries the command from the CNS out to the effector?
options: The sensory neuron
The integration center
The motor neuron
The receptor
questions.why: The motor neuron is the fourth component of a reflex arc. It carries the command from the integration center in the CNS out to the effector, the muscle or gland that responds. Motor neurons are multipolar, and in a spinal reflex their cell bodies sit in the anterior horn of the cord.
notes: The sensory neuron carries the signal in the other direction, from the receptor into the CNS. Pick it for a question about the component that brings the signal in.
The integration center is where the signal is processed inside the CNS, before anything is sent out. Choose it for a question about where the signal is processed.
Correct. The motor neuron carries the command out to the muscle or gland.
The receptor is at the start of the arc, where the stimulus is detected. It would be right for a question about the first component.
questions.answerText: The motor neuron

questions.q: In a withdrawal reflex, arm muscles contract to pull the hand off a hot stove. Which reflex arc component are these muscles?
options: The receptor
The integration center
The motor neuron
The effector
questions.why: The effector is the final component of a reflex arc, the muscle or gland that carries out the response. In a withdrawal reflex, the effectors are the skeletal muscles that pull the limb away from the painful stimulus. They act once the motor neurons deliver the command from the spinal cord.
notes: The receptor is in the skin of the hand, where the heat is detected, not in the muscles that move the arm. Pick it for a question about what senses the heat.
The integration center is the set of synapses in the spinal cord where the signal is processed. Choose it for a question about where the decision to withdraw is made.
The motor neuron carries the command to the muscles, but it is a neuron, not the muscle itself. It would be right for a question about the component just before the effector.
Correct. The muscles that carry out the response are the effector.
questions.answerText: The effector

questions.q: In a reflex arc, which component carries the signal from the receptor to the CNS?
options: The motor neuron
The integration center
The sensory neuron
The effector
questions.why: The sensory neuron is the second component of a reflex arc. It carries the signal from the receptor into the CNS, entering the spinal cord through the posterior root, with its cell body in the posterior root ganglion. There it reaches the integration center.
notes: The motor neuron carries the command the other way, out of the CNS to the effector. Pick it for a question about the component that carries the response out.
The integration center is where the signal is processed inside the CNS, after the sensory neuron delivers it. It would be right for a question about the middle of the arc.
Correct. The sensory neuron carries the signal into the CNS.
The effector is the muscle or gland that responds at the end of the arc. Choose it for a question about the final component.
questions.answerText: The sensory neuron

questions.q: A reflex whose effector is skeletal muscle is which type?
options: A monosynaptic reflex
A somatic reflex
A learned reflex
An autonomic reflex
questions.why: When reflexes are classified by their effector, those that act on skeletal muscle are somatic reflexes, matching the somatic nervous system that controls skeletal muscle. Those that act on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or glands are autonomic reflexes. The patellar reflex is a common somatic example.
notes: Monosynaptic describes a reflex with one synapse, a classification by synapse count rather than effector. Choose it for a question about the stretch reflex.
Correct. Reflexes acting on skeletal muscle are somatic.
Learned describes a reflex built by practice, a classification by origin. It would be right for a question about catching a suddenly dropped object.
An autonomic reflex acts on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or a gland, not skeletal muscle. Pick it for a reflex such as the pupillary light reflex.
questions.answerText: A somatic reflex

questions.q: Which tracts carry sensory information up the spinal cord to the brain?
options: Anterior roots
Ascending tracts
Descending tracts
Commissural fibers
questions.why: The white matter of the spinal cord contains ascending and descending tracts. Ascending tracts carry sensory information up the cord to the brain. Descending tracts carry motor commands in the opposite direction.
notes: The anterior roots carry motor axons out of the cord to muscles and glands; they are not tracts within the cord. They would be right for a question about where motor axons leave the cord.
Correct. Ascending tracts carry sensory input up to the brain.
Descending tracts carry motor commands down from the brain to the body. Pick them for a question about motor pathways.
Commissural fibers, such as the corpus callosum, connect the right and left cerebral hemispheres rather than running up the cord. Choose them for a question about links between the hemispheres.
questions.answerText: Ascending tracts

questions.q: A clinician taps just below the kneecap and watches the leg kick. Which reflex is being tested?
options: The pupillary light reflex
The withdrawal reflex
The blink reflex
The patellar reflex
questions.why: The patellar, or knee-jerk, reflex is triggered by tapping the patellar tendon below the kneecap, which stretches the muscle on the front of the thigh and makes it contract. This one test checks the whole reflex arc: the receptor, the sensory and motor neurons, and the spinal cord between them. A missing reflex points to a break somewhere along that pathway.
notes: The pupillary light reflex changes the size of the pupil in response to light. It would be right for a question about shining a light in the eye.
The withdrawal reflex pulls a limb away from a painful stimulus, such as a hot surface. Pick it for a question about pulling the hand off a stove.
The blink reflex closes the eyelids when something approaches or touches the eye. Choose it for a question about protecting the eye.
Correct. Tapping the patellar tendon tests the patellar (knee-jerk) reflex.
questions.answerText: The patellar reflex

questions.q: Which structure is present in a polysynaptic reflex but absent from a monosynaptic reflex?
options: A sensory neuron
A receptor
An interneuron
A motor neuron
questions.why: A monosynaptic reflex has one synapse, where the sensory neuron connects directly to the motor neuron. A polysynaptic reflex has two or more synapses because one or more interneurons sit between the sensory and motor neurons. Interneurons are what add the extra synapses, as in the withdrawal reflex.
notes: Every reflex arc has a sensory neuron, so it cannot be what separates the two types. Pick it for a question about the component that carries the signal into the CNS.
Every reflex arc begins with a receptor that detects the stimulus. It would be right for a question about the first component of the arc.
Correct. Interneurons add the extra synapses in a polysynaptic reflex.
Every reflex arc has a motor neuron to carry the command out. Choose it for a question about the component that reaches the effector.
questions.answerText: An interneuron

questions.q: A stroke on the left side of the brain causes weakness on the right side of the body. Which feature of the pathways explains this?
options: Convergence of neuronal pools
Saltatory conduction
Decussation of pathways
Serial processing
questions.why: Most sensory and motor pathways decussate, meaning they cross to the opposite side of the CNS along their route. As a result, the right half of the brain controls and senses the left half of the body, and the left half of the brain serves the right. A stroke that damages the left side of the brain therefore weakens the right side of the body.
notes: Convergence is many neurons feeding onto one, a wiring pattern that does not explain a left and right switch. Pick it for a question about many inputs meeting on one neuron.
Saltatory conduction is the jumping of the impulse between nodes of Ranvier on a myelinated axon. It would be right for a question about why myelinated axons conduct fast.
Correct. Most pathways cross to the opposite side, so each half of the brain controls the opposite half of the body.
Serial processing is a signal passing along a single chain of neurons. Choose it for a question about the step-by-step chain of a reflex arc.
questions.answerText: Decussation of pathways

questions.q: In any reflex arc, the integration center lies in which part of the nervous system?
options: The posterior root ganglion
The peripheral nervous system
The effector organ
The central nervous system
questions.why: The integration center is the third component of a reflex arc, made of one or more synapses where the incoming signal is processed. These synapses always lie in the CNS, in the spinal cord for spinal reflexes or in the brainstem for cranial reflexes. The other components connect the CNS to the receptor and effector out in the body.
notes: The posterior root ganglion holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons, but no processing synapses. Choose it for a question about where sensory cell bodies sit.
The PNS holds the receptor, the sensory and motor axons, and the effector side of the arc, but not the integration center. Pick the PNS for a question about where the nerves of the arc run.
The effector is the muscle or gland that responds at the end of the arc. It would be right for a question about which component carries out the response.
Correct. The integration center is always made of synapses in the brain or spinal cord.
questions.answerText: The central nervous system

questions.q: Which class of tracts carries motor commands from the brain down to the body?
options: Descending tracts
Commissural fibers
Posterior roots
Ascending tracts
questions.why: Descending tracts run in the white matter of the spinal cord and carry motor commands from the brain down toward the body. They reach motor neurons in the cord, which then carry the commands out to the muscles. Ascending tracts carry sensory information the other way, up to the brain.
notes: Correct. Descending tracts carry motor commands down the cord.
Commissural fibers, such as the corpus callosum, connect the two cerebral hemispheres. They would be right for a question about how the hemispheres communicate.
Posterior roots carry sensory axons into the cord from the body; they are roots, not tracts. Choose them for a question about where sensory axons enter the cord.
Ascending tracts carry sensory information up to the brain, the opposite direction. Pick them for a question about sensory pathways.
questions.answerText: Descending tracts

questions.q: A patient has no patellar reflex on one side. Along which structure could the break lie?
options: The cerebral cortex
The corpus callosum
The reflex arc
The cerebellum
questions.why: The patellar reflex depends on every link of its reflex arc: the receptor in the thigh muscle, the sensory neuron, the integration center in the spinal cord, the motor neuron, and the thigh muscle as the effector. Tapping the tendon tests all of these at once. If the reflex is missing, the break could be at any point along that arc.
notes: The cerebral cortex handles conscious sensation and voluntary movement, but the patellar reflex runs through the spinal cord without it. Pick the cortex for a question about a voluntary movement.
The corpus callosum is the band of white matter connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, and it plays no part in a spinal reflex. Choose it for a question about communication between the hemispheres.
Correct. A missing reflex points to a break somewhere along the arc.
The cerebellum coordinates movement, but the patellar reflex can occur without it. It would be right for a question about smooth, coordinated movement.
questions.answerText: The reflex arc

questions.q: A withdrawal reflex pulls the hand off a hot surface using skeletal muscle, with interneurons in the spinal cord. Which description fits this reflex?
options: Monosynaptic and autonomic
Polysynaptic and autonomic
Monosynaptic and somatic
Polysynaptic and somatic
questions.why: Reflexes can be described by synapse count and by effector at the same time. The withdrawal reflex has interneurons between the sensory and motor neurons, so it has two or more synapses and is polysynaptic. Its effector is skeletal muscle in the arm, so it is also a somatic reflex.
notes: Both labels are wrong here: interneurons make the reflex polysynaptic, and skeletal muscle makes it somatic. This choice reverses both classifications.
Polysynaptic is right, but the effector is skeletal muscle, so the reflex is somatic. Autonomic would fit a reflex acting on smooth muscle, such as the pupillary light reflex.
Somatic is right, but interneurons add synapses, so the reflex is polysynaptic. Monosynaptic and somatic would describe the stretch reflex.
Correct. Interneurons make it polysynaptic, and skeletal muscle makes it somatic.
questions.answerText: Polysynaptic and somatic

questions.q: A spinal cord injury in the mid-back cuts through the tracts of the white matter. Why can the person no longer move the legs voluntarily?
options: The brain can no longer produce any motor commands at all
Descending tracts cannot carry commands past the injury
Sensory receptors in the legs stop detecting all stimuli
Ascending tracts can no longer carry commands down to the legs
questions.why: The white matter of the spinal cord holds ascending tracts, which carry sensory information up, and descending tracts, which carry motor commands down. A cord injury interrupts both, so function is lost below the level of the injury while everything above it is spared. Voluntary leg movement is lost because the descending tracts can no longer deliver the brain's commands to the motor neurons below the injury.
notes: The brain above the injury is undamaged and can still issue commands; they simply cannot get past the injured cord. Function above the injury is spared.
Correct. Motor commands from the brain cannot pass the damaged tracts.
The receptors in the legs still work, but their signals cannot travel up past the injury. Even working receptors would not restore voluntary movement, which depends on descending commands.
Ascending tracts carry sensory information up to the brain, not commands down. Their loss explains the loss of feeling below the injury, not the loss of movement.
questions.answerText: Descending tracts cannot carry commands past the injury

questions.q: A goalkeeper who has trained for years blocks a sudden shot before having time to think about it. Based on whether it is inborn or practiced, which class of reflex fits this response?
options: An autonomic reflex
A learned reflex
A monosynaptic reflex
An innate reflex
questions.why: When reflexes are classified by origin, innate reflexes are present from birth and learned reflexes are built through practice and repetition. The goalkeeper's save is fast and automatic only because of years of training, so it is a learned reflex. Catching a suddenly dropped object is another common example.
notes: An autonomic reflex acts on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or a gland, while a save uses skeletal muscle. Choose autonomic for a question about the pupillary light reflex.
Correct. A fast, automatic response built through years of practice is learned.
A monosynaptic reflex has only one synapse, like the stretch reflex, and it is classified by synapse count rather than by origin. It would be right for a question about the stretch reflex.
An innate reflex is present from birth without practice, such as the blink reflex. Pick innate when no training was needed.
questions.answerText: A learned reflex

questions.q: In a cross-section of the spinal cord, which region is butterfly-shaped and holds the neuron cell bodies?
options: The white matter
The gray matter
The anterior white commissure
The posterior median sulcus
questions.why: The inner, butterfly-shaped core of the spinal cord is gray matter, made of neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated fibers. Its projections are called horns. This arrangement is the reverse of the cerebrum, where the gray matter lies on the outside as the cortex.
notes: White matter is the outer region of the cord, made of myelinated axons sorted into columns. Pick it if the question asked which region carries the ascending and descending tracts.
Correct. The butterfly-shaped core is gray matter.

The anterior white commissure is a thin bridge of white matter that crosses between the two sides of the cord. It would be the answer if the question asked which white matter structure connects the right and left halves.

The posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove down the back of the cord. Pick it if the question asked which groove, together with the anterior median fissure, divides the cord into right and left halves.
questions.answerText: The gray matter

questions.q: What is the conus medullaris?
options: The tapered inferior end of the spinal cord
The fluid-filled channel at the center of the cord
The sensory root entering the back of the cord
The bundle of nerve roots below the cord
questions.why: The conus medullaris is the cone-shaped, tapered end of the spinal cord. In the adult it lies at about the level of the disc between L1 and L2, well above the bottom of the vertebral column. Below it, only nerve roots and the filum terminale continue down the vertebral canal.
notes: Correct. The conus medullaris is the tapered end of the cord.
This describes the central canal, the small CSF channel continuous with the fourth ventricle. It would be the answer for a question about the fluid channel inside the cord.
This describes the posterior (dorsal) root, the sensory root of a spinal nerve. Pick it if the question asked which root carries sensory axons into the cord.

This describes the cauda equina, the hair-like bundle of nerve roots that descends past the conus medullaris. Pick it if the question asked what hangs in the vertebral canal below the end of the cord.
questions.answerText: The tapered inferior end of the spinal cord

questions.q: What does the posterior (dorsal) root of a spinal nerve carry?
options: Motor axons from the cord out to muscles
Ascending tracts running up the cord to the brain
Both sensory and motor axons mixed together
Sensory axons from the periphery into the cord
questions.why: Each spinal nerve connects to the cord by two roots. The posterior (dorsal) root is the sensory root, carrying sensory axons from receptors in the body into the back of the cord, and it bears a swelling, the dorsal root ganglion, that holds the sensory neuron cell bodies. Posterior is sensory in, anterior is motor out.
notes: Motor axons leaving the cord travel in the anterior (ventral) root. Pick this if the question asked about the ventral root.

Ascending tracts are bundles of axons in the white matter columns inside the cord, carrying sensory signals up to the brain. Pick them if the question asked what runs within the white matter of the cord.
Mixed sensory and motor axons are found in the spinal nerve itself, formed where the posterior and anterior roots join. This would be the answer for a question about the spinal nerve.
Correct. The posterior root carries sensory axons into the cord.
questions.answerText: Sensory axons from the periphery into the cord

questions.q: In a cross-section of the spinal cord, the white matter is divided into what structural units?
options: Columns
Ganglia
Horns
Gyri
questions.why: The white matter of the spinal cord surrounds the gray matter and is divided into anterior, posterior, and lateral white columns on each side. Each column holds tracts, which are bundles of axons that share a common origin and destination. Ascending tracts carry sensory signals up and descending tracts carry motor signals down.
notes: Correct. Spinal white matter is divided into columns.
Ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system, such as the dorsal root ganglion. Pick a ganglion if the question asked where sensory cell bodies sit outside the cord.
Horns are the projections of the cord's gray matter (posterior, lateral, and anterior horns). Pick horns if the question asked how the gray matter is divided.
Gyri are the raised folds of the cerebral cortex, not features of the spinal cord. They would be the answer for a question about the surface of the cerebrum.
questions.answerText: Columns

questions.q: Where is the cauda equina located relative to the conus medullaris?
options: Above it, in the cervical region of the cord
Lateral to it, outside the vertebral column
Inside it, as the central canal
Below it, within the vertebral canal
questions.why: The spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris near the L1 to L2 disc, but the nerve roots for the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal spinal nerves must still travel down to their exit points. These roots form the cauda equina, a hair-like bundle that hangs in the vertebral canal below the conus. Its name means horse's tail.
notes: The cervical region of the cord is far above the conus and holds the cervical enlargement, where upper limb nerves arise. Pick the cervical region if the question asked about the cervical enlargement.

Once spinal nerves leave the vertebral canal through the intervertebral foramina, they lie outside the vertebral column. The cauda equina is still inside the canal, so this describes spinal nerves after they exit.

The central canal is the CSF channel that runs through the center of the cord. It would be the answer if the question asked about the fluid-filled channel inside the cord, not the bundle of roots below it.
Correct. The cauda equina hangs below the conus medullaris inside the vertebral canal.
questions.answerText: Below it, within the vertebral canal

questions.q: What does the anterior (ventral) root of a spinal nerve carry?
options: Both sensory and motor axons mixed together
Sensory axons from the periphery into the cord
Motor axons from the cord out to muscles
The cell bodies of sensory neurons
questions.why: The anterior (ventral) root is the motor root. It carries axons from motor neurons whose cell bodies sit in the anterior and lateral horns of the gray matter, out of the front of the cord toward skeletal muscles, smooth muscle, and glands. It joins the posterior root to form the mixed spinal nerve.
notes: Sensory and motor axons travel together in the spinal nerve, formed where the two roots join. This would be the answer if the question asked about the spinal nerve.
Sensory axons entering the cord travel in the posterior (dorsal) root. Pick this if the question asked about the dorsal root.
Correct. The anterior root carries motor axons out of the cord.
Sensory neuron cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglion on the posterior root. Pick this if the question asked what the dorsal root ganglion holds; only the posterior root has a ganglion.
questions.answerText: Motor axons from the cord out to muscles

questions.q: On a cross-section of the spinal cord, a student points to the gray matter that holds the cell bodies of somatic motor neurons driving skeletal muscle. Which part of the gray matter is this?
options: The posterior (dorsal) horn
The lateral horn
The anterior (ventral) horn
The gray commissure
questions.why: The gray matter of the cord is shaped into horns. The anterior (ventral) horn holds somatic motor nuclei, the cell bodies of motor neurons whose axons leave through the anterior root and make skeletal muscle contract. Damage to these cell bodies causes weakness or paralysis of the muscles served by that segment.
notes: The posterior horn holds interneurons and receives the incoming axons of sensory neurons. Pick it if the question asked where sensory input first enters the gray matter.

The lateral horn holds autonomic motor nuclei, the neurons that serve smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, and it is present only in the T1 to L2 segments. Pick it for a question about autonomic motor neurons.
Correct. The anterior horn holds somatic motor neuron cell bodies.

The gray commissure is the bridge of gray matter that connects the two sides of the cord and surrounds the central canal. It would be the answer if the question asked what crosses the midline around the central canal.
questions.answerText: The anterior (ventral) horn

questions.q: Which spinal cord structure is the small fluid-filled channel running through the center of the cord?
options: The central canal
The conus medullaris
The cauda equina
The dorsal root
questions.why: The central canal is a narrow channel in the middle of the spinal cord's gray matter, surrounded by the gray commissure. It holds cerebrospinal fluid and is continuous above with the fourth ventricle of the brain. Like the ventricles, it is lined by ependymal cells.
notes: Correct. The central canal is the CSF channel at the center of the cord.
The conus medullaris is the tapered lower end of the spinal cord near the L1 to L2 disc. It would be the answer if the question asked where the cord ends.
The cauda equina is the bundle of nerve roots in the vertebral canal below the end of the cord. Pick it if the question asked what hangs below the conus medullaris.
The dorsal root is the sensory root that enters the back of the cord. Pick it if the question asked which root carries sensory axons in.
questions.answerText: The central canal

questions.q: Which region of a spinal cord cross-section is the outer layer of myelinated axons organized into columns?
options: The gray commissure
The gray matter
The white matter
The posterior horn
questions.why: White matter is made of myelinated axons, and the fatty myelin makes it look pale. In the spinal cord it forms the outer region, divided into anterior, posterior, and lateral columns that contain the ascending and descending tracts. This is the reverse of the cerebrum, where white matter lies inside and gray matter forms the outer cortex.
notes: The gray commissure is the bar of gray matter that crosses the midline around the central canal. Pick it if the question asked what connects the two halves of the gray butterfly.
The gray matter is the inner butterfly-shaped core of the cord, made of neuron cell bodies. Pick it if the question asked which region is divided into horns.
Correct. The outer layer of myelinated axons is the white matter.
The posterior horn is one projection of the gray matter, where sensory axons enter and interneurons sit. It would be the answer for a question about where sensory input first reaches the gray matter.
questions.answerText: The white matter

questions.q: After a fall, a patient has damage to the spinal cord that interrupts its ascending and descending tracts, and function is lost below the level of the damage. Which condition is this?
options: Spinal cord injury
Meningitis
Hydrocephalus
Stroke
questions.why: The ascending and descending tracts in the cord's white matter carry every signal between the brain and the body below. A spinal cord injury interrupts these tracts, so sensation and movement are lost below the level of the injury, while everything above it is spared. The higher the injury, the more of the body is affected.
notes: Correct. Damage to the cord's tracts with loss of function below the injury is a spinal cord injury.
Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, usually from infection, and is diagnosed by testing CSF. Pick it if the question described an infection of the membranes around the brain and cord.
Hydrocephalus is a buildup of cerebrospinal fluid that enlarges the ventricles and raises pressure inside the skull. It would be the answer for a question about blocked CSF flow.

A stroke is a loss of blood flow to part of the brain, and the deficit depends on which brain area is affected. Pick stroke if the question described sudden weakness on one side of the body after a blocked cerebral artery.
questions.answerText: Spinal cord injury

questions.q: Which structure is the bundle of nerve roots that hangs in the vertebral canal below the point where the spinal cord ends?
options: The lateral horn
The filum terminale
The conus medullaris
The cauda equina
questions.why: The spinal cord stops growing in length in early childhood while the vertebral column keeps growing, so the adult cord ends near the L1 to L2 disc. The roots of the lower spinal nerves continue down the canal to reach their exit points, forming a hair-like bundle called the cauda equina. These roots float in the CSF of the lumbar cistern.
notes: The lateral horn is part of the gray matter inside the cord, present only in the T1 to L2 segments, holding autonomic motor neurons. It would be the answer for a question about autonomic cell bodies in the cord.

The filum terminale is a single thread of pia mater, not a bundle of nerve roots, that runs from the conus to anchor the cord on the coccyx. Pick it if the question asked what anchors the lower end of the cord.
The conus medullaris is the tapered end of the cord itself, the point where the cauda equina begins. Pick it if the question asked where the cord ends.
Correct. The cauda equina is the bundle of roots below the end of the cord.
questions.answerText: The cauda equina

questions.q: Which part of the spinal cord gray matter lies toward the back of the cord and receives the incoming sensory axons?
options: The posterior white column
The lateral horn
The posterior (dorsal) horn
The anterior (ventral) horn
questions.why: The posterior (dorsal) horn is the gray matter projection toward the back of the cord. Sensory axons arrive through the posterior root and enter this horn, where many of them connect with interneurons. The sensory cell bodies themselves are not in the horn; they sit outside the cord in the dorsal root ganglion.
notes: The posterior white column is white matter made of tracts, many of them ascending sensory tracts, but it is not part of the gray matter. Pick it if the question asked where sensory tracts travel up toward the brain.
The lateral horn holds autonomic motor neurons and is found only in the T1 to L2 segments. It would be the answer for a question about autonomic output from the cord.
Correct. The posterior horn receives incoming sensory axons.
The anterior horn is toward the front of the cord and holds the cell bodies of somatic motor neurons. Pick it if the question asked where skeletal muscle motor neurons begin.
questions.answerText: The posterior (dorsal) horn

questions.q: A sensory signal from the skin reaches the spinal cord. Which root does it enter by, and which horn of gray matter does it reach first?
options: The ventral root, then the ventral horn
The dorsal root, then the dorsal horn
The ventral root, then the dorsal horn
The dorsal root, then the ventral horn
questions.why: Sensory axons travel in the spinal nerve, split off into the posterior (dorsal) root, and pass the dorsal root ganglion where their cell bodies sit. They enter the back of the cord and reach the posterior (dorsal) horn of the gray matter. Posterior is sensory in and anterior is motor out, so a sensory signal stays on the posterior side at entry.
notes: This is the motor side of the cord, used by signals leaving it. Pick the ventral horn and ventral root if the question traced a motor command from the cord out to a skeletal muscle.
Correct. Sensory signals enter by the dorsal root and reach the dorsal horn.
Sensory axons do not enter through the ventral root, which carries only motor axons out. This pairing mixes the motor root with the sensory horn.
The dorsal root is right, but the ventral horn holds motor neuron cell bodies. A sensory signal can reach the ventral horn later in a reflex, after passing through the dorsal horn first.
questions.answerText: The dorsal root, then the dorsal horn

questions.q: Which list orders these spinal cord features from most superior to most inferior: the junction with the medulla, the cervical enlargement, the conus medullaris, and the cauda equina?
options: Cervical enlargement, junction with the medulla, conus medullaris, cauda equina
Cauda equina, conus medullaris, cervical enlargement, junction with the medulla
Junction with the medulla, cervical enlargement, conus medullaris, cauda equina
Junction with the medulla, cervical enlargement, cauda equina, conus medullaris
questions.why: The spinal cord begins where it is continuous with the medulla oblongata at the foramen magnum. It widens at the cervical enlargement, where the nerves of the upper limbs arise, and later tapers to the conus medullaris near the L1 to L2 disc. The cauda equina, a bundle of nerve roots, hangs below the conus in the lower vertebral canal.
notes: This places the cervical enlargement above the medulla junction. The cord starts at the medulla, and the cervical enlargement lies below that, in the neck.
This is the correct sequence read from bottom to top. Pick it only if the question asked for the order from inferior to superior.
Correct. Medulla junction, cervical enlargement, conus medullaris, then cauda equina.
This places the cauda equina above the conus medullaris. The cauda equina is the bundle of roots that continues below the end of the cord, so it must come last.
questions.answerText: Junction with the medulla, cervical enlargement, conus medullaris, cauda equina

questions.q: In an adult, at about what level does the spinal cord end at the conus medullaris?
options: At the disc between L1 and L2
At the tip of the coccyx
At the disc between L4 and L5
At the foramen magnum
questions.why: The spinal cord stops lengthening at about 4 to 5 years of age while the vertebral column keeps growing, so in the adult the cord ends high in the lumbar region. Its tapered end, the conus medullaris, lies at about the disc between L1 and L2. Below that point only the cauda equina and filum terminale continue.
notes: Correct. The conus medullaris lies near the L1 to L2 disc.
The tip of the coccyx is where the filum terminale anchors, not where the cord itself ends. Pick it if the question asked where the filum terminale attaches.
The L4 to L5 level is below the end of the cord, one of the safe sites for a lumbar puncture needle. It would be the answer if the question asked where a spinal tap is performed.
The foramen magnum is where the spinal cord begins, continuous with the medulla oblongata. Pick it if the question asked where the cord starts.
questions.answerText: At the disc between L1 and L2

questions.q: Which widening of the spinal cord is where the nerves of the upper limbs arise?
options: The conus medullaris
The cauda equina
The lumbar enlargement
The cervical enlargement
questions.why: The cord is wider in two regions because more neurons are needed to serve the limbs. The cervical enlargement, from about C4 to T1, is where the nerves of the upper limbs arise, and these nerves form the brachial plexus. The lumbar enlargement lower down serves the lower limbs.
notes: The conus medullaris is the tapered end of the cord, a narrowing rather than a widening. It would be the answer if the question asked where the cord ends.
The cauda equina is the bundle of nerve roots below the end of the cord, not a widening of the cord itself. Pick it if the question asked what hangs in the lumbar cistern.
The lumbar enlargement is the lower widening of the cord, where the nerves of the lower limbs arise. Pick it if the question asked about the legs.
Correct. The cervical enlargement gives rise to the upper limb nerves.
questions.answerText: The cervical enlargement

questions.q: Which swelling on the posterior root of a spinal nerve holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons?
options: The anterior horn
The lateral horn
The posterior white column
The dorsal root ganglion
questions.why: The dorsal (posterior) root ganglion is a swelling on the posterior root, just outside the cord, that holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons for that segment. Only the posterior root has a ganglion. Because it lies outside the CNS, it is called a ganglion rather than a nucleus.
notes: The anterior horn holds the cell bodies of somatic motor neurons inside the gray matter of the cord. Pick it if the question asked where skeletal muscle motor neurons begin.
The lateral horn holds autonomic motor neuron cell bodies and is found only in the T1 to L2 segments. It would be the answer for a question about autonomic output from the cord.
The posterior white column is white matter made of axon tracts, not cell bodies. Pick it if the question asked where ascending sensory tracts run in the cord.
Correct. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies.
questions.answerText: The dorsal root ganglion

questions.q: Which part of a spinal nerve attaches it to the back of the spinal cord and carries sensory axons into the cord?
options: The ventral root
The dorsal root
The ventral ramus
The dorsal ramus
questions.why: The dorsal (posterior) root connects the back of the spinal cord to the spinal nerve and carries sensory axons into the cord. Along this root sits the dorsal root ganglion, which holds the cell bodies of those sensory neurons. Just past the cord, the dorsal root joins the ventral root to form one mixed spinal nerve.
notes: The ventral root attaches to the front of the cord and carries motor axons out. Pick it if the question asked about the motor root.
Correct. The dorsal root brings sensory axons into the back of the cord.

The ventral ramus is a branch that forms after the spinal nerve leaves the vertebral column. It supplies the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk, so pick it for the branch that builds the plexuses.

The dorsal ramus is a branch past the intervertebral foramen that supplies the deep back muscles and the skin of the back. It is a branch of the finished spinal nerve, not one of its attachments to the cord.
questions.answerText: The dorsal root

questions.q: What is the cluster of sensory neuron cell bodies sitting on the dorsal root of a spinal nerve called?
options: The posterior gray horn
A sympathetic trunk ganglion
The dorsal root ganglion
The ventral root
questions.why: The dorsal root ganglion is a swelling on the dorsal (posterior) root, just outside the spinal cord, that holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons for that spinal segment. Their axons carry signals from receptors in the body through the dorsal root and into the cord. Because the cluster lies outside the CNS, it is called a ganglion rather than a nucleus.
notes: The posterior gray horn lies inside the cord and holds interneurons that receive the incoming sensory axons. Pick it for where sensory axons end inside the cord, not where their cell bodies sit.

A sympathetic trunk ganglion also lies beside the vertebral column, but it holds autonomic motor neurons, not sensory neurons. Pick it for the chain of ganglia linked to the spinal nerves by the rami communicantes.
Correct. The dorsal root ganglion holds the sensory cell bodies for its segment.
The ventral root carries motor axons out of the front of the cord and has no ganglion on it. Pick it for the motor root.
questions.answerText: The dorsal root ganglion

questions.q: Which root attaches a spinal nerve to the front of the spinal cord and carries motor axons out of the cord?
options: The dorsal root
The ventral ramus
The ventral root
The dorsal root ganglion
questions.why: The ventral (anterior) root attaches the spinal nerve to the front of the spinal cord and carries motor axons out of the cord. Most of these axons come from motor neuron cell bodies in the ventral gray horn. Just past the cord, the ventral root joins the dorsal root to form a mixed spinal nerve.
notes: The dorsal root attaches to the back of the cord and carries sensory axons in. Pick it for the sensory root.
The ventral ramus is a branch of the spinal nerve beyond the intervertebral foramen, not an attachment to the cord. Pick it for the branch that supplies the limbs and forms the plexuses.
Correct. The ventral root carries motor axons out of the front of the cord.
The dorsal root ganglion is the swelling on the dorsal root that holds sensory cell bodies. Pick it for where sensory neuron cell bodies sit.
questions.answerText: The ventral root

questions.q: A dorsal root ganglion contains the cell bodies of which neurons?
options: Sympathetic postganglionic neurons
Somatic motor neurons
Sensory neurons
Interneurons
questions.why: A dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons for one spinal segment. Each of these neurons sends one branch out toward receptors in the body and another through the dorsal root into the spinal cord. Because the cluster lies outside the CNS, it is called a ganglion rather than a nucleus.
notes: Sympathetic postganglionic cell bodies sit in the sympathetic trunk ganglia or the prevertebral ganglia. These also lie near the vertebral column, which makes them tempting, but they are motor ganglia of the autonomic system.
Somatic motor neuron cell bodies sit in the ventral (anterior) gray horn inside the cord, and their axons leave through the ventral root. Pick them for the ventral horn.
Correct. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies.
Interneurons sit entirely inside the CNS, for example in the posterior gray horn where sensory axons arrive. Pick them for the neurons that connect sensory input to motor output inside the cord.
questions.answerText: Sensory neurons

questions.q: An injury cuts the ventral roots of several spinal nerves. The muscles they served become paralyzed and slowly waste away, but skin sensation in the area stays normal. Which statement best explains this pattern?
options: The ventral roots carry only autonomic axons to the limb muscles
The ventral roots hold the cell bodies of the sensory neurons for the skin
The ventral roots carry motor axons, while sensory axons enter through the dorsal roots
The ventral roots carry sensory axons, while motor axons leave through the dorsal roots
questions.why: The ventral root carries the motor axons that leave the cord for skeletal muscle. When it is cut, the muscles lose their nerve supply, become paralyzed, and slowly shrink, a change called atrophy. Sensory axons enter through the separate dorsal root, so sensation from the skin is spared.
notes: Skeletal muscles are controlled by somatic motor axons, not autonomic axons. Autonomic axons serve cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands.
Sensory cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglion on the dorsal root, not on the ventral root. Pick the dorsal root ganglion for where sensory cell bodies are.
Correct. Cutting the motor roots paralyzes the muscles while leaving the sensory roots intact.
This reverses the two roots. The ventral root is motor and the dorsal root is sensory, which is the reason cutting the ventral roots spares skin sensation.
questions.answerText: The ventral roots carry motor axons, while sensory axons enter through the dorsal roots

questions.q: Where does the spinal cord lie?
options: Within the thoracic cavity
Within the abdominopelvic cavity
Within the cranial cavity
Within the vertebral canal
questions.why: The spinal cord runs down the vertebral canal, the tunnel formed by the stacked vertebral foramina. It is continuous with the medulla oblongata above and ends near the L1 to L2 disc. The cranial cavity and vertebral canal together make up the dorsal body cavity.
notes: The thoracic cavity is part of the ventral body cavity and holds the heart and lungs. Choose it for a question about those organs.
The abdominopelvic cavity is the lower part of the ventral body cavity and holds the digestive, urinary, and reproductive organs. It would be the answer for organs like the stomach or bladder.
The cranial cavity holds the brain, the other half of the dorsal body cavity. Pick it for a question about where the brain sits.
Correct. The spinal cord lies within the vertebral canal.
questions.answerText: Within the vertebral canal

questions.q: What is the tapered, cone-shaped end of the spinal cord called?
options: The lumbar enlargement
The cauda equina
The conus medullaris
The filum terminale
questions.why: The conus medullaris is the cone-shaped tip where the spinal cord ends, at about the disc between L1 and L2 in adults. Below it, the canal holds the cauda equina and the thin filum terminale rather than cord tissue. Its name means cone of the cord.
notes: The lumbar enlargement is a widening of the cord behind the lower thoracic vertebrae (about T9 to T12) that gives rise to the nerves of the lower limbs. It would be the answer for a question about the wide part just above the end.
The cauda equina is the bundle of nerve roots that hangs below the conus medullaris. Pick it for a question about the horse-tail of roots in the lower canal.
Correct. The conus medullaris is the tapered end of the spinal cord.
The filum terminale is a thread of pia mater that extends from the conus medullaris down to the coccyx. Choose it for a question about what anchors the cord below.
questions.answerText: The conus medullaris

questions.q: What is the bundle of nerve roots that descends past the end of the spinal cord called?
options: The conus medullaris
The cauda equina
The denticulate ligaments
The filum terminale
questions.why: The spinal cord ends near L1 to L2, but the nerve roots for the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal spinal nerves must still travel down to their exit points. These long roots hang together in the lower vertebral canal and look like a horse's tail, which is what cauda equina means. They float in CSF in the lumbar cistern.
notes: The conus medullaris is the tapered end of the cord itself, just above the cauda equina. Pick it for a question about where the cord ends.
Correct. The cauda equina is the bundle of roots below the end of the cord.
The denticulate ligaments are tooth-like extensions of pia mater that anchor the cord to the dura along its length. They would be the answer for a question about side-to-side anchoring.
The filum terminale is a single thread of pia mater, not a bundle of nerve roots, running from the conus medullaris to the coccyx. Choose it for a question about anchoring the cord.
questions.answerText: The cauda equina

questions.q: Which part of a spinal nerve's connection to the cord carries only sensory axons into the cord?
options: The anterior (ventral) ramus
The anterior (ventral) root
The posterior (dorsal) root
The posterior (dorsal) ramus
questions.why: Each spinal nerve connects to the cord by two roots. The posterior root is the sensory root; it carries sensory axons from receptors into the cord and has a ganglion holding the sensory cell bodies. A simple rule is posterior is sensory in, anterior is motor out.
notes: The anterior ramus is a mixed branch of the spinal nerve that serves the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk and forms the plexuses. It would be the answer for a question about what forms the brachial plexus.
The anterior root is the motor root and carries motor axons out of the cord. Pick it for a question about the motor root.
Correct. The posterior root is the sensory root.

The posterior ramus is a branch of the spinal nerve after the roots have joined, so it carries both sensory and motor axons to the back. Choose it for a question about the branch serving the deep back muscles and skin.
questions.answerText: The posterior (dorsal) root

questions.q: Which root of a spinal nerve carries motor axons out of the spinal cord?
options: The anterior (ventral) root
The dorsal root ganglion
The posterior (dorsal) root
The gray commissure
questions.why: The anterior root is the motor root. Its axons start from motor neuron cell bodies in the anterior and lateral gray horns and leave the cord to reach muscles and glands. It joins the posterior root just beyond the ganglion to form the mixed spinal nerve.
notes: Correct. The anterior root carries motor axons out of the cord.
The dorsal root ganglion is the swelling on the posterior root that holds sensory cell bodies. Choose it for a question about where sensory neuron cell bodies sit.
The posterior root is the sensory root, carrying sensory axons into the cord. Pick it for a question about the sensory root.
The gray commissure is the bridge of gray matter around the central canal that connects the two sides of the cord. It would be the answer for a question about that internal bridge.
questions.answerText: The anterior (ventral) root

questions.q: What does the posterior (dorsal) root ganglion contain?
options: Cell bodies of somatic motor neurons
Cell bodies of autonomic motor neurons
Interneurons that link sensory to motor
Cell bodies of sensory neurons
questions.why: A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system. The posterior root ganglion is the swelling on the posterior root that holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons for that spinal segment. Only the posterior root has a ganglion, so if a question puts cell bodies on a root, it is the posterior one.
notes: Somatic motor neuron cell bodies sit inside the cord in the anterior gray horn. Pick them for a question about the anterior horn.
Autonomic motor neuron cell bodies inside the cord sit in the lateral gray horn of the T1 to L2 segments. Choose them for a question about the lateral horn.
Interneurons sit in the gray matter of the cord, especially the posterior horn. They would be the answer for a question about what the posterior horn holds besides incoming sensory axons.
Correct. The posterior root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies.
questions.answerText: Cell bodies of sensory neurons

questions.q: In a cross-section of the spinal cord, where is the gray matter?
options: Only within the dorsal root ganglia
In an outer layer around the white matter
Only in a thin ring around the central canal
In the inner, butterfly-shaped core
questions.why: In the spinal cord, gray matter forms an H or butterfly shape in the center, and white matter wraps around it on the outside. This is the reverse of the cerebrum, where gray matter forms the outer cortex. The wings of the butterfly are the gray horns, and the central canal sits in the middle of the crossbar.
notes: The dorsal root ganglia hold sensory cell bodies, but they sit outside the cord on the posterior roots. Choose them for a question about where sensory cell bodies are found.
An outer layer of gray matter is the pattern of the cerebral cortex, not the spinal cord. Pick it for a question about where gray matter lies in the cerebrum.
The gray commissure does surround the central canal, but the gray matter also spreads out into the anterior, posterior, and lateral horns. This option describes only the crossbar.
Correct. Spinal cord gray matter forms the inner, butterfly-shaped core.
questions.answerText: In the inner, butterfly-shaped core

questions.q: Which gray horn contains autonomic motor nuclei and is present only in the T1 to L2 segments?
options: The anterior horn
The gray commissure
The lateral horn
The posterior horn
questions.why: The lateral horn is a small side projection of gray matter between the anterior and posterior horns. It holds the cell bodies of autonomic motor neurons that serve organs, smooth muscle, and glands. It appears only in the T1 to L2 segments, which is where the sympathetic outflow leaves the cord.
notes: The anterior horn holds somatic motor nuclei that drive skeletal muscle, and it is present at every level. Pick it for a question about motor neurons to skeletal muscle.
The gray commissure is the bridge of gray matter around the central canal, not a horn. It would be the answer for a question about what connects the two sides of the gray matter.
Correct. The lateral horn holds autonomic motor nuclei in the T1 to L2 segments.
The posterior horn holds interneurons and the incoming axons of sensory neurons, and it is present at every level. Choose it for a question about sensory input to the cord.
questions.answerText: The lateral horn

questions.q: Which gray horn of the spinal cord holds the somatic motor nuclei that drive skeletal muscle?
options: The posterior (dorsal) horn
The anterior (ventral) horn
The lateral horn
The gray commissure
questions.why: The anterior horn is the front wing of the gray matter butterfly. It holds the cell bodies of somatic motor neurons, whose axons leave through the anterior root to make skeletal muscles contract. It is present at every level of the cord and is especially large in the cervical and lumbar enlargements, where the limb muscles are served.
notes: The posterior horn holds interneurons and receives the incoming axons of sensory neurons. Pick it for a question about sensory input to the gray matter.
Correct. The anterior horn holds somatic motor nuclei for skeletal muscle.
The lateral horn holds autonomic motor nuclei that serve organs, smooth muscle, and glands, and it is found only in the T1 to L2 segments. Choose it for a question about autonomic outflow.
The gray commissure is the bridge of gray matter around the central canal joining the two sides. It would be the answer for a question about that bridge.
questions.answerText: The anterior (ventral) horn

questions.q: What is the small cerebrospinal fluid channel at the center of the spinal cord called?
options: The anterior median fissure
The cerebral aqueduct
The fourth ventricle
The central canal
questions.why: The central canal is a tiny channel running the length of the spinal cord in the middle of the gray commissure. It is lined by ependymal cells and holds cerebrospinal fluid. At its upper end it is continuous with the fourth ventricle.
notes: The anterior median fissure is a deep groove on the outside front of the cord, not a fluid channel. It would be the answer for a question about the groove down the front of the cord.
The cerebral aqueduct is the narrow CSF channel through the midbrain that joins the third and fourth ventricles. Pick it for a question about the midbrain.
The fourth ventricle is the CSF space between the brainstem and cerebellum, and the central canal continues down from it. Choose it for the cavity behind the pons.
Correct. The central canal is the CSF channel at the center of the cord.
questions.answerText: The central canal

questions.q: What are the sensory tracts that conduct impulses up the spinal cord toward the brain called?
options: Association tracts
Ascending tracts
Descending tracts
Commissural tracts
questions.why: Tracts in the spinal cord white matter are named by the direction they carry signals. Ascending tracts carry sensory impulses up toward the brain, such as the spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature. Descending tracts carry motor commands down from the brain.
notes: Association tracts link gyri within one cerebral hemisphere, such as the arcuate fasciculus. They would be the answer for a question about connections on one side of the cerebrum.
Correct. Ascending tracts carry sensory impulses up toward the brain.
Descending tracts are motor tracts that carry impulses down from the brain to the cord. Pick them for a question about motor commands.
Commissural tracts connect the two cerebral hemispheres, as the corpus callosum does. Choose them for a question about cerebral white matter between hemispheres.
questions.answerText: Ascending tracts

questions.q: Which two enlargements widen the spinal cord?
options: The cervical and thoracic enlargements
The thoracic and sacral enlargements
The dorsal and ventral enlargements
The cervical and lumbar enlargements
questions.why: The cord widens where it must serve the limbs, because many more neurons are needed there. The cervical enlargement, from C4 to T1, gives rise to the nerves of the upper limbs, and the lumbar enlargement, behind the lower thoracic vertebrae (about T9 to T12), gives rise to the nerves of the lower limbs. The thoracic cord between them is the narrowest part.
notes: This pairs the correct cervical enlargement with the thoracic region, which is actually the narrowest part of the cord. Only the regions serving limbs are enlarged.
The thoracic region is the narrowest part of the cord, not an enlargement. This option misses both limb regions.
Dorsal and ventral describe the back and front of the cord, such as the dorsal and ventral roots, not enlargements. Pick those terms for a question about the roots.
Correct. The cervical and lumbar enlargements serve the upper and lower limbs.
questions.answerText: The cervical and lumbar enlargements

questions.q: What is the thread of pia mater that anchors the lower end of the spinal cord to the coccyx called?
options: The denticulate ligament
The filum terminale
The cauda equina
The conus medullaris
questions.why: The filum terminale is a thin thread of pia mater that continues down from the conus medullaris. It runs through the lumbar cistern among the roots of the cauda equina and attaches to the coccyx. Along the way it picks up a covering of dura at the end of the dural sac.
notes: The denticulate ligaments are tooth-like extensions of pia mater that anchor the cord to the dura along its sides. They would be the answer for side-to-side anchoring along the length of the cord.
Correct. The filum terminale anchors the cord to the coccyx.
The cauda equina is the bundle of nerve roots below the end of the cord, not an anchoring thread. Pick it for a question about the horse-tail of roots.
The conus medullaris is the tapered end of the cord itself, where the filum terminale begins. Choose it for a question about where the cord ends.
questions.answerText: The filum terminale

questions.q: What is the deep groove running down the front of the spinal cord called?
options: The central canal
The anterior median fissure
The posterior median sulcus
The longitudinal fissure
questions.why: Two grooves run the full length of the cord and divide it into right and left halves. The anterior median fissure is the deep groove down the front, and the posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove down the back. Remember that fissures are deeper than sulci, here as in the brain.
notes: The central canal is the CSF channel inside the cord, not a surface groove. Choose it for a question about the channel in the gray commissure.
Correct. The anterior median fissure is the deep groove down the front of the cord.
The posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove down the back of the cord. Pick it for the posterior groove.
The longitudinal fissure is in the brain and separates the two cerebral hemispheres. It would be the answer for the groove between the hemispheres.
questions.answerText: The anterior median fissure

questions.q: In the central nervous system, what is a bundle of axons that shares a common origin and destination called?
options: A ganglion
A nerve
A tract
A nucleus
questions.why: Clusters of cell bodies and bundles of axons get different names depending on whether they are in the CNS or the PNS. In the CNS, a bundle of axons is a tract and a cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus. In the PNS, a bundle of axons is a nerve and a cluster of cell bodies is a ganglion.
notes: A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies in the PNS, such as the dorsal root ganglion. It would be the answer for cell body clusters outside the CNS.
A nerve is a bundle of axons in the peripheral nervous system. Pick it if the question asks about axon bundles outside the brain and cord.
Correct. A CNS bundle of axons is a tract.
A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies in the CNS, not a bundle of axons. Choose it for a question about gray matter clusters such as cranial nerve nuclei.
questions.answerText: A tract

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the arrangement of gray and white matter in the spinal cord and the cerebrum?
options: Cord: gray outside, white inside, the reverse of the cerebrum
Both have gray matter outside and white matter inside
Cord: gray inside, white outside, the reverse of the cerebrum
Both have gray matter inside and white matter outside
questions.why: In the spinal cord, gray matter forms the butterfly-shaped core and white matter tracts surround it. In the cerebrum, gray matter forms the outer cortex and white matter fills the inside. Both contain gray and white matter; only the arrangement is reversed.
notes: This flips the cord's pattern. Gray matter outside and white inside is the arrangement of the cerebrum, not the cord.
This describes only the cerebrum, with its outer cortex. Pick it for a question about the cerebrum alone.
Correct. The cord has gray inside and white outside, while the cerebrum has gray outside and white inside.
This describes only the spinal cord. The cerebrum differs because its gray matter forms the outer cortex.
questions.answerText: Cord: gray inside, white outside, the reverse of the cerebrum

questions.q: Tiny bundles of axons attach in a row along the back or the front of the cord and merge to form each root. What are these small bundles called?
options: Tracts
Rami
Rootlets
Horns
questions.why: Each root does not leave the cord as one cable. Instead, a row of small rootlets fans out from the cord surface and gathers into a single posterior or anterior root. The two roots then join to form the spinal nerve.
notes: Tracts are bundles of axons inside the white matter of the CNS that run up or down the cord. Pick them for a question about ascending or descending pathways.
Rami are the branches a spinal nerve splits into after it leaves the intervertebral foramen. They would be the answer for a question about the anterior and posterior branches of a spinal nerve.
Correct. Rootlets merge to form each root.
Horns are projections of the gray matter inside the cord, such as the anterior and posterior horns. Choose them for a question about the butterfly-shaped gray matter.
questions.answerText: Rootlets

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the adult spinal cord typically end?
options: At the L1 to L2 level
At the T6 level
At the L4 to L5 level
At the S2 level
questions.why: The adult spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris near the disc between L1 and L2. The vertebral canal continues much lower, so below this point the canal holds only the cauda equina and CSF in the lumbar cistern. This is why a lumbar puncture is done lower, at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5.
notes: Correct. The adult cord typically ends near the L1 to L2 level.
T6 is in the middle of the thoracic region, well above the end of the cord. The cord continues through the rest of the thoracic segments and the lumbar enlargement before ending.
L4 to L5 is below the end of the cord and is a common site for a lumbar puncture. Pick it for a question about where the needle is placed for a spinal tap.
S2 is roughly where the dural sac and subarachnoid space end, well below the end of the cord. Choose it for a question about where the lumbar cistern stops, not the cord.
questions.answerText: At the L1 to L2 level

questions.q: Which spinal cord segment has the largest diameter and a large amount of white matter in an oval shape?
options: The lumbar segment
The sacral segment
The thoracic segment
The cervical segment
questions.why: White matter is thickest at the top of the cord because almost every tract is still running there, carrying signals for the whole body below. The cervical segments also serve the upper limbs, so they are wide and oval. White matter thins as you move down the cord, since fewer tracts are still traveling.
notes: Lumbar segments are almost circular with less white matter than the cervical segments. Choose lumbar for a nearly round section with large anterior horns.
Sacral segments are relatively small, with more gray matter and little white matter. They would be the answer for a small section that is mostly gray.
Thoracic segments have a small diameter with little gray matter and a small lateral horn. Pick thoracic for a cross-section that is small and shows a lateral horn.
Correct. Cervical segments are the largest, oval, and rich in white matter.
questions.answerText: The cervical segment

questions.q: Which gray horn would you expect to see in a thoracic segment but not in a cervical segment?
options: The anterior horn
The lateral horn
The gray commissure
The posterior horn
questions.why: The lateral horn holds autonomic motor nuclei and is present only in the T1 to L2 segments. A cervical section therefore shows anterior and posterior horns but no lateral horn. Spotting that small side projection is one way to tell a thoracic section from a cervical one.
notes: The anterior horn holds somatic motor nuclei and is present at every level of the cord. It would not help tell a thoracic section from a cervical one.
Correct. The lateral horn appears in the T1 to L2 segments but not in cervical ones.
The gray commissure is the bridge of gray matter around the central canal, present at all levels, and it is not a horn. Choose it for a question about the connection between the two sides.
The posterior horn receives sensory input and is present at every level. Pick it for a question about where sensory axons enter the gray matter.
questions.answerText: The lateral horn

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares ascending and descending tracts of the spinal cord?
options: Ascending are sensory and run down; descending are motor and run up
Ascending are motor and run up; descending are sensory and run down
Ascending are sensory and run up; descending are motor and run down
Both carry sensory and motor signals in either direction
questions.why: The names tell the direction. Ascending tracts carry sensory signals up toward the brain, such as the spinothalamic tract. Descending tracts carry motor commands down from the brain, such as the corticospinal tract. Each tract carries signals in one direction only.
notes: This keeps the correct signal type but reverses the direction. Ascending means going up, so these tracts run toward the brain, not away from it.
This swaps the type of signal. Sensory information travels up to the brain and motor commands travel down, so ascending tracts cannot be motor.
Correct. Ascending tracts are sensory and run up, and descending tracts are motor and run down.
Each tract carries one kind of signal in one direction. A mixed, two-way bundle better describes a spinal nerve, which carries sensory and motor axons together.
questions.answerText: Ascending are sensory and run up; descending are motor and run down

questions.q: The cervical enlargement of the spinal cord gives rise to the nerves of which body region?
options: The lower limbs
The upper limbs
The pelvic organs
The thoracic wall
questions.why: The cervical enlargement runs from about C4 to T1. The arms need many motor and sensory neurons for their detailed movement and sensation, so this part of the cord holds extra neurons and is wider. Its nerves form the brachial plexus, which supplies the upper limbs.
notes: The lower limbs are served by the lumbar enlargement, behind the lower thoracic vertebrae (about T9 to T12). Pick it if the question names the lumbar enlargement.
Correct. The cervical enlargement gives rise to the nerves of the upper limbs.
The pelvic organs get their nerves from the lower part of the cord, far below the cervical enlargement in the neck. The cervical enlargement serves the upper limbs only.
The thoracic wall is served by spinal nerves from the thoracic segments, which form the narrowest part of the cord. Choose it for a question about the intercostal region.
questions.answerText: The upper limbs

questions.q: Which bridge of gray matter surrounds the central canal and connects the two sides of the cord?
options: The lateral horn
The gray commissure
The anterior white commissure
The posterior median sulcus
questions.why: The gray commissure is the crossbar of the gray matter butterfly. It connects the right and left halves of the gray matter, and the central canal runs through its middle. A commissure is any bridge that connects two sides.
notes: The lateral horn is a side projection of gray matter in the T1 to L2 segments, holding autonomic motor nuclei. Choose it for a question about autonomic outflow.
Correct. The gray commissure surrounds the central canal and joins the two sides.

The anterior white commissure is also a bridge between the two sides, but it is made of white matter and lies in front of the gray commissure. Pick it if the question asks for the white matter bridge.
The posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove down the back surface of the cord. It would be the answer for the groove on the posterior side.
questions.answerText: The gray commissure

questions.q: A clinician performs a lumbar puncture between the L3 and L4 spines. Why is this site safe for the spinal cord?
options: The dura ends at L2, so no membranes are pierced
The denticulate ligaments pull the cord aside there
The central canal widens into a large reservoir there
The cord ends near L1 to L2, above the needle site
questions.why: The spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris near the L1 to L2 disc, but the subarachnoid space continues lower as the lumbar cistern. A needle placed between L3 and L4 enters this pool of CSF where only the loose roots of the cauda equina float, and they tend to drift aside. The cord itself is safely above the needle.
notes: The dura continues below L2, and a lumbar puncture needle does pass through it and the arachnoid to reach CSF. The dural sac ends around S2.
The denticulate ligaments anchor the cord to the dura along its sides, but they end with the cord. Pick them for a question about side-to-side anchoring.
The central canal is a tiny channel inside the cord, and it does not form a reservoir below. The CSF pool used for a tap is the lumbar cistern, part of the subarachnoid space.
