Correct. The cord ends near L1 to L2, so a needle lower down meets only the cauda equina and CSF.
questions.answerText: The cord ends near L1 to L2, above the needle site

questions.q: In shingles, a virus reactivates and causes a rash along the exact strip of skin served by one spinal segment. Where did the virus lie dormant?
options: In the posterior root ganglion
In the anterior gray horn
In the lateral gray horn
In the posterior gray horn of the cord
questions.why: The varicella zoster virus, which causes chickenpox, hides for decades in sensory neuron cell bodies. For a spinal segment, those cell bodies sit in the posterior root ganglion. When the virus reactivates, it travels down that ganglion's sensory axons, so the rash follows the one strip of skin, or dermatome, that the ganglion serves.
notes: Correct. The virus hides in the sensory cell bodies of the posterior root ganglion.
The anterior gray horn holds somatic motor neuron cell bodies inside the cord. Pick it for a question about motor neurons to skeletal muscle.
The lateral gray horn holds autonomic motor neurons in the T1 to L2 segments. It would be the answer for a question about autonomic outflow.

The posterior gray horn receives incoming sensory axons and holds interneurons, but the sensory cell bodies themselves sit outside the cord in the ganglion. Choose it for a question about where sensory axons synapse.
questions.answerText: In the posterior root ganglion

questions.q: After a spinal cord injury, a patient loses sensation and movement everywhere below the injury but keeps normal function above it. Damage to which structures explains this pattern?
options: The ascending and descending tracts
The dorsal root ganglia below the injury
The roots of the spinal nerves at that level
The denticulate ligaments
questions.why: The ascending and descending tracts in the white matter carry every signal between the brain and the body below. When they are cut at one level, nothing below that level can send sensation up or receive motor commands from above. Everything served by segments above the injury still connects to the brain, so it keeps working.
notes: Correct. Cutting the ascending and descending tracts disconnects the body below the injury from the brain.
The dorsal root ganglia below the injury are undamaged and still hold their sensory cell bodies. The problem is that their signals cannot travel past the injury to the brain.
Damage to the roots at one level affects only the strip of skin and the muscles served by that one segment. Pick this for a narrow, band-like loss, not loss of everything below.
The denticulate ligaments anchor the cord to the dura and carry no signals. Choose them for a question about how the cord is held in place.
questions.answerText: The ascending and descending tracts

questions.q: A spinal cord cross-section is relatively small and is mostly gray matter, with only a thin rim of white matter. Which segment is it most likely from?
options: A thoracic segment
A lumbar segment
A cervical segment
A sacral segment
questions.why: White matter thins as you go down the cord because fewer tracts are still running at each lower level. By the sacral segments, little white matter remains, so a sacral section is relatively small and has more gray matter than white matter.
notes: A thoracic segment has a small diameter with little gray matter and a small lateral horn. Choose it for a small section with thin gray horns and a lateral horn.
A lumbar segment is almost circular, with less white matter than cervical but still a sizable white rim. It would be the answer for a nearly round section with large anterior horns.
A cervical segment is the largest and oval, with a large amount of white matter. Pick it for a big section that is mostly white.
Correct. Sacral segments are small, with more gray matter and little white matter.
questions.answerText: A sacral segment

questions.q: A spinal cord cross-section is almost circular and fairly large, with less white matter than a cervical section. Which segment is it most likely from?
options: A thoracic segment
A lumbar segment
A cervical segment
A coccygeal segment
questions.why: Lumbar segments sit in the lumbar enlargement, so they are fairly large with big anterior horns for the lower limbs. They are almost circular in outline and carry less white matter than cervical segments, because fewer tracts are still running that low. Shape and the amount of white matter are the main clues for identifying a segment.
notes: A thoracic segment has a small diameter with little gray matter and a lateral horn. It would be the answer for a small section showing a lateral horn.
Correct. Lumbar segments are nearly circular with less white matter than cervical ones.
A cervical segment is large and oval with abundant white matter. Pick it for the widest, mostly white section.
The coccygeal segment is the smallest and looks like the lower sacral segments. Choose it for a tiny section at the very end of the cord.
questions.answerText: A lumbar segment

questions.q: You pull your hand off a hot stove before you even feel the pain. Why is this withdrawal reflex faster than a conscious response?
options: The cerebellum sends the command because it is closer to the limb
The signal skips the sensory neuron and goes straight to the muscle
The arc is completed in the spinal cord without a trip to the brain
The dorsal root ganglion sends the motor command to the muscle
questions.why: In a reflex arc, a sensory neuron carries the signal into the spinal cord, gray matter there connects it to a motor neuron, and the motor neuron carries the command out to the muscle. The whole loop runs through the cord, so it is much shorter than a path up to the brain and back. The brain is informed afterward, which is why you feel the pain a moment later.
notes: The cerebellum coordinates movement but is not part of a spinal withdrawal reflex. Choose it for a question about smoothing and coordinating movement.
Every reflex arc starts with a sensory neuron that detects the stimulus. Without it, the cord would never learn that the stove is hot.
Correct. The spinal cord completes the reflex arc, so the response does not wait for the brain.
The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies and does not send motor commands. Motor commands leave through motor neurons in the anterior horn and the anterior root.
questions.answerText: The arc is completed in the spinal cord without a trip to the brain

questions.q: White matter is made mostly of myelinated axons. In the spinal cord, white matter surrounds the central gray matter. What does this outer white matter do?
options: It produces cerebrospinal fluid for the central canal
It is where reflex connections between neurons are made
It forms tracts that carry signals up and down the cord
It holds the motor neuron cell bodies that drive muscles
questions.why: Myelinated axons are built for carrying signals quickly over long distances. In the cord, these axons are bundled into ascending and descending tracts in the outer white columns, forming highways between the brain and body. The central gray matter, with its cell bodies, handles local processing such as reflex connections.
notes: CSF is made by the choroid plexus in the brain's ventricles. It would be the answer for a question about where cerebrospinal fluid is produced.
Reflex connections are made in the gray matter, where sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons meet. Choose gray matter for a question about where reflexes are integrated.
Correct. The outer white matter forms ascending and descending tracts.
Motor neuron cell bodies sit in the anterior gray horn, part of the central gray matter. Pick that for a question about where somatic motor neurons are.
questions.answerText: It forms tracts that carry signals up and down the cord

questions.q: A surgeon cuts only the posterior roots of one spinal segment. What is the most likely result in the area served by that segment?
options: Loss of sensation, with movement preserved
Loss of movement, with sensation preserved
No change, because the anterior root takes over
Loss of both sensation and movement
questions.why: The posterior root is the sensory root, carrying sensory axons into the cord. Cutting it stops sensation from that segment from reaching the cord and brain. The anterior, motor root is untouched, so motor commands still reach the muscles and voluntary movement remains.
notes: Correct. Cutting the posterior roots removes sensation but spares the motor pathway.
Loss of movement with sensation spared would follow cutting the anterior roots, which carry the motor axons. Pick this if the question named the anterior roots.
The anterior root carries only motor axons and cannot take over sensory work. Each root has its own direction of traffic, so losing one removes that function.
Loss of both would follow cutting the spinal nerve itself, after the two roots have joined. Choose this for damage to the mixed spinal nerve.
questions.answerText: Loss of sensation, with movement preserved

questions.q: A spinal cord injury in the neck paralyzes far more of the body than a similar injury in the lower back. Why does the level of injury matter so much?
options: The cervical cord is not protected by any vertebrae
Lower injuries also damage the brainstem above them
Signals for all regions below must pass the injury site
The cervical cord holds the only motor neurons for the body
questions.why: The tracts in the cord carry signals between the brain and every region below each level. An injury in the neck blocks the signals for the arms, trunk, and legs, while an injury in the lower back blocks only the regions below it. The higher the injury, the more of the body is disconnected from the brain.
notes: The cervical cord is enclosed by the cervical vertebrae like the rest of the cord. Protection is not what differs between the levels.
An injury in the lower back damages the cord at that level, not the brainstem far above it. This reverses the direction of the effect.
Correct. Every signal to and from regions below the injury must pass through it, so higher injuries cut off more.
Motor neurons for each region sit in the anterior horns at many levels along the whole cord, not only in the neck. The lumbar enlargement, for example, holds the motor neurons for the legs.
questions.answerText: Signals for all regions below must pass the injury site

questions.q: Which list gives the protective coverings of the spinal cord in order, from outside to inside?
options: Vertebra, epidural space, pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
Vertebra, dura mater, epidural space, pia mater, arachnoid mater
Vertebra, epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
Vertebra, subdural space, arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
questions.why: The cord is protected by bone, then the fat-filled epidural space, then three meninges. The tough dura mater is outermost, the lacy arachnoid mater is in the middle, and the thin pia mater clings to the cord itself. Remembering that the names run from tough mother to tender mother keeps the order straight.
notes: This reverses the three meninges. The pia mater clings to the cord surface, so it is the innermost layer, not the one next to the epidural space.
The epidural space lies between the bone and the dura, so it comes before the dura, not after it. The arachnoid is also always outside the pia.
Correct. Bone, epidural space, dura, arachnoid, and pia run from outside to inside.
The subdural space lies between the dura and the arachnoid, not between the bone and the dura. This list also puts the arachnoid outside the dura.
questions.answerText: Vertebra, epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater

questions.q: In a lumbar puncture, the needle collects cerebrospinal fluid from which space?
options: The epidural space
The subdural space
The subarachnoid space
The central canal
questions.why: Cerebrospinal fluid around the cord fills the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater. Below the end of the cord this space widens into the lumbar cistern. The needle passes through the skin, ligaments, epidural space, dura, and arachnoid before CSF appears.
notes: The epidural space lies outside the dura and holds fat and veins, not CSF. Pick it for a question about where an epidural injection is given.
The subdural space between the dura and arachnoid is only a potential space with a thin film of fluid. Choose it for a question about where a subdural hematoma forms.
Correct. CSF is drawn from the subarachnoid space in the lumbar cistern.
The central canal is a tiny channel inside the cord, and the cord ends above the needle site. It would be the answer for the CSF channel at the center of the cord.
questions.answerText: The subarachnoid space

questions.q: In a newborn the spinal cord reaches lower in the vertebral canal than in an adult. Why does the adult cord end well above the bottom of the vertebral column?
options: The lower end of the cord turns into the filum terminale with age
The column keeps growing after the cord stops lengthening
The cauda equina pulls the cord upward during growth
The cord shrinks after birth as unused neurons die off
questions.why: The spinal cord stops lengthening at about 4 to 5 years of age, but the vertebral column keeps growing through childhood and adolescence. As the column outgrows the cord, the end of the cord ends up higher in the canal, near L1 to L2. The nerve roots below stretch down to reach their own exit points, forming the cauda equina.
notes: The filum terminale is a thread of pia mater that extends below the cord, not converted cord tissue. Choose it for a question about what anchors the cord to the coccyx.
Correct. The vertebral column outgrows the spinal cord.
The cauda equina is a result of the mismatch in growth, not its cause. Its long roots form because they must reach exit points far below the end of the cord.
The cord does not shrink. It simply stops growing in length while the bony column keeps getting longer.
questions.answerText: The column keeps growing after the cord stops lengthening

questions.q: The lumbar enlargement is wider than the thoracic cord just above it. What explains the extra width?
options: It holds extra neurons for the lower limb nerves
It stores CSF for the lumbar cistern below it
It holds the dorsal root ganglia for the whole body
It holds the cardiac and respiratory centers
questions.why: The legs need many motor and sensory neurons for movement and sensation. The lumbar enlargement, behind the lower thoracic vertebrae (about T9 to T12), holds those extra neurons, mostly in larger gray horns, and gives rise to the nerves of the lower limbs. The cervical enlargement does the same job for the upper limbs.
notes: Correct. The lumbar enlargement holds the extra neurons that serve the lower limbs.

CSF fills the subarachnoid space around the cord and is made by the choroid plexus in the ventricles, not stored inside the cord. Choose the lumbar cistern for a question about the CSF pool below the cord.
Dorsal root ganglia sit outside the cord on each posterior root, one pair per segment. They would be the answer for a question about where sensory cell bodies are found.
The cardiac and respiratory centers are in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem. Pick them for a question about the vital centers.
questions.answerText: It holds extra neurons for the lower limb nerves

questions.q: How does the spinal dura mater differ from the cranial dura mater?
options: The spinal dura lies inside the arachnoid, on the cord
The spinal dura is one layer, not fused to bone
The spinal dura has two layers fused to the vertebrae
The spinal dura forms the dural venous sinuses
questions.why: The cranial dura has two layers, an outer periosteal layer attached to the skull and an inner meningeal layer. Around the spinal cord, the dura is a single tough layer, and it is not fused to the vertebrae. The gap between the spinal dura and the bone is the epidural space, which is why epidural injections are given in the vertebral canal.
notes: The dura is always the outermost meninx, both in the skull and around the cord. The layer on the cord is the pia mater, which would be the answer for the innermost membrane.
Correct. The spinal dura is a single layer separated from bone by the epidural space.
This describes the cranial dura, where the outer layer is attached to the skull. Pick it if the question asked about the dura inside the cranium.
The dural venous sinuses form where the two layers of the cranial dura separate, so they are a cranial feature. Choose them for a question about how venous blood drains from the brain.
questions.answerText: The spinal dura is one layer, not fused to bone

questions.q: What is the epidural space, and what fills it?
options: Between arachnoid and pia; filled with cerebrospinal fluid
Between dura and arachnoid; a potential space with a fluid film
Inside the central canal of the cord; filled with CSF
Between spinal dura and vertebrae; filled with fat and veins
questions.why: The epidural space lies between the spinal dura mater and the bone of the vertebral canal, outside the dura (epi means upon). It is filled with fat and veins. It is a real space along the spinal cord, but inside the cranium it is only a potential space, and it is where anesthetic is placed in an epidural injection.
notes: This describes the subarachnoid space, where CSF circulates around the brain and cord. It would be the answer for the space a lumbar puncture reaches.
This describes the subdural space, a potential space only, with a thin film of fluid. Pick it if the question asked where a subdural hematoma forms.

The central canal is the narrow channel running down the center of the spinal cord gray matter, continuous with the fourth ventricle. Choose it for a question about the CSF channel inside the cord itself.
Correct. The epidural space lies outside the spinal dura and holds fat and veins.
questions.answerText: Between spinal dura and vertebrae; filled with fat and veins

questions.q: What do the denticulate ligaments and the filum terminale have in common?
options: Both are bundles of nerve roots that hang below the conus
Both are bands of arachnoid that return CSF to the blood
Both are extensions of pia mater that anchor the spinal cord
Both are folds of dura mater that divide the cranial cavity
questions.why: The denticulate ligaments and the filum terminale are both made of pia mater, the innermost meninx, and both hold the spinal cord in place. The denticulate ligaments are tooth-like extensions along each side of the cord that anchor it to the dura. The filum terminale is a thread of pia that runs from the conus medullaris down to anchor on the coccyx.
notes: The bundle of nerve roots below the conus medullaris is the cauda equina. It would be the answer for the horse-tail of roots in the lower vertebral canal, which the filum terminale runs through.
The structures that return CSF to the blood are the arachnoid granulations, which project into the dural venous sinuses. Choose them if the question asked how CSF is reabsorbed.
Correct. Both are pia mater, one anchoring the sides of the cord and one anchoring its end.
Folds of dura that divide the cranial cavity are the dural reflections, such as the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. Pick them for a question about partitions inside the skull.
questions.answerText: Both are extensions of pia mater that anchor the spinal cord

questions.q: Why is a lumbar puncture done between the L3 and L4 or the L4 and L5 vertebrae?
options: The epidural space holds the most CSF in the lower lumbar region
The cord ends near L1 to L2, so the needle reaches CSF below it
The subarachnoid space ends at L2, so CSF pools only above it
The cord is thickest there, so the needle can find it easily
questions.why: The spinal cord is shorter than the vertebral column and ends at the conus medullaris near the L1 to L2 disc in an adult. The subarachnoid space continues below it as the lumbar cistern, a pool of CSF holding only the floating nerve roots of the cauda equina. A needle placed between L3 and L4 or L4 and L5 reaches this CSF without risk of hitting the cord, and the roots drift aside.
notes: The epidural space holds fat and veins, not CSF; it is the site of an epidural injection. The CSF drawn in a lumbar puncture comes from the subarachnoid space, deeper, past the dura and arachnoid.
Correct. Below the end of the cord, the lumbar cistern holds CSF and only floating nerve roots.
It is the cord, not the subarachnoid space, that ends near L1 to L2. The subarachnoid space continues lower as the lumbar cistern, which is exactly why the tap works.
The goal of a lumbar puncture is to avoid the cord, not to find it, and the cord does not even reach this level. The needle is placed where there is CSF and no cord at all.
questions.answerText: The cord ends near L1 to L2, so the needle reaches CSF below it

questions.q: What is the cauda equina?
options: The thread of pia mater anchoring the cord to the coccyx
The bundle of nerve roots below the conus medullaris
The enlarged CSF-filled space below the end of the cord
The tapered, cone-shaped lower end of the spinal cord
questions.why: Because the spinal cord ends near the L1 to L2 disc, the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots must travel down the vertebral canal to reach their exit points. This bundle of roots hanging below the conus medullaris looks like a horse's tail, which is what cauda equina means. The roots float in the CSF of the lumbar cistern.
notes: This describes the filum terminale, which runs down among the roots of the cauda equina. It would be the answer for the pial thread that anchors the cord.
Correct. The cauda equina is the horse-tail of nerve roots below the end of the cord.
This describes the lumbar cistern, the enlarged subarachnoid space where a lumbar puncture draws CSF. The cauda equina floats inside it, which is why the two are easy to confuse.
This describes the conus medullaris, the tapered end of the cord. Pick it if the question asked where the spinal cord itself stops.
questions.answerText: The bundle of nerve roots below the conus medullaris

questions.q: In a cross-section of the spinal cord, where are the gray matter and white matter located?
options: White inside, gray outside
Gray and white evenly mixed
Gray inside, white outside
Gray in front, white in back
questions.why: In the spinal cord, the gray matter forms an inner core of neuron cell bodies shaped like a butterfly, and the white matter surrounds it on the outside. The outer white matter is made of myelinated axons organized into columns that hold the ascending and descending tracts. This is the reverse of the cerebrum, where the gray cortex is on the outside.
notes: This is the arrangement in the cerebrum, where the gray cortex covers the white matter. Pick it if the question asked about the brain rather than the spinal cord.
Gray and white matter form separate regions in the cord, a gray core and a white outer layer, not an even mix. Gray nuclei scattered among white tracts is the pattern of the brainstem.
Correct. The cord has a gray core wrapped in white matter.

Gray matter does have anterior and posterior horns, but white matter surrounds it on all sides, not just at the back. This mix-up confuses the horns of the gray matter with the location of the white matter.
questions.answerText: Gray inside, white outside

questions.q: What shape does the gray matter form in a cross-section of the spinal cord?
options: A crescent along the back
A butterfly or H shape
A thin outer ring
A solid circle
questions.why: In cross-section, the gray matter of the cord looks like a butterfly or the letter H. Its projections are the horns: the posterior horns point toward the back, the anterior horns point toward the front, and small lateral horns appear in the T1 to L2 segments. A bridge called the gray commissure crosses the middle and surrounds the central canal.
notes: The gray matter reaches both front and back, so it is not a crescent on one side. This mix-up may come from remembering only the posterior horns.
Correct. The cord's gray matter forms a butterfly or H shape.
A thin outer ring describes the cerebral cortex covering the brain, not the cord's gray matter. Pick it if the question asked about gray matter in the cerebrum.
The gray matter is not a solid circle; its horns project toward the front, back, and sides, with white matter filling in between. This choice ignores the horns.
questions.answerText: A butterfly or H shape

questions.q: The spinal cord relays signals between the brain and the body and also serves as a reflex center. Which statement explains how its gray and white matter divide these two jobs?
options: Outer white holds the motor neuron cell bodies; central gray holds only sensory axons
Central gray carries signals to and from the brain; outer white integrates reflexes
Central gray makes cerebrospinal fluid; outer white tracts absorb it back into the blood
Central gray integrates reflexes; outer white tracts carry signals to and from the brain
questions.why: The gray matter in the center of the cord holds cell bodies, interneurons, and synapses, so it is where signals are integrated, meaning combined and processed into a response, as in a spinal reflex. The white matter around it is made of myelinated axons organized into ascending tracts that carry sensory signals up to the brain and descending tracts that carry motor commands down. Processing happens in the gray core and long-distance conduction happens in the white shell.
notes: Motor neuron cell bodies sit in the anterior horn of the gray matter, not in the white matter. This mix-up confuses where cell bodies live with where axons run.
This reverses the two tissues. Gray matter holds the synapses where processing happens, while the white matter tracts carry signals over distance.

Cerebrospinal fluid is made mainly by the choroid plexuses in the ventricles of the brain, not by the cord's gray matter, and the white matter does not absorb it. Pick the choroid plexus for a question about where cerebrospinal fluid is produced.
Correct. Gray matter processes, and white matter tracts conduct up and down the cord.
questions.answerText: Central gray integrates reflexes; outer white tracts carry signals to and from the brain

questions.q: Which list gives the five components of a reflex arc in order?
options: Receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector
Effector, motor neuron, integration center, sensory neuron, receptor
Receptor, integration center, sensory neuron, motor neuron, effector
Receptor, motor neuron, integration center, sensory neuron, effector
questions.why: A reflex arc is a short, fixed pathway, which is why reflexes are fast. The receptor detects the stimulus, and the sensory neuron carries the signal to the CNS. The integration center, one or more synapses in the CNS, processes the signal. The motor neuron then carries the command out to the effector, the muscle or gland that carries out the response.
notes: Correct. Signal in, processing in the CNS, command out to the effector.
This is the whole arc written backward. A reflex starts with a stimulus at the receptor and ends with the effector's response, not the other way around.
The integration center sits in the CNS, so the signal needs the sensory neuron to get there first. This order puts processing before the signal has even reached the cord.
This order swaps the two neurons. The sensory neuron must come first to carry the signal in from the receptor, and the motor neuron comes after integration to carry the command out.
questions.answerText: Receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector

questions.q: What is a reflex?
options: A conscious decision made in the cerebral cortex
A signal that travels only along sensory neurons
A slow, voluntary response that must be learned by practice
A fast, automatic, predictable response to a stimulus
questions.why: A reflex is a fast, automatic, predictable response to a stimulus. It is fast because it runs along a short, fixed pathway, the reflex arc, and it is predictable because the same stimulus produces the same response each time. Pulling your hand away from a hot stove and the knee-jerk at the doctor's office are familiar examples.
notes: A conscious decision in the cerebral cortex is a voluntary action, which takes longer than a reflex. Many reflexes are completed in the spinal cord before the brain is even aware of the stimulus.
A reflex uses both a sensory neuron to carry the signal in and a motor neuron to carry the command out. A signal that only travels inward would produce a sensation, not a response.
Reflexes are fast and automatic rather than slow and voluntary. Some reflexes are learned through repetition, such as catching a dropped object, but even those run automatically once learned.
Correct. Fast, automatic, and predictable are the defining features of a reflex.
questions.answerText: A fast, automatic, predictable response to a stimulus

questions.q: In a reflex arc, what is the effector?
options: The muscle or gland that responds
The neuron that carries the command out of the CNS
The CNS synapse where the signal is processed
The receptor that first detects the stimulus
questions.why: The effector is the last link of the reflex arc: the muscle or gland that carries out the response. In the knee-jerk reflex the effector is the thigh muscle that kicks the leg forward. In an autonomic reflex the effector is smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or a gland, such as the smooth muscle of the iris in the pupillary light reflex.
notes: Correct. The effector is the muscle or gland that produces the response.
The neuron that carries the command out of the CNS is the motor neuron, the link just before the effector. Choose it if the question asked which neuron delivers the command.
The synapses where the signal is processed in the CNS form the integration center. This would be the answer if the question asked where the reflex is processed.
The receptor is the first link of the arc, the structure that detects the stimulus. Pick it if the question asked which component starts the reflex.
questions.answerText: The muscle or gland that responds

questions.q: Why can a spinal reflex such as the knee-jerk happen without any input from the brain?
options: Its effector is a gland that acts on its own
Its receptors send signals straight to the muscle
Its integration center is in the spinal cord
Its sensory neuron is also its motor neuron
questions.why: In a spinal reflex, the sensory neuron enters the cord and synapses in the gray matter, either directly on a motor neuron or through interneurons. The cord itself is the integration center, so the command goes back out without waiting for the brain. The brain may become aware of the event afterward through ascending tracts, but it is not needed to produce the response.
notes: The effector of the knee-jerk is skeletal muscle, not a gland, and no effector acts without a command from a motor neuron. A gland would be the effector in an autonomic reflex such as salivation.
Receptors cannot signal a muscle directly. The signal must travel along a sensory neuron to the CNS and back out along a motor neuron, even in the fastest reflex.
Correct. The cord's gray matter processes the signal, so the brain is not needed.
The sensory and motor neurons are separate cells. The sensory neuron carries the signal into the cord, and a different neuron, the motor neuron, carries the command out to the muscle.
questions.answerText: Its integration center is in the spinal cord

questions.q: A clinician taps just below a patient's kneecap and the leg kicks. What does this single test check, and what would a missing response suggest?
options: The whole reflex arc; a break somewhere along that pathway
Only the brain's motor cortex; a stroke on the same side
Only the thigh muscle; weakness in that muscle alone
Only the receptor; loss of skin sensation over the knee
questions.why: The patellar, or knee-jerk, reflex is a somatic stretch reflex. Tapping the tendon below the kneecap stretches the thigh muscle, receptors in the muscle send signals along sensory neurons into the cord, and motor neurons carry the command back to make the muscle contract. Because the test depends on every link (receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, and effector), a missing reflex means the pathway is broken somewhere along the way.
notes: Correct. The test runs the entire arc, so a missing response points to a break anywhere along it.

The knee-jerk is completed in the spinal cord and does not need the motor cortex. A stroke is tested by voluntary movement and strength, and it would affect the opposite side of the body, not the same side.
The muscle is only the effector, the last link of the arc. A weak muscle could reduce the kick, but a missing reflex could just as easily come from a damaged nerve or cord segment.
The receptors for this reflex sense muscle stretch, not touch on the skin, and they are only the first link. Skin sensation would be tested by touching the skin, not by tapping the tendon.
questions.answerText: The whole reflex arc; a break somewhere along that pathway

questions.q: Where does the spinal cord begin and end in an adult?
options: From the medulla oblongata to the L1 to L2 disc
From the pons to the second sacral vertebra
From the medulla oblongata to the L4 to L5 disc
From the medulla oblongata to the tip of the coccyx
questions.why: The spinal cord is continuous with the medulla oblongata at the foramen magnum and runs down the vertebral canal. In an adult it is about 42 to 45 cm (16 to 18 inches) long and ends at the conus medullaris, a tapered tip near the disc between L1 and L2. Below that point the canal holds only the cauda equina, the bundle of nerve roots that continues downward.
notes: Correct. The cord starts at the medulla and ends near the L1 to L2 disc.
The pons sits above the medulla in the brainstem, so the cord does not begin there, and the cord ends far above the sacrum. This choice puts both ends of the cord in the wrong place.
The L4 to L5 level is well below the end of the cord. It is a common site for a lumbar puncture needle, because only the cauda equina lies there and the cord is safely out of reach.
The coccyx is where the filum terminale, a thread of pia mater, anchors the cord. Pick the coccyx if the question asked where the filum terminale attaches, not where the cord ends.
questions.answerText: From the medulla oblongata to the L1 to L2 disc

questions.q: Which two regions of the spinal cord are visibly enlarged?
options: Cervical and lumbar enlargements
Thoracic and sacral enlargements
Lumbar and coccygeal enlargements
Cervical and thoracic enlargements
questions.why: The cord widens in two places where the nerves to the limbs arise. The cervical enlargement, from C4 to T1, holds the extra neurons that serve the upper limbs. The lumbar enlargement, behind the lower thoracic vertebrae (about T9 to T12), holds the extra neurons that serve the lower limbs. More limb muscle and skin to serve means more neurons, and that extra gray matter makes the cord wider.
notes: Correct. The cervical and lumbar enlargements serve the upper and lower limbs.

Neither region is enlarged. The thoracic cord serves the trunk rather than a limb, so it is narrow, and the sacral segments are relatively small. Pick thoracic if the question asked which region of the cord is narrow between the two enlargements.
The lumbar enlargement is real, but the coccygeal segment at the very end of the cord is tiny, not enlarged. This choice gets one of the two right.
The cervical enlargement is real, but the thoracic cord is narrow, not an enlargement. This choice gets one of the two right.
questions.answerText: Cervical and lumbar enlargements

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the anterior median fissure and the posterior median sulcus?
options: Shallow front groove and deep back groove; they split the cord into right and left
Deep front groove and shallow back groove; they split gray matter from white matter
Deep front groove and shallow back groove; they split the cord into right and left
Two gaps between vertebrae where the spinal nerves leave the vertebral canal
questions.why: Two grooves run the full length of the spinal cord. The anterior median fissure is the deep groove down the front, and the posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove down the back. Together they divide the cord into right and left halves. A fissure is a deep cleft and a sulcus is a shallower groove, which helps you remember which is which.
notes: This reverses the depths. The anterior groove is the deep fissure, and the posterior groove is the shallower sulcus.

The grooves are described correctly, but they divide the cord into right and left halves, not gray from white. Gray matter is the inner butterfly and white matter surrounds it, with no groove between them.
Correct. The deep fissure is in front and the shallow sulcus is in back, and together they split the cord into halves.
The gaps between vertebrae where spinal nerves exit are the intervertebral foramina. Pick these if the question asked where a spinal nerve leaves the vertebral canal.
questions.answerText: Deep front groove and shallow back groove; they split the cord into right and left

questions.q: Why does the adult spinal cord end near L1 to L2 even though the vertebral column runs much lower?
options: The cord stops growing at about age 4 or 5, but the column keeps growing
The lower part of the cord breaks down into the cauda equina during puberty
The column stops growing in childhood while the cord keeps shrinking
The filum terminale pulls the cord upward a little more each year
questions.why: The spinal cord stops lengthening at about 4 to 5 years of age, while the vertebral column keeps growing into adulthood. As a result, the end of the cord sits higher and higher relative to the vertebrae, finishing near the L1 to L2 disc. The nerve roots for the lower segments must run down the canal to reach their exits, forming the cauda equina. This is why a lumbar puncture needle can be placed below L2 without hitting the cord.
notes: Correct. The cord stops lengthening in early childhood while the column keeps growing.
The cauda equina is the bundle of nerve roots below the conus medullaris, not a broken-down piece of cord. It forms because those roots must travel down to reach their lower exit points.
This reverses the growth story. It is the column that keeps growing and the cord that stops, and the cord does not shrink.
The filum terminale is a thread of pia mater that anchors the cord to the coccyx; it does not pull the cord upward. Pick it if the question asked what anchors the lower end of the cord.
questions.answerText: The cord stops growing at about age 4 or 5, but the column keeps growing

questions.q: What are the two roots that connect each spinal nerve to the spinal cord?
options: The posterior sensory root and the anterior motor root
The posterior ramus and the anterior ramus
The posterior motor root and the anterior sensory root
The medial sensory root and the lateral motor root
questions.why: Each spinal nerve connects to the cord by two roots. The posterior (dorsal) root is the sensory root, bringing sensory axons into the cord, and it carries a swelling called the posterior root ganglion. The anterior (ventral) root is the motor root, carrying motor axons out of the cord. The two roots join just past the cord to form one mixed spinal nerve.
notes: Correct. The posterior root is sensory and the anterior root is motor.

The posterior and anterior rami are branches of the spinal nerve after it leaves the intervertebral foramen, not roots attached to the cord. Pick the rami if the question asked how a spinal nerve divides after it exits.
This swaps the roles. Posterior is sensory in and anterior is motor out, and only the posterior root has a ganglion.
Spinal nerve roots attach to the front and back of the cord, not its medial and lateral sides. This choice gets the functions right but uses the wrong directional terms.
questions.answerText: The posterior sensory root and the anterior motor root

questions.q: Shingles causes a painful rash along one strip of skin on one side of the body. Where does the virus hide, and why does the rash follow a single strip?
options: Posterior root ganglion; it holds one segment's sensory cell bodies
Anterior horn; it holds motor cell bodies for one segment
Posterior root ganglion; it holds motor cell bodies for one limb
Sympathetic trunk ganglia; they hold sensory cell bodies for the trunk
questions.why: The chickenpox virus can hide for decades in the posterior root ganglia. Each ganglion holds the sensory neuron cell bodies for one spinal segment, and their axons serve one strip of skin, called a dermatome. When the virus reactivates as shingles, it travels out along those sensory axons, so the rash and pain follow that one strip on one side of the body.
notes: Correct. The virus hides in a posterior root ganglion, which serves one segment's strip of skin.

The anterior horn holds somatic motor neuron cell bodies inside the cord, and it does not serve skin. Pick the anterior horn if the question asked where the cell bodies that drive skeletal muscle sit.
The location is right, but the posterior root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies, not motor ones, and it serves one segment rather than a whole limb.

The sympathetic trunk ganglia hold autonomic motor cell bodies, not the sensory cell bodies that serve the skin. They would be the answer for a question about the chain of ganglia beside the vertebral column.
questions.answerText: Posterior root ganglion; it holds one segment's sensory cell bodies

questions.q: Which list names the three gray horns of the spinal cord?
options: Medial, intermediate, and lateral horns
Superior, middle, and inferior horns
Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar horns
Posterior, lateral, and anterior horns
questions.why: The butterfly of gray matter projects into horns. The posterior (dorsal) horn holds interneurons and the incoming sensory axons, the anterior (ventral) horn holds the somatic motor nuclei that drive skeletal muscle, and the small lateral horn holds autonomic motor nuclei. The lateral horn appears only in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments.
notes: The horns are named posterior, lateral, and anterior. Medial and intermediate are not names of gray horns, so this choice only gets the lateral horn right.

Superior and inferior describe positions along the length of the cord, but the horns are seen in cross-section, pointing front, back, and sideways. This choice uses directional terms for the wrong plane.
Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar are regions of the cord, not horns. Pick these if the question asked how the cord is divided along its length.
Correct. The posterior, lateral, and anterior horns make up the gray matter.
questions.answerText: Posterior, lateral, and anterior horns

questions.q: What does the anterior (ventral) gray horn of the spinal cord contain?
options: Autonomic motor nuclei for smooth muscle and glands
Somatic motor nuclei for skeletal muscle
Interneurons and incoming sensory axons
Ascending tracts that carry sensation upward
questions.why: The anterior horn holds the somatic motor nuclei, clusters of motor neuron cell bodies whose axons leave through the anterior root to drive skeletal muscle contraction. Remember the pattern of the cord: posterior is sensory in, anterior is motor out. Damage to the anterior horn cells causes weakness of the muscles that segment controls.
notes: Autonomic motor nuclei sit in the lateral horn, present in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments. This would be the answer for a question about the lateral horn.
Correct. The anterior horn holds the somatic motor nuclei.
Interneurons and incoming sensory axons are found in the posterior (dorsal) horn. Pick this if the question asked what the posterior horn contains.
Ascending tracts are bundles of myelinated axons in the white matter, not part of the gray horns. Choose this for a question about the white columns of the cord.
questions.answerText: Somatic motor nuclei for skeletal muscle

questions.q: In which segments of the spinal cord is a lateral gray horn present?
options: Sacral and coccygeal segments only
Thoracic and upper lumbar segments
Every segment of the cord
Cervical segments only
questions.why: The lateral horn holds autonomic motor nuclei, specifically the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons. The sympathetic division leaves the cord from T1 to L2, so the lateral horn appears only in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments. Its presence is one way to recognize a thoracic section of the cord.
notes: The sacral segments do carry parasympathetic outflow from S2 to S4, but they do not form a lateral horn, and the coccygeal segment is the smallest part of the cord. This mix-up comes from linking any autonomic outflow with a lateral horn.
Correct. The lateral horn appears only where the sympathetic division leaves the cord, from T1 to L2.
Most cord segments have only posterior and anterior horns. The lateral horn is limited to the region where sympathetic fibers leave the cord.
The cervical segments have large anterior horns for the upper limbs but no lateral horn. This choice may come from linking the cervical enlargement with extra gray matter.
questions.answerText: Thoracic and upper lumbar segments

questions.q: What is the central canal of the spinal cord, and what is it continuous with?
options: A CSF channel in the gray commissure, continuous with the third ventricle
A CSF channel in the gray commissure, continuous with the fourth ventricle
A blood channel in the white matter, continuous with the vertebral arteries
A CSF channel in the white matter, continuous with the lateral ventricles
questions.why: The central canal is a tiny channel of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) running down the center of the cord, surrounded by the gray commissure, the bar of gray matter that joins the two sides. It is lined by ependymal cells. At its upper end it opens into the fourth ventricle of the brainstem, the ventricle closest to the cord.
notes: The third ventricle sits in the diencephalon, higher up, and connects to the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct. The canal joins the fourth ventricle, the one directly above the cord.
Correct. The central canal is a CSF channel continuous with the fourth ventricle.

The central canal carries CSF, not blood, and it sits in the gray commissure at the center of the cord. Pick the vertebral arteries for a question about the vessels that join to form the basilar artery.

The central canal sits in the gray commissure, not the white matter, and the lateral ventricles are deep within the cerebral hemispheres, far from the cord. Pick the lateral ventricles if the question asked which ventricles lie in the cerebrum.
questions.answerText: A CSF channel in the gray commissure, continuous with the fourth ventricle

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the ascending and descending tracts of the spinal cord?
options: Ascending tracts carry sensory signals up; descending tracts carry motor commands down
Ascending tracts carry motor commands up; descending tracts carry sensory signals down
Ascending tracts leave the cord as nerves; descending tracts stay within the cord
Ascending tracts run in the gray horns; descending tracts run in the white columns
questions.why: Tracts are bundles of axons in the white columns of the cord that share a common origin and destination. Ascending tracts are sensory and carry impulses up toward the brain. Descending tracts are motor and carry commands down from the brain to motor neurons in the cord. A spinal cord injury cuts both kinds, which is why sensation and movement are lost below the level of injury.
notes: Correct. Ascending tracts are sensory and go up; descending tracts are motor and go down.
This swaps the roles. Sensation travels up to the brain, and motor commands come down from it.
Tracts are CNS structures by definition, so neither kind leaves the cord as a nerve. Axons that leave the cord do so through the anterior roots, which are part of the PNS.
Both kinds of tracts run in the white columns. The gray horns hold cell bodies and interneurons, not long tracts.
questions.answerText: Ascending tracts carry sensory signals up; descending tracts carry motor commands down

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a somatic reflex and an autonomic reflex?
options: Somatic: skeletal muscle effector. Autonomic: smooth or cardiac muscle, or a gland
Somatic reflexes are all learned; autonomic reflexes are all present from birth
Somatic reflexes have one synapse; autonomic reflexes have two or more synapses
Somatic: smooth muscle or gland effector. Autonomic: skeletal muscle effector
questions.why: Somatic and autonomic reflexes are named for their effector. A somatic reflex acts on skeletal muscle, as in the patellar (knee-jerk) reflex. An autonomic reflex acts on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or a gland, as in the pupillary light reflex, where the pupil narrows in bright light. Other reflex names are based on different features, such as the number of synapses or whether the reflex is inborn.
notes: Correct. Somatic reflexes act on skeletal muscle, and autonomic reflexes act on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or glands.

Learned versus innate is a separate way of naming reflexes. The knee-jerk is a somatic reflex present from birth, and catching a dropped object is a learned somatic reflex, so somatic reflexes are not all learned.
One synapse versus several is the monosynaptic versus polysynaptic split, which cuts across both groups. The withdrawal reflex, for example, is somatic and polysynaptic.
This swaps the effectors. Skeletal muscle belongs to the somatic system, while smooth muscle and glands belong to the autonomic system.
questions.answerText: Somatic: skeletal muscle effector. Autonomic: smooth or cardiac muscle, or a gland

questions.q: What is another name for an autonomic reflex?
options: A somatic reflex
A stretch reflex
A visceral reflex
An acquired reflex
questions.why: Reflexes sorted by their effector are either somatic or autonomic. A somatic reflex acts on skeletal muscle, while an autonomic reflex, also called a visceral reflex, acts on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or a gland. The pupillary light reflex, which constricts the pupil using the smooth muscle of the iris, is the course example.
notes: A somatic reflex is the other half of the pair, with skeletal muscle as its effector, as in the patellar reflex.
A stretch reflex, such as the patellar reflex, is the course example of a monosynaptic reflex. It acts on skeletal muscle, so it is somatic.
Correct. An autonomic reflex is also called a visceral reflex, because its effector is smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or a gland.
Acquired reflex is another name for a learned reflex, one built through practice. That name sorts reflexes by whether they are inborn, not by effector.
questions.answerText: A visceral reflex

questions.q: How many pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain?
options: Eight pairs
Thirty-one pairs
Twelve pairs
Ten pairs
questions.why: Twelve pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain and brainstem. They are numbered with Roman numerals I to XII, from front to back, by where they attach. Even though they connect to the brain, they belong to the peripheral nervous system because they run out to the head, neck, and trunk.
notes: Eight is the number of cervical spinal nerve pairs. Pick it if the question asked how many spinal nerves arise in the neck region.
Thirty-one is the number of spinal nerve pairs, which arise from the spinal cord rather than the brain. Pick it if the question asked how many spinal nerves there are.
Correct. The cranial nerves are numbered I through XII, so there are twelve pairs.
Ten counts only cranial nerves III through XII, the nerves below the forebrain. It leaves out the olfactory and optic nerves, which attach above the brainstem, so it falls short of the total.
questions.answerText: Twelve pairs

questions.q: Cranial nerve I is which nerve?
options: The oculomotor nerve
The trigeminal nerve
The olfactory nerve
The optic nerve
questions.why: Cranial nerve I is the olfactory nerve, the nerve of smell. Its fibers begin in the olfactory epithelium high in the nasal cavity and pass up through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to the olfactory bulb. It is a sensory nerve and one of only two cranial nerves that attach above the brainstem.
notes: The oculomotor nerve is cranial nerve III and moves most of the eye muscles, raises the eyelid, and constricts the pupil. Its name starts like olfactory, which is why students mix them up.
The trigeminal nerve is cranial nerve V, the largest cranial nerve, carrying facial sensation and serving the chewing muscles. Pick it for the fifth cranial nerve.
Correct. The olfactory nerve is cranial nerve I and carries smell.
The optic nerve is cranial nerve II and carries vision from the retina. Pick it for the second cranial nerve.
questions.answerText: The olfactory nerve

questions.q: Cranial nerve II is which nerve?
options: The abducens nerve
The oculomotor nerve
The optic nerve
The olfactory nerve
questions.why: Cranial nerve II is the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the retina to the brain. It leaves the orbit through the optic canal of the sphenoid bone, and the two optic nerves meet at the optic chiasm. Like the olfactory nerve, it is purely sensory and attaches above the brainstem.
notes: The abducens nerve is cranial nerve VI, a motor nerve that turns the eye outward. It works on the eye but carries no vision, so it is not cranial nerve II.
The oculomotor nerve is cranial nerve III. It moves the eye rather than seeing with it, so pick it for most eye movements, lifting the eyelid, and constricting the pupil.
Correct. The optic nerve is cranial nerve II and carries vision.
The olfactory nerve is cranial nerve I, the nerve of smell. Pick it for the first cranial nerve.
questions.answerText: The optic nerve

questions.q: What is the number of the vagus nerve among the cranial nerves?
options: Cranial nerve XI
Cranial nerve X
Cranial nerve VIII
Cranial nerve IX
questions.why: The vagus nerve is cranial nerve X. Its name means wanderer, because it is the only cranial nerve that travels well past the head and neck into the chest and abdomen. It is a mixed nerve that leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the thoracic and abdominal organs.
notes: Cranial nerve XI is the accessory nerve, a motor nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. It also leaves through the jugular foramen, right beside the vagus.
Correct. The vagus nerve is cranial nerve X.
Cranial nerve VIII is the vestibulocochlear nerve, the sensory nerve for hearing and balance. Pick it for the nerve that enters through the internal acoustic meatus.

Cranial nerve IX is the glossopharyngeal nerve, which carries taste from the back of the tongue and helps with swallowing. It shares the jugular foramen with the vagus, which makes the two easy to confuse.
questions.answerText: Cranial nerve X

questions.q: Cranial nerve VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve, is associated with which special senses?
options: Hearing and balance
Smell and taste
Vision and eye movement
Facial sensation and chewing
questions.why: The vestibulocochlear nerve is a sensory nerve with two parts named for where they start. The cochlear part carries hearing from the cochlea, and the vestibular part carries balance information from the vestibule and semicircular canals of the inner ear. It enters the skull through the internal acoustic meatus alongside the facial nerve.
notes: Correct. The cochlear part serves hearing and the vestibular part serves balance.
Smell is carried by the olfactory nerve (I), and taste by the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves (VII and IX). No single nerve does both.
Vision is carried by the optic nerve (II), and eye movement by the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves (III, IV, VI). Pick this pair for those nerves.
Facial sensation and chewing belong to the trigeminal nerve (V). Pick this pair if the question asked about cranial nerve V.
questions.answerText: Hearing and balance

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the organs of the chest and abdomen?
options: The facial nerve
The trigeminal nerve
The vagus nerve
The accessory nerve
questions.why: The vagus nerve, cranial nerve X, carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the organs of the chest and abdomen. It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and travels down the neck into the thorax and abdomen, reaching the heart, the lungs, and much of the digestive tract. This long reach is why its name means wanderer.
notes: The facial nerve (VII) does carry parasympathetic fibers, but only to glands of the head such as the tear glands and some salivary glands. Pick it for tear or saliva production.
The trigeminal nerve (V) carries sensation from the face and serves the chewing muscles. It is not one of the four cranial nerves that carry parasympathetic fibers (III, VII, IX, and X).
Correct. The vagus nerve carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the thoracic and abdominal organs.
The accessory nerve (XI) is a motor nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. It leaves through the jugular foramen right beside the vagus, which is why students confuse them.
questions.answerText: The vagus nerve

questions.q: Cranial nerve V, the trigeminal nerve, has which two main functions?
options: Tongue movement and swallowing
Hearing and balance
Smell and vision
Facial sensation and chewing
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve is a mixed nerve and the largest cranial nerve. Its sensory fibers carry touch, pain, and temperature from the face through three branches (ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular), and its motor fibers travel with the mandibular branch to the muscles of chewing. The name comes from a Latin word for triplets, a reminder of those three branches.
notes: Tongue movement belongs to the hypoglossal nerve (XII), and swallowing to the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves (IX and X). Pick this pair for nerves of the lower brainstem.
Hearing and balance belong to the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII). Pick this pair for that nerve.
Smell and vision belong to the olfactory (I) and optic (II) nerves, the two purely sensory nerves at the front of the list.
Correct. The trigeminal nerve carries facial sensation and serves the chewing muscles.
questions.answerText: Facial sensation and chewing

questions.q: Which cranial nerve moves the tongue?
options: The facial nerve
The hypoglossal nerve
The accessory nerve
The glossopharyngeal nerve
questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve, cranial nerve XII, is a motor nerve that moves the tongue. Its name means under the tongue, which describes its path, and it leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal of the occipital bone. It is the last of the twelve cranial nerves.
notes: The facial nerve (VII) controls the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue. Pick it for taste on the front of the tongue, not tongue movement.
Correct. The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue.
The accessory nerve (XI) is a motor nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Pick it for turning the head and shrugging the shoulders.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) carries taste and sensation from the back of the tongue and helps with swallowing, but it does not move the tongue. Its glosso- root (tongue) is what makes it tempting.
questions.answerText: The hypoglossal nerve

questions.q: Which motor cranial nerve leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and serves muscles of the neck and shoulder?
options: The vagus nerve
The accessory nerve
The hypoglossal nerve
The glossopharyngeal nerve
questions.why: The accessory nerve, cranial nerve XI, is a motor nerve to two large muscles of the neck and shoulder, the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius. Most of its fibers start in the upper cervical spinal cord, rise into the skull through the foramen magnum, and then leave through the jugular foramen. Weakness turning the head or shrugging the shoulders points to this nerve.
notes: The vagus nerve (X) also exits the jugular foramen, but it is a mixed nerve serving the organs of the chest and abdomen, the voice, and swallowing. Pick it for parasympathetic supply to the viscera.
Correct. The accessory nerve is a motor nerve that exits the jugular foramen and serves neck and shoulder muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve (XII) is a motor nerve too, but it leaves through the hypoglossal canal and moves the tongue. Pick it for tongue movement.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) shares the jugular foramen, but it is mixed and serves taste on the back of the tongue and swallowing. Pick it for the throat and posterior tongue.
questions.answerText: The accessory nerve

questions.q: Through which opening does the hypoglossal nerve leave the skull?
options: The jugular foramen
The stylomastoid foramen
The foramen ovale
The hypoglossal canal
questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve, cranial nerve XII, leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal, a small tunnel in the occipital bone just above each occipital condyle. From there it runs forward beneath the tongue to reach the tongue muscles. The nerve and the canal share the same name, which makes this pairing easy to remember.
notes: The jugular foramen carries cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It sits right beside the hypoglossal canal, so pick it for the glossopharyngeal, vagus, or accessory nerve.
The stylomastoid foramen is where the facial nerve (VII) exits to reach the muscles of facial expression. Pick it for the facial nerve's final exit from the skull.
The foramen ovale in the sphenoid bone carries the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (V3). Pick it for the nerve branch to the lower jaw and chewing muscles.
Correct. The hypoglossal nerve exits through the hypoglossal canal.
questions.answerText: The hypoglossal canal

questions.q: Which cranial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue?
options: The vagus nerve
The glossopharyngeal nerve
The facial nerve
The trigeminal nerve
questions.why: The facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, is a mixed nerve. Its motor fibers control the muscles of facial expression, its sensory fibers carry taste from the front of the tongue, and its parasympathetic fibers drive tear and saliva production. It enters the internal acoustic meatus and exits to the face through the stylomastoid foramen.
notes: The vagus nerve (X) serves the organs of the chest and abdomen, the voice, and swallowing. Pick it for the parasympathetic supply to the heart and gut.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) carries taste from the back of the tongue and helps with swallowing. Pick it for the posterior tongue and throat.
Correct. The facial nerve moves the face and carries taste from the front of the tongue.
The trigeminal nerve (V) carries sensation from the face and serves the chewing muscles. Students confuse feeling the face with moving the face; pick the trigeminal nerve for facial touch and pain.
questions.answerText: The facial nerve

questions.q: Which cranial nerve is classified as a mixed nerve?
options: The trigeminal nerve
The vestibulocochlear nerve
The hypoglossal nerve
The optic nerve
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve (V) is a mixed nerve, carrying sensory axons from the face and motor axons to the chewing muscles. Only four cranial nerves are mixed: V, VII, IX, and X. The rest carry only sensory signals (I, II, and VIII) or mainly motor signals (III, IV, VI, XI, and XII).
notes: Correct. The trigeminal nerve carries both sensory and motor axons.
The vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) has two parts, which makes it look complex, but both parts are sensory (hearing and balance). Pick it as a sensory cranial nerve.
The hypoglossal nerve (XII) is a motor nerve that moves the tongue. Pick it as an example of a motor cranial nerve.
The optic nerve (II) is purely sensory and carries vision. Pick it as an example of a sensory cranial nerve.
questions.answerText: The trigeminal nerve

questions.q: Which choice correctly lists cranial nerves I, II, and VIII in numerical order with the sense each one carries?
options: Optic for smell, olfactory for vision, vestibulocochlear for hearing and balance
Olfactory for smell, optic for vision, vestibulocochlear for taste and balance
Olfactory for smell, optic for vision, vestibulocochlear for hearing and balance
Olfactory for smell, oculomotor for vision, vestibulocochlear for hearing and balance
questions.why: Cranial nerve I, the olfactory nerve, carries smell; cranial nerve II, the optic nerve, carries vision; and cranial nerve VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve, carries hearing and balance. These three are the purely sensory cranial nerves. Each name hints at its sense, since olfaction means smell and optic refers to sight.
notes: This swaps the olfactory and optic nerves, giving each the other's sense and number. The mix-up happens because both names start with O.
Taste is not carried by cranial nerve VIII; it travels in the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves (VII and IX). The cochlear part of VIII carries hearing.
Correct. I is olfactory for smell, II is optic for vision, and VIII is vestibulocochlear for hearing and balance.
The oculomotor nerve is cranial nerve III and moves the eye; it does not carry vision. Pick oculomotor for eye movement and pupil constriction.
questions.answerText: Olfactory for smell, optic for vision, vestibulocochlear for hearing and balance

questions.q: Through which opening does the vagus nerve leave the skull?
options: The hypoglossal canal
The jugular foramen
The foramen magnum
The internal acoustic meatus
questions.why: The vagus nerve, cranial nerve X, leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, the opening between the temporal and occipital bones where the internal jugular vein also begins. It shares this opening with the glossopharyngeal (IX) and accessory (XI) nerves. Because the three run together, a tumor or fracture at the jugular foramen can affect all three at once.
notes: The hypoglossal canal carries the hypoglossal nerve (XII) to the tongue. Pick it for cranial nerve XII.
Correct. The vagus nerve exits through the jugular foramen.
The foramen magnum is where the brainstem joins the spinal cord. The spinal part of the accessory nerve climbs up through it, but no cranial nerve leaves the skull this way.
The internal acoustic meatus carries the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves. Pick it for those two nerves.
questions.answerText: The jugular foramen

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil?
options: The trochlear nerve (IV)
The oculomotor nerve (III)
The abducens nerve (VI)
The ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal (V1)
questions.why: The oculomotor nerve (III) carries parasympathetic fibers that relay in the ciliary ganglion and then reach the muscle that constricts the pupil. It is one of the four cranial nerves with a parasympathetic part (III, VII, IX, and X). The same nerve also moves most of the eye muscles and raises the eyelid.
notes: The trochlear nerve (IV) is a motor nerve to the superior oblique muscle and carries no parasympathetic fibers. Pick it for that one eye muscle.
Correct. The oculomotor nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil.
The abducens nerve (VI) is a motor nerve to the lateral rectus, which turns the eye outward. Pick it for looking to the side.
The ophthalmic branch (V1) of the trigeminal nerve carries sensation from the surface of the eye, the forehead, and the nose. Pick it for touch and pain from the cornea.
questions.answerText: The oculomotor nerve (III)

questions.q: The cranial nerves are numbered with Roman numerals I to XII. What does the numbering follow?
options: The order of their skull openings, lateral to medial
Where they attach, from anterior to posterior
Their class, with sensory nerves numbered first
Their size, from largest to smallest
questions.why: The cranial nerves are numbered by the order in which they attach to the brain, from front to back. The olfactory nerve (I) attaches farthest forward, under the frontal lobe, and the higher numbers attach farther back. So CN I and II, which attach above the brainstem, come first, and III through XII follow in order down the brainstem, with most of XI coming from the upper cervical spinal cord.
notes: Skull openings do not set the numbers, and several nerves share one opening, such as IX, X, and XI in the jugular foramen. Pick the openings for a question about where a nerve exits the skull.
Correct. The numbers follow the attachment points from anterior to posterior.
The classes are mixed throughout the list. Sensory nerves are I, II, and VIII, so sensory nerves are not grouped first.
Size does not set the order. The largest nerve is the trigeminal (V) and the smallest is the trochlear (IV), which sit side by side in the numbering.
questions.answerText: Where they attach, from anterior to posterior

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell?
options: The optic nerve (CN II)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The facial nerve (CN VII)
The olfactory nerve (CN I)
questions.why: The olfactory nerve, CN I, is a purely sensory nerve that carries smell. Its fibers start in the olfactory epithelium at the roof of the nasal cavity, pass up through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, and reach the olfactory bulb. From there the olfactory tract carries the signals back toward the cortex.
notes: The optic nerve, CN II, is the other purely sensory nerve at the front of the list, and it carries vision. Pick it for a question about sight.

The trigeminal nerve, CN V, carries general sensation such as touch and pain from the face, including the inside of the nose, but not smell itself. It would be the answer for a question about facial sensation.
The facial nerve, CN VII, carries taste from the front of the tongue, a sense students often mix up with smell. Choose it for a question about taste or facial expression.
Correct. CN I, the olfactory nerve, carries smell.
questions.answerText: The olfactory nerve (CN I)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries vision?
options: The optic nerve (CN II)
The trochlear nerve (CN IV)
The olfactory nerve (CN I)
The oculomotor nerve (CN III)
questions.why: The optic nerve, CN II, is purely sensory and carries visual signals from the retina. It leaves the orbit through the optic canal of the sphenoid bone, and the two optic nerves meet at the optic chiasm. Several other cranial nerves move the eye, but only CN II carries what the eye sees.
notes: Correct. CN II, the optic nerve, carries vision.
The trochlear nerve, CN IV, moves the eye but does not carry vision, and it is the smallest cranial nerve. It would be the answer for a question about the smallest cranial nerve.
The olfactory nerve, CN I, carries smell. Pick it for a question about the sense of smell.
The oculomotor nerve, CN III, moves most of the eye, raises the eyelid, and constricts the pupil, but carries no visual information. Choose it for a question about eye movement or a drooping eyelid.
questions.answerText: The optic nerve (CN II)

questions.q: Which is the largest cranial nerve?
options: The vagus nerve (CN X)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The optic nerve (CN II)
The facial nerve (CN VII)
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve, CN V, is the largest cranial nerve. It is mixed, carrying sensation from the face and motor fibers to the muscles of chewing. Its name means triplets, because it splits into three branches, V1, V2, and V3, and each leaves the skull through its own opening.
notes: The vagus nerve, CN X, travels the farthest, reaching the thoracic and abdominal organs, which makes students guess it is the largest. Pick it for a question about the cranial nerve with the longest reach.
Correct. CN V, the trigeminal nerve, is the largest cranial nerve.
The optic nerve, CN II, is a thick sensory nerve for vision, but it is not the largest. Pick it for a question about vision.
The facial nerve, CN VII, is a mixed nerve for facial expression and taste, but it is not the largest. Choose it for a question about facial expression.
questions.answerText: The trigeminal nerve (CN V)

questions.q: Which is the smallest cranial nerve?
options: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
The accessory nerve (CN XI)
The trochlear nerve (CN IV)
The abducens nerve (CN VI)
questions.why: The trochlear nerve, CN IV, is the smallest cranial nerve. It is purely motor, arises from a nucleus in the midbrain, and passes through the superior orbital fissure to an eye muscle. Its name comes from trochlea, meaning pulley, after the pulley-like loop its muscle's tendon runs through.
notes: The hypoglossal nerve, CN XII, is the motor nerve of the tongue and exits through the hypoglossal canal. It would be the answer for a question about tongue movement.

The accessory nerve, CN XI, is a motor nerve to neck and shoulder muscles that exits through the jugular foramen. It is not the smallest, so choose it for a question about the purely motor nerve whose nucleus sits in the upper cervical spinal cord.
Correct. CN IV, the trochlear nerve, is the smallest cranial nerve.

The abducens nerve, CN VI, is also a small motor nerve to an eye muscle, but its nucleus is in the pons and it is not the smallest. Pick it for a question about the motor nerve from the pons that passes through the superior orbital fissure.
questions.answerText: The trochlear nerve (CN IV)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries hearing and balance?
options: The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The facial nerve (CN VII)
The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
questions.why: The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII, is purely sensory. Its cochlear part carries hearing from the cochlea, and its vestibular part carries balance information from the vestibule and semicircular canals. It enters the skull through the internal acoustic meatus alongside the facial nerve.
notes: The trigeminal nerve, CN V, carries sensation from the face and controls the muscles of chewing. It would be the answer for a question about facial sensation.

The facial nerve, CN VII, shares the internal acoustic meatus with CN VIII, but it controls facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue. Pick it for a question about facial expression.
Correct. CN VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve, carries hearing and balance.
The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, carries taste from the back of the tongue and helps with swallowing. Choose it for a question about taste from the back of the tongue.
questions.answerText: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve controls movement of the tongue?
options: The facial nerve (CN VII)
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
The accessory nerve (CN XI)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve, CN XII, is a purely motor nerve that moves the tongue. Its name means under the tongue, which is where it runs. It arises from the hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla and leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal.
notes: The facial nerve, CN VII, carries taste from the front of the tongue and controls facial expression. It would be the answer for a question about Bell's palsy.
Correct. CN XII, the hypoglossal nerve, moves the tongue.
The accessory nerve, CN XI, is purely motor too, but it moves neck and shoulder muscles. Pick it for a question about shrugging the shoulders or turning the head.

The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, also has glosso in its name, but it carries taste from the back of the tongue and helps with swallowing rather than moving the tongue. Choose it for a question about taste from the back of the tongue.
questions.answerText: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve provides autonomic control of the thoracic and abdominal organs?
options: The accessory nerve (CN XI)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
The vagus nerve (CN X)
questions.why: The vagus nerve, CN X, is a mixed nerve whose name means wanderer. After leaving the skull through the jugular foramen, it travels down the neck into the thorax and abdomen, carrying parasympathetic fibers to the heart, lungs, and much of the digestive tract. It also serves the voice and swallowing.
notes: The accessory nerve, CN XI, exits beside the vagus through the jugular foramen but is purely motor to neck and shoulder muscles. Pick it for a question about those muscles.
The trigeminal nerve, CN V, carries facial sensation and controls chewing, and it stays in the head. It would be the answer for a question about facial sensation.

The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, also uses the jugular foramen and carries some parasympathetic fibers, but only to the parotid gland in the head. Choose it for a question about the parotid gland or taste from the back of the tongue.
Correct. CN X, the vagus nerve, provides autonomic control of the thoracic and abdominal organs.
questions.answerText: The vagus nerve (CN X)

questions.q: Which three cranial nerves are purely sensory?
options: CN X, CN XI, and CN XII
CN I, CN II, and CN VIII
CN V, CN VII, and CN IX
CN III, CN IV, and CN VI
questions.why: The purely sensory cranial nerves carry special senses only: the olfactory nerve (I) for smell, the optic nerve (II) for vision, and the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) for hearing and balance. In the memory aid Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most, the S letters fall on I, II, and VIII.
notes: CN X is mixed, while CN XI and XII are purely motor. This set would only fit a question about the last three cranial nerves.
Correct. CN I, II, and VIII are the purely sensory cranial nerves.
CN V, VII, and IX are mixed nerves, carrying both sensory and motor fibers. Choose them, along with CN X, for a question about the mixed cranial nerves.
CN III, IV, and VI are the three motor nerves that move the eye. Pick them for a question about the nerves to the eye muscles.
questions.answerText: CN I, CN II, and CN VIII

questions.q: Which four cranial nerves are mixed, carrying both sensory and motor signals?
options: CN I, CN II, CN III, and CN IV
CN VIII, CN X, CN XI, and CN XII
CN V, CN VII, CN IX, and CN X
CN III, CN IV, CN VI, and CN XII
questions.why: The mixed cranial nerves are the trigeminal (V), facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX), and vagus (X). Each serves a region where it must both sense and move something, such as the face or the throat. In the memory aid Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most, the B letters fall on V, VII, IX, and X.
notes: CN I and II are purely sensory, and CN III and IV are motor. This set is simply the first four nerves in order.
CN VIII is sensory and CN XI and XII are motor, so only CN X in this set is mixed. Choose this group only for a question about the last nerves on the list.
Correct. CN V, VII, IX, and X are the mixed cranial nerves.
CN III, IV, VI, and XII are all motor nerves. Pick them, along with CN XI, for a question about the motor cranial nerves.
questions.answerText: CN V, CN VII, CN IX, and CN X

questions.q: Through which skull opening does the olfactory nerve (CN I) pass?
