options: The superior orbital fissure
The jugular foramen
The cribriform plate
The optic canal
questions.why: The cribriform plate is the sieve-like horizontal part of the ethmoid bone in the roof of the nasal cavity. Many small olfactory fibers pass up through its tiny holes, the olfactory foramina, to reach the olfactory bulb lying on top of it. A fracture here can tear these fibers and cause loss of smell.
notes: The superior orbital fissure carries CN III, IV, VI, and the V1 branch of CN V into the orbit. It would be the answer for the nerves that move the eye.
The jugular foramen carries CN IX, X, and XI. Choose it for a question about the glossopharyngeal, vagus, or accessory nerve.
Correct. CN I passes through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.
The optic canal of the sphenoid bone carries the optic nerve, CN II. Pick it for a question about the path of the nerve for vision.
questions.answerText: The cribriform plate

questions.q: Through which skull opening does the optic nerve (CN II) pass?
options: The optic canal
The foramen ovale
The hypoglossal canal
The cribriform plate
questions.why: The optic canal is a short tunnel in the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone at the back of the orbit. The optic nerve passes through it from the eye to reach the optic chiasm inside the skull. Its name matches the nerve, which makes it one of the easier foramina to remember.
notes: Correct. CN II passes through the optic canal of the sphenoid bone.
The foramen ovale of the sphenoid bone carries the V3 branch of the trigeminal nerve. Choose it for a question about the mandibular branch.
The hypoglossal canal carries the hypoglossal nerve, CN XII. It would be the answer for the nerve of the tongue.
The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone carries the olfactory nerve, CN I. Pick it for a question about smell.
questions.answerText: The optic canal

questions.q: Which purely motor cranial nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure and has its nucleus in the pons?
options: The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The oculomotor nerve (CN III)
The abducens nerve (CN VI)
The trochlear nerve (CN IV)
questions.why: Four nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure: CN III, CN IV, the V1 branch of CN V, and CN VI. Of these, the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei are in the midbrain, while the trigeminal and abducens nuclei are in the pons. The trigeminal nerve is mixed, so the only purely motor nerve that fits every clue is the abducens.
notes: The trigeminal nerve has nuclei in the pons and its V1 branch uses the superior orbital fissure, but it is mixed, not purely motor. It would be the answer for a question about facial sensation.
The oculomotor nerve is purely motor and uses the superior orbital fissure, but its nucleus is in the midbrain. Pick it for a question about the nerve that raises the eyelid and constricts the pupil.
Correct. The abducens nerve is purely motor, uses the superior orbital fissure, and arises from the pons.
The trochlear nerve is purely motor and uses the superior orbital fissure, but its nucleus is also in the midbrain. Choose it for a question about the smallest cranial nerve.
questions.answerText: The abducens nerve (CN VI)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve controls facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue?
options: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The facial nerve (CN VII)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
questions.why: The facial nerve, CN VII, is a mixed nerve. Its motor fibers control facial expression, its sensory fibers carry taste from the front of the tongue, and its parasympathetic fibers drive tear and saliva production. It enters the internal acoustic meatus and leaves the skull at the stylomastoid foramen.
notes: The hypoglossal nerve, CN XII, moves the tongue but carries no taste. It would be the answer for a question about tongue movement.
The trigeminal nerve, CN V, carries touch and pain from the face and controls chewing, but not facial expression or taste. Pick it for a question about facial sensation.
Correct. CN VII controls facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue.
The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, carries taste from the back of the tongue rather than the front. Choose it for a question about taste from the back of the tongue.
questions.answerText: The facial nerve (CN VII)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve is purely motor, exits through the jugular foramen, and has its nucleus in the upper cervical spinal cord?
options: The vagus nerve (CN X)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
The accessory nerve (CN XI)
questions.why: The accessory nerve, CN XI, is unusual because its motor nucleus sits in the upper cervical spinal cord, just below the brainstem. Its rootlets rise through the foramen magnum into the skull and then leave through the jugular foramen with CN IX and CN X. It is purely motor and moves muscles of the neck and shoulder.
notes: The vagus nerve also exits through the jugular foramen, but it is mixed and its nuclei sit in the medulla. Pick it for a question about autonomic control of the thoracic and abdominal organs.
The glossopharyngeal nerve also exits through the jugular foramen, but it is mixed and its nuclei are in the medulla. Choose it for a question about taste from the back of the tongue.

The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor with a medullary nucleus, but it exits through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. It would be the answer for a question about the nerve of the tongue.
Correct. CN XI is purely motor, uses the jugular foramen, and has its nucleus in the upper cervical cord.
questions.answerText: The accessory nerve (CN XI)

questions.q: Besides CN IX and CN X, which other cranial nerve passes through the jugular foramen?
options: The accessory nerve (CN XI)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The abducens nerve (CN VI)
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
questions.why: The jugular foramen lies between the temporal and occipital bones, and the internal jugular vein drains out through it. Three cranial nerves run beside the vein: the glossopharyngeal (IX), the vagus (X), and the accessory (XI). Learning the opening gives you all three nerves at once.
notes: Correct. CN XI joins CN IX and CN X in the jugular foramen.
The trigeminal nerve's three branches leave through the superior orbital fissure, the foramen rotundum, and the foramen ovale. Pick it for a question about those three openings.
The abducens nerve, CN VI, passes through the superior orbital fissure into the orbit. It would be the answer for a nerve that uses that fissure.
The hypoglossal nerve, CN XII, leaves through its own hypoglossal canal, just next to the jugular foramen. Choose it for a question about the hypoglossal canal.
questions.answerText: The accessory nerve (CN XI)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve passes through the hypoglossal canal of the occipital bone?
options: The accessory nerve (CN XI)
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
The vagus nerve (CN X)
questions.why: The hypoglossal canal is a small tunnel in the occipital bone just above the occipital condyle. It carries the hypoglossal nerve, CN XII, which shares its name. The nerve then runs below the tongue to move it.
notes: The accessory nerve, CN XI, leaves through the jugular foramen, not the hypoglossal canal. Choose it for the purely motor nerve that exits beside the vagus.
Correct. CN XII passes through the hypoglossal canal.

The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, leaves through the jugular foramen, not the hypoglossal canal, even though it also has glosso in its name. It would be the answer for taste from the back of the tongue.
The vagus nerve, CN X, leaves through the jugular foramen, not the hypoglossal canal. Pick it for a question about the nerve to the thoracic and abdominal organs.
questions.answerText: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

questions.q: How is the facial nerve (CN VII) classified?
options: Mixed
Special sensory only
Motor only
Sensory only
questions.why: The facial nerve carries motor fibers that control facial expression and sensory fibers that carry taste from the front of the tongue. It also carries parasympathetic fibers to the tear and salivary glands. Because it carries both sensory and motor signals, it is classified as mixed.
notes: Correct. CN VII is mixed, carrying both sensory and motor fibers.
Taste is a special sense, but CN VII also carries motor fibers, so it cannot be special sensory only. Choose special sensory only for nerves like the olfactory or optic nerve.
Purely motor nerves, such as CN III, IV, VI, XI, and XII, carry no sensory fibers. CN VII cannot be motor only because it carries taste.
Purely sensory nerves, such as CN I, II, and VIII, carry no motor fibers. CN VII cannot be sensory only because it moves the muscles of facial expression.
questions.answerText: Mixed

questions.q: A patient cannot raise one eyelid, cannot move that eye in most directions, and has a pupil on that side that will not constrict. Which cranial nerve is affected?
options: The trochlear nerve (CN IV)
The oculomotor nerve (CN III)
The abducens nerve (CN VI)
The optic nerve (CN II)
questions.why: The oculomotor nerve, CN III, controls most eye movements, raises the upper eyelid, and constricts the pupil through its parasympathetic fibers. Losing all three functions on one side points to CN III. Its nuclei are in the midbrain, and it reaches the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
notes: The trochlear nerve, CN IV, controls only one eye movement and has nothing to do with the eyelid or pupil. Choose it for a question about the smallest cranial nerve.
Correct. CN III controls most eye movements, the eyelid, and pupil constriction.

The abducens nerve, CN VI, controls only one eye movement and does not raise the eyelid or constrict the pupil. It would be the answer for the purely motor nerve from the pons that uses the superior orbital fissure.
The optic nerve, CN II, carries vision but moves nothing. Pick it for a patient who has lost sight in one eye.
questions.answerText: The oculomotor nerve (CN III)

questions.q: Which cranial nerves attach above the brainstem rather than to it?
options: The olfactory (I) and optic (II) nerves
The vagus (X) and accessory (XI) nerves
The facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves
The oculomotor (III) and trochlear (IV) nerves
questions.why: The olfactory nerve attaches to the cerebrum through the olfactory bulb, and the optic nerve attaches to the diencephalon through the optic chiasm and tracts. Cranial nerves III through XII attach to the brainstem, except that most of CN XI comes from the upper cervical spinal cord. So CN I and II are the only two that attach above the brainstem.
notes: Correct. CN I and CN II attach to the cerebrum and diencephalon, above the brainstem.

The vagus nerve attaches to the medulla, and the accessory nerve comes mostly from the upper cervical spinal cord, so both attach at or below the bottom of the brainstem. Choose them for a question about nerves that exit through the jugular foramen.
The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves attach near the junction of the pons and medulla. They would be the answer for the nerves that enter the internal acoustic meatus.
The oculomotor and trochlear nerves attach to the midbrain, the top of the brainstem. Pick them for a question about the cranial nerves with midbrain nuclei.
questions.answerText: The olfactory (I) and optic (II) nerves

questions.q: The dorsal motor nucleus and the nucleus ambiguus of the vagus nerve (CN X) lie in which brain region?
options: The cerebellum
The midbrain
The pons
The medulla oblongata
questions.why: The vagus nerve attaches to the side of the medulla oblongata, in the groove behind the olive, and its nuclei, including the dorsal motor nucleus and the nucleus ambiguus, sit there. The medulla holds the nuclei of IX, X, and XII. This fits the general rule that cranial nerve nuclei run in number order from the midbrain down.
notes: The cerebellum holds no cranial nerve nuclei. It would be the answer for a question about coordination and balance.
The midbrain holds the nuclei for CN III and IV. Pick it for a question about the oculomotor or trochlear nucleus.
The pons holds the nuclei for CN V through VIII. Choose it for a question about the trigeminal, abducens, or facial nucleus.
Correct. The vagus nuclei lie in the medulla oblongata.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries taste from the back of the tongue, helps with swallowing, and serves the parotid gland?
options: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
The vagus nerve (CN X)
The facial nerve (CN VII)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
questions.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, is named for the tongue (glosso) and the pharynx. It is mixed: it carries taste from the back of the tongue, helps with swallowing, and sends parasympathetic fibers to the parotid salivary gland. It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen.
notes: The hypoglossal nerve, CN XII, moves the tongue but carries no taste. It would be the answer for a question about tongue movement.

The vagus nerve, CN X, also helps with swallowing and voice, but it serves the thoracic and abdominal organs rather than the parotid gland. Choose it for a question about autonomic control of the viscera.
The facial nerve, CN VII, carries taste from the front of the tongue, not the back. Pick it for a question about taste from the front of the tongue.
Correct. CN IX carries taste from the back of the tongue, helps with swallowing, and serves the parotid gland.
questions.answerText: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

questions.q: The V2 (maxillary) branch of the trigeminal nerve passes through which skull opening?
options: The superior orbital fissure
The foramen ovale
The optic canal
The foramen rotundum
questions.why: Each of the three trigeminal branches has its own exit from the skull. V1 leaves through the superior orbital fissure, V2 through the foramen rotundum, and V3 through the foramen ovale, all in the sphenoid bone. A handy order to remember is Standing Room Only: superior orbital fissure, rotundum, ovale.
notes: The superior orbital fissure carries V1, the ophthalmic branch, along with CN III, IV, and VI. Choose it if the question names V1.
The foramen ovale carries V3, the mandibular branch. Pick it if the question names V3.
The optic canal carries the optic nerve, CN II, not any trigeminal branch. It would be the answer for the nerve of vision.
Correct. V2 passes through the foramen rotundum.
questions.answerText: The foramen rotundum

questions.q: How is the trigeminal nerve (CN V) classified?
options: Special sensory only
Motor only
Mixed
Sensory only
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve carries general sensation, such as touch and pain, from the face, and it also carries motor fibers to the muscles of chewing. Because it carries both sensory and motor signals, it is classified as mixed. Most of its fibers are sensory, which is why students sometimes call it sensory only.
notes: Special senses are smell, vision, taste, hearing, and balance. CN V carries general sensation like touch and pain, not a special sense, so this label fits nerves like CN I or CN II instead.
CN V does have motor fibers for chewing, but it also carries facial sensation, so it cannot be motor only. Choose motor only for nerves like CN III or CN XII.
Correct. CN V is mixed, carrying facial sensation and motor fibers for chewing.
CN V carries a great deal of facial sensation, but it also moves the muscles of chewing, so it cannot be sensory only. Pick sensory only for CN I, II, or VIII.
questions.answerText: Mixed

questions.q: The cochlear and vestibular nuclei connected to CN VIII sit at the junction of which two regions?
options: The midbrain and the pons
The medulla and the spinal cord
The pons and the medulla
The cerebrum and the diencephalon
questions.why: The vestibulocochlear nerve attaches at the pontomedullary junction, where the pons meets the medulla. Its cochlear and vestibular nuclei lie right at that border. This is why CN VIII is listed among the nerves of the pons and also among the nerves of the medulla.
notes: The midbrain holds the nuclei for CN III and IV, above the pons. Pick this pair for a question about the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei.
The CN VIII nuclei do not sit at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord. The upper cervical cord just below that junction holds the accessory (CN XI) nucleus instead.
Correct. The CN VIII nuclei sit at the junction of the pons and medulla.
The cerebrum and diencephalon receive CN I and CN II, the two nerves that attach above the brainstem. Choose them for a question about smell and vision.
questions.answerText: The pons and the medulla

questions.q: A tumor at the jugular foramen causes trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, and weakness shrugging one shoulder. Which set of cranial nerves is compressed?
options: CN VII, CN VIII, and CN XII
CN IX, CN X, and CN XI
CN III, CN IV, and CN VI
CN V, CN VII, and CN VIII
questions.why: The jugular foramen carries the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and accessory (XI) nerves side by side. A mass there can press on all three at once. The glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves serve swallowing and the voice, and the accessory nerve serves the shoulder, producing this recognizable cluster of signs.
notes: CN VII and VIII pass through the internal acoustic meatus, and CN XII passes through the hypoglossal canal. This set mixes nerves from two different openings.
Correct. CN IX, X, and XI pass through the jugular foramen together.
CN III, IV, and VI move the eye and pass through the superior orbital fissure. Pick them for a mass at that fissure causing double vision.
CN V, VII, and VIII serve facial sensation, facial expression, and hearing. Choose them for a mass near the pons that affects the face and ear.
questions.answerText: CN IX, CN X, and CN XI

questions.q: A patient wakes up with one side of the face drooping and cannot close that eye or smile on that side. Which cranial nerve is involved in this Bell's palsy?
options: The accessory nerve (CN XI)
The facial nerve (CN VII)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The oculomotor nerve (CN III)
questions.why: Bell's palsy is a sudden weakness of the facial nerve, CN VII, which controls facial expression. Each facial nerve serves only its own side, so the affected side droops while the other side works normally. Taste from the front of the tongue can also be affected because CN VII carries it.
notes: The accessory nerve, CN XI, moves the neck and shoulder. Choose it for a patient who cannot shrug one shoulder.
Correct. Bell's palsy is a weakness of CN VII.
The trigeminal nerve, CN V, carries facial sensation and controls chewing. Its classic disorder is trigeminal neuralgia, a stabbing facial pain, so pick it for that problem.

The oculomotor nerve, CN III, raises the eyelid and moves most of the eye but does not close the eye or move the face. It would be the answer for a drooping eyelid with a pupil that will not constrict.
questions.answerText: The facial nerve (CN VII)

questions.q: A clinician finds that a patient's tongue is weak on one side and looks for the lesion at the hypoglossal (CN XII) nucleus. Which brain region holds that nucleus?
options: The upper cervical cord
The midbrain
The medulla oblongata
The pons
questions.why: The hypoglossal nucleus lies in the medulla oblongata, near the midline. Testing each cranial nerve helps localize brainstem lesions because each nucleus has a fixed home. A weak tongue from a CN XII problem points the clinician to the medulla.
notes: The upper cervical cord holds the accessory (CN XI) nucleus, not the hypoglossal nucleus. It would be the answer for a question about where the CN XI nucleus sits.
The midbrain holds the nuclei for CN III and IV. Pick it for a patient with a drooping eyelid and a pupil that will not constrict.
Correct. The hypoglossal nucleus is in the medulla oblongata.
The pons holds the nuclei for CN V through VIII. Choose it for a weak abducens or facial nerve.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.q: A patient has brief, stabbing pain along the cheek and jaw on one side of the face. Which cranial nerve is the source of this trigeminal neuralgia?
options: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
The facial nerve (CN VII)
questions.why: Trigeminal neuralgia is a stabbing facial pain that follows the branches of CN V, the trigeminal nerve, which carries touch and pain from the face. The cheek is served by V2 and the jaw by V3, so pain along these areas matches the nerve's branches. The anatomy of the nerve predicts exactly where the pain appears.
notes: The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, serves the throat and the back of the tongue. Choose it for a question about taste from the back of the tongue or swallowing.
The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII, carries hearing and balance, not facial sensation. It would be the answer for hearing loss or dizziness.
Correct. Trigeminal neuralgia comes from CN V, the nerve of facial sensation.
The facial nerve, CN VII, controls facial movement rather than facial pain. Pick it for a drooping face, as in Bell's palsy.
questions.answerText: The trigeminal nerve (CN V)

questions.q: A patient's eye movement problem is traced to a nucleus in the midbrain. The nerve involved is purely motor, but the eyelid and pupil are normal. Which nerve is most likely affected?
options: The oculomotor nerve (CN III)
The trochlear nerve (CN IV)
The optic nerve (CN II)
The abducens nerve (CN VI)
questions.why: Two cranial nerves have their motor nuclei in the midbrain, the oculomotor (III) and the trochlear (IV), and both move the eye. The oculomotor nerve also raises the eyelid and constricts the pupil, so a normal eyelid and pupil point away from it. That leaves the trochlear nerve, the smallest cranial nerve, which moves the eye through a single muscle.
notes: The oculomotor nerve does have its nucleus in the midbrain, but damage would also cause a drooping eyelid and a pupil that will not constrict. Pick it when those signs are present.
Correct. The trochlear nerve is the purely motor eye nerve with a midbrain nucleus that leaves the eyelid and pupil alone.
The optic nerve carries vision and is sensory, not motor, and it attaches to the diencephalon rather than the midbrain. It would be the answer for loss of sight.
The abducens nerve is purely motor and moves the eye, but its nucleus is in the pons, not the midbrain. Choose it for a lesion localized to the pons.
questions.answerText: The trochlear nerve (CN IV)

questions.q: The twelve pairs of cranial nerves belong to which division of the nervous system?
options: The central nervous system
The peripheral nervous system
The enteric nervous system
Only the autonomic division of the PNS
questions.why: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The cranial nerves arise from the brain and brainstem but travel outside them to reach their targets, so they are part of the peripheral nervous system, just like the spinal nerves. Some cranial nerves carry autonomic fibers, but most also carry somatic sensory or motor fibers.
notes: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord themselves. The cranial nerves connect to it but lie outside it, so pick the CNS for a question about the brain or cord.
Correct. The cranial nerves are part of the peripheral nervous system.
The enteric nervous system is the network of neurons in the wall of the digestive tract. Choose it for a question about the nerve plexuses within the gut wall.
Only CN III, VII, IX, and X carry autonomic fibers, and even they carry other types too. Most cranial nerves are sensory or somatic motor, so the autonomic division alone is too narrow.
questions.answerText: The peripheral nervous system

questions.q: The vagus nerve (CN X) reaches far beyond the head to the heart, lungs, and digestive tract. What type of fibers does it carry to these organs?
options: Sympathetic fibers from the thoracic cord
Parasympathetic (visceral motor) fibers
Somatic motor fibers to trunk muscles
Special sensory fibers for hearing
questions.why: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic, or rest-and-digest, fibers to the heart, lungs, and much of the digestive tract. These visceral motor fibers slow the heart and promote digestion. A single cranial nerve reaching so many organs is why the vagus is called the wanderer.
notes: Sympathetic fibers leave the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord from the lateral horns, not from a cranial nerve. Pick this for a question about the sympathetic division.
Correct. The vagus carries parasympathetic fibers to the thoracic and abdominal organs.
Skeletal muscles of the trunk are served by spinal nerves, not the vagus. Choose spinal nerves for a question about trunk muscles.
Hearing is carried by the vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII. It would be the answer for a question about the sense of hearing.
questions.answerText: Parasympathetic (visceral motor) fibers

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the optic nerve (CN II) and the facial nerve (CN VII)?
options: CN II is purely sensory, while CN VII is mixed
Both are purely motor nerves
CN II is mixed, while CN VII is purely sensory
CN II is purely motor, while CN VII is purely sensory
questions.why: Each cranial nerve carries the kinds of fibers its job needs. The optic nerve only carries vision into the brain, so it is purely sensory. The facial nerve both moves the muscles of facial expression and carries taste, so it is mixed.
notes: Correct. CN II is purely sensory and CN VII is mixed.
Neither nerve is purely motor. The optic nerve carries vision, and the facial nerve carries taste as well as motor fibers.
This reverses the two nerves. The optic nerve carries only vision, and the facial nerve has motor fibers for expression, so neither label fits here.
The optic nerve moves nothing, so it cannot be motor, and the facial nerve has motor fibers, so it cannot be purely sensory.
questions.answerText: CN II is purely sensory, while CN VII is mixed

questions.q: A fracture runs through the superior orbital fissure. Which group of cranial nerves is most at risk?
options: CN IX, X, and XI
CN III, IV, V1, and VI
CN II, III, IV, and VI
CN VII and VIII only
questions.why: The superior orbital fissure is the slit between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid at the back of the orbit. The nerves that move the eye, CN III, IV, and VI, pass through it along with V1, the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. Damage here can cause eye movement problems and numbness of the forehead together.
notes: CN IX, X, and XI pass through the jugular foramen. They would be the answer for a lesion causing swallowing, voice, and shoulder problems.
Correct. CN III, IV, V1, and VI pass through the superior orbital fissure.
CN III, IV, and VI do use the superior orbital fissure, but CN II, the optic nerve, passes through the separate optic canal. Pick a group with CN II for a fracture involving the optic canal.
CN VII and VIII pass through the internal acoustic meatus in the temporal bone. Choose them for a fracture affecting facial movement and hearing.
questions.answerText: CN III, IV, V1, and VI

questions.q: Visual signals leave the retina in the optic nerve, pass through the optic chiasm, and travel in the optic tract to which relay nucleus?
options: The lateral geniculate nucleus
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus
The vestibular nuclei of the brainstem
The olfactory bulb
questions.why: The optic nerve carries visual signals from the retina back to the optic chiasm, where fibers from the two eyes partly cross. The pathway then continues as the optic tract to the lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay nucleus of the thalamus. From there the signals are passed on to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
notes: Correct. The optic tract carries visual signals to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.

The Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain belongs to CN III and sends the signals that constrict the pupil. It would be the answer for a question about the parasympathetic nucleus of the oculomotor nerve.
The vestibular nuclei at the pons and medulla receive balance signals from CN VIII. Choose them for a question about the pathway for balance.
The olfactory bulb receives smell signals from the olfactory epithelium and sends them along the olfactory tract. Pick it for the pathway of CN I.
questions.answerText: The lateral geniculate nucleus

questions.q: Taste from the front of the tongue and taste from the back of the tongue are carried by which two cranial nerves?
options: Facial (VII) and glossopharyngeal (IX)
Trigeminal (V) and hypoglossal (XII)
Olfactory (I) and vestibulocochlear (VIII)
Hypoglossal (XII) and accessory (XI)
questions.why: Taste is a special sense carried by mixed cranial nerves. The facial nerve, CN VII, carries taste from the front of the tongue, and the glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX, carries taste from the back. Both send these signals to nuclei in the brainstem.
notes: Correct. CN VII carries taste from the front of the tongue and CN IX from the back.

The trigeminal nerve carries general touch and pain from the front of the tongue, not taste, and the hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue. Pick this pair for a question about touch and movement of the tongue.
The olfactory nerve carries smell and the vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance. Choose this pair for a question about two purely sensory cranial nerves.
Both of these nerves are purely motor, moving the tongue and the neck and shoulder muscles. They would be the answer for a question about motor nerves near the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal.
questions.answerText: Facial (VII) and glossopharyngeal (IX)

questions.q: The facial nerve (CN VII) enters the temporal bone through the internal acoustic meatus. Through which opening does it leave the skull to reach the face?
options: The jugular foramen
The stylomastoid foramen
The hypoglossal canal
The foramen ovale of the sphenoid
questions.why: The facial nerve travels through a canal in the temporal bone after entering the internal acoustic meatus with CN VIII. It exits the skull at the stylomastoid foramen, between the styloid and mastoid processes. From there its branches fan out across the face to the muscles of facial expression.
notes: The jugular foramen carries CN IX, X, and XI. Pick it for a question about the glossopharyngeal, vagus, or accessory nerve.
Correct. CN VII leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.
The hypoglossal canal carries CN XII to the tongue. It would be the answer for the nerve of tongue movement.
The foramen ovale carries V3, the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve. Choose it for a question about the nerve to the muscles of chewing.
questions.answerText: The stylomastoid foramen

questions.q: Which four cranial nerves carry parasympathetic (visceral motor) fibers?
options: CN I, II, and VIII
CN IV, VI, XI, and XII
CN III, VII, IX, and X
CN V, VII, IX, and X
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibers travel in four cranial nerves. CN III constricts the pupil, CN VII drives tear and saliva production, CN IX serves the parotid gland, and CN X serves the thoracic and abdominal organs. These nerves already reach the glands and organs involved, so they carry the signals that regulate them.
notes: These are the purely sensory cranial nerves for smell, vision, hearing, and balance. They would be the answer for a question about the sensory nerves.
These are purely motor nerves to skeletal muscles of the eye, neck, shoulder, and tongue. Choose them for a question about somatic motor cranial nerves.
Correct. CN III, VII, IX, and X carry parasympathetic fibers.
This is close to the list of mixed nerves, but CN V is not parasympathetic, and CN III, which is, is missing. Pick V, VII, IX, and X for a question about the mixed cranial nerves.
questions.answerText: CN III, VII, IX, and X

questions.q: A patient wakes up unable to close one eye, raise that eyebrow, or smile on the same side of the face. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
options: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
questions.why: The facial nerve (CN VII) is a mixed cranial nerve whose motor job is facial expression; it leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen and fans out across the face. When it fails on one side, as in Bell palsy, expression on that whole side goes slack, so the eye will not close, the forehead will not wrinkle, and the mouth droops. Because it also carries taste from the front of the tongue and drives tears and saliva, those can be affected too.
notes: The hypoglossal nerve controls movement of the tongue. It would be the answer for a patient whose tongue drifts to one side when stuck out.
The oculomotor nerve controls most eye movements, raises the upper eyelid, and constricts the pupil. Damage would cause a drooping eyelid and trouble moving the eye, not loss of the smile.
Correct. Loss of expression on one whole side of the face points to the facial nerve.

The trigeminal nerve carries sensation from the face and controls the muscles of chewing. Pick it if the patient lost feeling in the face or had trouble clenching the jaw while facial expression stayed normal.
questions.answerText: Facial nerve (CN VII)

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries sensation from the face and also controls the muscles of chewing?
options: Facial nerve (CN VII)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Vagus nerve (CN X)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the largest cranial nerve and is mixed, carrying both sensory and motor fibers. Its three branches, ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3), carry sensation from the face, and the mandibular branch also carries the motor fibers for chewing. Its nuclei are in the pons.
notes: The facial nerve controls facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue, but it is not the main sensory nerve of the face. Pick it if the question asked which nerve is involved in Bell palsy.
Correct. The trigeminal nerve is the sensory nerve of the face and the motor nerve for chewing.
The vagus nerve gives autonomic control of the thoracic and abdominal organs and serves the voice and swallowing. Choose it for the cranial nerve that travels down into the trunk.

The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the back of the tongue, helps with swallowing, and drives saliva from the parotid gland. It would be the answer for a question about the back of the tongue and throat.
questions.answerText: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)

questions.q: Which three cranial nerves control the movements of the eyeball?
options: Oculomotor (III), trigeminal (V), and abducens (VI)
Trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), and facial (VII)
Optic (II), oculomotor (III), and trochlear (IV)
Oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), and abducens (VI)
questions.why: Three motor cranial nerves move the eyeball, and all three pass through the superior orbital fissure. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) handles most eye movements and also raises the eyelid and constricts the pupil, the trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the smallest cranial nerve, and the abducens nerve (CN VI) turns the eye outward. The optic nerve carries vision but does not move the eye.
notes: The trigeminal nerve is the odd one out: its ophthalmic branch carries sensation from the eye region but does not move the eye. The trochlear nerve belongs in its place.
The trigeminal nerve carries facial sensation and controls chewing, and the facial nerve controls facial expression. Only the abducens in this set moves the eye.
The optic nerve carries vision from the retina, so it is purely sensory and moves nothing. Swap it for the abducens nerve and the set would be right.
Correct. CN III, IV, and VI are the three eye-movement nerves.
questions.answerText: Oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), and abducens (VI)

questions.q: How many pairs of cranial nerves are there, and where do they arise?
options: 12 pairs, from the brain
12 pairs, from the spinal cord
24 pairs, from the brain
31 pairs, from the spinal cord
questions.why: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, numbered I to XII from front to back by where they attach to the brain. The olfactory (I) and optic (II) nerves attach to the cerebrum and diencephalon, and nerves III through XII attach to the brainstem, except that most of XI comes from the upper cervical spinal cord. Like the spinal nerves, they are part of the peripheral nervous system.
notes: Correct. There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, and they arise from the brain.
The count is right, but cranial nerves attach to the brain, not the spinal cord. That is what makes them cranial rather than spinal.
Twenty-four is the number of individual cranial nerves, counting left and right separately. Cranial nerves are counted in pairs, so the answer is 12 pairs.
There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves, and they arise from the spinal cord. Pick this if the question asked about spinal nerves.
questions.answerText: 12 pairs, from the brain

questions.q: Which cranial nerve is the vagus, and what makes its reach unusual?
options: CN X; it reaches beyond the head into the thorax and abdomen
CN X; it carries only hearing and balance from the ear
CN IX; it reaches beyond the head into the thorax and abdomen
CN XI; its roots arise partly from the upper spinal cord
questions.why: The vagus is cranial nerve X, a mixed nerve that leaves the skull through the jugular foramen. Its name means wanderer, because it travels far beyond the head and neck, down into the thorax and abdomen. It carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the chest and abdominal organs, which is why one nerve can slow the heart and drive digestion, and it also serves voice and swallowing.
notes: Correct. The vagus is CN X, and it wanders into the thorax and abdomen.
Hearing and balance are carried by CN VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve. Pick CN VIII if the question asked which nerve serves the inner ear.

CN IX is the glossopharyngeal nerve, which serves taste from the back of the tongue, swallowing, and saliva from the parotid gland. It shares the jugular foramen with the vagus but stays in the head and neck.
CN XI is the accessory nerve, whose nucleus sits in the upper cervical spinal cord. It is not the vagus, so pick it only if the question asked which cranial nerve has roots in the cord.
questions.answerText: CN X; it reaches beyond the head into the thorax and abdomen

questions.q: Which cranial nerves carry vision and smell?
options: Optic (II) for vision; olfactory (I) for smell
Olfactory (I) for vision; optic (II) for smell
Oculomotor (III) for vision; olfactory (I) for smell
Optic (II) for vision; trigeminal (V) for smell
questions.why: The first two cranial nerves are both purely sensory and both serve special senses. The olfactory nerve (CN I) carries smell from the nasal cavity through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The optic nerve (CN II) carries vision from the retina through the optic canal. These two are the only cranial nerves that attach above the brainstem.
notes: Correct. The optic nerve carries vision and the olfactory nerve carries smell.
This swaps the two nerves. Olfactory refers to smell (as in the olfactory bulb), and optic refers to the eye and vision.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) moves most of the eye muscles, raises the eyelid, and constricts the pupil, but it does not carry vision. Pick it if the question asked which nerve controls most eye movements.
The trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries general sensation from the face, such as touch and pain, but not the special sense of smell. It would be the answer for a question about facial sensation.
questions.answerText: Optic (II) for vision; olfactory (I) for smell

questions.q: Which statement correctly matches two mixed cranial nerves to their main jobs?
options: Vagus (X): facial expression; trigeminal (V): face sensation and chewing
Trigeminal (V): facial expression; facial (VII): face sensation and chewing
Facial (VII): facial expression; glossopharyngeal (IX): chewing
Facial (VII): facial expression; trigeminal (V): face sensation and chewing
questions.why: Both nerves are mixed and both serve the face, so they are easy to confuse. The facial nerve (CN VII) controls facial expression and also carries taste from the front of the tongue and drives tear and saliva production. The trigeminal nerve (CN V), the largest cranial nerve, has three branches that carry sensation from the face, and it also controls chewing. A drooping face points to CN VII, as in Bell's palsy, while stabbing facial pain points to CN V, as in trigeminal neuralgia.
notes: The vagus (CN X) serves the thoracic and abdominal organs, voice, and swallowing, not facial expression. It would be the answer for a question about the nerve that reaches into the abdomen.
This swaps the two nerves. The facial nerve moves the face for expression, while the trigeminal nerve feels the face and moves the jaw for chewing.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) serves taste from the back of the tongue, swallowing, and saliva from the parotid gland, not chewing. Pick it if the question asked which nerve carries taste from the back of the tongue.
Correct. CN VII runs facial expression, and CN V carries face sensation and controls chewing.
questions.answerText: Facial (VII): facial expression; trigeminal (V): face sensation and chewing

questions.q: A patient cannot shrug one shoulder or turn the head against resistance. Which cranial nerve is most likely damaged?
options: Facial nerve (VII)
Vagus nerve (X)
Accessory nerve (XI)
Hypoglossal nerve (XII)
questions.why: The accessory nerve (CN XI) is a motor nerve to the muscles that turn the head and shrug the shoulders. Its nucleus sits in the upper cervical spinal cord, its rootlets rise into the skull through the foramen magnum, and it leaves through the jugular foramen. Weak shrugging and weak head turning on one side are the classic signs of damage to this nerve.
notes: The facial nerve (CN VII) controls facial expression. Choose it if one side of the face drooped, as in Bell's palsy.
The vagus nerve (CN X) serves voice, swallowing, and the thoracic and abdominal organs. It would be the answer for hoarseness or trouble swallowing, though it shares the jugular foramen with CN XI.
Correct. Weak shrugging and head turning point to the accessory nerve.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) moves the tongue. Pick it if the patient's tongue deviated to one side when stuck out.
questions.answerText: Accessory nerve (XI)

questions.q: A nociceptor is a sensory receptor named for detecting which kind of stimulus?
options: Chemicals
Light
Temperature
Pain
questions.why: Sensory receptors are named for the kind of stimulus they detect. Nociceptors respond to potentially damaging stimuli, such as extreme heat, crushing, or cutting, and produce the sensation of pain. The other stimulus types are mechanical force (mechanoreceptors), temperature (thermoreceptors), light (photoreceptors), and chemicals (chemoreceptors).
notes: Chemicals in solution, such as smell and taste molecules, are detected by chemoreceptors. It would be right for a question about chemoreceptors.
Light is detected by photoreceptors in the retina. Pick light for a question about photoreceptors.
Changes in temperature are detected by thermoreceptors. Choose temperature for a question about thermoreceptors.
Correct. Nociceptors respond to potentially damaging stimuli and produce the sensation of pain.
questions.answerText: Pain

questions.q: Sensory receptors can be named by location. Which term names receptors that detect stimuli inside the body, in the organs and blood vessels?
options: Exteroceptors
Photoreceptors
Proprioceptors
Interoceptors
questions.why: Receptors can be classified by where they sit. Interoceptors, also called visceroceptors, detect stimuli inside the body, in the organs and blood vessels. Exteroceptors detect stimuli at or near the surface, and proprioceptors detect body position and movement in the muscles, tendons, and joints.
notes: Exteroceptors detect stimuli at or near the body surface, such as touch, temperature, and the special senses. Pick them for a question about receptors in the skin.
Photoreceptors are named for their stimulus, light, not their location; they are in the retina. They would be right for a question about which receptors detect light.
Proprioceptors detect the position and movement of the body and sit in muscles, tendons, and joints. Choose them for a question about sensing where a limb is.
Correct. Interoceptors (visceroceptors) sense conditions inside the body.
questions.answerText: Interoceptors

questions.q: Which receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints detect the position and movement of the body?
options: Exteroceptors
Nociceptors
Interoceptors
Proprioceptors
questions.why: Proprioceptors are receptors located in muscles, tendons, and joints that detect the position and movement of the body. They let you know where a limb is without looking at it. The receptor that senses stretch in the patellar reflex is one example of a proprioceptor in muscle.
notes: Exteroceptors detect stimuli at or near the body surface, such as touch and temperature on the skin. Pick them for a question about receptors near the surface.
Nociceptors respond to potentially damaging stimuli and produce pain; they are named for their stimulus, not their location. They would be right for a question about pain receptors.
Interoceptors detect stimuli inside the organs and blood vessels. Choose them for a question about sensing conditions in the viscera.
Correct. Proprioceptors sense body position and movement.
questions.answerText: Proprioceptors

questions.q: A receptor in the skin detects warmth. Which type of receptor is responding?
options: A mechanoreceptor
A thermoreceptor
A chemoreceptor
A photoreceptor
questions.why: Sensory receptors are named for the kind of stimulus they detect. Thermo means heat, so thermoreceptors respond to changes in temperature, including warmth and cold on the skin. If the heat became strong enough to damage tissue, nociceptors would also respond and produce pain.
notes: Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical force such as touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch. Pick it for a question about feeling pressure on the skin.
Correct. Thermoreceptors respond to changes in temperature.
Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals in solution, such as smell and taste molecules. Choose it for a question about taste or smell.
Photoreceptors respond to light and are found in the retina. It would be right for a question about vision.
questions.answerText: A thermoreceptor

questions.q: Which receptors in the retina of the eye respond to light?
options: Mechanoreceptors
Photoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
Chemoreceptors
questions.why: Sensory receptors are named for the kind of stimulus they detect. Photo means light, so photoreceptors respond to light, and they are found in the retina of the eye. The other stimulus types are mechanical force, temperature, chemicals, and potentially damaging stimuli that cause pain.
notes: Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical force such as touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch. Choose them for a question about touch.
Correct. Photo means light, and photoreceptors respond to it.
Thermoreceptors respond to changes in temperature. They would be right for a question about sensing warmth or cold.
Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals in solution, such as smell and taste molecules. Pick them for a question about taste or smell.
questions.answerText: Photoreceptors

questions.q: After bumping an elbow, a person rubs the spot. Which receptors detect the touch and pressure of the rubbing?
options: Mechanoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
Chemoreceptors
Nociceptors
questions.why: Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical force such as touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch. Rubbing the skin presses on and moves it, so mechanoreceptors in the skin detect the rubbing. The pain from the bump itself came from nociceptors, which respond to potentially damaging stimuli.
notes: Correct. Mechanoreceptors respond to touch and pressure.
Thermoreceptors respond to changes in temperature. Choose them for a question about sensing warmth or cold on the skin.
Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals in solution, such as taste and smell molecules. They would be right for a question about taste.
Nociceptors respond to potentially damaging stimuli and produce pain, so they are the receptors that signaled the bump itself. Pick them for a question about what detected the injury.
questions.answerText: Mechanoreceptors

questions.q: Which receptors respond to the chemicals dissolved in food that produce the sense of taste?
options: Photoreceptors
Mechanoreceptors
Nociceptors
Chemoreceptors
questions.why: Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals in solution. Taste and smell both depend on chemoreceptors, which detect molecules dissolved in saliva or in the moist lining of the nose. They are one of the five receptor types named for their stimulus.
notes: Photoreceptors respond to light and are found in the retina. Choose them for a question about vision.
Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical force such as touch and pressure, like the feel of food in the mouth. Pick them for a question about texture or pressure.
Nociceptors respond to potentially damaging stimuli and produce pain. They would be right for a question about pain from a burn.
Correct. Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals in solution, including taste molecules.
questions.answerText: Chemoreceptors

questions.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves arise from the spinal cord?
options: Twelve pairs
Thirty-three pairs
Twenty-four pairs
Thirty-one pairs
questions.why: Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves arise from the spinal cord: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. Each pair is named for the region of the vertebral column where it leaves and is numbered within that region. Every spinal nerve is a mixed nerve, carrying both sensory and motor axons.
notes: Twelve is the number of cranial nerve pairs, and also the number of thoracic spinal nerve pairs. Pick it if the question asked about nerves arising from the brain.
Thirty-three is the usual count of vertebrae before the sacral and coccygeal bones fuse. It comes from mixing up the bones of the column with the nerves that pass between them.
Twenty-four is the number of movable vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar). Students who assume one nerve per vertebra pick it, but the nerve count does not match the vertebra count.
Correct. Adding 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal gives 31 pairs.
questions.answerText: Thirty-one pairs

questions.q: Which connective tissue wrapping surrounds the entire nerve?
options: The periosteum
The endoneurium
The epineurium
The perineurium
questions.why: The epineurium is the outermost connective tissue wrapping of a nerve, a tough sheath that encloses the whole nerve. The prefix epi- means upon or over, which matches its place on the outside. Inside it, the axons are grouped into fascicles wrapped by perineurium, and each single axon is wrapped by endoneurium.
notes: The periosteum is the connective tissue membrane covering the outer surface of a bone. Its peri- prefix makes it look like a nerve wrapping, but it would be the answer only for a question about bone.
The endoneurium is the innermost wrapping, around each individual axon. Pick it if the question asked about the layer around one nerve fiber.
Correct. The epineurium is the outer sheath around the entire nerve.
The perineurium is the middle wrapping, around each fascicle (bundle of axons). Pick it if the question asked about the layer around one bundle inside the nerve.
questions.answerText: The epineurium

questions.q: Which connective tissue wrapping surrounds each individual axon within a nerve?
options: The epineurium
The perineurium
The endoneurium
The endomysium
questions.why: The endoneurium is the innermost wrapping, a delicate layer of connective tissue around each individual axon in a nerve. Endo- means within, so it is the wrapping deepest inside the nerve. Groups of these wrapped axons form fascicles bound by perineurium, and the whole nerve is enclosed by epineurium.
notes: The epineurium is the outermost layer around the entire nerve. Pick it for the tough outer sheath.
The perineurium surrounds a fascicle, a whole bundle of axons, not one axon. Pick it for the middle layer of the nerve.
Correct. The endoneurium wraps each single axon.

The endomysium is the connective tissue around each individual skeletal muscle fiber. It is the muscle version of the same idea, so pick it if the question asked about the wrapping of one muscle cell.
questions.answerText: The endoneurium

questions.q: What is the name for a nerve that carries both sensory and motor axons?
options: A motor nerve
A sensory nerve
A mixed nerve
A nerve tract
questions.why: A mixed nerve carries both sensory axons, which bring signals in toward the central nervous system, and motor axons, which carry commands out to muscles and glands. All 31 pairs of spinal nerves are mixed, and four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) are mixed as well. Nerves are classed as sensory, motor, or mixed by the kinds of axons they carry.
notes: A motor nerve carries mainly motor signals out to muscles, as cranial nerves III, IV, VI, XI, and XII do. Pick it for a nerve such as the hypoglossal nerve.
A sensory nerve carries only sensory signals into the brain, as cranial nerves I, II, and VIII do. Pick it for a nerve such as the olfactory nerve.
Correct. A nerve carrying both kinds of axons is a mixed nerve.
A tract is a bundle of axons inside the brain or spinal cord, not a peripheral nerve. Pick it for a pathway in the white matter of the cord.
questions.answerText: A mixed nerve

questions.q: What term names the area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve?
options: A ramus
A myotome
A plexus
A dermatome
questions.why: A dermatome is the strip of skin whose sensation is carried by the sensory axons of a single spinal nerve. Derma- means skin, and the strips line up in bands down the body in the same order as the spinal nerves. Clinicians use dermatome maps to work out which spinal nerve is involved from where a patient feels numbness or pain.
notes: A ramus is a branch of a spinal nerve just past the intervertebral foramen. Pick it for the branches that split off a spinal nerve.
A myotome is the group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve. Pick it if the question were about muscles rather than skin.
A plexus is a network formed by the anterior rami of several spinal nerves, such as the brachial plexus. Pick it for a network of nerves, not an area of skin.
Correct. The patch of skin served by one spinal nerve is a dermatome.
questions.answerText: A dermatome

questions.q: How many pairs of cervical spinal nerves are there?
options: Eight pairs
Seven pairs
Twelve pairs
Five pairs
questions.why: There are eight pairs of cervical spinal nerves, even though there are only seven cervical vertebrae. The first cervical nerve exits above the atlas, between the skull and C1, so the cervical nerves exit above their matching vertebrae until the eighth, which exits below C7. From the thoracic region down, each nerve exits below the vertebra of the same number.
notes: Correct. There are eight pairs of cervical nerves.
Seven is the number of cervical vertebrae, not cervical nerves. This is the most common mix-up, because students expect one nerve per vertebra.
Twelve is the number of thoracic spinal nerve pairs, matching the twelve thoracic vertebrae. Pick it if the question asked about the thoracic region.
Five is the number of lumbar pairs and also of sacral pairs. Pick it if the question asked about either of those regions.
questions.answerText: Eight pairs

questions.q: Which connective tissue wrapping surrounds a fascicle, a bundle of axons within a nerve?
options: The endoneurium
The perineurium
The perimysium
The epineurium
questions.why: The perineurium is the middle wrapping of a nerve, a layer of connective tissue around each fascicle. Peri- means around, and this layer surrounds a bundle of axons rather than a single axon or the whole nerve. It sits between the endoneurium inside and the epineurium outside.
notes: The endoneurium wraps each single axon, the smallest level. Pick it if the question asked about one nerve fiber.
Correct. The perineurium wraps each fascicle.
The perimysium wraps a fascicle of skeletal muscle fibers, not nerve fibers. The two terms share a prefix and the same idea, so pick perimysium only for a question about muscle.
The epineurium wraps the entire nerve. Pick it for the tough outer sheath around all the fascicles together.
questions.answerText: The perineurium

questions.q: The cervical plexus is formed mainly from the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
options: L1 to L4
C5 to T1
L4 to S4
C1 to C4
questions.why: The cervical plexus is built from the anterior rami of C1 to C4, with a small contribution from C5. It lies deep in the neck and serves the skin and muscles of the neck and upper shoulders. Its best-known branch is the phrenic nerve, which travels down to the diaphragm.
notes: L1 to L4 form the lumbar plexus in the lower back. Pick it for the plexus serving the lower abdominal wall and part of the lower limb.
C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus, just below the cervical plexus. Pick it for the plexus that serves the shoulder and the whole upper limb.
L4 to S4 form the sacral plexus. Pick it for the plexus serving the buttock, perineum, and most of the lower limb.
Correct. The cervical plexus comes mainly from C1 to C4.
questions.answerText: C1 to C4

questions.q: The brachial plexus is formed from the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
options: C5 to T1
L4 to S4
L1 to L4
C1 to C4
questions.why: The brachial plexus forms from the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1. These rami merge and sort in the lower neck and axilla (armpit) into the nerves of the upper limb. Because the arm sits at the level of the lower neck and upper chest, its nerves come from that part of the cord.
notes: Correct. The brachial plexus comes from C5 to T1.
L4 to S4 form the sacral plexus, which serves most of the lower limb. Students mixing up the upper and lower limb plexuses pick it.
L1 to L4 form the lumbar plexus, which serves the lower abdominal wall and the front and inner thigh. Pick it for that region.
C1 to C4 form the cervical plexus, which serves the neck and gives off the phrenic nerve. Pick it for the plexus just above the brachial plexus.
questions.answerText: C5 to T1

questions.q: The phrenic nerve, which supplies the diaphragm, arises from which plexus?
options: The sacral plexus
The cervical plexus
The brachial plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The phrenic nerve arises from the cervical plexus, mainly from C3, C4, and C5, and runs down through the thorax to the diaphragm. It is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing. The teaching phrase C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive is a reminder that a high neck injury can stop breathing.
notes: The sacral plexus (L4 to S4) gives rise to the sciatic nerve. Pick it for a nerve running down the back of the thigh.
Correct. The phrenic nerve leaves the cervical plexus and descends to the diaphragm.
The brachial plexus (C5 to T1) gives rise to the nerves of the upper limb, such as the median, ulnar, and radial nerves. Pick it for a nerve running down the arm.
The lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) gives rise to nerves such as the femoral nerve to the front of the thigh. Pick it for a nerve of the lower abdominal wall or anterior thigh.
questions.answerText: The cervical plexus

questions.q: The sciatic nerve, the largest nerve in the body, arises from which plexus?
options: The lumbar plexus
The cervical plexus
The sacral plexus
The brachial plexus
questions.why: The sciatic nerve is the largest branch of the sacral plexus, which forms from the anterior rami of L4 to S4. It leaves the pelvis deep to the gluteal muscles and runs down the back of the thigh, where it divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves. The sacral plexus serves the buttock, the perineum, and most of the lower limb.
notes: The lumbar plexus sits just above the sacral plexus and also serves the lower limb, which makes it a tempting choice. Pick it for the femoral or obturator nerve to the front and inner thigh.
The cervical plexus serves the neck and gives off the phrenic nerve. Pick it for the nerve to the diaphragm.
Correct. The sciatic nerve comes from the sacral plexus.
The brachial plexus serves the upper limb. Pick it for nerves such as the median or ulnar nerve.
questions.answerText: The sacral plexus

questions.q: Just after a spinal nerve leaves the vertebral column through the intervertebral foramen, it splits into branches. What are these branches called?
options: Rami
Roots
Fascicles
Ganglia
questions.why: Just past the intervertebral foramen, each spinal nerve divides into branches called rami (singular ramus). The posterior ramus supplies the deep back muscles and the skin of the back, and the anterior ramus supplies the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk. Smaller branches include the meningeal branch and the rami communicantes, which link to the sympathetic trunk.
notes: Correct. A spinal nerve splits into rami just past the intervertebral foramen.
The roots (dorsal and ventral) attach the spinal nerve to the cord on the inside, before the nerve forms. Pick roots for the attachments to the cord, not the branches outside the column.
Fascicles are bundles of axons inside a nerve, wrapped by perineurium. Pick them for the internal bundles of a nerve, not its branches.
Ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS, such as the dorsal root ganglion on the dorsal root. Pick them for a swelling of cell bodies, not a branch.
questions.answerText: Rami

questions.q: Spinal nerves regroup into networks called plexuses. Which part of the spinal nerves forms these plexuses?
options: The ventral roots
The dorsal roots
The ventral rami
The dorsal rami
questions.why: The ventral (anterior) rami of spinal nerves join and regroup into plexuses before their axons travel on to the body. This regrouping lets each region receive axons from several spinal nerves, so damage to one spinal nerve rarely erases all function in an area. The ventral rami of T2 to T12 are the exception; they run straight to the thoracic wall as the intercostal nerves.
notes: The ventral roots are motor roots that leave the cord. They join the dorsal roots to make the spinal nerve, which only later splits into rami, so the roots cannot form plexuses.
The dorsal roots are sensory roots that enter the cord inside the vertebral canal, before the spinal nerve even forms. Pick them for the sensory attachment to the cord.
Correct. The ventral rami form the plexuses.
The dorsal rami supply the deep back muscles and the skin of the back, and they do not form plexuses. Pick them for the branch that serves the back of the trunk.
questions.answerText: The ventral rami

questions.q: Which nerve plexus serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb?
options: The cervical plexus
The sacral plexus
The lumbar plexus
The brachial plexus
questions.why: The brachial plexus serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb. It forms from the anterior rami of C5 to T1 in the lower neck and passes through the axilla, giving rise to the nerves of the arm, forearm, and hand. Brachial means arm, which ties the name to its territory.
notes: The cervical plexus serves the neck and upper shoulders and gives off the phrenic nerve. Pick it for the neck or the diaphragm, not the whole limb.
The sacral plexus serves the buttock, the back of the thigh, and the leg and foot. It is the lower limb counterpart of the brachial plexus.
The lumbar plexus serves the lower abdominal wall and the front and inner thigh. Pick it for those regions of the lower body.
Correct. The brachial plexus serves the shoulder and the whole upper limb.
questions.answerText: The brachial plexus

questions.q: What does the epineurium surround?
options: A single axon
A single fascicle
A muscle fascicle
The entire nerve
questions.why: The epineurium surrounds the entire nerve, enclosing all of its fascicles along with the small blood vessels that supply the nerve. It is the outermost and toughest of the three nerve wrappings. Together with the perineurium, it holds a cut nerve's shape so a surgeon can line up the fascicles during repair.
notes: A single axon is wrapped by the endoneurium, the innermost layer. Pick it if the question asked about the endoneurium.
A single fascicle is wrapped by the perineurium, the middle layer. Pick it if the question asked about the perineurium.
A fascicle of muscle fibers is wrapped by the perimysium, which belongs to a muscle, not a nerve. Students mix up the nerve and muscle wrappings because both use the same prefixes.
Correct. The epineurium is the outer sheath around the entire nerve.
questions.answerText: The entire nerve

questions.q: A plexus forms from spinal nerves L1 to L4 and serves the lower abdominal wall and the front of the thigh. Which plexus is it?
options: The brachial plexus
The cervical plexus
The sacral plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The lumbar plexus forms from the anterior rami of L1 to L4 in the lower back. It serves the anterolateral abdominal wall, the external genitals, and part of the lower limb, mainly the front and inner thigh. Damage here causes weakness and sensory loss of the lower abdominal wall and the front and inner surfaces of the thigh.
notes: The brachial plexus forms from C5 to T1 and serves the shoulder and the whole upper limb. Pick it for the arm, not the thigh.
The cervical plexus forms from C1 to C4 and serves the neck and upper shoulders. Pick it for the plexus that gives off the phrenic nerve.
The sacral plexus forms from L4 to S4 and serves the buttock, the back of the thigh, and the leg and foot. It overlaps the lumbar plexus at L4, which is why the two are easy to confuse.
Correct. L1 to L4 build the lumbar plexus.
questions.answerText: The lumbar plexus

questions.q: A receptor is a bare dendrite tip with no connective tissue covering, and it detects pain and temperature. What is it?
options: A lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle
A tactile (Meissner) corpuscle
A free nerve ending
A muscle spindle
questions.why: A free nerve ending is the simplest sensory receptor, a bare dendrite tip with no capsule around it. Free nerve endings are found in the epithelium and connective tissue throughout the body. They detect pain, temperature, and some touch.
notes: A lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle is an encapsulated receptor with a layered capsule in the deep dermis and hypodermis. Pick it for deep pressure and vibration.
A tactile (Meissner) corpuscle is an encapsulated receptor in the dermal papillae of hairless skin. Pick it for fine, discriminative touch.
Correct. A bare dendrite tip that senses pain and temperature is a free nerve ending.
A muscle spindle is a stretch receptor inside skeletal muscle. Pick it for detecting how far a muscle is stretched.
questions.answerText: A free nerve ending

questions.q: The endoneurium of a nerve matches which wrapping in a skeletal muscle?
options: The epimysium
The endomysium
The perimysium
The sarcolemma
questions.why: The endoneurium wraps each single axon in a nerve, and the endomysium wraps each single muscle fiber in a skeletal muscle. Nerves and muscles are organized the same way, with one wrapping around each fiber, another around each fascicle, and an outer one around the whole organ. The shared prefixes line them up: endo- for one fiber, peri- for a fascicle, and epi- for the whole organ.
notes: The epimysium wraps the whole muscle, so it matches the epineurium of a nerve. Pick it if the question started from the epineurium.
Correct. Both the endoneurium and the endomysium wrap a single fiber.
The perimysium wraps a fascicle of muscle fibers, so it matches the perineurium of a nerve. Pick it if the question started from the perineurium.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of a muscle fiber, part of the cell itself rather than a connective tissue wrapping. Pick it for the cell membrane of a muscle fiber.
questions.answerText: The endomysium

questions.q: A sensory nerve ending is wrapped in a connective tissue capsule and detects touch and pressure. What is its structural class?
options: A nociceptor
A free nerve ending
An interoceptor
An encapsulated receptor
questions.why: Encapsulated receptors are nerve endings wrapped in a connective tissue capsule. Most of them are mechanoreceptors for touch, pressure, vibration, or stretch, such as the tactile (Meissner) corpuscles and lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscles. Structure is one of three ways receptors are classified, along with stimulus type and location.
notes: A nociceptor is classified by stimulus type; it responds to potentially damaging stimuli and produces pain. Pick it for pain receptors, most of which are free nerve endings.
A free nerve ending is the other structural class, a bare dendrite tip with no capsule. Pick it for receptors of pain and temperature.
An interoceptor is classified by location, not structure; it detects stimuli inside the body, in the organs and blood vessels. Pick it for a receptor in the wall of an organ.
Correct. A capsule of connective tissue makes it an encapsulated receptor.
questions.answerText: An encapsulated receptor

questions.q: An injury to the cervical plexus on one side also damages the phrenic nerve. Which structure is most directly weakened?
options: The muscles of the upper limb
The muscles of the lower abdominal wall
The diaphragm on that side
The tongue on that side
questions.why: The phrenic nerve leaves the cervical plexus, which forms mainly from C1 to C4, and it is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. If it is damaged on one side, the diaphragm on that side weakens and breathing is affected. Other cervical plexus damage shows up as weakness or numbness of the neck and shoulder.
notes: Weakness across the shoulder and whole upper limb points to the brachial plexus (C5 to T1). Pick it for an injury in the lower neck or axilla.
Weakness of the lower abdominal wall points to the lumbar plexus (L1 to L4). Pick it for an injury in the lower back.
Correct. The phrenic nerve is the motor supply to the diaphragm.
The tongue is moved by the hypoglossal nerve, a cranial nerve, not by a spinal nerve plexus. Pick it for damage to cranial nerve XII.
questions.answerText: The diaphragm on that side

questions.q: A virus that has been dormant in one dorsal root ganglion reactivates and causes a painful rash in a band of skin along one dermatome. Which disorder is it?
options: Carpal tunnel syndrome
Peripheral neuropathy
Bell palsy
Shingles
questions.why: Shingles is caused by the varicella zoster virus, the chickenpox virus, which can hide in a dorsal root ganglion for decades. When it reactivates, it travels along the sensory axons of that one spinal nerve, so the rash follows the dermatome that ganglion serves. This is why a shingles rash usually forms a band on one side of the body.
notes: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve at the wrist, causing numbness in the hand. Pick it for a wrist problem with no rash.
Peripheral neuropathy is damage to many peripheral nerves, often causing numbness in both hands and feet, as in long-term diabetes. Pick it for widespread, symmetrical numbness rather than one band.
Bell palsy is a sudden weakness of the facial nerve (VII) that droops one side of the face, with no dermatome rash. Pick it for facial paralysis.
Correct. A rash following one dermatome from a reactivated virus is shingles.
questions.answerText: Shingles

questions.q: Which choice lists the three connective tissue wrappings of a nerve from the smallest scale to the largest?
options: Endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium
Perineurium, endoneurium, epineurium
Epineurium, perineurium, endoneurium
Endoneurium, epineurium, perineurium
questions.why: From the smallest scale to the largest, the wrappings are the endoneurium around each axon, the perineurium around each fascicle, and the epineurium around the whole nerve. The prefixes give the order: endo- means within, peri- means around, and epi- means upon or over. Each wrapping is named for the level it surrounds.
notes: Correct. Axon, then fascicle, then whole nerve: endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium.
This starts with the fascicle layer and puts the axon layer second. It treats the perineurium as the innermost layer, which it is not.
This is the correct order run backward, from largest to smallest. Pick it if the question asked for the order from the outside in.
This puts the epineurium in the middle. It comes from mixing up epi- (outermost) with peri- (around a fascicle).
questions.answerText: Endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium

questions.q: Which choice lists the spinal nerve regions in order from the neck down toward the tailbone?
options: Cervical, thoracic, sacral, lumbar, coccygeal
Cervical, lumbar, thoracic, sacral, coccygeal
Thoracic, cervical, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal
Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal
questions.why: The spinal nerves are named for the region of the vertebral column where they leave, so they follow the same order as the column: cervical (8 pairs), thoracic (12), lumbar (5), sacral (5), and coccygeal (1). The neck comes first, then the chest, the lower back, the sacrum, and finally the tailbone. Knowing the order of the vertebral regions gives you the order of the nerve regions.
notes: This puts the sacral region above the lumbar region. The sacrum sits below the lumbar vertebrae and joins the hip bones.
This puts the lumbar region above the thoracic region. The lumbar vertebrae are in the lower back, below the rib-bearing thoracic vertebrae.
This puts the thoracic (chest) region above the cervical (neck) region. The neck is the top of the column, so cervical always comes first.
Correct. Neck, chest, lower back, sacrum, tailbone.
questions.answerText: Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal

questions.q: Which choice correctly names the plexus formed from C5 to T1, one nerve that comes from it, and the region that nerve serves?
options: Sacral plexus, median nerve, upper limb
Cervical plexus, phrenic nerve, upper limb
Brachial plexus, median nerve, upper limb
Brachial plexus, sciatic nerve, lower limb
questions.why: The anterior rami of C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus, which serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb. One of its major nerves is the median nerve, which runs down the front of the arm and forearm and passes through the carpal tunnel into the hand. Every part of the correct answer belongs to the upper limb, which is how the pieces fit together.
notes: The sacral plexus forms from L4 to S4 and serves the lower limb, so it cannot give rise to the median nerve. Pick the sacral plexus for the sciatic nerve.
The phrenic nerve does come from the cervical plexus, but it serves the diaphragm, not the upper limb, and the cervical plexus forms from C1 to C4. Pick this plexus and nerve for breathing.
Correct. C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus, which gives off the median nerve to the upper limb.
The sciatic nerve belongs to the sacral plexus and serves the lower limb. Only the plexus name is right here, which is a common half-remembered pairing.
questions.answerText: Brachial plexus, median nerve, upper limb

questions.q: Which choice correctly names the plexus formed from L4 to S4, its largest nerve, and the region that nerve serves?
options: Sacral plexus, sciatic nerve, back of thigh and leg
Lumbar plexus, sciatic nerve, back of thigh and leg
Sacral plexus, phrenic nerve, diaphragm
Sacral plexus, median nerve, hand and forearm
questions.why: The anterior rami of L4 to S4 form the sacral plexus, which serves the buttock, the perineum, and most of the lower limb. Its largest branch is the sciatic nerve, which runs down the back of the thigh and divides to supply the leg and foot. Damage to the sacral plexus causes weakness and sensory loss in the buttock, the back of the thigh, and the leg and foot.
notes: Correct. L4 to S4 form the sacral plexus, and its sciatic nerve runs down the back of the thigh into the leg.
The lumbar plexus forms from L1 to L4, and its main nerves (femoral and obturator) serve the front and inner thigh. The sciatic nerve does not come from it.
The phrenic nerve comes from the cervical plexus and serves the diaphragm. Only the plexus name is right here; pick the phrenic nerve for breathing.
The median nerve comes from the brachial plexus and serves the forearm and hand. Pick it for the upper limb, not the sacral plexus.
questions.answerText: Sacral plexus, sciatic nerve, back of thigh and leg

questions.q: Which choice traces the parts of a spinal nerve in order, from its attachments to the cord out to its branches beyond the vertebral column?
options: Dorsal and ventral roots, then the spinal nerve, then the rami
Rami, then the spinal nerve, then the dorsal and ventral roots
Dorsal and ventral roots, then the rami, then the spinal nerve
The spinal nerve, then the dorsal and ventral roots, then the rami
questions.why: A spinal nerve starts as two roots attached to the cord: the dorsal root, which is sensory, and the ventral root, which is motor. The two roots join to form the spinal nerve itself, which passes out through the intervertebral foramen. Just outside the foramen, the spinal nerve splits into its rami.
notes: Correct. Roots join to form the spinal nerve, which then splits into rami.
This is the correct sequence run backward, from the branches in toward the cord. Pick it if the question asked you to trace from the body inward.
This puts the rami before the spinal nerve. The rami are branches of the finished spinal nerve, so they cannot come before it.
This puts the spinal nerve before the roots, but the nerve is formed by the roots joining, so the roots must come first.
questions.answerText: Dorsal and ventral roots, then the spinal nerve, then the rami

questions.q: A cross section of a nerve shows several round bundles inside the thick outer layer, each outlined by its own thin ring of connective tissue. What are the bundles and their ring called?
options: Fascicles wrapped by endoneurium
Fascicles wrapped by perineurium
Axons wrapped by epineurium
Ganglia wrapped by perineurium
questions.why: On a nerve cross section, the thick outer ring is the epineurium. The round bundles inside it are fascicles, and each one is outlined by a thin ring of perineurium. The tiny circles packed inside a fascicle are single axons, each surrounded by endoneurium.
notes: The endoneurium is the thin wrapping around each single axon inside a fascicle. Pick it for the delicate layer between individual fibers.
Correct. The round bundles are fascicles, and the ring around each is the perineurium.

Single axons are the tiny circles inside each bundle, not the bundles themselves, and the epineurium surrounds the whole nerve, not each bundle. Pick the epineurium for the thick outer ring of the section.
Ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies, not bundles inside a nerve. Pick a ganglion for a swelling such as the dorsal root ganglion.
questions.answerText: Fascicles wrapped by perineurium

questions.q: What is a bundle of axons grouped together within a nerve called?
options: A ramus
A fascicle
