A tract
A ganglion
questions.why: A fascicle is a bundle of axons grouped together inside a nerve and wrapped by perineurium. A nerve is built from many fascicles held together by the epineurium. The same word is used in muscle, where a fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers.
notes: A ramus is a branch of a spinal nerve just past the intervertebral foramen. Pick it for a branch, not a bundle within the nerve.
Correct. A bundle of axons inside a nerve is a fascicle.
A tract is a bundle of axons inside the brain or spinal cord that share an origin and destination. Pick it for a bundle in the white matter of the CNS.
A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS. Pick it for a swelling of cell bodies, such as the dorsal root ganglion.
questions.answerText: A fascicle

questions.q: How many pairs of thoracic spinal nerves are there?
options: Five pairs
Seven pairs
Eight pairs
Twelve pairs
questions.why: There are twelve pairs of thoracic spinal nerves, one exiting below each of the twelve thoracic vertebrae. The thoracic region has more pairs than any other region. Most of their anterior rami run between the ribs as intercostal nerves instead of joining a plexus.
notes: Five is the number of lumbar pairs and also of sacral pairs. Pick it for either of those regions.
Seven is the number of cervical vertebrae. It comes from mixing up vertebrae and nerves, and it does not match any thoracic count.
Eight is the number of cervical nerve pairs. Pick it if the question asked about the neck region.
Correct. There are twelve pairs of thoracic nerves.
questions.answerText: Twelve pairs

questions.q: Which kinds of axons does every spinal nerve carry?
options: Only sensory axons, entering the cord
Only autonomic axons to the organs
Sensory and motor axons
Only motor axons, leaving the cord
questions.why: Every spinal nerve is a mixed nerve, carrying both sensory and motor axons. The sensory axons arrive through the dorsal root and the motor axons leave through the ventral root, and the two roots join to form one spinal nerve. From that point on, the nerve and its main branches carry both kinds of axons.
notes: Only sensory axons describes the dorsal root, before it joins the ventral root. Pick it for the dorsal root, not the spinal nerve.
Autonomic axons do travel in spinal nerves, but alongside sensory and somatic motor axons, never alone. Pick autonomic fibers for the rami communicantes that link to the sympathetic trunk.
Correct. All 31 pairs of spinal nerves are mixed.
Only motor axons describes the ventral root, before it joins the dorsal root. Pick it for the ventral root, not the spinal nerve.
questions.answerText: Sensory and motor axons

questions.q: Which branch of a spinal nerve supplies the deep muscles and skin of the back of the trunk?
options: The meningeal branch
The rami communicantes
The posterior ramus
The anterior ramus
questions.why: The posterior (dorsal) ramus supplies the deep muscles of the back and the skin over the posterior trunk. It is the smaller of the two main rami. Because its territory is the back, a problem in a posterior ramus stays in the back and does not reach the limbs.
notes: The meningeal branch re-enters the vertebral canal to supply the vertebrae, ligaments, blood vessels of the cord, and meninges. Pick it for structures inside the vertebral canal.
The rami communicantes are small branches that carry autonomic fibers to and from the sympathetic trunk. Pick them for the link between a spinal nerve and the sympathetic chain.
Correct. The posterior ramus serves the deep back muscles and the skin of the back.
The anterior ramus supplies the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk, and it forms the plexuses. Pick it for the limbs.
questions.answerText: The posterior ramus

questions.q: The anterior rami of which spinal nerves do not join a plexus but run straight to the thoracic wall?
options: T2 to T12
C1 to C4
L1 to L4
C5 to T1
questions.why: The anterior rami of T2 to T12 do not form a plexus. Instead, they run between the ribs as the intercostal nerves (T12, below the last rib, is called the subcostal nerve). They supply the intercostal muscles, the muscles of the abdominal wall, and the skin of the chest and abdomen. T1 joins the brachial plexus, and every other region also sends its anterior rami into a plexus.
notes: Correct. T2 to T12 run straight to the thoracic wall as intercostal nerves.
C1 to C4 form the cervical plexus, which serves the neck and gives off the phrenic nerve. Pick it for the neck.
L1 to L4 form the lumbar plexus, which serves the lower abdominal wall and the front and inner thigh. Pick it for that plexus.
C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus. T1 joins this plexus, which is why the intercostal list starts at T2.
questions.answerText: T2 to T12

questions.q: Which receptors respond to mechanical force such as touch, pressure, and stretch?
options: Chemoreceptors
Mechanoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
Photoreceptors
questions.why: Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical force such as touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch. They include the tactile corpuscles of the skin, the lamellar corpuscles that sense vibration, and the muscle spindles that sense stretch. Classifying by stimulus type asks what kind of change the receptor answers to.
notes: Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals dissolved in solution, such as smell and taste molecules. Pick them for taste buds or the olfactory epithelium.
Correct. Touch, pressure, and stretch are mechanical forces, sensed by mechanoreceptors.
Thermoreceptors respond to changes in temperature. Pick them for sensing heat or cold.
Photoreceptors respond to light and are found in the retina of the eye. Pick them for vision.
questions.answerText: Mechanoreceptors

questions.q: Which receptors detect the position and movement of the body from within the muscles, tendons, and joints?
options: Exteroceptors
Proprioceptors
Interoceptors
Nociceptors
questions.why: Proprioceptors detect the position and movement of the body. They sit in the skeletal muscles, tendons, and joint capsules, and include muscle spindles, tendon organs, and joint kinesthetic receptors. Proprio- means one's own, so these receptors report on the body's own position.
notes: Exteroceptors detect stimuli at or near the body surface, such as touch, temperature, and the special senses. Pick them for receptors in the skin.
Correct. Receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints that sense body position are proprioceptors.
Interoceptors (also called visceroceptors) detect stimuli inside the body, in the organs and blood vessels. Pick them for receptors in the wall of the stomach or an artery.
Nociceptors are classified by stimulus, not location; they respond to potentially damaging stimuli and produce pain. Pick them for pain receptors.
questions.answerText: Proprioceptors

questions.q: Where in the body are free nerve endings found?
options: Only within skeletal muscles
Only in the retina
In most body tissues
Only in the dermal papillae of hairless skin
questions.why: Free nerve endings are bare dendrite tips found in the epithelium and connective tissue throughout the body. Because they are nearly everywhere, almost any tissue can signal pain and temperature. They are the simplest receptors, with no connective tissue capsule around them.
notes: Muscle spindles sit within skeletal muscles and detect stretch. Pick this location for muscle spindles, not free nerve endings.
The retina holds photoreceptors, the receptors for light. Pick the retina if the question asked where photoreceptors are found.
Correct. Free nerve endings are spread through most tissues of the body.
The dermal papillae of hairless skin hold tactile (Meissner) corpuscles, the receptors for fine touch. Pick this location for those corpuscles.
questions.answerText: In most body tissues

questions.q: Which receptor in the deep dermis and hypodermis detects deep pressure and vibration?
options: Tactile (Merkel) discs
Bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles
Lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscles
Free nerve endings
questions.why: Lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscles are large encapsulated receptors in the deep dermis and hypodermis. Each one has a nerve ending surrounded by many layers of connective tissue, like the layers of an onion, which is where the name lamellar comes from. They detect deep pressure and vibration.
notes: Tactile (Merkel) discs sit in the deepest layer of the epidermis and detect light touch, not deep pressure. Pick them for light touch near the surface.
Bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles also sit in the deep dermis, but they detect steady deep pressure and stretching of the skin rather than vibration. Pick them for pressure that lasts.
Correct. Lamellar corpuscles in the deep dermis and hypodermis sense deep pressure and vibration.
Free nerve endings are bare dendrite tips that detect pain, temperature, and some touch, not deep pressure and vibration. Pick them for pain or temperature.
questions.answerText: Lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscles

questions.q: A receptor detects chemicals dissolved in solution, such as taste molecules. Which type of receptor is it?
options: A photoreceptor
A mechanoreceptor
A chemoreceptor
A thermoreceptor
questions.why: Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals in solution. Taste receptors in the taste buds and smell receptors in the olfactory epithelium are both chemoreceptors, because each detects molecules dissolved in saliva or mucus. Other chemoreceptors inside the body monitor the chemistry of the blood.
notes: A photoreceptor responds to light and is found in the retina. Pick it for vision.
A mechanoreceptor responds to mechanical force such as touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch. Pick it for receptors such as tactile corpuscles or muscle spindles.
Correct. A receptor for dissolved chemicals is a chemoreceptor.
A thermoreceptor responds to changes in temperature. Pick it for sensing heat or cold.
questions.answerText: A chemoreceptor

questions.q: A receptor in the deep dermis and the joint capsules senses continuous, steady pressure. Which receptor is it?
options: Free nerve endings
Bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles
Muscle spindles
Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles
questions.why: Bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles are encapsulated receptors in the deep dermis, the hypodermis, and the joint capsules. They respond to steady deep pressure and to stretching of the skin. Lamellar corpuscles sit in the same deep layers but sense vibration and deep pressure, so the kind of stimulus is what tells the two apart.
notes: Free nerve endings are bare dendrite tips that detect pain, temperature, and some touch, not steady pressure. Pick them for pain.
Correct. Bulbous corpuscles in the deep dermis and joint capsules sense steady pressure.
Muscle spindles lie within skeletal muscles and detect stretch. Pick them for how far a muscle is stretched.
Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae of hairless skin, close to the surface, and detect fine, discriminative touch. Pick them for the fingertips and lips.
questions.answerText: Bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles

questions.q: Which receptor, found within skeletal muscles, detects the stretch of a muscle?
options: Tendon organs
Lamellar corpuscles
Joint kinesthetic receptors
Muscle spindles
questions.why: Muscle spindles are proprioceptors that lie within skeletal muscles, among the ordinary muscle fibers. They detect the stretch of a muscle, telling the CNS how much the muscle is being lengthened. They are the receptors that start the knee-jerk stretch reflex.
notes: Tendon organs sit within tendons and detect the tension a contracting muscle places on its tendon. Pick them for pull on the tendon rather than stretch of the muscle.
Lamellar corpuscles sit in the deep dermis and hypodermis and detect deep pressure and vibration. Pick them for vibration.
Joint kinesthetic receptors sit in the capsules of synovial joints and detect joint position and movement. Pick them for the angle of a joint.
Correct. Muscle spindles inside skeletal muscle detect stretch.
questions.answerText: Muscle spindles

questions.q: Where are the stimuli that an exteroceptor detects?
options: Inside the organs and blood vessels
In the muscles, tendons, and joints
At or near the body surface
Only in the retina of the eye
questions.why: Exteroceptors detect stimuli at or near the body surface. They include the receptors for touch, pressure, pain, and temperature in the skin, along with most receptors of the special senses. Extero- means outside, so these receptors report on the world outside the body.
notes: Stimuli inside the organs and blood vessels are detected by interoceptors, also called visceroceptors. Pick this location for interoceptors.
Stimuli in the muscles, tendons, and joints are detected by proprioceptors, which report body position and movement. Pick this location for proprioceptors.
Correct. Exteroceptors respond to stimuli at or near the surface of the body.

The retina holds photoreceptors, which are named for their stimulus (light). They do count as exteroceptors, but this answer is far too narrow, since exteroceptors are spread across the whole body surface.
questions.answerText: At or near the body surface

questions.q: Which small branches of a spinal nerve carry autonomic fibers to and from the sympathetic trunk?
options: The rami communicantes
The dorsal roots
The meningeal branches
The posterior rami
questions.why: The rami communicantes are small branches that link a spinal nerve to the sympathetic trunk ganglion beside it. The white ramus carries sympathetic axons from the spinal nerve into the ganglion, and the gray ramus carries them back out to the spinal nerve. Communicantes means communicating, which describes their role as links.
notes: Correct. The rami communicantes link the spinal nerve to the sympathetic trunk.

The dorsal roots are sensory roots attached to the back of the cord, inside the vertebral canal. They connect the nerve to the cord, so they are not branches of the spinal nerve and do not reach the sympathetic trunk.
The meningeal branches re-enter the vertebral canal to supply the vertebrae, ligaments, and meninges. Pick them for structures inside the canal.
The posterior rami supply the deep back muscles and the skin of the back. Pick them for the back of the trunk.
questions.answerText: The rami communicantes

questions.q: Where does a spinal nerve split into its rami?
options: Just past the intervertebral foramen
Within the dorsal root ganglion
Inside the vertebral canal, right beside the cord
At the conus medullaris, where the cord ends
questions.why: A spinal nerve forms where the dorsal and ventral roots join, then passes out of the vertebral canal through the intervertebral foramen. Just past that opening, it splits into its rami. So the roots lie inside the vertebral canal, while the rami lie outside the vertebral column.
notes: Correct. The spinal nerve splits into rami just outside the intervertebral foramen.
The dorsal root ganglion sits on the dorsal root before the spinal nerve has even formed. Pick it for where the sensory cell bodies are.
Inside the vertebral canal beside the cord is where the dorsal and ventral roots run and join. Pick it for where the roots are, not the rami.
The conus medullaris is the tapered end of the spinal cord near the L1 to L2 disc, with the cauda equina below it. Pick it for where the cord ends.
questions.answerText: Just past the intervertebral foramen

questions.q: Which of these sensory receptors is an encapsulated receptor?
options: A hair follicle receptor
A free nerve ending in the epidermis
A lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle
A tactile (Merkel) disc
questions.why: A lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle is an encapsulated receptor: its nerve ending is wrapped in many layers of connective tissue. Other encapsulated receptors include the tactile (Meissner) corpuscles, bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles, muscle spindles, and tendon organs. Free nerve endings, Merkel discs, and hair follicle receptors are nonencapsulated, meaning their endings have no capsule.
notes: A hair follicle receptor is a nonencapsulated ending wrapped around a hair follicle that senses hair movement. Pick it for a receptor triggered by bending a hair.
A free nerve ending is the classic nonencapsulated receptor, a bare dendrite tip. Pick it for a receptor with no capsule that senses pain and temperature.
Correct. The lamellar corpuscle has a layered connective tissue capsule.

A tactile (Merkel) disc is a nonencapsulated ending in the deepest layer of the epidermis that senses light touch. Its name sounds like the encapsulated tactile (Meissner) corpuscle, which is the usual mix-up.
questions.answerText: A lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle

questions.q: Which branch of a spinal nerve re-enters the vertebral canal to supply the vertebrae and meninges?
options: The posterior ramus
The meningeal branch
The anterior ramus
The rami communicantes
questions.why: The meningeal branch is a small branch that turns back through the intervertebral foramen into the vertebral canal. It supplies the vertebrae, the ligaments, the blood vessels of the spinal cord, and the meninges. Its name tells you its main target, the membranes around the cord.
notes: The posterior ramus supplies the deep back muscles and the skin of the back. Pick it for the back of the trunk.
Correct. The meningeal branch returns into the vertebral canal.
The anterior ramus supplies the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk, and it forms the plexuses. Pick it for the limbs.
The rami communicantes carry autonomic fibers to and from the sympathetic trunk. Pick them for the link to the sympathetic chain.
questions.answerText: The meningeal branch

questions.q: Which receptor detects the tension a muscle places on its tendon?
options: Tendon organs
Muscle spindles
Hair follicle receptors
Joint kinesthetic receptors
questions.why: Tendon organs are proprioceptors within tendons, near the point where the muscle joins the tendon. They detect the tension a contracting muscle places on its tendon. Muscle spindles report stretch from inside the muscle, while tendon organs report pull from inside the tendon.
notes: Correct. Tendon organs sense the pull of a muscle on its tendon.
Muscle spindles lie within the muscle itself and detect stretch, not tendon tension. Pick them for how far a muscle is lengthened.
Hair follicle receptors wrap around hair follicles in the skin and detect movement of the hair. Pick them for a light touch that bends a hair.
Joint kinesthetic receptors sit in synovial joint capsules and detect joint position and movement. Pick them for the angle of a joint.
questions.answerText: Tendon organs

questions.q: A surgeon repairs a cut nerve by lining up its fascicles. Which connective tissue wrappings hold the nerve's shape so the fascicles can be matched?
options: The myelin sheath and neurilemma
The dura mater and arachnoid
The epineurium and perineurium
The endomysium and perimysium
questions.why: The epineurium wraps the whole nerve and the perineurium wraps each fascicle, and these two layers hold a cut nerve's shape. Because each fascicle stays outlined by its perineurium, a surgeon can line up the cut ends and stitch these layers together. This connective tissue framework is part of why peripheral nerves can be repaired.
notes: The myelin sheath and neurilemma are Schwann cell coverings around individual axons, not connective tissue wrappings. Pick them for the insulating layer around a single axon.
The dura mater and arachnoid are meninges that cover the brain and spinal cord. Pick them for membranes of the CNS, not a peripheral nerve.
Correct. The epineurium and perineurium hold the nerve and its fascicles in shape.
The endomysium and perimysium are the wrappings of a skeletal muscle, around each fiber and each fascicle of muscle. Pick them for repairing a muscle, not a nerve.
questions.answerText: The epineurium and perineurium

questions.q: The fingertips sense fine detail far better than the skin of the back. Which difference best explains this?
options: Larger dorsal root ganglia for the hand
Thicker myelin on their sensory axons
More tactile corpuscles and Merkel discs
No free nerve endings to compete for signals
questions.why: The fingertips are crowded with tactile (Meissner) corpuscles and tactile (Merkel) discs, the receptors for fine, discriminative touch. The more of these receptors packed into an area, the smaller the details that skin can tell apart. The skin of the back has far fewer of them, so it senses touch only crudely.
notes: A ganglion holds cell bodies, and its size does not set how much detail the skin can feel. The number of receptors in the skin is the deciding factor.
Myelin affects how fast a signal travels, not how finely the skin can tell two points apart. Students reach for myelin whenever a nerve works better, but receptor density is what matters here.
Correct. A dense supply of fine-touch receptors gives the fingertips their sharp sense of detail.
The fingertips do have free nerve endings, which is why they feel pain and temperature. Receptors do not compete with one another, so this explanation is a misconception.
questions.answerText: More tactile corpuscles and Merkel discs

questions.q: A nerve injury weakens the limbs but spares the muscles and skin of the back. Which branches of the spinal nerves were most likely involved?
options: The rami communicantes
The posterior rami
The anterior rami
The meningeal branches
questions.why: The anterior rami supply the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk, and they form the plexuses that send nerves into the limbs. An injury to the anterior rami or their plexuses affects the limbs, while the posterior rami, which serve the back, keep working. That is why the back is spared.
notes: The rami communicantes carry autonomic fibers to and from the sympathetic trunk. Pick them for the link to the sympathetic chain, not limb weakness.
The posterior rami serve the deep back muscles and skin of the back. Damage to them would affect the back, which is exactly what was spared here.
Correct. The anterior rami supply the limbs, so their injury shows up in the limbs.
The meningeal branches supply the vertebrae, ligaments, and meninges inside the vertebral canal. They do not reach the limbs.
questions.answerText: The anterior rami

questions.q: A patch of skin can still feel pain and temperature but cannot sense fine touch. Which receptors are still working there?
options: Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles
Free nerve endings
Lamellar corpuscles
Muscle spindles
questions.why: Free nerve endings sense pain, temperature, and some touch, so if pain and temperature remain, the free nerve endings are intact. Fine, discriminative touch depends on the tactile (Meissner) corpuscles and the Merkel discs, so those must be the receptors not working. Matching each remaining sensation to its receptor shows which receptors survived.
notes: Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles carry fine, discriminative touch, which is the sensation that was lost. Pick them for fine touch.
Correct. Pain and temperature come from free nerve endings.
Lamellar corpuscles sense deep pressure and vibration in the deep dermis and hypodermis. The scenario does not test those sensations, so nothing points to them.
Muscle spindles lie within skeletal muscle and sense stretch, not skin sensation. Pick them for proprioception.
questions.answerText: Free nerve endings

questions.q: Which region of the spinal cord gives rise to the most pairs of spinal nerves?
options: The sacral region, with 5 pairs
The lumbar region, with 5 pairs
The thoracic region, with 12 pairs
The cervical region, with 8 pairs
questions.why: The thoracic region has the most spinal nerve pairs, twelve, one for each thoracic vertebra. The cervical region has eight, the lumbar and sacral regions have five each, and the coccygeal region has one. Together they add up to 31 pairs.
notes: The sacral region also has 5 pairs. Pick it if the question asked about the nerves arising near the sacrum.
The lumbar region has 5 pairs. Pick it if the question asked about the lower back.
Correct. Twelve thoracic pairs is the largest count of any region.
The cervical region has 8 pairs, more than its 7 vertebrae, which makes it seem large. It still has fewer than the thoracic region.
questions.answerText: The thoracic region, with 12 pairs

questions.q: A cut peripheral nerve is more likely to regrow successfully when its connective tissue wrappings are lined up again. Which statement best explains why?
options: The wrappings fill the gap with connective tissue that conducts signals
The wrappings give regrowing axons a path back toward their targets
The wrappings hold neuron cell bodies that can build brand-new axons
The wrappings are made of myelin, which speeds up the regrowing fibers
questions.why: A cut peripheral axon can regrow from the part still attached to its cell body, and the neurolemma of its Schwann cells helps it do so. The epineurium and perineurium hold the cut nerve's shape, so a surgeon can stitch the ends back in line. Lined-up fascicles give the regrowing axons a path into the matching part of the far side of the nerve and on toward their targets.
notes: Connective tissue does not carry nerve signals; only axons do. Scar tissue in the gap actually blocks regrowth, which is why surgeons try to line up the ends closely.
Correct. Aligned wrappings act as guides that lead regrowing axons toward their targets.
Neuron cell bodies sit in ganglia or in the CNS, not in the connective tissue wrappings. This choice confuses a nerve, which is a bundle of axons, with a ganglion.
The wrappings are connective tissue, not myelin. Myelin comes from Schwann cells around individual axons, so pick myelin for the insulating layer, not the nerve wrappings.
questions.answerText: The wrappings give regrowing axons a path back toward their targets

questions.q: Every spinal nerve carries sensory and motor axons together. Which statement best explains why this arrangement works well?
options: One nerve can serve a region for both sensation and movement
Sensory axons act as insulation for the motor axons beside them
Each axon in a nerve carries signals in both directions
Mixing the axons lets sensory signals pass directly into muscles
questions.why: A mixed nerve carries sensory axons running toward the CNS and motor axons running away from it, side by side within the same connective tissue wrappings. Because one nerve does both jobs, a single route carries sensation from a region and commands back to the muscles of that same region. Each axon still carries its signals in one direction only.
notes: Correct. Bundling both kinds of axons lets one nerve serve a region for sensation and movement.
Insulation around axons comes from myelin made by Schwann cells, and protection comes from the connective tissue wrappings. Neighboring axons do not insulate each other.
Each axon is either sensory or motor and carries signals one way. The nerve as a whole carries traffic both ways only because it holds both kinds of axons.
Sensory axons end in the CNS, not on muscles. A sensory signal must reach the cord before any motor command goes back out to a muscle.
questions.answerText: One nerve can serve a region for both sensation and movement

questions.q: The sciatic nerve runs a long way down the back of the thigh and is stretched and pressed as the limb moves. Which feature of the nerve protects its axons from this wear?
options: The dura mater, which extends down the limb around the nerve
Its myelin sheaths, which form the outer covering of the nerve
A layer of periosteum that wraps the nerve along the femur
Its connective tissue wrappings, especially the epineurium
questions.why: A nerve is protected by its three connective tissue wrappings, and the outer epineurium is the toughest of them. These layers cushion the delicate axons and let the nerve bend and stretch a little as the limb moves and bears weight. The same wrappings also give a nerve some ability to heal after injury.
notes: The dura mater is the tough outer meninx around the brain and spinal cord. It does not run down the limb around the sciatic nerve, so it cannot protect the nerve in the thigh.
Myelin sheaths wrap individual axons and insulate them; they do not form the outer covering of a whole nerve. Pick myelin for the insulating layer around one axon.
Periosteum is the membrane covering the surface of a bone such as the femur. It does not wrap nerves.
Correct. The connective tissue wrappings, led by the epineurium, protect the nerve.
questions.answerText: Its connective tissue wrappings, especially the epineurium

questions.q: Which receptors sit in the dermal papillae of hairless skin, such as the fingertips, and detect fine, discriminative touch?
options: Bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles
Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles
Hair follicle receptors
Lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscles
questions.why: Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles are small encapsulated receptors in the dermal papillae of hairless skin. The dermal papillae are the bumps of dermis that push up into the epidermis, which puts these receptors close to the surface. They detect fine, discriminative touch and are packed most densely in the fingertips and lips.
notes: Bulbous (Ruffini) corpuscles sit in the deep dermis and joint capsules and detect continuous, steady pressure. Pick them for pressure that lasts.
Correct. Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles in the dermal papillae sense fine touch.
Hair follicle receptors wrap around hair follicles, so they cannot be found in hairless skin. Pick them for a touch that bends a hair.
Lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscles sit deep, in the deep dermis and hypodermis, and detect deep pressure and vibration. Pick them for vibration.
questions.answerText: Tactile (Meissner) corpuscles

questions.q: A peripheral nerve is often compared to a cable of many wires. Which description of a nerve's structure is accurate?
options: Many neuron cell bodies packed together and wrapped in perineurium
Many axons grouped into fascicles, all enclosed by an outer epineurium
Many axons running loosely side by side with no connective tissue around them
One very large axon wrapped in several layers of epineurium and perineurium
questions.why: A nerve is a bundle of many axons, much like a cable of many wires. The axons are grouped into fascicles, each wrapped by perineurium, and the whole nerve is enclosed by the epineurium, with endoneurium around each single axon. This lets one protected route carry signals for many different destinations.
notes: A cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion, not a nerve. Pick this description for a ganglion such as the dorsal root ganglion.
Correct. A nerve is many axons in fascicles, enclosed by epineurium.
Axons running side by side with no connective tissue wrappings describes a tract in the CNS. Peripheral nerves always have connective tissue wrappings.
A nerve holds many axons, not one, and the perineurium wraps fascicles inside the nerve. One axon wrapped by its own layer describes an axon in its endoneurium.
questions.answerText: Many axons grouped into fascicles, all enclosed by an outer epineurium

questions.q: Pressure on a peripheral nerve, as at the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome, causes numbness and tingling. Where are these symptoms mainly felt?
options: In the matching area of skin on the opposite side of the body
In the skin that nerve serves, beyond the point of pressure
In every dermatome below the level of the compressed nerve
Only at the exact spot where the nerve is being squeezed
questions.why: A peripheral nerve carries sensation from the area of skin it serves, so pressure on the nerve disrupts the signals from that whole territory. The numbness and tingling are felt in the skin the nerve supplies beyond the point of pressure, not only at the pressure spot. In carpal tunnel syndrome, the compressed median nerve produces symptoms mainly on the thumb side of the hand.
notes: Crossing to the opposite side happens in pathways inside the CNS, not in a peripheral nerve. A squeezed peripheral nerve affects the same side of the body.
Correct. Symptoms appear in the area the compressed nerve serves.
Loss in every dermatome below a certain level describes a spinal cord injury, which interrupts the tracts. Pick it for cord damage, not one compressed peripheral nerve.
The brain reads signals from a nerve as coming from where its endings are, not from where it is squeezed. That is why symptoms spread into the nerve's territory.
questions.answerText: In the skin that nerve serves, beyond the point of pressure

questions.q: A spinal nerve is formed where which two structures join?
options: The anterior and posterior rami
The posterior and anterior roots
Two anterior roots from neighboring segments
The posterior root and the filum terminale
questions.why: The posterior root brings sensory axons and the anterior root carries motor axons. Just beyond the dorsal root ganglion, the two roots join to form the spinal nerve, which is therefore a mixed nerve carrying both. The spinal nerve then exits through the intervertebral foramen and soon splits into rami.
notes: The rami are the branches the spinal nerve splits into after it forms, so this reverses the order. Pick the rami for a question about what the spinal nerve divides into.
Correct. The posterior and anterior roots join to form the spinal nerve.
Each spinal nerve gets one posterior and one anterior root from its own segment, not two anterior roots. Joining two motor roots would leave the nerve with no sensory axons.
The filum terminale is a thread of pia mater that anchors the cord to the coccyx and carries no axons. Choose it for a question about anchoring the end of the cord.
questions.answerText: The posterior and anterior roots

questions.q: Through which opening does a spinal nerve leave the vertebral canal?
options: The intervertebral foramen
The vertebral foramen
The foramen magnum
The transverse foramen
questions.why: The intervertebral foramen is the gap between the notches of two neighboring vertebrae. Each spinal nerve forms near this opening and passes out through it to reach the body. That is why a herniated disc or bone spur that narrows the foramen can pinch a spinal nerve.
notes: Correct. Spinal nerves exit through the intervertebral foramina.
The vertebral foramen is the large central hole in each vertebra; stacked together, they form the vertebral canal that holds the cord. Pick it for a question about where the spinal cord runs.
The foramen magnum is the large opening in the occipital bone where the medulla becomes the spinal cord. It would be the answer for where the brainstem meets the cord.
The transverse foramina are holes in the transverse processes of cervical vertebrae that carry the vertebral arteries. Choose them for a question about the vertebral artery's path.
questions.answerText: The intervertebral foramen

questions.q: What is a nerve plexus?
options: A bundle of axons traveling together inside the spinal cord
A cluster of neuron cell bodies lying outside the CNS
A network where the anterior rami of several spinal nerves regroup
A cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the brain or spinal cord
questions.why: A nerve plexus is a network where the anterior rami of neighboring spinal nerves weave together and then sort their axons into the named nerves that leave it. Because of this regrouping, each nerve leaving a plexus carries axons from more than one spinal nerve. Plexuses lie in the PNS (peripheral nervous system, the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord), close to the limbs and regions they serve.
notes: A bundle of axons inside the CNS is a tract. That would be the answer for a pathway of white matter running up or down the spinal cord.
A cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion, such as the dorsal root ganglion. Pick ganglion if the question asks for a PNS collection of cell bodies.
Correct. A plexus is where anterior rami mix and regroup before their axons travel on to the body.
A cluster of cell bodies inside the CNS is a nucleus. Pick nucleus if a question asks for a group of neuron cell bodies within the brain or spinal cord.
questions.answerText: A network where the anterior rami of several spinal nerves regroup

questions.q: Which branches of the spinal nerves join to form the nerve plexuses?
options: The dorsal roots
The anterior rami
The posterior rami
The ventral roots
questions.why: Each spinal nerve splits into rami (branches) soon after it leaves the intervertebral foramen. The anterior rami are the larger branches that supply the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk, and these are the branches that weave together into the cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal plexuses. The posterior rami stay segmental and never form plexuses.
notes: The dorsal roots carry sensory axons into the spinal cord before the spinal nerve forms. They would be the answer for the root that holds the dorsal root ganglion, not for plexus formation.
Correct. The anterior rami of neighboring spinal nerves join and regroup to form the plexuses.

The posterior rami are the smaller branches that run straight back to the deep back muscles and the skin of the back. They stay separate and do not form plexuses, so pick them only for a question about supply to the back.

The ventral roots carry motor axons out of the spinal cord and join the dorsal roots to form the spinal nerve. Pick them for the root that carries motor axons, but plexuses form only after the spinal nerve has divided into rami.
questions.answerText: The anterior rami

questions.q: In which region of the spine do the anterior rami NOT form a plexus?
options: The thoracic region
The cervical region
The sacral region
The lumbar region
questions.why: In the thoracic region, the anterior rami of T2 to T12 do not weave into a plexus. Instead they run between the ribs as the intercostal nerves, supplying the intercostal muscles, the abdominal wall muscles, and the skin of the chest and abdomen in orderly bands. Every other region of the spine sends its anterior rami into a plexus.
notes: Correct. The thoracic anterior rami run separately as intercostal nerves instead of forming a plexus.

The cervical anterior rami form the cervical plexus (C1 to C4) and help form the brachial plexus. Pick the cervical region if the question asks where the plexus that gives off the phrenic nerve arises.
The sacral anterior rami help form the sacral plexus (L4 to S4). Pick the sacral region for the plexus that serves the buttock and most of the lower limb.
The lumbar anterior rami form the lumbar plexus (L1 to L4). Pick this region for the plexus serving the anterolateral abdominal wall and front of the thigh.
questions.answerText: The thoracic region

questions.q: Which plexus is formed mainly by the anterior rami of C1 to C4?
options: The cervical plexus
The sacral plexus
The brachial plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The cervical plexus forms from the anterior rami of C1 to C4, with a small contribution from C5. It lies deep in the neck and supplies the skin and muscles of the neck and upper shoulders. It also gives rise to the phrenic nerve, which travels down to the diaphragm.
notes: Correct. C1 to C4 build the cervical plexus, which serves the neck.
The sacral plexus forms from L4 to L5 and S1 to S4. Pick it for the buttock, perineum, and most of the lower limb.
The brachial plexus forms from C5 to C8 and T1, just below the cervical plexus. Pick it for the plexus that serves the shoulder and entire upper limb.
The lumbar plexus forms from L1 to L4 in the lower back. Pick it for the anterolateral abdominal wall and the front and inner thigh.
questions.answerText: The cervical plexus

questions.q: Which plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C5 to C8 and T1?
options: The cervical plexus
The coccygeal plexus
The brachial plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The brachial plexus forms from the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1. These spinal levels sit right where the upper limb joins the trunk, and the plexus serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb. Its name comes from brachium, the Latin word for arm.
notes: The cervical plexus forms from C1 to C4, the levels just above the brachial plexus. Pick it for the neck, the upper shoulders, and the phrenic nerve.
The coccygeal plexus forms from S4, S5, and the coccygeal nerve (Co1) at the very bottom of the cord. Pick it for the small patch of skin over the coccyx.
Correct. C5 to T1 build the brachial plexus, the nerve network for the upper limb.
The lumbar plexus forms from L1 to L4. Pick it for the lower abdominal wall and the front of the thigh.
questions.answerText: The brachial plexus

questions.q: Which plexus is formed by the anterior rami of L1 to L4?
options: The cervical plexus
The brachial plexus
The sacral plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The lumbar plexus forms from the anterior rami of L1 to L4 in the posterior abdominal wall. It serves the anterolateral abdominal wall, the external genitals, and part of the lower limb, mainly the front and inner thigh. The plexuses are named for the spinal region that builds them, so lumbar levels form the lumbar plexus.
notes: The cervical plexus forms from C1 to C4. Pick it for the neck and the phrenic nerve.
The brachial plexus forms from C5 to T1. Pick it for the shoulder and upper limb.
The sacral plexus forms from L4 to L5 and S1 to S4, overlapping the lumbar plexus at L4. Pick it when the levels run down into the sacral nerves.
Correct. L1 to L4 build the lumbar plexus.
questions.answerText: The lumbar plexus

questions.q: Which plexus serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb?
options: The cervical plexus
The brachial plexus
The sacral plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The brachial plexus, built from C5 to T1, is the nerve network for the shoulder and the whole upper limb. The named nerves of the arm, forearm, and hand all leave this one plexus. That is why an injury to the brachial plexus can affect movement and sensation across the entire upper limb on that side.
notes: The cervical plexus (C1 to C4) serves the skin and muscles of the neck and the upper shoulders, not the rest of the limb. Pick it for the neck or for the phrenic nerve.
Correct. The brachial plexus serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb.
The sacral plexus (L4 to S4) serves the buttock, perineum, and most of the lower limb. Pick it for the back of the thigh, leg, and foot.
The lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) serves the lower abdominal wall and part of the lower limb. Pick it for the front and inner thigh.
questions.answerText: The brachial plexus

questions.q: Which nerve leaves the cervical plexus and descends through the thorax to reach the diaphragm?
options: The vagus nerve
The axillary nerve
The intercostal nerve
The phrenic nerve
questions.why: The phrenic nerve arises from the cervical plexus, from C3, C4, and C5, and runs down through the thorax beside the heart to the diaphragm. It is the only motor supply to the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing. That is why an injury to the cord at or above C3 to C5 can stop breathing.
notes: The vagus nerve is cranial nerve X. It leaves the brainstem, not a spinal plexus, and runs down the neck to the thoracic and abdominal organs. Pick it for a question about the cranial nerve that wanders to the viscera.
The axillary nerve is a terminal branch of the brachial plexus that wraps around the neck of the humerus. Pick it for a nerve found near the shoulder joint.
Intercostal nerves are the anterior rami of T2 to T12 running between the ribs. They are the answer for the thoracic wall, and they do not come from any plexus.
Correct. The phrenic nerve leaves the cervical plexus and runs to the diaphragm.
questions.answerText: The phrenic nerve

questions.q: Which plexus serves the buttocks, the perineum, and most of the lower limb?
options: The coccygeal plexus
The brachial plexus
The sacral plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The sacral plexus forms from L4 to L5 and S1 to S4 on the posterior wall of the pelvis. It serves the buttocks, the perineum (the region between the thighs that holds the external genitals and anus), and most of the lower limb. Its largest branch, the sciatic nerve, runs down the back of the thigh.
notes: The coccygeal plexus serves only a small patch of skin over the coccyx. Pick it for that tiny area, not for the whole buttock and limb.
The brachial plexus (C5 to T1) serves the shoulder and upper limb. Pick it for any region of the arm.
Correct. The sacral plexus serves the buttock, perineum, and most of the lower limb.
The lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) also reaches the lower limb, but only part of it, mainly the front and inner thigh, along with the lower abdominal wall. Pick it for those regions.
questions.answerText: The sacral plexus

questions.q: The anterior rami of T2 to T12 do not form a plexus. What nerves do they become?
options: The phrenic nerves
The intercostal nerves
The femoral nerves
The radial nerves
questions.why: The anterior rami of T2 to T12 skip the plexus stage and run one by one in the spaces between the ribs. These are the intercostal nerves (inter means between, costa means rib). Each one supplies a band of the thoracic wall muscles and skin, which is why the chest and abdomen show a very orderly, striped pattern of sensory supply.
notes: The phrenic nerves come from the cervical plexus (C3 to C5) and run to the diaphragm. Pick them for the nerve that powers breathing, not for nerves between the ribs.
Correct. The thoracic anterior rami run between the ribs as the intercostal nerves.
The femoral nerve is a branch of the lumbar plexus that enters the front of the thigh. Pick it for a nerve passing down the anterior thigh.
The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the brachial plexus that runs along the back of the arm. Pick it for a nerve on the posterior arm and forearm.
questions.answerText: The intercostal nerves

questions.q: Which plexus serves only a small area of skin over the coccyx?
options: The sacral plexus
The coccygeal plexus
The cervical plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The coccygeal plexus forms from the anterior rami of S4, S5, and the coccygeal nerve (Co1) at the very bottom of the spinal column. It supplies only a small patch of skin over the coccyx (tailbone). Its name matches the bone it lies beside.
notes: The sacral plexus sits just above the coccygeal plexus but serves a far larger area, including the buttock, perineum, and most of the lower limb. Pick it for those regions.
Correct. The coccygeal plexus supplies only the skin over the coccyx.
The cervical plexus is at the opposite end of the spine and serves the neck and upper shoulders. Pick it for numbness of the neck, not the skin over the tailbone.
The lumbar plexus serves the lower abdominal wall and the front and inner thigh. Pick it for a deficit in those areas.
questions.answerText: The coccygeal plexus

questions.q: Which plexus is formed by the anterior rami of L4 to L5 and S1 to S4?
options: The brachial plexus
The lumbar plexus
The sacral plexus
The coccygeal plexus
questions.why: The sacral plexus forms from the anterior rami of L4, L5, and S1 to S4, so it draws on two lumbar levels as well as four sacral ones. It lies on the posterior wall of the pelvis. It serves the buttock, the perineum, and most of the lower limb.
notes: The brachial plexus forms from C5 to T1. Pick it for the plexus serving the upper limb.
The lumbar plexus forms from L1 to L4. It shares L4 with the sacral plexus, which is why students mix them up, but it does not include any sacral nerves.
Correct. L4 to S4 build the sacral plexus.
The coccygeal plexus forms from S4, S5, and the coccygeal nerve (Co1). Pick it when the levels sit at the very bottom of the cord.
questions.answerText: The sacral plexus

questions.q: Which plexus serves the skin and muscles of the neck and upper shoulders?
options: The coccygeal plexus
The lumbar plexus
The brachial plexus
The cervical plexus
questions.why: The cervical plexus, built from C1 to C4 deep in the neck, supplies the skin and muscles of the neck and the upper part of the shoulders. It also sends the phrenic nerve down to the diaphragm. The plexuses run head to tail in the same order as the regions they serve, so the highest plexus serves the neck.
notes: The coccygeal plexus serves a small patch of skin over the coccyx. Pick it for numbness over the tailbone.
The lumbar plexus serves the lower abdominal wall and front of the thigh. Pick it for those lower regions.
The brachial plexus serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb. It sits just below the cervical plexus, so pick it when the deficit extends down the arm.
Correct. The cervical plexus serves the neck and upper shoulders.
questions.answerText: The cervical plexus

questions.q: Why do the anterior rami form a plexus instead of each spinal nerve running straight to its target?
options: Regrouping turns sensory axons into motor axons
Regrouping speeds up conduction along the axons
Regrouping lets each region receive axons from several spinal nerves
Regrouping adds new neuron cell bodies to the nerve
questions.why: In a plexus, axons from several spinal nerves mix and then sort into the named nerves that leave it. As a result, each body region receives axons from more than one spinal nerve. This works as a safety feature, because damage to one spinal nerve weakens an area without erasing all of its function.
notes: An axon keeps its function no matter where it travels, so a sensory axon stays sensory. Mixed nerves simply carry both kinds side by side.
Conduction speed depends on axon diameter and myelin, not on whether axons pass through a plexus. Pick myelination if a question asks what speeds up a nerve signal.
Correct. Regrouping gives each region input from several spinal nerves, which builds in overlap.
A plexus is made of axons, not cell bodies. A collection of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion, which is the answer for a question about where sensory cell bodies sit.
questions.answerText: Regrouping lets each region receive axons from several spinal nerves

questions.q: How are the principal nerve plexuses named?
options: For the body region where they sit or that they serve
For the cranial nerve they connect to
For the number of spinal nerves they contain
For the bone they pass through
questions.why: Each plexus is named for the body region where it sits or that it serves: cervical for the neck, brachial for the arm, lumbar for the lower back, sacral for the sacrum, and coccygeal for the coccyx. The names run head to tail in the same order as those regions, so a plexus name tells you roughly where it is and what it serves. The name is not an exact list of the spinal nerves that build it; the brachial plexus, for example, is built from C5 to T1.
notes: Correct. Plexus names describe the body region where they sit or the region they serve.

Plexuses are built from spinal nerves, not cranial nerves, and they do not connect to any cranial nerve by name. Cranial nerves are named and numbered on their own, from the olfactory nerve (I) to the hypoglossal nerve (XII).
No plexus is named for a count of its spinal nerves. The names are regional, and the count of contributing levels varies from plexus to plexus.
No plexus passes through a bone, and the names are not taken from openings. The sacral and coccygeal names point to the regions around those bones, not to a passage the nerves run through.
questions.answerText: For the body region where they sit or that they serve

questions.q: A patient injures the brachial plexus. Which body region loses movement and sensation?
options: The neck and diaphragm
The thoracic wall
The front of the thigh
The shoulder and upper limb
questions.why: The brachial plexus is the nerve network for the shoulder and the whole upper limb. Every named nerve of the arm, forearm, and hand leaves this plexus, so damage to it causes weakness and sensory loss across the shoulder and upper limb on the injured side. The location of a plexus injury predicts the region affected.
notes: The neck and diaphragm are served by the cervical plexus and its phrenic nerve. Pick that region for a cervical plexus injury.
The thoracic wall is served by the intercostal nerves, which do not form a plexus. Pick it for damage to the T2 to T12 anterior rami.
The front of the thigh is served by the lumbar plexus. Pick it for a lumbar plexus injury.
Correct. The brachial plexus serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb.
questions.answerText: The shoulder and upper limb

questions.q: Damage to which plexus could weaken the diaphragm and affect breathing?
options: The sacral plexus
The lumbar plexus
The brachial plexus
The cervical plexus
questions.why: The phrenic nerve, the only motor supply to the diaphragm, leaves the cervical plexus from C3 to C5. If the cervical plexus is damaged and the phrenic nerve is involved, the diaphragm on that side weakens and breathing is affected. The teaching phrase is C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.
notes: The sacral plexus serves the buttock and most of the lower limb. Pick it for weakness of the back of the thigh, leg, and foot.

The lumbar plexus serves the lower abdominal wall and front of the thigh. Students sometimes pick it because the diaphragm separates the thorax from the abdomen, but its nerve supply comes from the neck.
The brachial plexus (C5 to T1) sits just below the cervical plexus and serves the upper limb. Its injury causes arm weakness, not diaphragm weakness.
Correct. The phrenic nerve to the diaphragm arises from the cervical plexus.
questions.answerText: The cervical plexus

questions.q: A plexus injury causes weakness and sensory loss in the front and inner thigh and the lower abdominal wall. Which plexus was damaged?
options: The lumbar plexus
The sacral plexus
The brachial plexus
The coccygeal plexus
questions.why: The lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) serves the anterolateral abdominal wall, the external genitals, and the front and inner surfaces of the thigh. A deficit in exactly those areas points to the lumbar plexus. The neighboring sacral plexus covers the back of the thigh and the leg instead.
notes: Correct. The lumbar plexus serves the lower abdominal wall and the front and inner thigh.
The sacral plexus serves the buttock, the back of the thigh, and the leg and foot. Pick it when the deficit is on the posterior thigh and below the knee.
The brachial plexus serves the shoulder and upper limb. Pick it for weakness of the arm and hand.
The coccygeal plexus serves only the skin over the coccyx. Pick it for a small numb patch over the tailbone.
questions.answerText: The lumbar plexus

questions.q: A patient has weakness and sensory loss of the buttock, the back of the thigh, and the leg and foot. Which plexus is involved?
options: The lumbar plexus
The cervical plexus
The coccygeal plexus
The sacral plexus
questions.why: The sacral plexus (L4 to S4) serves the buttock, the perineum, the back of the thigh, and most of the leg and foot. Its largest branch, the sciatic nerve, runs down the back of the thigh. A deficit in that pattern points to the sacral plexus.
notes: The lumbar plexus serves the lower abdominal wall and the front and inner thigh. Pick it when the deficit is on the anterior thigh rather than the back of the limb.
The cervical plexus serves the neck and upper shoulders. Pick it for neck weakness or diaphragm problems.
The coccygeal plexus serves only the skin over the coccyx. It sits next to the sacral plexus, but its territory is tiny.
Correct. The sacral plexus serves the buttock, back of the thigh, leg, and foot.
questions.answerText: The sacral plexus

questions.q: Which pairing correctly gives the plexus the phrenic nerve leaves and the structure it reaches?
options: From the brachial plexus to the diaphragm
From the cervical plexus to the diaphragm
From the cervical plexus to the thoracic wall
From the brachial plexus to the thoracic wall
questions.why: The phrenic nerve leaves the cervical plexus, drawing on C3, C4, and C5, and descends through the thorax to the diaphragm. Because C5 also feeds the brachial plexus, students sometimes place the phrenic nerve there, but it is a cervical plexus branch. The thoracic wall is served by the intercostal nerves instead.
notes: The destination is right, but the brachial plexus serves the upper limb. The phrenic nerve shares the C5 level with the brachial plexus, which is the source of this mix-up.
Correct. The phrenic nerve runs from the cervical plexus to the diaphragm.
The plexus is right, but the thoracic wall is served by the intercostal nerves (T2 to T12). Pick the thoracic wall for a question about the nerves running between the ribs.
Neither half fits. The phrenic nerve leaves the cervical plexus, not the brachial plexus, and the thoracic wall is served by the intercostal nerves, which come from no plexus.
questions.answerText: From the cervical plexus to the diaphragm

questions.q: Why does damage to a single spinal nerve root usually weaken, but rarely fully paralyze, a limb region?
options: Each spinal nerve regenerates within a few hours
The thoracic intercostal nerves take over the limb
The dorsal root ganglion stores spare axons
Each region draws axons from several spinal nerves
questions.why: A plexus mixes axons from several spinal nerves before they leave as named nerves, so each limb region receives fibers from more than one spinal level. If one root is damaged, the fibers from the other levels still reach the region. The area is weakened, but the overlap keeps it from being completely paralyzed.
notes: Damaged peripheral axons can regrow, but slowly, over weeks to months, and not within hours. This choice confuses slow regeneration with the immediate protection that overlap gives.
The intercostal nerves stay in the thoracic wall and do not reroute to the limbs. Pick them for the nerves running between the ribs.
The dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons, not spare axons. Pick it for a question about where sensory cell bodies sit outside the spinal cord.
Correct. The overlap built by the plexus keeps some function when one root is lost.
questions.answerText: Each region draws axons from several spinal nerves

questions.q: An injury to a plexus itself, rather than to a single root, can take out a whole region at once. Why?
options: A plexus carries only sensory axons
A plexus lies inside the spinal cord
A plexus has no connective tissue covering
The injury sits where the region's nerves are gathered together
questions.why: Root injuries hit only one spinal level, and the overlap from other levels covers the gap. A plexus, however, is where all the axons headed for one region are gathered and sorted. Damage at that point catches fibers from every contributing level at once, so it can wipe out movement and sensation across the whole region.
notes: Plexuses carry both sensory and motor axons, which is why a plexus injury causes both weakness and numbness. Pick sensory only for a dorsal root.
Plexuses are part of the PNS and lie outside the spinal cord, in the neck, axilla, and posterior abdominal and pelvic walls. A structure inside the cord would be a tract or a nucleus.
Nerves and plexuses are wrapped in connective tissue (endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium). Pick those wrappings for a question about the layers around a nerve.
Correct. A plexus collects the axons for a whole region, so damage there affects them all.
questions.answerText: The injury sits where the region's nerves are gathered together

questions.q: Which plexus serves the anterolateral abdominal wall and the external genitals along with part of the lower limb?
options: The cervical plexus
The lumbar plexus
The brachial plexus
The sacral plexus
questions.why: The lumbar plexus forms from L1 to L4 in the posterior abdominal wall. It supplies the anterolateral abdominal wall (the front and sides of the belly), the external genitals, and part of the lower limb, mainly the front and inner thigh. Its location just behind the abdomen explains why its branches reach the abdominal wall.
notes: The cervical plexus serves the neck and upper shoulders. Pick it for the neck or the phrenic nerve.
Correct. The lumbar plexus serves the anterolateral abdominal wall, external genitals, and part of the lower limb.
The brachial plexus serves the shoulder and upper limb. Pick it for any region of the arm or hand.
The sacral plexus serves the perineum, buttock, and most of the lower limb. Pick it for the back of the thigh and the leg, not the abdominal wall.
questions.answerText: The lumbar plexus

questions.q: The teaching phrase C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive refers to which nerve and plexus?
options: The radial nerve from the brachial plexus
The femoral nerve from the lumbar plexus
The intercostal nerves from the thoracic rami
The phrenic nerve from the cervical plexus
questions.why: The phrase reminds you that the phrenic nerve, which supplies the diaphragm, carries fibers from C3, C4, and C5 and arises from the cervical plexus. Because the diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing, a high cervical injury above these levels can stop breathing. The phrase is a way to remember both the levels and the stakes.
notes: The radial nerve is a brachial plexus branch running along the back of the arm and forearm. Pick it for a nerve on the posterior upper limb.
The femoral nerve is a lumbar plexus branch that enters the front of the thigh. Pick it for a nerve of the anterior thigh.
The intercostal nerves come from T2 to T12 and serve the thoracic wall between the ribs. Pick them for the chest wall, not the diaphragm levels in this phrase.
Correct. The phrenic nerve from the cervical plexus carries C3 to C5 fibers to the diaphragm.
questions.answerText: The phrenic nerve from the cervical plexus

questions.q: Which plexus, if injured, produces numbness limited to a small patch of skin over the coccyx?
options: The lumbar plexus
The cervical plexus
The sacral plexus
The coccygeal plexus
questions.why: The coccygeal plexus forms from S4, S5, and the coccygeal nerve (Co1), and its only territory is a small area of skin over the coccyx. Damage to it therefore produces a small numb patch over the tailbone and nothing more. The size of the deficit matches the size of the territory.
notes: The lumbar plexus serves the lower abdominal wall and front of the thigh. Pick it for numbness on the anterior thigh.
The cervical plexus serves the neck and upper shoulders. Pick it for numbness of the neck.
The sacral plexus lies just above it and serves the buttock, perineum, and most of the lower limb. Its injury causes a much larger deficit down the back of the leg.
Correct. The coccygeal plexus serves only the skin over the coccyx.
questions.answerText: The coccygeal plexus

questions.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury high in the neck cannot breathe without a ventilator. Which nerve and plexus best explain this?
options: The vagus nerve from the brainstem
The axillary nerve from the brachial plexus
The phrenic nerve from the cervical plexus
The intercostal nerves from the thoracic rami
questions.why: The diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing, and its only motor supply is the phrenic nerve, which arises from the cervical plexus at C3 to C5. A cord injury above these levels cuts the diaphragm off from the brain, so the patient cannot breathe without support. That is the meaning behind C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.
notes: The vagus nerve is a cranial nerve that leaves the brainstem and supplies the heart, lungs, and gut. It does not power the diaphragm, so pick it for a question about cranial nerve X and the viscera.
The axillary nerve leaves the brachial plexus and wraps around the neck of the humerus. Its loss affects the shoulder, not breathing.
Correct. A high cervical injury cuts off the phrenic nerve, which powers the diaphragm.
The intercostal nerves serve the muscles between the ribs, which help breathing but cannot replace the diaphragm. They also arise below the neck, from T2 to T12.
questions.answerText: The phrenic nerve from the cervical plexus

questions.q: After a motorcycle crash that forced the head away from the shoulder, a rider loses movement and sensation across the whole upper limb. Which structure was most likely stretched or torn?
options: The lumbar plexus
The brachial plexus
The sacral plexus
The cervical plexus
questions.why: The brachial plexus runs from the lower neck (C5 to T1) across the shoulder region into the arm. Forcing the head and shoulder apart stretches this network, and because all the upper limb nerves pass through it, the whole limb can lose movement and sensation. A deficit covering the entire upper limb points to the plexus rather than a single named nerve.
notes: The lumbar plexus lies in the posterior abdominal wall and serves the abdominal wall and front of the thigh. Pick it for a lower limb deficit on the anterior thigh.
Correct. A whole upper limb deficit after a neck and shoulder stretch points to the brachial plexus.
The sacral plexus lies in the pelvis and serves the buttock and most of the lower limb. Pick it for a deficit in the back of the leg.
The cervical plexus sits higher in the neck and serves the neck and upper shoulders. Pick it for neck weakness or diaphragm problems.
questions.answerText: The brachial plexus

questions.q: A pelvic fracture damages the sacral plexus. Which pattern of deficits would you expect?
options: Weakness of the front and inner thigh and lower abdominal wall
Numbness limited to a small patch of skin over the coccyx
Weakness and numbness across the shoulder and whole upper limb
Weakness of the buttock, back of the thigh, and the leg and foot
questions.why: The sacral plexus lies on the posterior wall of the pelvis, so a pelvic fracture can injure it directly. It serves the buttock, the perineum, the back of the thigh, and most of the leg and foot. Damage therefore causes weakness and sensory loss in that territory.
notes: This is the lumbar plexus pattern. Pick it for an injury to the L1 to L4 network in the posterior abdominal wall.
This is the coccygeal plexus pattern. Pick it for an injury to the smallest plexus at the bottom of the spine.
This is the brachial plexus pattern. Pick it for an injury in the lower neck and axilla.
Correct. The sacral plexus serves the buttock, back of the thigh, leg, and foot.
questions.answerText: Weakness of the buttock, back of the thigh, and the leg and foot

questions.q: A herniated disc presses on a single cervical spinal nerve root. The patient has some arm weakness but can still move every part of the arm. Which feature of the nervous system explains the preserved movement?
options: The myelin sheath around each axon
The crossing of tracts in the brainstem
The dorsal root ganglion beside the cord
The overlap created by the brachial plexus
questions.why: The brachial plexus mixes axons from C5 to T1, so each part of the arm receives fibers from more than one spinal level. When one root is compressed, the fibers from the other levels still arrive, which leaves the arm weaker but still able to move. This overlap is the built-in safety feature of a plexus.
notes: Myelin insulates axons and speeds signals, but it cannot replace fibers that are compressed at the root. Pick myelin for a question about conduction speed or the job of Schwann cells.
Crossing of tracts (decussation) explains why each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. It has nothing to do with spared function after a root injury.
The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies on the dorsal root. Pick it for where sensory cell bodies sit, not for why movement is preserved.
Correct. Fibers from other spinal levels still reach the arm through the plexus.
questions.answerText: The overlap created by the brachial plexus

questions.q: A clinician must predict the deficit from an injury to the plexus formed from C5 to T1. Which region will be affected?
options: The neck and diaphragm
The skin over the coccyx
The buttock and lower limb
The shoulder and upper limb
questions.why: The plexus formed from C5 to T1 is the brachial plexus. It serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb, so its injury causes weakness and sensory loss across that whole limb on the injured side. To answer this kind of question, first name the plexus from its levels, then recall its territory.
notes: The neck and diaphragm are served by the cervical plexus (C1 to C4), which sits just above C5. Pick this region for an injury at those higher levels.
The skin over the coccyx is served by the coccygeal plexus at the bottom of the spine. Pick it for an S4 to coccygeal level injury.
The buttock and most of the lower limb are served by the sacral plexus (L4 to S4). Pick this region for an injury in the pelvis.
Correct. C5 to T1 is the brachial plexus, which serves the shoulder and upper limb.
questions.answerText: The shoulder and upper limb

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the named nerves that leave a plexus?
options: Each carries axons from more than one spinal level
Each carries only sensory axons to the skin
Each carries axons from exactly one spinal level
Each returns to the spinal cord at a lower level
questions.why: Inside a plexus, axons from several anterior rami mix and are sorted into new bundles. Each named nerve that leaves the plexus, such as the radial or femoral nerve, therefore carries axons from more than one spinal level. This is why one muscle can receive input from more than one level of the spinal cord.
notes: Correct. Plexus branches carry axons pooled from several spinal levels.

The main plexus branches, such as the radial, median, and femoral nerves, carry motor axons to muscles as well as sensory axons, so they are not all sensory. The root that carries only sensory axons is the posterior root, before the spinal nerve forms.
One level per nerve describes the intercostal nerves of the thorax, which skip the plexus stage. Pick this for a T2 to T12 anterior ramus, not a plexus branch.
Peripheral nerves travel out to their targets and do not loop back into the cord at a lower level. This choice describes a pathway that does not exist.
questions.answerText: Each carries axons from more than one spinal level

questions.q: The nerves to the shoulder, forearm, and hand all leave one network. Where do the axons in these nerves come from?
options: From the C7 spinal nerve alone
From C5 to T1, mixed in the brachial plexus
From C1 to C4 through the cervical plexus
From the thoracic intercostal nerves
questions.why: All of the nerves of the upper limb leave the brachial plexus, which gathers the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1. Inside the plexus these axons are sorted so that each named nerve heads to its own part of the limb while still carrying fibers from several levels. One organized network supplies the whole limb.
notes: C7 is only one of the five levels feeding the brachial plexus. Choosing a single level ignores the mixing that happens in the plexus.
Correct. The upper limb nerves carry axons from C5 to T1 sorted in the brachial plexus.
The cervical plexus (C1 to C4) serves the neck and gives off the phrenic nerve. Pick it for the neck, not the forearm and hand.
The intercostal nerves run between the ribs and serve the thoracic wall. Pick them for the chest wall, not the upper limb.
questions.answerText: From C5 to T1, mixed in the brachial plexus

questions.q: A deep wound in the armpit affects movement and sensation across much of the arm at once. Why can one small injury have such widespread effects?
options: The armpit holds the spinal cord segments for the arm
Many arm nerves pass together through the brachial plexus there
Injury in the armpit spreads upward into the cervical plexus
The arm has only one nerve, so any injury affects all of it
questions.why: The brachial plexus extends from the lower neck into the axilla (armpit), and the named nerves of the arm are packed close together as they pass through it. A single wound in that area can therefore damage several of these nerves at the same time. That is why the deficit spreads across much of the limb instead of staying in one spot.
notes: Spinal cord segments sit inside the vertebral canal, not in the armpit. Pick the cervical enlargement of the cord for the cord region that serves the upper limbs.
Correct. Many arm nerves run together through the plexus in the armpit, so one wound can hit several.
Nerve damage does not travel up into a different plexus. The cervical plexus would be the answer for a neck or diaphragm deficit.
The upper limb has several named nerves, including the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, and ulnar nerves. This choice misses that the brachial plexus divides into many nerves.
questions.answerText: Many arm nerves pass together through the brachial plexus there

questions.q: The nerves to the lower limb come from plexuses separate from those serving the upper limb. Which plexuses supply the lower limb?
options: The lumbar and sacral plexuses
The brachial and lumbar plexuses
The cervical and coccygeal plexuses
The brachial and cervical plexuses
questions.why: Each limb is supplied by the plexuses formed at the spinal levels where that limb joins the trunk. The lower limb draws on the lumbar plexus (L1 to L4), which serves part of the limb such as the front and inner thigh, and the sacral plexus (L4 to S4), which serves most of the rest. The upper limb draws on the brachial plexus instead.
notes: Correct. The lumbar and sacral plexuses together supply the lower limb.
The lumbar plexus is right, but the brachial plexus serves the upper limb. This mix-up comes from pairing one upper limb plexus with one lower limb plexus.
The cervical plexus serves the neck and the coccygeal plexus serves only skin over the coccyx. Neither reaches the lower limb.
The brachial plexus serves the upper limb and the cervical plexus serves the neck. Pick this pair for nerves of the arm and neck.
questions.answerText: The lumbar and sacral plexuses

questions.q: The sciatic nerve runs down the back of the thigh and carries fibers from several spinal levels. Which plexus does it leave?
options: The lumbar plexus
The coccygeal plexus
The brachial plexus
The sacral plexus
questions.why: The sciatic nerve is the largest branch of the sacral plexus and the largest nerve in the body. It leaves the pelvis deep to the gluteal muscles and runs down the back of the thigh. Because it carries fibers from several lumbar and sacral levels, damage to any one of those levels weakens it only partly.
notes: The lumbar plexus sends its main branches to the front and inner thigh, such as the femoral and obturator nerves. Pick it for a nerve on the anterior or medial thigh.
The coccygeal plexus serves only skin over the coccyx and gives off no large limb nerve. It sits next to the sacral plexus, which leads to the mix-up.
The brachial plexus serves the upper limb. Pick it for any nerve of the arm, such as the radial or median nerve.
Correct. The sciatic nerve is the largest branch of the sacral plexus.
questions.answerText: The sacral plexus

questions.q: The brachial plexus lies in the lower neck and armpit, and the lumbar and sacral plexuses lie in the posterior abdominal wall and pelvis. What do these locations have in common?
options: Each sits at the far end of the limb it serves
Each sits close to where its limb joins the trunk
Each lies inside the vertebral canal
Each lies between a pair of ribs
questions.why: Each limb plexus forms near the root of its limb, at the spinal levels where that limb attaches to the trunk. This lets the anterior rami regroup right before they fan out as named nerves into the nearby limb. The brachial plexus sits at the root of the upper limb, and the lumbar and sacral plexuses sit at the root of the lower limb.
notes: Plexuses lie at the root of a limb, not at its far end. The named nerves leaving the plexus are what travel down to the hand or foot.
Correct. Each plexus sits near the root of the limb it supplies.
The vertebral canal holds the spinal cord and nerve roots. Plexuses form after the spinal nerves have left the canal, so pick the vertebral canal for where the cord and roots lie.
The spaces between the ribs hold the intercostal nerves, which do not form a plexus. Pick this location for T2 to T12 anterior rami.
questions.answerText: Each sits close to where its limb joins the trunk

questions.q: A tumor on the posterior wall of the pelvis presses on a plexus, causing tingling and weakness in the buttock, the back of the thigh, and the leg. Which plexus is compressed?
options: The sacral plexus
The brachial plexus
The coccygeal plexus
The lumbar plexus
questions.why: The sacral plexus lies on the posterior pelvic wall, right where this tumor sits. Many of the lower limb nerves, including the sciatic nerve, pass through it together, so pressure there causes symptoms spread across the buttock, the back of the thigh, and the leg. Matching both the location and the territory points to the sacral plexus.
notes: Correct. The sacral plexus sits on the posterior pelvic wall and serves the buttock, back of the thigh, and leg.
The brachial plexus lies in the lower neck and armpit and serves the upper limb. Pick it for tingling down the arm.
The coccygeal plexus is at the bottom of the pelvis too, but it serves only skin over the coccyx. Its compression would not cause weakness down the leg.
The lumbar plexus lies higher, in the posterior abdominal wall, and serves the front and inner thigh. Pick it for symptoms on the anterior thigh and lower abdominal wall.
questions.answerText: The sacral plexus

questions.q: How is a spinal nerve formed, and what kind of axons does it carry?
options: Posterior and anterior roots join; it carries sensory and motor axons
Rootlets from the brainstem join; it carries only sensory axons
Posterior and anterior rami join; it carries only motor axons
Anterior rami from several levels join; it carries only motor axons
questions.why: Rootlets along the cord gather into two roots on each side. The posterior root brings sensory axons and the anterior root carries motor axons, and the two roots join to form the spinal nerve. Because it holds axons from both roots, every spinal nerve is a mixed nerve, carrying sensory and motor axons together.
notes: Correct. The two roots join, so every spinal nerve is mixed.
Rootlets attach along the spinal cord, not the brainstem, and spinal nerves are mixed, not purely sensory. Nerves that arise from the brainstem are cranial nerves.
The rami are branches that split off after the spinal nerve has formed, not the parts that build it. Every spinal nerve and both of its rami carry sensory as well as motor axons.
Anterior rami from several levels weaving together form a nerve plexus, not a single spinal nerve. Pick this if the question asked how a plexus such as the brachial plexus is built.
questions.answerText: Posterior and anterior roots join; it carries sensory and motor axons

questions.q: What is a nerve?
options: A single long process carrying an impulse away from a cell body
A bundle of axons that runs within the brain or spinal cord
A cluster of neuron cell bodies lying outside the CNS
A PNS bundle of axons wrapped in connective tissue
questions.why: A nerve is a cordlike organ of the peripheral nervous system: many axons, some myelinated and some not, bundled together and wrapped in three layers of connective tissue. The axons are grouped into fascicles, and the connective tissue protects them and holds the nerve together. A nerve can carry sensory axons, motor axons, or both.
