notes: A single long process carrying an impulse away from a cell body is one axon, one nerve fiber. A nerve contains many axons bundled together.
A bundle of axons within the brain or spinal cord is a tract. Pick tract if the question asked about a bundle of axons in the CNS.
A cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion. This would be the answer for a question about the posterior root ganglion.
Correct. A nerve is a bundle of PNS axons wrapped in connective tissue.
questions.answerText: A PNS bundle of axons wrapped in connective tissue

questions.q: Which list gives the connective tissue wrappings of a nerve from innermost to outermost?
options: Endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium
Perineurium, endoneurium, epineurium
Epineurium, perineurium, endoneurium
Endomysium, perimysium, epimysium
questions.why: The three nerve wrappings nest from the inside out, and each prefix tells you the level. Endo means within, so the endoneurium wraps each individual axon. Peri means around, so the perineurium wraps each fascicle, a bundle of axons. Epi means upon, so the epineurium wraps the entire nerve.
notes: Correct. Endoneurium, then perineurium, then epineurium.
The perineurium wraps a whole fascicle, so it cannot be inside the endoneurium, which wraps a single axon. This order mixes up the two inner layers.
These are the right three layers in reverse order, from outermost to innermost. Students pick it when they mix up the meanings of endo and epi.
Endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium are the matching wrappings of a skeletal muscle, not a nerve. Pick this list if the question asked about muscle wrappings.
questions.answerText: Endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium

questions.q: In a peripheral nerve, what is a fascicle?
options: The outer wrapping of the whole nerve
A bundle of axons grouped together
A single axon with its myelin
A cluster of neuron cell bodies
questions.why: A fascicle is a bundle of axons grouped together within a nerve, wrapped by the perineurium. A nerve contains many fascicles, all held together by the outer epineurium. Skeletal muscle uses the same word for a bundle of muscle fibers, so the term always means a bundle.
notes: The outer wrapping of the whole nerve is the epineurium. This would be the answer if the question asked for the outermost nerve layer.
Correct. A fascicle is a bundle of axons inside a nerve.
A single axon with its myelin is one nerve fiber, wrapped by the endoneurium. Pick this if the question asked what the endoneurium surrounds.
A cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion, not a fascicle. Fascicles hold axons, not cell bodies.
questions.answerText: A bundle of axons grouped together

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the endoneurium and the epineurium?
options: Endoneurium wraps each fascicle; epineurium wraps each axon
Endoneurium wraps the whole nerve; epineurium wraps each axon
Endoneurium wraps each muscle fiber; epineurium wraps each muscle
Endoneurium wraps each axon; epineurium wraps the whole nerve
questions.why: The endoneurium is the innermost connective tissue wrapping, around each individual axon. The epineurium is the outermost wrapping, around the entire nerve. Between them, the perineurium wraps each fascicle. The prefixes help: endo means within, and epi means upon.
notes: The layer around each fascicle is the perineurium, and the epineurium is outermost, not around single axons. This choice scrambles all three levels.
This reverses the two layers. Endo means within, so the endoneurium is the innermost wrapping, and epi means upon, so the epineurium is the outermost.
Wrappings around muscle fibers and whole muscles are the endomysium and epimysium. This choice confuses the nerve terms with their muscle counterparts.
Correct. Endoneurium is around each axon, and epineurium is around the whole nerve.
questions.answerText: Endoneurium wraps each axon; epineurium wraps the whole nerve

questions.q: Nerve wrappings follow the same pattern as muscle wrappings. Which nerve layer matches the perimysium, the layer around each muscle fascicle?
options: Perineurium
Neurolemma
Endoneurium
Epineurium
questions.why: Both muscles and nerves are bundles of long structures wrapped at three levels. In muscle, the endomysium wraps each fiber, the perimysium wraps each fascicle, and the epimysium wraps the whole muscle. In a nerve, the endoneurium wraps each axon, the perineurium wraps each fascicle, and the epineurium wraps the whole nerve. The perineurium matches the perimysium because both surround a fascicle.
notes: Correct. The perineurium and perimysium both wrap a fascicle.
The neurolemma is the outer layer of a Schwann cell around a PNS axon, not a connective tissue wrapping. Choose it if the question asked which structure guides a cut peripheral axon as it regrows.
The endoneurium wraps each single axon, so it matches the endomysium around each muscle fiber. Pick it if the question asked for the counterpart of the endomysium.
The epineurium wraps the whole nerve, so it matches the epimysium around the whole muscle. It would be the answer for the counterpart of the epimysium.
questions.answerText: Perineurium

questions.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there, and what kind of nerve is each one?
options: 12 pairs, all mixed nerves
31 pairs, all motor nerves
31 pairs, all mixed nerves
33 pairs, all mixed nerves
questions.why: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves, one pair for each segment of the spinal cord. Every one is a mixed nerve, because it forms where a sensory posterior root and a motor anterior root join. The 12 pairs of cranial nerves are counted separately, and some of them are purely sensory or mainly motor.
notes: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, not spinal nerves. Pick 12 pairs if the question asked how many nerves arise from the brain.
The count is right, but spinal nerves are not purely motor. Each one carries sensory axons from the posterior root along with motor axons from the anterior root.
Correct. There are 31 pairs, and every one is mixed.

The count of 33 matches the usual number of vertebrae, not spinal nerves. The nerve count differs because there are 8 cervical nerves for only 7 cervical vertebrae, and just 1 coccygeal nerve for about 4 small coccygeal vertebrae.
questions.answerText: 31 pairs, all mixed nerves

questions.q: How are the 31 pairs of spinal nerves divided by region?
options: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal
8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacral, 1 coccygeal
8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 coccygeal
8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal
questions.why: The spinal nerves are named for the region of the vertebral column where they leave: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal pair, for a total of 31. The counts mostly match the vertebrae, with one well-known exception: there are 8 cervical nerves but only 7 cervical vertebrae, because the first cervical nerve leaves between the skull and C1.
notes: Seven is the number of cervical vertebrae, not cervical nerves. There are 8 cervical nerve pairs because the first one leaves between the skull and C1.
The sacrum is one fused bone in the adult, but it still passes 5 pairs of sacral nerves. This mix-up comes from counting the fused bone instead of its segments.
The coccyx is made of about four small fused vertebrae, but there is only one pair of coccygeal nerves. This choice counts the bones instead of the nerves.
Correct. Eight cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal make 31 pairs.
questions.answerText: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal

questions.q: What does the posterior (dorsal) ramus of a spinal nerve supply?
options: Deep muscles and skin of the posterior trunk
Muscles and skin of the limbs and the front of the trunk
The vertebrae, spinal ligaments, and meninges
The ganglia of the sympathetic trunk
questions.why: Just past the intervertebral foramen, each spinal nerve splits into rami, or branches. The posterior ramus turns backward to supply the deep muscles of the back and the skin over the posterior surface of the trunk. Because of this, a posterior ramus problem stays in the back, while limb problems point to the anterior rami or the plexuses they form.
notes: Correct. The posterior ramus serves the deep back muscles and the skin of the back.
The limbs and the front and sides of the trunk are supplied by the anterior (ventral) ramus. Pick this if the question asked what the anterior ramus supplies.
The vertebrae, ligaments, and meninges are supplied by the meningeal branch, which re-enters the vertebral canal. This would be the answer for a question about the meningeal branch.

The ganglia of the sympathetic trunk are reached by the rami communicantes, the small branches that link the spinal nerve to the trunk, not by the posterior ramus. Choose them for a question about how autonomic fibers reach the sympathetic trunk.
questions.answerText: Deep muscles and skin of the posterior trunk

questions.q: What does the anterior (ventral) ramus of a spinal nerve supply, and what do the anterior rami form?
options: Limbs and the anterior and lateral trunk; they form the plexuses
The meninges and vertebrae; they form the sympathetic trunk
Limbs and the anterior and lateral trunk; they form the cauda equina
Deep back muscles and posterior skin; they form the plexuses
questions.why: The anterior ramus is the larger branch of a spinal nerve. It supplies the muscles and skin of the limbs and of the front and sides of the trunk. In most regions the anterior rami of neighboring nerves weave together into networks called plexuses (cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal) before sending nerves to the body. The anterior rami of T2 to T12 are the exception and run as intercostal nerves.
notes: Correct. The anterior rami supply the limbs and front and sides of the trunk and form the plexuses.
The meninges and vertebrae are supplied by the meningeal branch, and the sympathetic trunk is a chain of autonomic ganglia. This choice confuses the anterior ramus with two other structures.
The territory is right, but the cauda equina is the bundle of nerve roots inside the vertebral canal below the end of the cord. It forms before the nerves exit, so the rami cannot form it.

The deep back muscles and posterior skin are supplied by the posterior (dorsal) ramus, and the posterior rami do not form plexuses. Pick this territory if the question asked about the posterior ramus.
questions.answerText: Limbs and the anterior and lateral trunk; they form the plexuses

questions.q: Which list gives the four large nerve plexuses that serve the neck and limbs, in order from superior to inferior?
options: Cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral
Brachial, cervical, sacral, lumbar
Cervical, brachial, thoracic, lumbar
Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral
questions.why: The plexuses run head to tail in the same order as the cord regions that build them. The cervical plexus (C1 to C4) serves the neck and shoulders, the brachial plexus (C5 to T1) serves the upper limb, the lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) serves the abdominal wall and part of the thigh, and the sacral plexus (L4 to S4) serves the buttock and most of the lower limb. A tiny coccygeal plexus below them serves only the skin over the coccyx.
notes: Correct. Cervical, brachial, lumbar, and sacral run from top to bottom.
These are the right four plexuses in the wrong order. The cervical plexus forms above the brachial plexus, and the lumbar plexus forms above the sacral plexus.
There is no thoracic plexus. The thoracic anterior rami run straight to the chest wall as intercostal nerves instead of forming a network.
This list leaves out the brachial plexus and adds a thoracic plexus that does not exist. The thoracic anterior rami are the one group that does not form a plexus.
questions.answerText: Cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral

questions.q: Which plexus gives rise to the phrenic nerve, the nerve that runs down through the thorax to the diaphragm?
options: Lumbar plexus
Cervical plexus
Brachial plexus
Sacral plexus
questions.why: The phrenic nerve leaves the cervical plexus in the neck and travels down through the thorax to the diaphragm. The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C1 to C4, and the phrenic nerve's fibers come mainly from C3 to C5. The teaching phrase 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive' is a reminder that a high cervical injury can stop breathing.
notes: The lumbar plexus forms from L1 to L4 and serves the lower abdominal wall and part of the thigh, well below the diaphragm. It would be the answer for a nerve running into the front of the thigh.
Correct. The phrenic nerve comes from the cervical plexus.
The brachial plexus forms from C5 to T1 and serves the shoulder and upper limb. Pick it if the question asked which plexus gives rise to the nerves of the arm.
The sacral plexus forms from L4 to S4 and gives rise to the sciatic nerve. Choose it if the question asked about the nerve running down the back of the thigh.
questions.answerText: Cervical plexus

questions.q: Which plexus serves the upper limb, and which spinal nerves form it?
options: Cervical plexus, C1 to C4
Brachial plexus, C5 to T1
Lumbar plexus, L1 to L4
Brachial plexus, C1 to C4
questions.why: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1, and it serves the shoulder and the entire upper limb. Brachial means arm. These segments match the cervical enlargement of the cord, where the extra neurons for the upper limb sit. Damage to this plexus causes weakness and sensory loss across the shoulder and the whole limb on that side.
notes: The cervical plexus forms from C1 to C4 and serves the neck and upper shoulders, and it gives off the phrenic nerve. Pick it if the question asked which plexus serves the neck.
Correct. The brachial plexus forms from C5 to T1 and serves the upper limb.
The lumbar plexus forms from L1 to L4 and serves the lower abdominal wall and part of the lower limb. It would be the answer for a question about the front of the thigh.
The plexus name is right, but C1 to C4 are the levels of the cervical plexus. The brachial plexus begins just below it, at C5.
questions.answerText: Brachial plexus, C5 to T1

questions.q: Which plexus gives rise to the sciatic nerve?
options: Brachial plexus
Lumbar plexus
Coccygeal plexus
Sacral plexus
questions.why: The sciatic nerve, the largest nerve in the body, comes from the sacral plexus. This plexus is formed by the anterior rami of L4 to S4 and serves the buttock, the perineum, and most of the lower limb. The sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis and runs down the back of the thigh, which is why sacral plexus damage affects the back of the thigh, the leg, and the foot.
notes: The brachial plexus (C5 to T1) gives rise to the nerves of the upper limb, not the lower limb. It would be the answer for a nerve in the arm.
The lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) gives rise to the femoral and obturator nerves, which run into the front and inner thigh. Pick it if the question asked which plexus gives rise to the femoral nerve.
The coccygeal plexus is tiny and serves only a small patch of skin over the coccyx. Choose it if the question asked which plexus serves the skin over the tailbone.
Correct. The sciatic nerve comes from the sacral plexus.
questions.answerText: Sacral plexus

questions.q: Most anterior rami weave together into plexuses. Which group of anterior rami is the exception and runs straight to its targets instead?
options: Anterior rami of L1 to L4
Anterior rami of T2 to T12
Anterior rami of C1 to C4
Anterior rami of L4 to S4
questions.why: The anterior rami of T2 to T12 do not form a plexus. They run between the ribs as the intercostal nerves (T12, below the last rib, is the subcostal nerve) and supply the intercostal muscles, the abdominal wall muscles, and the skin of the chest and abdomen. T1 is not part of this group because it joins the brachial plexus.
notes: The anterior rami of L1 to L4 form the lumbar plexus, serving the lower abdominal wall and part of the thigh. They would be the answer for the rami that build the lumbar plexus.
Correct. The anterior rami of T2 to T12 run as intercostal nerves without forming a plexus.
The anterior rami of C1 to C4 form the cervical plexus, which serves the neck and gives off the phrenic nerve. Pick them if the question asked which rami build the cervical plexus.
The anterior rami of L4 to S4 form the sacral plexus, which gives rise to the sciatic nerve. Choose them if the question asked which rami build the sacral plexus.
questions.answerText: Anterior rami of T2 to T12

questions.q: Which list names sensory receptor types classified by the kind of stimulus they detect?
options: Free nerve endings and encapsulated nerve endings
Multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar sensory neurons
Exteroceptors, interoceptors, and proprioceptors
Thermoreceptors, photoreceptors, nociceptors
questions.why: Receptors are classified three ways: by stimulus, by location, and by structure. By stimulus, mechanoreceptors respond to touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch; thermoreceptors to temperature; photoreceptors to light; chemoreceptors to chemicals such as taste and smell molecules; and nociceptors to potentially damaging stimuli, producing pain. Each name tells you what the receptor responds to.
notes: Free and encapsulated nerve endings are classified by structure, whether the ending is bare or wrapped in a connective tissue capsule. This would be the answer for a question about receptor structure.
Multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar are the structural classes of neurons, not receptor types. Choose this list for a question about neuron shapes.

Exteroceptors, interoceptors, and proprioceptors are classified by location: the body surface, the internal organs, and the muscles, tendons, and joints. Pick this list if the question asked how receptors are classified by where they sit.
Correct. These receptors are named for the stimulus they detect.
questions.answerText: Thermoreceptors, photoreceptors, nociceptors

questions.q: What do nociceptors detect?
options: Pain from potentially damaging stimuli
Stretch of a skeletal muscle
Changes in temperature
Chemicals such as taste and smell molecules
questions.why: Nociceptors respond to stimuli that could damage tissue, such as extreme heat, crushing pressure, or harmful chemicals, and they produce the sensation of pain. Many are free nerve endings, bare dendrite tips found in most body tissues. The root noci comes from the Latin word for harm.
notes: Correct. Nociceptors detect potentially damaging stimuli and produce pain.
The stretch of a skeletal muscle is detected by muscle spindles, a type of proprioceptor. Choose them if the question asked which receptor senses muscle stretch.
Changes in temperature are detected by thermoreceptors. Pick them if the question asked which receptors sense warm and cold.
Chemicals such as taste and smell molecules are detected by chemoreceptors. They would be the answer for a question about the receptors of taste and smell.
questions.answerText: Pain from potentially damaging stimuli

questions.q: What is the general job of a sensory receptor?
options: Release neurotransmitter onto the next neuron at a synapse
Detect a stimulus and trigger a signal in a sensory neuron
Carry a motor command from the CNS to a muscle or gland
Process incoming signals and decide on a response
questions.why: A sensory receptor is the first link in any sensory pathway or reflex arc. It monitors changes inside or outside the body, and when it detects a stimulus it triggers a signal in a sensory neuron, which carries the signal toward the CNS. Without receptors, the nervous system would have no input to process.
notes: Releasing neurotransmitter onto the next cell is the job of the synaptic end bulbs of an axon. Choose it if the question asked how a signal crosses a synapse.
Correct. A receptor detects a stimulus and starts a signal in a sensory neuron.
Carrying a motor command from the CNS to a muscle or gland is the job of a motor neuron. Pick it if the question asked what an efferent neuron does.

Processing signals and deciding on a response is the integrative function of the CNS, carried out at the integration center. It would be the answer for a question about the integration center of a reflex arc.
questions.answerText: Detect a stimulus and trigger a signal in a sensory neuron

questions.q: On a model, you trace a small branch from a sympathetic trunk ganglion back into the L4 spinal nerve, and it looks gray. Which ramus is it, and could you also find a white ramus on the L4 nerve?
options: A white ramus communicans, and yes, white rami are on every spinal nerve
A gray ramus communicans, and no, white rami are found only from T1 to L2
A white ramus communicans, and no, white rami are only on cervical nerves
A gray ramus communicans, and yes, white rami are on every spinal nerve
questions.why: Rami communicantes link a spinal nerve to a sympathetic trunk ganglion. The gray ramus carries unmyelinated axons from the ganglion back to the spinal nerve and is found on every spinal nerve. The white ramus carries myelinated axons into the ganglion and is found only on the T1 to L2 nerves, because only those cord segments have lateral horns.
notes: A branch that looks gray and runs from the ganglion back to the nerve is a gray ramus. Gray rami, not white rami, are the ones on every spinal nerve.
Correct. A gray ramus runs from the ganglion back to the spinal nerve, and white rami are found only on T1 to L2, so L4 has none.
The branch is a gray ramus, and white rami are on the T1 to L2 nerves, not the cervical nerves.
The ramus is right, but white rami are found only from T1 to L2. L4 is below that range.
questions.answerText: A gray ramus communicans, and no, white rami are found only from T1 to L2

questions.q: A skin slide shows a receptor deep in the hypodermis that looks like a cut onion, with many layers of capsule around one dendrite. Which receptor is it, what does it detect, and what is its structural class?
options: A tactile corpuscle; light touch; encapsulated
A tactile disc; deep pressure; nonencapsulated
A lamellar corpuscle; deep pressure; encapsulated
A lamellar corpuscle; light touch; nonencapsulated
questions.why: Lamellar means layered, and on a slide a lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle looks like a cut onion, with many capsule layers around one dendrite. It sits deep, in the deep dermis and hypodermis, and detects deep pressure and vibration. Because its nerve ending is wrapped in a connective tissue capsule, it is an encapsulated receptor.
notes: A tactile (Meissner) corpuscle is small and sits up in a dermal papilla near the surface, where it senses light touch. The deep, onion-like receptor is lamellar.
Tactile (Merkel) discs are bare endings in the stratum basale of the epidermis that sense light touch. They have no layered capsule and are not deep.
Correct. The deep, onion-like receptor is a lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle, an encapsulated receptor for deep pressure and vibration.
The receptor is right, but it detects deep pressure and vibration, and its layered capsule makes it encapsulated.
questions.answerText: A lamellar corpuscle; deep pressure; encapsulated

questions.q: The autonomic nervous system has two divisions. Which one prepares the body for fight or flight, such as during exercise or an emergency?
options: The parasympathetic division
The somatic division
The sympathetic division
The enteric division
questions.why: The autonomic nervous system, the involuntary motor branch of the PNS, has two divisions that usually act in opposite directions. The sympathetic division is the fight-or-flight division, supporting exercise and emergencies. The parasympathetic division is the rest-and-digest division, supporting routine activities.
notes: The parasympathetic division is the rest-and-digest division that supports routine activities such as digestion. Pick it for a question about the body at rest.
The somatic nervous system is the voluntary motor branch to skeletal muscle and is not part of the autonomic system. Choose it for a question about voluntary movement.
Correct. The sympathetic division is the fight-or-flight division.
The enteric nervous system is the network of neurons in the wall of the GI tract that can run the gut on its own. It would be right for a question about the nervous system of the gut.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: What is another name for the autonomic nervous system?
options: The central nervous system
The sensory nervous system
The visceral motor system
The somatic motor system
questions.why: The autonomic nervous system is also called the visceral motor system because it sends motor commands to the viscera, the internal organs. Its effectors are cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands, and it works without conscious control. The somatic motor system, by contrast, controls skeletal muscle voluntarily.
notes: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The ANS is a motor division of the peripheral nervous system, with only its first neurons starting in the CNS.

The sensory (afferent) division carries input toward the CNS. The ANS does have some sensory neurons from the organs, but it is defined by its motor output to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands, so sensory nervous system is not another name for it.
Correct. The ANS is the visceral motor system.
The somatic motor system is the other motor division; it controls skeletal muscle voluntarily. Pick it for the system that moves your arm when you choose to.
questions.answerText: The visceral motor system

questions.q: Which three tissue types are the effectors of the autonomic nervous system?
options: Skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands
Smooth muscle, skeletal muscle, and bone
Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands
Glands, skeletal muscle, and cartilage
questions.why: The effectors of the autonomic nervous system are cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands. These tissues run the internal organs: the heartbeat, the walls of blood vessels and hollow organs, and the secretions of glands. Skeletal muscle is the one muscle type the ANS does not control, because it belongs to the voluntary somatic system.
notes: Skeletal muscle is controlled by the somatic motor system, not the ANS. Swapping it in for smooth muscle is the most common slip.
Skeletal muscle belongs to the somatic system, and bone is not an effector of any motor system. Pick skeletal muscle only for somatic control.
Correct. Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands are the autonomic effectors.
Skeletal muscle is somatic, and cartilage is a connective tissue that receives no motor commands. Only glands in this list are autonomic effectors.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands

questions.q: From which parts of the central nervous system does the sympathetic division arise?
options: The brainstem nuclei and the sacral cord, S2 to S4
The cervical cord, C1 to C8 only
The lower lumbar and coccygeal cord
The thoracic and upper lumbar cord, T1 to L2
questions.why: The sympathetic division arises from the thoracic and upper lumbar segments of the spinal cord, T1 to L2. Its preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral gray horns of those segments, which is why it is also called the thoracolumbar division. The parasympathetic division leaves from the two ends instead, the brainstem and S2 to S4.
notes: The brainstem and S2 to S4 are the origins of the parasympathetic division, the craniosacral outflow. Pick them for the parasympathetic division.
No autonomic fibers leave the cervical cord. The head and neck do receive sympathetic fibers, but they climb up the sympathetic trunk from the thoracic segments.

No autonomic fibers leave the cord from the lower lumbar or coccygeal segments. The lower lumbar segments sit in the gap between the sympathetic outflow, which ends at L2, and the parasympathetic outflow, which starts at S2, and the coccygeal segment lies below S4, past the end of the parasympathetic outflow.
Correct. The sympathetic division leaves the cord from T1 to L2.
questions.answerText: The thoracic and upper lumbar cord, T1 to L2

questions.q: What does the term thoracolumbar outflow describe?
options: Sensory fibers entering the cord through the dorsal roots
Parasympathetic fibers leaving the brainstem and S2 to S4
Somatic motor fibers leaving the thoracic and lumbar ventral horns
Sympathetic fibers leaving the cord from T1 to L2
questions.why: Thoracolumbar outflow describes the sympathetic preganglionic fibers leaving the spinal cord from segments T1 to L2. The name joins the two regions involved, thoracic and lumbar. It is the reason the sympathetic division is also called the thoracolumbar division.
notes: Sensory fibers entering through the dorsal roots are input, not outflow. Outflow always means motor fibers leaving the CNS.
Parasympathetic fibers leaving the brainstem and S2 to S4 make up the craniosacral outflow. Pick it for the parasympathetic division.
Somatic motor fibers leave the ventral horn at every level of the cord to reach skeletal muscle. They are not autonomic, so they are not part of the thoracolumbar outflow.
Correct. Thoracolumbar outflow is the sympathetic exit from T1 to L2.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic fibers leaving the cord from T1 to L2

questions.q: Where in the spinal cord do the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons sit?
options: In the ventral gray horn
In the lateral gray horn
In the dorsal gray horn
In the dorsal root ganglion
questions.why: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral gray horn, a small projection of gray matter between the dorsal and ventral horns. The lateral horn is found in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, matching the T1 to L2 origin of the sympathetic division. The axons of these neurons leave the cord through the ventral root.
notes: The ventral gray horn holds somatic motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle. Pick it for the cell bodies of motor neurons to skeletal muscle.
Correct. The lateral horn holds the sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies.
The dorsal gray horn holds interneurons and receives incoming sensory axons. Pick it for where sensory input arrives in the cord.
The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies and lies outside the cord. Pick it for sensory cell bodies.
questions.answerText: In the lateral gray horn

questions.q: What is the sympathetic trunk also called?
options: The sympathetic chain
The thoracic splanchnic nerve
The cauda equina
The celiac plexus
questions.why: The sympathetic trunk is also called the sympathetic chain because its ganglia are linked one after another like beads on a string. A trunk runs on each side of the vertebral column from the base of the skull to the coccyx. The ganglia along it are the sympathetic trunk ganglia, also called paravertebral ganglia.
notes: Correct. The sympathetic trunk is the sympathetic chain.
The thoracic splanchnic nerves branch off the sympathetic trunk and carry fibers forward to the prevertebral ganglia in the abdomen. They leave the chain rather than forming it.
The cauda equina is the bundle of spinal nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord; its name means horse's tail. Pick it for the roots in the lower vertebral canal.
The celiac plexus is the large autonomic network around the celiac trunk in the abdomen, also called the solar plexus. Pick it for the plexus behind the stomach.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic chain

questions.q: From which spinal cord segments do the pelvic splanchnic nerves arise?
options: The lumbar segments L3 to L5
The cervical segments C1 to C8
The sacral segments S2 to S4
The thoracic segments T1 to T12
questions.why: The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from the S2 to S4 segments of the spinal cord and carry the sacral part of the parasympathetic outflow. They supply the pelvic organs, such as the urinary bladder, the lower large intestine, and the reproductive organs. Together with the four parasympathetic cranial nerves, they make up the craniosacral outflow.
notes: L3 to L5 fall in the gap between the sympathetic outflow, which ends at L2, and the parasympathetic outflow, which starts at S2. No autonomic fibers leave there.
The cervical segments send out no autonomic fibers. Pick them for the spinal nerves that form the cervical plexus and most of the brachial plexus.
Correct. The pelvic splanchnic nerves come from S2 to S4.
The thoracic segments are part of the sympathetic outflow, and they give rise to the thoracic splanchnic nerves, which are sympathetic. Pick them for those nerves.
questions.answerText: The sacral segments S2 to S4

questions.q: What is the celiac plexus also called?
options: The pulmonary plexus
The hypogastric plexus
The solar plexus
The cardiac plexus
questions.why: The celiac plexus is also called the solar plexus. It is the largest autonomic plexus and surrounds the celiac trunk, the first large unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta, behind the stomach. The nickname comes from the way its fibers radiate outward like rays of the sun.
notes: The pulmonary plexus lies at the root of each lung and supplies the bronchial tree. Pick it for the lungs.
The hypogastric plexus lies low in the abdominopelvic cavity and supplies the pelvic organs. Pick it for the bladder and rectum.
Correct. The celiac plexus is the solar plexus.
The cardiac plexus supplies the heart and lies at the base of the heart in the thorax. Pick it for the heart.
questions.answerText: The solar plexus

questions.q: Where does the cell body of an autonomic preganglionic neuron sit?
options: In a dorsal root ganglion
In an autonomic ganglion
In the brain or spinal cord
In the wall of the effector organ
questions.why: The cell body of an autonomic preganglionic neuron sits in the central nervous system, either in a brainstem nucleus or in the lateral gray matter of the spinal cord. Its thin, lightly myelinated axon then runs out to an autonomic ganglion, where it synapses with the second neuron. The first neuron of the pathway always starts in the CNS.
notes: A dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies, not autonomic motor neurons. Pick it for sensory cell bodies.
An autonomic ganglion holds the cell body of the second neuron, the postganglionic neuron. Pick it for the postganglionic cell body.
Correct. The preganglionic cell body sits in the CNS.
The wall of the effector organ is where parasympathetic terminal (intramural) ganglia sit, so it holds postganglionic cell bodies, not preganglionic ones.
questions.answerText: In the brain or spinal cord

questions.q: An autonomic preganglionic axon runs from the CNS to which structure?
options: To the dorsal gray horn
Directly to the effector organ
To a skeletal muscle
To an autonomic ganglion
questions.why: The preganglionic axon leaves the CNS and runs to an autonomic ganglion, where it synapses with a postganglionic neuron. The postganglionic axon then carries the signal the rest of the way to the effector. This synapse in a ganglion is the one feature the somatic motor pathway does not have.
notes: The dorsal gray horn is inside the cord and receives incoming sensory axons. A preganglionic axon is leaving the CNS, not entering the dorsal horn.
Running straight from the CNS to the target is the somatic pattern, with one neuron and no ganglion. The autonomic pathway always adds a second neuron.
Skeletal muscle is the effector of the somatic system. Autonomic axons serve cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands.
Correct. The preganglionic axon ends in an autonomic ganglion.
questions.answerText: To an autonomic ganglion

questions.q: Where does the cell body of an autonomic postganglionic neuron sit?
options: In the dorsal root ganglion
In the brainstem
In the autonomic ganglion
In the lateral horn of the spinal cord
questions.why: The postganglionic neuron is the second neuron of the autonomic pathway. Its cell body sits in the autonomic ganglion, where it receives the synapse from the preganglionic axon, and its unmyelinated axon runs on to the effector. The word postganglionic means after the ganglion, describing the axon that leaves it.
notes: The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies, not autonomic motor neurons. Pick it for sensory cell bodies.
The brainstem holds the preganglionic cell bodies of the cranial parasympathetic outflow. Pick it for the first neuron of a parasympathetic pathway in a cranial nerve.
Correct. The postganglionic cell body sits in the autonomic ganglion.
The lateral horn holds sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies, the first neuron of the pathway. Pick it for the sympathetic preganglionic neuron.
questions.answerText: In the autonomic ganglion

questions.q: A motor pathway reaches a skeletal muscle through a single neuron with no ganglion along the way. Which system is this?
options: The sympathetic division
The parasympathetic division
The somatic motor system
The autonomic nervous system
questions.why: The somatic motor system uses one motor neuron that runs from the CNS straight to a skeletal muscle, with no ganglion in between. Its cell body sits in the ventral gray horn or a brainstem motor nucleus. The autonomic system, by contrast, always uses two neurons with a synapse in a ganglion.
notes: The sympathetic division uses two neurons, with a ganglion close to the spinal cord. It does not drive skeletal muscle contraction.
The parasympathetic division uses two neurons, with a ganglion near or in the target organ. Its effectors are cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands, not skeletal muscle.
Correct. One neuron straight to skeletal muscle is the somatic pattern.
The autonomic nervous system always uses a two-neuron chain with a ganglion. Pick it for any pathway with a preganglionic and postganglionic neuron.
questions.answerText: The somatic motor system

questions.q: A preganglionic fiber synapses in a ganglion of the sympathetic trunk. Which division does it belong to?
options: The somatic motor system
The sensory division
The parasympathetic division
The sympathetic division
questions.why: The sympathetic trunk ganglia (paravertebral ganglia) belong to the sympathetic division. Many sympathetic preganglionic axons leave the cord in the T1 to L2 spinal nerves, enter the trunk through a white ramus communicans, and synapse in a trunk ganglion close to the vertebral column. Parasympathetic fibers do not synapse in the sympathetic trunk; they synapse in terminal ganglia near or in the organ.
notes: The somatic motor system uses one neuron and no ganglion, so it has no preganglionic fibers at all.
The sensory division carries input toward the CNS and has no preganglionic fibers. Its cell bodies sit in sensory ganglia such as the dorsal root ganglion.
Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers synapse in terminal ganglia near or within the target organ. Pick this division for a ganglion in the wall of an organ.
Correct. A synapse in the sympathetic trunk marks the sympathetic division.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X carry fibers of which autonomic division?
options: The somatic motor system only
The enteric nervous system
The sympathetic division
The parasympathetic division
questions.why: Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X carry the cranial part of the parasympathetic division. The oculomotor nerve (III) constricts the pupil, the facial (VII) and glossopharyngeal (IX) nerves drive tear and saliva production, and the vagus (X) serves the thoracic and abdominal organs. The rest of the parasympathetic outflow leaves from the sacral cord, S2 to S4.
notes: Several of these nerves do carry somatic motor fibers too, but not only those. The autonomic fibers they carry are parasympathetic.
The enteric nervous system is the network of plexuses inside the wall of the gut. It does not travel in cranial nerves, although the vagus does connect to it.
The sympathetic division leaves only from T1 to L2. Sympathetic fibers reach the head by climbing the sympathetic trunk, not by traveling in these cranial nerves.
Correct. These four cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibers.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: The adrenal medulla works like a modified ganglion of which autonomic division?
options: The sympathetic division
The parasympathetic division
The enteric nervous system
The somatic motor system
questions.why: The adrenal medulla, the inner part of the adrenal gland, works like a modified sympathetic ganglion. Sympathetic preganglionic fibers reach it directly, and its cells, which are related to postganglionic neurons, release epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood instead of onto a nearby organ. This is how a fight-or-flight response spreads through the bloodstream as well as through nerves.
notes: Correct. The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion.
The parasympathetic division does not supply the adrenal medulla. Pick it for terminal ganglia near or within organs.
The enteric nervous system lies in the wall of the gut. It does not include the adrenal gland.
The somatic motor system drives skeletal muscle with a single neuron and has no ganglia, so it has nothing to modify into a gland.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: Where are the prevertebral ganglia located?
options: In front of the vertebral column, near large abdominal arteries
Near or within the walls of the target organs they supply
Inside the lateral gray horns of the thoracic spinal cord
Alongside the vertebral column, linked together in a vertical chain
questions.why: Prevertebral (collateral) ganglia lie anterior to the vertebral column, clustered around the large arteries that branch off the abdominal aorta. They include the celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, aorticorenal, and renal ganglia, each named for the artery it sits beside. Like the trunk ganglia, they belong to the sympathetic division, but they sit farther forward.
notes: Correct. Prevertebral ganglia sit in front of the vertebral column by the abdominal arteries.
Near or within the target organ describes the parasympathetic terminal ganglia. Pick it for terminal or intramural ganglia.
The lateral gray horns hold the sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies, which are inside the CNS. A ganglion by definition lies outside the CNS.
A vertical chain alongside the vertebral column describes the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral) ganglia. Pick it for paravertebral ganglia.
questions.answerText: In front of the vertebral column, near large abdominal arteries

questions.q: Intramural ganglia belong to which broader group of autonomic ganglia?
options: Terminal ganglia
Dorsal root ganglia
Prevertebral ganglia
Paravertebral ganglia
questions.why: Intramural ganglia are terminal ganglia that sit within the wall of the organ they supply; intramural means within the wall. Terminal ganglia are the parasympathetic ganglia, located near or within the target organ. Because the ganglion is so close to the organ, the parasympathetic postganglionic axon is very short.
notes: Correct. Intramural ganglia are a kind of terminal ganglion.
Dorsal root ganglia hold sensory neuron cell bodies and are not autonomic ganglia. Pick them for sensory cell bodies.
Prevertebral ganglia are sympathetic ganglia in front of the vertebral column near the abdominal arteries. Pick them for the celiac or mesenteric ganglia.
Paravertebral ganglia form the sympathetic trunk beside the vertebral column, far from the organs. Pick them for the chain ganglia.
questions.answerText: Terminal ganglia

questions.q: Splanchnic nerves carry autonomic fibers toward which destination?
options: The cerebral cortex
The skin of the back
The visceral organs
The skeletal muscles
questions.why: Splanchnic means relating to the viscera, and splanchnic nerves carry autonomic fibers toward the internal organs of the abdomen and pelvis. The thoracic splanchnic nerves carry sympathetic fibers from the trunk to the prevertebral ganglia, and the pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 to the pelvic organs. In both cases the target is the viscera, not skeletal muscle or skin.
notes: The cerebral cortex is part of the CNS and is not a target of any peripheral nerve. Ascending tracts, not splanchnic nerves, carry signals there.
The skin of the back is supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves. Pick it for the posterior rami.
Correct. Splanchnic nerves head for the visceral organs.
Skeletal muscles are reached by somatic motor axons in the spinal and cranial nerves. Pick them for the somatic system.
questions.answerText: The visceral organs

questions.q: Which description fits an autonomic plexus?
options: A cluster of sensory neuron cell bodies just beside the cord
A network of spinal nerve anterior rami serving a limb
A single large nerve that runs to one organ
A network of autonomic axons and ganglia around the organs
questions.why: An autonomic plexus is a network of autonomic axons and ganglia in the thorax, abdomen, or pelvis. Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers often travel together through these networks before spreading out to the organs. The cardiac, pulmonary, celiac, mesenteric, hypogastric, and renal plexuses are examples.
notes: A cluster of sensory cell bodies beside the cord is a dorsal root ganglion. Pick it for where sensory neuron cell bodies sit.
A network of anterior rami serving a limb is a somatic nerve plexus, such as the brachial or sacral plexus. Pick it for the spinal nerve plexuses.
A single nerve to one organ is not a network. A plexus is defined by many fibers joining and branching.
Correct. An autonomic plexus is a network of autonomic axons and ganglia.
questions.answerText: A network of autonomic axons and ganglia around the organs

questions.q: Where is the pulmonary plexus located?
options: At the base of the heart
Around the esophagus in the thorax
Deep in the pelvis
At the root of each lung
questions.why: The pulmonary plexus lies at the root of each lung, where the bronchi and pulmonary vessels enter at the hilum. Its fibers follow the bronchi into the lung to supply the bronchial tree. It receives fibers from both the vagus nerve and the sympathetic trunk.
notes: The base of the heart is where the cardiac plexus lies. Pick it for the plexus that supplies the heart.
The esophageal plexus wraps around the esophagus in the thorax, formed mainly by the vagus nerves. Pick it for the esophagus.
The hypogastric plexus lies deep in the pelvis and supplies the pelvic organs. Pick it for the bladder and rectum.
Correct. The pulmonary plexus sits at the root of each lung.
questions.answerText: At the root of each lung

questions.q: The hypogastric plexus supplies autonomic fibers to which organs?
options: The organs of the head
The organs of the pelvis
The organs of the chest
The organs of the upper abdomen
questions.why: The hypogastric plexus supplies autonomic fibers to the pelvic organs, such as the urinary bladder, the rectum, and the reproductive organs. Hypogastric means below the stomach, which describes its low position in the abdominopelvic cavity. It receives parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) as well as sympathetic fibers.
notes: The organs of the head receive parasympathetic fibers through cranial nerves and the terminal ganglia of the head, such as the ciliary and otic ganglia. The hypogastric plexus sits low in the pelvis, far from the head.
Correct. The hypogastric plexus supplies the pelvic organs.
The organs of the chest are supplied by the cardiac, pulmonary, and esophageal plexuses. Pick the chest for those plexuses.
The upper abdominal organs are supplied mainly by the celiac plexus. Pick the upper abdomen for the celiac (solar) plexus.
questions.answerText: The organs of the pelvis

questions.q: The cardiac plexus delivers autonomic fibers to which organ?
options: The stomach
The heart
The lungs
The esophagus
questions.why: The cardiac plexus is a network of autonomic fibers at the base of the heart that supplies the heart. Sympathetic fibers in this plexus speed the heart, and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve slow it. The plexus lies in the thorax close to the pulmonary plexus.
notes: The stomach is supplied mainly through the celiac plexus in the abdomen. Pick it for the celiac (solar) plexus.
Correct. Cardiac means heart, and the cardiac plexus supplies the heart.
The lungs are supplied by the pulmonary plexus at the root of each lung. Pick the lungs for that plexus.
The esophagus is supplied by the esophageal plexus, formed mainly by the vagus nerves in the thorax. Pick it for that plexus.
questions.answerText: The heart

questions.q: The esophageal plexus is found in which body cavity?
options: The cranial cavity
The abdomen
The pelvis
The thorax
questions.why: The esophageal plexus surrounds the esophagus in the thorax, in the posterior mediastinum. It forms mainly from the two vagus nerves, which branch and weave around the esophagus as they travel down. Just above the diaphragm, the fibers regroup into vagal trunks that pass into the abdomen with the esophagus.
notes: The cranial cavity holds the brain, not any autonomic trunk plexus. Pick it for the cranial nerve nuclei, not a plexus.
The abdomen holds the celiac, mesenteric, and renal plexuses. The esophagus passes through the diaphragm only at its very end, so its plexus sits above.
The pelvis holds the hypogastric plexus, which supplies the pelvic organs. Pick it for that plexus.
Correct. The esophageal plexus lies in the thorax.
questions.answerText: The thorax

questions.q: A ganglion lies in a vertical chain alongside the vertebral column. Which type of ganglion is it?
options: A prevertebral ganglion
A terminal ganglion
An intramural ganglion
A paravertebral ganglion
questions.why: Paravertebral ganglia, also called sympathetic trunk ganglia, form a vertical chain on each side of the vertebral column. Para- means beside, which matches their position next to the vertebrae. They belong to the sympathetic division and run from the base of the skull to the coccyx.
notes: A prevertebral ganglion sits in front of the vertebral column near the large abdominal arteries, not in a chain beside it. Pre- means in front, para- means beside.
A terminal ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion near or within the target organ. Pick it for a ganglion close to the organ.
An intramural ganglion is a terminal ganglion inside the wall of an organ. Pick it for a ganglion in the wall of the bladder or gut.
Correct. The chain beside the vertebral column is made of paravertebral ganglia.
questions.answerText: A paravertebral ganglion

questions.q: An autonomic division has short preganglionic axons and long postganglionic axons. Which division is it?
options: The parasympathetic division
The sympathetic division
The somatic motor system
The enteric nervous system
questions.why: In the sympathetic division the ganglia sit close to the spinal cord, in the sympathetic trunk or the prevertebral ganglia. That makes the preganglionic axon short and the postganglionic axon long, since the second neuron must travel all the way out to the organ. The parasympathetic division is the reverse, with a long preganglionic axon and a short postganglionic one.
notes: The parasympathetic division has long preganglionic and short postganglionic axons, because its ganglia sit at the organ. Pick it for the reverse pattern.
Correct. Ganglia near the cord give the sympathetic division short preganglionic and long postganglionic axons.
The somatic motor system uses a single neuron with no ganglion, so it has no preganglionic or postganglionic axons.
The enteric nervous system is the network inside the gut wall. It is not described by preganglionic and postganglionic lengths.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: An autonomic division has its ganglia near or within the walls of the target organs. Which division is it?
options: The visceral sensory system
The parasympathetic division
The sympathetic division
The somatic motor system
questions.why: The parasympathetic division has its ganglia, the terminal ganglia, near or within the walls of the target organs. Its preganglionic axons therefore run a long way from the brainstem or sacral cord, and its postganglionic axons are short. Terminal ganglia inside the organ wall are also called intramural ganglia.
notes: The visceral sensory system carries input from the organs to the CNS, with its cell bodies in sensory ganglia. It is not a motor division with ganglia at the organs.
Correct. Terminal ganglia at the organ mark the parasympathetic division.
The sympathetic division has its ganglia close to the spinal cord, in the sympathetic trunk or the prevertebral ganglia. Pick it for ganglia near the vertebral column.
The somatic motor system has no ganglia at all; one neuron runs straight to skeletal muscle.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: Which of these is a prevertebral ganglion?
options: The otic ganglion
The celiac ganglion
The ciliary ganglion
The dorsal root ganglion
questions.why: The celiac ganglion is a prevertebral (collateral) ganglion, one of the sympathetic ganglia that sit in front of the vertebral column around the large abdominal arteries. It lies beside the celiac trunk. The other prevertebral ganglia are the superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, aorticorenal, and renal ganglia.
notes: The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic terminal ganglion of the head that serves the parotid salivary gland. Pick it as one of the four terminal ganglia of the head.
Correct. The celiac ganglion is a prevertebral ganglion.
The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic terminal ganglion in the orbit, serving the eye with fibers from the oculomotor nerve. Its name looks like celiac, which is the usual mix-up.
The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies and is not an autonomic ganglion. Pick it for sensory cell bodies.
questions.answerText: The celiac ganglion

questions.q: During surgery high in the chest, a structure is cut that runs as a chain of ganglia beside the vertebral column. Which structure was cut?
options: The vagus nerve
The sympathetic trunk
The celiac plexus
The pelvic splanchnic nerves
questions.why: The sympathetic trunk is a chain of ganglia that runs on each side of the vertebral column from the base of the skull to the coccyx. In the thorax it lies along the heads of the ribs, beside the vertebral bodies. Cutting it interrupts the sympathetic fibers traveling through that part of the chain.
notes: The vagus nerve does run through the thorax, but it travels beside the esophagus and is a single nerve, not a chain of ganglia.
Correct. A chain of ganglia beside the vertebral column is the sympathetic trunk.
The celiac plexus lies in the abdomen around the celiac trunk, below the diaphragm. Pick it for the network behind the stomach.
The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from S2 to S4 and lie in the pelvis. Pick them for parasympathetic supply to the pelvic organs.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic trunk

questions.q: Which of these ganglia of the head is a parasympathetic terminal ganglion?
options: The ciliary ganglion
The celiac ganglion
The superior cervical ganglion
The trigeminal ganglion
questions.why: The ciliary ganglion is one of the four named parasympathetic terminal ganglia of the head, along with the pterygopalatine, submandibular, and otic ganglia. It sits in the orbit behind the eye and relays parasympathetic fibers from the oculomotor nerve (III) to the muscles that constrict the pupil. As a terminal ganglion, it lies close to the organ it serves.
notes: Correct. The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic terminal ganglion of the head.
The celiac ganglion is a sympathetic prevertebral ganglion in the abdomen, beside the celiac trunk. Its name looks like ciliary, but it is not in the head at all.
The superior cervical ganglion is the top ganglion of the sympathetic trunk, in the neck. It sends sympathetic fibers to the head, so pick it for the sympathetic supply to the head.
The trigeminal ganglion holds the sensory cell bodies of the trigeminal nerve (V). It is a sensory ganglion, not an autonomic one.
questions.answerText: The ciliary ganglion

questions.q: An autonomic division leaves the CNS only from the brainstem and the sacral cord. Which division is it?
options: The parasympathetic division
The enteric nervous system
The sympathetic division
The somatic motor system
questions.why: The parasympathetic division leaves the CNS from the brainstem, through cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X, and from the sacral cord, S2 to S4. These two ends of the CNS give it the name craniosacral division. The sympathetic division fills the middle instead, leaving from T1 to L2.
notes: Correct. Brainstem plus sacral cord is the craniosacral, or parasympathetic, outflow.
The enteric nervous system lies in the wall of the gut and is largely independent of the CNS. It does not leave the CNS at all.
The sympathetic division leaves from the middle of the cord, T1 to L2, the thoracolumbar outflow. Pick it for the thoracic and upper lumbar segments.

The somatic motor system sends motor neurons from the brainstem motor nuclei and the anterior horns along the whole cord to skeletal muscle. It is not limited to the two ends of the CNS and is not autonomic.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the chest and most of the abdomen. Which nerves carry parasympathetic fibers to the pelvic organs?
options: The pelvic splanchnic nerves
The sympathetic trunks
The thoracic splanchnic nerves
The glossopharyngeal nerves
questions.why: The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from S2 to S4 and carry the sacral parasympathetic fibers to the pelvic organs, such as the bladder, the rectum and lower colon, and the reproductive organs. They pass through the hypogastric plexus on the way. The vagus nerve covers the chest and most of the abdomen, and the pelvic splanchnic nerves take over below that.
notes: Correct. The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry the sacral parasympathetic outflow to the pelvis.
The sympathetic trunks are chains of sympathetic ganglia. They carry no parasympathetic fibers.
The thoracic splanchnic nerves carry sympathetic fibers from the thoracic sympathetic trunk to the prevertebral ganglia. They share the word splanchnic, but they belong to the other division.
The glossopharyngeal nerves (IX) carry parasympathetic fibers, but only to the parotid salivary gland in the head. Pick them for saliva from the parotid gland.
questions.answerText: The pelvic splanchnic nerves

questions.q: What does the celiac plexus supply?
options: The urinary bladder and the rectum
Most of the upper abdominal organs
The heart and the great vessels
The bronchial tree of both lungs
questions.why: The celiac (solar) plexus is the largest autonomic plexus. It surrounds the celiac trunk, and its fibers spread out to supply most of the upper abdominal organs. The intestines are supplied mainly by the superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses, and the pelvic organs by the hypogastric plexus.
notes: The bladder and rectum are pelvic organs supplied by the hypogastric plexus. Pick them for the hypogastric plexus.
Correct. The celiac plexus supplies most of the upper abdominal organs.
The heart and great vessels are supplied by the cardiac plexus at the base of the heart. Pick them for the cardiac plexus.
The bronchial tree is supplied by the pulmonary plexus at the root of each lung. Pick it for the pulmonary plexus.
questions.answerText: Most of the upper abdominal organs

questions.q: An autonomic neuron has its cell body inside an autonomic ganglion and sends its axon out to a gland. Which neuron is this?
options: A somatic motor neuron
A preganglionic neuron
A postganglionic neuron
A sensory neuron
questions.why: A postganglionic neuron is the second neuron of the autonomic pathway. Its cell body sits in the autonomic ganglion, and its unmyelinated axon runs from the ganglion to the effector, here a gland. The name means after the ganglion, which describes the path of its axon.
notes: A somatic motor neuron runs from the CNS straight to skeletal muscle, with no ganglion. Pick it for voluntary muscle control.
A preganglionic neuron has its cell body in the brain or spinal cord and sends its axon to the ganglion. Pick it for the first neuron of the pathway.
Correct. A cell body in the ganglion with an axon to the effector is a postganglionic neuron.
A sensory neuron carries input toward the CNS, and its cell body sits in a sensory ganglion such as the dorsal root ganglion. It does not send commands to a gland.
questions.answerText: A postganglionic neuron

questions.q: Which autonomic plexus supplies the kidneys and ureters?
options: The hypogastric plexus
The cardiac plexus
The renal plexus
The pulmonary plexus
questions.why: The renal plexus supplies the kidneys and ureters. It forms around the renal arteries, which branch from the abdominal aorta, and its fibers follow those arteries into each kidney. Many autonomic plexuses are named for the organ or vessel they wrap around, and renal means kidney.
notes: The hypogastric plexus supplies the pelvic organs, including the urinary bladder. Because the bladder continues the urinary pathway, students sometimes extend this plexus up to the kidneys.
The cardiac plexus supplies the heart. Pick it for the plexus at the base of the heart.
Correct. Renal means kidney, and the renal plexus supplies the kidneys and ureters.
The pulmonary plexus supplies the bronchial tree at the root of each lung. Pick it for the lungs.
questions.answerText: The renal plexus

questions.q: In an autonomic pathway to the stomach, the second neuron sits in the stomach wall and its axon travels only a few millimeters. Which division does this describe?
options: The parasympathetic division
The somatic motor system
The sympathetic division
The visceral sensory system
questions.why: A second neuron sitting in the wall of the organ means the ganglion is an intramural (terminal) ganglion, and terminal ganglia belong to the parasympathetic division. Because the ganglion is at the organ, the postganglionic axon is very short, while the preganglionic axon, here traveling in the vagus nerve, is long. Sympathetic pathways show the opposite pattern.
notes: Correct. A ganglion in the organ wall with a short postganglionic axon is parasympathetic.
The somatic motor system has only one neuron and no ganglion, so it has no second neuron at all.
The sympathetic division has its ganglia near the spinal cord, so its postganglionic axons are long. Pick it for a second neuron in a chain or prevertebral ganglion.
The visceral sensory system carries input from the organs toward the CNS. It is not a two-neuron motor pathway ending at the organ.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: A preganglionic cell body sits in the lateral gray horn of a thoracic spinal segment. To which division does this neuron belong?
options: The sympathetic division
The parasympathetic division
The enteric nervous system
The somatic motor system
questions.why: The lateral gray horn of segments T1 to L2 holds the preganglionic cell bodies of the sympathetic division. A thoracic segment falls within that range, so this neuron is sympathetic. Its axon will leave through the ventral root and head for the sympathetic trunk.
notes: Correct. A preganglionic cell body in a thoracic lateral horn is sympathetic.
Parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in brainstem nuclei and in segments S2 to S4. A thoracic segment is outside the parasympathetic outflow.
The enteric nervous system has its neurons in the gut wall, not in the spinal cord. Pick it for the myenteric or submucosal plexus.
Somatic motor neurons sit in the ventral gray horn and have no preganglionic stage. Pick them for a cell body in the ventral horn.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: Which choice lists, in order, the structures an autonomic motor command passes through from start to target?
options: CNS, preganglionic neuron, postganglionic neuron, ganglion, effector
Ganglion, preganglionic neuron, CNS, postganglionic neuron, effector
CNS, preganglionic neuron, ganglion, postganglionic neuron, effector
CNS, postganglionic neuron, ganglion, preganglionic neuron, effector
questions.why: Every autonomic command starts with a preganglionic neuron whose cell body is in the CNS. Its axon runs to an autonomic ganglion and synapses with a postganglionic neuron, whose axon carries the signal the rest of the way to the effector (cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, or a gland). The ganglion always sits between the two neurons.
notes: This puts both neurons before the ganglion. The ganglion is where the two neurons meet, so it must sit between them.
This starts at the ganglion instead of the CNS. Every autonomic command begins in the brain or spinal cord.
Correct. CNS, preganglionic neuron, ganglion, postganglionic neuron, effector.
This swaps the two neurons. Pre- means before the ganglion and post- means after it, so the preganglionic neuron must come first.
questions.answerText: CNS, preganglionic neuron, ganglion, postganglionic neuron, effector

questions.q: Which combination correctly pairs the sympathetic division with its outflow and a type of ganglion it uses?
options: Sympathetic division, craniosacral outflow, paravertebral (chain) ganglia
Sympathetic division, craniosacral outflow, terminal ganglia
Sympathetic division, thoracolumbar outflow, terminal ganglia
Sympathetic division, thoracolumbar outflow, paravertebral (chain) ganglia
questions.why: The sympathetic division leaves the cord from T1 to L2, the thoracolumbar outflow, and many of its fibers synapse in the paravertebral (chain) ganglia of the sympathetic trunk beside the vertebral column. Its other ganglia, the prevertebral ganglia, also sit near the vertebral column. Craniosacral outflow and terminal ganglia both belong to the parasympathetic division.
notes: The ganglia are right, but craniosacral outflow (brainstem and S2 to S4) is the parasympathetic origin.
Craniosacral outflow and terminal ganglia are both parasympathetic features. This choice describes the parasympathetic division with the wrong name attached.
The outflow is right, but terminal ganglia near or in the organ belong to the parasympathetic division.
Correct. Thoracolumbar outflow and chain ganglia both belong to the sympathetic division.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic division, thoracolumbar outflow, paravertebral (chain) ganglia

questions.q: Which combination correctly pairs the parasympathetic division with its outflow and the length of its preganglionic axon?
options: Parasympathetic division, thoracolumbar outflow, short preganglionic axon
Parasympathetic division, thoracolumbar outflow, long preganglionic axon
Parasympathetic division, craniosacral outflow, short preganglionic axon
Parasympathetic division, craniosacral outflow, long preganglionic axon
questions.why: The parasympathetic division leaves the CNS from the brainstem and S2 to S4, the craniosacral outflow. Its ganglia sit near or within the target organs, so its preganglionic axons must travel a long way and its postganglionic axons are short. The sympathetic division is the reverse on both points.
notes: Thoracolumbar outflow and a short preganglionic axon are both sympathetic features. Pick this combination for the sympathetic division.
The axon length is right, but thoracolumbar outflow (T1 to L2) is the sympathetic origin.
The outflow is right, but a short preganglionic axon belongs to the sympathetic division, whose ganglia sit near the cord.
Correct. Craniosacral outflow with a long preganglionic axon is the parasympathetic pattern.
questions.answerText: Parasympathetic division, craniosacral outflow, long preganglionic axon

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the two autonomic divisions on ganglion location and postganglionic axon length?
options: Sympathetic ganglia lie near the organ with long postganglionic axons; parasympathetic ganglia lie near the cord with short ones
Sympathetic ganglia lie near the organ with short postganglionic axons; parasympathetic ganglia lie near the cord with long ones
Sympathetic ganglia lie near the cord with short postganglionic axons; parasympathetic ganglia lie near the organ with long ones
Sympathetic ganglia lie near the cord with long postganglionic axons; parasympathetic ganglia lie near the organ with short ones
questions.why: The sympathetic ganglia sit close to the spinal cord, so the postganglionic axon has to run a long way out to the organ. The parasympathetic ganglia sit near or within the organ, so the postganglionic axon is short. Where the ganglion sits decides how long the axon leaving it must be.
notes: This puts the sympathetic ganglia at the organ and the parasympathetic ganglia near the cord, which is backward, and the lengths do not fit those locations either.
This swaps the two divisions completely. Sympathetic ganglia are near the cord, and parasympathetic ganglia are at the organ.
The ganglion locations are right, but the axon lengths are reversed. A ganglion near the cord must send a long axon to reach a distant organ.
Correct. Ganglia near the cord give long postganglionic axons; ganglia at the organ give short ones.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic ganglia lie near the cord with long postganglionic axons; parasympathetic ganglia lie near the organ with short ones

questions.q: A sympathetic command travels from the spinal cord to a distant organ. Which list names, in order, the structures it passes through?
options: Sympathetic chain ganglion, lateral horn, preganglionic axon, postganglionic axon, effector
Lateral horn, preganglionic axon, sympathetic chain ganglion, postganglionic axon, effector
Lateral horn, postganglionic axon, sympathetic chain ganglion, preganglionic axon, effector
Dorsal horn, preganglionic axon, terminal ganglion, postganglionic axon, effector
questions.why: A sympathetic command starts at a preganglionic cell body in the lateral gray horn of a segment between T1 and L2. The preganglionic axon leaves through the ventral root and synapses in a sympathetic chain ganglion, and the postganglionic axon then runs out to the effector. Preganglionic always comes before the ganglion and postganglionic after it.
notes: This starts at the chain ganglion instead of the cord. Every autonomic command begins with a cell body in the CNS, here the lateral horn.
Correct. Lateral horn, preganglionic axon, chain ganglion, postganglionic axon, effector.
This swaps the two axons. The preganglionic axon must reach the ganglion before the postganglionic axon can leave it.
The dorsal horn receives sensory input and holds no autonomic motor neurons, and terminal ganglia are parasympathetic. This list mixes in two wrong structures.
questions.answerText: Lateral horn, preganglionic axon, sympathetic chain ganglion, postganglionic axon, effector

questions.q: Which set of structures all belong to the parasympathetic division?
options: Cranial nerve X, the pelvic splanchnic nerves, and terminal ganglia
The sympathetic trunk, the thoracic splanchnic nerves, and prevertebral ganglia
Cranial nerve X, the sympathetic trunk, and paravertebral ganglia
The pelvic splanchnic nerves, the lateral horn, and chain ganglia
questions.why: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) carries the cranial parasympathetic outflow to the chest and abdomen, the pelvic splanchnic nerves carry the sacral outflow from S2 to S4, and terminal ganglia are where parasympathetic fibers synapse near or in the organ. All three belong to the craniosacral, or parasympathetic, division. The sympathetic trunk, the lateral horn, and the chain and prevertebral ganglia all belong to the sympathetic division.
notes: Correct. The vagus nerve, pelvic splanchnic nerves, and terminal ganglia are all parasympathetic.
Every item here is sympathetic: the trunk, the thoracic splanchnic nerves, and the prevertebral ganglia. Pick this set for the sympathetic division.
The vagus nerve is parasympathetic, but the sympathetic trunk and its paravertebral ganglia are sympathetic. Only one item fits.
The pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic, but the lateral horn and chain ganglia are sympathetic. Only one item fits.
questions.answerText: Cranial nerve X, the pelvic splanchnic nerves, and terminal ganglia

questions.q: Which of these effectors is controlled by the somatic motor system rather than the autonomic nervous system?
options: The salivary glands
Cardiac muscle of the heart
Skeletal muscle of the arm
Smooth muscle of the bronchioles
questions.why: Skeletal muscle, such as the muscles of the arm, is controlled by the somatic motor system, normally under voluntary control. The autonomic nervous system controls the other three kinds of effector: cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands. Sorting by tissue type is the quickest way to tell which motor system is in charge.
notes: Glands, including the salivary glands, are autonomic effectors. Pick them for autonomic control of secretion.
Cardiac muscle is an autonomic effector; the ANS speeds or slows the heart. Pick it for autonomic control.
Correct. Skeletal muscle is the effector of the somatic motor system.
Smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchioles is an autonomic effector; the sympathetic division opens the airways. Pick it for autonomic control.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle of the arm

questions.q: Which two divisions make up the autonomic nervous system?
options: The somatic and enteric motor divisions
The sympathetic and somatic motor divisions
The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
The afferent (sensory) and efferent (motor) divisions
questions.why: The autonomic nervous system has two divisions, the sympathetic and the parasympathetic. They usually act in opposite directions on the same organ: the sympathetic division prepares the body for action (fight or flight), and the parasympathetic division conserves energy (rest and digest). The enteric nervous system in the gut wall works alongside them but is described separately.
notes: The somatic system is a separate motor system for skeletal muscle, not part of the ANS. The enteric system is described separately as well.
The sympathetic division is right, but the somatic motor system controls skeletal muscle and is not autonomic.
Correct. The ANS has a sympathetic and a parasympathetic division.
Afferent and efferent divide the whole peripheral nervous system into sensory and motor parts. The ANS sits entirely on the efferent (motor) side.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions

questions.q: How many motor neurons does the autonomic pathway use between the CNS and the effector?
options: Two, with a synapse in a ganglion
One, running straight to the effector
Three, with two ganglia
None, since it relies on sensory neurons only
questions.why: The autonomic motor pathway always uses two neurons in a row. The preganglionic neuron runs from the CNS to an autonomic ganglion and synapses there, and the postganglionic neuron carries the signal on to the effector. The somatic pathway, by comparison, uses only one motor neuron.
notes: Correct. Two neurons, with a synapse in a ganglion.
One neuron running straight to the effector is the somatic pattern for skeletal muscle. Pick it for the somatic motor system.
No autonomic pathway uses three motor neurons. Students sometimes count the ganglion as an extra neuron, but it is simply where the two neurons meet.
The ANS is a motor system that sends commands out to effectors. Sensory neurons carry input in the other direction.
questions.answerText: Two, with a synapse in a ganglion

questions.q: What is the first neuron of the autonomic two-neuron pathway called?
options: The interneuron
The preganglionic neuron
The sensory neuron
The postganglionic neuron
questions.why: The first neuron of the autonomic pathway is the preganglionic neuron. Its cell body sits in the brain or spinal cord, and its thin, lightly myelinated axon runs out to an autonomic ganglion. Pre- means before, so this is the neuron before the ganglion.
notes: An interneuron lies entirely within the CNS and links other neurons. It is not one of the two motor neurons of the autonomic chain.
Correct. The preganglionic neuron comes first.
A sensory neuron carries input toward the CNS. The autonomic two-neuron pathway is motor, carrying commands outward.
The postganglionic neuron is the second neuron, with its cell body in the ganglion. Pick it for the neuron after the ganglion.
questions.answerText: The preganglionic neuron

questions.q: Which of these axons is typically unmyelinated?
options: The preganglionic axon
A somatic motor axon to skeletal muscle
The postganglionic axon
A sensory axon from a lamellar corpuscle
questions.why: In the autonomic pathway, the preganglionic axon is lightly myelinated and the postganglionic axon is unmyelinated. Myelin is the fatty wrapping around an axon, and postganglionic axons lack it. The synapse in the ganglion marks the switch from the lightly myelinated first axon to the unmyelinated second one.
notes: The preganglionic axon is lightly myelinated, so it does have some myelin. Pick it if the question asked which autonomic axon has myelin.
Somatic motor axons to skeletal muscle are myelinated, which helps them carry fast commands. Pick them for a myelinated motor axon.
Correct. Autonomic postganglionic axons are unmyelinated.
Sensory axons from lamellar corpuscles are myelinated. Pick them for a myelinated sensory axon.
questions.answerText: The postganglionic axon

questions.q: By what other name is the sympathetic division known?
options: The craniosacral division
The enteric division
The somatic division
The thoracolumbar division
questions.why: The sympathetic division is also called the thoracolumbar division because its preganglionic neurons leave the spinal cord from the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, T1 to L2. The name is a map of where the division begins. Its partner, the parasympathetic division, is the craniosacral division.
notes: The craniosacral division is the parasympathetic division, which leaves from the brainstem and S2 to S4. Pick it for the parasympathetic division.
The enteric nervous system is the network in the gut wall, not another name for the sympathetic division.
The somatic division controls skeletal muscle and is not autonomic. Pick it for voluntary motor control.
Correct. The sympathetic division is the thoracolumbar division.
questions.answerText: The thoracolumbar division

questions.q: By what other name is the parasympathetic division known?
options: The craniosacral division
The thoracolumbar division
The enteric division
The somatic division
questions.why: The parasympathetic division is also called the craniosacral division because its preganglionic neurons leave from the brainstem (through cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X) and from the sacral cord, S2 to S4. Cranio- refers to the head and sacral to the lowest part of the cord. Its partner, the sympathetic division, is the thoracolumbar division.
notes: Correct. The parasympathetic division is the craniosacral division.
The thoracolumbar division is the sympathetic division, which leaves from T1 to L2. Pick it for the sympathetic division.
