The enteric nervous system is the network in the gut wall. It is not another name for the parasympathetic division, though the vagus nerve connects to it.
The somatic division controls skeletal muscle and is not autonomic. Pick it for voluntary motor control.
questions.answerText: The craniosacral division

questions.q: A cross section of the thoracic spinal cord shows a small lateral gray horn on each side. Which cell bodies does the lateral horn hold?
options: Sympathetic postganglionic neurons
Sympathetic preganglionic neurons
Somatic motor neurons
Sensory neurons
questions.why: The lateral gray horn holds the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons. It is found in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, T1 to L2, which is exactly where the sympathetic division leaves the cord. The axons of these neurons exit through the ventral root and head for the sympathetic trunk.
notes: Sympathetic postganglionic cell bodies sit in the sympathetic trunk and prevertebral ganglia, outside the CNS. Pick them for a sympathetic ganglion.
Correct. The lateral horn holds sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies.
Somatic motor neurons sit in the ventral gray horn and drive skeletal muscle. Pick them for the ventral horn.
Sensory neuron cell bodies sit outside the cord in the dorsal root ganglia. Pick them for the dorsal root ganglion.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons

questions.q: From which structures does the parasympathetic division arise?
options: Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and cord segments S2 to S4
The lateral gray horns of the spinal segments from T1 to L2
The dorsal root ganglia of the sacral spinal nerves
The lateral gray horns found in every segment of the spinal cord
questions.why: The parasympathetic division arises from the nuclei of four cranial nerves in the brainstem (III, VII, IX, and X) and from the S2 to S4 segments of the spinal cord. These two ends of the CNS give it the name craniosacral division. The middle of the cord, T1 to L2, belongs to the sympathetic division instead.
notes: Correct. Four cranial nerves plus S2 to S4 make up the craniosacral outflow.
The lateral gray horns of T1 to L2 are the origin of the sympathetic division. Pick them for the sympathetic division.
The dorsal root ganglia hold sensory neuron cell bodies, not autonomic motor neurons. Pick them for sensory cell bodies.
The lateral horn is not found in every segment; it appears in the thoracic and upper lumbar cord. Neither division arises from every segment.
questions.answerText: Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and cord segments S2 to S4

questions.q: Which phrase describes the overall role of the sympathetic division?
options: Producing cerebrospinal fluid
Fight or flight
Forming new memories
Rest and digest
questions.why: The sympathetic division is the fight-or-flight division. It takes over during exercise, excitement, emergency, and embarrassment, preparing the body for action by speeding the heart, opening the airways, dilating the pupils, and slowing digestion. Its effects spread through many organs at once.
notes: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced by the choroid plexuses in the ventricles of the brain. Pick it for the choroid plexus, not the ANS.
Correct. The sympathetic division prepares the body for fight or flight.
Forming new memories is a job of brain structures in the limbic system, such as the hippocampus. It is not an autonomic role.
Rest and digest is the role of the parasympathetic division, which conserves energy and runs digestion. Pick it for the parasympathetic division.
questions.answerText: Fight or flight

questions.q: Which phrase describes the overall role of the parasympathetic division?
options: Sensory relay to the cortex
Rest and digest
Voluntary movement
Fight or flight
questions.why: The parasympathetic division is the rest-and-digest division. It conserves energy and runs routine housekeeping such as digestion, defecation, and urination, while slowing the heart and constricting the pupils. It usually pulls each organ in the opposite direction from the sympathetic division.
notes: Relaying sensory signals to the cortex is a job of the thalamus in the diencephalon. It is not an autonomic role.
Correct. The parasympathetic division handles rest and digest.
Voluntary movement is controlled by the somatic motor system acting on skeletal muscle. Pick it for the somatic system.
Fight or flight is the role of the sympathetic division, which prepares the body for action. Pick it for the sympathetic division.
questions.answerText: Rest and digest

questions.q: What are the parasympathetic ganglia, located near or within the target organ, called?
options: Dorsal root ganglia
Prevertebral ganglia
Terminal ganglia
Sympathetic trunk ganglia
questions.why: The parasympathetic ganglia are called terminal ganglia because they sit at the end of the pathway, near or within the wall of the target organ. Those inside the organ wall are also called intramural ganglia. The four named terminal ganglia of the head are the ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular, and otic ganglia.
notes: Dorsal root ganglia hold sensory neuron cell bodies and are not autonomic. Pick them for sensory cell bodies.
Prevertebral ganglia are sympathetic ganglia in front of the vertebral column near the abdominal arteries. Pick them for the celiac or mesenteric ganglia.
Correct. Parasympathetic ganglia at the organ are terminal ganglia.
Sympathetic trunk ganglia form the chain beside the vertebral column. They are sympathetic, far from the organs.
questions.answerText: Terminal ganglia

questions.q: How far does each sympathetic trunk extend along the vertebral column?
options: Only along the cervical vertebrae
Only from T1 to L2, where the outflow leaves
From the base of the skull to the coccyx
From the brainstem to the S2 to S4 segments
questions.why: Each sympathetic trunk runs the whole length of the vertebral column, from the base of the skull to the coccyx. Preganglionic fibers enter it only from T1 to L2, but they can travel up or down the chain before synapsing, which is how sympathetic fibers reach the head and the lower limbs. That is why the trunk is much longer than the region of sympathetic outflow.
notes: The trunk does have ganglia in the neck, but it continues down the thoracic, lumbar, and sacral regions as well.
T1 to L2 is where sympathetic fibers enter the trunk, not the full length of the trunk. The chain continues above and below so it can serve the whole body.
Correct. The trunk runs from the base of the skull to the coccyx.
The brainstem and S2 to S4 are the origins of the parasympathetic division. They describe the craniosacral outflow, not the length of a sympathetic structure.
questions.answerText: From the base of the skull to the coccyx

questions.q: Which enteric plexus lies between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers of the gut wall?
options: The myenteric plexus
The celiac plexus
The submucosal plexus
The cardiac plexus
questions.why: The myenteric plexus lies in the muscularis externa, between the circular and longitudinal layers of smooth muscle in the gut wall. My- refers to muscle and enteric refers to the intestine, so the name describes a nerve network among the gut muscles. It mainly controls the movement of the gut.
notes: Correct. The myenteric plexus sits between the two muscle layers.
The celiac plexus surrounds the celiac trunk outside the gut and supplies most of the upper abdominal organs. It is not one of the enteric plexuses within the gut wall.
The submucosal plexus lies in the submucosa, closer to the lumen than the muscle layers, and mainly controls the secretions of the gut. Pick it for gut secretion.
The cardiac plexus is an autonomic plexus at the base of the heart. It is not in the gut wall.
questions.answerText: The myenteric plexus

questions.q: Which is the largest autonomic plexus, surrounding the celiac trunk?
options: The hypogastric plexus
The celiac plexus
The pulmonary plexus
The cardiac plexus
questions.why: The celiac plexus, also called the solar plexus, is the largest autonomic plexus. It surrounds the celiac trunk, the first large unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta, and supplies most of the upper abdominal organs. The celiac ganglia sit inside it, and many sympathetic fibers synapse there.
notes: The hypogastric plexus lies low in the abdominopelvic cavity and supplies the pelvic organs. Pick it for the bladder and rectum.
Correct. The celiac plexus is the largest and wraps the celiac trunk.
The pulmonary plexus lies at the root of each lung and supplies the bronchial tree. Pick it for the lungs.
The cardiac plexus lies at the base of the heart and supplies the heart. Pick it for the heart.
questions.answerText: The celiac plexus

questions.q: A patient's pupils dilate, heart speeds up, and digestion slows. Which division is dominant?
options: The somatic motor system
The sympathetic division
The enteric nervous system
The parasympathetic division
questions.why: Dilated pupils, a faster heart, and slowed digestion are classic effects of the sympathetic division. Together they prepare the body for action, the fight-or-flight response. The parasympathetic division would produce the opposite pattern: constricted pupils, a slower heart, and active digestion.
notes: The somatic motor system controls skeletal muscle, not the pupils, heart, or gut. Pick it for voluntary movement.
Correct. These are fight-or-flight effects of the sympathetic division.
The enteric nervous system runs the gut wall, and here digestion is slowing, not being driven. It also has no control over the pupils or heart.
The parasympathetic division constricts the pupils, slows the heart, and stimulates digestion, the opposite of this pattern. Pick it for a person resting after a meal.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: How does the somatic motor pathway differ from the autonomic motor pathway in the number of motor neurons?
options: Somatic uses one neuron; autonomic uses two
Both use a single neuron from the CNS to the effector
Both use two neurons with a ganglion in between
Somatic uses two neurons; autonomic uses one
questions.why: The somatic motor pathway uses one neuron that runs from the CNS straight to skeletal muscle. The autonomic pathway uses two, a preganglionic neuron from the CNS and a postganglionic neuron from a ganglion to the effector. The synapse in the ganglion is the feature the somatic system lacks.
notes: Correct. One neuron for somatic, two for autonomic.
A single neuron describes only the somatic system. The autonomic system always adds a second neuron after the ganglion.
Two neurons with a ganglion describes only the autonomic system. The somatic system has no ganglion on its motor path.
This reverses the two systems. The autonomic system is the one with a ganglion, so it is the one with two neurons.
questions.answerText: Somatic uses one neuron; autonomic uses two

questions.q: Somatic motor neurons always excite their effector. What effect can autonomic motor neurons have on their effectors?
options: Always excitation
It has no direct effect on the effector
Always inhibition
Either excitation or inhibition
questions.why: Somatic motor neurons always excite skeletal muscle, causing it to contract. Autonomic motor neurons can either excite or inhibit their effectors, depending on the division and the organ. For example, the sympathetic division speeds the heart but slows digestion, and the parasympathetic division does the reverse.
notes: Always excitation is true of the somatic system acting on skeletal muscle. Pick it for the somatic system.
Autonomic motor neurons act directly on cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands. That is the whole purpose of the visceral motor system.
If autonomic neurons only inhibited, nothing could speed the heart or stimulate digestion. Each division excites some organs and inhibits others.
Correct. Autonomic neurons can excite or inhibit.
questions.answerText: Either excitation or inhibition

questions.q: In the somatic motor system, where does the cell body of the single motor neuron to a limb muscle sit?
options: In the dorsal root ganglion
In the ventral gray horn
In the lateral gray horn
In an autonomic ganglion
questions.why: The somatic motor neuron to a limb muscle has its cell body in the ventral (anterior) gray horn of the spinal cord. Its axon leaves through the ventral root and runs, without any ganglion, all the way to the skeletal muscle. This single-neuron path is the main structural difference from the two-neuron autonomic pathway.
notes: The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies. Pick it for sensory neurons, not motor neurons.
Correct. Somatic motor neurons sit in the ventral gray horn.
The lateral gray horn holds sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies. Pick it for the first neuron of a sympathetic pathway.
An autonomic ganglion holds postganglionic cell bodies. The somatic pathway has no ganglion at all.
questions.answerText: In the ventral gray horn

questions.q: Where are the ganglia of the sympathetic division located?
options: Inside the brainstem
Inside the dorsal root ganglion
Close to the spinal cord
Close to or within the effector organ
questions.why: Sympathetic ganglia sit close to the spinal cord, either in the sympathetic trunk beside the vertebral column or in the prevertebral ganglia just in front of it. This placement gives the sympathetic division short preganglionic axons and long postganglionic axons. Parasympathetic ganglia, by contrast, sit close to or within the effector organ.
notes: The brainstem is part of the CNS, and ganglia by definition lie outside the CNS. The brainstem holds the parasympathetic preganglionic nuclei instead.
The dorsal root ganglion is a sensory ganglion on the dorsal root. Autonomic ganglia are separate structures.
Correct. Sympathetic ganglia lie close to the spinal cord.
Close to or within the effector organ describes the parasympathetic terminal ganglia. Pick it for the parasympathetic division.
questions.answerText: Close to the spinal cord

questions.q: Which group of sympathetic ganglia lies anterior to the vertebral column, near the large abdominal arteries?
options: The prevertebral ganglia
The terminal ganglia
The dorsal root ganglia
The sympathetic trunk ganglia
questions.why: The prevertebral ganglia, also called collateral ganglia, are sympathetic ganglia that lie anterior to the vertebral column near the large abdominal arteries. They include the celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, aorticorenal, and renal ganglia. Pre- means in front of, which describes their position relative to the vertebrae.
notes: Correct. The prevertebral ganglia sit in front of the vertebral column by the abdominal arteries.
Terminal ganglia are parasympathetic and sit near or within the target organ. Pick them for a ganglion at the organ.
Dorsal root ganglia hold sensory cell bodies on the dorsal roots. Pick them for sensory neurons.
The sympathetic trunk ganglia lie beside the vertebral column in a chain, not in front of it. Pick them for the paravertebral chain.
questions.answerText: The prevertebral ganglia

questions.q: Which enteric plexus controls the secretions of the gut?
options: The hypogastric plexus
The submucosal plexus
The cardiac plexus
The myenteric plexus
questions.why: The submucosal plexus lies in the submucosa, between the mucosa and the muscularis externa. Its place next to the mucosa, where the glands are, fits its job of mainly controlling the secretions of the gut. The myenteric plexus, farther out between the muscle layers, mainly controls movement instead.
notes: The hypogastric plexus is an autonomic plexus that supplies the pelvic organs. It sits outside the gut wall.
Correct. The submucosal plexus controls gut secretions.
The cardiac plexus supplies the heart and is not in the gut wall. Pick it for the heart.
The myenteric plexus lies between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers and controls gut movement. Pick it for movement of the gut.
questions.answerText: The submucosal plexus

questions.q: Which list traces, in order, a parasympathetic command from the brainstem to the heart?
options: Brainstem nucleus, vagus nerve, terminal ganglion near the heart, short postganglionic axon, heart
Brainstem nucleus, vagus nerve, sympathetic chain ganglion, long postganglionic axon, heart
Lateral horn of T1, preganglionic axon, terminal ganglion near the heart, short postganglionic axon, heart
Brainstem nucleus, phrenic nerve, terminal ganglion near the heart, short postganglionic axon, heart
questions.why: The parasympathetic supply to the heart starts in a brainstem nucleus of the vagus nerve (CN X). The long preganglionic axon travels in the vagus nerve, through the cardiac plexus, to a terminal ganglion near or in the heart, and a short postganglionic axon carries the signal the rest of the way. This follows the parasympathetic pattern of a long first axon and a short second one.
notes: Correct. Brainstem, vagus nerve, terminal ganglion, short postganglionic axon, heart.
Parasympathetic fibers do not synapse in the sympathetic chain, and a long postganglionic axon is a sympathetic feature. This list mixes the two divisions.
The lateral horn of T1 is a sympathetic origin, not a parasympathetic one. Parasympathetic fibers to the heart start in the brainstem.
The phrenic nerve comes from the cervical plexus and is the motor supply to the diaphragm. It carries no parasympathetic fibers to the heart.
questions.answerText: Brainstem nucleus, vagus nerve, terminal ganglion near the heart, short postganglionic axon, heart

questions.q: Which organs do the superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses supply?
options: The urinary bladder and uterus
The small and large intestine
The kidneys and the ureters
The heart and the bronchial tree
questions.why: The superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses supply the small and large intestine. They surround the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, which carry blood to the intestines, and their fibers follow those arteries. They sit just below the celiac plexus along the abdominal aorta.
notes: The urinary bladder and uterus are pelvic organs supplied by the hypogastric plexus. Pick them for the hypogastric plexus.
Correct. The mesenteric plexuses supply the intestines.
The kidneys and ureters are supplied by the renal plexus around the renal arteries. Pick them for the renal plexus.
The heart and bronchial tree are supplied by the cardiac and pulmonary plexuses in the thorax. Pick them for those plexuses.
questions.answerText: The small and large intestine

questions.q: A person's heart rate rises at the start of exercise, even before the sympathetic division speeds it up. Which change best explains the early rise?
options: The enteric system stimulates the heart
The sympathetic trunk is cut on both sides
Parasympathetic input is withdrawn
The somatic system contracts the heart
questions.why: At rest, parasympathetic input from the vagus nerve holds the heart at a slower rate. Because the two divisions pull in opposite directions, easing off this parasympathetic brake lets the heart rate rise even before the sympathetic division begins to speed it up. This shows how the body can adjust an organ by withdrawing one division, not only by pushing with the other.
notes: The enteric nervous system lives in the wall of the gut and does not supply the heart. Pick it for gut movement and secretion.
Cutting the sympathetic trunk would remove the input that speeds the heart, so it could not explain a rise. Pick it for a loss of sympathetic effects.
Correct. Withdrawing the parasympathetic brake lets the heart rate climb.
The somatic system controls skeletal muscle only; cardiac muscle is an autonomic effector. Pick the somatic system for the leg muscles used in exercise.
questions.answerText: Parasympathetic input is withdrawn

questions.q: A single cranial nerve slows the heart, constricts the airways, and drives digestion all at once. Which nerve, through its long reach, does this?
options: The accessory nerve (CN XI)
The phrenic nerve
The vagus nerve (CN X)
The trigeminal nerve (CN V)
questions.why: The vagus nerve, cranial nerve X, carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the organs of the chest and abdomen. It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and travels down through the neck and thorax into the abdomen, branching to the heart, lungs, and digestive tract. Its long reach is why one nerve can slow the heart, constrict the airways, and drive digestion at the same time.
notes: The accessory nerve (XI) leaves the skull beside the vagus but is a motor nerve to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Pick it for turning the head and shrugging.
The phrenic nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus, not a cranial nerve, and it is the motor supply to the diaphragm. It does not reach the heart or the gut.
Correct. The vagus nerve reaches the heart, lungs, and digestive tract.
The trigeminal nerve (V) carries facial sensation and serves the chewing muscles. It carries no parasympathetic fibers to the organs.
questions.answerText: The vagus nerve (CN X)

questions.q: A section of bowel keeps moving food along even after its connection to the CNS is cut. Which system explains this independence?
options: The enteric nervous system
The cervical plexus
The sympathetic division
The somatic nervous system
questions.why: The enteric nervous system is the network of neurons in the wall of the digestive tract, built around the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. It is independent enough to be called the brain of the gut: smooth muscle keeps contracting in rhythm and glands keep secreting even when the link to the CNS is cut. That is why a denervated bowel can still move food along.
notes: Correct. The enteric nervous system can run the gut on its own.
The cervical plexus serves the neck and diaphragm and has no role in the bowel. Pick it for the phrenic nerve.
The sympathetic division reaches the gut from the CNS through the trunk and splanchnic nerves. Cutting the CNS connection removes it, and it slows digestion rather than driving it.
The somatic nervous system controls skeletal muscle through nerves from the CNS. Cutting the link to the CNS would stop it, and the gut wall is mostly smooth muscle anyway.
questions.answerText: The enteric nervous system

questions.q: A cluster of neuron cell bodies sits within the wall of the urinary bladder, where parasympathetic fibers synapse. Which type of ganglion is it?
options: A dorsal root ganglion
A sympathetic trunk ganglion
A prevertebral ganglion
A terminal ganglion
questions.why: A ganglion in the wall of an organ where parasympathetic fibers synapse is a terminal ganglion, specifically an intramural one. The parasympathetic fibers to the bladder arrive in the pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4 and synapse right at the organ. Short postganglionic axons then reach the smooth muscle of the bladder wall.
notes: A dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies on the dorsal root, not autonomic synapses. Pick it for sensory neurons.
A sympathetic trunk ganglion lies beside the vertebral column, far from the bladder. Pick it for the paravertebral chain.
A prevertebral ganglion is a sympathetic ganglion in front of the vertebral column near the abdominal arteries. Pick it for the celiac or mesenteric ganglia.
Correct. A parasympathetic ganglion in the organ wall is a terminal (intramural) ganglion.
questions.answerText: A terminal ganglion

questions.q: After a large meal, a resting person has constricted pupils, a slow heart rate, and active digestion. Which division is dominant?
options: The sympathetic division
The somatic motor system
The parasympathetic division
The enteric nervous system
questions.why: Constricted pupils, a slower heart, and stimulated digestion are effects of the parasympathetic division, the rest-and-digest division. After a meal at rest, the body conserves energy and focuses on housekeeping such as digestion. The sympathetic division would produce the opposite pattern.
notes: The sympathetic division would dilate the pupils, speed the heart, and slow digestion. Pick it for a person under stress.
The somatic motor system controls skeletal muscle and has no say over the pupils, heart, or gut. Pick it for voluntary movement.
Correct. These are rest-and-digest effects of the parasympathetic division.
The enteric nervous system helps run digestion inside the gut wall, but it cannot constrict the pupils or slow the heart. Only one of the three signs fits it.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how the autonomic nervous system controls the organs?
options: It works only during sleep and shuts off when we are awake
It works voluntarily, so we decide how fast the heart beats
It works by sending signals straight from the brain to skeletal muscle
It works involuntarily, adjusting the organs without conscious effort
questions.why: The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary motor division. It adjusts cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands without conscious effort or awareness, so vital work such as the heartbeat and digestion continues while we sleep or focus on other things. Emotion and pain can influence it, but most of its activity cannot be consciously changed.
notes: The ANS works around the clock, awake or asleep. The heart and gut never stop needing control.
Voluntary control describes the somatic system acting on skeletal muscle. We cannot simply decide how fast the heart beats.
Signals straight to skeletal muscle with one neuron describe the somatic motor system. The ANS uses two neurons and targets cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands.
Correct. The ANS controls the organs involuntarily.
questions.answerText: It works involuntarily, adjusting the organs without conscious effort

questions.q: After a stressful event ends, which part of the nervous system brings the heart rate back down and restarts digestion?
options: The parasympathetic division
The sympathetic division
The adrenal medulla
The somatic motor system
questions.why: The parasympathetic division restores resting conditions after activity. It slows the heart, constricts the pupils, and stimulates digestion, conserving energy for routine housekeeping. Because it pulls the organs in the opposite direction from the sympathetic division, it gives the body a way back from fight or flight.
notes: Correct. The parasympathetic division restores rest and digest.
The sympathetic division is what sped the heart and slowed digestion in the first place. Pick it for the stress response itself.
The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion whose hormones extend the fight-or-flight response. It prolongs the stress effects rather than ending them.
The somatic motor system controls skeletal muscle and has no control over the heart rate or the gut.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: Many organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers that push them in opposite directions. What does this dual supply allow?
options: Two-way adjustment, speeding up or slowing down the organ as needed
Twice the force in one direction, since both divisions excite the organ
A backup, since the second division takes over only if the first is cut
Voluntary control, since one division is always under conscious command
questions.why: With two divisions pulling in opposite directions, an organ can be turned up or down. The sympathetic division speeds the heart while the parasympathetic division slows it, and the balance between them sets the rate. The body can also adjust an organ by easing off one division rather than only by pushing with the other.
notes: Correct. Opposing inputs let the body adjust an organ in either direction.
The two divisions usually have opposite effects on the same organ, not the same effect. Treating them as partners pushing one way is a common misconception.
Both divisions are active at the same time, and their balance sets the organ's activity. Neither one is a spare waiting for the other to fail.
Both divisions are involuntary. Neither is under conscious command; voluntary control belongs to the somatic system.
questions.answerText: Two-way adjustment, speeding up or slowing down the organ as needed

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares where the two autonomic divisions leave the central nervous system?
options: Sympathetic from the middle of the cord; parasympathetic from the two ends
Sympathetic from the two ends; parasympathetic from the middle of the cord
Both divisions leave only through cranial nerves of the brainstem
Both divisions leave from every segment of the cord, from C1 to S5
questions.why: The sympathetic division leaves from the middle of the spinal cord, T1 to L2, which is why it is called thoracolumbar. The parasympathetic division leaves from the two ends of the CNS, the brainstem (through cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X) and the sacral cord at S2 to S4, which is why it is called craniosacral. The two other names are a map of where each division begins.
notes: Correct. Sympathetic from T1 to L2; parasympathetic from the brainstem and S2 to S4.
This swaps the two divisions. The middle of the cord (T1 to L2) is sympathetic, and the ends are parasympathetic.
Only part of the parasympathetic division leaves through cranial nerves. The sympathetic division uses spinal nerves T1 to L2, and the sacral parasympathetic fibers leave from S2 to S4.
Neither division leaves from every segment. The cervical, lower lumbar, and coccygeal segments send out no autonomic fibers.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic from the middle of the cord; parasympathetic from the two ends

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the somatic and autonomic nervous systems by what each one controls?
options: Somatic runs smooth and cardiac muscle; autonomic runs skeletal muscle and glands
Somatic runs skeletal muscle; autonomic runs smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands
Somatic carries only sensory input; autonomic carries only motor output to organs
Somatic runs skeletal muscle and glands; autonomic runs only cardiac and smooth muscle
questions.why: The somatic and autonomic systems are both motor divisions of the PNS, and they are told apart by the effector they control. The somatic system is voluntary and sends commands to skeletal muscle. The autonomic system is involuntary and sends commands to the visceral effectors: smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. The autonomic system also uses two motor neurons in a row with a ganglion between them, while the somatic system reaches its muscle with one.
notes: This statement swaps the two systems. Skeletal muscle is the voluntary muscle the somatic system controls, while smooth and cardiac muscle are involuntary and belong to the autonomic system.
Correct. Skeletal muscle is the somatic effector, and smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands are the autonomic effectors.

Both systems are motor systems that carry commands out from the CNS, so neither is purely sensory. This mix-up comes from confusing the sensory and motor sides of the PNS with the somatic and autonomic split.
Glands are autonomic effectors, not somatic ones. The somatic system controls only skeletal muscle, and the autonomic system controls glands along with cardiac and smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: Somatic runs skeletal muscle; autonomic runs smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands

questions.q: A fire alarm startles a student. Her heart races, her pupils dilate, and her airways open. Which division of the nervous system is driving these changes?
options: The parasympathetic division
The sympathetic division
The somatic nervous system
The enteric nervous system
questions.why: A racing heart, dilated pupils, and open airways are fight or flight effects, the job of the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system. It takes over during exercise, excitement, and emergencies. Its preganglionic fibers leave the spinal cord from T1 to L2, which is why it is also called the thoracolumbar division.
notes: The parasympathetic division is the rest and digest division, and it does the opposite here: it constricts the pupils, slows the heart, and narrows the airways. Pick it if the student were relaxing after a meal.
Correct. These are classic fight or flight effects of the sympathetic division.

The somatic nervous system controls skeletal muscle, which we move by choice. It would be the answer if the question asked what lets the student run for the exit, but heart rate, pupil size, and airway diameter are involuntary.
The enteric nervous system is the network of neurons in the wall of the GI tract that runs gut movement and secretion. It fits a question about the brain of the gut, not heart rate or pupils.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: How many motor neurons are in an autonomic motor pathway, and where do they meet?
options: Two neurons, which synapse in an autonomic ganglion
Three neurons, which synapse in two separate ganglia
Two neurons, which synapse in the posterior root ganglion
One neuron, running straight from the CNS to the organ
questions.why: Every autonomic motor pathway uses two neurons in a row. The preganglionic neuron has its cell body in the brain or spinal cord and sends its axon out to an autonomic ganglion. There it synapses with the postganglionic neuron, whose cell body sits in the ganglion and whose axon runs on to the effector. The somatic system, by contrast, reaches skeletal muscle with a single motor neuron.
notes: Correct. Two neurons meet at a synapse in an autonomic ganglion.
An autonomic motor pathway has exactly two motor neurons and one ganglion between them. This choice adds an extra neuron and an extra ganglion that the pathway does not have.

The posterior root ganglion holds sensory neuron cell bodies, and no synapse happens there. Autonomic neurons synapse in autonomic ganglia, such as the sympathetic trunk ganglia or the terminal ganglia near organs.
One motor neuron running straight from the CNS to its target describes the somatic system, which controls skeletal muscle. Pick this if the question asked about a somatic motor pathway.
questions.answerText: Two neurons, which synapse in an autonomic ganglion

questions.q: What are the two divisions of the autonomic nervous system?
options: Sympathetic and parasympathetic
Central and peripheral nervous systems
Somatic and enteric nervous systems
Afferent and efferent divisions
questions.why: The autonomic nervous system has two divisions that usually act in opposite directions on the same organ. The sympathetic division prepares the body for action (fight or flight), and the parasympathetic division conserves energy and runs routine housekeeping (rest and digest). Because they pull against each other, the body can fine-tune an organ by easing off one division as well as by pushing the other.
notes: Correct. The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions make up the ANS.

The central and peripheral nervous systems are the two main divisions of the whole nervous system. Pick them if the question asked about the top-level split into brain and cord versus everything else.
The somatic system is the voluntary motor division that runs skeletal muscle, and the enteric system is the network in the gut wall. Both sit beside the ANS rather than inside it.
Afferent and efferent describe direction, toward or away from the CNS. They would be the answer if the question asked how the PNS is split into sensory and motor sides.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic and parasympathetic

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the general roles of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions?
options: Sympathetic prepares for fight or flight; parasympathetic supports rest and digest
Sympathetic supports rest and digest; parasympathetic prepares for fight or flight
Both prepare the body for action, but sympathetic acts only on the heart
Sympathetic controls skeletal muscle; parasympathetic controls smooth muscle and glands
questions.why: The sympathetic division takes over during exercise, excitement, and emergencies: it dilates the pupils, speeds the heart, opens the airways, and slows digestion. The parasympathetic division conserves energy and runs routine housekeeping such as digestion, defecation, and urination: it constricts the pupils, slows the heart, and stimulates digestion. The two usually act on the same organs in opposite directions.
notes: Correct. Sympathetic is fight or flight, and parasympathetic is rest and digest.
This swaps the two divisions. The sympathetic division is fight or flight, and the parasympathetic division is rest and digest.
Only the sympathetic division prepares the body for action, and it acts on many organs, not just the heart. The parasympathetic division does the opposite, conserving energy.
Neither autonomic division controls skeletal muscle; that is the job of the somatic system. Both autonomic divisions act on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic prepares for fight or flight; parasympathetic supports rest and digest

questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces an autonomic motor command from the CNS to the organ it controls?
options: Preganglionic neuron, posterior root ganglion, motor neuron, effector
Postganglionic neuron, autonomic ganglion, preganglionic neuron, effector
Preganglionic neuron, autonomic ganglion, postganglionic neuron, effector
Anterior horn motor neuron, straight to the skeletal muscle effector
questions.why: The preganglionic neuron has its cell body in the brain or spinal cord, and its lightly myelinated axon runs out to an autonomic ganglion. In the ganglion it synapses with the postganglionic neuron, whose unmyelinated axon carries the signal the rest of the way. The command ends at the effector tissue: cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, or a gland. Pre means before and post means after, so the names tell you which side of the ganglion each neuron is on.
notes: The posterior root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies and is not part of an autonomic motor pathway. The autonomic synapse happens in an autonomic ganglion.
This swaps the two neurons. The preganglionic neuron comes first, before the ganglion, and the postganglionic neuron comes after it.
Correct. Preganglionic neuron, ganglion, postganglionic neuron, then the effector.
A single anterior horn motor neuron running straight to skeletal muscle is the somatic motor pathway. Pick this if the question asked how a command reaches a skeletal muscle.
questions.answerText: Preganglionic neuron, autonomic ganglion, postganglionic neuron, effector

questions.q: Where are the ganglia of the parasympathetic division located?
options: Near or within the wall of the target organ
Anterior to the vertebral column near the aorta
In a chain beside the vertebral column
On the posterior roots just outside the cord
questions.why: Parasympathetic ganglia are called terminal ganglia because they sit at the end of the line, near or within the wall of the organ they control. As a result, the parasympathetic preganglionic axon is long and the postganglionic axon is short. Four named terminal ganglia are found in the head: the ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular, and otic ganglia.
notes: Correct. Parasympathetic ganglia sit near or within the target organ.

Ganglia in front of the vertebral column near the large abdominal arteries are the sympathetic prevertebral ganglia, such as the celiac ganglion. They would be the answer for a question about collateral ganglia.
The chain of ganglia beside the vertebral column is the sympathetic trunk. Pick it if the question asked where sympathetic trunk (paravertebral) ganglia sit.
The swellings on the posterior roots are the posterior root ganglia, which hold sensory cell bodies and are not autonomic. Choose them for a question about where sensory neuron cell bodies sit.
questions.answerText: Near or within the wall of the target organ

questions.q: Where do the preganglionic neurons of each autonomic division arise in the CNS?
options: Sympathetic: C1 to C4; parasympathetic: L1 to L4 and sacrum
Both divisions: the lateral horns from T1 to L2 only
Sympathetic: brainstem and S2 to S4; parasympathetic: T1 to L2
Sympathetic: T1 to L2; parasympathetic: brainstem and S2 to S4
questions.why: The two divisions are first told apart by where their fibers leave the CNS. Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral gray horns of the T1 to L2 cord segments, which is why it is called the thoracolumbar division. Parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in the nuclei of four cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, and X) in the brainstem and in the S2 to S4 segments, which is why it is called the craniosacral division.
notes: C1 to C4 and L1 to L4 are the levels that form the cervical and lumbar nerve plexuses, not autonomic origins. This mix-up confuses plexus levels with autonomic outflow.
Only the sympathetic division arises from the lateral horns of T1 to L2. The parasympathetic division arises from the brainstem and the sacral cord, at the two ends of the CNS.
This swaps the two divisions. The thoracolumbar (T1 to L2) origin belongs to the sympathetic division, and the craniosacral origin belongs to the parasympathetic division.
Correct. Sympathetic is thoracolumbar, and parasympathetic is craniosacral.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic: T1 to L2; parasympathetic: brainstem and S2 to S4

questions.q: A chain of autonomic ganglia runs down each side of the vertebral column from the base of the skull to the coccyx. Which division do these ganglia belong to?
options: Somatic nervous system
Enteric nervous system
Sympathetic division
Parasympathetic division
questions.why: This chain is the sympathetic trunk, and its ganglia are also called paravertebral ganglia, meaning beside the vertebrae. Sympathetic ganglia sit close to the spinal cord, either in this chain or in the prevertebral ganglia just in front of the vertebral column. Parasympathetic ganglia, by contrast, sit near or within the target organ.
notes: The somatic nervous system has no ganglia in its motor pathway, because a single motor neuron runs straight from the cord to skeletal muscle. This choice confuses autonomic ganglia with the somatic pathway.
The enteric nervous system is made of networks within the wall of the GI tract, such as the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. It would be the answer for a question about the neurons in the gut wall.
Correct. The chain beside the vertebral column is the sympathetic trunk.

Parasympathetic ganglia are terminal ganglia located near or within the wall of the target organ, not in a chain beside the spine. Pick parasympathetic if the ganglion sat in the wall of the bladder or near the eye.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic division

questions.q: A tumor destroys neuron cell bodies in the lateral gray matter of the T5 segment of the spinal cord. Which autonomic neuron is lost, and where would its axon have ended?
options: The preganglionic neuron, whose axon ended in a ganglion
The preganglionic neuron, whose axon ended on the effector
A somatic motor neuron, whose axon ended on skeletal muscle
The postganglionic neuron, whose axon ended on the effector
questions.why: The autonomic system uses two motor neurons in a row. The preganglionic neuron has its cell body in the CNS, in a brainstem nucleus or the lateral gray matter of the spinal cord, and its axon ends in an autonomic ganglion. There it synapses with the postganglionic neuron, whose axon carries the signal to the effector.
notes: Correct. Preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral gray matter, and their axons end in an autonomic ganglion.
The neuron is right, but a preganglionic axon ends in an autonomic ganglion. The second neuron carries the signal on to the effector.
Somatic motor cell bodies sit in the anterior horn of the cord, not the lateral gray matter. The lateral gray matter holds autonomic preganglionic neurons.
Postganglionic cell bodies sit in an autonomic ganglion outside the CNS, not in the lateral gray matter of the cord.
questions.answerText: The preganglionic neuron, whose axon ended in a ganglion

questions.q: You are told that a ganglion contains synapses between neurons. Is it an autonomic ganglion or a posterior root ganglion, and whose cell bodies does it hold?
options: A posterior root ganglion, holding postganglionic cell bodies
An autonomic ganglion, holding preganglionic cell bodies
A posterior root ganglion, holding sensory cell bodies
An autonomic ganglion, holding postganglionic motor cell bodies
questions.why: Two kinds of ganglia are easy to mix up. A posterior root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies and has no synapses. An autonomic ganglion holds motor cell bodies, the postganglionic neurons, and it is where the preganglionic axon synapses with them.
notes: Postganglionic cell bodies sit in autonomic ganglia. A posterior root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies and has no synapses.
The ganglion type is right, but preganglionic cell bodies are in the CNS. Only their axons reach the ganglion.
A posterior root ganglion does hold sensory cell bodies, but it has no synapses. A ganglion with synapses is autonomic.
Correct. Synapses happen in autonomic ganglia, where preganglionic axons meet the cell bodies of postganglionic motor neurons.
questions.answerText: An autonomic ganglion, holding postganglionic motor cell bodies

questions.q: An unmyelinated axon is traced to the smooth muscle of a blood vessel, and its cell body sits in a ganglion. If you follow the pathway back one neuron, what do you reach, and where is that neuron's cell body?
options: A second postganglionic neuron, from a cell body in another ganglion
A preganglionic axon, from a cell body in the brainstem or cord
A sensory neuron, from a cell body in a posterior root ganglion
A myelinated somatic axon, from a cell body in the anterior horn
questions.why: An unmyelinated axon from a ganglion cell body to smooth muscle is a postganglionic axon. It received its signal in the ganglion from a preganglionic axon, which is thin and lightly myelinated. The preganglionic cell body sits in the CNS, in a brainstem nucleus or the lateral gray matter of the spinal cord.
notes: The autonomic pathway uses exactly two motor neurons. The neuron before the postganglionic one is preganglionic, with its cell body in the CNS.
Correct. The unmyelinated axon is postganglionic, so one step back is the lightly myelinated preganglionic neuron whose cell body is in the CNS.
Posterior root ganglia hold sensory cell bodies and have no synapses. The motor command reaching this ganglion comes from a preganglionic neuron.
Somatic motor neurons run straight to skeletal muscle with no ganglion. They do not feed an autonomic ganglion.
questions.answerText: A preganglionic axon, from a cell body in the brainstem or cord

questions.q: Which of these ions is present at a much higher concentration inside a cell than in the extracellular fluid?
options: K+
Cl-
Ca2+
Na+
questions.why: Intracellular K+ runs about 140 mEq/L against roughly 4 mEq/L outside, a gradient the Na+/K+ ATPase rebuilds continuously. Na+ is the mirror image, about 145 mEq/L outside and 15 mEq/L inside. Cl- is also higher outside, near 105 mEq/L against about 10 mEq/L inside. Ca2+ shows the steepest gradient of all, but it points inward: free Ca2+ inside a resting cell is only about 0.0001 mM.
questions.answerText: K+

questions.q: What is the typical extracellular sodium concentration in a healthy adult?
options: 45 mEq/L
145 mEq/L
290 mEq/L
15 mEq/L
questions.why: Plasma Na+ is held near 145 mEq/L, and it is the dominant extracellular cation. The value of 15 mEq/L is the intracellular Na+ concentration, which is the other half of the gradient. 45 mEq/L does not correspond to either compartment. 290 is the number to remember for plasma osmolarity in mOsm/L, a total particle count rather than a sodium concentration.
questions.answerText: 145 mEq/L

questions.q: What is the typical intracellular potassium concentration?
options: 14 mEq/L
40 mEq/L
140 mEq/L
4 mEq/L
questions.why: Cells hold roughly 140 mEq/L of K+, which makes K+ the dominant intracellular cation. 4 mEq/L is the extracellular value, so picking it flips the gradient. 14 and 40 mEq/L do not match either compartment; 14 is close to intracellular Na+, which is a different ion entirely.
questions.answerText: 140 mEq/L

questions.q: What is the typical extracellular potassium concentration in plasma?
options: 10 mEq/L
24 mEq/L
1 mEq/L
4 mEq/L
questions.why: Plasma K+ sits in a narrow band around 4 mEq/L, roughly 3.5 to 5.0, which is why small absolute changes matter so much for excitable tissue. 1 mEq/L would be a severe deficit incompatible with normal function. 10 mEq/L is dangerous hyperkalemia rather than a normal value. 24 mEq/L is close to the plasma bicarbonate figure, a different solute.
questions.answerText: 4 mEq/L

questions.q: What is the approximate free calcium concentration inside a resting cell?
options: 1 mM
10 mM
questions.why: Free cytosolic Ca2+ is held near 0.0001 mM, which is 100 nM, by pumps in the plasma membrane and the sarcoplasmic or endoplasmic reticulum. About 1 mM is the free extracellular value, so choosing it reverses the gradient. 0.01 mM would still be a hundredfold too high for a resting cell and would trigger contraction or secretion. 10 mM exceeds even extracellular calcium.

questions.q: How is chloride distributed across the membrane of a typical cell?
options: Roughly equal on both sides at about 50 mEq/L
Higher outside, about 105 mEq/L out and 10 mEq/L in
Higher inside, about 105 mEq/L in and 10 mEq/L out
Higher outside, about 20 mEq/L out and 2 mEq/L in
questions.why: Cl- follows Na+ in the extracellular fluid, so it is concentrated outside at roughly 105 mEq/L against about 10 mEq/L inside. Reversing that puts the anion where the negatively charged proteins already are, which the membrane potential actively prevents. The 20 and 2 mEq/L pair has the right direction but the wrong magnitude for plasma. Equal concentrations would give Cl- an equilibrium potential of 0 mV, which is not what cells show.
questions.answerText: Higher outside, about 105 mEq/L out and 10 mEq/L in

questions.q: The chemical component of the driving force on an ion is set by what?
options: The number of open channels available for that ion
The valence, or electrical charge, of the ion
The difference in that ion's concentration across the membrane
The membrane potential across the lipid bilayer
questions.why: The chemical, or concentration, component is pure diffusion: the ion is pushed from where it is crowded toward where it is not. The membrane potential is the electrical component, the other half of the pair you are asked to separate. The number of open channels sets how fast the ion actually moves, not how hard it is pushed. Valence enters the electrical component, since it determines how the potential pulls on the ion.
questions.answerText: The difference in that ion's concentration across the membrane

questions.q: The electrical component of the driving force on an ion depends on the membrane potential and what property of the ion?
options: Its extracellular concentration
Its diffusion coefficient
Its hydrated radius
Its charge
questions.why: An electrical field pushes on charge, so the sign and size of the ion's valence decide which way and how strongly the membrane potential moves it. A negative interior pulls cations in and pushes anions out. Hydrated radius and diffusion coefficient affect how easily the ion passes a channel, not the force the voltage exerts. Extracellular concentration belongs to the chemical component.
questions.answerText: Its charge

questions.q: A neuron sits at a resting membrane potential of -70 mV. Which way do the chemical and the electrical forces push Na+?
options: Chemical inward, electrical inward
Chemical inward, electrical outward
Chemical outward, electrical inward
Chemical outward, electrical outward
questions.why: Na+ is about ten times more concentrated outside, so diffusion pushes it in, and the negative interior attracts the positive ion, so the electrical force pushes it in as well. That is why Na+ has the largest net driving force of any ion at rest and why opening Na+ channels depolarizes so sharply. The options that put a force outward describe K+ or Cl- instead, whose two components oppose each other at rest.
questions.answerText: Chemical inward, electrical inward

questions.q: At a resting membrane potential of -70 mV, which way does the electrical force alone push K+?
options: Into the cell, because K+ is concentrated outside
Into the cell, because the interior is negative
Out of the cell, because K+ is concentrated inside
Out of the cell, because the interior is negative
questions.why: The electrical force is about voltage and charge only: a negative interior attracts the positive K+ ion inward. The option saying K+ leaves because it is concentrated inside states the chemical force correctly but answers the wrong half of the question, and that is exactly the confusion this card is testing. A negative interior cannot push a cation out. K+ is not concentrated outside, so that reasoning fails on the facts.
questions.answerText: Into the cell, because the interior is negative

questions.q: At a resting membrane potential of -70 mV, which way does the electrical force push Cl-?
options: Out of the cell, because Cl- is more concentrated inside
Into the cell, because the interior is negative
Out of the cell, because the negative interior repels a negative ion
Into the cell, because Cl- is more concentrated outside
questions.why: Cl- carries a negative charge, so the negative interior repels it and the electrical force points outward. A negative interior attracts cations and repels anions, which is why the same voltage moves Na+ and Cl- in opposite directions. The two options built on concentration describe the chemical component, not the electrical one, and one of them also states the gradient backwards.
questions.answerText: Out of the cell, because the negative interior repels a negative ion

questions.q: Which way does the chemical gradient push Cl- in a typical cell, and why?
options: Out of the cell, because intracellular Cl- is about ten times extracellular Cl-
Into the cell, because the interior is electrically negative
Out of the cell, because the interior is electrically negative
Into the cell, because extracellular Cl- is about ten times intracellular Cl-
questions.why: Chloride sits near 105 mEq/L outside and 10 mEq/L inside, so diffusion drives it inward. The option reversing those numbers has the gradient backwards. The two options that appeal to the negative interior are describing the electrical force, which for Cl- actually points outward and partly cancels the chemical push. Separating those two components is the whole point of this competency.
questions.answerText: Into the cell, because extracellular Cl- is about ten times intracellular Cl-

questions.q: At rest, what is the net electrochemical driving force on Ca2+?
options: Strongly inward, because the concentration gradient and the negative interior both favor entry
Strongly outward, because free intracellular Ca2+ is far above extracellular Ca2+
Near zero, because the chemical and electrical forces cancel each other exactly
Inward electrically but outward chemically, giving a small net force
questions.why: Extracellular Ca2+ is about ten thousand times the free cytosolic level, and the doubly positive ion is also pulled in by the negative interior, so both components point the same way. That enormous inward force is why opening a few Ca2+ channels can raise cytosolic Ca2+ fast enough to trigger contraction or secretion. Intracellular Ca2+ is very low, not high, so the outward option fails on the facts. Because the forces add rather than oppose, the net force is not near zero.
questions.answerText: Strongly inward, because the concentration gradient and the negative interior both favor entry

questions.q: The Na+/K+ ATPase is inhibited and intracellular Na+ climbs from 15 to 30 mEq/L while extracellular Na+ stays at 145. What happens to the inward chemical driving force on Na+?
options: It increases, because there is more Na+ in the cell
It decreases, because the concentration gradient is less steep
It is unchanged, because extracellular Na+ did not change
It reverses, so the chemical force now pushes Na+ out
questions.why: The chemical force depends on the ratio across the membrane, and that ratio falls from roughly 10 to roughly 5, so the inward push weakens. More Na+ inside works against entry, not for it. The gradient is a comparison of two compartments, so a change on either side changes it. The force would only reverse if intracellular Na+ rose above 145 mEq/L, which pump failure alone does not accomplish.
questions.answerText: It decreases, because the concentration gradient is less steep

questions.q: Extracellular K+ is raised from 4 to 10 mEq/L while intracellular K+ stays at 140. What happens to the outward chemical driving force on K+?
options: It is unaffected, because intracellular K+ did not change
It reverses, so the chemical force now pushes K+ inward
It gets smaller, because the gradient is less steep
It gets larger, because there is more K+ in the system
questions.why: The outward push on K+ comes from the ratio of inside to outside, which falls from about 35 to about 14, so the chemical force weakens even though it still points outward. It would only reverse if extracellular K+ exceeded 140 mEq/L. Total K+ in the system is not what matters; the difference between the two compartments is. And because the gradient is a ratio, raising the outside value changes it even with the inside held fixed.
questions.answerText: It gets smaller, because the gradient is less steep

questions.q: A neuron with an equilibrium potential for K+ of -90 mV is voltage clamped from -70 mV to 0 mV. What happens to the net driving force on K+?
options: It reverses, so K+ now moves into the cell
It is unchanged, because the K+ concentrations did not change
It falls to zero, because there is no longer any voltage across the membrane
It increases, because the negative interior that had opposed K+ exit is gone
questions.why: Net driving force is the distance between the membrane potential and the ion's equilibrium potential. At -70 mV that distance is 20 mV; at 0 mV it is 90 mV, so the outward push on K+ more than quadruples. The chemical gradient never went away, so removing the opposing electrical force unmasks it rather than canceling it. K+ would only move inward if the membrane potential were driven below -90 mV.
questions.answerText: It increases, because the negative interior that had opposed K+ exit is gone

questions.q: A cell is voltage clamped to +61 mV, which is exactly its equilibrium potential for Na+. Voltage gated Na+ channels are then opened. What happens?
options: There is almost no net Na+ movement, because the driving force is near zero
Na+ leaves rapidly, because the interior is now positive
Na+ entry continues normally, because movement depends only on the concentration gradient
Na+ enters rapidly, because the channels are open
questions.why: At the equilibrium potential the electrical force exactly balances the concentration gradient, so open channels carry ions both ways with no net flux. Open channels provide a path; they do not provide a push. Net efflux would require clamping above +61 mV, where the electrical force finally exceeds the chemical one. And ion movement never depends on the concentration gradient alone, which is why the electrochemical driving force is the quantity we track.
questions.answerText: There is almost no net Na+ movement, because the driving force is near zero

questions.q: Extracellular Cl- is lowered from 110 to 11 mEq/L while intracellular Cl- stays at 11 mEq/L. A cell resting at -70 mV then opens its Cl- channels. Predict what happens to the membrane potential.
options: It hyperpolarizes, because Cl- entry always adds negative charge
It depolarizes, because Cl- now leaves the cell
Nothing changes, because Cl- cannot move without a concentration gradient
It depolarizes, because Cl- now enters the cell faster
questions.why: With equal Cl- on both sides the chemical force is gone, so only the electrical force acts, and a -70 mV interior pushes the negative ion out. Losing negative charge makes the interior less negative, so the cell depolarizes toward 0 mV, which is the new equilibrium potential for Cl-. Cl- entry hyperpolarizes only when the extracellular concentration is high, which is the normal condition this experiment removed. Cl- moves readily here because the electrical force alone is enough.
questions.answerText: It depolarizes, because Cl- now leaves the cell

questions.q: During a brief influx, free intracellular Ca2+ rises tenfold from 0.0001 mM to 0.001 mM while extracellular Ca2+ stays near 1 mM. What happens to the inward driving force on Ca2+?
options: It increases, because more Ca2+ is now available to move
It disappears, because intracellular Ca2+ has risen ten times
It falls only slightly, because the gradient is still about a thousandfold
It reverses, so Ca2+ now leaves through the same channels
questions.why: A tenfold rise sounds dramatic, but it takes the gradient from ten thousandfold to one thousandfold, and the negative interior still pulls Ca2+ in, so the force remains large. That is precisely why Ca2+ works so well as a signal: the cell can raise cytosolic Ca2+ enough to change protein behavior without meaningfully spending the gradient. Reversal would require intracellular Ca2+ to exceed the extracellular level. Having more Ca2+ inside opposes further entry rather than promoting it.
questions.answerText: It falls only slightly, because the gradient is still about a thousandfold

questions.q: What does the Nernst equation calculate for a single ion?
options: The membrane potential that the cell will actually rest at with all ions present
The rate at which that ion crosses the membrane through open channels
The concentration the ion will reach inside the cell at steady state
The membrane potential at which the electrical force balances that ion's concentration gradient
questions.why: The Nernst equation answers one question: what voltage would hold this ion still despite its concentration gradient. That voltage is the equilibrium potential. The potential a cell actually rests at depends on several ions weighted by permeability, which is the Goldman equation instead. Nernst says nothing about flux rate, since that depends on open channels, and it does not predict a final concentration, because it assumes the concentrations you feed it.
questions.answerText: The membrane potential at which the electrical force balances that ion's concentration gradient

questions.q: The equilibrium potential for Na+ is about +60 mV. What does the positive sign tell you?
options: Na+ is more concentrated inside the cell than outside
The inside of the cell would have to be positive to stop Na+ from moving in, so at rest Na+ tends to enter
Na+ leaves the cell whenever its channels open
The resting membrane potential of a neuron is positive
questions.why: Na+ is crowded outside the cell, so its concentration gradient pushes it inward. The only thing that could hold it still is a positive interior repelling it, which is why E_Na is positive. At a resting potential of about -70 mV the inside is nowhere near positive, so Na+ tends to enter whenever its channels open. Na+ is concentrated outside, not inside, the resting potential is negative, and Na+ moves in, not out, when its channels open at rest.
questions.answerText: The inside of the cell would have to be positive to stop Na+ from moving in, so at rest Na+ tends to enter

questions.q: The equilibrium potential for K+ is about -90 mV. What does the negative sign tell you?
options: The inside of the cell would have to be negative to hold K+ in, so at any potential above -90 mV K+ tends to leave
K+ is more concentrated outside the cell than inside
K+ enters the cell whenever its channels open
The membrane is not permeable to K+
questions.why: K+ is crowded inside the cell, so its gradient pushes it outward. A negative interior pulls back on the positive K+ ions, and at about -90 mV that pull exactly balances the push. At the resting potential of about -70 mV the inside is not negative enough to hold K+ in, so K+ leaks out. K+ is concentrated inside, it leaves rather than enters at rest, and the sign says nothing about permeability; the resting membrane is actually quite permeable to K+.
questions.answerText: The inside of the cell would have to be negative to hold K+ in, so at any potential above -90 mV K+ tends to leave

questions.q: Which two things set the sign and size of an ion's equilibrium potential?
options: How many channels for that ion are open and how fast they open
The activity of the Na+/K+ pump and the amount of ATP available
The ion's concentration gradient across the membrane and the ion's charge
The cell's resting membrane potential and its size
questions.why: An equilibrium potential depends only on how unevenly the ion is spread across the membrane and on the charge it carries. The direction of the gradient and the sign of the charge set the sign, and the steepness of the gradient sets the size. The number of open channels changes how much the ion affects the membrane potential, not where its own balance point sits. The pump builds the gradients over time but does not appear in the equilibrium potential itself, and the resting potential is a result of the equilibrium potentials, not an input to them.
questions.answerText: The ion's concentration gradient across the membrane and the ion's charge

questions.q: What is the approximate equilibrium potential for Na+ in a typical neuron?
options: -90 mV
-60 mV
+60 mV
questions.why: With about 145 mEq/L outside and 15 mEq/L inside, the roughly tenfold gradient gives an equilibrium potential near +60 mV, and the positive sign says the interior would have to be positive to hold Na+ still. About -90 mV is the value for K+, whose gradient runs the other way. Around +120 mV belongs to Ca2+, whose gradient is far steeper. A value of -60 mV would require Na+ to be concentrated inside.
questions.answerText: +60 mV

questions.q: What is the approximate equilibrium potential for K+ in a typical neuron?
options: -90 mV
-70 mV
-60 mV
+90 mV
questions.why: Roughly 4 to 5 mEq/L outside against about 140 to 150 mEq/L inside gives an equilibrium potential near -90 mV, and the negative sign says a negative interior is what holds K+ from leaking out. About -70 mV is the resting membrane potential, which sits near E_K but not on it because the membrane also leaks some Na+. A value of +90 mV would require K+ to be concentrated outside.
questions.answerText: -90 mV

questions.q: What is the approximate equilibrium potential for Ca2+ in a typical cell?
options: +60 mV
0 mV
questions.why: The Ca2+ gradient is enormous, roughly ten thousand times more Ca2+ outside than inside, so a large positive interior would be needed to hold it out, about +120 mV. That large positive value means the inward driving force on Ca2+ at rest is huge. About +60 mV is the Na+ value, whose gradient is only about tenfold. A negative value would require Ca2+ to be concentrated inside the cell.

questions.q: If an ion is at the same concentration inside and outside the cell, what is its equilibrium potential?
options: +61 mV
0 mV
-61 mV
questions.why: With equal concentrations there is no concentration gradient pushing the ion either way, so no voltage is needed to balance it and the equilibrium potential is 0 mV. That means the ion is held still only when there is no voltage across the membrane, and at any other membrane potential it will move. The other values would all require a gradient in one direction or the other.
questions.answerText: 0 mV

questions.q: A neuron sits at -70 mV. The equilibrium potential for Na+ is +60 mV. If Na+ channels open, which way does Na+ move and what happens to the membrane potential?
options: Na+ leaves the cell and the membrane hyperpolarizes
There is no net movement, because both forces cancel at -70 mV
Na+ leaves the cell and the membrane moves toward +60 mV
Na+ enters the cell and the membrane depolarizes toward +60 mV
questions.why: An open channel always moves its ion in the direction that pulls the membrane potential toward that ion's equilibrium potential. The membrane is at -70 mV and E_Na is +60 mV, so both the concentration gradient and the negative interior push Na+ inward, and the entering positive charge depolarizes the cell toward +60 mV. Na+ would leave only if the membrane were more positive than +60 mV. The forces cancel only at E_Na itself, and hyperpolarization is the opposite of what Na+ entry does.
questions.answerText: Na+ enters the cell and the membrane depolarizes toward +60 mV

questions.q: In a neuron where the equilibrium potential for Cl- is -70 mV, the membrane is also sitting at -70 mV. What happens when Cl- channels open?
options: Cl- rushes in and the cell hyperpolarizes sharply
There is little or no net Cl- movement, because the membrane is already at E_Cl
Cl- rushes out and the cell depolarizes
Cl- moves in and the cell depolarizes
questions.why: At an ion's equilibrium potential the electrical force and the concentration force on that ion are equal and opposite, so opening its channels produces no net flow. Here the membrane is already at E_Cl, so the voltage barely changes. Opening Cl- channels still matters, though: it holds the membrane near -70 mV and makes it harder for excitatory input to push the cell to threshold. Net movement in either direction would require the membrane to be away from E_Cl.
questions.answerText: There is little or no net Cl- movement, because the membrane is already at E_Cl

questions.q: The membrane potential is -50 mV and the equilibrium potential for Cl- is -70 mV. When Cl- channels open, which way does Cl- move and what happens to the membrane potential?
options: Cl- enters the cell and the membrane moves toward -70 mV
Cl- leaves the cell and the membrane moves toward -70 mV
Cl- enters the cell and the membrane depolarizes
Cl- does not move, because Cl- channels only open at threshold
questions.why: The membrane at -50 mV is more positive than E_Cl, so the open channels move Cl- in the direction that brings the membrane back toward -70 mV. That means Cl- enters, carrying negative charge in and making the inside more negative. Cl- leaving would take negative charge out and make the inside more positive, which moves the membrane away from E_Cl. Cl- entry hyperpolarizes rather than depolarizes. Cl- channels do not wait for threshold; many are ligand gated.
questions.answerText: Cl- enters the cell and the membrane moves toward -70 mV

questions.q: In terms of its effect on the membrane potential, Cl- entering a cell is most like which of these?
options: Na+ entering the cell
Ca2+ entering the cell
K+ leaving the cell
K+ entering the cell
questions.why: What changes the membrane potential is the movement of charge. Cl- carries a negative charge, so bringing it in makes the inside more negative. Taking positive charge out does the same thing, which is exactly what K+ leaving does. Na+ or Ca2+ entering brings positive charge in and depolarizes the cell, and so would K+ entering. This is why the direction rule for an anion looks reversed compared with a cation.
questions.answerText: K+ leaving the cell

questions.q: Plasma K+ rises well above normal (hyperkalemia). What happens to the equilibrium potential for K+ and to the resting membrane potential?
options: E_K becomes more negative and the cell hyperpolarizes
E_K does not change, because K+ inside the cell stays the same
E_K becomes more positive than E_Na
E_K becomes less negative and the resting potential depolarizes
questions.why: With more K+ outside, the gradient pushing K+ out of the cell is smaller, so less negative interior is needed to hold it in and E_K becomes less negative. The resting membrane is mostly permeable to K+, so the resting potential follows E_K and depolarizes. That is why hyperkalemia makes heart and nerve cells unstable. E_K depends on the ratio of outside to inside, so changing the outside alone does change it. E_K does not become more negative with more outside K+, and it does not climb anywhere near E_Na.
questions.answerText: E_K becomes less negative and the resting potential depolarizes

questions.q: A neuron sits at -70 mV and its equilibrium potential for K+ is -90 mV. If K+ channels open, which way does K+ move and why?
options: Out of the cell, moving the membrane potential toward -90 mV
Out of the cell, moving the membrane potential toward 0 mV
There is no net movement, because the membrane potential is already negative
Into the cell, moving the membrane potential toward -90 mV
questions.why: An open channel always moves its ion in the direction that carries the membrane potential toward that ion's equilibrium potential. Since -70 mV is positive of E_K, K+ leaves, taking positive charge with it and hyperpolarizing the cell toward -90 mV. K+ would enter only if the membrane potential were driven below -90 mV. Losing positive charge cannot push the cell toward 0 mV, and net movement stops only when the two values match.
questions.answerText: Out of the cell, moving the membrane potential toward -90 mV

questions.q: Which change would make the equilibrium potential for Na+ more positive?
options: Opening more Na+ channels
Raising the extracellular Na+ concentration
Raising the intracellular Na+ concentration
Lowering the extracellular Na+ concentration
questions.why: E_Na depends only on the Na+ gradient and its charge. Making the outside even richer in Na+ makes the gradient steeper, so a more positive interior would be needed to hold Na+ out, and E_Na becomes more positive. Raising inside Na+ or lowering outside Na+ flattens the gradient and makes E_Na less positive. Opening more channels changes how strongly Na+ pulls the membrane toward E_Na, but it does not move E_Na itself.
questions.answerText: Raising the extracellular Na+ concentration

questions.q: A drug depolarizes a neuron from -70 mV to -50 mV. The equilibrium potential for K+ is -90 mV. How does the driving force on K+ change, and what happens when K+ channels open?
options: The driving force falls, so K+ leaves more slowly
The driving force is unchanged, because E_K did not change
The driving force rises, so K+ leaves faster and pulls the membrane back toward -90 mV
The driving force reverses, so K+ now enters the cell
questions.why: Driving force is the distance between the membrane potential and the ion's equilibrium potential. At -70 mV the membrane is 20 mV away from E_K; at -50 mV it is 40 mV away, so the push on K+ to leave is larger and K+ exits faster when its channels open, repolarizing the cell. This is part of why K+ channels are so effective at bringing a depolarized cell back down. E_K is the same, but the driving force depends on both numbers. The direction would reverse only if the membrane dropped below -90 mV.
questions.answerText: The driving force rises, so K+ leaves faster and pulls the membrane back toward -90 mV

questions.q: A cell rests at -70 mV. E_Na is +60 mV, E_K is -90 mV, E_Cl is -70 mV and E_Ca is +120 mV. Which ion has the largest driving force pushing it into the cell?
options: Na+
K+
Cl-
Ca2+
questions.why: The driving force is the gap between the membrane potential and each ion's equilibrium potential. From -70 mV, Ca2+ is 190 mV away from its balance point, Na+ is 130 mV away, K+ is 20 mV away in the outward direction, and Cl- is at its balance point with no net push. So Ca2+ has the largest inward driving force, which is why even a few open Ca2+ channels let Ca2+ flood in, as happens at the axon terminal. Na+ has a large inward push too, but smaller than Ca2+. K+ is pushed out, not in.
questions.answerText: Ca2+

questions.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV. Opening K+ channels moves the membrane potential only a little, while opening the same number of Na+ channels moves it a lot. Why?
options: -70 mV is close to E_K but far from E_Na, so the driving force on Na+ is much larger
K+ channels are always closed at rest
Na+ ions are smaller than K+ ions and move faster
K+ has no concentration gradient across the membrane
questions.why: The resting potential sits about 20 mV from E_K (-90 mV) but about 130 mV from E_Na (+60 mV). Opening K+ channels can only pull the membrane the short distance down toward -90 mV, while opening Na+ channels unleashes a large push toward +60 mV. K+ leak channels are actually open at rest, which is why the resting potential sits near E_K. Ion size is not the reason, and K+ has a steep gradient, high inside and low outside.
questions.answerText: -70 mV is close to E_K but far from E_Na, so the driving force on Na+ is much larger

questions.q: A neuron is bathed in a solution in which extracellular Na+ has been lowered to 15 mEq/L, matching its intracellular Na+ of 15 mEq/L. Predict the equilibrium potential for Na+ and what happens to the peak of an action potential.
options: E_Na becomes -61 mV and the cell hyperpolarizes at the peak
E_Na becomes 0 mV, so the action potential can no longer overshoot above 0 mV
E_Na is unchanged, because it is set by intracellular Na+ alone
E_Na becomes +61 mV and the overshoot roughly doubles
questions.why: With equal concentrations there is no gradient left to push Na+ in, so E_Na becomes 0 mV. The upstroke of an action potential drives the membrane toward E_Na and can never pass it, so the peak can no longer rise above 0 mV and the overshoot disappears. E_Na does not become negative, because nothing now pushes Na+ outward either. It is not set by inside Na+ alone; it depends on the ratio of outside to inside. And a doubled overshoot would require an even steeper gradient.
questions.answerText: E_Na becomes 0 mV, so the action potential can no longer overshoot above 0 mV

questions.q: What is the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron?
options: 0 mV
-40 mV
-70 mV
questions.why: A neuron at rest sits near -70 mV, close to but slightly positive of the K+ equilibrium potential. A value of 0 mV would mean no charge separation at all, which no living cell maintains. About -40 mV is nearer the resting potential of a pacemaker cell that leaks Na+ heavily. Around -120 mV is more negative than E_K, so no combination of resting permeabilities could produce it.
questions.answerText: -70 mV

questions.q: The resting membrane potential sits closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
options: Na+
Ca2+
Cl-
K+
questions.why: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to anything else, so the Goldman weighting pulls the membrane potential close to E_K, near -90 mV. E_Na is about +60 mV, and if the membrane favored Na+ the cell would rest positive instead. E_Ca is even further positive at about +120 mV. E_Cl is close to the resting potential in many cells, but chloride follows the membrane potential rather than setting it.
questions.answerText: K+

questions.q: Which channels are the most numerous open channels in a resting neuron membrane?
options: K+ leak channels
Voltage gated Ca2+ channels
Ligand gated Cl- channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
questions.why: Leak channels for K+ are open continuously and vastly outnumber other open channels at rest, which is what makes the membrane predominantly K+ permeable.
