Voltage gated Na+ and Ca2+ channels are almost all closed at -70 mV and open only when the membrane depolarizes. Ligand gated Cl- channels open only when a transmitter such as GABA binds, so they contribute nothing at rest without input.
questions.answerText: K+ leak channels

questions.q: When we say the resting membrane potential is -70 mV, what is negative relative to what?
options: The outside of the cell relative to the inside
The inside of the cell relative to the outside
The membrane itself relative to the cytosol
The cytosol relative to the nucleus
questions.why: By convention the extracellular fluid is the zero reference and the recording electrode is inside, so a reading of -70 mV means the cytosol is 70 mV negative to the bath. Reversing the reference would report +70 mV for the same cell, which is why the convention has to be stated. The membrane is the insulator that holds the charge separation, not one of the two compartments, and the nucleus is not a reference point for this measurement.
questions.answerText: The inside of the cell relative to the outside

questions.q: Why is the resting membrane potential not exactly equal to the equilibrium potential for K+?
options: Chloride sits at equilibrium across the resting membrane
The Nernst equation does not apply to living cell membranes
A small resting Na+ permeability pulls the potential positive of E_K
K+ leak channels are closed while the cell is at rest
questions.why: Resting permeability to K+ is high but not exclusive, and the steady trickle of Na+ inward keeps the membrane potential about 20 mV positive of E_K. If the membrane were perfectly K+ selective, the resting potential would be -90 mV instead of -70 mV. K+ leak channels are open at rest, not closed. Chloride being near equilibrium is true in many cells but it explains stability, not the offset from E_K, and the Nernst equation works fine on living membranes.
questions.answerText: A small resting Na+ permeability pulls the potential positive of E_K

questions.q: The Na+/K+ ATPase exports three Na+ for every two K+ it imports. What is its direct contribution to the resting membrane potential?
options: About 30 mV of extra negativity
About 3 to 4 mV of extra positivity
None, because the pump is electrically neutral
About 3 to 4 mV of extra negativity
questions.why: Because the pump moves one more positive charge out than it brings in, it is electrogenic and adds a few millivolts of negativity directly. The much larger role of the pump is indirect: it builds and maintains the gradients that the Nernst and Goldman relationships then use. A 3 to 2 stoichiometry cannot be neutral, and it cannot make the interior more positive since net positive charge leaves. Thirty millivolts overstates the direct effect by roughly tenfold.
questions.answerText: About 3 to 4 mV of extra negativity

questions.q: How does the Goldman equation differ from the Nernst equation?
options: It combines several ions, each weighted by its relative membrane permeability
It calculates the equilibrium potential more precisely for one ion
It applies only to divalent ions
It ignores concentration gradients and uses permeability alone
questions.why: Goldman handles the real membrane, where Na+, K+, and Cl- all contribute and permeability decides how loudly each ion votes. Nernst handles one ion in isolation and assumes it is the only one that can move. Goldman still uses concentration gradients; permeability is a weighting factor layered on top of them. Valence is not what distinguishes the two equations, and Goldman is not a refinement of a single ion equilibrium potential.
questions.answerText: It combines several ions, each weighted by its relative membrane permeability

questions.q: What is the typical resting membrane potential of a skeletal muscle fiber?
options: -70 mV
-90 mV
-30 mV
-55 mV
questions.why: Skeletal muscle rests near -90 mV, more negative than a neuron because its membrane is even more selectively permeable to K+ and it has a large resting chloride conductance that holds it there. About -70 mV is the neuronal figure. About -55 mV is closer to a typical threshold voltage, not a resting value. About -30 mV is far positive of anything a resting skeletal muscle fiber maintains.
questions.answerText: -90 mV

questions.q: Extracellular K+ rises from 4 to 8 mEq/L. Which way does the resting membrane potential move?
options: It does not change, because intracellular K+ is unchanged
It depolarizes past 0 mV
It depolarizes, becoming less negative
It hyperpolarizes, becoming more negative
questions.why: Raising extracellular K+ shrinks the K+ gradient, so E_K becomes less negative, and because the resting membrane follows E_K closely the resting potential follows it up. This is the mechanism behind the cardiac and neuromuscular effects of hyperkalemia. Hyperpolarization would require lowering extracellular K+ instead. The resting potential tracks a ratio, so a change on either side matters, and a doubling of extracellular K+ shifts it by roughly 18 mV, nowhere near 0 mV.
questions.answerText: It depolarizes, becoming less negative

questions.q: Extracellular K+ falls from 4 to 2 mEq/L. Which way does the resting membrane potential move?
options: It stays the same, because K+ permeability did not change
It moves toward E_Na
It depolarizes toward threshold
It hyperpolarizes, becoming more negative
questions.why: Halving extracellular K+ steepens the K+ gradient, so E_K becomes more negative and the resting potential follows, sitting further from threshold. That extra negativity is why hypokalemia makes excitable cells harder to fire. Depolarization is the hyperkalemic direction, not the hypokalemic one. Permeability did not change, but the driving force did, and Vm moves toward E_K, not toward E_Na, whenever K+ dominates.
questions.answerText: It hyperpolarizes, becoming more negative

questions.q: A cell's membrane permeability to K+ increases while all concentrations stay the same. What happens to the resting membrane potential?
options: It hyperpolarizes toward E_K
It depolarizes toward E_Na
It moves to exactly 0 mV
It is unchanged, because the K+ gradient did not change
questions.why: In the Goldman weighting, the ion with the highest permeability dominates the membrane potential, so raising K+ permeability pulls Vm closer to E_K near -90 mV. It cannot pass E_K, because at that point K+ movement stops. Depolarization toward E_Na would follow a rise in Na+ permeability instead. A value of 0 mV would require the gradients to vanish, which is not what a permeability change does.
questions.answerText: It hyperpolarizes toward E_K

questions.q: A cell's membrane permeability to Na+ increases while all concentrations stay the same. What happens to the resting membrane potential?
options: It hyperpolarizes toward E_K
It depolarizes toward E_Na
It is unchanged, because the Na+ gradient did not change
It depolarizes all the way to +60 mV
questions.why: Giving Na+ a bigger vote in the Goldman weighting drags the membrane potential away from E_K and toward E_Na at about +60 mV. How far it travels depends on how much the permeability ratio shifts, so a modest change gives a modest depolarization rather than a jump to E_Na itself. Reaching +60 mV would require Na+ permeability to swamp K+ permeability entirely, as it briefly does at the peak of an action potential. Hyperpolarization is the response to more K+ permeability, not more Na+ permeability.
questions.answerText: It depolarizes toward E_Na

questions.q: A drug blocks half of a neuron's K+ leak channels. Predict the effect on the resting membrane potential.
options: The cell depolarizes, because K+ now enters through the remaining channels
The cell hyperpolarizes, because less K+ can leave
The cell depolarizes, because the relative contribution of Na+ permeability rises
Nothing changes, because the K+ gradient is unaffected
questions.why: What matters is the ratio of permeabilities, so cutting K+ permeability gives the ongoing Na+ leak more weight and pulls the resting potential positive. Blocking K+ exit does not add negative charge; the negativity comes from K+ leaving in the first place, so less K+ exit means less negativity. The gradients are unchanged, but the membrane potential depends on permeability as well as gradients. K+ still leaves rather than enters, since Vm remains positive of E_K.
questions.answerText: The cell depolarizes, because the relative contribution of Na+ permeability rises

questions.q: Extracellular Na+ is lowered from 145 to 120 mEq/L and the resting membrane potential barely changes. Why?
options: Na+ has no meaningful equilibrium potential while the cell is at rest
The Na+/K+ ATPase immediately restores the extracellular Na+ level
The Na+ gradient is far too steep for so small a change to matter
Resting Na+ permeability is very low, so Na+ carries little weight at rest
questions.why: In the Goldman weighting an ion influences Vm in proportion to its permeability, and at rest the membrane is perhaps a hundred times more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so shifting E_Na hardly moves the resting potential. The same manipulation would visibly lower the peak of an action potential, when Na+ permeability is briefly dominant. Na+ has an equilibrium potential at all times, and the pump cannot change the composition of a large extracellular bath.
questions.answerText: Resting Na+ permeability is very low, so Na+ carries little weight at rest

questions.q: In a cell where E_Cl is -70 mV and the resting membrane potential is -70 mV, what happens when Cl- channels open?
options: The membrane potential holds steady, but the cell becomes harder to depolarize
Cl- floods into the cell until the membrane potential reaches E_Na
The cell hyperpolarizes sharply, moving toward -90 mV
The cell depolarizes steadily, moving toward 0 mV
questions.why: When Vm already equals E_Cl there is no net driving force, so no net chloride moves and the voltage holds. The added conductance still matters, because any attempt to depolarize the cell now meets an increased Cl- current pulling it back to -70 mV, an effect called shunting. Hyperpolarization would require E_Cl to be more negative than Vm, and depolarization would require it to be less negative. Chloride movement can never carry a cell toward E_Na.
questions.answerText: The membrane potential holds steady, but the cell becomes harder to depolarize

questions.q: Plasma K+ rises from 4 to 7 mEq/L and stays there. Trace what happens to a neuron's resting potential and then to its excitability.
options: E_K becomes more negative, so the cell hyperpolarizes and can no longer reach threshold
E_K becomes less negative so the cell depolarizes, and the sustained depolarization inactivates Na+ channels
E_K is unchanged, so the resting potential and excitability are both unaffected
E_K becomes less negative so the cell depolarizes, and its excitability then keeps rising without limit
questions.why: Step one is the Nernst effect: a smaller K+ gradient makes E_K less negative, and the resting potential follows. Step two is the channel effect: sitting closer to threshold briefly raises excitability, but a maintained depolarization drives voltage gated Na+ channels into their inactivated state, and inactivated channels cannot open again until the membrane repolarizes. That two step story is why severe hyperkalemia produces weakness and cardiac conduction failure rather than endless firing. Hyperpolarization is the hypokalemic direction, and E_K always responds to a change in either K+ compartment.
questions.answerText: E_K becomes less negative so the cell depolarizes, and the sustained depolarization inactivates Na+ channels

questions.q: Ouabain is applied to a neuron and completely blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase. Predict the immediate effect and the effect over the next hour on the resting membrane potential.
options: No immediate change, and then a hyperpolarization as intracellular Na+ accumulates over the hour
An immediate hyperpolarization from losing the pump current, and then no further change at all
An immediate depolarization of a few mV from losing the pump current, then a larger one as the gradients run down
An immediate depolarization of about 30 mV, and then a slow return to the original resting potential
questions.why: The pump contributes in two ways on two timescales. Losing its direct electrogenic current removes only about 3 to 4 mV of negativity, so the immediate change is small. Over minutes to an hour, intracellular Na+ climbs and intracellular K+ falls, E_K becomes far less negative, and the resting potential collapses toward zero, which is the large delayed effect. Because the pump exports net positive charge, losing it can only depolarize, never hyperpolarize, and nothing restores the gradients while it is blocked.
questions.answerText: An immediate depolarization of a few mV from losing the pump current, then a larger one as the gradients run down

questions.q: Cell A has a resting permeability ratio of K+ to Na+ of 100 to 1. Cell B has a ratio of 10 to 1. Both have identical ion gradients. Which cell has the more negative resting membrane potential, and why?
options: They are identical, because the two cells have identical ion gradients
Cell A, because a higher permeability ratio makes E_K more negative
Cell B, because a larger relative Na+ permeability adds negativity
Cell A, because the heavier K+ weighting pulls its membrane potential closer to E_K
questions.why: Gradients set the equilibrium potentials, and permeability decides which equilibrium potential the membrane sits near. With K+ outvoting Na+ a hundred to one, cell A rests very close to E_K near -90 mV, while cell B, with Na+ carrying ten times more relative weight, rests noticeably positive of that. Na+ entry always adds positive charge, so a larger Na+ share can only depolarize. Identical gradients are not enough, because permeability is the second variable, and permeability cannot change E_K, which depends on concentrations alone.
questions.answerText: Cell A, because the heavier K+ weighting pulls its membrane potential closer to E_K

questions.q: At the peak of an action potential, Na+ permeability rises several hundredfold, yet the membrane potential peaks near +30 mV rather than reaching E_Na at about +60 mV. Why?
options: K+ permeability persists while Na+ channels are already beginning to inactivate
The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps Na+ back out fast enough to cap the peak
The Na+ concentration gradient reverses during the upstroke
The membrane potential can never rise above 0 mV in any cell
questions.why: Reaching E_Na would require the membrane to be permeable to Na+ and nothing else. In reality K+ leak and delayed rectifier channels keep pulling the membrane potential negative while Na+ channels are already entering their inactivated state, so the two effects halt the upstroke short of +60 mV. The Na+ gradient barely changes during a single spike, since only a tiny number of ions cross. The overshoot proves the membrane potential can exceed 0 mV, and the pump moves far too slowly to shape a millisecond event.
questions.answerText: K+ permeability persists while Na+ channels are already beginning to inactivate

questions.q: What opens a voltage gated channel?
options: A rise in extracellular temperature
A change in the membrane potential
Binding of a chemical messenger
Physical stretch of the membrane
questions.why: Voltage gated channels carry charged segments in the protein that move when the electrical field across the membrane changes, and that movement swings the gate. Chemical messenger binding is what opens a ligand gated channel. Physical stretch opens a mechanically gated channel. Temperature does gate a few specialized sensory channels, but it is not the defining stimulus for the voltage gated class.
questions.answerText: A change in the membrane potential

questions.q: What opens a ligand gated channel?
options: Phosphorylation of the channel by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Depolarization of the membrane past a threshold voltage
Binding of a specific chemical messenger to the channel protein
Deformation of the surrounding patch of membrane
questions.why: A ligand gated channel is a receptor and a pore in one molecule, so when the transmitter or hormone binds, the pore opens directly and quickly. Depolarization is the trigger for voltage gated channels, and deformation is the trigger for mechanically gated ones. The Na+/K+ ATPase is a pump that phosphorylates itself; it does not gate other channels.
questions.answerText: Binding of a specific chemical messenger to the channel protein

questions.q: What opens a mechanically gated channel?
options: A sustained shift in the membrane potential
Binding of a neurotransmitter to the channel
A fall in the intracellular ATP concentration
Physical deformation of the membrane, such as stretch
questions.why: Mechanically gated channels are pulled open by tension in the membrane or by the cytoskeletal elements attached to them, which is what makes touch, hearing, and stretch sensation possible. Voltage shifts and transmitter binding define the other two gated classes. ATP sensitive channels do exist, notably in pancreatic beta cells, but they are gated by a bound nucleotide rather than by mechanical force.
questions.answerText: Physical deformation of the membrane, such as stretch

questions.q: Which channel type has no true gate and stays open most of the time?
options: The leak channel
The mechanically gated channel
The voltage gated channel
The ligand gated channel
questions.why: Leak channels sit open essentially all the time, and their steady K+ conductance is what makes the resting membrane predominantly K+ permeable. The other three classes are defined by the stimulus that opens them, and all three are mostly closed in a resting cell. That difference is why leak channels set the resting potential while gated channels produce changes away from it.
questions.answerText: The leak channel

questions.q: Where are voltage gated Na+ channels most densely concentrated in a neuron?
options: The postsynaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction
The axon hillock and the axon membrane
The stereocilia of inner ear hair cells
The membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.why: The axon hillock carries the highest density of voltage gated Na+ channels, which is why it is the trigger zone where an action potential is initiated and then propagated along the axon. The postsynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction is packed with ligand gated nicotinic receptors instead. Hair cell stereocilia carry mechanically gated channels. The endoplasmic reticulum has Ca2+ release channels, not the Na+ channels that drive the upstroke.
questions.answerText: The axon hillock and the axon membrane

questions.q: Which location is a classic example of ligand gated channels in action?
options: The T tubule membrane during propagation
The node of Ranvier
The motor end plate of a skeletal muscle fiber
The lamellated capsule of a Pacinian corpuscle
questions.why: At the motor end plate, acetylcholine released from the motor neuron binds nicotinic receptors that are themselves cation channels, and the pore opens on binding. Nodes of Ranvier are dense with voltage gated Na+ channels for saltatory conduction. The Pacinian corpuscle houses mechanically gated channels for pressure sensing. T tubules propagate an action potential using voltage gated channels.
questions.answerText: The motor end plate of a skeletal muscle fiber

questions.q: Where would you find mechanically gated channels doing their defining job?
options: In the presynaptic terminal during transmitter release
In the sarcoplasmic reticulum of cardiac muscle
In the initial segment of a motor neuron axon
In the stereocilia of inner ear hair cells
questions.why: Sound bends the stereocilia, tension on the tip links pulls the mechanically gated channels open, and that is the conversion of a physical stimulus into an electrical signal. Presynaptic terminals rely on voltage gated Ca2+ channels for release. The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca2+ through ligand and voltage coupled release channels. The initial segment is the voltage gated Na+ channel territory that starts an action potential.
questions.answerText: In the stereocilia of inner ear hair cells

questions.q: Which channel type is primarily responsible for setting the resting membrane potential?
options: K+ leak channels
Voltage gated Ca2+ channels
Ligand gated cation channels
Mechanically gated channels
questions.why: Because K+ leak channels are the main open pathway at rest, the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to any other ion, and the resting potential settles near E_K. Voltage gated Ca2+ channels are closed at rest and open only with depolarization. Ligand gated channels wait for a transmitter, and mechanically gated channels wait for a physical stimulus, so none of them contribute to a resting, unstimulated membrane.
questions.answerText: K+ leak channels

questions.q: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction opens its pore when acetylcholine binds it. How is this channel classified?
options: Voltage gated
Ligand gated
Mechanically gated
Nongated leak
questions.why: The stimulus that opens the pore is a bound chemical messenger, so by definition the channel is ligand gated, even though the ions that flow through it then change the voltage. Classification follows the stimulus that opens the gate, not the consequence. A voltage gated channel would need a change in membrane potential first, a mechanically gated one would need deformation, and a leak channel would need nothing at all because it is already open.
questions.answerText: Ligand gated

questions.q: A neuron ending in the wall of the carotid sinus fires more rapidly when a rise in arterial pressure distends the vessel. Which channel type is doing the initial transduction?
options: Voltage gated
Nongated leak
Mechanically gated
Ligand gated
questions.why: The stimulus here is physical stretch of the vessel wall pulling on the nerve ending, so the first channels to open are mechanically gated ones, and the resulting depolarization is what later recruits voltage gated channels to fire action potentials. Ligand gated channels would require a chemical messenger, and none is being applied. Voltage gated channels do participate, but downstream, after the mechanical event has already depolarized the ending. Leak channels do not respond to stimuli at all.
questions.answerText: Mechanically gated

questions.q: A channel is closed at -70 mV and opens as the membrane potential moves to -50 mV. How is it classified?
options: Ligand gated
Nongated leak
Mechanically gated
Voltage gated
questions.why: The only thing that changed was the membrane potential, and the channel responded, which is the definition of voltage gating. A leak channel would already have been open at -70 mV. A mechanically gated channel would require deformation of the membrane, and a ligand gated channel would require a messenger to bind, neither of which was supplied in this description.
questions.answerText: Voltage gated

questions.q: A Pacinian corpuscle in the skin depolarizes when the overlying tissue is pressed. Which channel type opens first?
options: Mechanically gated
Ligand gated
Voltage gated
Nongated leak
questions.why: Pressure deforms the lamellae and the nerve ending inside them, and that deformation pulls mechanically gated channels open, producing the receptor potential. Voltage gated channels come next, converting a large enough receptor potential into action potentials, but they are not the transducer. No chemical messenger is involved, so ligand gating does not apply, and leak channels have no stimulus to respond to.
questions.answerText: Mechanically gated

questions.q: A GABA-A receptor opens a chloride pore when GABA binds. Classify the channel and predict its effect on a neuron resting at -70 mV with an E_Cl of -75 mV.
options: Voltage gated, and it produces a large depolarization
Ligand gated, and it produces a small hyperpolarization
Ligand gated, and it produces a large depolarization
Mechanically gated, and it produces a small hyperpolarization
questions.why: GABA binding opens the pore, so the channel is ligand gated. Because E_Cl of -75 mV lies just below the resting potential of -70 mV, the small driving force lets Cl- enter and nudges the membrane potential toward -75 mV, a modest hyperpolarization that also shunts incoming excitation. Depolarization would require E_Cl to be positive of the resting potential, which happens in some immature neurons. Nothing here is opened by voltage or by mechanical force.
questions.answerText: Ligand gated, and it produces a small hyperpolarization

questions.q: A channel in a cell membrane opens when intracellular Ca2+ binds to a site on its cytoplasmic side. How is it classified?
options: Leak, because Ca2+ is always present in the cytosol
Voltage gated, because Ca2+ carries charge
Ligand gated, with an intracellular ligand
Mechanically gated, because Ca2+ influx stretches the membrane
questions.why: Ligand gating is defined by a chemical binding to the channel, and nothing in the definition requires the chemical to arrive from outside the cell. Calcium activated K+ channels work exactly this way and help repolarize cells after Ca2+ entry. The fact that Ca2+ is charged does not make the channel voltage gated, since the trigger is binding rather than a field change. Ca2+ influx does not stretch the membrane, and a channel that requires a trigger is not a leak channel.
questions.answerText: Ligand gated, with an intracellular ligand

questions.q: Which channel type produces the rapid upstroke of an action potential?
options: Mechanically gated channels
K+ leak channels
Ligand gated cation channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
questions.why: Once the membrane reaches threshold, voltage gated Na+ channels open, and because they open in response to the very depolarization they cause, the result is a fast regenerative upstroke. K+ leak channels oppose depolarization rather than driving it. Ligand gated channels can produce the graded depolarization that brings a cell to threshold, but they do not generate the spike. Mechanically gated channels transduce physical stimuli at sensory endings and are not present along the axon.
questions.answerText: Voltage gated Na+ channels

questions.q: A toxin blocks voltage gated Na+ channels on a skeletal muscle fiber but leaves the nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate untouched. A motor neuron then fires. What happens at the muscle fiber?
options: An end plate potential still appears, but no muscle action potential follows and the fiber does not contract
Both the end plate potential and the muscle action potential occur completely normally
The end plate potential is blocked, but the muscle action potential still propagates normally
No end plate potential appears at all, because acetylcholine can no longer bind
questions.why: The two channel classes are independent, so blocking one leaves the other working. Acetylcholine binds its ligand gated receptors and the local end plate potential develops on schedule, but the propagated action potential requires voltage gated Na+ channels in the surrounding sarcolemma, and those are blocked, so the signal dies where it started and no contraction follows. Binding is unaffected because the toxin targets a different protein, and an action potential cannot propagate without the channels that generate it.
questions.answerText: An end plate potential still appears, but no muscle action potential follows and the fiber does not contract

questions.q: A mutation slows the inactivation of voltage gated Na+ channels in skeletal muscle. Predict the effect on the membrane potential and on firing.
options: Na+ entry stops sooner, so action potentials become shorter and the fiber is harder to excite
Na+ entry continues longer, so the fiber stays depolarized and tends to fire repeatedly after a single stimulus
The resting potential becomes more negative and the fiber cannot reach threshold
The channels never open, so no action potential occurs at all
questions.why: Inactivation is the built in stop signal that ends the upstroke, so slowing it lets Na+ keep entering and holds the membrane depolarized past its usual repolarization point. A membrane that lingers near threshold retriggers easily, which produces bursts of activity and the sustained stiffness seen in myotonic disorders. Shortened spikes would follow faster inactivation, not slower. Activation is untouched, so the channels still open normally and the resting potential is not made more negative.
questions.answerText: Na+ entry continues longer, so the fiber stays depolarized and tends to fire repeatedly after a single stimulus

questions.q: Sound bends the stereocilia of a cochlear hair cell. Put the next steps in the right order, remembering that the endolymph bathing the stereocilia is unusually rich in K+.
options: Ligand gated channels open first, and then Ca2+ enters and depolarizes the cell
Voltage gated Na+ channels open first, and then K+ leaves and the cell hyperpolarizes
Mechanically gated channels open, K+ enters and depolarizes the cell, Ca2+ channels open, and transmitter is released
Mechanically gated channels open, K+ leaves and hyperpolarizes the cell, and transmitter release stops
questions.why: Bending puts tension on the tip links and pulls the mechanically gated channels open, and because endolymph is rich in K+ while the hair cell interior is negative, K+ moves into the cell instead of out of it, which is the reverse of what K+ normally does elsewhere. That depolarization then opens voltage gated Ca2+ channels at the base of the cell, and Ca2+ entry triggers transmitter release onto the auditory nerve. Nothing in this chain begins with a voltage change or with a chemical messenger, so the mechanically gated step has to come first.
questions.answerText: Mechanically gated channels open, K+ enters and depolarizes the cell, Ca2+ channels open, and transmitter is released

questions.q: A drug increases how long GABA-A channels stay open each time GABA binds. Predict the effect on a postsynaptic neuron that is receiving excitatory input.
options: More Na+ moves per binding event, so the neuron reaches its threshold more easily
The neuron depolarizes, because a longer channel open time always adds positive charge
Nothing changes, because the amount of GABA released is not altered at all
More Cl- moves per binding event, so the neuron is held nearer E_Cl and is harder to fire
questions.why: Holding the pore open longer increases the total chloride charge that moves for each release event, so the inhibitory effect deepens even though no extra GABA was released. The membrane is pulled toward E_Cl and the added conductance shunts incoming excitatory current, so a larger depolarizing input is needed to reach threshold. GABA-A pores pass Cl-, not Na+, so excitability cannot rise. And a change in open time changes the response to a given amount of transmitter, which is why the unchanged GABA release does not make the drug ineffective.
questions.answerText: More Cl- moves per binding event, so the neuron is held nearer E_Cl and is harder to fire

questions.q: What does depolarization mean?
options: The membrane potential becomes less negative, moving toward zero
The membrane potential becomes more negative than rest
The membrane potential returns to rest after a change
The membrane potential rises above zero
questions.why: Depolarization is any reduction in the charge separation across the membrane, so the interior becomes less negative and the potential moves toward zero. Becoming more negative than rest is hyperpolarization. Returning to rest after a change is repolarization. Rising above zero is the overshoot, which is one particular part of a large depolarization rather than the definition of the term.
questions.answerText: The membrane potential becomes less negative, moving toward zero

questions.q: What does repolarization mean?
options: The membrane potential becomes more negative than its resting value
The membrane potential returns toward its resting value after a depolarization
The membrane potential becomes less negative than its resting value
The membrane potential holds steady at rest with no change
questions.why: Repolarization is the recovery phase: the membrane potential travels back down toward the resting value it started from. Going past that value into more negative territory is hyperpolarization, which often follows repolarization but is a separate phase. Becoming less negative than rest is depolarization. A membrane simply sitting at rest is not repolarizing, because nothing is being restored.
questions.answerText: The membrane potential returns toward its resting value after a depolarization

questions.q: What does hyperpolarization mean?
options: The membrane potential exceeds zero and becomes positive
The membrane potential becomes less negative than its resting value
The membrane potential becomes more negative than its resting value
The membrane potential returns to its resting value from a positive peak
questions.why: Hyperpolarization increases the charge separation, so the interior becomes more negative than rest and the cell is further from threshold and harder to excite. Becoming less negative is depolarization. Returning from a positive peak toward rest is repolarization. Crossing above zero is the overshoot, which is the opposite end of the range from hyperpolarization.
questions.answerText: The membrane potential becomes more negative than its resting value

questions.q: What does the overshoot refer to on a membrane potential tracing?
options: The steepest part of the falling phase
The delay between the stimulus and the start of the response
The portion of the tracing where the membrane potential dips below the resting value
The portion of the tracing where the membrane potential is above 0 mV
questions.why: Overshoot names the stretch of the tracing where the interior has actually become positive relative to the outside, typically peaking near +30 mV in a neuron. Dipping below the resting value is the after-hyperpolarization, at the other end of the tracing. The steepest falling segment is part of repolarization. The delay before a response is latency, which is a timing measure rather than a voltage region.
questions.answerText: The portion of the tracing where the membrane potential is above 0 mV

questions.q: A cell's membrane potential moves from -70 mV to -50 mV. What is this change called?
options: Depolarization
Overshoot
Hyperpolarization
Repolarization
questions.why: The interior became less negative, which is depolarization, and in this case the cell also moved closer to threshold. Hyperpolarization would be a move toward more negative values. Repolarization would require the cell to be returning from a previous displacement rather than moving away from rest. Overshoot would require the potential to pass 0 mV, and -50 mV is still well below it.
questions.answerText: Depolarization

questions.q: A cell's membrane potential moves from -70 mV to -85 mV. What is this change called?
options: Repolarization
Hyperpolarization
Depolarization
Overshoot
questions.why: The interior became more negative than rest, so this is hyperpolarization, and the cell now sits further from threshold. Depolarization would move the value toward zero. Overshoot requires crossing above 0 mV. Repolarization describes a return toward rest, but here the cell is moving away from rest in the negative direction.
questions.answerText: Hyperpolarization

questions.q: On an action potential tracing, the after-hyperpolarization follows immediately after which phase?
options: The initial depolarization
The overshoot
Repolarization
The resting phase
questions.why: The sequence runs depolarization, overshoot, repolarization, and then after-hyperpolarization, because slow K+ channels stay open a little past the point where the membrane reaches its resting value. The overshoot comes before repolarization, not after it. The resting phase is where the tracing began and where it finally returns. The initial depolarization is two phases too early.
questions.answerText: Repolarization

questions.q: Which ion movement most commonly produces hyperpolarization in a neuron?
options: K+ entering the cell
Ca2+ entering the cell
Na+ entering the cell
K+ leaving the cell
questions.why: K+ efflux carries positive charge out of the cell, leaving the interior more negative, which is why an increase in K+ conductance is the standard route to hyperpolarization. Na+ entry and Ca2+ entry both bring positive charge in and depolarize. K+ entering the cell would also depolarize, though at a normal resting potential K+ moves outward rather than inward.
questions.answerText: K+ leaving the cell

questions.q: A tracing rises from -70 mV to +30 mV and then falls back to -70 mV. What is the falling portion called?
options: Repolarization
Hyperpolarization
Depolarization
Overshoot
questions.why: The membrane is traveling back toward its resting value after being displaced, which is the definition of repolarization, and it is driven mostly by K+ leaving through delayed rectifier channels. It would only count as hyperpolarization if the tracing continued past -70 mV into more negative territory. Depolarization is the rising portion. Overshoot names the segment above 0 mV, which occurs during the rise and the earliest part of the fall.
questions.answerText: Repolarization

questions.q: On a tracing that rises from -70 mV to a peak of +30 mV, which part is the overshoot?
options: The whole rise from -70 mV to +30 mV
The segment where the membrane potential is above 0 mV
The segment between -70 mV and threshold
The peak value of +30 mV only
questions.why: Overshoot means the membrane potential has gone past zero and reversed polarity, so the interior is briefly positive. The whole rise from -70 mV is the depolarizing phase, of which the overshoot is only the upper part. The stretch between rest and threshold is the subthreshold portion of the depolarization. The single peak value is the maximum reached, not the whole region above zero.
questions.answerText: The segment where the membrane potential is above 0 mV

questions.q: A wave of Na+ rushes into a neuron through open channels. What change in membrane potential results?
options: No change, because Cl- follows Na+ and cancels it
Hyperpolarization, because charge is moving across the membrane
Depolarization, because positive charge is added to the interior
Repolarization, because Na+ restores the resting value
questions.why: Adding positive charge to a negative interior reduces the charge separation, so the membrane potential moves toward and possibly past zero. Hyperpolarization would require the interior to become more negative, which Na+ entry cannot do. Na+ entry displaces the membrane from rest rather than restoring it, so it is not repolarization. Cl- movement is a separate event that depends on its own driving force and does not automatically cancel a Na+ current.
questions.answerText: Depolarization, because positive charge is added to the interior

questions.q: After returning through -70 mV, a tracing continues down to -80 mV before drifting slowly back to -70 mV. Name this feature and its usual cause.
options: After-hyperpolarization, caused by voltage gated Na+ channels reopening
Repolarization, caused by the Na+/K+ ATPase restoring the gradients
Overshoot, caused by continued Na+ entry through open channels
After-hyperpolarization, caused by K+ channels staying open past repolarization
questions.why: Voltage gated K+ channels are slow to close, so K+ keeps leaving after the membrane has already reached its resting value, briefly carrying the potential below rest. That undershoot contributes to the relative refractory period. Overshoot is the opposite excursion, above 0 mV. Reopening Na+ channels would depolarize rather than hyperpolarize. The pump restores gradients over minutes and is far too slow to shape a feature lasting a few milliseconds.
questions.answerText: After-hyperpolarization, caused by K+ channels staying open past repolarization

questions.q: A neuron's membrane potential moves from -85 mV back to -70 mV. Is this depolarization or hyperpolarization?
options: Depolarization, because the interior became less negative
Neither, because the cell only returned to rest
Hyperpolarization, because the cell has not reached threshold
Hyperpolarization, because the value is still negative
questions.why: These terms describe the direction of change, not the absolute value, so any move toward zero is depolarization even when the potential stays negative the whole time. A value being negative does not make the change hyperpolarizing. Returning to rest still counts as a change with a direction, and here that direction is depolarizing. Threshold is a separate landmark and has no bearing on what to call the movement.
questions.answerText: Depolarization, because the interior became less negative

questions.q: A stimulus moves a neuron's membrane potential from -70 mV to -62 mV, and it decays back to -70 mV without any spike. How should this be classified?
options: An after-hyperpolarization
A subthreshold graded depolarization
An action potential of reduced size
A graded hyperpolarization
questions.why: The membrane became less negative, so the change was depolarizing, and because it never reached threshold it stayed graded and simply decayed. Action potentials are all or none, so there is no such thing as a smaller one; either threshold is reached and a full spike fires or it is not. Hyperpolarization would move the value below -70 mV. An after-hyperpolarization only occurs following a spike, and no spike occurred here.
questions.answerText: A subthreshold graded depolarization

questions.q: Cl- enters a neuron whose membrane potential is -70 mV and whose E_Cl is -75 mV. What change results?
options: No change, because Cl- is always at equilibrium
A large depolarization toward 0 mV
A small hyperpolarization toward -75 mV
A small depolarization toward -65 mV
questions.why: Chloride carries negative charge inward, so the interior becomes slightly more negative, and the movement stops once the membrane potential reaches E_Cl at -75 mV. The size of the change is limited by how far the resting potential sits from E_Cl, which here is only 5 mV. Depolarization would require E_Cl to be positive of the resting potential. Chloride is often close to equilibrium but not exactly at it, which is why a small current flows here.
questions.answerText: A small hyperpolarization toward -75 mV

questions.q: A tracing starts at -70 mV, rises to +30 mV, falls to -80 mV, and then drifts back to -70 mV. Which sequence of phases does this describe?
options: Depolarization, then hyperpolarization, then an overshoot, then repolarization
Overshoot, then depolarization, then repolarization, then a return to rest
Repolarization, then depolarization with an overshoot, then hyperpolarization, then a return to rest
Depolarization including an overshoot, then repolarization, then hyperpolarization, then a return to rest
questions.why: The rise from -70 mV is depolarization, and the part of that rise above 0 mV is the overshoot, so the overshoot is contained within the depolarizing phase rather than being a separate step before or after it. The fall from +30 mV back toward rest is repolarization, driven by K+ efflux. Continuing past -70 mV down to -80 mV is hyperpolarization, and the slow drift up is the return to rest. Any ordering that puts repolarization or hyperpolarization before the initial rise reverses the direction of the event.
questions.answerText: Depolarization including an overshoot, then repolarization, then hyperpolarization, then a return to rest

questions.q: Extracellular K+ rises and a neuron's membrane potential settles at -60 mV and stays there. Analyze what this does to excitability over time.
options: It is a sustained depolarization, which first brings the cell nearer threshold but then inactivates Na+ channels
It is a sustained depolarization, so the cell fires continuous action potentials for as long as it lasts
It is not a depolarization at all, because no action potential ever occurred
It is a sustained hyperpolarization, so the cell becomes progressively harder to excite
questions.why: Moving from -70 mV to -60 mV is depolarization by definition, whether or not a spike follows, and initially the smaller gap to threshold does make the cell easier to fire. The second step is what makes this interesting: a depolarization that is held rather than transient pushes voltage gated Na+ channels into inactivation, and inactivated channels cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, so excitability ends up reduced. That is why moderate hyperkalemia can cause weakness rather than continuous firing. Calling it hyperpolarization reverses the direction of the change.
questions.answerText: It is a sustained depolarization, which first brings the cell nearer threshold but then inactivates Na+ channels

questions.q: Two neurons are stimulated. One reaches a peak of +30 mV; the other peaks at -10 mV with no overshoot. What best explains the difference in the second neuron?
options: A more negative resting membrane potential in the second neuron
Less net Na+ entry during the upstroke, from fewer channels or a weaker gradient
Faster K+ efflux during the resting phase before the stimulus
A larger stimulus current applied to the second neuron membrane
questions.why: How high the peak goes depends on how completely Na+ permeability dominates and on how positive E_Na is, so either fewer available Na+ channels or a lower extracellular Na+ concentration will cut the peak short and remove the overshoot. Starting from a more negative resting potential changes where the upstroke begins, not how far past zero it can climb. K+ efflux at rest sets the resting potential rather than the peak. Stimulus size does not scale an action potential, because spikes are all or none once threshold is reached.
questions.answerText: Less net Na+ entry during the upstroke, from fewer channels or a weaker gradient

questions.q: On the same stretch of dendrite, an excitatory synapse opens Na+ channels at the exact moment an inhibitory synapse opens Cl- channels. Predict what happens to the membrane potential there.
options: It depolarizes and then overshoots, because two channel types are open at once
It depolarizes fully, because Na+ carries the larger driving force here
It changes very little, because the Cl- current offsets the depolarizing Na+ current
It hyperpolarizes strongly, because Cl- always overrides a Na+ current
questions.why: The membrane potential settles wherever the competing currents balance, so simultaneous depolarizing and hyperpolarizing currents largely cancel. There is a second effect worth naming: the open Cl- channels lower the membrane resistance, so the same Na+ current produces a smaller voltage change, which is called shunting inhibition. Na+ does have a large driving force, but that is exactly why the inhibitory input is placed to oppose it. Chloride does not automatically override anything; the outcome depends on the relative sizes of the two conductances.
questions.answerText: It changes very little, because the Cl- current offsets the depolarizing Na+ current

questions.q: In the membrane potential simulation you change extracellular K+ and record the resting membrane potential. Which is the independent variable?
options: The intracellular K+ concentration
The number of open K+ channels
The recorded resting membrane potential
The extracellular K+ concentration
questions.why: The independent variable is the one you set, and here that is the extracellular K+ concentration you type into the simulation. The recorded membrane potential is what responds, so it is the dependent variable. Intracellular K+ is held fixed as a control variable in this protocol. The number of open channels is a property of the model rather than something the exercise asks you to manipulate.
questions.answerText: The extracellular K+ concentration

questions.q: In that same protocol, which is the dependent variable?
options: The recorded resting membrane potential
The Nernst constant of 61 mV
The extracellular K+ concentration
The temperature of the simulated bath
questions.why: The dependent variable is the measurement that changes in response to what you set, and that is the membrane potential the electrode reports. Extracellular K+ is what you manipulate, so it is independent. Bath temperature is held at 37 C as a control. The 61 mV constant is fixed by temperature and physical constants, so it is not a variable in this experiment at all.
questions.answerText: The recorded resting membrane potential

questions.q: What does the intracellular microelectrode in the simulation actually measure?
options: The total electrical charge stored in the cytosol
The potential inside the cell relative to the outside bath
The concentration of K+ in the cytosol of the cell
The rate at which ions cross the cell membrane
questions.why: A membrane potential is always a difference between two points, so the recording electrode inside is compared against a reference electrode in the bath, and the bath is defined as zero. It does not report concentrations; those are what you set in the simulation. It does not report flux rate, which would require a current measurement instead. And it reports a potential difference across the membrane, not an absolute quantity of charge in the cytosol.
questions.answerText: The potential inside the cell relative to the outside bath

questions.q: In what units should you record the membrane potential values from this simulation?
options: mmHg
mEq/L
mV
mOsm/L
questions.why: Membrane potential is a voltage, and physiological voltages are small enough that millivolts are the working unit. mEq/L is the unit for the ion concentrations you set, not for the response you record. mOsm/L measures osmolarity, a particle count. mmHg measures pressure and belongs to cardiovascular and respiratory recordings.
questions.answerText: mV

questions.q: You graph resting membrane potential against extracellular K+ concentration. Which axis should carry extracellular K+?
options: Either one, since both are measured
Neither, since it is a control variable
The vertical y axis
The horizontal x axis
questions.why: Convention puts the independent variable on the x axis and the dependent variable on the y axis, so extracellular K+ goes across the bottom and membrane potential goes up the side. Putting the manipulated variable on the y axis inverts the graph and makes the slope hard to compare with the Nernst prediction. The choice is not arbitrary, and extracellular K+ is the variable you set rather than one you hold constant.
questions.answerText: The horizontal x axis

questions.q: In the simulation you raise extracellular K+ step by step and plot the resting membrane potential each time. What trend should the graph show?
options: The resting potential becomes less negative as extracellular K+ rises
The resting potential becomes more negative as extracellular K+ rises
The resting potential stays at -70 mV no matter how much K+ you add
The resting potential swings positive as soon as any K+ is added
questions.why: More K+ outside shrinks the gradient that pushes K+ out of the cell, so E_K becomes less negative, and because the resting membrane is mostly permeable to K+, the resting potential follows it upward. The resting potential is not fixed at -70 mV; that is just its value at normal K+. It becomes more negative only when extracellular K+ is lowered, and it reaches 0 mV only when K+ is equal on both sides.
questions.answerText: The resting potential becomes less negative as extracellular K+ rises

questions.q: Which manipulation should change the resting membrane potential more in this simulation, altering extracellular K+ or altering extracellular Na+?
options: Altering extracellular Na+
Altering extracellular K+
Both change it by about the same amount
Neither changes it, since the pump compensates
questions.why: The resting membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so K+ carries most of the weight in setting the resting potential and changing it produces a large shift. Changing extracellular Na+ moves E_Na a great deal but barely moves the resting potential, because Na+ has so little permeability to vote with. That asymmetry is the central finding the exercise is designed to demonstrate, and the pump cannot compensate for a change in a large external bath.
questions.answerText: Altering extracellular K+

questions.q: While you vary extracellular K+ in this experiment, what should be held constant?
options: The recorded membrane potential
The logarithm of extracellular K+
Intracellular K+ and the other ion concentrations
Nothing, since the simulation adjusts everything automatically
questions.why: Controlled variables are everything you deliberately keep fixed so the change you see can be attributed to the one variable you manipulated. Holding intracellular K+ and the other ions steady lets you compare each measured potential against a Nernst prediction that depends only on the value you changed. The membrane potential is the response, so holding it constant would defeat the experiment. The log of extracellular K+ changes whenever extracellular K+ does, so it cannot be held fixed.
questions.answerText: Intracellular K+ and the other ion concentrations

questions.q: You raise extracellular K+ tenfold, from 5 to 50 mEq/L, with intracellular K+ unchanged. Which way does the K+ equilibrium potential shift, and what does the resting potential do?
options: E_K becomes more negative and the cell hyperpolarizes
E_K does not change because intracellular K+ did not change
E_K becomes positive and the cell fires continuously
E_K becomes less negative and the resting potential depolarizes
questions.why: Raising the outside K+ shrinks the gradient pushing K+ out, so less negative interior is needed to hold K+ in and E_K becomes less negative. The resting potential follows E_K because K+ permeability dominates at rest, so the cell depolarizes. E_K depends on the outside to inside ratio, so changing only the outside still moves it. It stays negative here because K+ is still higher inside than outside.
questions.answerText: E_K becomes less negative and the resting potential depolarizes

questions.q: You lower extracellular K+ tenfold, from 5 to 0.5 mEq/L, with intracellular K+ unchanged. Which way does the resting membrane potential move?
options: It hyperpolarizes, because a steeper K+ gradient makes E_K more negative
It does not move, because intracellular K+ did not change
It depolarizes, because less K+ is available to carry charge
It swings positive, because Na+ now dominates
questions.why: With less K+ outside, the gradient pushing K+ out is steeper, so an even more negative interior is needed to hold K+ in and E_K becomes more negative. The resting potential follows E_K downward. Depolarization is what raising extracellular K+ does. Changing only the outside value still changes the balance point, because it depends on the ratio of outside to inside. Na+ permeability stays low at rest, so it does not take over.
questions.answerText: It hyperpolarizes, because a steeper K+ gradient makes E_K more negative

questions.q: You double extracellular Na+ in the simulation and the resting membrane potential changes by only about 1 mV. What does that result tell you?
options: The Na+ concentration you entered did not register in the model
Resting Na+ permeability is very low, so Na+ contributes little at rest
The Nernst equation does not apply to Na+ in living cells
The Na+ gradient is already at equilibrium in a resting cell
questions.why: Doubling extracellular Na+ moves E_Na by about 18 mV, but the resting membrane weights each ion by its permeability, and resting Na+ permeability is perhaps a hundredth of K+ permeability, so almost none of that shift reaches the recorded potential. The small change is real data rather than an input error. Nernst applies perfectly well to Na+; what it does not do by itself is predict a multi-ion resting potential. Na+ is very far from equilibrium at rest, which is precisely why it has such a large driving force.
questions.answerText: Resting Na+ permeability is very low, so Na+ contributes little at rest

questions.q: Intracellular K+ is 150 mEq/L and extracellular K+ is 5 mEq/L. If the membrane were permeable only to K+, where would the membrane potential settle?
options: At about -70 mV, the normal resting potential
At 0 mV
At E_K, about -90 mV
At E_Na, about +60 mV
questions.why: With only one ion able to cross, the membrane potential settles at that ion's equilibrium potential, here E_K, about -90 mV. A real neuron rests near -70 mV instead because the membrane also leaks some Na+, which pulls the potential a little positive of E_K. 0 mV would require equal K+ on both sides, and E_Na matters only when the membrane is permeable to Na+.
questions.answerText: At E_K, about -90 mV

questions.q: At 5 mEq/L extracellular K+ your simulated cell records -70 mV, but the Nernst prediction was about -90 mV. What accounts for the difference?
options: The electrode was measuring the outside bath relative to the inside
The simulation was not run at body temperature
Intracellular K+ must have risen during the measurement period
The membrane is not perfectly K+ selective, and the Na+ leak pulls it positive
questions.why: A Nernst prediction assumes only one ion can cross, so it gives the potential of an ideal K+ electrode. A real membrane also leaks Na+ inward, and that inward positive current holds the resting potential about 20 mV positive of E_K, which is exactly the gap you observed. Reversing the electrode reference would flip the sign to positive, not shift it by 20 mV. Temperature has only a small effect and was held at body temperature. Intracellular K+ was held constant as a control variable.
questions.answerText: The membrane is not perfectly K+ selective, and the Na+ leak pulls it positive

questions.q: At very high extracellular K+ concentrations, your measured points fall almost exactly on the Nernst line. Why does the fit improve there?
options: At high extracellular K+ the membrane acts almost as a pure K+ electrode
At high extracellular K+ the Nernst equation switches to the divalent form
At high extracellular K+ the Na+/K+ ATPase stops working entirely
At high extracellular K+ intracellular K+ falls to match the outside value
questions.why: Raising extracellular K+ increases K+ conductance and shrinks the gap between E_K and the resting potential, so the constant Na+ leak represents a much smaller share of the total current and the measured value converges on the pure K+ prediction. The deviation is largest at low extracellular K+, where E_K is most negative and the Na+ leak has the most room to pull the potential positive. The valence of K+ never changes, the pump does not shut off, and intracellular K+ is held constant by the protocol.
questions.answerText: At high extracellular K+ the membrane acts almost as a pure K+ electrode

questions.q: Intracellular K+ is fixed at 150 mEq/L. You run the simulation at extracellular K+ of 1.5, 15, and 150 mEq/L. How should the resting potentials compare?
options: All three should be about -70 mV
Most negative at 1.5 mEq/L, less negative at 15, and near 0 mV at 150
Near 0 mV at 1.5 mEq/L, and most negative at 150
Positive at 150 mEq/L, because K+ is now higher outside
questions.why: The lower the outside K+, the steeper the gradient pushing K+ out, and the more negative the interior must be to hold it in, so 1.5 mEq/L gives the most negative potential. At 150 mEq/L K+ is equal on both sides, so there is no gradient left and E_K is 0 mV. The potentials cannot all be the same, because E_K changes with the gradient. A positive value would require more K+ outside than inside, and 150 only matches the inside value.
questions.answerText: Most negative at 1.5 mEq/L, less negative at 15, and near 0 mV at 150

questions.q: Your measured values at extracellular K+ of 1.5, 15, and 150 mEq/L are -95, -60, and -2 mV, against predictions of -122, -61, and 0 mV. Where does the Nernst model fit worst, and why?
options: The fit is equally poor at all three values, because Nernst never applies to a real membrane
At the highest extracellular K+, because the membrane stops conducting K+ at that concentration
At the lowest extracellular K+, because the resting Na+ leak pulls the potential positive of E_K
At the middle value, because that is where measurement error is always largest
questions.why: The gaps are 27 mV, 1 mV, and 2 mV, so the model fails most dramatically at 1.5 mEq/L. The reason is that E_K is most negative there, giving the steady inward Na+ leak the largest distance over which to drag the membrane potential positive, while at high extracellular K+ the K+ conductance dominates so completely that the leak barely registers. K+ conduction does not stop at high concentrations, and there is no reason for random error to peak at the middle point. Nernst works well for a real membrane wherever one ion dominates permeability, which is the pattern this data set actually shows.
questions.answerText: At the lowest extracellular K+, because the resting Na+ leak pulls the potential positive of E_K

questions.q: You add a K+ channel blocker to the simulation and repeat the whole extracellular K+ series. What happens to the slope of the line relating membrane potential to the logarithm of extracellular K+?
options: The slope is unchanged, because E_K depends only on concentrations
The line becomes vertical, because the membrane potential no longer responds
The slope becomes steeper, because each K+ ion now carries more charge
The slope becomes shallower, because Na+ permeability now carries relatively more weight
questions.why: The 61 mV per decade slope is achieved only when K+ is essentially the sole permeant ion. Blocking K+ channels lowers K+ permeability, so the fixed Na+ leak takes a larger share of the Goldman weighting and the membrane potential responds less to every change in extracellular K+, flattening the line. E_K itself is untouched, since it depends only on the concentrations, but the measured potential no longer tracks it closely, which is why the slope changes even though the prediction does not. Charge per K+ ion is fixed at plus one, and the membrane still responds, just less.
questions.answerText: The slope becomes shallower, because Na+ permeability now carries relatively more weight

questions.q: You double extracellular Na+ and the resting membrane potential barely moves. If the simulation then triggers an action potential, what should happen to its peak?
options: The peak should become somewhat more positive, because E_Na rises and the peak moves toward E_Na
The peak should become more negative, because the larger gradient slows Na+ entry
The peak should be unchanged, for the same reason the resting potential was unchanged
The peak should drop to 0 mV
questions.why: The resting potential and the peak are set by different permeability conditions, and that contrast is the point of this pair of measurements. At rest Na+ permeability is very low, so E_Na hardly matters. At the peak Na+ permeability dominates, so the membrane potential approaches E_Na. A steeper Na+ gradient makes E_Na more positive, so the peak climbs. A steeper inward gradient speeds Na+ entry rather than slowing it, and a peak at 0 mV is what equal Na+ on both sides would produce.
questions.answerText: The peak should become somewhat more positive, because E_Na rises and the peak moves toward E_Na

questions.q: Which arrangement of processes defines a multipolar neuron?
options: Two processes, one dendrite and one axon, at opposite ends
One process that leaves the cell body and then splits in two
Many dendrites and a single axon leaving the cell body
Many axons and a single dendrite leaving the cell body
questions.why: Multipolar means many poles: numerous dendrites plus one axon, so the cell can gather input from thousands of synapses and send one output. A single process that branches in two is the pseudounipolar pattern of sensory ganglion cells. Two processes at opposite ends describe a bipolar neuron. No neuron carries many axons, because each cell has a single trigger zone and one all-or-none output line.
questions.answerText: Many dendrites and a single axon leaving the cell body

questions.q: Which structural class has exactly two processes, one dendrite and one axon, extending from opposite ends of the cell body?
options: Bipolar
Pseudounipolar
Multipolar
Anaxonic
questions.why: A bipolar neuron has one receptive process and one axon leaving from opposite poles, an arrangement that suits a cell relaying a signal straight through. Multipolar cells have many dendrites and one axon. Pseudounipolar cells have a single stalk that splits into peripheral and central branches. Anaxonic neurons have no process identifiable as an axon and are found in small numbers in the retina and brain.
questions.answerText: Bipolar

questions.q: In a pseudounipolar neuron, where does the cell body sit relative to the conducting pathway?
options: At the receptive end, where the stimulus is transduced
In line with the axon, midway along the conducting path
Inside the spinal cord, at the central end of the fiber
Off to one side of a single process the signal runs along
questions.why: The single stalk splits into a peripheral branch and a central branch, and the cell body hangs off that stalk, so the action potential travels straight past it. Putting the cell body at the receptive end describes a bipolar sensory cell such as an olfactory neuron. Placing it in line with the axon would force every signal through the soma and slow conduction. The cell body of these neurons lies in a ganglion outside the cord, not inside it.
questions.answerText: Off to one side of a single process the signal runs along

questions.q: A neuron whose axon carries signals from a skin receptor toward the spinal cord is called what?
options: An afferent neuron
An efferent neuron
An interneuron
A preganglionic neuron
questions.why: Afferent means carried toward the central nervous system, which is exactly what a sensory fiber does. Efferent is the opposite direction, out from the CNS to muscle or gland. An interneuron lies entirely inside the CNS and connects other neurons rather than reaching a receptor. A preganglionic neuron is a specific kind of efferent cell in the autonomic system, so it also points away from the CNS.
questions.answerText: An afferent neuron

questions.q: Which functional class accounts for the great majority of neurons in the human nervous system?
options: Sensory neurons
Motor neurons
Preganglionic autonomic neurons
Interneurons
questions.why: Interneurons vastly outnumber the other classes because almost all of the brain and spinal cord is devoted to processing between input and output. Sensory neurons are numerous but are limited to the afferent pathways. Motor neurons are the smallest group, since many inputs converge onto each one before it drives a muscle. Preganglionic autonomic cells are a small subset of the motor side.
questions.answerText: Interneurons

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of the pseudounipolar neurons that carry skin sensation located?
options: In the dorsal horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the dorsal root ganglion, outside the spinal cord
In the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the skin itself, next to the sensory ending
questions.why: These first-order sensory cell bodies cluster in the dorsal root ganglion, a swelling on the dorsal root just outside the cord. The dorsal horn holds the second-order neurons these fibers synapse on, not the sensory cell bodies themselves. The ventral horn holds somatic motor neurons. The peripheral ending in the skin is only the receptive terminal; the nucleus and protein synthesis stay in the ganglion.
questions.answerText: In the dorsal root ganglion, outside the spinal cord

questions.q: Bipolar neurons are found in which locations in the human body?
options: The dorsal root ganglia and the autonomic ganglia
The ventral horn and the cerebral cortex
The retina and the olfactory epithelium
The cerebellum and the hippocampus
questions.why: Bipolar cells serve special senses where a signal is passed straight along a short chain, notably the retina and the olfactory epithelium, with a similar pattern in the inner ear. Dorsal root ganglia hold pseudounipolar cells, and autonomic ganglia hold multipolar ones. The ventral horn, cortex, cerebellum and hippocampus are all populated by multipolar neurons that integrate many inputs.
questions.answerText: The retina and the olfactory epithelium

questions.q: A somatic motor neuron in the ventral horn belongs to which structural class?
options: Bipolar
Multipolar
Pseudounipolar
Anaxonic
questions.why: A motor neuron must sum input from descending tracts, afferent fibers and local interneurons before it fires, and the multipolar shape with many dendrites provides that receptive surface. Bipolar cells relay a single line of information and are limited to special sensory epithelia. Pseudounipolar cells are sensory, with cell bodies in ganglia. An anaxonic cell has no axon and so could not drive a muscle a meter away.
questions.answerText: Multipolar

questions.q: A retinal neuron has one short process ending on photoreceptors and a single axon leaving the opposite side of the cell body. Which structural class is it?
options: Multipolar
Bipolar
Pseudounipolar
Anaxonic
questions.why: Two processes leaving opposite poles is the definition of bipolar, and the retina is one of the few places this class appears. Multipolar would require many dendrites converging on the soma. Pseudounipolar would show a single stalk splitting into two branches with the soma set off to the side. An anaxonic cell would have no identifiable axon at all, so the described axon rules it out.
questions.answerText: Bipolar

questions.q: A neuron has its cell body in a dorsal root ganglion, a peripheral branch ending in a muscle spindle, and a central branch entering the spinal cord. Which structural class is it?
options: Pseudounipolar
Multipolar
Anaxonic
Bipolar
questions.why: One stalk that divides into a peripheral and a central branch, with the soma parked in a ganglion off to the side, is the pseudounipolar plan used by essentially all first-order somatic sensory neurons. Bipolar cells have their soma between the two processes rather than off to the side. Multipolar cells have many dendrites and are the integrating cells of the CNS. Anaxonic cells lack an axon and cannot project a meter to the cord.
questions.answerText: Pseudounipolar

questions.q: A neuron lies entirely within the spinal cord gray matter, receiving input from an incoming sensory fiber and synapsing on a motor neuron. Which functional class is it?
options: An afferent neuron
An efferent neuron
An interneuron
A postganglionic neuron
questions.why: A cell that begins and ends inside the central nervous system, bridging input to output, is by definition an interneuron. An afferent neuron would have to reach a receptor in the periphery. An efferent neuron would have to send its axon out of the CNS to a muscle or gland. A postganglionic autonomic neuron sits in a peripheral ganglion, outside the cord entirely.
questions.answerText: An interneuron

questions.q: An axon leaves the brainstem and ends on a salivary gland. Which functional class does this neuron belong to?
options: Efferent
Afferent
Interneuron
Second-order sensory
questions.why: The axon carries the signal away from the CNS to an effector, and a gland is an effector just as a muscle is, so the cell is efferent. Afferent would require the signal to travel toward the CNS from a receptor. An interneuron never leaves the CNS. A second-order sensory neuron carries sensation upward inside the CNS and does not innervate glands.
questions.answerText: Efferent

questions.q: Why does the multipolar shape suit a neuron that must combine input from thousands of other neurons?
options: Its single stalk lets signals bypass the cell body entirely
Its two processes keep the input and output paths separate
Its short axon prevents any loss of signal between cells
Its many dendrites give a large surface for synaptic input
questions.why: Dendritic branching multiplies membrane area, and each patch of that area can host synapses whose graded potentials then sum at the trigger zone. Bypassing the soma through a single stalk is the pseudounipolar arrangement, which favors speed rather than integration. Separating input from output along two processes describes a bipolar relay cell. Multipolar axons are often long, and axon length is not what makes the cell a good integrator.
questions.answerText: Its many dendrites give a large surface for synaptic input

questions.q: In a pseudounipolar sensory neuron, what happens to an action potential traveling from the skin toward the spinal cord when it reaches the level of the cell body?
options: It stops, and a new potential is started in the central branch
It is amplified by the cell body before it continues centrally
It stays on the shared stalk and bypasses the cell body
It reverses direction and travels back toward the receptor
questions.why: The soma sits on a side stalk, so the impulse runs continuously from the peripheral branch into the central branch without a synapse or a detour, which keeps conduction fast. Nothing stops and restarts, because there is no synapse within a single neuron. The cell body does not amplify impulses; action potential size is set by the axon membrane. Backward travel is prevented by the refractory period behind the impulse.
questions.answerText: It stays on the shared stalk and bypasses the cell body

questions.q: A peripheral ganglion is examined and every neuron in it has a single process leaving a round cell body wrapped by satellite cells. Which functional class are these neurons?
options: Somatic efferent neurons supplying skeletal muscle
Afferent neurons carrying sensation to the CNS
Interneurons of the spinal cord gray matter
Postganglionic sympathetic neurons supplying blood vessels
questions.why: A single process is the pseudounipolar giveaway, and pseudounipolar cell bodies in peripheral ganglia are sensory, so this is a dorsal root or cranial sensory ganglion. Somatic motor cell bodies never sit in peripheral ganglia; they stay in the ventral horn or brainstem. Interneurons are confined to the CNS. Postganglionic sympathetic neurons do live in peripheral ganglia, but they are multipolar and would show several dendrites.
questions.answerText: Afferent neurons carrying sensation to the CNS

questions.q: A single spinal dorsal root is cut. Predict the effect in the region that root serves and name the class of neuron lost.
options: Movement is lost, sensation is spared, multipolar efferents cut
Sensation is lost, movement is spared, pseudounipolar afferents cut
Both are lost, because the root carries afferent and efferent fibers
Neither is lost, because interneurons reroute around the cut root
questions.why: The dorsal root carries only the central branches of pseudounipolar sensory neurons, so cutting it removes input while leaving the ventral root motor output intact. Lost movement with spared sensation describes a ventral root lesion instead. Afferent and efferent fibers do travel together, but only after the two roots join to form the spinal nerve, so at the root itself they are separable. Interneurons cannot substitute for information that never reaches the cord.
questions.answerText: Sensation is lost, movement is spared, pseudounipolar afferents cut

questions.q: After an injury, a muscle is paralyzed but skin sensation over that muscle is normal. Which neurons were damaged and where do their cell bodies lie?
options: Pseudounipolar afferents with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion
Bipolar relay neurons with cell bodies inside the dorsal horn
Multipolar efferents with cell bodies in the ventral horn
Interneurons with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion
questions.why: Preserved sensation with lost movement isolates the lesion to the efferent limb, and somatic motor neurons are multipolar cells whose somata sit in the ventral horn. Damaging pseudounipolar afferents would have produced the opposite pattern, numbness with intact strength. Bipolar neurons are not found in the spinal cord at all. Interneurons live in the CNS, not in a peripheral ganglion, so that pairing is impossible.
questions.answerText: Multipolar efferents with cell bodies in the ventral horn

questions.q: A disease destroys the bipolar neurons of the retina while photoreceptors and ganglion cells survive. What is the predicted result?
options: Light is still transduced but the signal cannot reach the ganglion cells
Ganglion cells fire continuously once their normal inhibition is removed
Vision is unaffected, since photoreceptors contact ganglion cells directly
Light is no longer transduced, so no receptor potential is generated
questions.why: Bipolar cells are the relay in the retinal chain from photoreceptor to ganglion cell, so losing them breaks the path even though transduction and the output neurons are intact. Photoreceptors do not synapse directly on ganglion cells, which is why the bipolar layer matters. Loss of a relay removes drive rather than removing inhibition, so continuous firing is not expected. Transduction happens in the photoreceptor outer segment and is untouched here.
questions.answerText: Light is still transduced but the signal cannot reach the ganglion cells

questions.q: A toxin destroys most interneurons in the spinal cord gray matter but spares afferent and efferent neurons. Which response is most impaired?
options: Transduction at the sensory receptor in the skin
Transmission at the neuromuscular junction
The monosynaptic stretch reflex, such as the knee jerk
Polysynaptic withdrawal reflexes from a painful stimulus
questions.why: A withdrawal reflex routes the afferent signal through one or more interneurons before reaching motor neurons, so removing interneurons breaks the circuit. Receptor transduction is a property of the afferent ending and needs no interneuron. Neuromuscular transmission happens between a motor neuron and muscle, well outside the cord. The stretch reflex is the useful contrast: its afferent synapses directly on the motor neuron, so it survives when interneurons are lost.
questions.answerText: Polysynaptic withdrawal reflexes from a painful stimulus

questions.q: Which type of electrical signal do the dendrites of a neuron carry?
options: Graded potentials that vary in size with the input
All-or-none action potentials of fixed amplitude
End plate potentials generated by acetylcholine
Pacemaker potentials that depolarize on a set schedule
questions.why: Dendritic membrane responds to transmitter with graded potentials whose amplitude tracks how much transmitter bound and which fade as they spread toward the soma. Action potentials are all-or-none and begin only at the trigger zone, where voltage-gated Na+ channels are dense. End plate potentials are the graded response of skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction, not of a dendrite. Pacemaker potentials belong to cardiac nodal and some smooth muscle cells.
questions.answerText: Graded potentials that vary in size with the input
