questions.q: Which region of a neuron is the trigger zone, where action potentials are initiated?
options: The tips of the dendrites, where transmitter first binds
The axon hillock and the initial segment of the axon
The center of the cell body, next to the nucleus
The axon terminal, just before transmitter is released
questions.why: The trigger zone is the cone-shaped hillock plus the first stretch of axon, the place where summed graded potentials are read against threshold. Dendritic tips receive input but lack the channel density to fire. The soma conducts graded signals toward the hillock but does not initiate them. The terminal is the output end, and by the time the impulse arrives there the decision to fire has already been made.
questions.answerText: The axon hillock and the initial segment of the axon

questions.q: Which membrane property of the trigger zone explains why the action potential starts there rather than on a dendrite?
options: It has the thinnest membrane in the whole neuron
It has the largest surface area of any neuronal region
It has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels
It has the greatest number of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps
questions.why: Packing voltage-gated Na+ channels into the hillock and initial segment lowers the threshold there, so that region reaches firing level before any other part of the cell. Membrane thickness is essentially uniform across a cell and is not what sets excitability. Dendrites, not the hillock, carry the largest surface area, which is why they receive input rather than initiate output. Na+/K+ ATPase maintains the gradients over minutes and hours but does not generate the upstroke of an action potential.
questions.answerText: It has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels

questions.q: What kind of signal travels along the axon?
options: Graded potentials that shrink as they travel
Receptor potentials proportional to stimulus strength
Action potentials of constant, all-or-none amplitude
Slow waves that set a rhythm for firing
questions.why: Once threshold is crossed the axon regenerates the same size impulse at every point along its length, which is what lets a signal reach a target a meter away without fading. Graded potentials do shrink with distance, which is exactly why they cannot serve as the long-distance signal. Receptor potentials are graded events at sensory endings. Slow waves are a smooth muscle phenomenon, not a feature of axons.
questions.answerText: Action potentials of constant, all-or-none amplitude

questions.q: What is the immediate result of an action potential arriving at the axon terminal?
options: Transmitter is synthesized from precursors delivered by the soma
The Na+/K+ ATPase reverses and pumps Na+ back inward
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ enters the terminal
The terminal membrane becomes permanently depolarized
questions.why: Depolarization of the terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and the Ca2+ that rushes in is the signal that makes vesicles fuse and release transmitter. The Na+/K+ ATPase never reverses under physiological conditions; it restores gradients in one direction only. Transmitter synthesis happens over minutes to hours and is not the immediate event triggered by one impulse. The terminal repolarizes within milliseconds, so permanent depolarization would mean the cell had failed.
questions.answerText: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ enters the terminal

questions.q: Which function belongs to the cell body of a neuron?
options: Synthesizing the proteins that the rest of the neuron needs
Releasing neurotransmitter onto the next cell in the circuit
Initiating the action potential once threshold is reached
Regenerating the impulse at each node along the axon
questions.why: The soma holds the nucleus and the rough endoplasmic reticulum seen as Nissl substance, so it makes the channels, enzymes and cytoskeletal proteins that keep a long axon working. Initiating the impulse is the job of the trigger zone just downstream. Transmitter release happens at the terminal. Regeneration of the impulse at nodes is an axonal event and does not involve the cell body at all.
questions.answerText: Synthesizing the proteins that the rest of the neuron needs

questions.q: What is the axon hillock?
options: The swelling at the end of the axon that stores vesicles
The gap in the myelin sheath along the length of the axon
The branching region where dendrites leave the cell body
The cone-shaped part of the cell body where the axon begins
questions.why: The hillock is the tapering region of the soma from which the axon emerges, and together with the initial segment it forms the trigger zone. The swelling at the far end is the axon terminal, the release site. Dendrites arise from the soma too, but that region has no special name and no concentration of voltage-gated channels. A gap in myelin is a node of Ranvier, which lies far downstream along the axon.
questions.answerText: The cone-shaped part of the cell body where the axon begins

questions.q: Which statement describes a graded potential?
options: Its size varies with the stimulus and it decays with distance
It travels the length of the axon without losing amplitude
It cannot be summed with other potentials in the same cell
It is the same size no matter how strong the stimulus is
questions.why: Graded means the response scales with the input, and because current leaks across the membrane as it spreads, the signal is smaller the farther it travels from where it started. A fixed size regardless of stimulus describes the all-or-none action potential. Traveling without decrement is also an action potential property, achieved by regenerating the signal. Summation is precisely what graded potentials are for, since it is how the trigger zone adds up its inputs.
questions.answerText: Its size varies with the stimulus and it decays with distance

questions.q: Two identical excitatory synapses fire, one on a distal dendrite and one on the cell body near the hillock. Which produces the larger depolarization at the trigger zone?
options: The dendritic synapse, because dendrites amplify their own input
The synapse on the cell body, because its signal decays less
Both equally, because graded potentials do not lose amplitude
Neither, because only the axon can carry signals to the hillock
questions.why: A graded potential loses amplitude as it spreads, so the input starting closest to the trigger zone arrives with more of its depolarization intact. Dendrites do not amplify; they receive and conduct passively in most neurons. Loss of amplitude with distance is the defining weakness of graded potentials, so equality is not expected. The soma and dendrites conduct these local currents perfectly well toward the hillock, which is how integration happens at all.
questions.answerText: The synapse on the cell body, because its signal decays less

questions.q: A sensory stimulus is doubled in strength. What happens to the action potentials the neuron sends down its axon?
options: They become twice as large but keep the same frequency
They become both larger and more frequent
They stay the same size but occur more frequently
They stop, because the axon is overloaded by the input
questions.why: The all-or-none rule fixes action potential amplitude, so intensity has to be coded some other way, and the nervous system uses firing frequency. Doubling the amplitude would violate the all-or-none property of the axon membrane. Since amplitude cannot change, the combined option fails for the same reason. Very strong input increases firing rate up to a limit set by the refractory period, but it does not silence the axon.
questions.answerText: They stay the same size but occur more frequently

questions.q: A drug blocks the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the axon terminal only. Predict what happens when an action potential reaches that terminal.
options: The impulse fails partway along the axon before reaching the terminal
The impulse arrives normally but no transmitter is released
The trigger zone can no longer reach threshold and stops firing
Transmitter is released continuously instead of in response to firing
questions.why: Conduction along the axon depends on voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels, so the impulse still arrives; what is lost is the Ca2+ entry that couples arrival to vesicle fusion. Conduction failure would require blocking axonal Na+ channels rather than terminal Ca2+ channels. The trigger zone lies far upstream of the drug and is unaffected. Blocking Ca2+ entry removes the release signal rather than making release continuous.
questions.answerText: The impulse arrives normally but no transmitter is released

questions.q: An action potential is recorded at the trigger zone and again halfway down an unbranched axon. How do the two amplitudes compare?
options: The two are the same, because the impulse is regenerated as it travels
The midpoint signal is larger, because the axon narrows along its length
The midpoint signal is about half as large, because current leaks out
The midpoint signal is smaller only if the stimulus was weak
questions.why: Each patch of axon membrane opens its own voltage-gated Na+ channels and rebuilds the impulse at full size, so amplitude is preserved from hillock to terminal. Decay with distance is a property of graded potentials, which do not regenerate. Axon diameter affects conduction speed rather than impulse height, and a narrowing axon would not raise amplitude. Stimulus strength sets firing frequency, not the size of any single action potential.
questions.answerText: The two are the same, because the impulse is regenerated as it travels

questions.q: Two excitatory synapses on different dendrites of the same neuron are active at the same instant, and together they bring the trigger zone to threshold. What is this called?
options: Temporal summation
Saltatory conduction
Accommodation
Spatial summation
questions.why: Inputs arriving at the same moment from different places on the cell add together at the trigger zone, which is spatial summation. Temporal summation is the other route to threshold, where one input repeats quickly enough that each graded potential builds on the last. Saltatory conduction describes impulses jumping between nodes along a myelinated axon, a different process entirely. Accommodation is the loss of excitability during a slow depolarization.
questions.answerText: Spatial summation

questions.q: An inhibitory synapse on the cell body produces a hyperpolarizing graded potential just as an excitatory input arrives. What is the effect at the trigger zone?
options: The excitatory input is blocked from reaching the trigger zone
The inhibitory signal cancels the action potential after it starts
The two sum, so the membrane is less likely to reach threshold
The threshold voltage itself is shifted to a more negative value
questions.why: Graded potentials add algebraically, so a hyperpolarizing input subtracts from a depolarizing one and the net voltage at the trigger zone falls short of threshold more easily. An action potential, once started, runs to completion and cannot be canceled midway. The excitatory potential is not blocked; it still spreads to the hillock and simply meets opposition. Threshold is a property of the channels at the trigger zone and does not move because of a synaptic input.
questions.answerText: The two sum, so the membrane is less likely to reach threshold

questions.q: You want to record a signal whose amplitude changes when you change how much transmitter is applied. Which region should you place the electrode in?
options: The middle of the axon
A dendrite or the cell body
The initial segment, just past the hillock
A node of Ranvier along the axon
questions.why: Only the graded signals of the dendrites and soma scale with input size, so that is where a dose-dependent amplitude shows up. The axon carries all-or-none impulses whose amplitude is fixed no matter how strong the input was. A node of Ranvier is simply a point on the axon and follows the same all-or-none rule. The initial segment is where the graded signal is converted into a fixed-size impulse, so recordings there already show the all-or-none output.
questions.answerText: A dendrite or the cell body

questions.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV and fires at -55 mV. One excitatory input starts as a 15 mV depolarization at a dendrite but has decayed to 5 mV by the time it reaches the trigger zone. How many such inputs must arrive together to fire the cell?
options: Two
Five
One, because the dendritic value is what counts
Three
questions.why: The cell needs 15 mV of depolarization at the trigger zone to move from -70 to -55, and each input delivers 5 mV there, so three simultaneous inputs are required. Two would give only 10 mV and leave the membrane at -60 mV, still below threshold. Using the 15 mV starting value ignores the decay that happens on the way, which is the whole point of the calculation. Five would be more than needed, since 15 mV is reached at three.
questions.answerText: Three

questions.q: A local anesthetic is applied to a narrow band in the middle of an axon, blocking voltage-gated Na+ channels there only. Predict the recordings at the trigger zone and at the axon terminal.
options: No impulse at either site, because the whole neuron is silenced
Normal impulses at the trigger zone but none at the terminal
Normal impulses at both sites, since the block affects only speed
Impulses at the terminal only, arriving from the opposite direction
questions.why: Synaptic input and threshold detection happen upstream of the drug, so the trigger zone fires normally, but the impulse cannot regenerate through the blocked band and dies there, leaving the terminal silent. The neuron is not silenced everywhere, because the anesthetic reaches only the treated band. Blocking Na+ channels prevents regeneration outright rather than slowing it. Nothing generates impulses distal to the block, so the terminal has no other source.
questions.answerText: Normal impulses at the trigger zone but none at the terminal

questions.q: A neuron is altered so that the threshold at its trigger zone moves from -55 mV to -45 mV, with the resting potential unchanged at -70 mV. What is the predicted effect on the cell?
options: It needs more summed input to fire, so it fires less readily
It fires at the same rate, since threshold does not affect firing
It fires continuously, since the resting potential now exceeds threshold
It fires more readily, since threshold is now closer to zero
questions.why: The gap between rest and threshold widens from 15 mV to 25 mV, so more excitatory input must sum at the trigger zone before an impulse is produced. Being closer to zero is not the same as being easier to reach; what matters is the distance from the resting potential. Threshold sets the firing decision directly, so it certainly affects rate. The resting potential of -70 mV is still well below -45 mV, so spontaneous firing would not occur.
questions.answerText: It needs more summed input to fire, so it fires less readily

questions.q: A neuron fires steady trains of action potentials even when every synapse onto it is blocked. Which change best explains this?
options: Its cell body has stopped synthesizing membrane proteins
Its dendrites have lost the ability to generate graded potentials
Its axon terminal is releasing transmitter without Ca2+ entry
Its resting potential has drifted up to threshold at the trigger zone
questions.why: With no synaptic drive, the only way the trigger zone can keep reaching threshold is for the membrane potential itself to sit at or above threshold, which happens when the resting potential becomes less negative. Losing dendritic graded potentials would reduce firing, not cause it. Runaway release at the terminal would affect the next cell downstream and could not generate impulses at the trigger zone. Halting protein synthesis in the soma degrades the neuron over days rather than driving it to fire.
questions.answerText: Its resting potential has drifted up to threshold at the trigger zone

questions.q: Which glial cell forms the myelin sheath around axons in the brain and spinal cord?
options: The oligodendrocyte
The astrocyte
The Schwann cell
The microglial cell
questions.why: Oligodendrocytes wrap central axons, sending out several arms so that one cell myelinates segments on many different axons. Astrocytes support synapses and the blood brain barrier but make no myelin. Schwann cells do make myelin, but only in the peripheral nervous system. Microglia are the immune cells of the CNS and remove debris rather than insulate axons.
questions.answerText: The oligodendrocyte

questions.q: Which glial cell myelinates axons in peripheral nerves?
options: The satellite cell
The oligodendrocyte
The Schwann cell
The ependymal cell
questions.why: Schwann cells wrap peripheral axons, one cell per internode, and the same cell type also ensheathes unmyelinated peripheral fibers. Satellite cells are the other peripheral glia, but they surround cell bodies in ganglia rather than axons. Oligodendrocytes do the equivalent job in the CNS only. Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and have no role in myelination.
questions.answerText: The Schwann cell

questions.q: Which glial cell lines the ventricles of the brain and helps produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid?
options: The oligodendrocyte
The astrocyte
The microglial cell
The ependymal cell
questions.why: Ependymal cells form the epithelium lining the ventricles and central canal, and their cilia keep cerebrospinal fluid moving while specialized ependymal cells of the choroid plexus secrete it. Astrocytes touch capillaries and help regulate what enters the brain, but they do not secrete cerebrospinal fluid. Microglia are phagocytes. Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating cells of the CNS.
questions.answerText: The ependymal cell

questions.q: Which cell serves as the resident phagocyte and immune defender of the central nervous system?
options: The astrocyte
The satellite cell
The microglial cell
The ependymal cell
questions.why: Microglia patrol the CNS, engulf pathogens and dead cells, and prune damaged synapses, which makes them the immune arm of nervous tissue. Astrocytes react to injury by forming a scar, but they are not phagocytes. Satellite cells support neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia. Ependymal cells line fluid spaces and have no defensive role.
questions.answerText: The microglial cell

questions.q: Which glial cell takes up excess K+ from the extracellular fluid around active neurons?
options: The astrocyte
The microglial cell
The Schwann cell
The oligodendrocyte
questions.why: Astrocytes soak up the K+ that leaks out during repeated action potentials and spread it through their network, which keeps extracellular K+ near 4 mEq/L and keeps neurons from drifting toward threshold. Oligodendrocytes insulate axons and take no part in ion buffering. Microglia respond to damage. Schwann cells are peripheral and support single axons rather than managing the ionic environment of the brain.
questions.answerText: The astrocyte

questions.q: Which cells surround and support neuron cell bodies inside peripheral ganglia?
options: Microglia
Astrocytes
Ependymal cells
Satellite cells
questions.why: Satellite cells form a capsule around the somata in dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, regulating the chemical environment much as astrocytes do centrally. Astrocytes perform that role, but only inside the CNS. Ependymal cells are confined to the ventricles and central canal. Microglia are also CNS residents and are phagocytic rather than supportive.
questions.answerText: Satellite cells

questions.q: Which glial cell is the most abundant in the central nervous system?
options: The microglial cell
The ependymal cell
The astrocyte
The Schwann cell
questions.why: Astrocytes are the most numerous glia in the brain and spinal cord, which fits the breadth of their jobs: potassium buffering, transmitter clearance, metabolic support and induction of the blood brain barrier. Microglia are a small fraction of the total. Ependymal cells are limited to the lining of fluid spaces. Schwann cells are numerous but are peripheral cells and are not found in the CNS at all.
questions.answerText: The astrocyte

questions.q: Which glial cell clears glutamate from the synaptic cleft after excitatory transmission?
options: The astrocyte
The microglial cell
The oligodendrocyte
The ependymal cell
questions.why: Astrocyte processes wrap synapses and carry transporters that pull glutamate out of the cleft, ending the signal and protecting neurons from overexcitation. Microglia sample the environment for damage but do not perform transmitter reuptake. Oligodendrocytes contact axons rather than synapses. Ependymal cells line the ventricles, far from most synapses.
questions.answerText: The astrocyte

questions.q: How does the relationship between a myelinating cell and the axons it serves differ between the CNS and the PNS?
options: One Schwann cell serves many axons, while an oligodendrocyte serves one
One oligodendrocyte serves several axons, one Schwann cell serves one
Both cell types wrap exactly one internode on exactly one axon
Both cell types wrap the entire length of a single axon by themselves
questions.why: An oligodendrocyte extends multiple processes and myelinates an internode on each of several nearby central axons, while a Schwann cell wraps its whole body around a single internode of a single peripheral axon. Giving the Schwann cell the many-axon job reverses the two cell types. Restricting both to one internode on one axon ignores the branching of oligodendrocytes. No glial cell myelinates a whole axon by itself, which is why nodes of Ranvier exist between successive cells.
questions.answerText: One oligodendrocyte serves several axons, one Schwann cell serves one

questions.q: Astrocyte potassium uptake fails in a region of cortex during heavy neuronal activity. Predict what happens to the neurons there.
options: Nothing changes, because the Na+/K+ ATPase handles all K+ removal
Extracellular K+ falls, the neurons hyperpolarize and become silent
Extracellular Na+ rises, so action potentials become larger than normal
Extracellular K+ rises, the neurons depolarize and become more excitable
questions.why: Each action potential leaks K+ into a small extracellular space, and if astrocytes do not take it up, the K+ equilibrium potential moves toward zero and drags the resting potential closer to threshold. Falling K+ would hyperpolarize cells, which is the opposite of what unbuffered activity produces. Sodium influx during firing tends to lower extracellular Na+ slightly rather than raise it. The pump helps restore gradients but works too slowly on its own to hold extracellular K+ steady during bursts of firing.
questions.answerText: Extracellular K+ rises, the neurons depolarize and become more excitable

questions.q: Bacteria reach the brain tissue of a patient. Which glial cell population responds first by multiplying and engulfing the invaders?
options: Oligodendrocytes
Microglia
Satellite cells
Ependymal cells
questions.why: Microglia are derived from the same lineage as macrophages, and they proliferate and phagocytose when they detect pathogens or debris in nervous tissue. Oligodendrocytes are highly specialized for making myelin and cannot phagocytose. Ependymal cells line fluid spaces and provide no defense. Satellite cells exist only in peripheral ganglia, so they cannot respond to an infection in the brain.
questions.answerText: Microglia

questions.q: A narrow ependymal-lined channel between two ventricles becomes blocked while cerebrospinal fluid continues to be produced upstream. What is the immediate consequence?
options: Production stops at once, so total fluid volume stays normal
Fluid accumulates upstream and pressure inside the ventricle rises
The blood brain barrier opens to let the extra fluid escape
Astrocytes take over fluid production to bypass the block
questions.why: Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted continuously, so if the outflow path is closed the fluid backs up behind the obstruction and stretches the ventricle. Secretion by choroid plexus does not shut off in response to a downstream block. The blood brain barrier controls solute movement between blood and brain and is not a drainage route. Astrocytes support the barrier but do not secrete cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.answerText: Fluid accumulates upstream and pressure inside the ventricle rises

questions.q: A drug blocks astrocyte glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses. Predict the effect on the postsynaptic neuron.
options: Glutamate lingers in the cleft, so excitation lasts longer than normal
Glutamate is never released, so the neuron receives no excitation at all
Glutamate is converted to an inhibitory transmitter in the cleft
The postsynaptic membrane becomes impermeable to Na+ and Ca2+
questions.why: Astrocyte uptake is the main way glutamate is removed, so blocking it leaves transmitter bound to receptors and prolongs the excitatory postsynaptic potential, an effect that can become damaging if it continues. Release from the presynaptic terminal is a separate process and is untouched. Nothing in the cleft converts glutamate into an inhibitory transmitter. Postsynaptic channel proteins are not blocked by a transporter inhibitor.
questions.answerText: Glutamate lingers in the cleft, so excitation lasts longer than normal

questions.q: Astrocyte end feet help induce tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells. What does this predict about which substances enter the brain easily?
options: All molecules cross freely, since the junctions only slow blood flow
Only large proteins cross, because they are carried across in vesicles
Small lipid-soluble molecules cross while water-soluble ones need carriers
Water-soluble molecules cross freely and lipid-soluble ones are excluded
questions.why: Tight junctions close off the path between endothelial cells, so entry has to be through the cell membranes, which favors small lipid-soluble molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and many anesthetics. Free passage for everything is exactly what the barrier prevents. Large proteins are the least likely to cross, not the most. Saying water-soluble molecules pass freely reverses the chemistry, since it is lipid solubility, not water solubility, that lets a substance slip through a membrane.
questions.answerText: Small lipid-soluble molecules cross while water-soluble ones need carriers

questions.q: A peripheral nerve is crushed but the connective tissue sheath stays intact. Which glial cell makes regrowth of the severed axons possible?
options: The oligodendrocyte
The astrocyte
The Schwann cell
The ependymal cell
questions.why: Schwann cells survive the injury, clear debris with macrophages, and line up in columns that guide the regrowing axon back toward its target, which is why peripheral nerves can recover. Oligodendrocytes are central cells, and the molecules they leave behind actively inhibit regrowth. Astrocytes react to central injury by forming a dense scar that also blocks regeneration. Ependymal cells have no role in peripheral repair.
questions.answerText: The Schwann cell

questions.q: An autoimmune attack targets a protein found only in oligodendrocyte myelin. Which pattern of deficits is predicted?
options: Weakness in the hands and feet only, with the brain entirely spared
Loss of cerebrospinal fluid production and enlarging ventricles
Loss of sensation in dorsal root ganglia with normal central conduction
Brain, spinal cord and optic nerve lesions with peripheral nerves spared
questions.why: Oligodendrocytes myelinate only central axons, and the optic nerve is a central tract despite its name, so an antibody against their myelin produces scattered central lesions while Schwann cell myelin in peripheral nerves is untouched. A pure hands and feet pattern points to peripheral myelin instead. Cerebrospinal fluid production depends on ependymal cells, which carry different proteins. Dorsal root ganglion cell bodies are supported by satellite cells, so they are not the target here.
questions.answerText: Brain, spinal cord and optic nerve lesions with peripheral nerves spared

questions.q: During a stroke, astrocytes near the damaged tissue lose ATP and can no longer run their glutamate transporters. Trace the consequence for nearby neurons.
options: Glutamate is trapped inside astrocytes, so nearby synapses go silent
Glutamate builds up, drives excess Ca2+ entry, and injures nearby neurons
Neurons hyperpolarize and are protected from further damage
Myelin is stripped from nearby axons by the excess transmitter
questions.why: Glutamate uptake is an active process, so when ATP fails the transmitter accumulates, overstimulates receptors, and lets enough Ca2+ into neurons to trigger destructive enzymes, which is how injury spreads into tissue that was initially viable. Failing transporters leave glutamate outside the astrocyte rather than trapping it inside. Excess glutamate depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizes its targets. Demyelination is an immune or metabolic process affecting the myelinating cell, not a direct action of transmitter.
questions.answerText: Glutamate builds up, drives excess Ca2+ entry, and injures nearby neurons

questions.q: The narrow passage draining one ventricle is obstructed by a tumor. Put the resulting events in the right order.
options: The ventricle collapses, then secretion rises to refill the space
Secretion continues, fluid accumulates, the ventricle expands on brain tissue
Microglia secrete extra fluid to flush the obstruction away
Astrocytes absorb the extra fluid, so pressure never changes
questions.why: Choroid plexus secretion is not regulated by downstream pressure, so it continues, fluid piles up behind the block, and the expanding ventricle compresses the surrounding tissue. A ventricle upstream of a block fills rather than collapses. Microglia are phagocytes and secrete no fluid. Astrocytes buffer ions and support the barrier but cannot absorb a continuously produced fluid volume fast enough to prevent a rise in pressure.
questions.answerText: Secretion continues, fluid accumulates, the ventricle expands on brain tissue

questions.q: The same patient severs a nerve in the forearm and a tract in the spinal cord. The forearm recovers function over months while the cord deficit is permanent. Which glial difference best explains this?
options: Schwann cells guide peripheral regrowth while central glia obstruct it
Central neurons lack cell bodies capable of protein synthesis after injury
Peripheral axons are shorter, so they need less axonal transport to regrow
Microglia remove peripheral debris but are absent from the spinal cord
questions.why: The peripheral environment is permissive because Schwann cells proliferate, form guiding columns, and release growth factors, while the central environment is hostile because oligodendrocyte myelin carries inhibitory molecules and reactive astrocytes build a glial scar. Peripheral axons are often the longer of the two, so length does not explain the difference. Central neurons retain full protein synthesis in the soma. Microglia are abundant in the spinal cord and clear debris there as well.
questions.answerText: Schwann cells guide peripheral regrowth while central glia obstruct it

questions.q: What is a node of Ranvier?
options: A short gap in the myelin sheath where the axon membrane is exposed
The junction between an axon terminal and its target cell
The point where an axon branches into several collaterals
The layer of myelin laid down by a single glial cell
questions.why: Nodes are the bare patches between successive myelin segments, and they are where ions can actually cross the membrane. The junction with a target cell is a synapse, a different structure entirely. A branch point is a collateral and has nothing to do with myelin. The stretch of myelin made by one glial cell is the internode, which is the insulated region between two nodes.
questions.answerText: A short gap in the myelin sheath where the axon membrane is exposed

questions.q: What is the name for the way an action potential travels along a myelinated axon?
options: Continuous conduction
Electrotonic spread
Saltatory conduction
Antidromic conduction
questions.why: Saltatory comes from the Latin for jumping, and it describes the impulse being regenerated only at the nodes so that it appears to leap from node to node. Continuous conduction is the slower pattern seen in unmyelinated axons, where every patch of membrane must fire in sequence. Electrotonic spread is the passive, decremental flow of current, which is what happens under the myelin between nodes. Antidromic conduction means travel in the direction opposite the normal one.
questions.answerText: Saltatory conduction

questions.q: What does the myelin sheath do to the electrical properties of the axon membrane it covers?
options: It lowers membrane resistance and raises membrane capacitance
It raises membrane resistance and lowers membrane capacitance
It raises both membrane resistance and membrane capacitance
It leaves both unchanged and simply protects the axon from injury
questions.why: Stacking many lipid layers around the axon makes it much harder for ions to leak out, which is high resistance, and separates the charges farther apart, which is low capacitance. Both changes push more of the local current forward inside the axon to the next node. Lowering resistance would do the opposite and let current escape. Myelin does provide some mechanical protection, but the reason it speeds conduction is electrical.
questions.answerText: It raises membrane resistance and lowers membrane capacitance

questions.q: Which axon conducts action potentials fastest?
options: A small diameter unmyelinated axon
A large diameter myelinated axon
A small diameter myelinated axon
A large diameter unmyelinated axon
questions.why: Diameter and myelination both raise conduction velocity, so the fastest fibers in the body have both, reaching about 100 m/s. Small unmyelinated fibers are the slowest, near 1 m/s, and they carry slow pain and temperature. Either factor alone helps: a large unmyelinated axon or a small myelinated one falls in between. The two effects work through the same principle, which is getting current farther down the axon before it leaks away.
questions.answerText: A large diameter myelinated axon

questions.q: Where are voltage-gated Na+ channels concentrated along a myelinated axon?
options: Spread evenly along the entire axon under the myelin
At the nodes of Ranvier
In the myelin sheath itself, between the lipid layers
Only at the axon terminal, where transmitter is released
questions.why: Channels are clustered in the bare nodal membrane, which is the only place ions can cross, so that is where the impulse is regenerated. Spreading them evenly would waste them, since the membrane under the myelin cannot pass current across itself anyway. Myelin is made of stacked glial membrane and holds no functional axonal Na+ channels. The terminal has voltage-gated Ca2+ channels for release, but Na+ channels are needed all along the axon to keep the impulse alive.
questions.answerText: At the nodes of Ranvier

questions.q: What is myelin mostly made of?
options: Lipid, in many wrapped layers of glial cell membrane
Collagen fibers secreted into the space around the axon
Extracellular fluid trapped between connective tissue sheets
Dense cytoskeletal protein extending out of the axon
questions.why: Myelin is glial plasma membrane wrapped repeatedly around the axon, and because membrane is largely lipid the sheath is an excellent electrical insulator. Collagen surrounds nerves in the connective tissue sheaths but is not myelin. Trapped fluid would conduct current rather than block it, defeating the purpose. Cytoskeletal protein such as neurofilament fills the inside of the axon rather than forming the sheath.
questions.answerText: Lipid, in many wrapped layers of glial cell membrane

questions.q: Roughly how fast does a large myelinated axon conduct compared with a small unmyelinated one?
options: About 10 m/s versus about 9 m/s
About 100 m/s versus about 1 m/s
About 1 m/s versus about 100 m/s
About 1000 m/s versus about 100 m/s
questions.why: The fastest human fibers run near 100 m/s and the slowest unmyelinated C fibers near 1 m/s, roughly a hundredfold spread, which is why touch reaches awareness well before slow burning pain. A difference of only 10 percent would not produce that everyday experience. Pairing 1 m/s with the myelinated fiber reverses the two, giving the insulated axon the slower speed. Nothing in the body conducts at 1000 m/s; that is far beyond what any axon achieves.
questions.answerText: About 100 m/s versus about 1 m/s

questions.q: Besides myelination, which axon property most affects conduction velocity?
options: The length of the axon
The number of dendrites on the cell body
The amount of transmitter stored in the terminal
Axon diameter
questions.why: A wider axon offers less internal resistance to the flow of current along its core, so depolarization spreads farther and faster ahead of the impulse. Axon length changes how long the trip takes but not the speed of travel. Dendrite number affects how much input the cell integrates, not how fast its output moves. Stored transmitter matters at the synapse after the impulse has already arrived.
questions.answerText: Axon diameter

questions.q: Myelin is stripped from a stretch of axon while the nodes keep their Na+ channels. Predict what happens to conduction through that stretch.
options: Conduction speeds up, because current no longer has to cross the sheath
Current leaks across the bare internode and the next node may not fire
Conduction is unchanged, since the nodes still have their channels
The axon fires continuously, because the membrane is now unprotected
questions.why: Myelin keeps local current inside the axon so it arrives at the next node still strong enough to open Na+ channels there; without it, current escapes across the exposed membrane and the depolarization arriving downstream may fall below threshold, slowing conduction or blocking it. Removing insulation cannot speed conduction, since the whole advantage came from the insulation. Intact nodal channels are not enough if too little current reaches them. Bare membrane between nodes has few voltage-gated channels, so spontaneous firing is not the expected result.
questions.answerText: Current leaks across the bare internode and the next node may not fire

questions.q: A demyelinating disease affects the largest myelinated sensory fibers first. Which sensation is most likely to be lost earliest?
options: Slow burning pain
Itch from the skin surface
Warm temperature sensation
Vibration and position sense
questions.why: Vibration and proprioception travel on the largest, most heavily myelinated afferents, so they are the first modalities to fail when myelin is the target. Slow burning pain runs on unmyelinated C fibers, which have no myelin to lose and are therefore spared early. Warm temperature also travels on unmyelinated fibers. Itch is likewise carried by small unmyelinated afferents, so it persists while position sense fades.
questions.answerText: Vibration and position sense

questions.q: Two axons have the same diameter, but one is myelinated and one is not. What accounts for the myelinated axon conducting faster?
options: It regenerates the impulse only at nodes rather than at every patch
It has a larger resting potential, so it starts closer to threshold
It has more Na+/K+ ATPase pumps to restore its gradients faster
It carries a larger action potential, which travels farther per step
questions.why: Opening channels takes time, so an axon that must fire every square micrometer of membrane in sequence is slow, while one that can skip the insulated internodes and fire only at nodes covers the same distance in far fewer steps. Pump density affects long-term gradient maintenance, not the speed of a single impulse. Resting potential is about the same in both axons and is not what myelin changes. Action potential amplitude is set by the ion gradients and is essentially the same in both.
questions.answerText: It regenerates the impulse only at nodes rather than at every patch

questions.q: A person with partial demyelination notices that symptoms worsen when body temperature rises, for example in a hot bath. What does this suggest about the affected axons?
options: Heat destroys myelin directly, so the damage is permanent each time
They have lost all their nodal Na+ channels and cannot conduct at all
They are conducting at the edge of failure, so a small change blocks them
Heat increases transmitter release, which fatigues the muscles
questions.why: Where myelin is thinned, each node barely receives enough current to reach threshold, so anything that shortens the time channels stay open, as warming does, can push conduction from marginal to blocked, and symptoms return until the temperature falls. Complete loss of nodal channels would produce a fixed deficit rather than one that comes and goes. A hot bath does not strip myelin, which is why the change is reversible. The problem is conduction along the axon, not transmitter release at the synapse.
questions.answerText: They are conducting at the edge of failure, so a small change blocks them

questions.q: A signal must travel 1 m from the toe to the spinal cord. How long does it take on a fiber conducting at 50 m/s compared with one conducting at 1 m/s?
options: About 50 ms versus about 100 ms
About 2 ms versus about 100 ms
About 20 ms versus about 50 ms
About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms
questions.why: Time equals distance divided by velocity, so 1 m at 50 m/s takes 1/50 of a second, which is 20 ms, and 1 m at 1 m/s takes a full second, or 1000 ms. That fiftyfold gap is why a sharp prick registers almost instantly while the aching pain behind it arrives about a second later. The values of 50 ms, 2 ms and 100 ms come from dividing in the wrong direction or from mixing seconds with milliseconds.
questions.answerText: About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms

questions.q: Imagine an axon whose myelin is normal but whose internodes are made much shorter, so nodes occur far more often. What happens to conduction velocity?
options: It rises, because more nodes mean more Na+ channels overall
It is unchanged, since only myelin thickness matters
It falls, because the impulse is regenerated more times per meter
It falls to zero, because current cannot cross a short internode
questions.why: Each regeneration costs the time it takes Na+ channels to open, so packing in extra nodes adds delays without adding distance covered per step. More channels do not help if the limiting factor is how many times you must stop and rebuild the signal. Internode length matters alongside sheath thickness, so the property is not fixed by thickness alone. Conduction still succeeds; a short internode passes current easily, it is just an unnecessary stop.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the impulse is regenerated more times per meter

questions.q: A patient has patchy demyelination in the optic nerve. Vision is dim and blurred rather than absent, and a recording shows the visual response arriving late but still present. What explains this pattern?
options: Conduction is slowed and partly blocked, so a late, scattered signal arrives
The photoreceptors have been destroyed, so no signal is generated
The optic nerve axons are cut, so no signal can reach the brain at all
The brain is ignoring the signal, though conduction is entirely normal
questions.why: Patchy demyelination leaves some fibers conducting slowly, some blocked, and the surviving impulses arriving at scattered times, which produces a delayed and weakened response rather than an absent one. Destroyed photoreceptors would abolish the signal at its source, and no delayed response would be recorded. Cut axons would likewise give no response. A normal-conduction explanation cannot account for a measured delay.
questions.answerText: Conduction is slowed and partly blocked, so a late, scattered signal arrives

questions.q: A nerve conduction study shows greatly slowed velocity with response amplitude close to normal. What does this point to?
options: Loss of many axons with the remaining ones normally myelinated
Failure of transmitter release at the neuromuscular junction
A muscle disease with normal nerve function throughout
Demyelination with the axons themselves largely intact
questions.why: Velocity depends on the insulation and the geometry of the fibers, while amplitude depends on how many axons are firing, so slow but full-sized responses say the wiring is intact and the insulation is not. Losing axons would drop the amplitude while leaving the surviving fast fibers at close to normal speed, the opposite pattern. A junction problem shows up as a fading response with repeated stimulation rather than slowed conduction. Muscle disease would not slow a nerve at all.
questions.answerText: Demyelination with the axons themselves largely intact

questions.q: An immune attack strips myelin from motor axons in the peripheral nerves of the legs over a few days. Predict the combination of findings.
options: Loss of slow pain first, with strength and reflexes preserved
Weakness with exaggerated reflexes, because the muscles are irritable
Weakness with reduced reflexes, while slow pain sensation is preserved
No weakness, because unmyelinated motor fibers take over the work
questions.why: Motor axons to skeletal muscle are large and heavily myelinated, so stripping myelin blocks or delays their impulses and both voluntary strength and the reflex response fall away, while unmyelinated C fibers carrying slow pain keep working. Reflexes depend on those same large fibers, so they weaken rather than increase. Slow pain rides on fibers with no myelin to lose, so it is not the first casualty. There are no unmyelinated motor fibers to skeletal muscle that could substitute.
questions.answerText: Weakness with reduced reflexes, while slow pain sensation is preserved

questions.q: A motor axon 1 m long normally conducts at 50 m/s. Demyelination drops its velocity to 5 m/s. How much extra delay does a command now take to reach the muscle, and what is the functional result?
options: About 180 ms extra, so movements become slow and poorly timed
About 20 ms extra, too small to change anything the person notices
About 2 s extra, so voluntary movement becomes impossible
No extra delay, because the impulse amplitude is unchanged
questions.why: One meter at 50 m/s takes 20 ms and at 5 m/s takes 200 ms, so the difference is 180 ms, a delay long enough to disrupt the timing that smooth movement and balance depend on. The 20 ms figure is the normal transit time rather than the added delay. Two seconds would require a velocity near 0.5 m/s, well below what this axon still manages. Conduction time depends on velocity, not amplitude, so unchanged amplitude does not protect the timing.
questions.answerText: About 180 ms extra, so movements become slow and poorly timed

questions.q: Which motor protein carries cargo down the axon away from the cell body?
options: Dynein
Kinesin
Myosin
Tubulin
questions.why: Kinesin walks toward the plus end of a microtubule, which in an axon points away from the soma, so kinesin is the anterograde motor. Dynein walks the other way and handles retrograde traffic. Myosin is a motor too, but it moves along actin filaments and drives muscle contraction and short-range movements. Tubulin is not a motor at all; it is the subunit that polymerizes into the microtubule track.
questions.answerText: Kinesin

questions.q: Which motor protein carries cargo back up the axon toward the cell body?
options: Kinesin
Dynein
Actin
Myosin
questions.why: Dynein moves toward the minus end of a microtubule, which in an axon points back toward the soma, making it the retrograde motor. Kinesin is its anterograde counterpart. Actin is a filament protein, not a motor, and it forms the track that myosin uses. Myosin does not carry cargo the length of an axon, since actin filaments do not run continuously along it.
questions.answerText: Dynein

questions.q: Which cytoskeletal element serves as the track for fast axonal transport?
options: Neurofilaments
Actin microfilaments
Microtubules
Collagen fibrils
questions.why: Microtubules run lengthwise through the axon with a consistent orientation, which gives the motor proteins both a road and a sense of direction. Actin microfilaments are concentrated just under the membrane and in the terminal, where they support short-range movement. Neurofilaments provide structural support and set axon caliber, and they are themselves cargo of slow transport rather than a track. Collagen is an extracellular protein and is not inside the axon at all.
questions.answerText: Microtubules

questions.q: What does fast anterograde transport carry to the axon terminal?
options: Worn out organelles being returned for breakdown
Neurofilaments and other structural proteins of the cytoskeleton
Membrane-bound organelles such as vesicles and mitochondria
Free ribosomes that will synthesize protein in the terminal
questions.why: Fast anterograde transport moves membrane-enclosed cargo, so vesicles carrying transmitter enzymes, membrane proteins and mitochondria all travel this way at a few hundred millimeters per day. Worn organelles travel the other direction, back to the soma, by retrograde transport. Cytoskeletal proteins move by slow transport, which is a hundred times slower. Axon terminals contain almost no ribosomes, which is precisely why protein has to be shipped from the cell body.
questions.answerText: Membrane-bound organelles such as vesicles and mitochondria

questions.q: What does fast retrograde transport carry back to the cell body?
options: Used organelles and growth factor signals picked up at the terminal
Newly made synaptic vesicles ready to be filled with transmitter
Fresh mitochondria heading toward the energy demands of the synapse
Soluble enzymes needed for transmitter synthesis in the terminal
questions.why: Retrograde traffic returns worn organelles for recycling and delivers signals such as nerve growth factor that the terminal has taken up, telling the soma the target has been reached. Newly made vesicles are anterograde cargo, since they are built in the cell body. Mitochondria travel both ways, but fresh ones heading to the synapse are moving anterograde. Enzymes for transmitter synthesis are also delivered outward, not returned.
questions.answerText: Used organelles and growth factor signals picked up at the terminal

questions.q: What does slow axonal transport carry, and at roughly what rate?
options: Synaptic vesicles and transmitter enzymes, at about 400 mm per day
Cytoskeletal proteins and soluble enzymes, at about 1 mm per day
Membrane receptors in vesicles, at about 50 mm per hour
Mitochondria and membrane proteins, at about 100 mm per day
questions.why: Slow transport moves the axon's structural material, the neurofilaments, tubulin and cytosolic enzymes, at a rate measured in a millimeter or so per day, and it is anterograde only. Synaptic vesicles are fast anterograde cargo, moving hundreds of millimeters per day. Mitochondria are also fast cargo. Membrane receptors travel inside vesicles and therefore also use the fast system.
questions.answerText: Cytoskeletal proteins and soluble enzymes, at about 1 mm per day

questions.q: A virus is taken up at a nerve terminal in the skin and later appears in the neuron cell body in the spinal cord. Which transport process moved it?
options: Fast anterograde transport, driven by kinesin
Slow transport, driven by cytoskeletal assembly
Simple diffusion along the length of the axon
Fast retrograde transport, driven by dynein
questions.why: Movement from the terminal back to the soma is retrograde by definition, and dynein is the motor that walks in that direction, which is how viruses such as rabies and toxins such as tetanus reach the central nervous system. Anterograde transport would carry the virus the wrong way, out toward the terminal. Slow transport is anterograde only and far too slow. Diffusion over a distance of a meter would take years and is not a viable route.
questions.answerText: Fast retrograde transport, driven by dynein

questions.q: A virus lying dormant in a dorsal root ganglion cell body reactivates and produces a rash in the skin served by that neuron. Which transport process delivered it?
options: Fast retrograde transport, driven by dynein
Fast anterograde transport, driven by kinesin
Slow transport of cytoskeletal proteins
Transport through the bloodstream to the skin
questions.why: Moving from the cell body out to the peripheral ending is anterograde, and kinesin is the motor for that direction, which is why the rash appears in exactly the skin field served by that one ganglion. Retrograde transport is the route the virus took originally, on its way in from the skin. Slow transport carries structural proteins and would take far too long for a rash that develops over days. A bloodborne route would scatter the rash rather than confining it to one sensory territory.
questions.answerText: Fast anterograde transport, driven by kinesin

questions.q: A drug depolymerizes microtubules inside an axon. Predict the effect on axonal transport.
options: Only anterograde transport fails, since dynein uses actin instead
Only retrograde transport fails, since kinesin does not need a track
Transport speeds up, because cargo is no longer tethered to a track
Both fast anterograde and fast retrograde transport fail
questions.why: Kinesin and dynein both walk on microtubules, differing only in which end they head toward, so destroying the track stops traffic in both directions and the terminal is cut off from the cell body. Dynein does not use actin; that is myosin. Kinesin cannot move cargo without a track any more than dynein can. Removing the track leaves cargo stranded rather than free to travel faster.
questions.answerText: Both fast anterograde and fast retrograde transport fail

questions.q: A severed peripheral axon regrows at roughly 1 mm per day. Which transport process sets that pace?
options: Fast anterograde transport of synaptic vesicles
Diffusion of ions into the growing tip
Fast retrograde transport of growth factor signals
Slow transport of cytoskeletal proteins
questions.why: A regrowing axon has to build new cytoskeleton along its whole new length, and tubulin and neurofilaments arrive only by slow transport at about a millimeter per day, which matches the observed regeneration rate almost exactly. Fast anterograde transport runs hundreds of times faster and is not the bottleneck. Retrograde signals report back to the soma but do not supply building material. Ion movement is not what limits the construction of a new axon segment.
questions.answerText: Slow transport of cytoskeletal proteins

questions.q: A motor neuron axon is 1000 mm long and fast anterograde transport runs at 400 mm per day. About how long does a newly made vesicle take to reach the terminal?
options: About 2.5 hours
About 25 days
About 2.5 days
About 400 days
questions.why: Dividing 1000 mm by 400 mm per day gives 2.5 days, a reminder that even the fast system takes real time over the length of a limb. Getting hours instead of days means the rate was read as millimeters per hour. Twenty-five days would follow from a rate of 40 mm per day, ten times too slow. Four hundred days confuses the rate with the answer.
questions.answerText: About 2.5 days

questions.q: A mutation disables dynein in a group of motor neurons. Predict what happens to the neuron over time.
options: New material still reaches the terminal, but nothing returns, and the cell fails
Nothing changes, because kinesin can carry cargo in either direction
The terminal is starved of vesicles at once, so transmission stops within hours
The axon regrows faster, because retrograde traffic no longer blocks the track
questions.why: Kinesin is intact, so outward delivery continues, but the neuron loses the return line that clears worn organelles and carries trophic signals such as nerve growth factor back to the nucleus, and without that feedback the cell slowly degenerates. Immediate loss of transmission would require the anterograde motor to fail. Kinesin is directional and cannot substitute for dynein. Removing traffic in one direction does not accelerate growth, since growth depends on outward supply and on the trophic signals that are now lost.
questions.answerText: New material still reaches the terminal, but nothing returns, and the cell fails

questions.q: In one experiment kinesin is blocked, and in another dynein is blocked, both at the midpoint of a long axon. Where does cargo pile up in each case?
options: Kinesin block piles cargo on the soma side, dynein block on the terminal side
Both blocks pile cargo on the terminal side of the axon
Both blocks pile cargo on the cell body side of the axon
Kinesin block piles cargo on the terminal side, dynein block on the soma side
questions.why: Cargo accumulates behind the stalled motor, and anterograde cargo approaches the block from the soma side while retrograde cargo approaches it from the terminal side, so the swelling appears on opposite sides in the two experiments. Having both pile up in the same place would require both motors to travel in the same direction. Putting the kinesin pile on the terminal side reverses the directions the two motors travel.
questions.answerText: Kinesin block piles cargo on the soma side, dynein block on the terminal side

questions.q: An axon 500 mm long is cut near the cell body. Fast anterograde transport runs at 400 mm per day and slow transport at 1 mm per day. Compare the two delivery times and explain what this predicts about recovery.
options: Fast cargo takes about a day, slow cargo about 500 days, so recovery takes months
Both take about a day, so recovery should be complete within a week
Fast cargo takes 500 days and slow cargo about a day, so recovery is quick
Neither matters, because a cut axon is rebuilt from the terminal inward
questions.why: Dividing 500 mm by each rate gives about 1.25 days for the fast system and 500 days for the slow system, and since the new axon must be built from cytoskeletal proteins carried by slow transport, that slower figure is what governs the timeline, which is why nerve recovery is measured in months. Equal times would require the two systems to run at the same rate, and they differ by several hundredfold. Giving the fast system the 500 day figure swaps the two rates. Regrowth proceeds outward from the surviving stump, supplied by the cell body, not inward from a terminal that is no longer connected.
questions.answerText: Fast cargo takes about a day, slow cargo about 500 days, so recovery takes months

questions.q: Which structures make up the central nervous system?
options: The brain, the spinal cord, and the cranial nerves
The brain and the spinal cord
The spinal cord and the spinal nerves
The brain, the spinal cord, and the sensory receptors
questions.why: The central nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord, and it acts as the integrating center for neural reflexes. Cranial and spinal nerves are bundles of peripheral axons that carry signals to and from the CNS, so they belong to the peripheral nervous system. Sensory receptors sit out in the body and feed the sensory division of the peripheral nervous system.
questions.answerText: The brain and the spinal cord

questions.q: Which division of the peripheral nervous system carries information toward the central nervous system?
options: The efferent division
The autonomic division
The somatic motor division
The sensory, or afferent, division
questions.why: Sensory, or afferent, neurons carry information from sensory receptors in toward the brain and spinal cord. The efferent division carries commands the other way, out from the CNS to target cells. The somatic motor and autonomic divisions are the two branches of that outgoing efferent division, so neither carries information inward.
questions.answerText: The sensory, or afferent, division

questions.q: What does the somatic motor division of the nervous system control?
options: Skeletal muscles
Cardiac muscle and smooth muscle
Exocrine glands and some endocrine glands
The smooth muscle in the wall of the intestines
questions.why: Somatic motor neurons carry commands from the CNS to skeletal muscle. Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, exocrine glands, some endocrine glands, and some adipose tissue are the targets of the autonomic division instead. Intestinal smooth muscle is controlled by the enteric nervous system and the autonomic division, not by somatic motor neurons.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscles

questions.q: What is the enteric nervous system?
options: The branch of the autonomic division that slows the heart
The part of the spinal cord that controls the digestive tract
A network of neurons in the wall of the digestive tract
The sensory neurons that carry taste to the brain
questions.why: The enteric nervous system is a network of neurons in the walls of the digestive tract. It is often controlled by the autonomic division, but it can also work on its own as an integrating center. Slowing the heart is a job of the parasympathetic branch of the autonomic division. The spinal cord is part of the CNS, while enteric neurons sit out in the gut wall. Neurons carrying taste toward the brain are sensory, or afferent, neurons.
questions.answerText: A network of neurons in the wall of the digestive tract

questions.q: Many internal organs receive input from both sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons. What is the usual relationship between the two?
options: They always produce the same effect, which doubles the response
They often have opposing effects on the same target
They act on different organs and never share a target
One carries sensory information and the other carries motor commands
questions.why: Sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons are the two branches of the autonomic division, and it is common for the two to exert antagonistic, or opposing, control over a single target. They do share targets, since many internal organs receive both, so they are not limited to separate organs. They do not simply double one response. Both branches are efferent, carrying commands out from the CNS, so neither is sensory.
questions.answerText: They often have opposing effects on the same target

questions.q: A patient can feel a pin prick on the leg but cannot move the leg muscles. Assuming the brain, spinal cord, and muscles are normal, which division is most likely damaged?
options: The sensory division of the peripheral nervous system
The enteric nervous system
The autonomic division
The somatic motor division
questions.why: Feeling the pin prick shows the sensory, or afferent, pathway still works, so the sensory division is not the problem. Losing movement of skeletal muscle points to the somatic motor division, which carries commands from the CNS to skeletal muscle. The autonomic division controls cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands, not skeletal muscle. The enteric nervous system sits in the gut wall and has no role in moving the leg.
questions.answerText: The somatic motor division

questions.q: A neuron carries a stretch signal from a muscle into the spinal cord. Which part of the nervous system does it belong to?
options: The sensory, or afferent, division of the peripheral nervous system
The central nervous system
The somatic motor division
The autonomic division
questions.why: Any neuron that carries information from a receptor in toward the CNS is a sensory, or afferent, neuron, part of the peripheral nervous system. The somatic motor division carries commands out to skeletal muscle, the opposite direction. The autonomic division also carries commands outward, to organs and glands. The CNS contains the interneurons that integrate the signal once it arrives, but this neuron is the one bringing it in.
questions.answerText: The sensory, or afferent, division of the peripheral nervous system

questions.q: The central nervous system can produce activity with no measurable output to the efferent divisions. Which example stays entirely inside the CNS?
options: Pulling a hand away from a hot stove
Salivating at the smell of food
Thinking through a problem while sitting still
The heart speeding up during exercise
questions.why: Thinking and dreaming are complex brain functions that can take place entirely within the CNS, with no signal sent out to muscles or glands. Pulling a hand from a stove uses sensory input and a somatic motor output to skeletal muscle. Salivating uses a smell signal coming in and an autonomic output to a gland going out. A faster heart rate is an autonomic output to cardiac muscle.
questions.answerText: Thinking through a problem while sitting still

questions.q: A signal from food in the gut wall triggers a response in intestinal smooth muscle without involving the brain or the spinal cord. What does this show?
options: The response must travel through the somatic motor division
The enteric nervous system can act as its own integrating center
Sensory neurons in the gut connect straight to skeletal muscle
The autonomic division is required for every digestive response
questions.why: The enteric nervous system can function on its own as an integrating center, so a local gut response can happen without the brain or spinal cord. It is often controlled by the autonomic division, but not every response requires that control. The somatic motor division only controls skeletal muscle, and intestinal muscle is smooth muscle, which also rules out a connection to skeletal muscle.
questions.answerText: The enteric nervous system can act as its own integrating center

questions.q: What defines a graded potential?
options: A membrane potential change whose size varies with stimulus strength
A membrane potential change of fixed size once threshold is crossed
A membrane potential change carried by voltage gated Na+ channels
A membrane potential change that spreads without losing any size
questions.why: A graded potential is produced when gated channels open and let ions cross, and the more channels that open, the larger the voltage change, so its size reports stimulus strength. A change of fixed size once threshold is crossed describes the action potential, which is all or none. Voltage gated Na+ channels drive the action potential upstroke, while graded potentials come mostly from chemically and mechanically gated channels. Spreading without losing size describes regenerative propagation down an axon, not the decremental spread of a graded potential.
questions.answerText: A membrane potential change whose size varies with stimulus strength

questions.q: In a typical multipolar neuron, where are graded potentials mainly produced?
options: At the nodes of Ranvier along the axon
On the dendrites and cell body
At the trigger zone where voltage gated Na+ channels cluster
Along the myelinated internodes of the axon
questions.why: Dendrites and the cell body carry the chemically gated channels that synaptic transmitters open, so this is where postsynaptic graded potentials arise and then spread toward the trigger zone. The nodes of Ranvier and the trigger zone are dense in voltage gated Na+ channels and are where action potentials are generated and regenerated. Myelinated internodes are insulated and have very few channels of any kind, which is exactly why current passes them without much leak.
questions.answerText: On the dendrites and cell body

questions.q: At a chemical synapse, which class of ion channel opens to produce the postsynaptic graded potential?
options: Chemically gated channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
Mechanically gated channels
Voltage gated K+ channels
questions.why: A neurotransmitter binds a receptor and opens chemically gated (ligand gated) channels, and the ion flow through them is what shifts the postsynaptic membrane potential. Mechanically gated channels do produce graded potentials, but in sensory receptors responding to stretch or pressure, not at a chemical synapse. Voltage gated Na+ and K+ channels respond to membrane potential rather than transmitter, and they shape the action potential once the graded potential reaches the trigger zone.
questions.answerText: Chemically gated channels

questions.q: What is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)?
options: A graded hyperpolarization that moves the membrane away from threshold
An all or none depolarization generated at the trigger zone
A graded depolarization that moves the membrane toward threshold
A steady depolarization that lasts as long as the stimulus without decay
questions.why: An EPSP is a local depolarization, usually from Na+ entry through chemically gated channels, that brings the membrane potential closer to threshold and so raises the chance of firing. A graded hyperpolarization is the inhibitory postsynaptic potential, the IPSP, which does the opposite. An all or none depolarization at the trigger zone is the action potential itself. EPSPs are brief and decay both over time and over distance, so a steady undecaying response does not describe them.
questions.answerText: A graded depolarization that moves the membrane toward threshold

questions.q: Which ion movement most often produces an inhibitory postsynaptic potential?
options: Cl- moving into the cell
Ca2+ moving into the cell
K+ moving into the cell
Na+ moving into the cell
questions.why: Cl- entry adds negative charge to the inside of the cell, hyperpolarizing it and pushing the membrane potential away from threshold. K+ movement also hyperpolarizes, but K+ leaves the cell rather than entering, since its gradient points outward. Na+ entry and Ca2+ entry both add positive charge inside and are depolarizing, so they produce excitatory rather than inhibitory potentials.
questions.answerText: Cl- moving into the cell

questions.q: In the spread of a graded potential, what does current leak refer to?
options: Positive charge escaping back across the membrane through open channels
Ions being pumped back out by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Charge lost to the friction of the cytosol as current flows lengthwise
Current passing to a neighboring cell through gap junctions
questions.why: As charge spreads sideways inside the cell, some of it slips back out across the membrane through open leak channels, so less and less current is left to change the potential farther along. Charge lost to the friction of the cytosol is the other factor, cytoplasmic resistance, and the two act together. The Na+/K+ ATPase restores concentration gradients over minutes and is far too slow to shape a single graded potential. Gap junction current is a feature of electrical synapses, not of decay within one neuron.
questions.answerText: Positive charge escaping back across the membrane through open channels

questions.q: What does the term cytoplasmic resistance describe?
options: The opposition the cytosol offers to current flowing lengthwise inside the cell
The opposition the membrane offers to ions crossing from inside to outside
The opposition the extracellular fluid offers to current returning to the source
The opposition myelin offers to charge leaking out of the internode
questions.why: Cytoplasm is a conductor, but a poor one, so current spreading lengthwise inside a dendrite or axon loses strength the farther it has to travel. The opposition of the membrane to ions crossing it is membrane resistance, which is the property that leak channels lower and myelin raises. Extracellular fluid does carry the return current, but its resistance is small and is not what the term names. Myelin insulation raises membrane resistance rather than cytoplasmic resistance.
questions.answerText: The opposition the cytosol offers to current flowing lengthwise inside the cell

questions.q: As a graded potential spreads away from the point where it started, what happens to its amplitude?
options: It grows larger with distance
It stays the same at every distance
It reverses sign a short distance away
It gets smaller with distance
questions.why: Graded potentials spread passively, and current leaks out across the membrane while the cytoplasm resists flow, so the voltage change shrinks the farther it travels. This decay is why a graded potential can only signal over short distances and why neurons need action potentials for long ones. An amplitude that stays constant describes a regenerating action potential, which is rebuilt at every point along the axon. Nothing in passive spread flips the sign of the potential, and growth with distance would require an energy source that passive spread does not have.
questions.answerText: It gets smaller with distance

questions.q: A stimulus opens twice as many chemically gated channels as before on a dendrite. What is the result?
options: A graded potential of the same amplitude that spreads faster
A graded potential of larger amplitude
A graded potential of the same amplitude repeated twice
An action potential of larger amplitude at the trigger zone
questions.why: More open channels means more ions crossing per unit time, more charge moved, and therefore a bigger voltage change, which is exactly what makes graded potentials graded. Passive spread speed is set by the cable properties of the cell, not by how many channels the stimulus opened. Nothing about a stronger stimulus splits the response into two events. The action potential option is the classic trap: a bigger graded potential can make an action potential more likely, but it never makes the action potential itself bigger, because that response is all or none.
questions.answerText: A graded potential of larger amplitude

questions.q: Two EPSPs arrive at the same synapse two milliseconds apart, and the second builds on the tail of the first. What is this called?
options: Spatial summation
Temporal summation
Divergence to two targets
Convergence of two pathways
questions.why: Two inputs at one location arriving close together in time overlap before the first decays, and their depolarizations add, which is temporal summation. Spatial summation is the same addition, but of inputs arriving at the same moment from different locations on the neuron. Convergence and divergence describe wiring patterns, how many neurons feed into one cell or how many cells one neuron contacts, not the adding of overlapping potentials.
questions.answerText: Temporal summation

questions.q: Two different presynaptic neurons fire at the same instant onto separate dendrites, and their EPSPs add at the trigger zone. What is this called?
options: Temporal summation
Facilitation of a single synapse
Spatial summation
Recruitment of additional axons
questions.why: Inputs at different places on the same neuron arriving at the same moment sum where their spreading currents meet, and that is spatial summation. Temporal summation would require the inputs to be separated in time at one site rather than separated in space at one instant. Facilitation describes a synapse becoming more effective with use, which is a change in one synapse rather than the addition of two. Recruitment refers to bringing more axons into a population response, which happens across cells, not within one postsynaptic neuron.
questions.answerText: Spatial summation

questions.q: An EPSP measured at the dendrite is 15 mV, but at the trigger zone 500 micrometers away it is only 4 mV. What best explains the drop?
options: The Na+/K+ ATPase pumped the excess Na+ back out along the way
Voltage gated Na+ channels inactivated partway down the dendrite
Charge leaked out across the membrane while the cytoplasm resisted the flow
The membrane entered a refractory period between the two recording sites
questions.why: Passive spread loses current two ways at once: some charge escapes through open membrane channels, and the cytosol resists the lengthwise flow of what is left, so the recorded voltage falls steadily with distance. The Na+/K+ ATPase works on a timescale of many seconds to minutes and cannot account for a change occurring in a fraction of a millisecond. Voltage gated Na+ channels are sparse on dendrites and are not what carries a spreading EPSP. Refractory periods follow action potentials, and no action potential has occurred here.
questions.answerText: Charge leaked out across the membrane while the cytoplasm resisted the flow

questions.q: One dendrite is twice the diameter of another, which lowers its cytoplasmic resistance. How far does a graded potential spread in the wider one?
options: A shorter distance, because the larger volume dilutes the charge
Farther, but only if the dendrite is myelinated
The same distance, because diameter affects only action potentials
Farther, because less current is lost to internal resistance
questions.why: A wider cylinder of cytoplasm is an easier path for current, the same way a wide pipe carries water with less pressure loss, so more of the original charge reaches a given distance and the potential decays less. Charge is not diluted by volume in any way that matters here; what matters is the resistance of the path. Diameter affects passive spread in every process, which is why it also affects action potential conduction velocity. Myelin helps by reducing leak across the membrane, but the diameter effect is real with or without it.
questions.answerText: Farther, because less current is lost to internal resistance

questions.q: A toxin holds extra K+ leak channels open along a dendrite. What happens to the distance a graded potential can spread?
options: It becomes longer, because K+ carries the signal along the dendrite
It becomes shorter, because more current escapes across the membrane
It stays the same, because leak channels do not carry current
It becomes longer, because the resting potential is now more stable
questions.why: Extra open channels lower membrane resistance, so spreading current has more escape routes and the potential dies out over a shorter distance. K+ leaving through leak channels carries charge out of the cell rather than along it; the lengthwise carrier of a graded potential is current flowing through the cytoplasm. Leak channels certainly do carry current, and that is exactly the problem. A more stable resting potential is not an advantage for spread, since the cost of stability here is a shorter distance.
questions.answerText: It becomes shorter, because more current escapes across the membrane

questions.q: An EPSP of 6 mV and an IPSP of 4 mV reach the trigger zone at the same moment. What is the net change in membrane potential?
options: About 10 mV of depolarization
No net change, since opposite inputs cancel completely
About 2 mV of hyperpolarization
About 2 mV of depolarization
questions.why: Graded potentials sum algebraically, so a 6 mV depolarization plus a 4 mV hyperpolarization leaves roughly 2 mV of net depolarization. Adding the two magnitudes to get 10 mV would treat the inhibitory input as if it were excitatory. A net hyperpolarization would require the IPSP to be the larger of the two, which it is not. Complete cancellation happens only when the two are equal in size, so it is the right answer for a 4 mV EPSP paired with a 4 mV IPSP, not for this pair.
questions.answerText: About 2 mV of depolarization
