questions.why: A wider axon offers a lower resistance path for current flowing lengthwise, so the local current from an active patch reaches farther ahead and brings distant membrane to threshold sooner, which speeds conduction. There is more membrane to depolarize in a wide axon, but the drop in internal resistance outweighs it, which is why the giant axons of invertebrates are fast. Myelination is a second major factor, not the only one. Pump density affects long term gradient maintenance, not the speed of a single action potential.
questions.answerText: It increases velocity, because a wider cytoplasmic path resists current less

questions.q: How does myelination affect conduction velocity?
options: It increases velocity by adding voltage gated Na+ channels along the internode
It increases velocity by reducing current leak across the internodal membrane
It decreases velocity by insulating the axon from the extracellular fluid
It increases velocity by widening the axon inside the myelin sheath
questions.why: Myelin wraps the internode in many layers of membrane, which raises membrane resistance so that local current stays inside the axon and travels far enough to reach the next node quickly. Voltage gated Na+ channels are concentrated at the nodes and are actually excluded from the internode, so myelin does not add them along it. Insulation is the mechanism of the speed increase, not a drag on it. Myelin surrounds the axon rather than expanding the cytoplasmic core, so the diameter effect is separate.
questions.answerText: It increases velocity by reducing current leak across the internodal membrane

questions.q: What is saltatory conduction?
options: Action potentials skipping over the nodes and regenerating under the myelin
Action potentials traveling in both directions away from the trigger zone at once
Action potentials regenerating only at the nodes while current jumps the internodes
Action potentials passing from one axon to a neighboring axon in the nerve
questions.why: In a myelinated axon the voltage gated channels sit at the nodes, so the action potential is rebuilt there while the depolarizing current spreads passively and rapidly beneath the insulated internodes, which is what saltatory means. Skipping the nodes reverses the arrangement, since the nodes are the only places with the channels needed to regenerate the signal. Bidirectional spread from a stimulus site is a separate phenomenon and occurs in unmyelinated axons too. Action potentials do not hop between separate axons.
questions.answerText: Action potentials regenerating only at the nodes while current jumps the internodes

questions.q: In a myelinated axon, where is the action potential regenerated?
options: Beneath the thickest part of the myelin sheath
At the nodes of Ranvier
At the axon terminal only
Uniformly along the entire internode
questions.why: Nodes of Ranvier are short gaps in the myelin packed with voltage gated Na+ channels, and they are the only stretches of a myelinated axon where the membrane can produce a fresh action potential. Under the myelin there are almost no voltage gated channels, so nothing can be regenerated there. The axon terminal converts the arriving action potential into transmitter release rather than serving as the site of propagation. Regeneration along the whole internode describes continuous conduction in an unmyelinated axon.
questions.answerText: At the nodes of Ranvier

questions.q: Which fiber type conducts action potentials most rapidly?
options: Small diameter unmyelinated fibers
Large diameter myelinated fibers
Large diameter unmyelinated fibers
Small diameter myelinated fibers
questions.why: Speed rises with diameter and with myelination, so the fastest axons in the body combine both, reaching roughly 100 m/s in the largest myelinated fibers that serve proprioception and skeletal muscle. Small unmyelinated fibers sit at the other extreme, near 1 m/s, and carry slow pain and autonomic signals. A small myelinated fiber or a large unmyelinated one has one advantage but not the other, so each falls in between.
questions.answerText: Large diameter myelinated fibers

questions.q: What does myelin do to current leak across the internodal membrane?
options: It has no effect on leak but lowers cytoplasmic resistance
It increases leak, which speeds repolarization at each node
It reduces leak, so more current reaches the next node
It reduces leak only in unmyelinated regions of the axon
questions.why: Wrapping the axon in many layers of lipid membrane drastically raises the resistance of the path out of the cell, so the current spreading forward inside the axon stays inside and arrives at the next node with enough strength to reach threshold. Increased leak would be a handicap, draining the very current that has to reach the next node. Myelin acts on the membrane, not on the cytoplasm, so cytoplasmic resistance is unchanged. Describing unmyelinated regions as myelinated is a contradiction.
questions.answerText: It reduces leak, so more current reaches the next node

questions.q: What are typical conduction velocities for the fastest myelinated fibers and for unmyelinated fibers?
options: About 10 m/s and about 1 m/s
About 100 m/s and about 50 m/s
About 100 m/s and about 1 m/s
About 1000 m/s and about 100 m/s
questions.why: Large myelinated fibers reach roughly 100 m/s, while small unmyelinated fibers crawl along near 1 m/s, a hundredfold range that explains why touch reaches awareness long before slow burning pain. A top speed of 10 m/s underestimates the fastest fibers by an order of magnitude. Fifty meters per second is typical of a medium myelinated fiber, not of an unmyelinated one. A thousand meters per second is faster than any biological axon conducts.
questions.answerText: About 100 m/s and about 1 m/s

questions.q: What is continuous conduction?
options: Passive spread of a graded potential along an unmyelinated axon
Sequential regeneration of the action potential at every adjacent patch of membrane
Regeneration of the action potential only at points where Schwann cells are absent
Conduction that continues after the stimulus has been removed
questions.why: In an unmyelinated axon, voltage gated channels are spread along the whole membrane, so each small patch depolarizes its neighbor to threshold and the action potential is rebuilt step by step without skipping anything, which is slower than jumping node to node. Passive spread without regeneration describes a graded potential, and it decays rather than propagating. Regeneration at gaps in a sheath describes saltatory conduction in a myelinated axon. Conduction certainly continues past the stimulus, but that is true of any propagating action potential and is not what the term names.
questions.answerText: Sequential regeneration of the action potential at every adjacent patch of membrane

questions.q: Rank these four axons from fastest to slowest: a 20 micrometer myelinated fiber, a 2 micrometer myelinated fiber, a 20 micrometer unmyelinated fiber, and a 1 micrometer unmyelinated fiber.
options: 1 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated, 20 micrometer myelinated
20 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated
2 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated
20 micrometer unmyelinated, 20 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated
questions.why: Both factors push in the same direction, so the fiber that is both large and myelinated is fastest and the one that is both small and unmyelinated is slowest, with the two mixed cases in between. The ordering that starts with the 1 micrometer unmyelinated fiber lists the same four in exactly reverse order, slowest first. The two orderings that put a small fiber ahead of a large one with the same insulation contradict the diameter rule. Where the two middle fibers fall relative to each other depends on the exact numbers, but both clearly sit between the extremes.
questions.answerText: 20 micrometer myelinated, 20 micrometer unmyelinated, 2 micrometer myelinated, 1 micrometer unmyelinated

questions.q: An action potential travels 15 cm along a nerve in 3 ms. What is the conduction velocity?
options: 5 m/s
45 m/s
50 m/s
questions.why: Convert first: 15 cm is 0.15 m and 3 ms is 0.003 s, and 0.15 divided by 0.003 gives 50 m/s, a value typical of a medium sized myelinated fiber. Five meters per second would come from dividing 15 by 3 and then mishandling the unit conversion by a factor of ten. Forty five is what you get by subtracting rather than dividing. Five hundred is off by a factor of ten in the other direction and exceeds any biological conduction velocity.
questions.answerText: 50 m/s

questions.q: A segment of myelin is destroyed along an axon, leaving the underlying membrane intact but with few voltage gated Na+ channels. What happens to conduction there?
options: It speeds up, because the current no longer has to jump from node to node
It reverses direction when it reaches the damaged segment of the axon
It is unchanged, because the axon still has its normal diameter and gradients
It slows and may fail, because current leaks out before reaching the next node
questions.why: The bare stretch has low membrane resistance and almost no voltage gated Na+ channels, so current leaks out across it and the depolarization arriving at the next node may be too small to reach threshold, producing slowing or outright conduction block. Removing myelin removes the insulation that made saltatory conduction fast, so speeding up is the opposite of what occurs. Diameter still matters, but it cannot compensate for the loss of insulation on a channel poor membrane. Nothing about demyelination reverses the direction of travel.
questions.answerText: It slows and may fail, because current leaks out before reaching the next node

questions.q: Why does saltatory conduction cost less ATP than continuous conduction over the same distance?
options: Fewer ions cross the membrane, so the Na+/K+ ATPase has less to restore
Myelin supplies ATP to the axon along the internode
Action potentials in myelinated axons are smaller and use less charge
The axon uses passive diffusion rather than active transport at the nodes
questions.why: Ion movement is confined to the small nodal patches rather than occurring over the whole membrane surface, so far less Na+ enters and less K+ leaves per action potential and the pump spends much less ATP restoring the gradients. Myelin is made by supporting cells and insulates the axon; it does not feed it ATP. Action potentials in myelinated axons are full sized, so the savings do not come from smaller signals. The pump uses ATP in both cases, and passive diffusion through channels is what the pump has to reverse.
questions.answerText: Fewer ions cross the membrane, so the Na+/K+ ATPase has less to restore

questions.q: Two axons have the same diameter, but one is myelinated and one is not. Which conducts faster and why?
options: The myelinated one, because insulation lets local current reach the next node quickly
The unmyelinated one, because every patch of its membrane can regenerate the signal
They conduct at the same speed, since diameter is the only factor that matters
The unmyelinated one, because it has less membrane capacitance to charge
questions.why: High membrane resistance under the myelin keeps current inside the axon so it spreads rapidly to the next node, and the time consuming step of opening channels happens only at the nodes rather than at every point, so the myelinated axon wins easily. Regenerating at every patch sounds thorough but is exactly what makes continuous conduction slow, since each step takes the same fraction of a millisecond. Diameter matters but is not the only factor. Myelin actually lowers effective membrane capacitance, so the capacitance argument favors the myelinated fiber, not the bare one.
questions.answerText: The myelinated one, because insulation lets local current reach the next node quickly

questions.q: A painful stimulus produces a sharp, well localized sensation followed a second later by a dull ache. Which fibers carry each?
options: Slow unmyelinated C fibers first, then fast myelinated A delta fibers
Both are carried by A delta fibers, with the delay caused by the refractory period
Both are carried by C fibers, with the delay caused by processing in the brain
Fast myelinated A delta fibers first, then slow unmyelinated C fibers
questions.why: A delta fibers are small but myelinated and conduct at roughly 20 m/s, so their signal arrives first as the sharp fast pain, while unmyelinated C fibers conduct near 1 m/s and deliver the dull slow pain a noticeable interval later. Putting the C fibers first ignores that unmyelinated fibers are the slowest in the body. If both sensations came from one fiber type, the delay would have to come from somewhere else, and neither central processing nor the refractory period stretches to a full second.
questions.answerText: Fast myelinated A delta fibers first, then slow unmyelinated C fibers

questions.q: In a myelinated axon, why does the spacing of the nodes of Ranvier matter?
options: Local current must still be above threshold when it reaches the next node
The Na+/K+ ATPase can only work at evenly spaced intervals
Widely spaced nodes would raise the amplitude of the action potential
Nodes must be spaced closely enough for myelin to remain attached
questions.why: Current spreading under the internode decays as it goes, so nodes have to be close enough that the depolarization arriving at the next one is still large enough to open its Na+ channels, and spacing them too far apart causes conduction to fail. The pump is distributed along the membrane and does not require particular spacing. Node spacing does not change action potential amplitude, which is all or none. Myelin attachment is a matter of the supporting cell wrapping the axon, not of a threshold current requirement.
questions.answerText: Local current must still be above threshold when it reaches the next node

questions.q: A nerve conduction study on a patient shows conduction velocity reduced from 55 m/s to 25 m/s, while the size of the response is nearly normal. What does this pattern suggest?
options: Loss of axons, since fewer fibers would be contributing to the response
A shortened refractory period in the surviving fibers
A rise in threshold at the stimulating electrode
Demyelination, since insulation is lost but the axons themselves are intact
questions.why: Velocity depends on insulation and diameter while response size depends on how many axons are firing, so a large drop in speed with a preserved response points to intact axons that have lost myelin. Axon loss would do the reverse, shrinking the response while the surviving fibers still conduct at close to normal speed. A raised stimulating threshold would mean a larger stimulus was needed, not slower conduction once firing occurred. Refractory period sets maximum firing frequency, not the velocity of a single action potential.
questions.answerText: Demyelination, since insulation is lost but the axons themselves are intact

questions.q: A signal must travel 1 m from the toe to the spinal cord. Compare the arrival time in an axon conducting at 50 m/s and one conducting at 1 m/s.
options: About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms, a difference of nearly a second
About 2 ms versus about 100 ms, a difference of about 98 ms
About 20 ms versus about 100 ms, a difference of 80 ms
About 50 ms versus about 1000 ms, a difference of 950 ms
questions.why: Time is distance divided by velocity, so 1 m at 50 m/s takes 0.02 s or 20 ms, and 1 m at 1 m/s takes a full second, which is why slow C fiber pain lags so noticeably behind fast touch from the same spot. The options offering 100 ms for the slow fiber use 10 m/s rather than 1 m/s. Two milliseconds would require 500 m/s. Fifty milliseconds inverts the calculation, multiplying by the velocity instead of dividing.
questions.answerText: About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms, a difference of nearly a second

questions.q: Conduction velocity in a child's motor nerves rises steadily during the first two years of life. What two developmental changes account for this?
options: Increasing action potential amplitude and lengthening of the axons
Increasing Na+/K+ ATPase density and rising body temperature
Shortening of the refractory period and rising extracellular K+
Progressive myelination and increasing axon diameter
questions.why: Both factors that set conduction velocity are still developing: axons grow thicker, which lowers internal resistance, and supporting cells lay down myelin, which cuts current leak and converts continuous conduction into saltatory conduction. Pump density maintains gradients over time but does not speed a single action potential, and core body temperature is already adult like at birth. Refractory period governs maximum firing rate rather than velocity, and rising extracellular K+ would impair excitability. Action potential amplitude is all or none, and a longer axon adds travel time rather than speed.
questions.answerText: Progressive myelination and increasing axon diameter

questions.q: An axon's diameter doubles. This lowers cytoplasmic resistance but also increases the total membrane surface area available for current leak. Why does conduction still get faster?
options: Leak does not actually increase, because the membrane thickens as the axon widens
The extra membrane adds voltage gated Na+ channels that speed regeneration
Internal resistance falls faster than leak rises, so local current reaches farther ahead
The larger axon has a lower threshold, so less depolarization is needed downstream
questions.why: Internal resistance depends on the cross sectional area, which scales with the square of the radius, while leak depends on the circumference, which scales with the radius alone, so widening the axon helps the internal path more than it hurts the membrane path and the net effect is a longer reach for local current and faster conduction. Membrane thickness is fixed at about the same value in all cells, so it does not compensate. Channel density per unit area stays roughly the same, so extra channels are not the explanation. Threshold is a property of the channels and does not fall with diameter.
questions.answerText: Internal resistance falls faster than leak rises, so local current reaches farther ahead

questions.q: What is the normal range for plasma K+ concentration?
options: About 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L
About 8 to 12 mEq/L
About 135 to 145 mEq/L
About 95 to 105 mEq/L
questions.why: Plasma K+ is held in a narrow band near 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L, and even small departures shift the resting potential enough to change excitability in nerve and cardiac muscle. The range of 135 to 145 mEq/L belongs to plasma Na+, and 95 to 105 mEq/L belongs to Cl-. Eight to twelve is close to the intracellular Cl- value and is not a plasma potassium range.
questions.answerText: About 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L

questions.q: Which ion's gradient has the largest influence on the resting membrane potential?
options: Na+
Ca2+
Cl-
K+
questions.why: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to anything else, so the resting potential sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential and follows changes in extracellular K+ closely. Na+ has a steep gradient but very low resting permeability, so it pulls the resting potential only a little positive of the K+ value. Ca2+ has the steepest gradient of all but almost no resting conductance in a typical axon. Cl- distributes near equilibrium in many cells and tends to follow the potential rather than set it.
questions.answerText: K+

questions.q: What is hyperkalemia?
options: An elevated concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid
An elevated concentration of K+ inside the cell
A reduced concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid
A reduced concentration of Ca2+ in the extracellular fluid
questions.why: Clinical ion names refer to the plasma and extracellular concentration, so hyperkalemia means extracellular K+ is above about 5.0 mEq/L. Intracellular K+ is already high in every cell and is not what the term describes. A reduced extracellular value is hypokalemia, the mirror condition. Reduced extracellular Ca2+ is hypocalcemia, a different ion with a different mechanism of action on excitability.
questions.answerText: An elevated concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid

questions.q: What does hypokalemia do to the resting membrane potential?
options: It makes the resting potential less negative
It makes the resting potential more negative
It leaves the resting potential unchanged
It drives the resting potential above threshold
questions.why: Lowering extracellular K+ steepens the K+ gradient, which makes the K+ equilibrium potential more negative, and because the resting membrane follows K+ closely the resting potential is pulled with it, moving the cell farther from threshold. A less negative resting potential is what hyperkalemia produces. The resting potential does change, and quite noticeably, because K+ dominates resting permeability. Nothing about low extracellular K+ drives a cell toward threshold.
questions.answerText: It makes the resting potential more negative

questions.q: What does hyperkalemia do to the resting membrane potential?
options: It makes the resting potential more negative
It leaves the resting potential unchanged
It reverses the polarity of the resting potential
It makes the resting potential less negative
questions.why: Raising extracellular K+ flattens the K+ gradient, so the K+ equilibrium potential becomes less negative and the resting potential follows it upward toward threshold. A more negative resting potential results from hypokalemia. The resting potential is highly sensitive to extracellular K+, so no change is not an option. Full reversal of polarity requires a large inward current, which nothing in hyperkalemia provides.
questions.answerText: It makes the resting potential less negative

questions.q: Local anesthetics such as lidocaine act by blocking which channel?
options: Voltage gated K+ channels
K+ leak channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
Chemically gated Cl- channels
questions.why: Lidocaine and related drugs bind inside the pore of the voltage gated Na+ channel, so the inward current that drives the upstroke cannot develop and no action potential is generated in the treated nerve. Blocking voltage gated K+ channels would prolong action potentials rather than abolish them. Leak channels set the resting potential and are not the target. Chemically gated Cl- channels are the target of a different class of drugs, and opening rather than blocking them is what produces inhibition.
questions.answerText: Voltage gated Na+ channels

questions.q: What is the approximate equilibrium potential for K+ in a typical neuron?
options: About -90 mV
About -70 mV
About -55 mV
About +60 mV
questions.why: With roughly 140 mEq/L inside and 4 mEq/L outside, the Nernst equation puts the K+ equilibrium potential near -90 mV, which is the value the membrane approaches during afterhyperpolarization. About -70 mV is the resting potential, which sits positive of the K+ equilibrium potential because of a small Na+ leak. About -55 mV is threshold. About +60 mV is the Na+ equilibrium potential, the target during the upstroke.
questions.answerText: About -90 mV

questions.q: Which phase of the action potential is abolished first when voltage gated Na+ channels are blocked?
options: The afterhyperpolarization
The depolarizing upstroke
The repolarization phase
The resting phase before the stimulus
questions.why: The upstroke is carried entirely by Na+ entering through voltage gated Na+ channels, so blocking them removes it, and with no upstroke there is nothing left for the later phases to follow. Afterhyperpolarization and repolarization both depend on K+ channels that open only after a depolarization has occurred, so they disappear as a consequence rather than as the primary effect. The resting phase is maintained by leak channels and the pump and persists whether or not Na+ channels are blocked.
questions.answerText: The depolarizing upstroke

questions.q: Extracellular K+ rises from 4 to 6 mEq/L. Which way does the resting membrane potential move, and what is the immediate effect on excitability?
options: Away from threshold, making the cell less excitable
Toward threshold, making the cell more excitable at first
It does not move, so excitability is unchanged
Toward threshold, but the cell becomes less excitable immediately
questions.why: A smaller K+ gradient means a less negative K+ equilibrium potential, so the resting potential drifts up from about -70 mV toward threshold and a smaller stimulus now suffices, which is why mild hyperkalemia is initially excitatory. Moving away from threshold is what hypokalemia does. The resting potential is very sensitive to extracellular K+, so no change is wrong. Reduced excitability does come later, but only once the depolarization is large enough to inactivate Na+ channels.
questions.answerText: Toward threshold, making the cell more excitable at first

questions.q: Extracellular K+ reaches 7.5 mEq/L and the resting potential settles near -55 mV. Why does the cell become inexcitable rather than fire continuously?
options: The K+ equilibrium potential is now above threshold
The Na+/K+ ATPase stops working when extracellular K+ is this high
Sustained depolarization inactivates the voltage gated Na+ channels
Threshold rises above the new resting potential
questions.why: Inactivation gates close in response to depolarization and reopen only on repolarization, so a membrane held near threshold accumulates inactivated Na+ channels until too few are available to generate an upstroke, and the cell falls silent despite sitting close to threshold. The K+ equilibrium potential has moved up but is still well below threshold. The pump actually works faster with more extracellular K+, since K+ is its substrate on the outside. Threshold itself does not move; what changes is how many Na+ channels can respond when it is reached.
questions.answerText: Sustained depolarization inactivates the voltage gated Na+ channels

questions.q: A patient's plasma K+ falls to 2.5 mEq/L. Predict the effect on nerve and muscle excitability.
options: Increased excitability, because the K+ gradient across the membrane is steeper
Reduced excitability, because the Na+ channels have become inactivated
No change, because intracellular K+ is unchanged by the plasma value
Reduced excitability, because the resting potential moves farther from threshold
questions.why: Lower extracellular K+ makes the K+ equilibrium potential more negative and hyperpolarizes the cell, so a larger depolarization is needed to reach threshold and the cell is harder to excite. A steeper K+ gradient does hyperpolarize the cell, but hyperpolarization reduces excitability rather than increasing it. Intracellular K+ is indeed nearly unchanged, but the resting potential depends on the ratio across the membrane, so the outside value matters enormously. Na+ channel inactivation is the mechanism in hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia; here the channels are, if anything, more available than usual.
questions.answerText: Reduced excitability, because the resting potential moves farther from threshold

questions.q: Lidocaine is injected around a sensory nerve. What happens to the receptor potential at the sensory ending and to the action potentials in the axon?
options: Both the receptor potential and the resulting action potentials are abolished
Both continue, but the action potentials are smaller than normal
The receptor potential is abolished but action potentials continue
The receptor potential still forms, but no action potentials are generated
questions.why: Receptor potentials come from mechanically or chemically gated channels, which lidocaine does not block, so the local graded response survives, but without voltage gated Na+ channels that depolarization can never be converted into a propagating action potential and nothing reaches the central nervous system. Abolishing both would require blocking the sensory transduction channels as well. Losing the receptor potential while keeping action potentials reverses the order of events in the pathway. Smaller action potentials would occur with partial block, but a full block produces none at all.
questions.answerText: The receptor potential still forms, but no action potentials are generated

questions.q: A cell is bathed in a solution with extracellular K+ lowered from 4 to 2 mEq/L. Which way does the K+ equilibrium potential move?
options: It becomes more negative
It becomes less negative
It becomes positive
It does not change, since intracellular K+ is unchanged
questions.why: The Nernst equation depends on the ratio of outside to inside concentration, and halving the outside value makes that ratio smaller, driving the equilibrium potential further below zero, toward roughly -108 mV. Becoming less negative is the direction taken when extracellular K+ rises. A positive value would require extracellular K+ to exceed intracellular K+, which is far from the case. Holding intracellular K+ constant does not protect the equilibrium potential, because the ratio is what matters.
questions.answerText: It becomes more negative

questions.q: Which single measurement best distinguishes a cell in hyperkalemia from a cell in hypokalemia?
options: The peak of the action potential
The resting membrane potential
The conduction velocity of the axon
The duration of the absolute refractory period
questions.why: The two conditions push the resting potential in opposite directions, depolarized in hyperkalemia and hyperpolarized in hypokalemia, so the baseline voltage separates them immediately. The action potential peak can fall in hyperkalemia through Na+ channel inactivation, but it does not move in a clean opposite direction in hypokalemia. Conduction velocity and refractory duration can both be affected indirectly, but neither gives the clear, opposite signed answer that the resting potential does.
questions.answerText: The resting membrane potential

questions.q: A patient's plasma K+ climbs steadily from 5 to 7 mEq/L. Describe how excitability changes over that climb.
options: It falls steadily throughout, because K+ always stabilizes the membrane
It rises steadily throughout, because the resting potential just keeps approaching threshold
It rises at first as the resting potential nears threshold, then falls as Na+ channels inactivate
It is unchanged until K+ exceeds 10 mEq/L, when the cell suddenly depolarizes
questions.why: Two effects overlap: bringing the resting potential closer to threshold makes firing easier, but holding the membrane depolarized progressively inactivates Na+ channels, and beyond a point the second effect dominates and the cell cannot fire at all. Steady loss of excitability throughout ignores the early phase, which is why rising K+ can first cause tingling and cramping. Steady gain throughout is the classic half learned answer, since it tracks only the distance to threshold and forgets inactivation. Excitability changes measurably well before 10 mEq/L, so a sudden all or nothing switch does not describe the progression.
questions.answerText: It rises at first as the resting potential nears threshold, then falls as Na+ channels inactivate

questions.q: A dentist injects lidocaine near a sensory nerve before drilling. Trace what happens from the stimulus to the perceived sensation.
options: The receptors no longer respond, so no receptor potential and no signal are produced
Action potentials still travel but arrive too slowly to be perceived as pain
Receptor potentials still form, but the axon cannot generate action potentials
The brain receives the signal but cannot interpret it because the fibers are blocked
questions.why: Drilling still deforms and damages tissue, so transduction channels still open and a graded receptor potential still develops, but with voltage gated Na+ channels blocked the trigger zone cannot convert that depolarization into a propagating action potential, and the pathway falls silent at that step. The receptors themselves use chemically and mechanically gated channels that lidocaine does not affect. Slower conduction would delay the sensation rather than abolish it. Nothing reaches the brain at all, so an interpretation problem in the brain is not the issue.
questions.answerText: Receptor potentials still form, but the axon cannot generate action potentials

questions.q: An axon in an experimental bath has a resting potential of -60 mV instead of -70 mV, and its action potentials have a lower peak than normal. Which change to the bath explains both findings?
options: Extracellular Na+ has been raised
Extracellular K+ has been raised
Extracellular Cl- has been lowered
Extracellular K+ has been lowered
questions.why: Raising extracellular K+ makes the K+ equilibrium potential less negative and depolarizes the resting membrane, and that sustained depolarization inactivates a fraction of the Na+ channels so fewer are available for the upstroke, which lowers the peak, so one change accounts for both observations. Raising extracellular Na+ would raise the peak rather than lower it and would barely touch the resting potential. Lowering Cl- has little effect in an axon where Cl- carries small resting current. Lowering K+ would hyperpolarize the cell, moving the resting potential the wrong way.
questions.answerText: Extracellular K+ has been raised

questions.q: Extracellular Na+ is halved in a nerve bath. Predict the effect on the resting potential and on the action potential peak.
options: The resting potential barely moves, but the peak falls noticeably
The resting potential falls sharply while the peak is unchanged
Both the resting potential and the peak fall sharply
Neither value changes, because the pump restores the gradient
questions.why: Membrane potential at any moment reflects the equilibrium potential of the most permeant ion, so at rest, when K+ permeability rules, cutting extracellular Na+ has only a small effect, while at the peak, when Na+ permeability rules, the less positive Na+ equilibrium potential pulls the peak down noticeably. Equal effects on both would require Na+ to dominate permeability at rest, which it does not. A large fall in resting potential with an unchanged peak reverses which phase depends on Na+. The pump moves ions across the membrane and cannot change what is dissolved in the bath.
questions.answerText: The resting potential barely moves, but the peak falls noticeably

questions.q: In a neuron simulation, tetrodotoxin (TTX) is applied. Which channel does it block?
options: K+ leak channels
Voltage gated K+ channels
Voltage gated Na+ channels
The Na+/K+ ATPase
questions.why: TTX plugs the pore of the voltage gated Na+ channel, which is why it is the standard tool for removing the depolarizing upstroke in a simulation. Voltage gated K+ channels are blocked by tetraethylammonium instead. Leak channels are not the target of either classic blocker. The Na+/K+ ATPase is inhibited by ouabain, a different agent working on a pump rather than a channel.
questions.answerText: Voltage gated Na+ channels

questions.q: In a neuron simulation, tetraethylammonium (TEA) is applied. Which channel does it block?
options: Voltage gated Na+ channels
Chemically gated Na+ channels
Voltage gated K+ channels
Voltage gated Ca2+ channels
questions.why: TEA blocks the delayed rectifier voltage gated K+ channel, so in a simulation it is used to slow repolarization and remove the afterhyperpolarization. Voltage gated Na+ channels are the target of tetrodotoxin. Chemically gated channels respond to transmitter and are not part of the axonal action potential machinery being tested. Voltage gated Ca2+ channels matter at the axon terminal but do not shape the axonal action potential in these simulations.
questions.answerText: Voltage gated K+ channels

questions.q: In an action potential simulation, what does the stimulus setting control?
options: The number of Na+ channels present in the membrane
The size of the depolarization delivered to the membrane
The resting potential the membrane returns to
The conduction velocity of the simulated axon
questions.why: The stimulus control sets how large a depolarizing current is injected, which determines whether the membrane reaches threshold and, with repeated stimuli, how often it fires. Channel numbers are properties of the simulated membrane, adjusted separately or by applying a blocker. The resting potential is set by the ion concentrations and leak permeabilities in the model. Conduction velocity depends on the modeled diameter and myelination, not on how hard the membrane is pushed.
questions.answerText: The size of the depolarization delivered to the membrane

questions.q: On a simulated action potential tracing, what does the vertical axis show?
options: Stimulus current in milliamperes
Membrane potential in millivolts
Ion concentration in mEq/L
Channel conductance in siemens
questions.why: The standard action potential tracing plots membrane potential in millivolts against time in milliseconds, so the vertical excursion from about -70 mV up to about +30 mV is the action potential itself. Stimulus current is what the experimenter sets, and it appears as an input rather than as the plotted response. Ion concentrations change negligibly during an action potential and are not what the trace displays. Conductance curves can be plotted separately in some simulations but are not the default trace.
questions.answerText: Membrane potential in millivolts

questions.q: On a normal simulated tracing, what value does the peak of the action potential reach?
options: About -55 mV
About -30 mV
About +90 mV
About +30 mV
questions.why: A healthy simulated neuron peaks near +30 mV, short of the Na+ equilibrium potential because K+ channels open and Na+ channels inactivate before the membrane gets there. About -55 mV is the threshold line on the same plot, not the peak. About -30 mV is a point on the rising phase. About +90 mV exceeds the Na+ equilibrium potential and is not reachable.
questions.answerText: About +30 mV

questions.q: In a simulation, a suprathreshold stimulus is delivered and the trace shows only a small bump that decays back to the resting potential. What does this indicate?
options: An action potential of reduced amplitude was generated
The resting potential has shifted to a new value
An action potential was generated but conducted away before recording
No action potential was generated
questions.why: A small decaying bump is the passive response of the membrane to injected current, a graded potential, and the absence of any regenerative upstroke means no action potential occurred. A reduced amplitude action potential would still show a clear rapid rise and fall rather than a passive decay. A recording electrode on the stimulated membrane sees the action potential where it starts, so conduction away is not an explanation. The trace returns to its original baseline, so the resting potential has not shifted.
questions.answerText: No action potential was generated

questions.q: In an action potential simulation, what does the threshold stimulus mean?
options: The stimulus that produces the largest action potential
The smallest stimulus that produces an action potential
The stimulus that produces the fastest conduction velocity
The stimulus that produces the shortest refractory period
questions.why: Threshold stimulus is found by increasing the stimulus in small steps until an action potential first appears, and that value marks the boundary between subthreshold and suprathreshold. Since action potentials are all or none, no stimulus produces a larger one, so a stimulus that yields the largest action potential is something that does not exist. Conduction velocity and refractory period are properties of the membrane and are not set by the size of the stimulus.
questions.answerText: The smallest stimulus that produces an action potential

questions.q: Which phase of the simulated action potential does TEA prolong?
options: Repolarization
The rising phase to the peak
The resting phase before the stimulus
The delay between the stimulus and threshold
questions.why: Repolarization is driven by K+ leaving through voltage gated K+ channels, so blocking those channels with TEA removes the main outward current and the membrane takes much longer to return toward rest. The rising phase depends on Na+ entry and is unaffected by a K+ channel blocker. The resting phase is maintained by leak channels rather than by the voltage gated K+ channels TEA blocks. The delay to threshold depends on the stimulus size and on passive membrane properties.
questions.answerText: Repolarization

questions.q: TTX is added in the simulation and a stimulus well above the previous threshold is delivered. What does the tracing show?
options: A normal action potential with a delayed onset
A small passive depolarization with no action potential
An action potential with a normal peak but slow repolarization
An action potential with a reduced peak and a normal afterhyperpolarization
questions.why: With voltage gated Na+ channels blocked there is no regenerative inward current, so the injected stimulus produces only the passive depolarization it delivers directly and the membrane decays back to rest. A delayed but normal action potential would require working Na+ channels. Slow repolarization with a normal peak is the TEA pattern, since it leaves the Na+ channels intact. A reduced peak is what partial Na+ block produces, but a full block leaves no action potential at all.
questions.answerText: A small passive depolarization with no action potential

questions.q: TEA is added in the simulation and a suprathreshold stimulus is delivered. What does the tracing show?
options: A normal upstroke with slowed repolarization and little afterhyperpolarization
No response beyond the stimulus artifact, with the membrane staying at rest
A reduced upstroke with normal repolarization and normal afterhyperpolarization
A normal upstroke followed by a deeper and longer afterhyperpolarization
questions.why: TEA leaves the Na+ channels untouched, so the upstroke is normal, but removing the delayed K+ current slows the return to rest and eliminates the overshoot below rest that those same lingering K+ channels normally cause. No response at all is the TTX pattern. A reduced upstroke would point to a Na+ channel problem instead. A deeper afterhyperpolarization would require more K+ efflux, which is the opposite of what a K+ channel blocker does.
questions.answerText: A normal upstroke with slowed repolarization and little afterhyperpolarization

questions.q: With TTX present, the simulated stimulus is increased fivefold and still produces no action potential. How should this be interpreted?
options: The stimulus is still below the new threshold and should be raised further
The membrane is in a refractory period that a stronger stimulus will overcome
The recording electrode has failed and should be repositioned
The block is on the channels themselves, so no stimulus size can restore firing
questions.why: Threshold has meaning only if Na+ channels are available to carry the regenerative current, and when those channels are plugged the membrane can be depolarized as far as you like without an action potential ever developing. Raising the stimulus further is the intuitive move but it cannot work, and recognizing that is the point of the experiment. The electrode is clearly working, since the passive depolarization is recorded. The membrane is not refractory, because no action potential preceded this stimulus.
questions.answerText: The block is on the channels themselves, so no stimulus size can restore firing

questions.q: A simulated tracing shows a normal resting potential and a normal time course, but the peak reaches only +5 mV instead of +30 mV. What is the most likely cause?
options: A fraction of the voltage gated K+ channels is blocked
The stimulus was delivered below threshold
The Na+/K+ ATPase has been inhibited
A fraction of the voltage gated Na+ channels is blocked
questions.why: The height of the peak depends on how much Na+ current the membrane can generate, so removing some of the Na+ channels lowers the peak while leaving the overall shape and timing recognizable. Blocking K+ channels would stretch repolarization rather than shorten the climb. Inhibiting the pump degrades gradients over minutes and would show up first as a drifting resting potential. A subthreshold stimulus would give no action potential at all rather than a small one, since the response is all or none.
questions.answerText: A fraction of the voltage gated Na+ channels is blocked

questions.q: A simulated action potential has a normal peak and normal repolarization but no afterhyperpolarization at all. Which manipulation best explains this?
options: Partial block of the voltage gated Na+ channels
An increase in extracellular Na+
Partial block of the voltage gated K+ channels
A decrease in extracellular Na+
questions.why: Afterhyperpolarization exists because voltage gated K+ channels remain open past the return to rest, so reducing their number removes the extra K+ efflux and the trace stops at the resting potential, and a partial block can do this while leaving repolarization close to normal. Na+ channel block would show up in the upstroke and the peak. Changing extracellular Na+ shifts the peak by changing the Na+ equilibrium potential and does not selectively remove the tail of the trace.
questions.answerText: Partial block of the voltage gated K+ channels

questions.q: In the simulation, the stimulus is increased from just above threshold to three times threshold, and repeated stimuli are delivered. What changes on the tracing?
options: The action potentials become taller while keeping the same spacing
The action potentials come closer together while keeping the same height
The action potentials become wider while keeping the same height
The action potentials arrive at the recording site sooner after leaving the trigger zone
questions.why: Stronger stimulation drives the membrane back to threshold sooner after each recovery, so the frequency rises while each action potential stays the same size, which is the simulation demonstrating frequency coding. Taller action potentials would violate the all or none principle. Width is set by channel kinetics and does not change with stimulus strength. Conduction time depends on the axon's cable properties, not on how hard the trigger zone is pushed.
questions.answerText: The action potentials come closer together while keeping the same height

questions.q: A simulated response grows steadily as the stimulus is increased and never rises above 0 mV. What is being recorded?
options: A graded potential rather than an action potential
An action potential with partial Na+ channel block
An action potential recorded far from the trigger zone
An afterhyperpolarization following a subthreshold stimulus
questions.why: Growing in proportion to the stimulus is the definition of a graded response, and the absence of any overshoot confirms that the regenerative Na+ current never took over. A partially blocked action potential has a lower peak but is still all or none, so it does not scale smoothly with the stimulus. Action potentials are the same size wherever along the axon they are recorded, so distance does not explain a graded response. Afterhyperpolarization is a hyperpolarization and requires a preceding action potential.
questions.answerText: A graded potential rather than an action potential

questions.q: A simulation applies enough TTX to block half the Na+ channels. Predict what happens to the threshold stimulus and to the peak of the action potentials that still occur.
options: Threshold falls and the peak rises, because the remaining channels open more readily
Threshold is unchanged and the peak falls, since threshold depends only on voltage
Threshold rises and the peak falls, because less Na+ current is available
Threshold rises and the peak is unchanged, since amplitude is all or none
questions.why: With half the channels gone, more depolarization is needed before the inward current can outrun the outward one, so the stimulus required rises, and the total inward current available at any voltage is smaller, so the peak is lower. The remaining channels have unchanged gating and do not compensate by opening more readily. Threshold is a voltage, but which voltage is enough depends on the density of available channels, so it does shift. All or none applies to a given membrane in a given state, and a state with fewer Na+ channels has a lower all or none amplitude.
questions.answerText: Threshold rises and the peak falls, because less Na+ current is available

questions.q: TEA is applied and the simulated neuron is then driven with rapid repeated stimuli. Predict the effect on the maximum firing frequency.
options: It rises, because K+ channels no longer oppose depolarization
It is unchanged, because firing frequency is set by the stimulus strength alone
It falls, because the prolonged action potential lengthens the refractory period
It falls, because the action potential amplitude is reduced
questions.why: Na+ channels can only recover from inactivation once the membrane repolarizes, so a trace that takes far longer to come back down keeps the membrane refractory for longer and the next action potential cannot start as soon, lowering the ceiling on firing rate. The removal of an opposing outward current does make it easier to depolarize, but the rate limiting step is recovery from inactivation, not the ease of depolarizing. Stimulus strength drives the rate toward the ceiling but does not set the ceiling. Amplitude is essentially preserved with TEA, since the Na+ channels are untouched.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the prolonged action potential lengthens the refractory period

questions.q: A simulated tracing shows a normal upstroke and peak, repolarization taking three times as long as the control, and no afterhyperpolarization. Which blocker was used?
options: A voltage gated K+ channel blocker such as TEA
A voltage gated Na+ channel blocker such as TTX
A Na+/K+ ATPase inhibitor such as ouabain
A blocker of chemically gated channels at the synapse
questions.why: Reading the trace backward, an intact upstroke and peak clear the Na+ channels of suspicion, while slowed repolarization and a missing afterhyperpolarization both point at the delayed K+ current that normally ends the action potential. TTX would have removed the action potential entirely rather than stretching its tail. Pump inhibition acts over minutes and would show as a drifting baseline rather than a reshaped single action potential. Chemically gated channels are at synapses and play no part in shaping the axonal waveform.
questions.answerText: A voltage gated K+ channel blocker such as TEA

questions.q: Both TTX and TEA are applied to the simulated neuron at once, then a large stimulus is delivered. What does the tracing show and why?
options: A passive depolarization only, since without Na+ channels nothing can start
A prolonged action potential, because the K+ channel block dominates the result
A normal action potential, because the two blockers cancel each other out
A hyperpolarization, because K+ efflux is left unopposed by Na+ entry
questions.why: The Na+ current is the event that starts everything, so removing it means there is nothing for the K+ block to prolong and the trace shows only the passive response to the injected current. A prolonged action potential requires an action potential to exist in the first place. The two blockers act on different channels and cannot cancel; each removes a current, and neither restores the other. A K+ block reduces efflux rather than leaving it unopposed, so a hyperpolarization is the wrong direction.
questions.answerText: A passive depolarization only, since without Na+ channels nothing can start

questions.q: What is a compound action potential?
options: The graded potential recorded at a sensory ending
A single action potential recorded from one large axon
An action potential that travels in both directions at once
The summed electrical response of all the axons in a nerve
questions.why: A nerve contains many axons, and a surface electrode records the sum of their individual action potentials as one wave, which is why it is called compound. A recording from one axon is a single unit action potential and is all or none. Bidirectional travel can occur after mid nerve stimulation but is not what the term describes. A graded potential at a sensory ending is a receptor potential, recorded at a single ending rather than from a whole nerve.
questions.answerText: The summed electrical response of all the axons in a nerve

questions.q: Is the compound action potential all or none?
options: Yes, because each axon in the nerve is all or none
No, because each axon fires with a different amplitude
Yes, because the whole nerve either fires together or does not fire
No, its size grows as more axons are recruited by a stronger stimulus
questions.why: Every individual axon is all or none, but axons have different thresholds, so a stronger stimulus brings more of them into the response and the summed wave grows, which makes the compound response graded. Reasoning from the behavior of one axon to the behavior of the whole nerve is the trap here. The nerve does not fire as a unit; each axon decides independently. Individual axons do not vary in amplitude; the variation in the compound response comes from how many are firing.
questions.answerText: No, its size grows as more axons are recruited by a stronger stimulus

questions.q: How is conduction velocity calculated from a nerve recording?
options: Distance traveled divided by conduction time
Conduction time divided by distance traveled
Distance traveled multiplied by conduction time
Stimulus strength divided by conduction time
questions.why: Velocity is distance per unit time, so measuring how far the signal traveled and how long it took gives the answer directly, usually reported in meters per second. Dividing time by distance gives the reciprocal, which is a delay per unit length rather than a velocity. Multiplying the two gives a quantity with no physical meaning here. Stimulus strength determines how many axons fire, not how fast the action potentials travel.
questions.answerText: Distance traveled divided by conduction time

questions.q: What is latency in a nerve conduction recording?
options: The time from the peak of the recorded response back to baseline
The time from the stimulus to the onset of the recorded response
The duration of the compound action potential itself
The interval between two successive stimuli
questions.why: Latency is the delay between delivering the stimulus and seeing the response arrive at the recording electrode, and it is the raw measurement from which conduction velocity is calculated. The fall from peak to baseline is part of the waveform's shape rather than its arrival time. The duration of the wave reflects the spread of fiber velocities in the nerve. The interval between stimuli is set by the experimenter and is a separate parameter.
questions.answerText: The time from the stimulus to the onset of the recorded response

questions.q: Which axons contribute to the earliest part of a compound action potential?
options: The smallest unmyelinated axons
The axons closest to the recording electrode
The largest myelinated axons
The axons with the lowest resting potential
questions.why: The earliest arrival belongs to the fastest fibers, and the fastest fibers are the large myelinated ones, so the leading edge of the compound response reflects them. Small unmyelinated axons are the slowest and contribute to the late, low components of the wave. All the axons in a nerve travel essentially the same distance to the electrode, so proximity does not sort the arrivals. Resting potential differences affect excitability rather than conduction speed.
questions.answerText: The largest myelinated axons

questions.q: In what units is nerve conduction velocity usually reported?
options: Meters per second
Millivolts per millisecond
Milliseconds per centimeter
Millimeters per minute
questions.why: Conduction velocity is a speed and is conventionally given in meters per second, which puts human nerves in a convenient range of roughly 1 to 100 m/s. Millivolts per millisecond is a rate of voltage change, which describes the steepness of the upstroke rather than travel speed. Milliseconds per centimeter is a delay per unit length, the reciprocal of velocity. Millimeters per minute is a speed but on a timescale suited to growth rather than to electrical signaling.
questions.answerText: Meters per second

questions.q: Why does a compound action potential often show more than one peak?
options: Because each axon fires more than once per stimulus
Because groups of fibers with different conduction velocities arrive at different times
Because the stimulus is delivered more than once
Because the recording electrode picks up both the depolarization and the repolarization
questions.why: A nerve carries fiber groups with very different diameters and degrees of myelination, and each group arrives as its own bump, so the summed wave separates into peaks as the recording distance grows. A single stimulus produces one action potential per axon, so repeated firing is not the explanation. Multiple stimuli would be visible as multiple stimulus artifacts. Depolarization and repolarization within one wave shape a single deflection rather than producing separate peaks.
questions.answerText: Because groups of fibers with different conduction velocities arrive at different times

questions.q: What is the stimulus artifact on a nerve conduction tracing?
options: The first action potentials arriving from the fastest fibers in the nerve
Noise from the muscle beneath the electrode contracting after the stimulus
The stimulator current picked up directly by the recording electrode
The afterhyperpolarization that follows the compound action potential
questions.why: Current from the stimulator spreads through the tissue and reaches the recording electrode almost instantly, producing a sharp deflection that marks time zero for measuring latency. The arrival of the fastest fibers comes after a real conduction delay and is the response, not the artifact. Muscle activity produces its own later potentials and is a different signal. Afterhyperpolarization follows the response rather than preceding it.
questions.answerText: The stimulator current picked up directly by the recording electrode

questions.q: Two recording sites are 12 cm apart and the response onset differs by 2 ms between them. What is the conduction velocity of the fastest fibers?
options: 6 m/s
24 m/s
60 m/s
questions.why: Convert to base units first: 12 cm is 0.12 m and 2 ms is 0.002 s, and 0.12 divided by 0.002 is 60 m/s, a normal value for a large myelinated nerve. Six meters per second comes from dropping a factor of ten in the length conversion. Twenty four comes from multiplying rather than dividing. Six hundred exceeds any biological conduction velocity by roughly a factor of six.
questions.answerText: 60 m/s

questions.q: Why is conduction velocity usually calculated from the difference between two recording sites rather than from a single latency?
options: Subtracting cancels out the effect of temperature on the nerve fibers
Subtracting removes the fixed delay before conduction actually begins
A single site cannot detect the compound action potential reliably enough
Two sites are needed because each one records only half of the fibers
questions.why: Some of the latency at any single site is spent getting the axons to fire in the first place, and that delay is the same at both sites, so subtracting the two latencies leaves only the time spent traveling the known distance between them. Temperature does affect conduction, but it affects both sites equally and is not what the subtraction is designed to remove. One electrode records the compound response perfectly well; the problem is interpreting its latency. Both electrodes see the same population of fibers, just at different times.
questions.answerText: Subtracting removes the fixed delay before conduction actually begins

questions.q: The stimulus to a nerve is increased and the compound action potential grows larger. What does this show?
options: Each axon is producing a larger action potential
The axons are conducting more rapidly
More axons are being recruited into the response
The refractory period has shortened
questions.why: Individual axons are all or none, so the only way the summed wave can grow is for additional axons, with higher thresholds, to start contributing. Larger individual action potentials are ruled out by the all or none principle. Conduction velocity is a fixed property of each axon and does not rise with stimulus strength. Refractory period is a membrane property and is not affected by how hard the nerve is stimulated.
questions.answerText: More axons are being recruited into the response

questions.q: A compound action potential is recorded first at 4 cm and then at 20 cm from the stimulus site. How does the shape of the wave change with distance?
options: It becomes taller and narrower as the signal builds
It stays exactly the same, since action potentials do not decay
It spreads out and flattens as the fiber groups separate in time
It reverses polarity because the electrode is now past the fastest fibers
questions.why: Fast and slow fibers start together but pull apart as they travel, so at longer distances their contributions no longer overlap and the summed wave becomes broader and lower, a phenomenon called temporal dispersion. The wave does not build with distance; each axon carries the same action potential the whole way. It is true that individual action potentials do not decay, but the compound wave still changes shape because of differences in arrival time. Polarity depends on electrode arrangement, not on distance.
questions.answerText: It spreads out and flattens as the fiber groups separate in time

questions.q: A nerve conducts at 50 m/s. How long does a signal take to travel 0.5 m?
options: 1 ms
10 ms
25 ms
100 ms
questions.why: Time is distance divided by velocity, so 0.5 m divided by 50 m/s gives 0.01 s, which is 10 ms. One millisecond would require a velocity of 500 m/s. Twenty five milliseconds comes from multiplying 0.5 by 50 and misplacing the units. One hundred milliseconds corresponds to a velocity of 5 m/s, which is ten times too slow for this nerve.
questions.answerText: 10 ms

questions.q: Which point on the compound action potential should be used to calculate the velocity of the fastest fibers?
options: The onset of the response
The peak of the response
The point where the response returns to baseline
The midpoint of the falling phase
questions.why: The fastest fibers are the first to arrive, so the very beginning of the deflection marks their arrival time and is the correct point for calculating their velocity. The peak reflects the arrival of the largest group of fibers rather than the quickest ones. The return to baseline marks the arrival of the slowest contributors. The falling phase midpoint has no clear physiological meaning as an arrival time.
questions.answerText: The onset of the response

questions.q: A compound action potential recorded 12 cm from the stimulus begins at 2 ms and its last component arrives at 6 ms. What are the velocities of the fastest and slowest contributing fibers?
options: About 6 m/s and about 2 m/s
About 60 m/s and about 20 m/s
About 20 m/s and about 60 m/s
About 24 m/s and about 72 m/s
questions.why: Each velocity is 0.12 m divided by the relevant time, so 0.12 divided by 0.002 gives 60 m/s for the earliest arrivals and 0.12 divided by 0.006 gives 20 m/s for the last, a range consistent with a mix of large and medium myelinated fibers. The values near 6 and 2 m/s drop a factor of ten in the length conversion. Assigning 20 m/s to the fastest fibers reverses the relationship, since arriving earlier means moving faster. The pair near 24 and 72 m/s comes from multiplying instead of dividing.
questions.answerText: About 60 m/s and about 20 m/s

questions.q: One nerve study shows a conduction velocity of 25 m/s with a compound response of near normal size. Another shows a velocity of 52 m/s with a compound response one third of normal size. What does each pattern suggest?
options: The first suggests loss of axons and the second suggests demyelination
Both suggest loss of axons, differing only in severity
Both suggest demyelination, differing only in severity
The first suggests demyelination and the second suggests loss of axons
questions.why: Velocity reports the quality of insulation and fiber size, while response amplitude reports how many axons are firing, so slow conduction with a full sized response points to intact axons that have lost myelin, and normal speed with a small response points to fewer surviving axons that still conduct normally. Swapping the two interpretations ignores which measurement each pathology affects. Calling both demyelination cannot explain the reduced amplitude in the second study. Calling both axon loss cannot explain the slowing in the first.
questions.answerText: The first suggests demyelination and the second suggests loss of axons

questions.q: A student calculates conduction velocity by dividing the distance from the stimulator to a single recording electrode by the latency at that electrode. How will the result compare with the true velocity?
options: It will be an underestimate, because the latency includes a delay before conduction begins
It will be an overestimate, because the latency omits the time spent at the nodes
It will be correct, because the delay is negligible in a healthy nerve
It will be an underestimate, because the distance was measured along a curved path in the limb
questions.why: Part of the measured latency is spent bringing the axons to threshold rather than traveling, so dividing the full distance by a latency that includes that extra time makes the nerve look slower than it is, which is exactly why two site subtraction is the standard method. The nodal delays are part of conduction and are already included in a true velocity measurement. The initiation delay is a fraction of a millisecond but is a substantial share of a short latency, so it is not negligible. Path curvature is a real measurement concern but would make the assumed distance too short and the velocity too low for a different reason, and it is not the systematic error the single site method introduces.
questions.answerText: It will be an underestimate, because the latency includes a delay before conduction begins

questions.q: Stimulus intensity is raised step by step, and beyond a certain point the compound action potential stops growing. What has happened, and what is the stimulus called at that point?
options: Every axon in the nerve is now firing, and the stimulus is supramaximal
The axons have reached their maximum action potential amplitude, and the stimulus is at threshold
The nerve has entered a refractory period, and the stimulus is subthreshold
The recording electrode has saturated, and the stimulus is maximal
questions.why: The compound response grows only through recruitment, so once the highest threshold axons have been brought in there is nothing left to add and further increases in stimulus change nothing, which is why nerve studies deliberately use a supramaximal stimulus to guarantee a complete response. Individual action potentials never grow with stimulus strength, so a ceiling on amplitude per axon is not the explanation. Threshold names the stimulus that first excites the most sensitive axons, at the other end of the range. Nothing here indicates refractoriness or an equipment limit.
questions.answerText: Every axon in the nerve is now firing, and the stimulus is supramaximal

questions.q: What does Ohm's law say about current flow?
options: Current flow equals voltage multiplied by resistance
Current flow depends only on the number of open channels
Current flow is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance
Current flow rises as resistance rises
questions.why: Ohm's law says current (I) is directly proportional to the voltage difference (V) and inversely proportional to resistance (R), written I = V/R. Voltage equals current times resistance, so multiplying voltage by resistance is the wrong arrangement. Open channels matter because they change resistance, but voltage matters too. More resistance means less current, not more.
questions.answerText: Current flow is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance

questions.q: What is the conductance of an ion channel?
options: The ease with which ions flow through it
The voltage at which it opens
The speed at which a signal travels down the axon
The amount of ATP it uses to move ions
questions.why: Conductance, written G, is how easily ions flow through a channel, and it changes with the channel's gating state. The voltage at which a channel opens is a property of voltage-gated channels, not the definition of conductance. The speed of a signal down the axon is conduction, a different word for a different idea. Ion channels let ions move down their gradients and do not use ATP.
questions.answerText: The ease with which ions flow through it

questions.q: What are the two main sources of resistance to current flow in a neuron?
options: The extracellular fluid and the myelin
The nucleus and the axon terminal
The Na+/K+ ATPase and the leak channels
The cell membrane and the cytoplasm
questions.why: Resistance comes mainly from the cell membrane and from the cytoplasm inside the cell. The extracellular fluid also has resistance, but it is so small that it is usually ignored. Leak channels lower membrane resistance rather than create it, and the pump moves ions rather than resisting current. The nucleus and axon terminal are structures, not sources of resistance.
questions.answerText: The cell membrane and the cytoplasm

questions.q: Many ion channels in a patch of membrane open at once, and the electrochemical gradient stays the same. What happens to membrane resistance and to current across the membrane?
options: Resistance rises and current falls
Resistance falls and current rises
Resistance and current both fall
Neither changes, because resistance depends only on the cytoplasm
questions.why: A membrane with no open channels has very high resistance. Opening channels lowers membrane resistance, and by Ohm's law a lower resistance lets more current flow for the same driving force. Resistance does not rise when channels open, so current cannot fall. The membrane is one of the two main sources of resistance, so it does matter, not only the cytoplasm.
questions.answerText: Resistance falls and current rises

questions.q: Why can current travel farther through a larger-diameter neuron before it dies out?
options: Its membrane has more leak channels
Its cytoplasm has a different composition
Its internal resistance is lower
It has a more negative resting membrane potential
questions.why: Internal resistance falls as cell diameter increases, so current meets less resistance inside a wide neuron and spreads farther. Cytoplasm composition is about the same in all neurons, so it does not explain the difference. More leak channels would let more current escape and shorten the spread. Resting membrane potential does not depend on diameter.
questions.answerText: Its internal resistance is lower

questions.q: Two neurons get the same depolarizing stimulus on the cell body. Neuron A has many open leak channels in its cell body membrane, and neuron B has few. In which neuron will the graded potential spread farther, and why?
options: Neuron B, because fewer open leak channels mean higher membrane resistance and less current lost
Neuron A, because more open channels let more current flow down the cell
Neuron A, because leak channels regenerate the signal the way voltage-gated channels do
They spread equally, because only cytoplasmic resistance matters
questions.why: A graded potential shrinks as current leaks out through open channels and meets resistance in the cytoplasm. With fewer open leak channels, neuron B has higher membrane resistance, loses less current, and carries the graded potential farther. The current escaping through neuron A's extra leak channels leaves the cell rather than flowing down it. Leak channels do not regenerate a signal, and both membrane resistance and cytoplasmic resistance set how far current spreads.
questions.answerText: Neuron B, because fewer open leak channels mean higher membrane resistance and less current lost

questions.q: Which ion enters the axon terminal and triggers vesicle fusion at a chemical synapse?
options: Na+
K+
Ca2+
Cl-
questions.why: Depolarization of the terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and the Ca2+ that rushes in binds the vesicle sensor that drives fusion. Na+ entry carries the action potential along the axon and into the terminal, but Na+ itself does not trigger release. K+ leaves during repolarization rather than entering. Cl- movement is not part of the release step at the presynaptic terminal.
questions.answerText: Ca2+

questions.q: What opens the voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic terminal?
options: Binding of neurotransmitter to the vesicle membrane
Depolarization delivered by the arriving action potential
Hyperpolarization of the terminal below resting potential
Stretch of the terminal membrane by vesicle docking
questions.why: These channels are voltage gated, so the change in membrane potential produced by the invading action potential is the stimulus that opens them. Neurotransmitter binding acts on the postsynaptic side, not on the presynaptic channel. Hyperpolarization closes voltage-gated channels rather than opening them. Mechanical stretch opens a different family of channels not involved in this step.
questions.answerText: Depolarization delivered by the arriving action potential

questions.q: Where is neurotransmitter stored in the axon terminal before release?
options: In synaptic vesicles
Free in the cytosol of the terminal
Inside the mitochondria of the terminal
Bound to the outer face of the terminal membrane
questions.why: Transmitter is concentrated inside membrane-bound synaptic vesicles, which is what allows release in discrete packets called quanta. Free cytosolic transmitter exists but is the pool being loaded into vesicles, not the releasable store. Mitochondria supply ATP for the terminal and, for catecholamines, host the degrading enzyme MAO, but they do not store releasable transmitter. Transmitter bound to the outer membrane face would already be in the cleft.
questions.answerText: In synaptic vesicles

questions.q: By what process does a synaptic vesicle release its neurotransmitter into the cleft?
options: Endocytosis
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Exocytosis
questions.why: The vesicle membrane fuses with the terminal membrane and dumps its contents outward, which is exocytosis. Endocytosis is the reverse step that recovers vesicle membrane after release. Facilitated diffusion moves single solutes through a carrier and could not move a packaged quantum. Primary active transport is how transmitter is loaded into the vesicle in the first place, not how it leaves the cell.
questions.answerText: Exocytosis

questions.q: About how wide is the synaptic cleft at a typical chemical synapse?
options: About 2 to 4 micrometers
About 2 to 4 nm
About 200 to 400 nm
About 20 to 40 nm
questions.why: A cleft of roughly 20 to 40 nm is narrow enough that transmitter crosses by diffusion in well under a millisecond. A gap of 2 to 4 nm is the spacing at a gap junction, where the membranes nearly touch and channels bridge them. Gaps of 200 to 400 nm or several micrometers would make diffusion far too slow for rapid signaling.
questions.answerText: About 20 to 40 nm

questions.q: About how long is the synaptic delay at a fast chemical synapse?
options: About 0.005 ms
About 5 ms
About 0.5 ms
About 50 ms
questions.why: Roughly half a millisecond passes between the action potential reaching the terminal and the start of the postsynaptic response. A value near 0.005 ms is essentially instantaneous and describes an electrical synapse instead. Five milliseconds and fifty milliseconds are far too long for a fast ionotropic synapse, although slow metabotropic responses can build over hundreds of milliseconds.
questions.answerText: About 0.5 ms

questions.q: Which family of proteins pulls the vesicle membrane and the terminal membrane together so they can fuse?
options: The connexins
The SNARE proteins
The integrins
The aquaporins
questions.why: SNARE proteins on the vesicle and on the terminal membrane zipper together and force the two bilayers into contact, and the Ca2+ sensor then triggers fusion. Connexins build the channels of gap junctions at electrical synapses. Integrins anchor cells to extracellular matrix. Aquaporins are water channels and play no role in vesicle fusion.
questions.answerText: The SNARE proteins

questions.q: What happens immediately after neurotransmitter binds a receptor on the postsynaptic membrane at a fast synapse?
options: An ion channel in the postsynaptic membrane opens
An action potential fires in the postsynaptic dendrite
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open in the postsynaptic membrane
The transmitter is pumped back into the vesicle
questions.why: At a fast synapse the receptor is itself a ligand-gated ion channel, so binding opens the pore and ions flow, producing a graded postsynaptic potential. An action potential is not the next step, because dendrites conduct graded potentials and any spike begins later at the trigger zone. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels are a presynaptic feature of release, not the immediate postsynaptic event. Transmitter is not pulled straight back into a vesicle from the cleft.
questions.answerText: An ion channel in the postsynaptic membrane opens

questions.q: An axon terminal is bathed in a solution containing no calcium. An action potential arrives at the terminal. What happens?
options: The terminal releases neurotransmitter normally
The action potential fails to reach the terminal
The terminal releases neurotransmitter continuously
The terminal depolarizes but releases no neurotransmitter
questions.why: The action potential is carried by Na+ and K+, so it still invades the terminal, but with no Ca2+ outside there is nothing to enter and trigger fusion, and release fails. Normal release is impossible without the Ca2+ trigger. Conduction to the terminal does not require external Ca2+. Continuous release would require a sustained rise in terminal Ca2+, which is exactly what is missing.
questions.answerText: The terminal depolarizes but releases no neurotransmitter

questions.q: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins in the axon terminal. Which step of transmission fails first?
options: Conduction of the action potential into the terminal
Fusion of vesicles with the terminal membrane
Binding of transmitter to postsynaptic receptors
Entry of Ca2+ through voltage-gated channels
