questions.why: SNARE proteins are the fusion machinery, so cleaving them stops vesicles from merging with the terminal membrane and no transmitter reaches the cleft. Conduction into the terminal is unaffected because it depends on voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels. Ca2+ still enters normally, since its channels are intact. Receptor binding never gets tested, because nothing is released for the receptors to bind.
questions.answerText: Fusion of vesicles with the terminal membrane

questions.q: Extracellular calcium at a synapse is raised from 1 mM to 2.5 mM. What happens to the amount of transmitter released per action potential?
options: It increases, because more Ca2+ enters the terminal per spike
It decreases, because Ca2+ competes with Na+ entry
It is unchanged, because release is all or none
It decreases, because the vesicle pool is depleted faster
questions.why: Release rises steeply with terminal Ca2+, so a larger inward driving force for Ca2+ means more channels contribute more ions and more vesicles fuse. Ca2+ does not block the Na+ current enough to reduce release at this concentration. Release is graded in the number of quanta, not all or none like an action potential. Depletion can matter during long high frequency trains, but it is not what a single stronger stimulus does.
questions.answerText: It increases, because more Ca2+ enters the terminal per spike

questions.q: Tetrodotoxin blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels along an axon. Which event in synaptic transmission fails first?
options: Neurotransmitter is not loaded into vesicles
Postsynaptic receptors no longer bind transmitter
The action potential no longer reaches the terminal
Transmitter is not cleared from the cleft
questions.why: Without voltage-gated Na+ channels the axon cannot regenerate the spike, so the signal never arrives to depolarize the terminal and everything downstream stops. Vesicle loading uses a proton gradient and vesicular transporters and continues in the dark. Postsynaptic receptors remain fully functional, which is why applied transmitter still works. Clearance mechanisms are also untouched.
questions.answerText: The action potential no longer reaches the terminal

questions.q: Which step accounts for most of the roughly 0.5 ms synaptic delay?
options: Diffusion of transmitter across the cleft
Conduction of the action potential along the axon
Opening of the postsynaptic ligand-gated channel
Calcium entry and vesicle fusion in the terminal
questions.why: Ca2+ channels take time to open and the fusion machinery takes more time to act, and together they consume most of the delay. Diffusion across a 20 to 40 nm cleft is nearly instantaneous. Axonal conduction happens before the delay is measured, so it is not counted. Channel opening after binding is fast, on the order of tens of microseconds.
questions.answerText: Calcium entry and vesicle fusion in the terminal

questions.q: A drug slows the closing of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the axon terminal. What is the predicted effect on the postsynaptic response?
options: A smaller postsynaptic potential, because the terminal repolarizes faster
A larger postsynaptic potential, because more Ca2+ enters per spike
No change, because release depends only on spike amplitude
A smaller postsynaptic potential, because vesicles cannot dock
questions.why: Holding the Ca2+ channels open longer lets more Ca2+ accumulate in the terminal, more vesicles fuse, and the postsynaptic potential grows. Terminal repolarization is driven by K+ channels and is not what this drug changes. Release tracks terminal Ca2+, not spike amplitude alone, although a bigger spike does open more Ca2+ channels. Docking is a SNARE dependent step that this drug does not touch.
questions.answerText: A larger postsynaptic potential, because more Ca2+ enters per spike

questions.q: In the sequence at a chemical synapse, which event comes immediately before transmitter binds its receptor?
options: Opening of postsynaptic ion channels
Entry of Ca2+ into the terminal
Diffusion of transmitter across the synaptic cleft
Recycling of vesicle membrane by endocytosis
questions.why: Once exocytosis dumps transmitter into the cleft, it must diffuse the short distance to the postsynaptic membrane before it can bind. Postsynaptic channels open after binding, not before. Ca2+ entry is two steps earlier, before fusion. Endocytosis recovers membrane after release and runs on a slower timescale than the events of a single transmission.
questions.answerText: Diffusion of transmitter across the synaptic cleft

questions.q: A toxin is applied to a synapse. Stimulating the presynaptic axon now produces no postsynaptic potential, but squirting the same transmitter directly onto the postsynaptic cell produces a normal response. Where is the toxin acting?
options: On the presynaptic release machinery
On the postsynaptic receptors
On the enzyme that clears transmitter from the cleft
On the postsynaptic voltage-gated Na+ channels
questions.why: A normal response to applied transmitter proves the receptors and the postsynaptic membrane work, so the failure must lie upstream in release. If receptors were blocked, applied transmitter would also fail. Blocking clearance would prolong responses rather than abolish them. Damaged postsynaptic Na+ channels would affect spiking, but the graded response to applied transmitter would still appear.
questions.answerText: On the presynaptic release machinery

questions.q: Extracellular magnesium is raised at a synapse, and Mg2+ competes with Ca2+ at the presynaptic calcium channel. The postsynaptic potential shrinks. Raising extracellular Ca2+ then restores it. What does this show?
options: Mg2+ blocks the postsynaptic receptor, and the added Ca2+ displaces it from that site
Release depends on Ca2+ entry into the terminal, and Mg2+ reduces that entry
Mg2+ speeds clearance of transmitter from the cleft
Mg2+ prevents the action potential from reaching the axon terminal at all
questions.why: Competition at the presynaptic Ca2+ channel means less Ca2+ enters per spike, fewer vesicles fuse, and the response shrinks, and adding Ca2+ wins the competition back. A postsynaptic block would not be relieved by more extracellular Ca2+ acting presynaptically. Conduction to the terminal uses Na+ channels and is not the target here. Faster clearance would shorten the response rather than reduce its peak in this Ca2+ dependent way.
questions.answerText: Release depends on Ca2+ entry into the terminal, and Mg2+ reduces that entry

questions.q: A partial block of axonal Na+ channels reduces the action potential from about 100 mV in amplitude to about 60 mV. Trace the consequence at the terminal.
options: Transmitter release is unchanged but its clearance from the cleft slows
More Ca2+ channels open, more transmitter is released, and the postsynaptic potential is larger
Ca2+ entry into the terminal is unchanged because those channels are ligand gated rather than voltage gated, so the response is normal
Less depolarization opens fewer Ca2+ channels, less transmitter is released, and the postsynaptic potential is smaller
questions.why: Terminal Ca2+ channels are voltage gated, so a weaker depolarization opens fewer of them, terminal Ca2+ rises less, fewer vesicles fuse, and the postsynaptic potential falls. A smaller spike cannot open more channels. The presynaptic Ca2+ channels are voltage gated, not ligand gated. Clearance is handled by enzymes, transporters, and diffusion, none of which depend on spike amplitude.
questions.answerText: Less depolarization opens fewer Ca2+ channels, less transmitter is released, and the postsynaptic potential is smaller

questions.q: At an experimental synapse, vesicles dock at the active zone and Ca2+ entry is normal, but the number of vesicles that fuse per spike is far below normal. Adding more extracellular Ca2+ improves release only slightly. What is the most likely defect?
options: The fusion machinery downstream of Ca2+ is impaired
Postsynaptic receptors are desensitized
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels are blocked
The action potential fails to invade the terminal
questions.why: Normal docking and normal Ca2+ entry place the failure at the step between the Ca2+ signal and membrane fusion, and a poor rescue by extra Ca2+ confirms the trigger is not the limiting factor. Blocked Ca2+ channels are ruled out by the normal Ca2+ entry, and that defect would be largely rescued by more extracellular Ca2+. Desensitized receptors would be a postsynaptic problem and would not change the number of vesicles fusing. A spike that failed to invade would also abolish Ca2+ entry.
questions.answerText: The fusion machinery downstream of Ca2+ is impaired

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is the main excitatory transmitter of the central nervous system?
options: GABA
Glycine
Glutamate
Acetylcholine
questions.why: Glutamate carries most fast excitatory signaling in the brain and spinal cord, acting on AMPA and NMDA receptors that let cations in. GABA is its inhibitory counterpart in the brain. Glycine is the main inhibitory transmitter of the spinal cord and brainstem. Acetylcholine is excitatory at the neuromuscular junction but is a minor player among central fast synapses.
questions.answerText: Glutamate

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is the main inhibitory transmitter of the brain?
options: Glutamate
Dopamine
GABA
Serotonin
questions.why: GABA acting on GABA-A receptors opens Cl- channels and hyperpolarizes or stabilizes the postsynaptic membrane throughout the brain. Glutamate is the excitatory transmitter at most of the same circuits. Dopamine and serotonin are modulatory monoamines whose effect depends on the receptor subtype, so neither is the workhorse inhibitory transmitter.
questions.answerText: GABA

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is the main inhibitory transmitter of the spinal cord?
options: Glycine
GABA
Norepinephrine
Substance P
questions.why: Glycine opens Cl- channels on spinal interneurons and motor neurons and does most of the inhibitory work in the cord and brainstem. GABA is also inhibitory but dominates in the brain. Norepinephrine is a modulatory catecholamine. Substance P is an excitatory neuropeptide in pain pathways, the opposite of inhibitory.
questions.answerText: Glycine

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction onto skeletal muscle?
options: Norepinephrine
Acetylcholine
Glutamate
Dopamine
questions.why: Somatic motor neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors, always producing excitation and contraction. Norepinephrine is released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons onto smooth muscle, glands, and cardiac muscle, not onto skeletal muscle. Glutamate excites central neurons, not skeletal muscle fibers. Dopamine acts within the brain.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine

questions.q: Which three transmitters make up the catecholamines?
options: Acetylcholine, dopamine, and serotonin
Serotonin, histamine, and dopamine
Glutamate, GABA, and glycine
Dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine
questions.why: All three are built from tyrosine along one pathway, tyrosine to dopa to dopamine to norepinephrine to epinephrine, which is why they are grouped together. Serotonin and histamine are monoamines but are not catecholamines, since they lack the catechol ring and come from different precursors. Glutamate, GABA, and glycine are amino acid transmitters. Acetylcholine is in a class of its own.
questions.answerText: Dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine

questions.q: From which amino acid is serotonin synthesized?
options: Tyrosine
Tryptophan
Glutamate
Choline
questions.why: Tryptophan is hydroxylated and then decarboxylated to give serotonin, which is why dietary tryptophan matters for serotonin supply. Tyrosine is the precursor of the catecholamines, a common point of confusion because both are aromatic amino acids. Glutamate is the precursor of GABA. Choline combines with acetyl CoA to make acetylcholine.
questions.answerText: Tryptophan

questions.q: Substance P and the endorphins belong to which class of neurotransmitter?
options: The neuropeptides
The amino acid transmitters
The catecholamines
The purines
questions.why: Both are short chains of amino acids made in the cell body, packaged in large dense core vesicles, and released to act slowly and at low concentration. Catecholamines are small tyrosine derivatives. Amino acid transmitters such as glutamate and GABA are single amino acids, not chains. Purines such as ATP and adenosine are nucleotide based transmitters.
questions.answerText: The neuropeptides

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter do most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release onto their target organs?
options: Acetylcholine
Serotonin
Norepinephrine
Glycine
questions.why: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibers are adrenergic and release norepinephrine onto alpha and beta receptors on the heart, vessels, and glands. Acetylcholine is the transmitter at all autonomic ganglia and at parasympathetic targets, and also at sympathetic sweat gland fibers, which is the exception students most often miss. Serotonin and glycine act centrally and are not autonomic effector transmitters.
questions.answerText: Norepinephrine

questions.q: A drug increases how long GABA-A channels stay open. What happens to the excitability of neurons carrying those receptors?
options: Excitability rises, because Cl- leaves the cell and the resulting depolarization carries it toward threshold
Excitability rises, because GABA-A channels pass Na+
Excitability is unchanged, because Cl- movement carries no net charge across the membrane
Excitability falls, because more Cl- enters and the membrane is held away from threshold
questions.why: GABA-A receptors are Cl- channels, and in a neuron with the equilibrium potential for Cl- near or below rest, longer opening drives Cl- inward and resists depolarization. Cl- exit would require an equilibrium potential above the resting potential, which is not the usual case in these neurons. Cl- is a charged ion and its movement is a current. GABA-A channels are selective for Cl-, not Na+.
questions.answerText: Excitability falls, because more Cl- enters and the membrane is held away from threshold

questions.q: A neuron in a pain pathway releases substance P onto its target. What is the expected effect on the target neuron?
options: Excitation, since substance P is an excitatory neuropeptide in pain pathways
Inhibition, since substance P opens Cl- channels on the target neuron and hyperpolarizes it
No effect, since substance P acts only on blood vessels and not on neurons
Inhibition, since substance P is an opioid peptide
questions.why: Substance P is released by primary pain afferents in the dorsal horn and depolarizes second order neurons, which is how the signal is passed toward the brain. It does not open Cl- channels, the signature of GABA and glycine. It does act on vessels as well, but that is not its only target. The opioid peptides such as the endorphins are the inhibitory peptides that damp this same pathway.
questions.answerText: Excitation, since substance P is an excitatory neuropeptide in pain pathways

questions.q: Glutamate binds an NMDA receptor that has already lost its magnesium block. Sodium and calcium flow through the open channel. What kind of postsynaptic change is this?
options: An inhibitory, hyperpolarizing change
No net change, because Na+ and Ca2+ oppose each other
An excitatory, depolarizing change
An inhibitory change carried by Cl- entry
questions.why: Both Na+ and Ca2+ are cations at higher concentration outside the cell, so both move inward, add positive charge, and depolarize the membrane. Hyperpolarization requires cation exit or anion entry, neither of which happens here. Na+ and Ca2+ carry current in the same direction rather than canceling. Cl- does not pass the NMDA receptor channel.
questions.answerText: An excitatory, depolarizing change

questions.q: A synapse inside an autonomic ganglion is being studied. Which transmitter and receptor pair should be expected there, and what is the effect?
options: Norepinephrine on beta receptors, producing excitation
Acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors, producing excitation
GABA on GABA-A receptors, producing inhibition
Acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors, producing inhibition
questions.why: Every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic or parasympathetic, uses acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors, which are cation channels and therefore excitatory. Norepinephrine appears later in the sympathetic chain, at the postganglionic target, not in the ganglion. GABA is a central transmitter and is not used at autonomic ganglia. Muscarinic receptors are found at parasympathetic target organs rather than at the ganglionic synapse.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors, producing excitation

questions.q: Loss of dopamine-releasing neurons in the substantia nigra is expected to disturb which function most directly?
options: Fast excitatory transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Conduction speed along myelinated axons
Inhibition in the spinal cord
Control of movement
questions.why: The nigrostriatal dopamine pathway shapes the basal ganglia circuits that select and scale movement, so losing it produces rigidity, tremor, and slowed movement. The neuromuscular junction uses acetylcholine and is unaffected by nigral dopamine loss. Spinal inhibition relies on glycine and GABA. Conduction speed depends on myelin and axon diameter, not on dopamine.
questions.answerText: Control of movement

questions.q: Strychnine blocks glycine receptors in the spinal cord. What is the predicted effect on spinal motor neurons?
options: They become silent, because excitatory input is removed
They become overexcited, because inhibitory input is removed
They hyperpolarize, because Cl- entry increases
They are unaffected, because glycine acts only in the brain
questions.why: Glycine is the brake on spinal motor circuits, so blocking its receptor releases motor neurons from inhibition and produces spasm and convulsion. Glycine is inhibitory, so blocking it removes a brake rather than an accelerator. Blocking the receptor reduces Cl- entry rather than increasing it. Glycine receptors are concentrated in the cord and brainstem, not absent from them.
questions.answerText: They become overexcited, because inhibitory input is removed

questions.q: A newly described transmitter opens ligand-gated Cl- channels on a neuron whose equilibrium potential for Cl- is -70 mV and whose resting potential is -60 mV. How should this transmitter be classified?
options: Excitatory, because any channel opening adds current
Excitatory, because Cl- is a negative ion leaving the cell
Inhibitory, because Cl- entry pulls the membrane away from threshold
Neither, because Cl- channels do not change membrane potential
questions.why: With rest at -60 mV and the Cl- equilibrium at -70 mV, opening Cl- channels drives Cl- inward and moves the membrane toward -70 mV, further from threshold. Opening a channel does not automatically excite, since the direction depends on the ion and its driving force. Cl- moves inward here, not outward. Cl- channels do change membrane potential whenever the membrane sits away from the Cl- equilibrium potential.
questions.answerText: Inhibitory, because Cl- entry pulls the membrane away from threshold

questions.q: In a circuit, GABA neurons inhibit dopamine neurons, and those dopamine neurons project to the striatum. A drug blocks GABA-A receptors on the dopamine neurons. Predict the effect on dopamine release in the striatum.
options: Dopamine release decreases, because GABA normally excites the dopamine neurons
Dopamine release is unchanged, because GABA acts only on interneurons
Dopamine release decreases, because GABA-A blockade hyperpolarizes the dopamine neurons
Dopamine release increases, because the dopamine neurons are disinhibited
questions.why: Removing an inhibitory input leaves the dopamine neurons firing faster, and more firing means more transmitter released downstream, the pattern called disinhibition. GABA acting through GABA-A receptors inhibits rather than excites, so any answer that has GABA driving these neurons reverses the sign of the first step. The premise states GABA-A receptors sit on the dopamine neurons themselves. Blocking a Cl- channel removes hyperpolarizing influence rather than causing it.
questions.answerText: Dopamine release increases, because the dopamine neurons are disinhibited

questions.q: Acetylcholine released onto cardiac pacemaker cells opens K+ channels, while acetylcholine released onto skeletal muscle opens cation channels. A student concludes that acetylcholine is an inhibitory transmitter. What is the best correction?
options: The sign of the response is set by the receptor and the channel it controls, not by the transmitter itself
Acetylcholine is always excitatory, and the slowing seen in the heart is an artifact of the recording method
Acetylcholine is inhibitory only when released in small amounts
Acetylcholine becomes inhibitory only after acetylcholinesterase has modified it in the cleft
questions.why: The same molecule opens a K+ channel through a cardiac muscarinic receptor and hyperpolarizes, and opens a cation channel through a nicotinic receptor and depolarizes, so the receptor decides the sign. Calling the cardiac slowing an artifact ignores a well documented vagal effect. Amount released scales the size of a response, not its direction. Acetylcholinesterase splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending its action rather than reversing it.
questions.answerText: The sign of the response is set by the receptor and the channel it controls, not by the transmitter itself

questions.q: An opioid peptide binds receptors on the terminals of pain afferents and reduces calcium entry there. Trace the effect through to the second order neuron.
options: More substance P is released, so the second order neuron is driven harder and pain signaling rises sharply
Less substance P is released, so the second order neuron is depolarized less and pain signaling falls
Substance P release is unchanged, but the second order neuron becomes more excitable
Glycine release rises, so the afferent terminal is depolarized
questions.why: Transmitter release tracks terminal Ca2+, so cutting Ca2+ entry cuts substance P release, and the second order neuron receives a weaker excitatory drive. Reduced Ca2+ entry cannot raise release. If release fell, the postsynaptic drive falls with it rather than staying the same. Glycine is an inhibitory transmitter of the cord and is not what these afferents release.
questions.answerText: Less substance P is released, so the second order neuron is depolarized less and pain signaling falls

questions.q: A drug empties the vesicles of sympathetic postganglionic terminals of their catecholamine content. Predict the effect on transmission at those terminals and on resting blood pressure.
options: More norepinephrine is released per spike, alpha receptors on vascular smooth muscle are driven harder, and pressure rises
Release is unchanged, because catecholamines diffuse out of the terminal directly and never need to be packaged
Less norepinephrine is released per spike, vascular smooth muscle receives less alpha receptor drive, and blood pressure falls
Acetylcholine replaces norepinephrine at these terminals, so blood pressure rises
questions.why: Release is quantal, so emptying the vesicles removes the packets that would otherwise be released, sympathetic drive to vessels drops, and pressure falls. Depleting a store cannot increase what is released. Catecholamines do leak from cytosol but that slow route cannot substitute for stimulated exocytosis. Postganglionic sympathetic neurons do not switch to acetylcholine, except at the sweat glands where they were cholinergic all along.
questions.answerText: Less norepinephrine is released per spike, vascular smooth muscle receives less alpha receptor drive, and blood pressure falls

questions.q: What are the three routes that clear a neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft?
options: Exocytosis, endocytosis, and phagocytosis by the surrounding glial cells
Degradation, phosphorylation, and receptor binding at the postsynaptic membrane
Filtration, secretion, and reabsorption
Enzymatic degradation, reuptake, and diffusion away from the cleft
questions.why: Transmitter is either chopped up by an enzyme, carried back into a cell by a transporter, or simply drifts out of the cleft, and every synapse uses some mix of the three. Exocytosis and endocytosis handle vesicle traffic, not clearance from the cleft. Filtration, secretion, and reabsorption describe kidney handling of solutes. Phosphorylation modifies proteins and does not remove transmitter, and receptor binding is the signal rather than its termination.
questions.answerText: Enzymatic degradation, reuptake, and diffusion away from the cleft

questions.q: Which enzyme breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft?
options: Acetylcholinesterase
Monoamine oxidase
Catechol O methyltransferase
Carbonic anhydrase
questions.why: Acetylcholinesterase sits in the cleft, particularly at the neuromuscular junction, and splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline within about a millisecond. Monoamine oxidase degrades catecholamines and serotonin, and it works inside the terminal rather than in the cleft. Catechol O methyltransferase also acts on catecholamines. Carbonic anhydrase handles the reaction of CO2 with water and has nothing to do with transmitters.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholinesterase

questions.q: Which enzyme inside the axon terminal degrades catecholamines that are not repackaged into vesicles?
options: Acetylcholinesterase
Adenylyl cyclase
Monoamine oxidase
Sodium potassium ATPase
questions.why: Monoamine oxidase sits on the outer mitochondrial membrane of the terminal and destroys cytosolic norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin. Acetylcholinesterase acts on acetylcholine and works in the cleft. Adenylyl cyclase makes cyclic AMP in second messenger signaling. The Na+/K+ ATPase builds the sodium gradient that powers reuptake, so it supports clearance without degrading anything.
questions.answerText: Monoamine oxidase

questions.q: What is the main route by which glutamate is cleared from a central synapse?
options: Reuptake by transporters into astrocytes and neurons
Degradation by a specific enzyme released into the cleft
Filtration into the cerebrospinal fluid
Endocytosis of intact receptors
questions.why: Glutamate transporters on surrounding astrocytes and on the terminal pull glutamate out of the cleft, which both ends the signal and keeps concentrations low enough to avoid excitotoxicity. There is no cleft enzyme that destroys glutamate the way acetylcholinesterase destroys acetylcholine. Cerebrospinal fluid is not filtered at individual synapses. Receptor endocytosis changes sensitivity rather than removing transmitter.
questions.answerText: Reuptake by transporters into astrocytes and neurons

questions.q: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor blocks which protein?
options: The serotonin receptor on the postsynaptic membrane
Monoamine oxidase inside the terminal
The vesicular transporter that loads serotonin into vesicles
The serotonin transporter on the presynaptic terminal
questions.why: These drugs bind the plasma membrane serotonin transporter, so serotonin lingers longer in the cleft and keeps stimulating its receptors. Blocking the postsynaptic receptor would reduce signaling, the opposite effect. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors are a separate drug class that acts inside the terminal. The vesicular transporter loads transmitter into vesicles rather than recovering it from the cleft.
questions.answerText: The serotonin transporter on the presynaptic terminal

questions.q: Cocaine produces its central effects mainly by blocking which process?
options: Degradation of acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft
Reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine by their transporters
Release of GABA from inhibitory terminals
Binding of glutamate to NMDA receptors
questions.why: By blocking the dopamine and norepinephrine transporters, cocaine leaves these catecholamines in the cleft far longer than normal and exaggerates their signaling. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of drugs such as neostigmine, a different class entirely. Cocaine does not act primarily on GABA release. It is not an NMDA receptor blocker.
questions.answerText: Reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine by their transporters

questions.q: Neostigmine acts by blocking which molecule?
options: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
The choline transporter
Acetylcholinesterase
Monoamine oxidase
questions.why: Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine survives longer in the cleft and produces a larger and longer postsynaptic response. Blocking the nicotinic receptor is what curare does and would weaken transmission instead. The choline transporter recovers choline for resynthesis and is not this drug's target. Monoamine oxidase acts on catecholamines and serotonin, not acetylcholine.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholinesterase

questions.q: Which clearance route requires no enzyme and no membrane transporter?
options: Reuptake into the presynaptic terminal
Diffusion of transmitter out of the cleft
Reuptake into surrounding astrocytes
Degradation in the cleft
questions.why: Diffusion is passive, driven only by the concentration gradient out of the narrow cleft into surrounding fluid, so it uses no protein and no energy. Both forms of reuptake require a transporter protein and depend indirectly on the Na+ gradient. Degradation requires a specific enzyme. Diffusion is slow relative to the other two, which is why it dominates only where the other routes are absent, as with the neuropeptides.
questions.answerText: Diffusion of transmitter out of the cleft

questions.q: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is applied at the neuromuscular junction. What happens to the postsynaptic response to a single nerve stimulus?
options: It becomes smaller and briefer
It disappears completely
It is unchanged in size but delayed in onset
It becomes larger and lasts longer
questions.why: With the enzyme blocked, acetylcholine stays in the cleft, rebinds receptors, and keeps channels open, so the endplate potential grows and decays more slowly. A smaller and briefer response would follow from faster clearance or from receptor blockade. Onset is set by release and diffusion, which are unchanged. Complete loss of the response would require blocking release or blocking the receptor.
questions.answerText: It becomes larger and lasts longer

questions.q: A patient takes a drug that blocks the serotonin transporter. What is the immediate effect on serotonin in the synaptic cleft?
options: Its concentration rises and it acts on its receptors for longer
Its concentration falls because less is released
Its concentration is unchanged because diffusion compensates fully
Its concentration falls because degradation speeds up
questions.why: Reuptake is the main way serotonin leaves the cleft, so blocking the transporter leaves more transmitter available to bind receptors for a longer time. Release is a presynaptic process that this drug does not reduce. Diffusion continues but is far too slow to make up the difference. Blocking a transporter does not accelerate monoamine oxidase, and in fact less serotonin reaches the intracellular enzyme.
questions.answerText: Its concentration rises and it acts on its receptors for longer

questions.q: Monoamine oxidase inside sympathetic terminals is inhibited. What happens to the norepinephrine available for release?
options: More accumulates in the terminal and more is packaged into vesicles
Less accumulates, because synthesis stops
There is no change, because MAO acts only in the cleft
Less accumulates, because the reuptake transporter is blocked as well
questions.why: Monoamine oxidase destroys cytosolic catecholamine, so inhibiting it spares that pool and more transmitter is loaded into vesicles for later release. Synthesis from tyrosine is a separate pathway and continues. MAO is intracellular, on mitochondria in the terminal, not a cleft enzyme like acetylcholinesterase. Inhibiting MAO does not block the plasma membrane transporter, which is the target of a different drug class.
questions.answerText: More accumulates in the terminal and more is packaged into vesicles

questions.q: Transmitter is left in the cleft at high concentration for a long time. What is the most likely effect on the postsynaptic receptors?
options: They stop binding transmitter but keep their channels open
They become permanently more sensitive to transmitter
They convert into voltage-gated channels
They desensitize, and the response to further transmitter weakens
questions.why: Continued occupancy drives receptors into a desensitized state in which they are bound but closed, which is why unrelenting stimulation ends up depressing transmission. Prolonged exposure downregulates rather than upregulates sensitivity, and upregulation is what follows too little transmitter. Receptor type is fixed by the protein and does not switch to voltage gating. Channels do not remain open once the receptor desensitizes.
questions.answerText: They desensitize, and the response to further transmitter weakens

questions.q: Neuropeptides act for seconds or longer, while acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction acts for a few milliseconds. Which difference in clearance best explains this?
options: Peptides are never cleared from the cleft, so the signal ends only when new receptors are inserted
Peptides are cleared by a fast enzyme in the cleft, much as acetylcholinesterase clears acetylcholine
Peptides are cleared mainly by slow diffusion and extracellular peptidases, with no fast reuptake
Peptides are pumped back into vesicles directly from the cleft
questions.why: There is no rapid transporter that recovers peptides, so they linger until they diffuse away or are slowly cut by extracellular peptidases, which stretches their action out. Acetylcholine is unusual in having a dedicated fast cleft enzyme. Peptides are eventually cleared, so nothing requires new receptors to end the signal. No transmitter is pumped from the cleft straight into a vesicle.
questions.answerText: Peptides are cleared mainly by slow diffusion and extracellular peptidases, with no fast reuptake

questions.q: An organophosphate insecticide irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase. What is the predicted effect at the neuromuscular junction with repeated nerve stimulation?
options: Acetylcholine is cleared from the cleft faster, so the muscle responses weaken almost immediately
Acetylcholine accumulates, the endplate stays depolarized, and transmission eventually fails
Acetylcholine release stops, so the muscle relaxes at once
Acetylcholine is converted to norepinephrine at the endplate and the muscle relaxes
questions.why: With no enzyme to remove it, acetylcholine builds up, first causing sustained twitching and then a persistent depolarization that inactivates muscle Na+ channels and blocks further responses. Inhibiting the enzyme slows clearance rather than speeding it. Release from the motor neuron is unaffected by an enzyme inhibitor. Acetylcholine and norepinephrine are made by separate pathways and one does not convert into the other.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine accumulates, the endplate stays depolarized, and transmission eventually fails

questions.q: At a cholinergic synapse the postsynaptic current normally decays in about 1 ms. After an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is added, the decay stretches to about 10 ms while the peak changes little. What does this show about clearance at this synapse?
options: Enzymatic degradation is what normally ends the signal
Diffusion out of the cleft is what normally ends the signal
Reuptake of acetylcholine into the terminal is what normally ends the signal
Receptor desensitization is what normally ends the signal
questions.why: If removing one enzyme lengthens the decay tenfold, that enzyme was doing the work of terminating the signal, and the near normal peak shows release and receptor number were untouched. Diffusion still occurs and is what finally clears the transmitter in the treated case, but the change proves it was not the fast route before. Acetylcholine itself is not taken back up intact; only choline is recovered. Desensitization would shorten rather than lengthen the response.
questions.answerText: Enzymatic degradation is what normally ends the signal

questions.q: Astrocytic glutamate transporters are knocked out in a region of brain tissue. Predict the sequence of consequences at glutamate synapses there.
options: Glutamate release stops, so the synapses fall silent
Glutamate is degraded faster by an enzyme in the cleft, excitatory transmission fails, and the neurons fall silent
Glutamate accumulates in the cleft, NMDA receptors stay open, Ca2+ floods postsynaptic neurons, and cell injury follows
Glutamate is converted to GABA out in the cleft, inhibition rises, and neighboring neurons become harder to excite
questions.why: Reuptake is the only fast route for glutamate, so losing the transporters leaves the transmitter in the cleft, prolongs NMDA receptor opening, and the resulting Ca2+ load drives excitotoxic injury. There is no cleft enzyme that degrades glutamate, so faster degradation is not available. Presynaptic release is unaffected by a transporter knockout. Glutamate is converted to GABA inside GABAergic neurons by an intracellular enzyme, not out in the cleft.
questions.answerText: Glutamate accumulates in the cleft, NMDA receptors stay open, Ca2+ floods postsynaptic neurons, and cell injury follows

questions.q: A drug blocks the norepinephrine transporter at sympathetic terminals on the heart and blood vessels. Predict the effect on heart rate and on blood pressure.
options: Both fall, because less norepinephrine reaches the receptors
Heart rate rises but blood pressure falls, because the transporter is present only at vascular terminals
Both are unchanged, because circulating epinephrine, not local transmitter, sets these variables
Both rise, because norepinephrine stays in the cleft longer and drives beta and alpha receptors harder
questions.why: Reuptake is the dominant way norepinephrine leaves an adrenergic cleft, so blocking it raises the effective transmitter concentration, beta receptors speed the heart and alpha receptors constrict vessels, and pressure rises. Blocking clearance raises rather than lowers transmitter at the receptor. The transporter is present at both cardiac and vascular terminals. Circulating epinephrine contributes but does not override local sympathetic transmission.
questions.answerText: Both rise, because norepinephrine stays in the cleft longer and drives beta and alpha receptors harder

questions.q: Two synapses release the same transmitter. At synapse A a cleft enzyme destroys it within a millisecond. At synapse B there is no enzyme and no transporter, and clearance depends on diffusion. Compare the postsynaptic responses.
options: Synapse A gives a longer lasting response, because the enzyme holds transmitter in the cleft
Synapse B gives a longer lasting response, and repeated stimuli there summate more readily
The two responses have the same duration, since duration is set by the receptor alone
Synapse B gives a briefer response, because diffusion is the fastest clearance route
questions.why: Duration of a postsynaptic response depends on how long transmitter remains available, so slow diffusion at synapse B keeps receptors occupied longer and makes summation easier. An enzyme destroys transmitter rather than holding it. The receptor sets how the channel behaves once bound, but the time course of transmitter in the cleft also shapes the response. Diffusion out of a cleft is the slowest of the three routes, not the fastest.
questions.answerText: Synapse B gives a longer lasting response, and repeated stimuli there summate more readily

questions.q: What direction does the membrane potential move during an excitatory postsynaptic potential?
options: It stays at rest while the resistance falls
It hyperpolarizes, moving away from threshold
It depolarizes, moving closer to threshold
It moves to the equilibrium potential for K+
questions.why: An EPSP is by definition a depolarizing shift, for example from -70 mV toward -65 mV, that brings the cell nearer to firing. Hyperpolarization is the signature of an IPSP. A pure resistance change with no voltage shift describes shunting inhibition, a special case. Moving to the K+ equilibrium potential near -90 mV would be a strong hyperpolarization.
questions.answerText: It depolarizes, moving closer to threshold

questions.q: What direction does the membrane potential move during an inhibitory postsynaptic potential?
options: It hyperpolarizes, moving further from threshold
It rises to the Na+ equilibrium potential
It depolarizes toward threshold
It reverses in sign to a positive value
questions.why: An IPSP typically drives the membrane from -70 mV toward -75 mV or so, further from the roughly -55 mV threshold. Depolarization toward threshold is an EPSP. The Na+ equilibrium potential near +60 mV is approached during an action potential, not during inhibition. A postsynaptic potential is a small graded shift and does not carry the membrane to a positive value.
questions.answerText: It hyperpolarizes, moving further from threshold

questions.q: Which ion movement produces the excitatory postsynaptic potential at a glutamate AMPA receptor?
options: Net outward movement of K+
Net inward movement of Na+
Net inward movement of Cl-
Net outward movement of Ca2+
questions.why: The AMPA receptor is a nonselective cation channel, and because the driving force on Na+ is much larger than on K+ at rest, Na+ influx dominates and the membrane depolarizes. Net K+ exit would hyperpolarize the cell. Cl- entry is the inhibitory mechanism of GABA-A and glycine receptors. Ca2+ is far more concentrated outside than inside, so it never moves outward down its gradient.
questions.answerText: Net inward movement of Na+

questions.q: Which two ion movements can produce an inhibitory postsynaptic potential?
options: Na+ entering or Ca2+ entering
K+ entering the cell or Na+ leaving the cell
Cl- leaving the cell or Na+ entering
Cl- entering the cell or K+ leaving the cell
questions.why: Both moves make the inside more negative, Cl- by adding negative charge and K+ by removing positive charge, and both push the membrane away from threshold. Na+ or Ca2+ entry adds positive charge and is excitatory. Cl- leaving the cell would depolarize. K+ entering and Na+ leaving are not the directions these ions take down their normal gradients.
questions.answerText: Cl- entering the cell or K+ leaving the cell

questions.q: Are postsynaptic potentials graded or all or none?
options: All or none, in exactly the same way that the action potential is
Graded, so their size varies with the amount of transmitter bound
All or none in the dendrite and graded once they reach the soma
Graded only when the input happens to be inhibitory
questions.why: More transmitter opens more channels and produces a larger potential, which is exactly what makes summation possible. All or none behavior belongs to the action potential, where the regenerative Na+ current fixes the amplitude. Dendrites conduct graded potentials, not all or none events. Both EPSPs and IPSPs are graded.
questions.answerText: Graded, so their size varies with the amount of transmitter bound

questions.q: Where on a typical motor neuron are excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials generated?
options: On the dendrites and the cell body
At the nodes of Ranvier along the axon
At the axon terminal
Along the myelinated segment of the axon
questions.why: Synaptic input arrives on dendrites and soma, and the graded potentials produced there spread passively to the trigger zone. Nodes of Ranvier support saltatory conduction of an already formed action potential. The axon terminal is where transmitter is released, not where postsynaptic potentials are generated in that same neuron. Myelinated axon segments are insulated and carry no synaptic input.
questions.answerText: On the dendrites and the cell body

questions.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV with a threshold of -55 mV. A single small EPSP moves the membrane by about 1 mV. What does that tell you about firing?
options: One EPSP alone will fire the neuron
One EPSP sets the threshold to a new value
One EPSP will hyperpolarize the cell to -71 mV
One EPSP alone is far too small, so many must summate
questions.why: Fifteen millivolts separate rest from threshold, so a 1 mV depolarization gets nowhere near it and the cell depends on many inputs adding together. A single small EPSP cannot fire the cell. An EPSP depolarizes toward -69 mV rather than hyperpolarizing to -71 mV. Threshold is a property of the voltage-gated Na+ channels at the trigger zone and is not reset by a synaptic input.
questions.answerText: One EPSP alone is far too small, so many must summate

questions.q: How does a postsynaptic potential travel from a dendrite to the trigger zone?
options: By saltatory conduction between nodes
By regenerating itself at full size along the way
By passive spread, losing amplitude with distance
By release of transmitter at each point along the dendrite
questions.why: Graded potentials spread electrotonically, and current leaks out through the membrane so the signal decays as it travels. Saltatory conduction applies to action potentials on myelinated axons. Regeneration at full size is the property of an action potential, not a graded potential. Transmitter release happens at terminals rather than at successive points along a dendrite.
questions.answerText: By passive spread, losing amplitude with distance

questions.q: A transmitter opens Cl- channels on a neuron whose resting potential is -70 mV and whose Cl- equilibrium potential is also -70 mV. What is the recorded effect?
options: Almost no voltage change, but the membrane resists depolarization by other inputs
A large hyperpolarization that drives the membrane down to about -90 mV and holds it there
A steady depolarization that carries the membrane up toward threshold
No effect at all on the neuron, since no current flows
questions.why: With the membrane already sitting at the Cl- equilibrium potential there is no driving force, so no net current flows and the trace looks flat, yet the open channels lower membrane resistance and soak up incoming excitatory current, which is shunting inhibition. A shift to -90 mV would require the K+ equilibrium potential. Depolarization requires the Cl- equilibrium potential to lie above rest. Saying there is no effect misses the very real reduction in excitability.
questions.answerText: Almost no voltage change, but the membrane resists depolarization by other inputs

questions.q: A transmitter opens K+ channels on a neuron resting at -70 mV, with the K+ equilibrium potential at -90 mV. Which way does the membrane potential move?
options: Toward -55 mV, so this is an EPSP
Toward -90 mV, so this is an IPSP
Toward 0 mV, so this is an EPSP
It does not move, because K+ is already at equilibrium
questions.why: Opening a channel drives the membrane toward that ion's equilibrium potential, and -90 mV is below rest, so K+ leaves, the cell hyperpolarizes, and the event is inhibitory. Moving toward -55 mV or 0 mV would require an inward cation current. K+ is not at equilibrium at -70 mV, which is exactly why the driving force exists.
questions.answerText: Toward -90 mV, so this is an IPSP

questions.q: A ligand-gated channel opens that is equally permeable to Na+ and K+, giving it a reversal potential near 0 mV. A cell resting at -70 mV receives this input. What is the result?
options: A hyperpolarizing IPSP, because K+ exit dominates
No change, because the two ions cancel exactly
A depolarizing EPSP, because the net current is inward
A depolarization all the way to 0 mV
questions.why: At -70 mV the driving force on Na+ is about 130 mV inward while the driving force on K+ is only about 20 mV outward, so Na+ entry wins and the membrane depolarizes toward the 0 mV reversal potential. K+ exit does occur but is much smaller. The two currents do not cancel except at the reversal potential itself. A single small synaptic input moves the membrane a few millivolts, not all the way to the reversal potential.
questions.answerText: A depolarizing EPSP, because the net current is inward

questions.q: A synaptic input opens Cl- channels on a neuron sitting at -60 mV, with the Cl- equilibrium potential at -70 mV. Predict the response.
options: Cl- leaves and the membrane depolarizes toward -55 mV
No current flows, because Cl- channels are not gated by transmitter
Cl- enters and the membrane depolarizes toward -50 mV
Cl- enters and the membrane hyperpolarizes toward -70 mV
questions.why: The membrane sits 10 mV above the Cl- equilibrium potential, so the negative ion is driven inward and the cell moves down toward -70 mV, an inhibitory response. Cl- would leave only if the membrane were negative to the Cl- equilibrium potential, which is the situation in some immature neurons. Cl- entry adds negative charge and cannot depolarize. GABA-A and glycine receptors are transmitter gated Cl- channels.
questions.answerText: Cl- enters and the membrane hyperpolarizes toward -70 mV

questions.q: A recording shows the membrane potential of a neuron moving from -70 mV to -76 mV after a synapse is activated. How should this event be classified?
options: An IPSP
An EPSP
An action potential
A resting potential shift caused by the sodium potassium pump
questions.why: A 6 mV hyperpolarization in response to synaptic activation is an inhibitory postsynaptic potential, which moves the cell further from the roughly -55 mV threshold. An action potential is a large all or none spike toward positive voltages. An EPSP would move the potential upward toward threshold. The pump contributes only a few millivolts of steady offset and does not produce a stimulus locked event.
questions.answerText: An IPSP

questions.q: The amount of transmitter released at an excitatory synapse doubles. What happens to the EPSP recorded in the postsynaptic cell?
options: It becomes an IPSP, because too much transmitter is inhibitory
It stays the same size, because postsynaptic potentials are all or none
It grows larger, because more receptor channels open
It grows smaller, because the receptors saturate immediately
questions.why: EPSPs are graded, so more transmitter binds more receptors, opens more channels, and produces a bigger depolarization. All or none behavior belongs to action potentials, not synaptic potentials. Excess transmitter does not flip the sign of a response, since the sign is set by the ion channel involved. Saturation can flatten the top of the relationship at very high concentrations, but it does not shrink the response.
questions.answerText: It grows larger, because more receptor channels open

questions.q: Two identical EPSPs are generated, one at the far tip of a dendrite and one on the cell body. Which one produces the larger depolarization at the trigger zone?
options: The one at the dendritic tip, because it travels farther and gathers current
The one on the cell body, because less amplitude is lost in transit
They arrive equal, because graded potentials do not decay
The one at the dendritic tip, because dendrites are better insulated
questions.why: Graded potentials decay with distance as current leaks across the membrane, so the input closest to the trigger zone arrives with the most of its amplitude intact. Traveling farther loses current rather than gathering it. Graded potentials decay by definition, unlike action potentials. Dendrites are unmyelinated and leaky rather than well insulated.
questions.answerText: The one on the cell body, because less amplitude is lost in transit

questions.q: An experimenter holds a postsynaptic cell at several voltages and finds that a synaptic current reverses direction at 0 mV. What kind of synapse is this and what is the response at a resting potential of -70 mV?
options: A synapse with no net current at rest, giving pure shunting inhibition
An inhibitory synapse with a Cl- channel, giving a hyperpolarizing IPSP at rest
An inhibitory synapse with a K+ channel, giving a hyperpolarizing IPSP at rest
An excitatory synapse with a mixed cation channel, giving a depolarizing EPSP at rest
questions.why: A reversal potential of 0 mV is the signature of a channel permeable to both Na+ and K+, and at -70 mV the membrane is far below that value so current flows inward and depolarizes the cell. A Cl- channel would reverse near -70 mV and a K+ channel near -90 mV, both well below 0 mV. Pure shunting occurs when the reversal potential equals the resting potential, which is not the case here.
questions.answerText: An excitatory synapse with a mixed cation channel, giving a depolarizing EPSP at rest

questions.q: A neuron normally rests at -70 mV with a Cl- equilibrium potential of -75 mV. A transporter defect raises intracellular Cl- until the Cl- equilibrium potential is -55 mV. Predict what GABA-A activation now does to this cell.
options: Cl- still enters and the cell hyperpolarizes as before
GABA-A receptors stop responding to GABA entirely, so the cell no longer answers this input
Cl- leaves the cell, the membrane depolarizes toward -55 mV, and GABA becomes excitatory
The cell hyperpolarizes even further than before, all the way down to about -90 mV, and stays there
questions.why: Opening a channel drives the membrane toward that ion's equilibrium potential, so once the Cl- equilibrium potential sits above rest the same GABA-A channel depolarizes the cell instead of inhibiting it. Cl- entry requires the equilibrium potential to lie below the resting potential, which no longer holds. The receptor still binds GABA and still opens; only the driving force changed. A move to -90 mV would need a K+ conductance.
questions.answerText: Cl- leaves the cell, the membrane depolarizes toward -55 mV, and GABA becomes excitatory

questions.q: An inhibitory synapse is placed on the axon hillock of one neuron and on a distal dendrite of a second, otherwise identical, neuron. Both release the same amount of transmitter. Which inhibition is more effective at preventing firing, and why?
options: The one at the distal dendrite, because it stops the excitatory input before that input begins to spread
The one at the axon hillock, because it acts where the excitatory current must pass and where the spike begins
They are equally effective, because inhibition is all or none
The one at the distal dendrite, because dendritic membrane carries a much higher density of voltage-gated Na+ channels
questions.why: Inhibition near the trigger zone intercepts the summed excitatory current at the point of decision, and the conductance it opens shunts that current away just where the spike would be initiated. A distal dendritic IPSP blocks only the input from that one branch and decays before it reaches the hillock. Inhibition is graded, not all or none. The initial segment, not the dendrite, carries the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
questions.answerText: The one at the axon hillock, because it acts where the excitatory current must pass and where the spike begins

questions.q: A neuron shows a synaptic potential that is depolarizing at a resting potential of -80 mV but hyperpolarizing at -60 mV. What is the best interpretation?
options: The synapse opens Cl- channels with a reversal potential between the two, near -70 mV
The synapse opens Na+ selective channels, and the recording made at -60 mV must therefore be unreliable
The synapse switches its transmitter depending on the holding potential used
The synapse opens Ca2+ channels with a reversal potential near -70 mV
questions.why: A response that flips sign between two holding potentials places the reversal potential between them, and a value near -70 mV points to Cl-, so the same channel inhibits at -60 mV and depolarizes at -80 mV. A Na+ selective channel would reverse near +60 mV and depolarize at both holding potentials. A presynaptic terminal does not change transmitter with the postsynaptic holding potential. Ca2+ has a strongly positive equilibrium potential, nowhere near -70 mV.
questions.answerText: The synapse opens Cl- channels with a reversal potential between the two, near -70 mV

questions.q: What is temporal summation?
options: Adding the resting potential to the threshold potential
Adding postsynaptic potentials that arrive at the same moment from several synapses
Adding action potentials as they travel along one axon
Adding postsynaptic potentials that arrive from one synapse in rapid succession
questions.why: When a single presynaptic neuron fires again before the first potential has decayed, the two overlap in time and add, which is summation across time. Adding simultaneous inputs from several synapses is spatial summation. Action potentials cannot summate because each is all or none and is followed by a refractory period. The resting and threshold potentials are fixed reference values, not events that add.
questions.answerText: Adding postsynaptic potentials that arrive from one synapse in rapid succession

questions.q: What is spatial summation?
options: Adding two action potentials from the same axon
Adding postsynaptic potentials arriving at the same time from different synapses
Adding potentials that arrive one after another at a single synapse over time
Spreading one postsynaptic potential over a larger area of membrane
questions.why: Inputs on different parts of the dendritic tree and soma converge on the trigger zone, and their currents add when they arrive together, which is summation across space. Two action potentials from one axon cannot summate. Sequential inputs at one synapse describe temporal summation. Spreading of a single potential is passive conduction, not summation.
questions.answerText: Adding postsynaptic potentials arriving at the same time from different synapses

questions.q: Where in a typical motor neuron is the trigger zone that decides whether an action potential fires?
options: The distal tips of the dendrites
The nodes of Ranvier along the axon
The axon terminal at the synapse
The axon hillock and initial segment
questions.why: The initial segment carries the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels, so it has the lowest threshold and it is where the summed synaptic current is read out. Distal dendrites receive input but generate graded potentials rather than the decision to fire. The terminal releases transmitter after the spike arrives. Nodes of Ranvier propagate an already initiated action potential.
questions.answerText: The axon hillock and initial segment

questions.q: What is the usual threshold potential for a neuron whose resting potential is -70 mV?
options: About -55 mV
About -90 mV
About 0 mV
About +30 mV
questions.why: Threshold sits about 15 mV above rest, near -55 mV, and is the voltage at which enough Na+ channels open to become self reinforcing. A value near -90 mV is the K+ equilibrium potential, reached during strong hyperpolarization. Zero millivolts is roughly the reversal potential of a mixed cation synaptic channel. A value near +30 mV is the peak of the action potential itself.
questions.answerText: About -55 mV

questions.q: Which property of a postsynaptic potential makes temporal summation possible?
options: It is an all or none event, so its size cannot be reduced by later inputs
It travels along the dendrite faster than an action potential does
It lasts longer than the interval between the arriving action potentials
It reverses sign once it reaches the soma
questions.why: A postsynaptic potential lasts roughly 15 ms while an action potential lasts a few, so a second input arriving before the first decays lands on top of it. All or none behavior would prevent adding rather than allow it. Graded potentials spread passively and no faster than an action potential propagates. A postsynaptic potential does not change sign as it travels.
questions.answerText: It lasts longer than the interval between the arriving action potentials

questions.q: What kind of electrical events summate at the trigger zone?
options: Action potentials from the presynaptic neurons
Refractory periods
Graded postsynaptic potentials
Resting potentials of neighboring cells
questions.why: EPSPs and IPSPs are graded, so their currents add algebraically at the trigger zone and the sum decides whether threshold is reached. Presynaptic action potentials trigger transmitter release, but they do not themselves cross into the postsynaptic cell to be added. Refractory periods are intervals of reduced excitability, not events that add. Resting potentials of neighboring cells do not sum into this neuron.
questions.answerText: Graded postsynaptic potentials

questions.q: Why does the initial segment reach threshold before the dendrites do, given the same amount of depolarizing current?
options: It has the thickest myelin sheath
It has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels
It has the most synaptic vesicles
It has the highest concentration of ligand-gated Cl- channels
questions.why: Packing more voltage-gated Na+ channels into that patch of membrane means a smaller depolarization is enough to start the regenerative cycle, which is what a low threshold means. Myelin begins after the initial segment and insulates rather than lowers threshold. Synaptic vesicles are stored in terminals. Ligand-gated Cl- channels would raise the current needed to fire rather than lower it.
questions.answerText: It has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels

questions.q: What happens to the summed potential at the trigger zone when an EPSP and an IPSP of equal size arrive together?
options: They add to produce a doubled hyperpolarization
They add to produce a doubled depolarization
They produce an action potential regardless of size
They cancel and the membrane potential stays near rest
questions.why: The two currents flow in opposite directions, so an EPSP of 4 mV arriving with an IPSP of 4 mV leaves the membrane about where it started. Doubling in either direction would require both inputs to have the same sign. No action potential occurs, because threshold is never reached.
questions.answerText: They cancel and the membrane potential stays near rest

questions.q: One presynaptic neuron fires twice, 2 ms apart, onto the same synapse. What type of summation is at work?
options: Temporal summation
No summation, because the interval is too short
Spatial summation
Presynaptic facilitation
questions.why: A single input firing repeatedly in rapid succession produces overlapping potentials that add in time, the definition of temporal summation. Spatial summation requires inputs at different locations. A 2 ms interval is short enough for strong overlap, so summation certainly occurs. Presynaptic facilitation is a change in transmitter release caused by a third neuron, not simple addition of postsynaptic potentials.
questions.answerText: Temporal summation

questions.q: Three separate presynaptic neurons fire at the same instant onto three different dendritic synapses of one cell. What type of summation is this?
options: Temporal summation
Spatial summation
Long term potentiation
Postsynaptic inhibition
questions.why: Different synapses at different places delivering current at the same moment add across space, which is spatial summation. Temporal summation requires repeated firing over time at one input. Long term potentiation is a lasting strengthening of synapses, not the immediate addition of inputs. Postsynaptic inhibition would require inhibitory inputs, which are not described here.
questions.answerText: Spatial summation

questions.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV with a threshold of -55 mV. Three EPSPs of 5 mV each arrive together at the trigger zone. Does the cell fire?
options: Yes, the summed potential reaches -55 mV, exactly threshold
No, the summed potential reaches only -60 mV
No, because EPSPs cannot summate spatially
Yes, but only if an IPSP arrives at exactly the same moment
questions.why: Three inputs of 5 mV give 15 mV of depolarization, and -70 mV plus 15 mV is -55 mV, which is threshold, so the cell fires. Reaching only -60 mV would require just 10 mV of summed input. EPSPs summate spatially all the time, and that is the whole point of convergence. An IPSP would subtract from the total and make firing less likely.
questions.answerText: Yes, the summed potential reaches -55 mV, exactly threshold

questions.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV with a threshold of -55 mV. Two EPSPs of 6 mV each and one IPSP of 4 mV arrive together. What is the membrane potential at the trigger zone, and does the cell fire?
options: About -86 mV, so it does not fire
About -54 mV, so it fires
About -58 mV, so it fires
About -62 mV, so it does not fire
questions.why: The two EPSPs give 12 mV of depolarization and the IPSP subtracts 4 mV, leaving a net of 8 mV, so the membrane sits at -62 mV, still 7 mV short of threshold. Reaching -54 mV would require the IPSP to be ignored. A value of -58 mV would still be below threshold anyway, so that option is inconsistent with itself. A value of -86 mV would require the inputs to be almost entirely inhibitory.
questions.answerText: About -62 mV, so it does not fire

questions.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV with a threshold of -55 mV, and each EPSP at its trigger zone is worth 2 mV. How many simultaneous EPSPs are needed to fire it?
options: Four
Fifteen
Eight
Two
questions.why: The gap from rest to threshold is 15 mV, and at 2 mV per EPSP the cell needs 7.5 inputs, so eight are required to cross threshold. Four inputs supply only 8 mV and land at -62 mV. Fifteen would be the answer if each EPSP were worth 1 mV. Two inputs give only 4 mV of depolarization.
questions.answerText: Eight

questions.q: A presynaptic neuron fires twice with 100 ms between the two spikes, and each EPSP lasts about 15 ms. What is observed at the postsynaptic cell?
options: One large summated EPSP
Two separate EPSPs with no summation
An action potential after the second spike
An IPSP followed by an EPSP
questions.why: The first potential has fully decayed long before the second arrives, so there is nothing left to add to and the two events stand alone. Summation into one large EPSP would require the interval to be shorter than the duration of a single potential. Neither small EPSP alone reaches threshold. Nothing in the scenario introduces an inhibitory input.
questions.answerText: Two separate EPSPs with no summation

questions.q: An excitatory input drives a neuron at 5 Hz without firing it, but at 50 Hz the same input makes it fire. What explains the difference?
options: At 50 Hz each EPSP is individually larger than at 5 Hz
At 50 Hz the threshold of the neuron falls below rest
At 50 Hz the EPSPs overlap in time and summate to threshold
At 50 Hz the synapse switches from excitatory to inhibitory
questions.why: Fifty hertz means an interval of 20 ms, short enough for successive EPSPs to overlap and add, while 5 Hz leaves 200 ms and each potential decays fully. Individual EPSP size is set by transmitter released per spike, not by the rate itself. Threshold is a property of the trigger zone channels and does not drop below the resting potential. The sign of a synapse is fixed by its receptors and channels.
questions.answerText: At 50 Hz the EPSPs overlap in time and summate to threshold

questions.q: Four EPSPs of 4 mV each are generated together at a distal dendrite, and half their amplitude is lost by the time the signal reaches the trigger zone. At the same moment an IPSP of 3 mV arrives at the soma. With rest at -70 mV and threshold at -55 mV, does the neuron fire?
options: No, the trigger zone reaches about -65 mV
Yes, the trigger zone reaches about -54 mV
Yes, the trigger zone reaches about -51 mV
No, the trigger zone reaches about -73 mV
questions.why: The dendritic inputs sum to 16 mV, decay to 8 mV at the trigger zone, and the somatic IPSP subtracts 3 mV, leaving 5 mV of net depolarization and a potential of -65 mV, ten millivolts short. Reaching -54 mV would require ignoring the decay along the dendrite. Reaching -51 mV would require ignoring both the decay and the IPSP. A value of -73 mV would require net inhibition, which is not the case.
questions.answerText: No, the trigger zone reaches about -65 mV

questions.q: A neuron receives a steady excitatory drive that holds it at -58 mV, just below its threshold of -55 mV. An inhibitory interneuron that normally contributes a 5 mV IPSP is then silenced. Predict what happens.
options: The neuron hyperpolarizes and falls silent
The threshold rises to compensate and firing does not occur
Nothing changes, because inhibition acts only during action potentials
The membrane depolarizes past threshold and the neuron begins to fire
questions.why: Removing an inhibitory input takes away 5 mV of opposing current, so the excitatory drive that was being held at -58 mV can now carry the cell past -55 mV, an example of disinhibition. Removing inhibition cannot hyperpolarize the cell. Inhibitory inputs act continuously on the summed potential, not only during spikes. Threshold does not adjust itself to hold firing constant.
questions.answerText: The membrane depolarizes past threshold and the neuron begins to fire

questions.q: Two inputs converge on a neuron. Input A alone gives a 9 mV EPSP at the trigger zone, and input B alone gives a 9 mV EPSP. Fired together, they give 15 mV rather than 18 mV. What is the best explanation?
options: The open channels lower membrane resistance and reduce the driving force, so summation is less than perfectly additive
The two inputs must switch to inhibitory transmitters whenever they are activated together
One of the two inputs must have failed to release any transmitter on that particular trial
Postsynaptic potentials are all or none events, so their sum is capped at a fixed ceiling however many of them arrive together
questions.why: As the membrane depolarizes, the driving force on the inward current falls and the extra open channels shunt current, so real summation falls short of simple addition. Two excitatory inputs do not become inhibitory when paired. A failed release would give roughly 9 mV, not 15 mV. Postsynaptic potentials are graded, and there is no fixed cap short of the reversal potential.
questions.answerText: The open channels lower membrane resistance and reduce the driving force, so summation is less than perfectly additive

questions.q: A motor neuron fires when a sensory input arrives alone, but not when the same sensory input arrives together with a descending pathway. When the descending pathway is cut, the neuron fires again. What is the descending pathway doing?
options: Blocking conduction along the sensory axon itself
Delivering inhibitory input that subtracts from the summed excitation at the trigger zone
Raising the resting potential of the motor neuron to a value above its own threshold
Speeding the clearance of transmitter at the sensory synapse alone, so that its effect ends much sooner
questions.why: An input that prevents firing when present and permits it when removed is supplying inhibition that is subtracted from the excitatory total, and cutting it restores the net to threshold. Blocking conduction in the sensory axon would abolish the sensory response even when the descending pathway is cut. A resting potential above threshold would make the cell fire more, not less. Faster transmitter clearance is not something one neuron imposes on an unrelated synapse in this way.
questions.answerText: Delivering inhibitory input that subtracts from the summed excitation at the trigger zone

questions.q: Where does a neuron producing presynaptic inhibition make its synapse?
options: On the dendrite of the postsynaptic neuron
On the initial segment of the postsynaptic neuron
On the soma of the postsynaptic neuron
On the axon terminal of another presynaptic neuron
questions.why: Presynaptic inhibition works through an axoaxonic synapse, one terminal contacting another terminal, so it changes how much transmitter that one terminal releases. Contacts on a dendrite or soma of the target cell produce postsynaptic inhibition instead, which affects the whole cell. A synapse on the initial segment is also postsynaptic and is a particularly powerful form of it.
questions.answerText: On the axon terminal of another presynaptic neuron

questions.q: What is the main mechanism by which presynaptic inhibition reduces transmitter release?
options: It blocks postsynaptic receptors
It destroys transmitter inside the vesicles
It reduces Ca2+ entry into the terminal
It hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic cell body
questions.why: Less Ca2+ per spike means fewer vesicles fuse, so less transmitter is released from that terminal alone. Destroying vesicular transmitter is what a depleting drug does, not what a modulating neuron does. Blocking postsynaptic receptors would be a postsynaptic effect and would weaken every input using that receptor. Hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic soma is postsynaptic inhibition, a different arrangement entirely.
questions.answerText: It reduces Ca2+ entry into the terminal

questions.q: What does presynaptic facilitation do at the terminal it acts on?
options: It decreases the amount of transmitter released per action potential
It increases the number of postsynaptic receptors
It increases the amount of transmitter released per action potential
It shortens the refractory period of the postsynaptic cell
questions.why: Facilitation raises terminal Ca2+, often by prolonging the terminal action potential, so more vesicles fuse and the postsynaptic potential from that input grows. Reducing release is presynaptic inhibition, the opposite. Adding postsynaptic receptors is a postsynaptic change seen in long term potentiation. The refractory period is set by Na+ channel inactivation and is not a target of presynaptic modulation.
questions.answerText: It increases the amount of transmitter released per action potential

questions.q: What is the main advantage of presynaptic control over postsynaptic control?
options: Speed, because it acts before the action potential arrives
Selectivity, because only one input to the target cell is changed
Strength, because it always abolishes the response completely
Permanence, because its effect cannot be reversed
questions.why: Acting on a single terminal turns one input up or down while every other input to the same neuron continues unchanged, which is the point of the arrangement. It is not faster, since it still requires transmitter release and second messenger action at the terminal. It is graded rather than all or nothing. Its effect is reversible and lasts only as long as the modulating input is active.
questions.answerText: Selectivity, because only one input to the target cell is changed

questions.q: How does postsynaptic inhibition act on the target neuron?
options: It produces an IPSP that reduces the effect of every excitatory input to that cell
It reduces transmitter release from one selected presynaptic terminal and leaves the others alone
It removes receptors from a single dendritic spine
It blocks conduction along the presynaptic axon before the signal can arrive
questions.why: An inhibitory synapse on the soma or dendrite changes the membrane potential and conductance of the target cell, so all excitatory currents converging on that cell are opposed. Reducing release from one terminal is presynaptic inhibition. Removing receptors from a single spine is a plasticity mechanism, not classic postsynaptic inhibition. Blocking axonal conduction is not how synaptic inhibition works.
questions.answerText: It produces an IPSP that reduces the effect of every excitatory input to that cell

questions.q: Which receptor on a presynaptic terminal is commonly responsible for presynaptic inhibition in the central nervous system?
options: The nicotinic receptor
The AMPA receptor
The NMDA receptor
The GABA-B receptor
questions.why: GABA-B receptors on terminals act through G proteins to reduce Ca2+ channel opening and increase K+ conductance, cutting release from that terminal. Nicotinic receptors are excitatory cation channels. AMPA and NMDA receptors are the excitatory glutamate receptors of the postsynaptic membrane and do not mediate this inhibition.
questions.answerText: The GABA-B receptor

questions.q: A modulating neuron activates GABA-B receptors on an excitatory terminal, reducing Ca2+ channel opening there. What does the postsynaptic cell record?
options: A larger EPSP from that input, with no change in resting potential
A smaller EPSP from that input, with no change in resting potential
A hyperpolarization of the resting potential with normal EPSPs
A complete loss of all synaptic input to the cell
questions.why: Less Ca2+ entry means less transmitter from that terminal, so that one EPSP shrinks while the postsynaptic membrane itself is untouched and rests where it always did. A larger EPSP would follow from facilitation. A shift in resting potential is the fingerprint of postsynaptic inhibition. Other inputs to the cell are unaffected, which is the whole advantage of the presynaptic route.
questions.answerText: A smaller EPSP from that input, with no change in resting potential

questions.q: A neuron receives five excitatory inputs, and a circuit needs to suppress only the third one while leaving the other four intact. Which arrangement accomplishes this?
options: Presynaptic inhibition at the terminal of input three
Postsynaptic inhibition at the soma
An IPSP at the axon hillock
Blocking the postsynaptic receptor shared by all five inputs
questions.why: Only an axoaxonic contact on that one terminal changes that one input, which is what selectivity means. Postsynaptic inhibition at the soma damps every input at once. An IPSP at the hillock is even less selective, since it sits where all currents converge. Blocking a shared receptor would weaken all five inputs together.
questions.answerText: Presynaptic inhibition at the terminal of input three

questions.q: During presynaptic inhibition of one input, what happens to the resting membrane potential and input resistance of the postsynaptic neuron?
options: The resting potential falls and the input resistance falls
The resting potential rises and the input resistance rises
Both are unchanged, because nothing opens on the postsynaptic membrane
The resting potential is unchanged but the input resistance falls sharply
questions.why: Presynaptic inhibition acts entirely on the terminal, so the postsynaptic membrane opens no new channels and both its resting potential and its resistance stay put. A drop in both is what postsynaptic inhibition produces when Cl- or K+ channels open. A rise in resting potential and resistance does not follow from either mechanism. A resistance drop alone is the signature of shunting inhibition on the postsynaptic membrane.
questions.answerText: Both are unchanged, because nothing opens on the postsynaptic membrane

questions.q: A facilitating neuron blocks K+ channels in an axon terminal, so the terminal action potential lasts longer. Predict the effect on transmitter release from that terminal.
options: Release decreases, because the terminal cannot repolarize
Release stops, because the terminal becomes refractory
