Release is unchanged, because K+ does not affect vesicles
Release increases, because Ca2+ channels stay open longer
questions.why: Prolonging the depolarization keeps voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open longer, terminal Ca2+ rises higher, and more vesicles fuse. Slower repolarization increases rather than decreases release. K+ channels do not touch vesicles directly, but they set how long the terminal stays depolarized, which is what matters. Terminals do not enter a refractory block from a single lengthened spike.
questions.answerText: Release increases, because Ca2+ channels stay open longer

questions.q: An opioid peptide reduces pain signaling by acting on receptors located on the terminals of pain afferents. How should this modulation be classified?
options: Postsynaptic inhibition, because the second order neuron hyperpolarizes
Presynaptic inhibition, because it reduces release from a selected terminal
Presynaptic facilitation, because it changes release from a terminal
Spatial summation, because several inputs are combined
questions.why: The receptor sits on the terminal and the effect is less transmitter released, which is presynaptic inhibition acting on one specific input. Postsynaptic inhibition would require the modulation to change the membrane potential of the second order neuron itself. Facilitation would increase release rather than reduce it. Summation describes adding postsynaptic potentials, not modulating release.
questions.answerText: Presynaptic inhibition, because it reduces release from a selected terminal

questions.q: A recording from a postsynaptic neuron shows a smaller EPSP from input A, while its resting potential, its input resistance, and its response to directly applied transmitter are all normal. EPSPs from inputs B and C are also normal. Where is the modulation acting?
options: Postsynaptically, on the receptors shared by all inputs
On the axon of the postsynaptic neuron
Postsynaptically, at the axon hillock
Presynaptically, on the terminal of input A
questions.why: An unchanged postsynaptic membrane and an unchanged response to applied transmitter rule out the postsynaptic side, and the fact that only input A is weakened points to its terminal specifically. A change in shared receptors would weaken B and C too. A hillock effect would change the whole cell's excitability rather than one EPSP. The postsynaptic axon carries output and does not shape the size of an incoming EPSP.
questions.answerText: Presynaptically, on the terminal of input A

questions.q: In a second experiment on the same kind of neuron, the resting potential shifts from -70 mV to -76 mV, the input resistance falls, and EPSPs from all three inputs shrink by the same proportion. What is happening?
options: Postsynaptic inhibition, opening channels on the target cell membrane
Presynaptic inhibition at all three terminals at once
Presynaptic facilitation at one terminal
Loss of the presynaptic action potential in all three of the axons
questions.why: A hyperpolarized resting potential together with lower input resistance means new channels opened on the postsynaptic membrane, and their shunting effect scales down every input equally. Presynaptic inhibition at all three terminals would shrink the EPSPs but leave the resting potential and resistance untouched. Facilitation would enlarge an EPSP. Loss of the presynaptic spikes would abolish the EPSPs rather than shrink them proportionally.
questions.answerText: Postsynaptic inhibition, opening channels on the target cell membrane

questions.q: A drug destroys the axoaxonic synapse that had been inhibiting one of four excitatory inputs to a neuron. Predict what happens to the four inputs and to the firing of the cell.
options: All four of the excitatory inputs grow stronger together, and the cell fires far more often than it did before
That one input weakens further and the cell fires less often
That one input grows stronger, the other three are unchanged, and the cell is more likely to fire
The resting potential depolarizes by several millivolts and all four of the inputs shrink
questions.why: Removing a selective brake restores full release at that single terminal, which is exactly the selectivity that presynaptic control provides, and the extra excitatory current makes threshold easier to reach. All four strengthening would require the lost inhibition to have been postsynaptic. Losing an inhibitor cannot weaken the input it was suppressing. The postsynaptic resting potential was never changed by presynaptic inhibition, so it does not shift when that inhibition is removed.
questions.answerText: That one input grows stronger, the other three are unchanged, and the cell is more likely to fire

questions.q: What is long term potentiation?
options: A lasting decrease in synaptic strength that follows a prolonged period of synaptic inactivity
A brief increase in transmitter release that lasts only a few milliseconds
A lasting increase in synaptic strength that follows brief high frequency stimulation
A permanent change in the resting potential of a neuron
questions.why: After a short burst of high frequency stimulation, the same test stimulus produces a larger response for hours or longer, which is why LTP is treated as a cellular model of learning. A change lasting milliseconds is short term facilitation, not potentiation. A lasting decrease is long term depression, the mirror process. LTP changes the strength of specific synapses rather than the cell's resting potential.
questions.answerText: A lasting increase in synaptic strength that follows brief high frequency stimulation

questions.q: In which brain region has long term potentiation been studied most thoroughly?
options: The cerebellum
The hypothalamus
The medulla oblongata
The hippocampus
questions.why: Hippocampal circuits are laid out in orderly layers and are central to forming new memories, which made them the standard preparation for studying LTP. The cerebellum shows its own plasticity, better known for long term depression. The medulla handles autonomic reflexes such as breathing and blood pressure. The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and endocrine output.
questions.answerText: The hippocampus

questions.q: Which receptor acts as the coincidence detector in long term potentiation?
options: The NMDA receptor
The GABA-A receptor
The AMPA receptor
The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
questions.why: The NMDA receptor opens only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic membrane is already depolarized, so it reports that presynaptic and postsynaptic activity happened together. AMPA receptors open on glutamate binding alone and carry the ordinary fast EPSP. GABA-A receptors are inhibitory Cl- channels. Nicotinic receptors respond to acetylcholine and are not part of this pathway.
questions.answerText: The NMDA receptor

questions.q: Which ion blocks the NMDA receptor channel while the postsynaptic membrane is at its resting potential?
options: K+
Mg2+
Cl-
HCO3-
questions.why: Mg2+ sits in the pore at negative membrane potentials and is expelled when the membrane depolarizes, which is the voltage dependence that makes the receptor a coincidence detector. K+ moves through many channels but does not plug the NMDA pore. Cl- passes through inhibitory receptor channels. HCO3- matters in acid base handling and has no role here.
questions.answerText: Mg2+

questions.q: Which ion enters through the open NMDA receptor and triggers the changes that produce long term potentiation?
options: Cl-
Mg2+
Ca2+
H+
questions.why: NMDA receptor channels are unusual among glutamate receptors in passing Ca2+, and the rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ activates the kinases that strengthen the synapse. Cl- entry is inhibitory and does not pass this channel. Mg2+ blocks the channel rather than acting as the signal. H+ movement is not the trigger for plasticity.
questions.answerText: Ca2+

questions.q: Which receptor is inserted into the postsynaptic membrane during the expression of long term potentiation?
options: The AMPA receptor
The muscarinic receptor
The GABA-B receptor
The glycine receptor
questions.why: More AMPA receptors in the membrane means the same amount of released glutamate opens more channels and the EPSP is larger, which is how the strengthening is expressed. GABA-B receptors mediate slow inhibition and presynaptic damping. Muscarinic receptors respond to acetylcholine. Glycine receptors are inhibitory Cl- channels of the cord and brainstem.
questions.answerText: The AMPA receptor

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the synapses where long term potentiation is classically studied?
options: GABA
Glutamate
Acetylcholine
Norepinephrine
questions.why: These are excitatory glutamate synapses, and glutamate acting at both AMPA and NMDA receptors is what makes the coincidence detection possible. GABA is inhibitory and is not the transmitter at these synapses. Acetylcholine and norepinephrine modulate hippocampal circuits but are not the transmitter carrying the potentiated signal.
questions.answerText: Glutamate

questions.q: What is long term depression?
options: A failure of transmitter release caused by depletion of the vesicle pool during a long period of heavy activity
A brief hyperpolarization following an action potential
A lasting decrease in the resting membrane potential of the presynaptic neuron
A lasting decrease in synaptic strength, typically after prolonged low frequency stimulation
questions.why: Low frequency stimulation, often around 1 Hz for several minutes, weakens the synapse durably, largely by removing AMPA receptors from the postsynaptic membrane. A brief hyperpolarization after a spike is the afterhyperpolarization, a K+ current effect. Long term depression is about synaptic strength, not about a shifted resting potential. Vesicle depletion is a short term effect that recovers within seconds.
questions.answerText: A lasting decrease in synaptic strength, typically after prolonged low frequency stimulation

questions.q: What two conditions must be met at the same time for the NMDA receptor channel to open and pass current?
options: GABA must be bound and the presynaptic terminal must be depolarized
Glutamate must be bound and the postsynaptic membrane must be hyperpolarized
Glutamate must be bound and the postsynaptic membrane must be depolarized
Glycine must be bound and extracellular Ca2+ must be low
questions.why: Binding alone leaves the pore plugged by Mg2+, and depolarization alone gives nothing to open the gate, so both must occur together, which is what makes the receptor a detector of coincident activity. Hyperpolarization drives Mg2+ further into the pore and closes it more firmly. GABA does not act at this receptor. Glycine does serve as a co agonist, but the requirement being tested here is glutamate plus depolarization.
questions.answerText: Glutamate must be bound and the postsynaptic membrane must be depolarized

questions.q: A postsynaptic membrane depolarizes strongly during a burst of stimulation. What does this do at NMDA receptors that have glutamate bound?
options: Mg2+ leaves the pore and Ca2+ flows into the cell
Mg2+ enters the pore and current stops
Cl- flows into the cell and the synapse weakens
The receptor is removed from the membrane
questions.why: Depolarization pushes the positively charged Mg2+ out of the pore, unblocking the channel so that Na+ and Ca2+ can enter, and the Ca2+ signal starts the potentiating cascade. Mg2+ block deepens with hyperpolarization, not depolarization. NMDA receptor channels are cation channels and do not pass Cl-. Receptor removal from the membrane is a feature of long term depression rather than of unblocking.
questions.answerText: Mg2+ leaves the pore and Ca2+ flows into the cell

questions.q: A drug prevents new AMPA receptors from being inserted into the postsynaptic membrane. High frequency stimulation is then delivered. What is the predicted result?
options: The synapse is silenced completely
No Ca2+ enters and the EPSP does not grow
The EPSP grows normally, since receptor insertion is not required for this
Ca2+ still enters through NMDA receptors, but the EPSP does not grow
questions.why: Blocking insertion leaves the trigger intact, so the Ca2+ signal still occurs, but the expression step that would enlarge the response is missing. Ca2+ entry is an NMDA receptor event and is not prevented by an insertion blocker. Insertion of AMPA receptors is a main route by which the strengthening is expressed, so its loss matters. Existing AMPA receptors still work, so baseline transmission continues.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ still enters through NMDA receptors, but the EPSP does not grow

questions.q: After potentiation, the same amount of glutamate produces a larger EPSP at a synapse. What postsynaptic change best explains this?
options: Fewer AMPA receptors are present in the postsynaptic membrane
More AMPA receptors are present in the postsynaptic membrane
The Mg2+ block of the NMDA receptor has become permanent
The postsynaptic cell has hyperpolarized
questions.why: If the transmitter amount is fixed and the response is bigger, the postsynaptic side must be more responsive, and inserting AMPA receptors is the classic way that happens. Fewer receptors would shrink the response. A permanent Mg2+ block would abolish NMDA current and prevent future plasticity rather than enlarge the ordinary EPSP. Hyperpolarization would increase driving force somewhat but does not account for a lasting change of this kind.
questions.answerText: More AMPA receptors are present in the postsynaptic membrane

questions.q: A synapse is stimulated at 1 Hz for fifteen minutes. What is the expected outcome?
options: Long term depression, with AMPA receptors removed from the membrane
Long term potentiation, with AMPA receptors added to the membrane
No change at all, because the stimulation is too weak to matter
Presynaptic facilitation lasting several minutes
questions.why: Prolonged low frequency stimulation produces a small sustained rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ that favors phosphatases over kinases and drives receptor removal, weakening the synapse. Potentiation requires the brief, intense Ca2+ rise that only high frequency stimulation delivers. This protocol changes the synapse durably rather than leaving it untouched. Presynaptic facilitation requires a modulating input at the terminal, which is not part of this protocol.
questions.answerText: Long term depression, with AMPA receptors removed from the membrane

questions.q: Why does a single presynaptic action potential fail to induce long term potentiation, while a rapid train succeeds?
options: Only the train releases enough glutamate to occupy the AMPA receptors at the synapse
Only the train reaches the presynaptic terminal
Only the train depolarizes the postsynaptic cell enough to relieve the Mg2+ block
Only the train causes transmitter to diffuse all the way across the synaptic cleft
questions.why: A single EPSP is too small to move the membrane far from rest, so Mg2+ stays in the NMDA pore, while a train summates to a large depolarization that unblocks the channel and lets Ca2+ in. A single spike releases plenty of glutamate to bind AMPA receptors, which is why a normal EPSP appears. Single action potentials do reach the terminal. Diffusion across the cleft happens with every release event.
questions.answerText: Only the train depolarizes the postsynaptic cell enough to relieve the Mg2+ block

questions.q: High frequency stimulation is delivered while an NMDA receptor blocker is present. No potentiation develops. After the blocker is washed out, the baseline EPSP is normal. What does this experiment show?
options: AMPA receptors are the receptors required to induce potentiation
Potentiation depends on the amount of transmitter released rather than on the postsynaptic receptors at all
The presynaptic terminal was damaged by the stimulation
NMDA receptor activation is required to induce potentiation but not to carry ordinary transmission
questions.why: A normal baseline EPSP with the blocker removed proves the synapse works through AMPA receptors, and the failure to potentiate while NMDA receptors were blocked places the induction requirement squarely on them. AMPA receptors carry the baseline response and express the strengthening, but they are not the induction trigger. A damaged terminal would leave the baseline EPSP small. The experiment specifically implicates a postsynaptic receptor.
questions.answerText: NMDA receptor activation is required to induce potentiation but not to carry ordinary transmission

questions.q: The postsynaptic cell is voltage clamped at -70 mV during a high frequency train, so it cannot depolarize. Glutamate release is normal. Predict whether potentiation develops and explain the result.
options: Potentiation develops normally, because glutamate release is what matters
No potentiation, because Mg2+ remains in the NMDA pore and Ca2+ cannot enter
No potentiation, because glutamate cannot be released at -70 mV
Potentiation develops but is expressed presynaptically instead
questions.why: Holding the membrane at rest keeps the voltage dependent Mg2+ block in place, so even with glutamate bound the NMDA channel stays shut and the Ca2+ trigger never arrives. Release alone is not enough, which is exactly why the receptor is called a coincidence detector. Presynaptic release is unaffected by clamping the postsynaptic cell. Nothing about the clamp redirects expression to the terminal, since induction itself failed.
questions.answerText: No potentiation, because Mg2+ remains in the NMDA pore and Ca2+ cannot enter

questions.q: A chemical that binds calcium tightly is injected into the postsynaptic neuron before a high frequency train. Transmitter release and NMDA channel opening are both normal, but no potentiation develops. What does this identify?
options: Presynaptic Ca2+ entry is the trigger for potentiation
Glutamate binding alone is sufficient to trigger potentiation
A rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ is the trigger for potentiation
Mg2+ entry into the postsynaptic cell is the trigger for potentiation
questions.why: Everything upstream worked and only the postsynaptic Ca2+ signal was removed, so that signal is the necessary trigger for the cascade that strengthens the synapse. Presynaptic Ca2+ entry was normal, since release was normal, and the injected buffer stayed in the postsynaptic cell. Glutamate binding was also normal and clearly was not sufficient. Mg2+ leaves the pore during depolarization rather than serving as the signal.
questions.answerText: A rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ is the trigger for potentiation

questions.q: Two pathways converge on one hippocampal neuron. A weak pathway is stimulated alone and produces no lasting change. When the same weak stimulation is paired with strong stimulation of the other pathway, the weak pathway is potentiated. What accounts for this?
options: The strong pathway increased transmitter release at the terminals belonging to the weak pathway during the pairing
The strong pathway depolarized the cell, unblocking NMDA receptors at the weak pathway's active synapses
The weak pathway switched its transmitter to glutamate during pairing
The strong pathway removed AMPA receptors from the synapses made by the weak pathway
questions.why: Depolarization is a property of the whole postsynaptic cell, so the strong input supplies the voltage while the weak input supplies the glutamate, and only synapses receiving both meet the coincidence requirement. There is no axoaxonic contact described that would raise release at the weak terminals. Neurons do not swap transmitters over the course of an experiment. Removing AMPA receptors would weaken the synapse, the opposite of the result observed.
questions.answerText: The strong pathway depolarized the cell, unblocking NMDA receptors at the weak pathway's active synapses

questions.q: What structure joins the two cells at an electrical synapse?
options: A synaptic cleft of 20 to 40 nm
A tight junction
A desmosome
A gap junction
questions.why: A gap junction is a set of paired channels that lines up across a 2 to 4 nm gap and creates a continuous pore between the cytoplasm of the two cells. A tight junction seals the space between cells and blocks leakage rather than conducting current. A desmosome is a mechanical anchor. A wide cleft of 20 to 40 nm is the arrangement at a chemical synapse.
questions.answerText: A gap junction

questions.q: Which protein forms the channels of a gap junction?
options: Connexin
Actin
Synaptotagmin
Dystrophin
questions.why: Six connexin subunits form a connexon in each membrane, and two connexons align to make one continuous pore. Actin is a cytoskeletal filament. Synaptotagmin is the vesicle calcium sensor at chemical synapses. Dystrophin links the muscle cytoskeleton to the membrane and is unrelated to junctional channels.
questions.answerText: Connexin

questions.q: In which direction does current usually flow at an electrical synapse?
options: Only in one direction, from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic cell
Only in one direction, from the postsynaptic back to the presynaptic cell
In either direction, since the junction is usually bidirectional
Only when both of the coupled cells are hyperpolarized
questions.why: The pore is an open channel between two cytoplasms, so current flows whichever way the voltage difference drives it, and either cell can influence the other. One way transmission is the rule at chemical synapses, where transmitter is released from only one side. Restricting flow to a single direction in either sense misses the symmetry of the junction. Current flows whenever a voltage difference exists, not only during hyperpolarization.
questions.answerText: In either direction, since the junction is usually bidirectional

questions.q: About how long is the synaptic delay at an electrical synapse?
options: About 0.5 ms
About 2 ms
About 10 ms
Essentially zero
questions.why: Current passes directly through the open junction, so there is no release step and no measurable delay. A delay near 0.5 ms is the value at a fast chemical synapse, where Ca2+ entry and vesicle fusion take time. Two milliseconds and ten milliseconds are longer than even most chemical synapses require.
questions.answerText: Essentially zero

questions.q: What passes from one cell to the other through a gap junction channel?
options: Ions and small molecules, carrying current directly
Neurotransmitter that is still packaged inside its vesicles
Whole proteins and small organelles
Only water molecules and nothing else
questions.why: The pore is wide enough for ions and small molecules up to about 1000 daltons, so charge moves directly and the two cells share second messengers as well. Vesicles are not transferred at any synapse. The pore is far too narrow for proteins or organelles. Water can cross, but restricting the list to water would leave out the ion flow that makes the junction electrically useful.
questions.answerText: Ions and small molecules, carrying current directly

questions.q: In which tissue are electrical synapses at gap junctions essential for normal function?
options: Skeletal muscle fibers
Cardiac muscle
The neuromuscular junction
Myelinated peripheral axons
questions.why: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs let cardiac muscle cells depolarize as one unit, which is what allows the coordinated contraction of a chamber. Skeletal muscle fibers are electrically separate and each is driven by its own motor neuron. The neuromuscular junction is a chemical synapse using acetylcholine. Myelinated axons conduct along their own membrane and do not need gap junctions.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle

questions.q: Which type of synapse transmits faster, and what makes the difference?
options: The chemical synapse, because transmitter diffuses faster than current flows
The chemical synapse, because it amplifies the signal
They are equally fast, since both depend on ion movement
The electrical synapse, because current passes directly with no release step
questions.why: Skipping Ca2+ entry, vesicle fusion, diffusion, and receptor binding removes essentially all of the delay, so an electrical synapse transmits almost instantly. Diffusion of a transmitter across a cleft is slower than direct current flow through an open pore. The two are not equally fast, since the chemical synapse adds the release steps. Amplification is a real advantage of chemical synapses, but it costs time rather than saving it.
questions.answerText: The electrical synapse, because current passes directly with no release step

questions.q: Which type of synapse allows more modulation of the signal, and why?
options: The electrical synapse, because its gap junction channels are always open and freely conducting
Both equally, since both use voltage-gated channels
The chemical synapse, because release, receptors, and clearance can each be adjusted
The electrical synapse, because it can invert the sign of the signal it passes
questions.why: Every step of chemical transmission is a control point, so drugs, modulating neurons, and plasticity can turn the signal up, down, or off. Gap junction conductance can be adjusted somewhat by pH and Ca2+, but the range is narrow compared with a chemical synapse. Only the chemical synapse relies on the transmitter and receptor machinery that gives fine control. Inverting a signal, turning excitation into inhibition, is something only a chemical synapse does.
questions.answerText: The chemical synapse, because release, receptors, and clearance can each be adjusted

questions.q: A group of neurons must fire together in near perfect synchrony. Which arrangement best achieves this?
options: Electrical synapses linking them through gap junctions
Chemical synapses that use glutamate as their transmitter at each contact
Chemical synapses that use GABA as their transmitter
Presynaptic inhibition acting among the members of the group
questions.why: Direct electrical coupling shares current instantly across the group, so the cells depolarize together and fire as a unit. Glutamate synapses would excite the group but each with its own synaptic delay, blurring the timing. GABA synapses would inhibit rather than synchronize firing. Presynaptic inhibition damps selected inputs and does nothing to synchronize.
questions.answerText: Electrical synapses linking them through gap junctions

questions.q: Extracellular Ca2+ is removed from a preparation containing both an electrical and a chemical synapse. What happens at each?
options: Both fail, since both depend on Ca2+ entry
The chemical synapse fails while the electrical synapse continues to transmit
The electrical synapse fails while the chemical synapse continues to transmit
Both continue, since neither depends on extracellular Ca2+
questions.why: Vesicle fusion requires Ca2+ entry, so removing external Ca2+ silences the chemical synapse, while the gap junction simply passes current and needs no Ca2+ trigger. The electrical synapse is the one that survives, not the one that fails. Chemical transmission is strictly Ca2+ dependent, so saying both continue is wrong.
questions.answerText: The chemical synapse fails while the electrical synapse continues to transmit

questions.q: A signal passes through a chain of three electrically coupled cells and gets slightly smaller at each step, while a chemical synapse can produce a postsynaptic response larger than the presynaptic current. What does this comparison illustrate?
options: Electrical synapses can amplify a signal, while chemical synapses cannot
Neither type of synapse can change the size of a signal
Chemical synapses can amplify a signal, while electrical synapses cannot
Both types amplify equally, but at different speeds
questions.why: A chemical synapse spends energy to release many transmitter molecules that open many channels, so a small presynaptic signal can open a large postsynaptic current. An electrical synapse only divides existing current between the two cells, so the signal shrinks rather than grows. The chemical synapse clearly does change signal size. Equal amplification would erase the main functional difference between the two.
questions.answerText: Chemical synapses can amplify a signal, while electrical synapses cannot

questions.q: Current injected into cell A produces an immediate small depolarization in cell B with no measurable delay. The response persists when extracellular Ca2+ is removed and when transmitter receptors are blocked. What kind of synapse joins these cells?
options: An electrical synapse at a gap junction
A chemical synapse using acetylcholine
A chemical synapse using glutamate
An axoaxonic synapse producing presynaptic inhibition
questions.why: No delay, survival without extracellular Ca2+, and indifference to receptor blockade all point to direct current flow through gap junction channels. A glutamate synapse would be abolished by receptor blockade. An acetylcholine synapse would be abolished by removing Ca2+, which stops release. Presynaptic inhibition modulates release at a chemical terminal and cannot explain a direct, immediate coupling.
questions.answerText: An electrical synapse at a gap junction

questions.q: Two synapses are compared. Synapse X has a delay of about 1.5 ms and its response grows when an enzyme inhibitor is added to the cleft. Synapse Y has a delay too short to measure and is unaffected by the inhibitor. Identify each.
options: Both are electrical, but X has fewer gap junctions
X is electrical and Y is chemical
Both are chemical, but Y uses a faster transmitter
X is chemical and Y is electrical
questions.why: A measurable delay plus sensitivity to an enzyme that clears transmitter identifies the chemical synapse, since only there does an enzyme shape the response. The absence of both features marks the electrical synapse. Calling X electrical reverses the two clearest pieces of evidence. No transmitter is fast enough to erase the delay, and no gap junction is affected by a cleft enzyme.
questions.answerText: X is chemical and Y is electrical

questions.q: Gap junctions between cardiac muscle cells are partially uncoupled by a change in intracellular pH. Predict the consequences for conduction through the ventricle.
options: Conduction speeds up, because each cell now fires independently
Current spreads less easily from cell to cell, so conduction slows and the contraction becomes less coordinated
Conduction is unaffected, because cardiac muscle cells signal to one another through chemical synapses instead
Conduction stops immediately, because the gap junctions themselves carry the action potential from one cardiac cell to the next
questions.why: Cardiac cells depend on gap junctions to pass depolarizing current to their neighbors, so raising junctional resistance slows the spread and breaks up the coordinated wave of contraction. Independent firing would make conduction worse, not faster. Cardiac muscle cells are joined electrically rather than by chemical synapses. Partial uncoupling slows conduction rather than abolishing it, since each cell still regenerates its own action potential.
questions.answerText: Current spreads less easily from cell to cell, so conduction slows and the contraction becomes less coordinated

questions.q: In a synapse simulation, what does the vertical axis of the postsynaptic recording show?
options: Transmitter concentration in mmol/L
Current in nanoamperes through the stimulating electrode
Membrane potential in mV
Time in ms
questions.why: The postsynaptic trace plots the recorded membrane potential, which is why the baseline sits near -70 mV and events are read in millivolts. Transmitter concentration is a variable you set, not what the electrode reports. Stimulating current is an input to the presynaptic side. Time is plotted on the horizontal axis.
questions.answerText: Membrane potential in mV

questions.q: Before any stimulus is delivered in the simulation, what value should the postsynaptic trace sit at?
options: About -70 mV
About 0 mV
About +30 mV
About -90 mV
questions.why: The flat baseline before stimulation is the resting membrane potential, near -70 mV in a typical neuron. Zero millivolts would mean no charge separation across the membrane. A value near +30 mV is the peak of an action potential. A value near -90 mV is the K+ equilibrium potential, reached only during strong hyperpolarization.
questions.answerText: About -70 mV

questions.q: What does the stimulus frequency control in the simulation change?
options: The number of receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
How many presynaptic action potentials are delivered per second
The resting membrane potential of the postsynaptic neuron itself
The width of the synaptic cleft
questions.why: Frequency sets the rate of presynaptic firing, which is the variable that determines whether successive postsynaptic potentials overlap. Receptor number is set by a separate receptor availability control. Resting potential is a property of the postsynaptic cell that this control does not alter. Cleft width is a fixed anatomical feature in the model.
questions.answerText: How many presynaptic action potentials are delivered per second

questions.q: In the simulation, what does a receptor blocker control change?
options: The number of transmitter vesicles docked and waiting at the active zone
The speed of action potential conduction along the presynaptic axon
The amount of Ca2+ outside the terminal
The number of postsynaptic receptors available to bind transmitter
questions.why: A receptor blocker occupies receptors so fewer are free, which reduces the number of channels that transmitter can open. Docked vesicles belong to the presynaptic release settings. Extracellular Ca2+ is a separate presynaptic variable. Axonal conduction speed is upstream of the synapse and is not what a receptor blocker touches.
questions.answerText: The number of postsynaptic receptors available to bind transmitter

questions.q: What units are used on the time axis of the postsynaptic recording in the simulation?
options: Milliseconds
Seconds
Minutes
Microvolts
questions.why: Synaptic events unfold over a few to a few tens of milliseconds, so ms is the scale that makes an EPSP visible. Seconds and minutes are far too coarse and would compress every event into a vertical line. Microvolts are a unit of voltage, not of time.
questions.answerText: Milliseconds

questions.q: How is the amplitude of an EPSP measured from a simulation trace?
options: As the total time the trace is above baseline, in ms
As the peak voltage minus the resting baseline voltage, in mV
As the area under the whole trace
As the difference between threshold and the resting potential
questions.why: Amplitude is a height, so it is the number of millivolts from the flat baseline up to the peak of the event. Time above baseline is the duration, a different measurement. Area under the trace is a combined measure of size and duration, not amplitude. The gap between threshold and rest is a fixed property of the cell and does not vary with the EPSP.
questions.answerText: As the peak voltage minus the resting baseline voltage, in mV

questions.q: What does raising the extracellular calcium setting in the simulation affect?
options: The rate at which transmitter is degraded by enzymes in the cleft
The number of postsynaptic receptors in the membrane
The threshold of the postsynaptic trigger zone
The amount of transmitter released per presynaptic action potential
questions.why: Ca2+ entering the terminal triggers vesicle fusion, so more Ca2+ outside means more enters per spike and more transmitter is released. Receptor number is a postsynaptic setting. Threshold is a property of the postsynaptic voltage-gated Na+ channels. Degradation rate is controlled by the enzyme setting, not by Ca2+.
questions.answerText: The amount of transmitter released per presynaptic action potential

questions.q: On a postsynaptic trace in the simulation, how is an action potential recognized?
options: A slow drift of the baseline lasting several hundred milliseconds or more
A small 2 mV bump that decays within 15 ms
A rapid spike from threshold to about +30 mV followed by a fast return
A steady hyperpolarization held at -75 mV
questions.why: An action potential is an all or none event that overshoots to roughly +30 mV and repolarizes within a couple of milliseconds, so it dwarfs everything else on the trace. A slow baseline drift is usually an artifact or a change in a resting setting. A small decaying bump is a subthreshold EPSP. A maintained hyperpolarization is an inhibitory response.
questions.answerText: A rapid spike from threshold to about +30 mV followed by a fast return

questions.q: In the simulation the extracellular calcium is set to zero and the presynaptic axon is stimulated. What does the postsynaptic trace show?
options: A normal EPSP, because release does not need Ca2+
An action potential, because the terminal depolarizes
A flat trace at rest, because no transmitter is released
A hyperpolarization below -80 mV
questions.why: Vesicle fusion depends on Ca2+ entering the terminal, so with none available nothing is released and the postsynaptic cell sees nothing at all. Release absolutely requires Ca2+, which is the point of the manipulation. The presynaptic terminal does depolarize, but that event is not recorded by the postsynaptic electrode. Nothing in this setting opens inhibitory channels.
questions.answerText: A flat trace at rest, because no transmitter is released

questions.q: A student applies enough receptor blocker in the simulation to occupy half the postsynaptic receptors. Compared with the control run, what should the trace show?
options: An EPSP twice as large, with the baseline unchanged
An EPSP of normal size, with the baseline shifted down
No EPSP at all and a baseline shifted up
An EPSP about half as large, with the baseline unchanged
questions.why: Half the receptors free means about half as many channels open for the same transmitter, so the peak is roughly halved while the resting potential, which does not depend on these receptors, is untouched. A shifted baseline would require channels open at rest. Blocking half the receptors leaves the other half working, so some EPSP remains. Blocking receptors cannot enlarge a response.
questions.answerText: An EPSP about half as large, with the baseline unchanged

questions.q: The simulation is set so that each presynaptic action potential releases twice as many vesicles as the control run. What changes on the postsynaptic trace?
options: The EPSP amplitude increases
The EPSP amplitude decreases
The resting potential becomes more negative
The synaptic delay lengthens noticeably
questions.why: More vesicles mean more transmitter, more receptors bound, more channels open, and a larger depolarization, since postsynaptic potentials are graded. Releasing more transmitter cannot shrink the response. Resting potential depends on the leak conductances rather than on how much transmitter arrives. Delay is set by the release machinery and does not lengthen when release increases.
questions.answerText: The EPSP amplitude increases

questions.q: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is switched on in the simulation of a cholinergic synapse. What changes in the shape of the postsynaptic potential?
options: It decays more quickly and ends sooner
It decays more slowly and lasts longer
It reverses direction and becomes a hyperpolarization
It disappears entirely from the trace
questions.why: With the degrading enzyme inhibited, transmitter lingers in the cleft, keeps rebinding, and holds channels open, which stretches out the falling phase. Faster decay would follow from more clearance, not less. The sign of the response depends on which ions the receptor channel passes and is not changed by an enzyme. The response persists and in fact grows, so it does not vanish.
questions.answerText: It decays more slowly and lasts longer

questions.q: In the simulation, the postsynaptic receptor is switched from a Na+ permeable channel to a Cl- permeable channel, with the Cl- equilibrium potential set at -75 mV. What does the trace show after stimulation?
options: A larger depolarization than before
A small hyperpolarization, an IPSP
An action potential at lower stimulus intensity
No change from the control run
questions.why: Cl- entry drives the membrane from -70 mV toward -75 mV, which is a hyperpolarizing, inhibitory response. A larger depolarization would require a channel with a reversal potential above rest. Making the response inhibitory moves the cell away from threshold, so firing becomes harder, not easier. Changing the permeant ion changes the response, so the trace cannot look the same.
questions.answerText: A small hyperpolarization, an IPSP

questions.q: With single stimuli the simulation produces subthreshold EPSPs. The student raises the stimulus frequency until the EPSPs overlap. What should appear on the trace?
options: The potentials summate, the baseline climbs toward threshold, and an action potential eventually fires
Each potential stays exactly the same size however close together they arrive, and no action potential ever fires
The potentials cancel one another as they overlap and the trace flattens back to baseline
The resting potential drops toward -90 mV
questions.why: When intervals are shorter than the duration of a single EPSP, temporal summation stacks them and the membrane can reach threshold. Potentials stop staying isolated once they overlap, which is the whole point of raising frequency. Two excitatory events add rather than cancel. Nothing in this manipulation opens the K+ conductance that would carry the cell toward -90 mV.
questions.answerText: The potentials summate, the baseline climbs toward threshold, and an action potential eventually fires

questions.q: In the simulation, EPSP amplitude falls to a third of control. Raising extracellular Ca2+ to twice normal does not restore it, but removing the added drug does. Where is the drug acting?
options: On the presynaptic Ca2+ channels
On the enzyme that clears transmitter
On the postsynaptic receptors
On the presynaptic vesicle fusion proteins
questions.why: If more Ca2+ cannot rescue the response, the limiting step is not how much transmitter is released, which leaves the postsynaptic side as the site of action. A block of presynaptic Ca2+ channels would be at least partly overcome by raising extracellular Ca2+. Blocking clearance would enlarge and prolong the response rather than shrink it. A fusion protein defect is presynaptic and would also be helped somewhat by a stronger Ca2+ signal.
questions.answerText: On the postsynaptic receptors

questions.q: In a second run, EPSP amplitude again falls to a third of control, but this time raising extracellular Ca2+ restores it to normal. What does this indicate?
options: The manipulation removed postsynaptic receptors
The manipulation blocked clearance of transmitter from the cleft
The manipulation raised the postsynaptic threshold
The manipulation reduced transmitter release, a presynaptic effect
questions.why: A response that can be rescued by supplying more Ca2+ was limited by how much transmitter was released, which places the effect at the terminal. Missing receptors would not be replaced by extra Ca2+, since the postsynaptic cell would still have too few channels to open. A raised threshold would change firing rather than EPSP amplitude. Blocked clearance would produce a larger, longer response instead of a smaller one.
questions.answerText: The manipulation reduced transmitter release, a presynaptic effect

questions.q: In the simulation a single stimulus gives an 8 mV EPSP, five stimuli at 100 Hz fire an action potential, and five stimuli at 10 Hz do not. Rest is -70 mV and threshold is -55 mV. Explain the difference between the two trains.
options: At 100 Hz each individual EPSP is larger than at 10 Hz, because a faster train releases more transmitter from every vesicle that fuses, so each one starts higher
At 100 Hz the threshold of the cell falls all the way to the resting potential, so one EPSP is enough
At 10 Hz the EPSPs arrive during the refractory period of the one before and cancel each other out
At 100 Hz the 10 ms interval is shorter than the EPSP duration so the potentials summate, while at 10 Hz each has decayed before the next arrives
questions.why: An EPSP lasts roughly 15 ms, so spikes 10 ms apart overlap and add toward the 15 mV needed, while spikes 100 ms apart arrive on a fully recovered baseline. Individual EPSP size depends on transmitter released per spike, not on the interval. An excitatory input does not become inhibitory at lower frequency. Threshold is a fixed property of the trigger zone and does not shift to the resting potential.
questions.answerText: At 100 Hz the 10 ms interval is shorter than the EPSP duration so the potentials summate, while at 10 Hz each has decayed before the next arrives

questions.q: After a drug is added in the simulation, the postsynaptic baseline shifts from -70 mV to -78 mV and a train that used to fire the cell now produces only summating EPSPs that peak at -60 mV. Interpret both changes.
options: The drug opened an inhibitory conductance, so the cell starts further from threshold and the same excitation no longer reaches it
The drug raised the threshold of the trigger zone from -55 mV to -60 mV, so the summated EPSPs now fall a few millivolts short of it
The drug blocked presynaptic release, so the events left on the trace are artifacts rather than real EPSPs
The drug removed all of the postsynaptic receptors, so nothing but the shifted baseline is left on the trace
questions.why: A hyperpolarized baseline points to new Cl- or K+ channels opening at rest, and starting 8 mV lower means the same summated excitation stops short of the unchanged -55 mV threshold. Nothing in the trace reports a change in threshold itself, and a resting shift explains both observations with one mechanism. Release cannot have been blocked, since EPSPs are still visible. Removing all receptors would leave no EPSPs at all.
questions.answerText: The drug opened an inhibitory conductance, so the cell starts further from threshold and the same excitation no longer reaches it

questions.q: Neurocrine molecules are grouped into seven classes by structure. Which list names them?
options: Acetylcholine, amines, amino acids, peptides, steroids, sugars, and gases
Amines, amino acids, peptides, purines, gases, lipids, and ions
Acetylcholine, catecholamines, glutamate, GABA, glycine, peptides, and gases
Acetylcholine, amines, amino acids, peptides, purines, gases, and lipids
questions.why: The seven classes are acetylcholine, amines, amino acids, peptides, purines, gases, and lipids. Steroids and sugars are not classes of neurocrines, and ions such as Na+ carry current rather than act as signal molecules. Catecholamines, glutamate, GABA, and glycine are real neurocrines, but they are members of the amine and amino acid classes, not classes of their own.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine, amines, amino acids, peptides, purines, gases, and lipids

questions.q: Which neurocrine class includes nitric oxide?
options: Purines
Gases
Amino acids
Lipids
questions.why: Nitric oxide, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulfide are the gas class. Purines are adenosine, AMP, and ATP. The amino acid class includes glutamate, aspartate, GABA, and glycine. Lipid neurocrines include eicosanoids that bind cannabinoid receptors.
questions.answerText: Gases

questions.q: Serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and histamine belong to which neurocrine class?
options: Amines
Amino acids
Peptides
Purines
questions.why: These are amines, each made from a single amino acid: serotonin from tryptophan, histamine from histidine, and dopamine and norepinephrine from tyrosine. The amino acid class is the amino acids used directly as transmitters, such as glutamate, GABA, and glycine. Peptides are chains such as substance P and the opioid peptides. Purines are adenosine, AMP, and ATP.
questions.answerText: Amines

questions.q: Which three chemicals are the major neurocrine signals of the peripheral nervous system?
options: Glutamate, GABA, and glycine
Serotonin, dopamine, and histamine
Acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine
Substance P, enkephalins, and endorphins
questions.why: The peripheral nervous system secretes three major neurocrines: the neurotransmitters acetylcholine and norepinephrine and the neurohormone epinephrine. Glutamate, GABA, and glycine are amino acid transmitters of the CNS. Serotonin, dopamine, and histamine are amines active in the CNS. Substance P and the opioid peptides are peptides involved in pain pathways.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine

questions.q: Why do gases such as nitric oxide not need specific membrane receptors?
options: They are released only into the blood as hormones
They are broken down before they reach a target cell
They act only on the neuron that released them
They diffuse into target cells and bind directly to molecules inside
questions.why: The gases have no specific receptors because they diffuse into neurons or glial cells and bind directly to target molecules. They act as neurotransmitters and neuromodulators, not only as hormones in the blood. They do reach and affect other cells rather than breaking down first, and they are not limited to the cell that made them.
questions.answerText: They diffuse into target cells and bind directly to molecules inside

questions.q: Which neurocrine is in a chemical class by itself?
options: Glycine
Acetylcholine
Adenosine
Nitric oxide
questions.why: Acetylcholine forms its own class and is made from choline and acetyl CoA in the axon terminal. Glycine belongs to the amino acid class, adenosine to the purines, and nitric oxide to the gases.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine

questions.q: A drug activates the cannabinoid receptors in the brain. Which neurocrine class is it imitating, and through what type of receptor does that class act?
options: Lipids, acting through G protein coupled receptors
Peptides, acting through ion channel receptors
Purines, acting through ion channel receptors
Amines, acting through G protein coupled receptors
questions.why: The body's own ligands for cannabinoid receptors are lipid neurocrines, eicosanoids, and all lipid neurocrines bind G protein coupled receptors. Peptides such as the opioids are a different class. Some purine receptors are ion channels, but purines do not act on cannabinoid receptors. Many amines use G protein coupled receptors, but amines are not the cannabinoid ligands.
questions.answerText: Lipids, acting through G protein coupled receptors

questions.q: What is an ionotropic receptor?
options: A receptor that works through a second messenger system
A receptor found only on the presynaptic axon terminal
A receptor that is also an ion channel, so ligand binding opens or closes it
A receptor that pumps ions across the membrane using ATP
questions.why: Ionotropic receptors are receptor-channels, ligand-gated ion channels that change ion flow directly when a neurotransmitter binds, which is why they produce fast responses. Receptors that work through second messengers are G protein coupled, or metabotropic, receptors. Ionotropic receptors sit on the postsynaptic membrane at chemical synapses. They are channels, not ATP-driven pumps.
questions.answerText: A receptor that is also an ion channel, so ligand binding opens or closes it

questions.q: What kind of postsynaptic response comes from a neurotransmitter binding to a G protein coupled receptor?
options: A slow response that takes longer to begin and lasts longer
A fast response that lasts only a few milliseconds
An action potential, with no graded potential first
No response, because G protein coupled receptors are only presynaptic
questions.why: The signal has to pass through a second messenger system, so the response takes longer to start and lasts seconds to minutes. Fast, millisecond responses come from receptor-channels. Receptors create synaptic potentials, which are graded; an action potential only follows if the summed signal reaches threshold at the trigger zone. G protein coupled receptors are found on postsynaptic cells.
questions.answerText: A slow response that takes longer to begin and lasts longer

questions.q: How does a neuromodulator usually differ from a neurotransmitter?
options: It acts only in the peripheral nervous system
It is always released into the blood
It always hyperpolarizes its target
It acts at both synaptic and nonsynaptic sites and produces slower responses
questions.why: Neuromodulators act at synaptic and nonsynaptic sites and are slower acting, and most bind G protein coupled receptors. Chemicals released into the blood are neurohormones, a separate category. Neuromodulators can make a cell more or less likely to fire, so they do not always hyperpolarize. They act in the CNS as well as elsewhere.
questions.answerText: It acts at both synaptic and nonsynaptic sites and produces slower responses

questions.q: About how long does a fast synaptic potential last?
options: Several minutes
A few milliseconds
Several hours
Several seconds
questions.why: A fast synaptic potential begins quickly and lasts only a few milliseconds because it comes from directly opening a receptor-channel. Slow synaptic potentials last seconds to minutes. Changes lasting hours or longer, such as long-term potentiation, involve changes in the synapse itself.
questions.answerText: A few milliseconds

questions.q: A neuromodulator binds a G protein coupled receptor, and a second messenger closes K+ channels in the postsynaptic cell. What results?
options: An IPSP, because less K+ enters the cell
No change, because closing channels cannot change the membrane potential
An EPSP, because less K+ leaves and the cell depolarizes
An IPSP, because Cl- now enters the cell
questions.why: K+ normally leaks out of the cell, so closing K+ channels keeps positive charge inside, and the cell depolarizes, a slow EPSP. K+ leaves the cell rather than entering it, so less K+ entering is the wrong direction. Closing channels does change membrane potential, since it changes ion movement. Nothing in this pathway opens a Cl- channel.
questions.answerText: An EPSP, because less K+ leaves and the cell depolarizes

questions.q: Which change in a postsynaptic cell produces an IPSP?
options: Opening channels that let Cl- into the cell
Opening channels that let more Na+ into the cell
Closing K+ channels so that less K+ leaves
Opening channels that let Ca2+ into the cell
questions.why: Cl- entering adds negative charge, hyperpolarizing the cell and moving it away from threshold, which is an IPSP. More K+ leaving would also do this. Na+ or Ca2+ entering adds positive charge and depolarizes the cell, an EPSP. Keeping K+ inside by closing K+ channels also depolarizes the cell.
questions.answerText: Opening channels that let Cl- into the cell

questions.q: The same chemical can act as a neurotransmitter at one synapse and as a neuromodulator at another. What decides which role it plays?
options: The amount released from the axon terminal
How far it diffuses before it binds
Whether the presynaptic cell is in the CNS or the PNS
The receptor it binds to on the target cell
questions.why: The distinction depends on the receptor. Binding a receptor-channel at a synapse gives a rapid neurotransmitter response, while binding a G protein coupled receptor gives a slower neuromodulator response. The amount released changes the size of a response, not its type. Diffusion distance and the location of the presynaptic cell do not define the role.
questions.answerText: The receptor it binds to on the target cell

questions.q: A drug blocks every G protein coupled receptor at a synapse but leaves the receptor-channels working. Which postsynaptic responses remain?
options: Only the slow potentials and the changes in protein synthesis
Only the fast synaptic potentials
Both fast and slow potentials, because the neurotransmitter still binds
Neither, because every postsynaptic response needs a G protein
questions.why: Fast synaptic potentials come from receptor-channels, which still work, so they remain. Slow potentials and changes to existing or new proteins depend on G protein coupled receptors and their second messengers, so those are lost. Binding alone is not enough if the receptor is blocked, and fast responses do not use G proteins at all.
questions.answerText: Only the fast synaptic potentials

questions.q: A change at a synapse is still present days later. Which kind of postsynaptic response most likely set it up?
options: A slow response through a G protein coupled receptor that changes protein synthesis
A fast EPSP through a receptor-channel
A single action potential in the presynaptic neuron
Opening of a Cl- channel for a few milliseconds
questions.why: G protein coupled receptors can modify existing proteins or regulate the making of new proteins, and these slow responses are linked to neuron growth and to long-term memory. A fast EPSP and a brief Cl- current last only milliseconds. A single action potential releases a fixed amount of neurotransmitter and does not by itself create a lasting change.
questions.answerText: A slow response through a G protein coupled receptor that changes protein synthesis

questions.q: In a reflex arc, what does the receptor do?
options: It produces the response, such as a contraction or a secretion
It decides which motor neurons should be activated and how strongly
It detects the stimulus and converts it into an electrical signal
It carries the command from the spinal cord out to the effector muscle
questions.why: The receptor is the first element of the arc: it transduces a stimulus such as stretch, heat, or pressure into a receptor potential that can trigger action potentials in the sensory neuron. Carrying the command outward is the job of the motor neuron. Deciding which motor neurons fire is the job of the integrating center in the central nervous system. Producing the response is the job of the effector, the muscle or gland at the end of the arc.
questions.answerText: It detects the stimulus and converts it into an electrical signal

questions.q: Which component of a reflex arc carries information from the receptor into the central nervous system?
options: The interneuron in the spinal gray matter
The sensory neuron
The motor neuron
The effector organ
questions.why: The sensory, or afferent, neuron conducts the signal from the receptor into the spinal cord through the dorsal root. The motor neuron runs the other direction, out of the cord toward the effector. The interneuron lies entirely inside the central nervous system and never reaches the receptor. The effector is the muscle or gland that acts at the end of the arc, not a conducting element.
questions.answerText: The sensory neuron

questions.q: For a spinal reflex, where is the integrating center?
options: The gray matter of the spinal cord
The white matter columns of the spinal cord
The dorsal root ganglion
The primary motor cortex
questions.why: Integration means synapsing, and the synapses of a spinal reflex are made in the gray matter of the cord, where sensory terminals, interneurons, and motor neuron cell bodies meet. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies but contains no synapses. The motor cortex integrates voluntary movement, not spinal reflexes, which is why a reflex survives when the cord is cut off from the brain. White matter is myelinated axon tracts passing through, with no synapses.
questions.answerText: The gray matter of the spinal cord

questions.q: What counts as the effector in a reflex arc?
options: An interneuron pool in the gray matter
A sensory receptor ending
A neuron in the dorsal root ganglion
A muscle or a gland
questions.why: The effector is whatever carries out the response, and only muscle and gland tissue can do that. A receptor ending starts the arc rather than ending it. A dorsal root ganglion neuron is the sensory limb. An interneuron pool is part of the integrating center, and it acts on motor neurons rather than producing the response itself.
questions.answerText: A muscle or a gland

questions.q: What makes a reflex monosynaptic?
options: The pathway uses exactly one sensory neuron
There is a single synapse at the neuromuscular junction
Only one muscle takes part in the response
The sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron
questions.why: Monosynaptic counts synapses inside the central nervous system, and there is exactly one: sensory terminal onto motor neuron, with no interneuron between them. The number of sensory neurons is not what is being counted, since many Ia fibers converge on the same motor pool in a monosynaptic reflex. The number of muscles is also not the criterion. The neuromuscular junction is present in every reflex, monosynaptic or not, so it cannot distinguish them.
questions.answerText: The sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron

questions.q: What defines a polysynaptic reflex?
options: The motor neuron fires more than one action potential in a row
More than one muscle contracts during the reflex response
At least one interneuron lies between the sensory and motor neurons
The sensory neuron branches into several different spinal segments
questions.why: Polysynaptic means two or more central synapses, which requires at least one interneuron inserted into the pathway. Branching of an afferent into several segments happens in monosynaptic reflexes too and does not add a synapse in series. Multiple muscles contracting is a common consequence of interneurons but is not the definition. Repeated firing of the motor neuron changes the strength of the response, not the number of synapses in the arc.
questions.answerText: At least one interneuron lies between the sensory and motor neurons

questions.q: Which reflex is the standard example of a monosynaptic reflex?
options: The pupillary light reflex
The patellar stretch reflex
The flexor withdrawal reflex
The crossed extensor reflex
questions.why: In the patellar reflex the Ia afferent from the quadriceps spindle synapses directly on the alpha motor neurons of that same muscle, giving one central synapse and a very short latency. The flexor withdrawal reflex runs through chains of interneurons across several segments. The crossed extensor reflex adds interneurons that cross the midline. The pupillary light reflex passes through several brainstem nuclei, making it strongly polysynaptic.
questions.answerText: The patellar stretch reflex

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of the somatic motor neurons of a spinal reflex arc?
options: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the dorsal horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the lateral white column of the spinal cord
In the dorsal root ganglion
questions.why: Somatic motor neurons have their cell bodies in the ventral horn and send axons out through the ventral root to skeletal muscle. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies instead. The dorsal horn receives incoming sensory terminals and holds interneurons, not somatic motor neurons. White matter contains axons in transit and no neuronal cell bodies at all.
questions.answerText: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter

questions.q: One reflex in a limb has a latency of about 25 ms and another in the same limb has a latency of about 80 ms. What best explains the difference?
options: The slower reflex acts on a stronger and larger effector muscle
The faster reflex uses unmyelinated afferent fibers only
The slower reflex uses a shorter peripheral nerve pathway
The slower reflex has additional synapses in its central pathway
questions.why: Each central synapse costs roughly half a millisecond to a millisecond, and a polysynaptic pathway also uses smaller, slower afferents, so latency climbs well above the monosynaptic value. A shorter nerve path would make a reflex faster, not slower. Unmyelinated fibers conduct slowly, so they would belong to the slower reflex rather than the faster one. Effector strength changes the size of the response, not the delay before it begins.
questions.answerText: The slower reflex has additional synapses in its central pathway

questions.q: The dorsal root of a spinal nerve is cut. What happens to a reflex whose arc runs through that segment?
options: The reflex is exaggerated because inhibition has been removed
The reflex is lost because the sensory limb is interrupted
The reflex is lost because the motor limb is interrupted
The reflex is normal because the interneurons are intact
questions.why: The dorsal root carries afferent axons into the cord, so cutting it means the stimulus never reaches the integrating center and the arc cannot be completed. The motor limb leaves through the ventral root and is untouched, which is why the muscle can still be activated voluntarily. Intact interneurons cannot help when nothing arrives to excite them. Removing input removes excitation, so exaggeration is the opposite of what happens.
questions.answerText: The reflex is lost because the sensory limb is interrupted

questions.q: The ventral root of a spinal nerve is cut. What is the expected pattern of findings in the region it supplies?
options: Sensation is preserved but the reflex response is absent
Both sensation and the reflex response are lost
Sensation is lost but the reflex response is preserved
Both sensation and the reflex response are preserved
questions.why: The ventral root carries motor axons out, so cutting it removes the output limb while leaving the afferents in the dorsal root intact: the stimulus is still felt, but no contraction follows. Losing sensation while keeping the reflex is impossible, since the same afferents serve both. Preserving both would require an intact motor limb. Losing both is what a cut spinal nerve distal to the union of the two roots would produce, not a ventral root lesion alone.
questions.answerText: Sensation is preserved but the reflex response is absent

questions.q: A patient feels the tendon tap normally, and the muscle contracts when stimulated directly with an electrode, but no reflex contraction occurs. Which component is most likely at fault?
options: The extrafusal muscle fibers themselves
The sensory neuron running in the dorsal root
The alpha motor neuron or its synapse in the cord
The stretch receptor inside the muscle spindle
questions.why: Feeling the tap shows the receptor and afferent are working, and a muscle that contracts to direct stimulation shows the muscle itself is healthy, which leaves the efferent limb and its central synapse as the failure point. The receptor and the sensory neuron are cleared by the preserved sensation. The muscle fibers are cleared by the response to direct stimulation. Testing the limbs of the arc one at a time this way is how a reflex deficit gets localized.
questions.answerText: The alpha motor neuron or its synapse in the cord

questions.q: An autonomic reflex such as the baroreceptor reflex differs from a somatic reflex mainly in which component?
options: The receptor, which produces no receptor potential
The sensory neuron, which conducts without action potentials
The integrating center, which must be the cerebral cortex
The effector, which is cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, or gland
questions.why: Autonomic and somatic reflexes share the same general plan, and the clearest difference is the effector: autonomic output goes to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands rather than to skeletal muscle. Autonomic receptors transduce stimuli into receptor potentials just as somatic ones do. The integrating center for the baroreceptor reflex is in the medulla, not the cortex. Autonomic afferents conduct action potentials like any other sensory neuron.
questions.answerText: The effector, which is cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, or gland

questions.q: A spinal cord is transected at T4. Weeks later, a tap on the patellar tendon still produces a knee jerk. Why?
options: The brain still reaches the muscle through the sympathetic chain
The whole arc for that reflex lies below the level of the transection
The muscle generates the contraction on its own without neurons
The signal reroutes around the transection through the dorsal columns
questions.why: The patellar reflex is integrated in the L2 to L4 segments, all of which sit below T4 and remain connected to the leg, so the arc is intact even with no communication with the brain. The dorsal columns are ascending sensory tracts and are cut by the same transection, so they cannot serve as a detour. The sympathetic chain does not innervate skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle cannot generate its own contraction without motor neuron input.
questions.answerText: The whole arc for that reflex lies below the level of the transection

questions.q: Which change to a reflex arc would slow the reflex the most?
options: Increasing the strength of the stimulus
Warming the nerve by 1 C
Demyelination of the afferent axons
Insertion of one additional interneuron in the pathway
questions.why: Myelin is what makes saltatory conduction fast, so losing it can drop conduction velocity from tens of meters per second to a few, adding tens of milliseconds over a limb length. One extra interneuron adds only about half a millisecond to a millisecond of synaptic delay. Warming a nerve slightly speeds conduction rather than slowing it. A stronger stimulus recruits more fibers and can shorten latency a little, but it does not slow the reflex.
questions.answerText: Demyelination of the afferent axons

questions.q: A patient has no knee jerk on the right, normal touch sensation over the right thigh, and full strength when asked to extend the right knee. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: In the Ia afferent fibers from the quadriceps muscle spindles
In the alpha motor neurons of the right ventral horn of the cord
In the right corticospinal tract in the spinal cord
In the extrafusal fibers of the right quadriceps
questions.why: Full voluntary strength clears the alpha motor neurons and the muscle, and normal touch clears the cutaneous afferents, so the missing piece must be the specific afferent that starts the stretch reflex, the Ia fiber from the spindle. Alpha motor neuron damage would also weaken voluntary extension. Damaged extrafusal fibers would weaken the muscle as well. A corticospinal lesion causes weakness with brisker, not absent, reflexes, since it removes descending inhibition of the arc.
questions.answerText: In the Ia afferent fibers from the quadriceps muscle spindles

questions.q: A local anesthetic is applied to a mixed nerve and blocks the largest myelinated fibers first. Which is lost earlier, the stretch reflex or the sensation of sharp pain?
options: Both at the same time, because all fibers in a nerve are blocked together
The stretch reflex, because its Ia afferents are the largest fibers present
Neither, because anesthetics act only at the neuromuscular junction
Sharp pain, because pain fibers are the most sensitive to local anesthetics
questions.why: Ia spindle afferents are the largest diameter fibers in a peripheral nerve, so a block that works from largest to smallest silences them before it reaches the small fibers, and the tendon jerk disappears while pain is still felt. Sharp pain travels on small myelinated fibers, which are blocked later under this ordering. Fibers in a nerve are blocked in size order, not all at once. Local anesthetics block voltage gated Na+ channels along axons, not just at the junction.
questions.answerText: The stretch reflex, because its Ia afferents are the largest fibers present

questions.q: A toxin selectively blocks inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord. Predict the effect on the stretch reflex and on the antagonist muscle.
options: Both the stretch reflex and the antagonist response disappear, since the arc is interrupted
Only the antagonist is exaggerated and the stretched muscle falls silent
The stretch reflex disappears while the antagonist relaxes normally
The stretch reflex is exaggerated and the antagonist no longer relaxes, so both contract
questions.why: The excitatory monosynaptic limb is untouched, so the stretched muscle still contracts, and removing inhibitory interneurons both releases the motor pool from restraint and abolishes reciprocal inhibition, so the antagonist contracts along with it. The arc itself is not interrupted, so the reflex cannot vanish. The stretched muscle is driven by a direct excitatory synapse that needs no interneuron, so it cannot fall silent from this block. Blocking inhibition never selectively silences an excitatory pathway.
questions.answerText: The stretch reflex is exaggerated and the antagonist no longer relaxes, so both contract

questions.q: A reflex arc has an afferent path of 0.8 m conducting at 80 m/s, an efferent path of 0.8 m conducting at 80 m/s, and one central synapse costing about 0.5 ms. Roughly how long is the delay from stimulus to the arrival of the signal at the muscle?
options: About 21 ms
About 41 ms
About 2 ms
About 11 ms
questions.why: Each 0.8 m leg takes 0.8 divided by 80, which is 0.01 s or 10 ms, so the two legs total 20 ms, and adding the 0.5 ms synaptic delay gives about 21 ms. About 11 ms counts only one leg of the trip. About 41 ms would double the true conduction distance. About 2 ms is off by a factor of ten and would require conduction distances of centimeters rather than most of a limb.
questions.answerText: About 21 ms

questions.q: Which fibers inside a muscle spindle are wrapped by its sensory endings?
options: Capsules of the Golgi tendon organs
Collagen bundles of the tendon
Intrafusal muscle fibers
Extrafusal muscle fibers
questions.why: A spindle is a capsule containing a few small intrafusal fibers, and the sensory ending coils around their noncontractile middle so that stretching the middle deforms the ending. Extrafusal fibers are the ordinary force generating fibers outside the capsule. Tendon collagen is where Golgi tendon organs sit, not spindles. Golgi tendon organ capsules are a separate receptor entirely, located in the tendon.
questions.answerText: Intrafusal muscle fibers

questions.q: How is the muscle spindle arranged relative to the force generating muscle fibers?
options: In series with the extrafusal fibers
Outside the muscle in the joint capsule
In parallel with the extrafusal fibers
In series with the tendon at the muscle insertion
questions.why: Because the spindle lies side by side with the extrafusal fibers, stretching the whole muscle stretches the spindle too, and shortening the muscle unloads it. A receptor in series with the fibers would be loaded by the force those fibers generate, which is exactly how the Golgi tendon organ is arranged. Sitting in series at the insertion describes the tendon organ again. Joint capsule receptors report joint angle and are a different class of receptor.
questions.answerText: In parallel with the extrafusal fibers

questions.q: Which afferent fiber carries the primary sensory signal from the muscle spindle?
options: The group Ia afferent
The group III afferent
The group Ib afferent
The group IV afferent
questions.why: The primary annulospiral ending of the spindle sends its signal on a group Ia fiber, the largest and fastest afferent, which is why the stretch reflex has such a short latency. Group Ib fibers come from Golgi tendon organs and report tension. Group III and group IV fibers are small and carry pain and metabolic information from muscle. Group II fibers, not listed as the key here, carry the secondary spindle ending.
questions.answerText: The group Ia afferent

questions.q: Which motor neurons innervate the contractile ends of the intrafusal fibers?
options: Ib inhibitory interneurons
Gamma motor neurons
Postganglionic sympathetic neurons
Alpha motor neurons
questions.why: Gamma motor neurons supply only the intrafusal fibers, and by contracting their ends they stretch the sensory middle and reset spindle sensitivity. Alpha motor neurons supply the extrafusal fibers that generate force. Ib inhibitory interneurons act inside the cord on motor neurons and never leave the central nervous system. Sympathetic neurons innervate smooth muscle and glands, not skeletal muscle fibers of any kind.
questions.answerText: Gamma motor neurons

questions.q: Which motor neurons innervate the extrafusal fibers that generate the muscle force?
options: Renshaw interneurons
Group II afferent neurons
Gamma motor neurons
Alpha motor neurons
questions.why: Alpha motor neurons are the final common path to the extrafusal fibers, and their firing is what produces the contraction you can see. Gamma motor neurons go to the intrafusal fibers within the spindle and produce no useful force. Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons in the cord that feed back onto motor neurons. Group II fibers are afferents carrying information in, not motor fibers carrying commands out.
questions.answerText: Alpha motor neurons

questions.q: What is the adequate stimulus for the muscle spindle?
options: A change in the temperature of the muscle
A change in muscle length
A change in pressure inside the joint capsule
A change in muscle tension
questions.why: Because the spindle lies in parallel with the working fibers, what deforms its sensory ending is stretch, so it reports length and the rate at which length is changing. Tension is the stimulus for the Golgi tendon organ, which sits in series in the tendon. Joint capsule pressure is sensed by joint receptors. Temperature is sensed by thermoreceptors, which have no role in the stretch reflex.
questions.answerText: A change in muscle length

questions.q: In the stretch reflex, what happens to the muscle that was stretched?
options: It contracts
It relaxes
It is inhibited while its antagonist contracts
It stays unchanged until a command arrives from the brain
questions.why: Ia firing from the stretched spindle excites the alpha motor neurons of that same muscle directly, so the muscle contracts and resists the stretch, which is what keeps a limb position stable. Relaxation is the response of a muscle whose Golgi tendon organs are strongly loaded, not the response to stretch. Inhibition of the stretched muscle while the antagonist contracts is the reverse of the actual wiring. No brain command is needed, since the arc is complete within the cord.
questions.answerText: It contracts

questions.q: What is reciprocal inhibition in the stretch reflex?
options: An inhibitory interneuron reduces firing of the motor neurons to the stretched muscle
The spindle stops firing once the muscle has shortened
An inhibitory interneuron reduces firing of the motor neurons to the antagonist muscle
The Golgi tendon organ shuts down the muscle at high force
questions.why: A branch of the Ia afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron that suppresses the motor pool of the opposing muscle, so the antagonist relaxes and does not fight the reflex contraction. Inhibiting the stretched muscle itself would cancel the reflex, which is the opposite of what happens. Spindle unloading during shortening is a change in receptor firing, not an inhibitory circuit. Shutdown at high force is autogenic inhibition through Ib fibers, a different reflex.
questions.answerText: An inhibitory interneuron reduces firing of the motor neurons to the antagonist muscle

questions.q: The patellar tendon is tapped. Predict what the quadriceps and the hamstrings do.
options: Both contract together and stiffen the knee
Both relax and the leg drops
