The hamstrings contract and the quadriceps relax
The quadriceps contracts and the hamstrings relax
questions.why: The tap stretches the quadriceps spindles, and their Ia fibers excite quadriceps motor neurons directly while inhibiting the hamstring motor neurons through an inhibitory interneuron, so the knee extends smoothly. Contraction of the hamstrings would be the reflex of a muscle that had been stretched, which the tap did not do. Co-contraction would occur only if reciprocal inhibition were blocked. Both muscles relaxing describes loss of the reflex, not the normal response.
questions.answerText: The quadriceps contracts and the hamstrings relax

questions.q: A muscle is allowed to shorten quickly while gamma motor neurons stay silent. What happens to Ia firing from the spindle?
options: It falls, because the spindle is unloaded
It rises briefly and then stops because the receptor fatigues
It rises, because the shortening compresses the spindle
It is unchanged, because the spindle senses tension rather than length
questions.why: A spindle in parallel with shortening fibers goes slack, the sensory middle is no longer stretched, and firing drops or stops. Compression is not the stimulus for the spindle, so shortening cannot excite it that way. The spindle reports length, not tension, so an unchanged rate would only be expected of a tension receptor. Fatigue is not the issue here, since the same spindle fires again as soon as the muscle is stretched or gamma drive is restored.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the spindle is unloaded

questions.q: What does gamma coactivation accomplish during a voluntary contraction?
options: It silences the spindle so that the reflex cannot oppose the movement
It adds directly to the force that the whole muscle produces
It shortens the spindle with the muscle so it keeps reporting length changes
It converts the spindle into a detector of tension rather than of length
questions.why: Firing gamma neurons together with alpha neurons takes up the slack in the intrafusal fibers, so the spindle stays taut and can still sense an unexpected stretch during a shortening contraction. Intrafusal fibers are far too few and too small to add meaningful force. Silencing the spindle is what happens without gamma coactivation, which is the problem it solves. Nothing about gamma drive changes what the receptor measures, which remains length.
questions.answerText: It shortens the spindle with the muscle so it keeps reporting length changes

questions.q: How many synapses in the spinal cord does reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist require?
options: One, the same synapse the agonist uses
At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted
None, because the inhibition occurs at the muscle
Three or more, because the signal must cross to the other side
questions.why: The Ia fiber synapses on an inhibitory interneuron, which in turn synapses on the antagonist motor neuron, so this limb of the reflex is polysynaptic even though the agonist limb is monosynaptic. A single synapse would deliver excitation, since Ia afferents are excitatory. Inhibition of skeletal muscle never occurs at the muscle itself, only in the cord. The pathway stays on the same side, so no midline crossing is involved.
questions.answerText: At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted

questions.q: Which spindle ending responds best to the rate at which a muscle is being stretched?
options: The tendon organ on its group Ib fiber
The free nerve ending in the muscle belly
The secondary ending on its group II fiber
The primary ending on its group Ia fiber
questions.why: The primary ending is strongly dynamic: it fires a burst proportional to how fast the muscle is lengthening, which is why a brisk tap works so much better than a slow pull. The secondary ending is mainly static and reports steady length. The tendon organ reports force and is not part of the spindle. Free nerve endings in muscle carry pain and metabolic signals, not length information.
questions.answerText: The primary ending on its group Ia fiber

questions.q: A muscle is stretched steadily and then held at the new length. What Ia firing pattern is expected?
options: A steady rate during the stretch that increases when the length is held
A large burst during the stretch, then a lower steady rate at the new length
A burst during the stretch, then complete silence at the new length
No firing during the stretch, then a burst once the length is held
questions.why: The dynamic response tracks the velocity of stretch, so firing peaks while the length is changing, and the static response then holds a lower rate that encodes the new length. Firing cannot wait for the movement to stop, since velocity is highest during the stretch itself. A rate that rises after the stretch ends would mean velocity sensitivity in reverse. Complete silence at the new length would erase the position information the spindle exists to provide.
questions.answerText: A large burst during the stretch, then a lower steady rate at the new length

questions.q: Why does the stretch reflex help keep a limb steady when an unexpected load is added?
options: The load raises tension, and the spindle responds by inhibiting the muscle
The load shortens the muscle, and the reflex then relaxes it further
The load stretches the muscle, and the reflex contraction opposes it
The load excites the Golgi tendon organ, which then excites the muscle
questions.why: An added load lengthens the muscle a little, the spindles fire, and the resulting contraction pulls the limb back toward its original position, forming a negative feedback loop for length. A load lengthens rather than shortens the muscle, so the second option starts from the wrong direction. The spindle is excitatory to its own muscle, not inhibitory, and it responds to length rather than tension. The Golgi tendon organ does respond to tension, but its reflex effect on its own muscle is inhibition.
questions.answerText: The load stretches the muscle, and the reflex contraction opposes it

questions.q: Gamma motor neurons to a muscle are blocked while its alpha motor neurons are left intact. Predict the tendon jerk and the spindle behavior during a voluntary contraction.
options: The tendon jerk is exaggerated and the spindle fires faster as the muscle shortens further
The tendon jerk is normal, because gamma motor neurons act only on the antagonist
The tendon jerk is abolished and voluntary contraction becomes impossible too
The tendon jerk is weaker than normal and the spindle falls silent as the muscle shortens
questions.why: Without gamma drive the intrafusal fibers stay slack, so the resting sensitivity of the spindle drops and the tap produces a smaller Ia burst and a weaker jerk, and during shortening the unloaded spindle stops firing altogether. Exaggeration would require more spindle sensitivity, not less. Voluntary contraction is unaffected because alpha motor neurons still reach the extrafusal fibers. Gamma neurons supply the spindles of their own muscle, not the antagonist.
questions.answerText: The tendon jerk is weaker than normal and the spindle falls silent as the muscle shortens

questions.q: A large fiber sensory neuropathy destroys Ia afferents while sparing small fibers and all motor fibers. What pattern of findings is expected?
options: Tendon jerks are lost and position sense is impaired, while strength is preserved
Pain sensation is lost first and the tendon jerks become exaggerated over time
Strength is lost while tendon jerks and position sense remain entirely normal
Tendon jerks are exaggerated because descending inhibition has been removed
questions.why: Ia fibers are both the afferent limb of the tendon jerk and a major source of proprioceptive information, so losing them abolishes the jerk and degrades position sense while leaving intact motor axons and intact small pain fibers. Strength depends on motor fibers, which are spared. Pain travels on small fibers, which this neuropathy does not touch. Exaggerated reflexes come from removing descending inhibition in the cord, not from cutting the afferent limb, which can only weaken the reflex.
questions.answerText: Tendon jerks are lost and position sense is impaired, while strength is preserved

questions.q: A standing person sways slightly forward, which stretches the calf muscles. Trace what happens next.
options: Ib firing rises, the calf muscles are inhibited, and the person tips further forward
Ia firing rises, the calf muscles contract, and the body is pulled back toward upright
Ia firing rises, the shin muscles contract, and the forward sway increases
Ia firing falls, the calf muscles relax, and the forward sway continues
questions.why: Forward sway lengthens the calf, spindles fire, and the monosynaptic reflex contracts the same stretched muscle, which plantar flexes the ankle and restores the upright position without any conscious effort. Falling Ia firing would require the muscle to shorten, which forward sway does not do. Ib driven inhibition needs a large rise in tension, and it would worsen the sway rather than correct it. Contracting the shin muscles is what reciprocal inhibition prevents, since those are the antagonists here.
questions.answerText: Ia firing rises, the calf muscles contract, and the body is pulled back toward upright

questions.q: The inhibitory interneuron that mediates reciprocal inhibition at a joint is blocked, but the monosynaptic connection is intact. Predict the response to a tendon tap.
options: Only the antagonist contracts, so the joint moves in the opposite direction
Neither muscle contracts, because the reflex arc has been broken at its only synapse
The tapped muscle contracts, but its antagonist contracts too, so the joint stiffens
The tapped muscle relaxes while its antagonist contracts instead
questions.why: The direct Ia to alpha synapse is untouched, so the stretched muscle contracts on schedule, but with reciprocal inhibition gone the antagonist is no longer silenced and co-contracts, producing stiffness instead of a clean movement. The arc itself is not broken, so a complete loss of response is not possible. The antagonist has no excitatory drive of its own here, so it cannot act alone. Relaxation of the tapped muscle would require inhibiting the very pool the Ia fiber excites.
questions.answerText: The tapped muscle contracts, but its antagonist contracts too, so the joint stiffens

questions.q: Where is the Golgi tendon organ located?
options: In the connective tissue sheath around each fascicle
In the joint capsule next to the ligament
In the muscle belly, in parallel with the muscle fibers
In the tendon, in series with the muscle fibers
questions.why: The tendon organ sits at the junction of muscle and tendon so that all the force the fibers generate passes directly through it, which makes it a force meter. A receptor in parallel in the muscle belly is the spindle, and it measures length instead. Joint capsule receptors report joint angle and take no part in this reflex. A receptor inside the fascicle sheath would not be loaded by whole muscle force.
questions.answerText: In the tendon, in series with the muscle fibers

questions.q: Which afferent fiber carries the signal from the Golgi tendon organ?
options: The group Ib afferent
The group IV afferent
The group Ia afferent
The group II afferent
questions.why: Group Ib fibers are large and fast, matching the rapid protective role of the tendon organ reflex. Group Ia fibers carry the primary spindle signal about length and its rate of change. Group II fibers carry the secondary spindle ending, also a length signal. Group IV fibers are small unmyelinated fibers carrying pain and metabolic information from muscle.
questions.answerText: The group Ib afferent

questions.q: What is the adequate stimulus for the Golgi tendon organ?
options: Length of the muscle belly
Temperature within the tendon
Tension developed in the tendon
Rate of change of the joint angle
questions.why: Because the tendon organ is in series with the muscle fibers, whatever force they produce squeezes its collagen bundles onto the nerve endings, so its firing rate tracks tension. Muscle length is what the spindle measures. Joint angle and its rate of change are reported by joint receptors and, indirectly, by spindles. Temperature has no role in this receptor.
questions.answerText: Tension developed in the tendon

questions.q: What is the reflex response to strong Golgi tendon organ firing?
options: Inhibition of the motor neurons supplying that same muscle
Excitation of the gamma motor neurons of that same muscle
Inhibition of the motor neurons supplying the antagonist
Excitation of the motor neurons supplying that same muscle
questions.why: Ib input drives an inhibitory interneuron onto the motor pool of its own muscle, so rising tension reduces the drive that created it, a negative feedback loop for force. Excitation of the same muscle is the effect of spindle input, not tendon organ input. The antagonist is excited rather than inhibited by this reflex. Gamma motor neurons are not the target of the Ib pathway.
questions.answerText: Inhibition of the motor neurons supplying that same muscle

questions.q: How many synapses does the Golgi tendon organ reflex use inside the spinal cord before reaching the alpha motor neuron?
options: One, a direct inhibitory synapse
None, because the effect occurs at the neuromuscular junction
One, a direct excitatory synapse
At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted
questions.why: Ib afferents are excitatory, like all primary afferents, so producing inhibition requires them to excite an inhibitory interneuron first, making the pathway polysynaptic. A single excitatory synapse would produce contraction rather than relaxation. Primary afferents do not make inhibitory synapses directly, so a one synapse inhibitory arc does not exist here. Inhibition of skeletal muscle never happens at the neuromuscular junction, which is always excitatory.
questions.answerText: At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted

questions.q: What happens to the antagonist muscle when a Golgi tendon organ fires strongly?
options: It is unaffected
It is excited
It is inhibited
It is disconnected from its motor neurons
questions.why: The Ib pathway inhibits its own muscle and excites the antagonist, so the joint yields in the opposite direction and the dangerous force is relieved. Inhibiting the antagonist as well would leave the joint with no active control. Leaving the antagonist unaffected would waste the chance to unload the tendon. Motor neurons are never physically disconnected by a reflex, only excited or inhibited.
questions.answerText: It is excited

questions.q: Which of these receptors has its own motor innervation?
options: Both receptors receive motor innervation
Neither receptor receives motor innervation
The muscle spindle, through gamma motor neurons
The Golgi tendon organ, through Ib motor fibers
questions.why: Only the spindle contains contractile tissue, the ends of the intrafusal fibers, and gamma motor neurons adjust their length to set the sensitivity of the receptor. Group Ib is an afferent designation, so there is no such thing as a Ib motor fiber. The tendon organ is a purely passive collagen and nerve ending structure with no way to be reset centrally. Saying neither is innervated would leave the gamma system with nothing to do.
questions.answerText: The muscle spindle, through gamma motor neurons

questions.q: What is the name for the reflex effect a Golgi tendon organ has on its own muscle?
options: Reciprocal inhibition
Autogenic inhibition
Presynaptic facilitation
Recurrent inhibition
questions.why: Autogenic means acting on the source, so the term captures a receptor inhibiting the very muscle whose tension excited it. Reciprocal inhibition is the suppression of the antagonist during a stretch reflex, a different target. Recurrent inhibition is the Renshaw cell loop, in which a motor neuron collateral inhibits the motor pool. Presynaptic facilitation describes an increase in transmitter release at a terminal and is not a reflex name.
questions.answerText: Autogenic inhibition

questions.q: A muscle contracts hard isometrically against an immovable bar. Which receptor increases its firing the most?
options: The muscle spindle, because muscle length rises
Neither, because nothing moves
Both equally, because both receptors sense force
The Golgi tendon organ, because tension rises sharply
questions.why: An isometric contraction changes force without changing whole muscle length, which is exactly the condition that loads a series receptor and leaves a parallel one nearly unchanged. Muscle length does not rise during an isometric contraction, so the spindle has no reason to fire more. The absence of movement does not mean the absence of a stimulus, since tension is a stimulus. The two receptors sense different variables, so treating them as equal misses the whole contrast.
questions.answerText: The Golgi tendon organ, because tension rises sharply

questions.q: A completely relaxed muscle is stretched passively. Which statement is correct?
options: Both receptors are stimulated, but the spindle responds far more strongly
Neither receptor responds until the muscle contracts voluntarily
Only the tendon organ responds, because stretching raises the tension
Only the spindle responds, because a tendon itself cannot be stretched
questions.why: Passive stretch lengthens the parallel spindle strongly and puts only a small passive tension on the series tendon organ, so both fire but the spindle dominates. Passive tension is real but small, so calling the tendon organ the only responder overstates it. Tendons do take up passive load, so the claim that they cannot be stretched is wrong. Both receptors work perfectly well in a relaxed muscle and need no voluntary command.
questions.answerText: Both receptors are stimulated, but the spindle responds far more strongly

questions.q: Which receptor most directly helps hold grip force steady while carrying a heavy bag?
options: The Golgi tendon organ, which monitors force
The muscle spindle, which monitors force
The Golgi tendon organ, which monitors length
The muscle spindle, which monitors joint angle
questions.why: Steady force is a force problem, and the tendon organ is the receptor whose firing is proportional to the tension the muscle is producing, so it supplies the feedback that a force controller needs. The spindle does not monitor force, so pairing it with force is the common mix up. Length is the spindle variable and does not belong to the tendon organ. Joint angle is reported by joint receptors and again is not what a spindle measures directly.
questions.answerText: The Golgi tendon organ, which monitors force

questions.q: A receptor lies in series with the muscle fibers and inhibits its own muscle when it fires. Which receptor is described?
options: The nociceptor in the muscle belly
The joint capsule receptor
The muscle spindle
The Golgi tendon organ
questions.why: Series placement and autogenic inhibition are the two defining features of the tendon organ, and they belong together because a series receptor is the one loaded by force. A spindle is in parallel and excites its own muscle. A joint capsule receptor is outside the muscle entirely and reports position. A muscle nociceptor triggers withdrawal and pain responses and is not arranged in series to measure force.
questions.answerText: The Golgi tendon organ

questions.q: During a maximal lift the load suddenly feels as though it gives way and the muscle relaxes. Which reflex best explains this?
options: Reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist muscle
The stretch reflex driven by muscle spindles
Autogenic inhibition driven by Golgi tendon organs
The crossed extensor reflex
questions.why: At very high force the Ib input becomes strong enough to override the excitatory drive to the motor pool, and the muscle abruptly relaxes, unloading the tendon before it tears. The stretch reflex causes contraction, not sudden relaxation, so it cannot explain a give. Reciprocal inhibition acts on the opposing muscle and would not silence the one doing the lifting. The crossed extensor reflex involves the opposite limb and a painful stimulus.
questions.answerText: Autogenic inhibition driven by Golgi tendon organs

questions.q: How should the latencies of the stretch reflex and the Golgi tendon organ reflex compare?
options: The stretch reflex is slower because it also inhibits the antagonist
The tendon organ reflex is slower because of its extra interneuron
The tendon organ reflex is faster because Ib fibers are larger than Ia fibers
They are identical because both use a single central synapse
questions.why: Ia and Ib fibers conduct at about the same speed, so the difference in latency comes from the number of central synapses, and the extra inhibitory interneuron in the Ib pathway adds delay. Ib fibers are not larger than Ia fibers, so that reasoning fails at the premise. Only the stretch reflex has a single central synapse, so the two cannot be identical. The reciprocal inhibition limb of the stretch reflex runs in parallel with the direct limb and does not delay the agonist contraction.
questions.answerText: The tendon organ reflex is slower because of its extra interneuron

questions.q: A person lowers a heavy weight slowly, so the muscle is lengthening while generating high force. Predict the firing of the spindles and the tendon organs.
options: Both fire strongly, since the muscle is stretched and under high tension at once
Neither fires, since the whole movement is under voluntary cortical control
Only the spindles fire, since tension falls while the muscle is lengthening
Only the tendon organs fire, since the length of the muscle is not changing
questions.why: An eccentric contraction is the one condition that maximizes both variables at once, lengthening the parallel spindles while forcing high tension through the series tendon organs. Tension is high, not falling, during a controlled lowering, so the spindle only answer misreads the mechanics. Length is clearly changing during a lowering movement, so the tendon organ only answer misreads it in the other direction. Voluntary control of a movement does not switch off proprioceptors, which report during voluntary and passive movement alike.
questions.answerText: Both fire strongly, since the muscle is stretched and under high tension at once

questions.q: The Ib inhibitory interneurons serving a muscle are blocked while everything else is intact. Predict what happens during a maximal voluntary contraction.
options: The stretch reflex disappears along with the reflex braking effect
Force drops immediately, because the muscle loses its excitatory drive
Force continues to rise with no reflex braking, so tendon strain increases
The antagonist contracts instead of relaxing during the whole effort
questions.why: Removing the inhibitory interneuron removes the negative feedback loop for force, so the motor pool is no longer restrained at high tension and the tendon carries more load than it normally would. Excitatory drive comes from descending commands and is untouched, so force cannot collapse. The stretch reflex uses a different, monosynaptic excitatory pathway and continues to work. The antagonist is controlled by other interneurons and is not switched on by this block.
questions.answerText: Force continues to rise with no reflex braking, so tendon strain increases

questions.q: In a recording, afferent A fires briskly during passive stretch and goes silent during an active shortening contraction, while afferent B fires weakly during passive stretch and strongly during the active contraction. Identify the two afferents.
options: Both are Ib tendon organ afferents from different heads of the same muscle
A is a Ib tendon organ afferent and B is a Ia spindle afferent
Both are Ia spindle afferents from muscles on opposite sides of the joint
A is a Ia spindle afferent and B is a Ib tendon organ afferent
questions.why: Going silent during a shortening contraction is the signature of unloading a parallel receptor, and firing hardest when force is greatest is the signature of a series receptor, so A is the spindle and B is the tendon organ. Reversing the assignment would require a tension receptor to fall silent at high tension. Two spindles on opposite sides would both respond to length, and the antagonist spindle would be stretched rather than silent during shortening. Two tendon organs would both peak during the contraction, so their patterns would not differ this way.
questions.answerText: A is a Ia spindle afferent and B is a Ib tendon organ afferent

questions.q: A therapist holds a steady stretch on a tight muscle for 30 seconds and the muscle gradually relaxes, whereas a quick stretch of the same muscle makes it tighten. What accounts for the difference?
options: Sustained stretch recruits muscle spindles, whose excitation grows steadily the longer it is held
Sustained tension recruits Golgi tendon organs, whose inhibition outlasts a brief spindle response
Sustained stretch silences the Ib fibers, which removes all inhibition of the muscle
A fast stretch recruits Golgi tendon organs while a slow hold recruits the muscle spindles
questions.why: A quick stretch is a velocity stimulus that the dynamic spindle ending answers with a brief contraction, while a long hold keeps tension on the tendon and lets Ib driven autogenic inhibition dominate, so the muscle lets go. Spindle excitation adapts during a hold rather than growing. Sustained tension increases Ib firing rather than silencing it. The receptor assignments in the last option are reversed, since velocity is the spindle stimulus and force is the tendon organ stimulus.
questions.answerText: Sustained tension recruits Golgi tendon organs, whose inhibition outlasts a brief spindle response

questions.q: Which receptor starts the flexor withdrawal reflex?
options: A Golgi tendon organ
A Pacinian corpuscle
A nociceptor
A muscle spindle
questions.why: Withdrawal is triggered by tissue damaging stimuli, and nociceptors are the free nerve endings that detect them. A muscle spindle detects stretch and starts the stretch reflex instead. A Golgi tendon organ detects tension and produces autogenic inhibition. A Pacinian corpuscle detects vibration and rapid pressure change, which does not by itself drive withdrawal.
questions.answerText: A nociceptor

questions.q: Is the flexor withdrawal reflex monosynaptic or polysynaptic?
options: Polysynaptic
Monosynaptic on the stimulated side and polysynaptic on the other side
It uses no synapse within the spinal cord
Monosynaptic
questions.why: Nociceptive afferents reach flexor motor neurons only through chains of interneurons, and those interneurons also spread the signal across several segments, so the arc is polysynaptic throughout. A monosynaptic arrangement is limited to the stretch reflex. There is no side of this reflex that is monosynaptic, since even the ipsilateral limb runs through interneurons. Every spinal reflex has at least one synapse in the cord, so a synapse free arc is not possible.
questions.answerText: Polysynaptic

questions.q: In the flexor withdrawal reflex, which muscles contract on the stimulated side?
options: Only the muscles acting at the joint nearest the stimulus
The flexors
The extensors
Both the flexors and the extensors
questions.why: Flexion pulls the limb away from the stimulus, so flexor motor neurons are excited while extensor motor neurons are inhibited. Contracting the extensors would push the limb toward the stimulus. Contracting both would lock the limb in place and prevent escape. Interneurons spread the response across several segments, so the response usually involves several joints rather than only the nearest one.
questions.answerText: The flexors

questions.q: What happens to the extensors on the stimulated side during a withdrawal reflex?
options: They are excited
They contract after a short delay
They are unaffected by the reflex
They are inhibited
questions.why: Interneurons inhibit the extensor motor pool so the flexors can shorten the limb without opposition, the same reciprocal arrangement used in the stretch reflex. Exciting them would produce co-contraction and block the withdrawal. A delayed contraction of the extensors would return the limb toward the stimulus. Leaving them unaffected would leave resting extensor tone fighting the movement.
questions.answerText: They are inhibited

questions.q: In the crossed extensor reflex, what happens on the side opposite the painful stimulus?
options: The flexors contract
The extensors contract
Nothing, because the reflex is confined to one side
Both the flexors and the extensors relax
questions.why: Commissural interneurons cross the cord and excite extensor motor neurons on the opposite side so that limb can stiffen and take the body weight. Contralateral flexion would lift both limbs at once and drop the person. Relaxing both muscle groups would leave the supporting limb unable to bear load. The whole point of this reflex is that it is not confined to one side.
questions.answerText: The extensors contract

questions.q: What is the functional purpose of the crossed extensor reflex?
options: To support the body weight on the opposite limb while the stimulated limb withdraws
To pull the opposite limb away from the painful stimulus as well
To slow the withdrawal so that the moving limb is not injured by the movement
To carry the pain signal upward to the cerebral cortex for awareness
questions.why: Lifting one leg suddenly shifts all the body weight to the other, and the crossed reflex extends that limb at the same instant so balance is preserved. Withdrawing both limbs would remove all support. Slowing the withdrawal would defeat its protective purpose and is not what the crossed pathway does. Carrying pain to the cortex is the job of the ascending spinothalamic pathway, a separate route.
questions.answerText: To support the body weight on the opposite limb while the stimulated limb withdraws

questions.q: What allows a single withdrawal reflex to involve muscles at several joints?
options: Convergence of many afferents onto a single motor neuron
Spread of the signal from muscle to muscle along the limb
Branching of one motor neuron to several different muscles
Divergence of interneurons across several spinal segments
questions.why: One nociceptive afferent excites interneurons that ascend and descend in the cord and distribute the signal to many motor pools, which is divergence. Convergence describes many inputs onto one cell and would narrow the response rather than widen it. A motor neuron innervates fibers within a single muscle, so it cannot branch across muscles. Skeletal muscle fibers do not pass excitation to neighboring muscles.
questions.answerText: Divergence of interneurons across several spinal segments

questions.q: What is afterdischarge in the withdrawal reflex?
options: A second painful stimulus that follows shortly after the first
The inhibition of the flexors once withdrawal is complete
Continued motor neuron firing after the stimulus has stopped
The slow return of the limb to its original resting position
questions.why: Interneuron chains and reverberating loops keep delivering excitation to the motor pool for a period after the afferent volley ends, which is why a limb stays flexed after a brief stimulus. A second stimulus is an external event, not a property of the circuit. The passive return of the limb happens after the reflex ends and is not the discharge itself. Inhibition of the flexors is the opposite of continued flexor firing.
questions.answerText: Continued motor neuron firing after the stimulus has stopped

questions.q: A person standing barefoot steps on a tack with the right foot. Predict what the left leg does.
options: The left leg extends to bear the body weight
The left leg flexes so that both feet lift
The left leg does nothing until the person decides to shift
The left leg relaxes completely
questions.why: Crossed extensor output excites the contralateral extensors at the same time the right leg withdraws, so the left leg stiffens and supports the shifted weight. Flexing both legs would drop the person to the floor. Complete relaxation would collapse the supporting limb. The response is spinal and begins well before any voluntary decision can be made.
questions.answerText: The left leg extends to bear the body weight

questions.q: Why does the flexor withdrawal reflex have a longer latency than the patellar reflex?
options: It travels a longer distance within the peripheral nerve trunk
It uses smaller, slower afferents and adds interneurons in the pathway
Its effector muscles are larger and so take longer to contract fully
It must reach the cerebral cortex before any response can occur
questions.why: Nociceptive afferents are small and conduct slowly, and each interneuron in the chain adds synaptic delay, so both factors push the latency well above the monosynaptic value. Peripheral distances are similar for reflexes tested in the same limb. Muscle size affects the force and speed of the contraction, not the delay before it starts. The reflex is integrated in the cord, and cortical involvement is not required for the response.
questions.answerText: It uses smaller, slower afferents and adds interneurons in the pathway

questions.q: A stronger painful stimulus produces withdrawal at more joints than a weak one. What accounts for this?
options: Muscle fibers generate more force from exactly the same motor command
Afferent fibers conduct faster when the stimulus applied is stronger
More interneurons are recruited, spreading excitation to more segments
Motor neurons produce larger action potentials with stronger input
questions.why: A stronger stimulus recruits more afferents and drives interneuron pools harder, so excitation spreads to motor pools further up and down the cord and more joints join the movement. Conduction velocity is a property of fiber diameter and myelination and does not change with stimulus strength. Action potentials are all or none, so they do not grow larger. Muscle force here rises because more motor units are recruited, which is a consequence of the spread rather than the cause of it.
questions.answerText: More interneurons are recruited, spreading excitation to more segments

questions.q: A hand touches a hot pan. Which muscles are activated first in the withdrawal response?
options: The elbow extensors, which push the hand away
The shoulder abductors acting alone
The flexors and extensors together, which hold the arm steady
The elbow flexors, which pull the hand away
questions.why: Withdrawal is a flexion pattern, and flexing the elbow is the fastest way to move the hand off the source of injury. Extending the elbow would drive the hand further into the pan. The shoulder often joins the movement, but it does so through the same spreading interneurons rather than acting on its own. Co-contraction would freeze the arm in contact with the heat.
questions.answerText: The elbow flexors, which pull the hand away

questions.q: Which reflex depends on interneurons that cross to the opposite side of the spinal cord?
options: The crossed extensor reflex
The Golgi tendon organ reflex
The patellar stretch reflex
The flexor withdrawal reflex
questions.why: Only the crossed extensor reflex sends its signal through commissural interneurons to motor pools on the other side of the body. The flexor withdrawal reflex is ipsilateral, even though it spans several segments. The stretch reflex acts on one muscle and its antagonist on the same side. The tendon organ reflex likewise stays within the same side of the cord.
questions.answerText: The crossed extensor reflex

questions.q: Withdrawal begins before the person consciously feels the pain. What does that show about the integrating center?
options: Integration occurs in the cortex, which acts before it becomes aware of the pain
The reflex bypasses synapses entirely, which is why it seems instantaneous
Integration occurs in the cord, while conscious pain requires reaching the brain
Pain fibers conduct faster than the motor fibers used by the reflex arc
questions.why: The reflex arc closes locally in the cord over a few tens of milliseconds, while the ascending pathway and cortical processing needed for awareness take considerably longer, so the movement leads the sensation. Cortical integration would add the very delay that the timing rules out. Comparing conduction speeds does not explain awareness, which depends on the number and length of the pathways involved. The withdrawal arc is polysynaptic, so it is not synapse free and not instantaneous.
questions.answerText: Integration occurs in the cord, while conscious pain requires reaching the brain

questions.q: A person walking barefoot steps on broken glass with the left foot. Trace what the flexor withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes do together.
options: Both legs flex at once so that the person can lower to the ground safely
The left leg flexes and lifts while the right leg extends and takes the weight
The left leg extends to push off the glass while the right leg flexes
The left leg flexes and the right leg also flexes in order to shorten the stride
questions.why: Ipsilateral interneurons excite left flexors and inhibit left extensors, while commissural interneurons excite right extensors and inhibit right flexors, so escape and support happen in the same moment. Flexing both legs removes support and drops the body. Extending the injured leg would press the wound onto the glass. Flexing both legs also fails the balance requirement that the crossed pathway exists to meet.
questions.answerText: The left leg flexes and lifts while the right leg extends and takes the weight

questions.q: In a patient the commissural interneurons that cross the spinal cord are damaged while all ipsilateral circuits remain intact. Predict the response to a painful stimulus to one foot while the patient is standing.
options: Both legs extend, leaving the patient rigid
The stimulated leg extends and the other withdraws, reversing the pattern
Neither leg responds, because the whole reflex requires the crossing fibers
The stimulated leg withdraws but the other does not extend, so balance is lost
questions.why: The withdrawal limb of the response is entirely ipsilateral and survives, but the supporting extension on the other side depends on crossing fibers, so weight shifts to a limb that has not stiffened. The ipsilateral arc is intact, so a complete absence of response is not possible. Nothing in this lesion reverses the flexor and extensor assignments. Bilateral extension would require excitation of extensors on the stimulated side, which is actively inhibited.
questions.answerText: The stimulated leg withdraws but the other does not extend, so balance is lost

questions.q: Why does a painful stimulus to the hand of a seated person produce a different overall pattern than the same stimulus to the foot of a standing person?
options: The arm withdrawal reflex is monosynaptic while the leg withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic
The arm has few nociceptors, so the response there is largely voluntary rather than reflex
Crossed extension supports body weight, so it is prominent in the leg and minimal in the seated arm
Painful signals from the hand are integrated in the brainstem rather than in the spinal cord itself
questions.why: Both stimuli produce ipsilateral flexor withdrawal, but the crossed extension that preserves balance is only useful when the body weight must be transferred, which is the standing situation. The hand is densely supplied with nociceptors, so the first distractor fails at the premise. Both withdrawal reflexes are polysynaptic. Integration of both is spinal, with the brain informed afterward through ascending pathways.
questions.answerText: Crossed extension supports body weight, so it is prominent in the leg and minimal in the seated arm

questions.q: A withdrawal reflex is elicited with a stimulus lasting only 5 ms, yet the limb stays flexed for nearly a second. What best explains the prolonged contraction, and why does the patellar reflex not behave this way?
options: Slow conduction in the afferent and efferent fibers, which the patellar reflex does not have
Afterdischarge from reverberating interneuron circuits, which a monosynaptic arc does not have
Continued transmitter release at the neuromuscular junction, which the patellar reflex lacks
Prolonged receptor potentials in nociceptors combined with unusually slow flexor muscle fibers
questions.why: Once interneuron chains and loops are excited, they keep re-exciting the motor pool after the afferent volley has passed, and the multi-segmental spread keeps many motor neurons involved, so flexion outlasts the stimulus by orders of magnitude. Slow conduction shifts the start of the response by milliseconds and cannot stretch it to a second. Receptor potentials and muscle twitch duration are also far too brief to account for it. Neuromuscular transmission works the same way in both reflexes and stops when motor neuron firing stops.
questions.answerText: Afterdischarge from reverberating interneuron circuits, which a monosynaptic arc does not have

questions.q: What information does the dorsal column pathway carry?
options: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception
Unconscious proprioception bound for the cerebellum
Voluntary motor commands to skeletal muscle
Pain, temperature, and crude touch
questions.why: The dorsal columns carry the discriminative senses, the ones that need precise timing and a small receptive field, which is why vibration and joint position travel here. Pain and temperature ascend in the spinothalamic pathway instead. Voluntary motor commands descend in the corticospinal tract, so they move the opposite direction. Crude touch is largely a spinothalamic function, and confining the dorsal columns to it leaves vibration and proprioception unaccounted for.
questions.answerText: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception

questions.q: What information does the spinothalamic pathway carry?
options: Conscious proprioception from muscles and joints
Voluntary motor commands to skeletal muscle
Fine touch and vibration
Pain and temperature
questions.why: Spinothalamic fibers arise from dorsal horn neurons that receive small pain and temperature afferents, so this is the route by which a burn or a pinprick reaches consciousness. Fine touch and vibration travel in the dorsal columns. Conscious proprioception also uses the dorsal columns. Motor commands descend rather than ascend and belong to the corticospinal tract.
questions.answerText: Pain and temperature

questions.q: What does the corticospinal tract carry?
options: Autonomic commands to smooth muscle and glands
Voluntary motor commands from the cortex to spinal motor neurons
Proprioceptive information from muscle spindles to the cerebellum
Pain and temperature from the body up to the cortex
questions.why: The corticospinal tract is the main descending pathway for skilled voluntary movement, running from motor cortex to the ventral horn motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle. Pain and temperature ascend in the spinothalamic pathway. Unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum travels in the spinocerebellar tracts. Autonomic output leaves through preganglionic fibers of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, not the corticospinal tract.
questions.answerText: Voluntary motor commands from the cortex to spinal motor neurons

questions.q: Where does the dorsal column pathway cross the midline?
options: In the midbrain, at the level of the cerebral peduncle
In the thalamus, at the ventral posterolateral nucleus
In the spinal cord, a segment or two above where the fibers enter
In the medulla, at the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus
questions.why: The first order fiber ascends on its own side to the nucleus gracilis or cuneatus in the medulla, and only the second order fiber crosses there before ascending as the medial lemniscus. Crossing within a segment or two of entry is the spinothalamic arrangement, and confusing the two is what reverses lesion patterns. No crossing happens in the midbrain for this pathway. The thalamus is the relay to cortex, not a crossing point.
questions.answerText: In the medulla, at the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus

questions.q: Where does the spinothalamic pathway cross the midline?
options: In the spinal cord, a segment or two above where the fibers enter
In the midbrain, just below the thalamic relay
In the medulla, where the internal arcuate fibers cross the midline
In the pons, at the level of the medial lemniscus
questions.why: The second order neuron in the dorsal horn sends its axon through the anterior white commissure to the other side almost immediately, then ascends contralaterally, which is why a cord lesion here causes a deficit on the opposite side. Crossing in the medulla describes the dorsal column pathway. Nothing crosses in the pons for this pathway. A pathway that never crossed could not deliver body sensation to the opposite hemisphere.
questions.answerText: In the spinal cord, a segment or two above where the fibers enter

questions.q: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract cross the midline?
options: At the spinal cord segment where its fibers end
In the midbrain at the cerebral peduncles
At the pyramids of the medulla
In the internal capsule
questions.why: About 90 percent of corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla and then descend in the lateral column of the cord on the side they will control. Crossing at the target segment is not how the lateral tract is organized. The internal capsule and the cerebral peduncle are places these fibers pass through on the same side as the cortex that sent them, not places where they cross.
questions.answerText: At the pyramids of the medulla

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of the second order neurons of the spinothalamic pathway?
options: In the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
In the dorsal root ganglion beside the spinal cord
In the dorsal horn of the cord, near the level of entry
In the nucleus gracilis or cuneatus of the medulla
questions.why: Pain and temperature afferents synapse in the dorsal horn, and it is that dorsal horn neuron whose axon crosses and ascends, which is why the crossing happens so low. The dorsal root ganglion holds the first order cell body. The nucleus gracilis holds the second order cell body of the dorsal column pathway. The thalamic nucleus holds the third order neuron for both sensory pathways.
questions.answerText: In the dorsal horn of the cord, near the level of entry

questions.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays both dorsal column and spinothalamic input to the cerebral cortex?
options: The lateral geniculate nucleus
The ventral posterolateral nucleus
The medial geniculate nucleus
The anterior nucleus
questions.why: Both body sensory pathways converge on the ventral posterolateral nucleus, whose third order neurons project to the somatosensory cortex. The lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay. The medial geniculate nucleus is the auditory relay. The anterior nucleus belongs to limbic circuitry and carries no somatosensory relay function.
questions.answerText: The ventral posterolateral nucleus

questions.q: The dorsal column on the left side of the spinal cord is damaged at T6. Where is vibration sense lost?
options: On both sides of the body below T6
On the left side of the body above T6
On the right side of the body below T6
On the left side of the body below T6
questions.why: Dorsal column fibers ascend on the same side they entered and do not cross until the medulla, so a lesion in the cord takes out sensation from the same side, below the level of the injury. A contralateral deficit would require the fibers to have crossed already, which happens only above the medulla. Segments above the lesion send their fibers into the column above the damage, so they are unaffected. A bilateral loss would require damage to both columns.
questions.answerText: On the left side of the body below T6

questions.q: The spinothalamic tract on the right side of the spinal cord is cut at T10. Where is pain and temperature sensation lost?
options: On the left side of the body below the level of the lesion
On the left side of the body above the level of the lesion
On both sides of the body at the level of the lesion only
On the right side of the body below the level of the lesion
questions.why: These fibers cross within a segment or two of entering the cord, so the right side tract is already carrying signals that came from the left side of the body, and cutting it removes left sided pain and temperature below the injury. An ipsilateral deficit would be expected only if the pathway crossed higher up, as the dorsal columns do. Levels above the lesion enter the tract above the damage. A deficit confined to the level of the lesion describes damage to the crossing fibers themselves rather than the ascending tract.
questions.answerText: On the left side of the body below the level of the lesion

questions.q: The lateral corticospinal tract is damaged on the left side of the spinal cord at C7. Which side of the body is weak?
options: The left side, above the level of the lesion
The left side, below the level of the lesion
Both sides equally
The right side, below the level of the lesion
questions.why: These fibers crossed at the pyramids in the medulla, well above the cord, so by the time they reach C7 they are on the same side as the muscles they control and the weakness is ipsilateral to the cord lesion. A contralateral weakness would require the crossing to happen below C7, which it does not. Segments above the lesion receive their descending fibers before the damage. A bilateral deficit would require both lateral columns to be involved.
questions.answerText: The left side, below the level of the lesion

questions.q: A stroke damages corticospinal fibers in the right internal capsule, above the pyramids. Which side of the body is weak?
options: The left side of the body
The right side of the body
Neither side, because the fibers have not yet crossed
Both sides of the body equally
questions.why: The internal capsule lies above the pyramidal decussation, so fibers there still have their crossing ahead of them and control the opposite side of the body, giving a contralateral weakness. An ipsilateral weakness would be the answer for a lesion in the cord, below the crossing. A single sided capsular lesion cannot weaken both sides. The fact that the fibers have not yet crossed is exactly why the deficit appears on the other side, not why it is absent.
questions.answerText: The left side of the body

questions.q: A patient has lost pain and temperature sensation in the right leg but has normal vibration sense there. Which tract on which side is damaged?
options: The left dorsal column
The right spinothalamic tract
The right dorsal column
The left spinothalamic tract
questions.why: Signals from the right leg cross low in the cord and ascend in the left spinothalamic tract, so that is the tract carrying the lost information. The right spinothalamic tract carries the left side of the body. Either dorsal column would produce a vibration deficit, and vibration is preserved here, so the dorsal columns can be excluded on the pattern of loss alone.
questions.answerText: The left spinothalamic tract

questions.q: The medial lemniscus is damaged on the right side of the pons. Where is fine touch and vibration lost?
options: Only on the right side of the face
On both sides of the body
On the left side of the body
On the right side of the body
questions.why: The medial lemniscus forms after the dorsal column fibers have already crossed in the medulla, so a lesion above that point, such as in the pons, produces a contralateral deficit. An ipsilateral deficit would be expected only for a lesion below the crossing, in the cord. A one sided lesion cannot affect both sides. Facial sensation travels with the trigeminal system, so a body pathway lesion does not confine itself to the face.
questions.answerText: On the left side of the body

questions.q: Why does a spinothalamic lesion produce a sensory level a segment or two below the level of the injury rather than exactly at it?
options: Pain fibers cross in the medulla, well above the injury, so the level shifts downward
Fibers ascend a segment or two before crossing, so those entering just below the lesion escape it
The dorsal columns take over pain sensation for the top two segments below the lesion
Pain fibers conduct slowly, so the sensory deficit appears to lag behind the level of the injury
questions.why: Because the crossing is delayed by a segment or two, the fibers from dermatomes immediately below the lesion have already passed the damaged level on the other side, so the loss begins slightly lower than the injury. Conduction velocity has nothing to do with where a deficit appears on the body. The dorsal columns carry different modalities and cannot substitute for pain and temperature. Crossing in the medulla is the dorsal column arrangement, and if it applied here the deficit would be ipsilateral instead.
questions.answerText: Fibers ascend a segment or two before crossing, so those entering just below the lesion escape it

questions.q: The spinal cord is hemisected on the left at T10. Predict the pattern of deficits below the lesion.
options: Weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the right, with pain and temperature loss on the left
Loss of all sensation and of all strength on the left side only, with the right side normal
Weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the right
Weakness on the left together with loss of pain, temperature, and vibration all on the left
questions.why: Two of the three tracts cross above the lesion, so corticospinal weakness and dorsal column loss appear on the same side as the cut, while the spinothalamic tract crossed low and its loss appears on the opposite side, beginning a segment or two down. Reversing the sides swaps the crossed and uncrossed pathways. Losing everything on one side ignores that pain and temperature have already changed sides. Placing all deficits on the left leaves the low crossing of the spinothalamic tract unaccounted for.
questions.answerText: Weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the right

questions.q: A patient has weakness and loss of vibration sense in the right leg and loss of pain and temperature in the left leg, all below the level of the umbilicus. Where is the lesion?
options: A hemisection of the right side of the cord at about T10
A hemisection of the left side of the cord at about T10
A complete transection of the cord at T10
A lesion of the right internal capsule
questions.why: Motor and dorsal column deficits mark the side of a cord lesion because those tracts cross above it, so right sided weakness and right sided vibration loss place the injury on the right, and the crossed spinothalamic loss on the left confirms it. A left sided hemisection would give the mirror image of this pattern. An internal capsule lesion would produce weakness and sensory loss all on one side of the body, and would not spare the arm and trunk in this way. A complete transection would abolish everything on both sides below the level.
questions.answerText: A hemisection of the right side of the cord at about T10

questions.q: A cavity expands in the center of the cervical cord and interrupts the fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure at C5 to T1. Predict the sensory findings in the arms.
options: Loss of all sensation in one arm only
Loss of pain and temperature in both legs with the arms spared
Loss of vibration and position sense in both arms with pain and temperature preserved
Loss of pain and temperature in both arms with vibration and position sense preserved
questions.why: The crossing fibers of the spinothalamic pathway pass through the center of the cord, so a central cavity interrupts them bilaterally at those segments, while the dorsal columns sit posteriorly and are spared, producing a split pattern of loss. Losing vibration instead would require damage to the dorsal columns, which the cavity has not reached. A one sided total loss would require a hemisection rather than a central lesion. The legs are supplied by fibers that crossed lower down and are already ascending in the lateral column, so they escape.
questions.answerText: Loss of pain and temperature in both arms with vibration and position sense preserved

questions.q: A patient has weakness of the right arm and leg. If the lesion is in the spinal cord, which side is it on, and if the lesion is in the motor cortex, which side is it on?
options: The right side of the cord, or the left side of the cortex
The left side of the cord, or the right side of the cortex
The right side in both locations
The left side in both locations
questions.why: The pyramidal decussation is the dividing line: below it, in the cord, the fibers already serve the same side, so a cord lesion is ipsilateral to the weakness, while above it, in the cortex, the fibers have not crossed yet, so a cortical lesion is contralateral. Reversing both answers puts the decussation in the wrong place. Choosing the same side in both locations ignores the crossing entirely, which is the single most common error in reading these patterns.
questions.answerText: The right side of the cord, or the left side of the cortex

questions.q: Where is cerebrospinal fluid produced?
options: By the pia mater covering the cortex
At the choroid plexus in the ventricles
At the arachnoid granulations
By the endothelium of the dural venous sinuses
questions.why: Choroid plexus epithelium actively secretes CSF into the ventricles at roughly 500 mL per day. Arachnoid granulations are where the fluid is absorbed, the opposite end of the circuit. The pia is a thin covering membrane and does not secrete the fluid. The dural venous sinuses receive CSF rather than make it.
questions.answerText: At the choroid plexus in the ventricles

questions.q: Which of these is a function of cerebrospinal fluid?
options: It establishes the resting membrane potential of central neurons
It supplies the main metabolic fuel used by neurons in the cortex
It delivers oxygen to neurons in place of the cerebral blood supply
It supports the brain so that its effective weight is greatly reduced
questions.why: Floating in CSF reduces the effective weight of the brain from about 1400 g to roughly 50 g, which protects the base of the brain and its vessels from being crushed. Oxygen is delivered by blood through cerebral capillaries, not by CSF. Resting membrane potential is set by ion gradients and membrane permeability at each cell. Glucose is the fuel and arrives through the blood, although CSF composition does help keep the neuronal environment stable.
questions.answerText: It supports the brain so that its effective weight is greatly reduced

questions.q: Where does cerebrospinal fluid return to the blood?
options: Across the blood brain barrier into the brain capillaries
At the capillary beds of the choroid plexus in the ventricles
At the arachnoid granulations projecting into the dural sinuses
Through lymphatic vessels running within the pia mater
questions.why: Arachnoid granulations act as one way valves that let CSF pass into venous blood once CSF pressure exceeds venous pressure. Choroid plexus capillaries supply the fluid that becomes CSF, so flow there runs the other way. The blood brain barrier restricts movement between blood and brain tissue and is not the bulk drainage route. Classic lymphatic vessels do not run in the pia.
questions.answerText: At the arachnoid granulations projecting into the dural sinuses

questions.q: About how much cerebrospinal fluid is present in an adult at any one time?
options: About 1500 mL
About 15 mL
About 150 mL
About 500 mL
questions.why: Roughly 150 mL circulates at any moment, and since about 500 mL is produced each day the whole volume is replaced several times over. About 15 mL is far too small to fill the ventricles and subarachnoid space. About 500 mL is the daily production, a value students often mistake for the standing volume. About 1500 mL is closer to the mass of the brain itself in grams.
questions.answerText: About 150 mL

questions.q: What structure forms the blood brain barrier?
options: The thin layer of cerebrospinal fluid surrounding each neuron
Tight junctions between the endothelial cells of brain capillaries
Fenestrations in the endothelium of the brain capillary wall
The pia mater covering the entire outer surface of the brain
questions.why: Brain capillary endothelial cells are sealed to one another by continuous tight junctions, and astrocyte end feet wrap the vessel and help induce and maintain those junctions, so anything entering must pass through the cells rather than between them. Fenestrations are pores that make a capillary leaky, the opposite arrangement, and they are found in tissues such as the kidney glomerulus. The pia is a covering membrane, not a diffusion barrier at the capillary. CSF bathes the outside of the brain and ventricles and does not form the barrier.
questions.answerText: Tight junctions between the endothelial cells of brain capillaries

questions.q: Which property allows a substance to cross the blood brain barrier most easily by simple diffusion?
options: High lipid solubility
A strong net electrical charge
Tight binding to plasma albumin
Large molecular size
questions.why: With the paracellular route sealed, a molecule must dissolve into and pass through the endothelial cell membranes, and lipid solubility is exactly what allows that, which is why anesthetics and alcohol enter the brain within seconds. Large molecules cross poorly regardless of other properties. A charged molecule cannot enter a lipid bilayer without a transporter. A drug bound to albumin is held in the plasma and only its free fraction is available to cross.
questions.answerText: High lipid solubility

questions.q: How does glucose cross the blood brain barrier?
options: Through fenestrations between endothelial cells
By simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
By vesicular pinocytosis across the endothelial cell
By carrier mediated transport using GLUT1
questions.why: Glucose is polar and cannot pass through the membrane on its own, so the endothelium expresses abundant GLUT1 to carry it down its concentration gradient into the brain. Simple diffusion is the route for lipid soluble molecules only. Brain capillaries have no fenestrations, which is the whole point of the barrier. Pinocytosis is markedly limited in these endothelial cells, unlike in capillaries elsewhere.
questions.answerText: By carrier mediated transport using GLUT1

questions.q: How does the composition of cerebrospinal fluid compare with that of blood plasma?
options: CSF contains far more protein
CSF contains far less protein
CSF contains far more potassium
CSF and plasma have essentially identical composition
questions.why: CSF is a secreted fluid rather than a filtrate, so protein content is a small fraction of the plasma value, and K+ is also held slightly lower and more tightly regulated to keep neuronal excitability stable. High protein in CSF is an abnormal finding, not the normal state. High K+ in CSF would destabilize resting membrane potentials in neurons. Identical composition would defeat the purpose of a regulated extracellular environment.
questions.answerText: CSF contains far less protein

questions.q: Two drugs act equally well at the same brain receptor. Drug A is highly lipid soluble and drug B is fully ionized at body pH. Which reaches the brain better?
options: Drug A, because lipid soluble molecules diffuse through the endothelial membranes
Both equally, because the barrier excludes only large molecules
Drug B, because charged molecules are pulled across by the membrane potential
Neither, because every drug requires a specific transporter
questions.why: The barrier forces a transcellular route, so the ability to dissolve in membrane lipid decides passive entry and the lipid soluble drug wins easily. The small membrane potential across an endothelial cell cannot drag an ion through a lipid bilayer that offers it no path. Size matters, but charge and lipid solubility matter at least as much, so treating the barrier as a size filter is incomplete. Some substances do use transporters, but many drugs cross by simple diffusion without one.
questions.answerText: Drug A, because lipid soluble molecules diffuse through the endothelial membranes

questions.q: Dopamine given intravenously does not reach the brain, but L-dopa does. Why?
options: L-dopa dissolves in cerebrospinal fluid far better than dopamine does
L-dopa is smaller than dopamine and slips between the endothelial cells
L-dopa is carried by an amino acid transporter that dopamine cannot use
Dopamine is destroyed by the choroid plexus before it reaches brain tissue
questions.why: L-dopa is an amino acid and is recognized by the large neutral amino acid carrier in the endothelial membrane, giving it a route that polar dopamine simply does not have. Nothing slips between the endothelial cells, since tight junctions seal that path for both molecules. Choroid plexus destruction is not the limiting step, as the barrier blocks dopamine at the capillary. Both molecules are water soluble, so solubility in CSF is not what separates them.
questions.answerText: L-dopa is carried by an amino acid transporter that dopamine cannot use

questions.q: The cerebral aqueduct becomes blocked. Predict what happens.
options: CSF is rerouted through the arachnoid granulations with no change in pressure
CSF drains into the spinal canal and the brain shrinks
CSF production stops at once, so pressure falls
CSF accumulates above the block and pressure rises in the ventricles
questions.why: Choroid plexus secretion continues largely independent of pressure, so fluid keeps entering the ventricles upstream of the block while it can no longer reach the absorption sites, and the ventricles distend. Production does not shut off promptly when pressure rises, which is why obstruction is dangerous. Reaching the granulations requires passing the block, so no rerouting is available. Drainage downward is also blocked, so the brain tissue is compressed rather than allowed to shrink.
questions.answerText: CSF accumulates above the block and pressure rises in the ventricles

questions.q: A brain weighing about 1400 g in air presses on the floor of the skull with an effective weight of only about 50 g. What accounts for this?
options: The dura suspends the entire brain from the roof of the skull
It floats in cerebrospinal fluid, which provides buoyancy
Brain tissue is less dense than any fluid that surrounds it
The blood brain barrier holds the brain in position
questions.why: Because brain tissue and CSF have nearly the same density, the fluid supports almost the whole weight of the organ, which is why a brain removed from CSF deforms under its own mass. Dural folds do help stabilize the brain, but they do not carry its weight. The blood brain barrier controls chemical exchange and has no mechanical role. Brain tissue is very slightly denser than CSF, not less dense, so it does not simply float free.
questions.answerText: It floats in cerebrospinal fluid, which provides buoyancy

questions.q: Which region of the brain can respond to blood borne hormones and toxins despite the blood brain barrier?
options: The internal capsule, which contains no capillaries at all
The choroid plexus epithelium, which lacks tight junctions
The primary somatosensory cortex, which expresses extra transporters
The circumventricular organs, where the capillaries are leaky
questions.why: A few small regions bordering the ventricles, including the area postrema and parts of the hypothalamus, have fenestrated capillaries so the brain can sample the blood directly, which is how a vomiting reflex to circulating toxins is possible. The somatosensory cortex has an ordinary barrier and no special sampling role. Every region of the brain, including white matter tracts, is supplied by capillaries. The choroid plexus epithelium does have tight junctions, which is what makes it a blood to CSF barrier.
questions.answerText: The circumventricular organs, where the capillaries are leaky

questions.q: A drug is 99 percent bound to plasma albumin. What is the effect on its entry into the brain?
options: Entry is limited, because only the free fraction is available to cross
Entry is increased, because albumin is carried across along with it
Entry is prevented completely, because bound drug is chemically inactive
Entry is unaffected, because protein binding occurs only in the liver
questions.why: Only unbound drug can diffuse or be transported across the endothelium, so heavy protein binding leaves a small free concentration to drive entry and slows the rise of drug levels in the brain. Albumin itself is far too large to cross the barrier, so it cannot ferry the drug in. Binding happens in the plasma throughout the circulation, not only in the liver. Entry is reduced rather than abolished, since bound and free drug are in equilibrium and free drug is continuously replaced as it leaves.
questions.answerText: Entry is limited, because only the free fraction is available to cross

questions.q: Meningitis inflames the meninges and loosens the endothelial tight junctions. Predict the effect on an antibiotic that normally penetrates the brain poorly.
options: The antibiotic becomes trapped in the CSF and cannot return to the bloodstream
Penetration is unchanged, because the barrier depends only on lipid solubility
More antibiotic reaches the CSF while inflammation lasts, then less as it resolves
Less antibiotic reaches the CSF, because inflammation blocks the brain capillaries
questions.why: The barrier is a property of the junctions, so loosening them opens a paracellular route and raises drug entry, and the effect fades as the junctions reseal. Inflammation increases permeability rather than blocking flow. Lipid solubility governs the transcellular route but does not make the paracellular route irrelevant, so penetration is not fixed. Movement across a leaky barrier works in both directions, so trapping does not occur.
questions.answerText: More antibiotic reaches the CSF while inflammation lasts, then less as it resolves

questions.q: The arachnoid granulations are scarred after a hemorrhage while the choroid plexus continues to secrete at its normal rate. Predict what happens over the following days.
options: CSF volume falls, because secretion shuts down as soon as the pressure rises
Nothing changes, because production and absorption are independent of one another
CSF volume and pressure rise, because production continues while absorption falls
CSF is absorbed across the blood brain barrier instead, at exactly the same rate
questions.why: CSF volume is set by the balance of a nearly constant secretion rate against a pressure dependent absorption rate, so damaging absorption while secretion continues drives volume and pressure upward. Secretion is not strongly suppressed by rising pressure, which is exactly why the imbalance persists. The two processes are linked through volume, so they cannot be treated as independent. The blood brain barrier is not a bulk drainage route and cannot substitute for the granulations.
questions.answerText: CSF volume and pressure rise, because production continues while absorption falls

questions.q: Three substances are presented to the blood brain barrier: a small lipid soluble anesthetic, the amino acid phenylalanine, and a large plasma protein. Which crosses most readily and which least?
options: The plasma protein crosses most readily and the anesthetic least
All three cross at similar rates, because the barrier is only a size filter
Phenylalanine crosses most readily and the anesthetic least
The anesthetic crosses most readily and the plasma protein least
questions.why: A small lipid soluble molecule dissolves straight through the endothelial membranes with no carrier needed, phenylalanine has a carrier but is limited by how many transporters are available, and a large protein has neither route open to it. Ranking the protein first inverts every property that matters. Carrier mediated entry is real but slower and saturable, so it does not outrun free diffusion of a lipid soluble drug. Treating the barrier as a size filter ignores lipid solubility and transporters, the two factors doing most of the work.
questions.answerText: The anesthetic crosses most readily and the plasma protein least

questions.q: Mannitol, which cannot cross the blood brain barrier, is infused into the blood. Predict the effect on brain water.
options: Water moves from brain tissue into the blood, because plasma osmolarity rises
Water moves into the brain, because mannitol drags fluid across the barrier with it
The brain swells, because mannitol is taken up and converted to glucose by neurons
Nothing changes, because water cannot cross the barrier any better than mannitol
questions.why: A solute that stays in the plasma is an effective osmole across that barrier, so it raises the osmotic pressure of blood relative to brain tissue and pulls water out, lowering brain volume. Mannitol cannot drag water into a compartment it never enters. Water crosses the barrier freely even though mannitol does not, which is precisely what makes the osmotic effect possible. Mannitol is not metabolized to glucose by neurons.
questions.answerText: Water moves from brain tissue into the blood, because plasma osmolarity rises

questions.q: On the standard deep tendon reflex scale, which grade is recorded for a normal response?
questions.why: The scale runs from 0 to 4+, and 2+ is the expected brisk but not exaggerated response. A grade of 0 means no response at all even with reinforcement. A grade of 1+ means present but diminished, which is below normal though not always abnormal. A grade of 4+ means very brisk with clonus and points to loss of descending inhibition.

questions.q: What does a deep tendon reflex graded 4+ mean?
options: No response even with reinforcement
A normal, expected response
A very brisk response accompanied by clonus
A response that appears only with reinforcement
questions.why: A 4+ grade is the top of the scale and describes a hyperactive reflex with repetitive beats of clonus, which suggests an upper motor neuron problem. The normal response is 2+. A response requiring reinforcement is graded 1+ or is recorded with the reinforcement noted. No response at all is graded 0.
questions.answerText: A very brisk response accompanied by clonus

questions.q: Which spinal segments does the patellar reflex test?
options: L2 to L4
S1 and S2
T10 to T12
C5 and C6
questions.why: The quadriceps and its femoral nerve supply arise from L2 to L4, so a normal knee jerk tests the integrity of that arc. S1 is the ankle jerk. C5 and C6 give the biceps reflex. The T10 to T12 segments supply abdominal wall muscles and have no tendon jerk of this kind.
questions.answerText: L2 to L4

questions.q: Which spinal segment does the Achilles, or ankle jerk, reflex test?
options: S1
L4
C7
questions.why: The gastrocnemius and soleus draw their supply mainly from S1, so the ankle jerk is the standard test of that segment. L4 contributes to the knee jerk instead. C7 is tested by the triceps reflex. T12 supplies trunk musculature and no standard tendon jerk.
questions.answerText: S1

questions.q: Which deep tendon reflex tests the C5 and C6 segments?
options: The triceps reflex
The patellar reflex
The Achilles reflex
The biceps reflex
questions.why: The biceps and its musculocutaneous nerve supply come from C5 and C6, so tapping the biceps tendon tests those roots. The triceps reflex tests C7. The patellar reflex tests L2 to L4. The Achilles reflex tests S1.
questions.answerText: The biceps reflex

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Jendrassik maneuver during reflex testing?
options: To measure the latency of the reflex response accurately
To test the voluntary strength of the muscle being tapped
To reinforce a weak reflex so that it can be judged fairly
To relax the subject so that the reflex disappears entirely
questions.why: Having the subject pull interlocked fingers apart raises the background excitability of the motor pool in the leg, so a reflex that looked absent may appear, which prevents recording a false 0. It increases rather than suppresses the response. It provides no timing information, so latency must be measured some other way. It tests neither the strength nor the effort of the muscle being tapped.
questions.answerText: To reinforce a weak reflex so that it can be judged fairly

questions.q: About how long is the latency of the patellar reflex, from tendon tap to the start of contraction?
options: About 20 to 40 ms
About 150 to 250 ms
About 1 to 2 s
About 1 to 2 ms
questions.why: Conduction up and down the leg plus one synaptic delay adds up to a few tens of milliseconds, which is the signature of a monosynaptic spinal arc. One to two milliseconds is about the cost of a single synapse and far too short for the round trip. About 150 to 250 ms is the range of a simple voluntary reaction time. One to two seconds is longer than any reflex or voluntary reaction.
questions.answerText: About 20 to 40 ms

questions.q: What does the ruler drop test measure?
options: The latency of the patellar reflex
Nerve conduction velocity in the forearm
The maximum force of a muscle contraction
Voluntary reaction time
questions.why: The subject must see the ruler fall, decide to close the hand, and execute the movement, so the distance the ruler falls converts into a reaction time that includes central processing. A tendon reflex latency is an order of magnitude shorter and cannot be captured this way. The test records timing, not force. Conduction velocity requires stimulating a nerve at two points and comparing latencies.
questions.answerText: Voluntary reaction time

questions.q: A ruler is caught after falling 20 cm. Using d equal to one half g t squared, with g of 9.8 m/s squared, what is the reaction time?
options: About 0.45 s
About 0.20 s
About 0.02 s
About 2.0 s
questions.why: Rearranging gives t equal to the square root of two times 0.20 m divided by 9.8, which is the square root of about 0.041, or roughly 0.20 s, a typical simple reaction time. About 0.02 s would be shorter than a spinal reflex latency and is physically impossible for a visual response. About 0.45 s corresponds to a drop of roughly a meter. About 2.0 s is off by a factor of ten and would require a fall of nearly 20 m.
questions.answerText: About 0.20 s

questions.q: A subject responds to a stimulus with a measured latency of 180 ms. Is this a reflex or a voluntary response?
options: Voluntary, because 180 ms is far longer than a spinal reflex latency
Reflex, because voluntary responses always take less than 100 ms
Reflex, because spinal reflexes take about 200 ms
It cannot be decided, because latency says nothing about the pathway
