questions.q: Nociceptors adapt very little, and some sensitize instead. Why is that useful?
options: It allows pain to be located more precisely than touch
It keeps the pain fibers from conducting too quickly
Tissue damage keeps mattering, so the warning must not fade away
It prevents nociceptors from responding to more than one type of stimulus
questions.why: Adaptation is useful when a signal has already done its job, and a damaging stimulus never has, so a nociceptor that faded would let a person keep a hand on a hot pan. Pain is in fact localized less precisely than touch, not more. Adaptation rate has no bearing on conduction velocity, and many nociceptors are polymodal, responding to several stimulus types.
questions.answerText: Tissue damage keeps mattering, so the warning must not fade away

questions.q: You stop noticing the feeling of your shirt a minute after putting it on, though the shirt is still there. Which receptors explain this?
options: Phasic mechanoreceptors, which adapted to the steady pressure
Tonic mechanoreceptors, which continue to fire but are ignored
Nociceptors, which adapted once the pressure proved harmless
Thermoreceptors, which stopped reporting the warmth of the fabric
questions.why: The rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors of the skin fire as the shirt settles and then fall silent, so the CNS receives no ongoing touch signal at all, which is why moving the shirt makes you notice it again at once. Tonic receptors do keep some steady traffic going, but the disappearance of the sensation reflects adaptation in the periphery rather than a decision to ignore it. Nociceptors are not activated by a shirt, and the thermal signal is a separate sensation from the touch that fades.
questions.answerText: Phasic mechanoreceptors, which adapted to the steady pressure

questions.q: In an experiment the lamellae are peeled away from a Pacinian corpuscle, leaving the bare nerve ending. Steady pressure is then applied. What is the predicted result?
options: The ending stops responding to any applied pressure at all
The ending fires only at the offset of the applied pressure
The ending fires action potentials of much larger amplitude than before
The ending fires throughout the pressure rather than only at its onset
questions.why: The lamellae are what make the corpuscle phasic, because they slip under maintained pressure and stop transmitting force to the ending, so removing them leaves an ending that stays deformed and keeps firing. This is the cleanest demonstration that adaptation can be built into accessory structures rather than into the membrane. Transduction still works, so the response is not abolished, and spike height is fixed by the all or none rule.
questions.answerText: The ending fires throughout the pressure rather than only at its onset

questions.q: Arterial pressure must be monitored beat after beat, all day. What does that require of the carotid sinus baroreceptors?
options: They must adapt within a second so each beat is reported separately
They must adapt slowly enough to keep firing at a steady mean pressure
They must stop firing between beats to avoid saturating the pathway
They must switch from tonic to phasic behavior once pressure is stable
questions.why: A control system that corrects blood pressure needs a continuous readout of the current pressure, so the sensor has to keep reporting rather than falling silent, which is tonic behavior. A sensor that adapted in a second would leave the medulla blind between beats. Baroreceptors do reset over days if pressure stays high, but that is slow drift, not the moment to moment silence a phasic receptor would show.
questions.answerText: They must adapt slowly enough to keep firing at a steady mean pressure

questions.q: A person walks into a kitchen, notices a strong smell, and within a few minutes cannot detect it, though the odor molecules are still in the air. What accounts for this?
options: The odor molecules are cleared from the nasal mucosa within minutes
The olfactory nerve fatigues and can no longer conduct action potentials
Olfactory receptors adapt rapidly to a constant odor concentration
The cortex switches the labeled line for that odor to another modality
questions.why: Olfactory receptors are strongly phasic, so a steady concentration produces a burst of firing and then near silence, which is why a new smell in the same room is still detected while the old one is not. The molecules are still arriving, so clearance is not the explanation. Axons do not fatigue in this way over minutes, and labeled lines are fixed anatomy that the cortex cannot reassign.
questions.answerText: Olfactory receptors adapt rapidly to a constant odor concentration

questions.q: Two afferents are recorded during a five second skin indentation. Afferent A fires briskly for the whole five seconds. Afferent B fires for 100 ms at the start and 100 ms at the end. Which is which?
options: A is tonic and B is phasic
A is phasic and B is tonic
Both are tonic, but B has a higher threshold
Both are phasic, but A has a larger receptive field
questions.why: Continuous firing throughout the stimulus is the definition of slow adaptation, and brief bursts confined to onset and offset are the definition of rapid adaptation, so the recordings identify the two types directly. Threshold and receptive field size are separate properties that would change how easily and where each afferent responds, not how its firing decays over time. Reading the two patterns off a tracing is the practical form of this distinction.
questions.answerText: A is tonic and B is phasic

questions.q: Why would it be a poor design for the receptors that detect a light touch on the arm to adapt as slowly as nociceptors do?
options: Touch receptors would then be unable to code the intensity of a stimulus
The touch pathway would be too slow to reach cortex in time
Touch receptors would begin to report pain instead of pressure
The CNS would be flooded with signals about unchanging contact
questions.why: Adaptation is a filter that keeps the nervous system focused on new and changing information, and a steady, harmless contact carries no news after the first moment. Intensity coding by firing rate works in both tonic and phasic receptors, so it would not be lost. Conduction speed is unrelated to adaptation, and modality is fixed by the labeled line, so a touch receptor cannot start signaling pain.
questions.answerText: The CNS would be flooded with signals about unchanging contact

questions.q: A vibrating tuning fork is placed against the skin. Which adaptation property makes a receptor good at detecting the vibration?
options: Slow adaptation, so it can report the total time the fork is applied for
Rapid adaptation, so it can respond to each cycle of pressure change
Slow adaptation, so it can report the amplitude of each cycle
No adaptation at all, so no information is ever discarded
questions.why: Vibration is a rapid series of pressure changes, and only a receptor that resets quickly between them can fire in step with each cycle rather than blurring them together. A slowly adapting receptor stays partly depolarized from the previous cycle and loses the timing information. Reporting total application time or refusing to adapt at all would preserve less useful information, not more, for a stimulus whose content is the change itself.
questions.answerText: Rapid adaptation, so it can respond to each cycle of pressure change

questions.q: A patient has had untreated hypertension for years. Over that time the carotid sinus baroreceptors have reset to the higher pressure. What does the reflex now defend, and what does that mean for treatment?
options: It defends normal pressure, so the reflex opposes the hypertension continuously
It defends the new higher pressure, so lowering pressure triggers compensation
It defends nothing, because reset baroreceptors stop firing altogether
It defends only pulse pressure, since mean pressure is no longer sensed
questions.why: Resetting is adaptation on a slow time scale: the receptors come to treat the chronically high pressure as their new baseline, so they fire normally there and respond to changes around it. That is why a drug that lowers pressure is read as a fall and is met with reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction until the receptors reset again. If the reflex still defended the original normal, chronic hypertension would be self correcting, and reset receptors are still firing rather than silent.
questions.answerText: It defends the new higher pressure, so lowering pressure triggers compensation

questions.q: A drug converts the rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors of the skin into slowly adapting ones without changing anything else. Predict the effect on everyday sensation.
options: Steady contact would be felt continuously, and vibration would be felt poorly
Steady contact would still fade away, but vibration would be felt more sharply
Pain would be felt continuously and touch would disappear
Nothing would change, since perception is decided in the cortex
questions.why: Slow adaptation means the ending keeps reporting a constant pressure, so the shirt never stops being felt, and it also means the receptor cannot reset fast enough to follow each cycle of a vibration, so high frequency detection suffers. Fading contact requires the rapid adaptation the drug removed. Nociceptors are a separate population and are unaffected, and cortex can only work with the traffic the periphery sends.
questions.answerText: Steady contact would be felt continuously, and vibration would be felt poorly

questions.q: A recording during a ramp and hold indentation shows a high firing rate while the probe is moving in, a lower but steady rate while the probe is held, and a brief pause when the probe withdraws. How should this afferent be described?
options: Rapidly adapting, since the firing rate falls after the ramp
Slowly adapting, with an added sensitivity to the rate of change
Rapidly adapting, since firing stops when the probe withdraws
Non adapting, since firing never falls to zero during the hold
questions.why: The maintained firing during the hold is the defining feature and marks the afferent as slowly adapting, while the higher rate during the ramp shows it also reports how fast the skin is being indented, a dynamic component many tonic receptors have. A drop in rate after the ramp is not the same as adapting to silence, which is what rapidly adapting means. Firing that continues at a lower level is still adaptation, so calling it non adapting overstates the case.
questions.answerText: Slowly adapting, with an added sensitivity to the rate of change

questions.q: Imagine a hand in which every mechanoreceptor is phasic and none are tonic. Which everyday task becomes hardest?
options: Feeling a fly land on the skin
Detecting the buzz of a phone in the palm
Noticing the exact moment a held object begins to slip in the hand
Holding a glass with steady grip force without watching it
questions.why: Grip force control depends on a continuous report of how hard the fingers are pressing, and with only rapidly adapting receptors that report vanishes a moment after the grasp is stable, so the glass is squeezed or dropped without visual feedback. The other three tasks are all detections of change, which is precisely what phasic receptors do best. This is the clearest demonstration of why the body keeps both types rather than choosing one.
questions.answerText: Holding a glass with steady grip force without watching it

questions.q: Where is the cell body of the first order neuron of a somatosensory pathway?
options: In the dorsal horn of the spinal cord
In the dorsal root ganglion
In the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus
In the postcentral gyrus of the cortex
questions.why: The first order neuron runs from the receptor to the CNS with its cell body parked in the dorsal root ganglion, off to the side of the conducting axon. The dorsal horn is where many first order neurons synapse onto second order neurons, not where their cell bodies sit. The thalamus holds third order cell bodies, and the postcentral gyrus is the final destination rather than a cell body location for the pathway neurons.
questions.answerText: In the dorsal root ganglion

questions.q: Which sensations travel in the dorsal column medial lemniscus pathway?
options: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception
Pain, temperature, and crude touch
Pain and vibration only
Temperature and conscious proprioception but nothing else
questions.why: The dorsal columns carry the large fiber, high acuity information: two point discrimination, vibration, and joint position. Pain, temperature, and crude touch travel instead in the spinothalamic pathway on small diameter fibers. Keeping the two lists separate is what makes it possible to predict which sensations a given cord lesion will take.
questions.answerText: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception

questions.q: Where does the dorsal column pathway cross to the opposite side?
options: At the level of the spinal cord where the fiber enters
In the midbrain, just below the thalamus
In the medulla, after the second order neuron begins
It does not cross at all
questions.why: First order fibers ascend the cord on the same side, synapse in the gracile or cuneate nucleus of the medulla, and the second order axon then crosses as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus. Crossing near the level of entry is the spinothalamic arrangement, which is why the two pathways behave so differently after a cord lesion. Every conscious somatosensory pathway crosses at some point, since each hemisphere serves the opposite side of the body.
questions.answerText: In the medulla, after the second order neuron begins

questions.q: Where does the spinothalamic pathway cross to the opposite side?
options: In the medulla, at the internal arcuate fibers of the lemniscus
In the midbrain, at about the level of the red nucleus
It does not cross at all, so pain is felt on the same side
In the spinal cord, within a segment or two of where it enters
questions.why: Pain and temperature fibers synapse in the dorsal horn almost immediately, and the second order axon crosses in the anterior commissure and ascends on the opposite side. Crossing in the medulla is the dorsal column arrangement. Because both pathways cross somewhere, sensation always reaches the opposite hemisphere, but the level of crossing differs, and that difference produces the split findings of a cord hemisection.
questions.answerText: In the spinal cord, within a segment or two of where it enters

questions.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays somatosensory information from the body to the cortex?
options: The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
The ventral posterior lateral nucleus
The lateral geniculate nucleus
The anterior nucleus
questions.why: The ventral posterior lateral nucleus receives both the medial lemniscus and the spinothalamic tract from the body and sends third order axons to the postcentral gyrus. The medial geniculate is the auditory relay and the lateral geniculate the visual relay, both sensory but for other modalities. The anterior nucleus belongs to limbic circuitry rather than to a sensory relay.
questions.answerText: The ventral posterior lateral nucleus

questions.q: Where does the somatosensory pathway terminate in the cortex?
options: In the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
In the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
In the superior temporal gyrus
In the calcarine cortex of the occipital lobe
questions.why: Primary somatosensory cortex sits in the postcentral gyrus, immediately behind the central sulcus. The precentral gyrus just in front of that sulcus is primary motor cortex, and confusing the two reverses sensory and motor findings. The superior temporal gyrus is auditory cortex and the calcarine cortex is visual cortex.
questions.answerText: In the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe

questions.q: How many neurons in series carry a touch signal from the skin to the cortex?
options: One
Two
Four
Three
questions.why: The chain is first order from receptor to the CNS relay nucleus, second order from that nucleus to the thalamus, and third order from the thalamus to the cortex. A single neuron cannot span the distance and would give no place for the crossing and gating that occur at each synapse. Two would leave out the thalamic relay, which every conscious sensory pathway except olfaction passes through.
questions.answerText: Three

questions.q: What determines how much cortical territory a body region receives in the somatosensory homunculus?
options: The surface area of that region
The muscle mass of that region
The density of receptors in that region
The distance of that region from the brain
questions.why: Cortex is allocated by how much information a region sends, and that is set by receptor density, so densely innervated skin such as the fingertips and lips claims a huge strip while broad, sparsely innervated skin such as the back claims very little. Surface area and muscle mass do not predict representation, which is exactly why the map looks distorted. Distance from the brain has no bearing on cortical territory.
questions.answerText: The density of receptors in that region

questions.q: A pin is felt in the right hand. Which hemisphere processes it, and why?
options: The left hemisphere, because the pathway crossed in the spinal cord
The right hemisphere, because pain pathways stay on the same side
The left hemisphere, because pain pathways cross in the thalamus
Both hemispheres equally, because pain is not localized to one side
questions.why: Pain from the right hand enters the right dorsal horn, the second order axon crosses within a segment or two, and the spinothalamic tract ascends on the left to the left thalamus and left cortex. Pain pathways do cross, so a same side answer is wrong, and the crossing happens in the cord rather than in the thalamus, which relays without crossing. Pain localization is imprecise, but it is still lateralized.
questions.answerText: The left hemisphere, because the pathway crossed in the spinal cord

questions.q: The left dorsal column is damaged at the C5 level. Which deficit should you predict?
options: Loss of pain and temperature in the left arm
Loss of vibration and fine touch in the left arm
Loss of vibration and fine touch in the right arm
Loss of all sensation in both arms
questions.why: Dorsal column fibers ascend on the same side until they reach the medulla, so a lesion below that crossing point causes a deficit on the same side as the damage and below the level of the injury. Pain and temperature are spared because they have already crossed and are traveling in the spinothalamic tract on the other side. A contralateral deficit would require the lesion to be above the medullary crossing.
questions.answerText: Loss of vibration and fine touch in the left arm

questions.q: The lips occupy a far larger strip of somatosensory cortex than the entire back. What does that reflect?
options: The lips move more often than the back
The lips are closer to the brain than the back
The lips contain more muscle tissue per gram than the back does
The lips send far more afferent fibers per square centimeter
questions.why: Cortical territory scales with the number of incoming lines, and densely innervated skin with small receptive fields needs many cortical neurons to keep those lines separate. Movement frequency belongs to the motor homunculus rather than the sensory one, distance to the brain is irrelevant to allocation, and muscle mass predicts neither map. This is the same anatomy that gives the lips a two point threshold of a few millimeters.
questions.answerText: The lips send far more afferent fibers per square centimeter

questions.q: Put these structures in the order a vibration signal from the foot passes through them: medial lemniscus, gracile nucleus, postcentral gyrus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus.
options: Medial lemniscus, gracile nucleus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, postcentral gyrus
Gracile nucleus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, medial lemniscus, postcentral gyrus
Gracile nucleus, medial lemniscus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, postcentral gyrus
Ventral posterior lateral nucleus, gracile nucleus, medial lemniscus, postcentral gyrus
questions.why: The first order fiber ascends the dorsal column and synapses in the gracile nucleus in the medulla, the second order axon crosses and becomes the medial lemniscus, that tract ends in the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus, and the third order axon reaches the postcentral gyrus. Placing the medial lemniscus first ignores that the tract is made of second order axons. Putting the thalamus before the lemniscus or at the very start reverses the relay order.
questions.answerText: Gracile nucleus, medial lemniscus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, postcentral gyrus

questions.q: Pain fibers synapse in the dorsal horn as soon as they enter the cord, while fine touch fibers ascend for many segments first. What follows from that difference?
options: A cord lesion causes contralateral pain loss but ipsilateral touch loss
A cord lesion causes ipsilateral loss of both pain and touch below the level
A cord lesion causes contralateral loss of both pain and touch below the level
A cord lesion spares pain entirely, since it has already been relayed
questions.why: Because pain crosses at the level of entry, the fibers ascending on one side carry pain from the other side of the body, so damaging them takes pain from the opposite side. Touch fibers have not yet crossed, so damaging them takes touch from the same side. The split pattern is the whole diagnostic value of knowing where each pathway crosses, and relaying in the dorsal horn does not protect the pathway from a lesion higher up.
questions.answerText: A cord lesion causes contralateral pain loss but ipsilateral touch loss

questions.q: Compare the cortical representation of the hand with that of the trunk. Which is larger, and what does the size predict about acuity?
options: The trunk is larger, predicting a smaller two point threshold there
The hand is larger, predicting a much smaller two point threshold there
They are equal, since cortical area follows body surface area
The hand is larger, but two point thresholds are the same at both sites
questions.why: The hand occupies a disproportionate strip of the postcentral gyrus because it sends dense afferent input with small receptive fields, and that same anatomy produces a fingertip two point threshold of a few millimeters against several centimeters on the trunk. Cortical area follows innervation density rather than surface area, which is why the trunk gets so little despite being large. Cortical territory and acuity move together rather than independently.
questions.answerText: The hand is larger, predicting a much smaller two point threshold there

questions.q: A patient has a lesion of the right half of the spinal cord at T10. Below that level, what pattern of sensory loss should you predict?
options: Loss of all sensation on the right leg only
Loss of all sensation on the left leg only
Loss of vibration and fine touch on the right leg and loss of pain and temperature on the left leg
Loss of vibration and fine touch on the left leg and loss of pain and temperature on the right leg
questions.why: Dorsal column fibers from the right leg are still on the right side at T10, so cutting the right half takes fine touch and vibration from the right leg. Pain and temperature fibers from the left leg crossed near their entry and are ascending on the right, so the same cut takes those modalities from the left leg. Reversing the two sides is the common error, and it comes from forgetting that only one of the two pathways has already crossed at this level.
questions.answerText: Loss of vibration and fine touch on the right leg and loss of pain and temperature on the left leg

questions.q: A stroke damages the hand region of the right postcentral gyrus. What should the patient report?
options: Impaired touch and position sense in the right hand, with the left hand normal
Weakness of the right hand with normal sensation
Complete loss of pain sensation in both hands
Impaired touch and position sense in the left hand, with the right hand normal
questions.why: Third order axons from the right thalamus serve the right cortex, and the pathway carrying left hand information crossed long before, so a right cortical lesion produces a left sided sensory deficit. Weakness would follow damage to the precentral gyrus one gyrus forward, not to sensory cortex. Bilateral pain loss would require damage on both sides or at a midline structure, and cortical damage rarely abolishes pain awareness entirely.
questions.answerText: Impaired touch and position sense in the left hand, with the right hand normal

questions.q: A lesion is found in the left medial lemniscus in the pons. The dorsal columns and the postcentral gyrus are both intact. Which deficit follows?
options: Loss of fine touch and vibration on the right side of the body
Loss of fine touch and vibration on the left side of the body
Loss of pain and temperature on the left side of the body
No deficit, since the dorsal columns are intact
questions.why: The medial lemniscus is made of second order axons that have already crossed in the medulla, so the left lemniscus carries information from the right side of the body and a lesion there produces a right sided deficit. Intact dorsal columns only mean the signal reaches the medulla, and intact cortex only means the destination can still receive input, so neither rescues a break in the middle of the chain. Pain and temperature travel in the nearby spinothalamic tract and would be spared by a lesion confined to the lemniscus.
questions.answerText: Loss of fine touch and vibration on the right side of the body

questions.q: A violinist has practiced fingering with the left hand for twenty years. Recordings show that the cortical territory devoted to the left fingertips is larger than in a non musician. What does this show about the homunculus?
options: The homunculus is fixed at birth and the recording must be an artifact
Cortical territory is shaped by input and can change with sustained use
Practice increases receptor density, which is the only reason cortex expands
The left hemisphere grows overall, so every body region gains territory
questions.why: The map is allocated by input, and heavy, behaviorally important input over years strengthens and expands the cortical territory serving those fingers, which is why trained musicians show enlarged finger representations. A fixed map cannot account for reproducible findings like this one. Receptor density in adult skin does not increase with practice, and the expansion is specific to the trained fingers rather than a general growth of the hemisphere.
questions.answerText: Cortical territory is shaped by input and can change with sustained use

questions.q: Which fiber type carries fast pain?
options: Small myelinated A delta fibers
Unmyelinated C fibers
Large myelinated A beta fibers
Preganglionic autonomic B fibers
questions.why: A delta fibers are thin but myelinated, so they conduct at roughly 5 to 30 m/s and deliver the first, sharp signal from an injury. C fibers are unmyelinated and much slower, carrying slow pain. A beta fibers are the large touch and vibration fibers, and B fibers are autonomic, so neither carries pain at all.
questions.answerText: Small myelinated A delta fibers

questions.q: Which fiber type carries slow pain?
options: Large myelinated A alpha fibers
Small myelinated A delta fibers
Unmyelinated C fibers
Large myelinated A beta fibers
questions.why: C fibers have no myelin, conduct at about 0.5 to 2 m/s, and produce the dull, aching pain that follows an injury and lingers. A delta fibers carry the sharp first pain. A alpha fibers serve proprioception from muscle and A beta fibers serve touch, and both are far too fast and too large to be the slow pain line.
questions.answerText: Unmyelinated C fibers

questions.q: How would a patient describe fast pain?
options: Dull and hard to localize
Sharp and easy to localize
Burning and slow to build
Cramping and spread over a wide area
questions.why: Fast pain arrives on A delta fibers with relatively little convergence in the cord, so it is felt as a sharp prick at a definite spot, which is the sensation that makes a person pull the hand back. Dull, burning, and diffuse descriptions all belong to slow pain on C fibers. The two qualities often follow one another from the same injury, which is why a single stimulus can be felt twice.
questions.answerText: Sharp and easy to localize

questions.q: How would a patient describe slow pain?
options: Sharp and pinpointed to one spot
Brief and gone within a second
Felt only when the injured part is moved
Dull, aching or burning, and poorly localized
questions.why: Slow pain is carried by C fibers that converge heavily onto second order neurons, so the signal is smeared in space and the sensation is diffuse, aching, and persistent. Sharp and pinpointed describes fast pain on A delta fibers. Slow pain outlasts the stimulus rather than ending quickly, and it is present at rest rather than only on movement.
questions.answerText: Dull, aching or burning, and poorly localized

questions.q: What is referred pain?
options: Pain from an internal organ that is felt in a surface region of the body
Pain that spreads gradually to the surrounding skin as inflammation grows
Pain that persists after the injured tissue has fully healed
Pain that is felt on the side of the body opposite the injury
questions.why: Referred pain is a mislocalization: visceral afferents and somatic afferents converge on the same second order neurons, and the brain assigns the signal to the skin region it usually comes from. Spreading inflammation is a real process but it moves the actual source of the pain rather than misplacing it. Pain outlasting healing is chronic pain, and pain on the opposite side would indicate a central lesion.
questions.answerText: Pain from an internal organ that is felt in a surface region of the body

questions.q: What anatomical arrangement explains referred pain?
options: Visceral afferents cross the midline twice before reaching the thalamus
Visceral afferents travel in the dorsal columns rather than the spinothalamic tract
Visceral and somatic afferents converge onto the same second order neuron
Visceral afferents synapse directly in the thalamus with no spinal relay
questions.why: Because one dorsal horn neuron receives input from both the skin of a dermatome and a viscus that shares its spinal segment, activity on that neuron is ambiguous, and the brain interprets it according to the far more common source, which is skin. Visceral pain does travel in the spinothalamic system and does relay in the cord, so the other options misplace the pathway. The convergence itself, not the crossing pattern, is what produces the error.
questions.answerText: Visceral and somatic afferents converge onto the same second order neuron

questions.q: In the gate control theory, which afferent input closes the gate on pain transmission?
options: Additional C fiber input from the same region
Large diameter A beta touch fibers
Sympathetic postganglionic fibers
Second order spinothalamic axons
questions.why: Activity in large myelinated touch fibers excites inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, and those interneurons reduce transmission from nociceptive fibers to the projection neuron. More C fiber traffic opens the gate rather than closing it. Sympathetic fibers are motor to vessels and glands, and the spinothalamic axon is the output of the gate rather than an input to it.
questions.answerText: Large diameter A beta touch fibers

questions.q: Which of these are endogenous opioids?
options: Substance P, bradykinin, and histamine
Norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine
Glutamate, aspartate, and glycine
Endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins
questions.why: These three peptide families bind the same receptors that morphine binds and reduce pain transmission both in the dorsal horn and at higher levels. Substance P, bradykinin, and histamine work the other way, exciting or sensitizing nociceptors. Catecholamines and amino acid transmitters have many roles in the nervous system, but they are not the opioid peptides.
questions.answerText: Endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins

questions.q: Why is fast pain localized more precisely than slow pain?
options: A delta fibers have smaller receptive fields and less convergence
A delta fibers travel in the dorsal columns, which preserve fine detail
A delta fibers are more numerous than C fibers in every tissue
A delta fibers fire at higher frequencies, which improves localization
questions.why: Localization is a spatial code, so it depends on how narrow each line is and how much information is thrown away at the first synapse, and the A delta system keeps both tighter than the C fiber system. Both pain fiber types ascend in the spinothalamic tract, not the dorsal columns. C fibers actually outnumber A delta fibers in most tissues, and firing rate carries intensity rather than position.
questions.answerText: A delta fibers have smaller receptive fields and less convergence

questions.q: A person stubs a toe and immediately rubs it, which lessens the pain. What is the mechanism?
options: Rubbing warms the tissue and slows conduction in C fibers
Touch input on A beta fibers drives interneurons that close the gate
Rubbing releases endorphins from the skin into the local tissue
Rubbing physically shrinks the receptive fields of the nearby nociceptors
questions.why: Rubbing loads the large fiber touch system, and that traffic drives dorsal horn interneurons that inhibit transmission from nociceptors to the projection neuron, which is the everyday demonstration of gate control. A small change in skin temperature is not what does it. Endorphins act centrally rather than being released from skin, and receptive field size is anatomical and does not change with rubbing.
questions.answerText: Touch input on A beta fibers drives interneurons that close the gate

questions.q: During a heart attack, pain is often felt in the left arm and jaw rather than in the chest alone. Why?
options: The pain travels down the arm through the brachial plexus from the heart
Cardiac afferents cross to the left side and terminate in the arm area of cortex
Cardiac afferents converge with somatic afferents in the same spinal segments
Reduced cardiac output starves the arm muscles and causes them to ache
questions.why: Cardiac visceral afferents enter the cord around T1 to T5 and share second order neurons with skin and deep tissue of the left arm, shoulder, and jaw, so the brain refers the signal to the surface region it more often hears from. No nerve carries pain from the heart out into the arm. Cortical maps do not relabel a signal on their own, and arm muscle ischemia is not what makes the arm ache during a myocardial infarction.
questions.answerText: Cardiac afferents converge with somatic afferents in the same spinal segments

questions.q: An investigator gives naloxone, which blocks opioid receptors, before a painful test. Stress induced analgesia largely disappears. What does that show?
options: Pain fibers require opioid receptors in order to conduct at all
The dorsal horn gate depends entirely on large fiber touch input
Naloxone acts on the nociceptors in the skin to increase their firing
Endogenous opioids mediate a substantial part of that analgesia
questions.why: If blocking the receptors removes the effect, the effect was being produced by molecules acting at those receptors, which is a standard piece of pharmacological reasoning. Conduction in nociceptive fibers does not require opioid receptors and continues normally with naloxone present. Gate control by touch fibers is a separate mechanism that naloxone does not block, and naloxone works centrally rather than sensitizing skin receptors.
questions.answerText: Endogenous opioids mediate a substantial part of that analgesia

questions.q: A person steps on a sharp stone and feels a sharp pain almost immediately, then a dull ache about a second later. Why the delay between the two?
options: C fibers conduct much more slowly than A delta fibers
C fibers are activated only after inflammatory chemicals are released
The second pain travels a longer route through the brainstem
The thalamus deliberately delays the second signal to separate the two
questions.why: Both fiber types are activated by the same stone at the same instant, but unmyelinated C fibers conduct at around 1 m/s while myelinated A delta fibers conduct at ten or twenty times that, so from a foot the two arrivals are separated by about a second. Inflammatory chemicals do sensitize C fibers over minutes, but they are not needed for this first C fiber volley. Both pains share the spinothalamic route, and the thalamus does not insert delays.
questions.answerText: C fibers conduct much more slowly than A delta fibers

questions.q: Stimulating the periaqueductal gray in the midbrain produces analgesia. How does an event in the midbrain reduce a signal entering at the spinal cord?
options: It raises the threshold of the nociceptors in the skin directly
It blocks conduction in the spinothalamic tract at the level of the pons
It drives a descending pathway that inhibits transmission in the dorsal horn
It prevents the thalamus from relaying any sensory signal to cortex
questions.why: The periaqueductal gray projects through the raphe nuclei to the dorsal horn, where released serotonin and enkephalin reduce transmitter release from nociceptive terminals and quiet the projection neuron, so the message is turned down at the first synapse. Central structures cannot reach out and change the threshold of a skin receptor. Nothing blocks the ascending tract in the pons, and thalamic relay of other modalities continues normally, since the analgesia is specific to pain.
questions.answerText: It drives a descending pathway that inhibits transmission in the dorsal horn

questions.q: A patient has a neuropathy that has destroyed most A delta fibers in one leg while sparing C fibers. Predict what happens when that leg is pricked with a pin.
options: Neither the sharp pain nor the dull ache is felt
The sharp first pain is missing, but a delayed dull ache still develops
The sharp pain is felt normally, but no ache follows
Both pains are felt, but each arrives about a second later than normal
questions.why: A delta fibers carry the fast, sharp component and C fibers carry the slow, aching one, so losing one population removes one sensation and leaves the other intact. Total loss would require both populations to be gone. The sharp pain cannot be normal when its fibers are destroyed, and a uniform delay in both would suggest a general slowing rather than the selective loss described.
questions.answerText: The sharp first pain is missing, but a delayed dull ache still develops

questions.q: A transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulator delivers a buzzing sensation over a painful area and reduces the pain while it runs. Which explanation fits the physiology?
options: It fatigues the nociceptors in the skin until they stop transducing
It blocks conduction in C fibers by depolarizing them to inactivation
It stimulates the periaqueductal gray directly through the skin
It recruits large A beta fibers, whose input closes the dorsal horn gate
questions.why: Large myelinated fibers have the lowest electrical threshold, so a mild current recruits touch fibers first, which is why the sensation is a buzz rather than pain, and that touch traffic drives the inhibitory interneurons of the gate. Nociceptors do not fatigue in the way described, and a stimulus strong enough to inactivate C fibers would be intensely painful itself. Surface electrodes cannot reach a midbrain structure, though descending systems may add to the effect indirectly.
questions.answerText: It recruits large A beta fibers, whose input closes the dorsal horn gate

questions.q: After abdominal surgery, blood under the diaphragm irritates it and the patient reports pain at the top of the right shoulder. Work back from the finding to the mechanism.
options: Phrenic afferents enter at C3 to C5 and converge with shoulder afferents
Blood tracks up through the tissue planes and collects in the shoulder joint
The diaphragm and the shoulder share a single peripheral nerve trunk
Pain from the abdomen always refers upward because the spinothalamic tract ascends
questions.why: The diaphragm keeps the cervical innervation it had in the embryo, so its afferents arrive at spinal segments C3 to C5 and share second order neurons with the skin over the shoulder, and the brain assigns the signal to the shoulder. Blood does not travel to the shoulder joint, and the phrenic nerve is not shared with the shoulder skin, which is supplied by supraclavicular nerves from the same segments. Referral follows shared segments, not a general upward direction.
questions.answerText: Phrenic afferents enter at C3 to C5 and converge with shoulder afferents

questions.q: A soldier with a serious leg wound continues to move to safety and reports almost no pain until an hour later. Which combination of mechanisms best explains this?
options: The nociceptors adapted quickly, so they stopped firing after the injury
Descending inhibition and endogenous opioids reduce dorsal horn transmission
The A delta and C fibers were severed, so no signal reached the cord
The thalamus stopped relaying all somatosensory input during the emergency itself
questions.why: Under extreme stress the periaqueductal gray and raphe system drive inhibition of the first pain synapse and opioid peptides are released, which turns the signal down before it ever ascends, and the pain returns as that drive falls off. Nociceptors adapt poorly, so peripheral adaptation cannot account for an hour of relief. Severed fibers would produce permanent numbness rather than delayed pain, and touch and position sense are unaffected, so a global thalamic shutdown is ruled out.
questions.answerText: Descending inhibition and endogenous opioids reduce dorsal horn transmission

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure two point discrimination in the lab?
options: A tuning fork of known frequency
A two point caliper with an attached millimeter scale
A monofilament of calibrated bending force applied to the skin
A thermode set to a fixed temperature
questions.why: Two point discrimination is a distance measurement, so the tool must present two contacts a known number of millimeters apart, which is what the caliper or aesthesiometer does. A tuning fork tests vibration sense and a monofilament tests the force threshold for light touch, both useful but neither spatial. A thermode tests thermal thresholds and has nothing to do with spatial resolution.
questions.answerText: A two point caliper with an attached millimeter scale

questions.q: In a two point discrimination trial, what value is recorded as the threshold for that site?
options: The smallest separation at which the subject reliably reports two points
The largest separation at which the subject still reports one point
The average of all separations tested at that site
The separation at which the subject first feels any contact at all
questions.why: The threshold is the boundary between one and two, and by convention it is reported as the smallest distance that is reliably resolved as two. The largest distance felt as one sits just below that boundary and is a different number. Averaging every separation tested measures nothing in particular, and the distance at which contact is first felt is a force threshold rather than a spatial one.
questions.answerText: The smallest separation at which the subject reliably reports two points

questions.q: Why are trials with only one caliper point randomly mixed into the series?
options: To let the skin recover between two point trials
To measure the subject's reaction time as a second dependent variable
To check that the subject is discriminating rather than guessing
To calibrate the caliper against a known separation
questions.why: A subject who says two on every trial will appear to have superb acuity unless the protocol can catch it, and single point catch trials do exactly that. Recovery time is handled by pacing the trials, not by changing the stimulus. Reaction time is not part of this measurement, and the caliper is calibrated against its own scale rather than against the subject.
questions.answerText: To check that the subject is discriminating rather than guessing

questions.q: Why must both caliper points contact the skin at the same instant and with equal pressure?
options: Unequal pressure damages the receptors and raises the threshold permanently
Simultaneous contact is needed for the signals to reach the cortex together
Equal pressure keeps the caliper from bending and changing its separation
Staggered or unequal contact gives the subject a cue other than location
questions.why: The test is meant to isolate spatial resolution, so any other cue that reveals the presence of two contacts, such as one landing first or pressing harder, invalidates the measurement. Light caliper pressure does not damage receptors. Cortical arrival timing is not the issue, and a rigid caliper does not deform under the light forces used.
questions.answerText: Staggered or unequal contact gives the subject a cue other than location

questions.q: In the coin demonstration of adaptation, what does the subject report?
options: The sensation of the coin grows stronger as the skin warms
The sensation of the coin fades within a minute although it has not moved
The coin feels heavier the longer it rests on the skin
The coin is felt in a location a few centimeters away from where it rests
questions.why: Rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors stop firing during a steady, unchanging pressure, so the CNS receives no continuing touch signal and the coin drops out of awareness. A growing or heavier sensation would mean sensitization rather than adaptation. Mislocalization to a distant site describes referred sensation, which is a separate demonstration in this lab.
questions.answerText: The sensation of the coin fades within a minute although it has not moved

questions.q: In the lab demonstration of referred sensation, tapping the ulnar nerve where it crosses the elbow produces a sensation felt where?
options: In the little finger and the ring finger
At the elbow itself, where the tap was applied
In the thumb and the index finger
Diffusely over the whole forearm
questions.why: The ulnar nerve carries afferents from the medial hand, and stimulating those fibers anywhere along their length sends traffic on lines labeled for the little and ring fingers, so that is where the tingle is felt. Feeling it at the elbow would require the brain to track where along the axon the stimulus occurred, which it cannot do. The thumb and index finger are served by the median nerve, and the sensation is felt in a defined territory rather than diffusely.
questions.answerText: In the little finger and the ring finger

questions.q: Why does the subject keep their eyes closed throughout the two point testing?
options: Vision raises the firing rate of touch afferents
Closed eyes reduce the subject's overall skin temperature
Vision activates the same cortical region as touch
Seeing the caliper would let the subject infer the answer
questions.why: The measurement is a report of what the skin resolves, so any visual cue about how far apart the points are turns the trial into an inference rather than a discrimination. Vision does not change afferent firing or skin temperature. Visual and somatosensory cortex are distinct regions, so cortical overlap is not the concern here.
questions.answerText: Seeing the caliper would let the subject infer the answer

questions.q: In the adaptation demonstration, what quantity is actually recorded?
options: The mass of the object placed on the skin
The distance over which the sensation spreads across the skin
The time from placement until the sensation disappears
The number of receptors under the object
questions.why: Adaptation is a change over time, so the measured variable is how long the sensation persists before it fades, and comparing that time across sites or objects is what makes the demonstration quantitative. Mass is an independent variable the experimenter sets rather than the outcome. Spread of sensation and receptor counts cannot be measured with the equipment available in this lab.
questions.answerText: The time from placement until the sensation disappears

questions.q: A subject reports two points on every trial, including the single point catch trials. What should you conclude?
options: The data are unusable until the trials are repeated with better instruction
The subject has unusually fine acuity at that site
The caliper must be out of calibration, since the points read too far apart
The subject's receptive fields at that site are unusually small
questions.why: Catch trials exist to detect exactly this pattern, and failing them means the responses are not tracking the stimulus, so any threshold computed from them is meaningless. Fine acuity would show up as correct discrimination at small separations along with correct single point reports. A caliper error would not make single points feel double, and small receptive fields cannot produce two sensations from one contact.
questions.answerText: The data are unusable until the trials are repeated with better instruction

questions.q: Your group measures two point thresholds at the fingertip, the palm, the forearm, and the upper back. What order of thresholds should you predict from smallest to largest?
options: Upper back, forearm, palm, fingertip
Fingertip, palm, forearm, upper back
Palm, fingertip, upper back, forearm
Forearm, palm, fingertip, upper back
questions.why: Threshold tracks receptor density and receptive field size, and those grade steadily from the densely innervated fingertip through the palm and forearm to the sparsely innervated back. The reversed order would put the coarsest surface first. Placing the palm ahead of the fingertip or the forearm last contradicts the innervation density of those sites, and the predicted ranking is what the lab data should reproduce.
questions.answerText: Fingertip, palm, forearm, upper back

questions.q: A student presses one caliper point noticeably harder than the other. How does that bias the measured threshold?
options: It makes the threshold appear larger, because the harder point masks the lighter one
It leaves the threshold unchanged, since only separation matters
It makes the threshold unmeasurable, because the skin will be damaged
It makes the threshold appear smaller, because the difference in pressure is an extra cue
questions.why: Two contacts of different strength feel different from a single contact even when both fall inside one receptive field, so the subject can call two at separations the skin cannot actually resolve and the threshold looks better than it is. Masking is not what happens, since both points are suprathreshold for detection. Separation is not the only thing the subject can use, which is the whole reason the protocol controls pressure, and the light forces involved cause no damage.
questions.answerText: It makes the threshold appear smaller, because the difference in pressure is an extra cue

questions.q: A coin on the forearm has stopped being felt. A second coin is stacked on top of it and the sensation returns. Why?
options: The second coin covers additional skin containing unadapted receptors
Adding weight changes the stimulus, and phasic receptors report change
The receptors under the first coin have finished recovering by then anyway
The added weight recruits nociceptors, which do not adapt
questions.why: Phasic receptors report transitions, so any change in the load, including an increase, produces a fresh burst of firing and a fresh sensation, which then fades again. The second coin sits on the first and covers roughly the same skin, so new territory is not the explanation. The adapted receptors have not recovered while the stimulus is still present, and the weight of a coin is nowhere near a noxious level.
questions.answerText: Adding weight changes the stimulus, and phasic receptors report change

questions.q: The ulnar nerve tap makes the little finger tingle even though nothing touched the finger. Which principle does the demonstration confirm?
options: The labeled line principle, since sensation follows which fibers fire
Lateral inhibition, since the fingers on either side feel nothing at all
Adaptation, since the tingle fades quickly after the tap
Population coding, since many fibers are stimulated at once
questions.why: The stimulus is applied at the elbow and the sensation appears in the hand because those axons terminate centrally at the hand region of the map, which is the labeled line principle in its purest experimental form. Lateral inhibition sharpens borders and does not explain the mislocalization. The fading afterward and the number of fibers recruited are real but incidental to what this demonstration shows.
questions.answerText: The labeled line principle, since sensation follows which fibers fire

questions.q: A student records a two point threshold of 40 mm at the index fingertip. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The subject has an unusually dense fingertip innervation
A procedural error, since fingertip thresholds are only a few mm
The caliper was held perpendicular to the skin instead of at an angle
The subject adapted to the stimulus during the trial
questions.why: A value ten to twenty times the expected fingertip threshold points to how the measurement was made, most often the subject peeking, the points landing on the nail or on separate segments, or the series starting far too wide and never narrowing. Dense innervation would lower the number, not raise it. Perpendicular contact is the correct technique, and adaptation over a brief trial does not shift a spatial threshold this far.
questions.answerText: A procedural error, since fingertip thresholds are only a few mm

questions.q: Why is each site tested several times rather than once, with the results averaged?
options: Repeated testing gradually lowers the threshold through practice
Repeated testing warms the skin and improves receptor function
Repeated testing is needed to fully adapt the receptors before measuring
Single trials are noisy, and averaging reduces the effect of a guess
questions.why: A two point judgment near threshold is probabilistic, so any one trial may land either way, and several trials give a more stable estimate of where the boundary actually sits. Practice effects and skin warming are confounds to be avoided rather than reasons to repeat. Deliberately adapting the receptors before measuring would corrupt the measurement, since adapted receptors report less.
questions.answerText: Single trials are noisy, and averaging reduces the effect of a guess

questions.q: A lab group reports these thresholds: fingertip 3 mm, palm 11 mm, forearm 38 mm, back 52 mm. What can they conclude about receptive fields and cortical territory across the four sites?
options: Receptive fields grow from fingertip to back, and cortical territory per unit of skin grows with them
Receptive fields shrink from fingertip to back, while cortical territory per unit of skin grows
Receptive fields grow from fingertip to back, while cortical territory per unit of skin falls
Receptive fields are the same at all four sites, and only cortical territory differs
questions.why: A rising threshold means larger, more overlapping receptive fields, and fewer separate lines coming from a given area of skin means less cortex is needed to keep them apart, so the two measures move in opposite directions across the four sites. Fields and cortical territory cannot both grow, since dense innervation is what produces both small fields and a large cortical strip. Equal fields could not produce a seventeenfold spread in threshold.
questions.answerText: Receptive fields grow from fingertip to back, while cortical territory per unit of skin falls

questions.q: A classmate says the coin sensation faded only because the subject got bored and stopped paying attention. How would you modify the demonstration to test that claim?
options: Slide the coin slightly at a random moment and see whether sensation returns
Ask the subject to concentrate harder on the coin for the whole trial period
Repeat the trial with a heavier coin and time the fade again
Test a second subject and compare their fade times
questions.why: If attention were the explanation, moving the coin should change nothing, but if peripheral adaptation is the explanation, any change in the stimulus reactivates the phasic receptors and the sensation snaps back at once, which separates the two accounts cleanly. Instructing the subject to concentrate cannot be verified and does not distinguish the hypotheses. A heavier coin or a second subject changes the conditions without addressing whether the fade is peripheral or central.
questions.answerText: Slide the coin slightly at a random moment and see whether sensation returns

questions.q: A group reports identical two point thresholds of 25 mm at the fingertip and the palm. Which methodological error best explains this result?
options: The subject's eyes were closed, hiding the caliper from view
The caliper points were applied simultaneously and with equal pressure
Single point catch trials were included in the series
The series never narrowed below 25 mm, so the true threshold was missed
questions.why: A fingertip threshold near 3 mm can only be found by testing separations down in that range, and a series that stops at 25 mm will return 25 mm for any site whose true threshold is smaller, flattening the real differences. Closed eyes, simultaneous equal pressure, and catch trials are all correct procedure and would improve the data rather than distort it. When two very different sites give the same number, suspect a floor in the protocol before suspecting the physiology.
questions.answerText: The series never narrowed below 25 mm, so the true threshold was missed

questions.q: You want to show that a referred sensation really comes from stimulating the nerve trunk and not from the skin over the elbow. What control belongs in the design?
options: Tap the ulnar nerve harder and record whether the tingle grows
Tap nearby skin away from the nerve with equal force and note where it is felt
Tap the little finger directly and record whether it is felt there
Repeat the tap after the subject has adapted to a coin resting on the forearm skin
questions.why: The control has to hold the stimulus constant and change only whether the nerve trunk is under the point of contact, so an equally firm tap on nearby skin should be felt locally at the elbow if the nerve is what produces the referral. Tapping harder varies intensity rather than testing the hypothesis. Tapping the finger tests nothing that is in doubt, and an unrelated adaptation trial does not bear on where the sensation is assigned.
questions.answerText: Tap nearby skin away from the nerve with equal force and note where it is felt

questions.q: Which part of the eye does most of the bending of incoming light?
options: The vitreous humor
The lens
The cornea
The aqueous humor
questions.why: Light passes from air into the cornea, and that is the largest jump in refractive index anywhere in the eye, so the cornea supplies roughly two thirds of the total refractive power. The lens supplies the rest, and it matters because it is the part that can change shape, but its power is smaller. The vitreous humor and the aqueous humor have refractive indexes close to the tissues around them, so light passes through them with very little bending.
questions.answerText: The cornea

questions.q: Which muscle contracts so that the lens can round up for near vision?
options: The ciliary muscle
The sphincter pupillae
The dilator pupillae
The levator palpebrae superioris
questions.why: The ciliary muscle is a ring of smooth muscle, and when it contracts the ring narrows, which slackens the zonular fibers and lets the elastic lens spring into a rounder shape. The sphincter pupillae narrows the pupil during the near response but does not change lens shape. The dilator pupillae widens the pupil under sympathetic drive. The levator palpebrae raises the eyelid and has nothing to do with focusing.
questions.answerText: The ciliary muscle

questions.q: During accommodation for a near object, how does the lens change?
options: It flattens and loses refractive power
It becomes more rounded and gains refractive power
It slides backward toward the retina
It stays the same shape while the cornea steepens
questions.why: A rounder lens has more sharply curved surfaces, so it bends light more strongly, which is exactly what the diverging rays from a near object need. Flattening is what happens for distance vision, when the ciliary muscle relaxes. The human lens does not move forward or backward to focus, unlike a camera lens. The cornea has a fixed curvature and does not participate in accommodation.
questions.answerText: It becomes more rounded and gains refractive power

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that drive accommodation and pupillary constriction?
options: The oculomotor nerve, CN III
The trochlear nerve, CN IV
The abducens nerve, CN VI
The optic nerve, CN II
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibers travel with CN III, synapse in the ciliary ganglion, and innervate both the ciliary muscle and the sphincter pupillae. CN II is purely sensory and carries the incoming light signal, so it is the afferent limb rather than the motor output. CN IV and CN VI each move one extraocular muscle and carry no parasympathetic fibers to the inside of the eye.
questions.answerText: The oculomotor nerve, CN III

questions.q: Which autonomic division constricts the pupil, and which muscle does it act on?
options: Sympathetic, acting on the radial dilator muscle
Parasympathetic, acting on the circular sphincter muscle
Sympathetic, acting on the ciliary muscle
Parasympathetic, acting on the radial dilator muscle
questions.why: The iris has two muscle layers with opposite geometry, and the circular sphincter is the parasympathetic one, so when it shortens the pupil narrows. The sympathetic division acts on the radial dilator, whose fibers run like spokes, so shortening them pulls the pupil open. The ciliary muscle is parasympathetic but it shapes the lens rather than the pupil, and no autonomic division pairs the parasympathetic supply with the radial muscle.
questions.answerText: Parasympathetic, acting on the circular sphincter muscle

questions.q: What is the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
options: The oculomotor nerve
The trigeminal nerve
The ciliary ganglion
The optic nerve
questions.why: Light striking the retina is signaled to the midbrain over ganglion cell axons in the optic nerve, so CN II is the sensory arm of the reflex. The oculomotor nerve is the motor arm that carries the constriction command back to the iris. The trigeminal nerve carries corneal sensation, which drives the blink reflex rather than the light reflex. The ciliary ganglion sits on the motor side, where the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers synapse.
questions.answerText: The optic nerve

questions.q: Which three changes make up the near response?
options: Accommodation, convergence, and corneal flattening
Accommodation, divergence, and pupillary dilation
Corneal steepening, convergence, and pupillary dilation
Accommodation, convergence, and pupillary constriction
questions.why: Looking at something close requires more lens power, both eyes turned inward so the images land on corresponding retinal points, and a smaller pupil to sharpen the image. Divergence and pupillary dilation belong to the shift back toward distance viewing. The cornea does not change curvature in either direction, so any option built on corneal steepening or flattening describes something the eye cannot do.
questions.answerText: Accommodation, convergence, and pupillary constriction

questions.q: What unit expresses the refractive power of a lens?
options: The lumen
The millimeter of mercury
The decibel
The diopter
questions.why: Refractive power in diopters is the reciprocal of the focal length in meters, so a lens that focuses at 0.5 m has a power of 2 diopters. The lumen measures light output, which is about the source rather than the bending of rays. Millimeters of mercury measure pressure, including intraocular pressure, and decibels measure sound intensity.
questions.answerText: The diopter

questions.q: A student looks up from a distant clock to a book held 25 cm away. What happens to the tension on the zonular fibers?
options: It rises, because the ciliary muscle relaxes and the ciliary ring widens
It rises, because the ciliary muscle contracts and pulls the fibers tight
It does not change, because the zonular fibers are rigid
It falls, because the ciliary muscle contracts and the ciliary ring narrows
questions.why: The ciliary muscle is arranged as a ring around the lens, so contraction makes the ring smaller and moves the attachment points closer to the lens, which slackens the zonules and lets the lens round up. Rising tension with a relaxing muscle describes what happens on the way back to distance viewing. The idea that contraction tightens the fibers is the most common error here, because it assumes a muscle pulling on a rope rather than a sphincter closing down. The zonules are flexible and their tension changes constantly.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the ciliary muscle contracts and the ciliary ring narrows

questions.q: A light is shone into the right eye only. What happens to the left pupil?
options: It constricts, because of the consensual reflex
It dilates, because that eye is still in relative darkness
It does not change, because each optic nerve drives only its own eye
It constricts only if the light is moved to the left eye as well
questions.why: Signals from one optic nerve reach the pretectal area and then both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so a light in one eye constricts both pupils. That crossed connection is the whole point of testing the direct and consensual responses separately. The idea that each eye works alone would predict no consensual response at all, and dilation of the unlit eye would require sympathetic drive that the reflex does not produce.
questions.answerText: It constricts, because of the consensual reflex

questions.q: Eye drops that block muscarinic receptors are placed in one eye. What happens to near vision in that eye?
options: Near vision blurs, because the ciliary muscle cannot contract
Near vision is unchanged, because accommodation is sympathetic
Near vision sharpens, because the lens rounds up further
Distance vision blurs, because the lens is locked in a rounded shape
questions.why: Ciliary muscle contraction depends on acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors, so blocking those receptors leaves the muscle relaxed, the zonules taut, and the lens flat. A flat lens is set for distance, so far vision stays clear while near vision goes soft. Accommodation is parasympathetic, not sympathetic, and a lens locked in the rounded shape would be the result of a muscarinic agonist instead.
questions.answerText: Near vision blurs, because the ciliary muscle cannot contract

questions.q: In dim light the pupil dilates. What happens to the depth of focus?
options: It decreases, because a wide pupil admits more peripheral rays
It increases, because a wide pupil narrows the cone of light entering the eye
It is unchanged, because depth of focus depends only on lens power
It increases, because more light reaching the retina sharpens the image
questions.why: A wide pupil lets in rays that strike the lens far from its center, and those rays converge over a wider spread of distances, so only a narrow band of object distances stays sharp. A small pupil does the opposite and acts like the small aperture on a camera. Total light and lens power both change the image, but neither one is what sets depth of focus, which is governed by aperture size.
questions.answerText: It decreases, because a wide pupil admits more peripheral rays

questions.q: A surgeon flattens the central cornea. What happens to the refractive power of the eye and to the focal point?
options: Power falls and the focal point moves forward, in front of the retina
Power rises and the focal point moves forward, away from the retina
Power falls and the focal point moves backward, toward the retina
Power rises and the focal point moves backward, behind the retina
questions.why: A flatter surface bends light less, so refractive power drops and the rays converge farther back inside the eye. That is why flattening the cornea corrects myopia, where the image was landing in front of the retina. The pairings that raise power with a backward shift, or lower power with a forward shift, reverse the relationship between power and focal length, which are inversely related.
questions.answerText: Power falls and the focal point moves backward, toward the retina

questions.q: A frightened person's pupils widen. Which muscle and which transmitter produced this?
options: The circular sphincter pupillae, with acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors
The ciliary muscle, with acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors
The radial dilator pupillae, with norepinephrine on alpha receptors
The circular sphincter pupillae, with norepinephrine on alpha receptors
questions.why: Fear raises sympathetic outflow, and sympathetic postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto alpha receptors of the radial dilator muscle, which pulls the pupil open. Acetylcholine on the sphincter would narrow the pupil instead. Acetylcholine on the ciliary muscle changes lens shape rather than pupil size. Pairing norepinephrine with the sphincter mixes the transmitter of one pathway with the muscle of the other.
questions.answerText: The radial dilator pupillae, with norepinephrine on alpha receptors

questions.q: An object is moved from 6 m away to 30 cm away. What must happen to the refractive power of the eye for the image to stay on the retina?
options: It must fall, because near objects need less bending
It must stay the same, because the cornea does all of the focusing
It must rise, because rays from a near object arrive diverging
It must fall, because the eyeball lengthens during near work
questions.why: Rays from a distant object arrive nearly parallel, but rays from a near object are still spreading when they reach the eye, so more bending is needed to bring them to a point on the retina. That extra power comes from the lens rounding up. The cornea does most of the baseline focusing but cannot change, and the eyeball does not change length from moment to moment.
questions.answerText: It must rise, because rays from a near object arrive diverging

questions.q: A swimmer with normal eyes opens them underwater without goggles and everything looks badly blurred. What explains this?
options: Water and cornea have almost the same refractive index, so the cornea loses its power
Water keeps the ciliary muscle from contracting, so accommodation fails
Water raises corneal refractive power beyond what the lens can offset
Water clouds the aqueous humor and scatters the light before it reaches the photoreceptors
questions.why: Bending happens at an interface only when the two media differ in refractive index, and water is close enough to corneal tissue that the largest refracting surface in the eye stops working. The lens alone cannot supply the missing two thirds of the power, so images focus far behind the retina. Goggles restore an air interface in front of the cornea, which is why they fix the problem instantly. Water does not touch ciliary muscle function or the clarity of the aqueous humor, which sits behind the cornea.
questions.answerText: Water and cornea have almost the same refractive index, so the cornea loses its power

questions.q: Shining a light in the right eye constricts both pupils. Shining the same light in the left eye constricts neither pupil. Where is the lesion?
options: The left optic nerve, the afferent limb from that eye
The left oculomotor nerve, the efferent limb to that eye
The right optic nerve, the afferent limb from that eye
The right oculomotor nerve, the efferent limb to that eye
questions.why: Because light in the right eye constricts both pupils, both motor limbs and both iris muscles must be working, so the problem has to be on the sensory side. Since light in the left eye produces nothing at all, the signal is never leaving that eye, which places the lesion in the left optic nerve. A left CN III lesion would leave the left pupil fixed even when the right eye is lit, which is not what happened. A right optic nerve lesion would abolish the response to right sided light, and a right CN III lesion would leave the right pupil fixed.
questions.answerText: The left optic nerve, the afferent limb from that eye

questions.q: In an older adult the lens has hardened and can no longer round up, although the ciliary muscle still contracts normally. When this person looks at a near object, what happens?
options: Refractive power stays near its distance value and the near image falls behind the retina
Refractive power rises normally and the near image falls on the retina
Refractive power drops below its distance value and the near image falls in front of the retina
Refractive power rises too far and the near image falls in front of the retina
questions.why: Ciliary contraction only slackens the zonules, so the shape change depends on the elasticity of the lens itself, and a stiff lens stays flat no matter how hard the muscle works. With power stuck at the distance setting, the strongly diverging rays from a near object are still converging when they pass the retina, so the focal point lands behind it and near print blurs. Power cannot fall below the resting value, because nothing pulls the lens flatter than the fully tensed zonules do. Excess power with a focal point in front of the retina describes myopia, which is the opposite problem.
questions.answerText: Refractive power stays near its distance value and the near image falls behind the retina

questions.q: A drug that stimulates muscarinic receptors is placed in the eye. Trace its effect on the ciliary muscle, the lens, and the focus of the eye.
options: The ciliary muscle relaxes, the lens flattens, and the eye is set for distance
The ciliary muscle contracts, the lens rounds, and the eye is locked in near focus
The ciliary muscle relaxes, the lens rounds, and the eye is set for near
The ciliary muscle contracts, the lens flattens, and the eye is set for distance
questions.why: A muscarinic agonist mimics the parasympathetic input, so the ciliary ring contracts, the zonules slacken, the elastic lens rounds up, and refractive power rises to its near setting and stays there. Distance objects then focus in front of the retina and look blurred, which patients describe as an induced nearsightedness. The two options that pair contraction with flattening or relaxation with rounding break the link between zonular tension and lens shape, and full relaxation with distance focus is what a muscarinic blocker would produce.
questions.answerText: The ciliary muscle contracts, the lens rounds, and the eye is locked in near focus

questions.q: Which molecule inside a rod actually absorbs the photon?
options: Retinal
Opsin
Transducin
Guanylyl cyclase
questions.why: Retinal is the light absorbing chromophore, a derivative of vitamin A, and its shape change is the only step in vision that light itself performs. Opsin is the protein that holds retinal and shapes which wavelengths it absorbs best, but opsin alone does not capture the photon. Transducin is the G protein activated afterward, and guanylyl cyclase is the enzyme that rebuilds cyclic GMP during recovery.
questions.answerText: Retinal

questions.q: What two parts make up rhodopsin?
options: The protein opsin plus all-trans retinal
The protein transducin plus cyclic GMP
The protein opsin plus 11-cis retinal
The enzyme phosphodiesterase plus 11-cis retinal
questions.why: Rhodopsin is a G protein coupled receptor, opsin, with 11-cis retinal bound in its core as a built in ligand waiting to be changed by light. All-trans retinal is the product formed after a photon is absorbed, and once it forms, the pigment is bleached rather than resting. Transducin and phosphodiesterase are downstream signaling proteins, not components of the pigment itself.
questions.answerText: The protein opsin plus 11-cis retinal

questions.q: What happens to retinal when it absorbs a photon?
options: It is phosphorylated and released from the disc membrane
It isomerizes from the all-trans form to the 11-cis form
It isomerizes from the 11-cis form to the all-trans form
It binds a molecule of cyclic GMP and changes charge
questions.why: The photon straightens a bend in the retinal molecule, converting 11-cis to all-trans, and that new shape forces a conformational change in the surrounding opsin that activates it. The reverse conversion, all-trans back to 11-cis, happens later in the pigment epithelium during regeneration and requires energy rather than light. Retinal is not phosphorylated by the photon, and it never binds cyclic GMP.
questions.answerText: It isomerizes from the 11-cis form to the all-trans form

questions.q: Which G protein does activated rhodopsin turn on?
options: Gustducin
Transducin
Golf
Calmodulin
questions.why: Transducin is the retina specific G protein, and activated rhodopsin loads it with GTP so that its alpha subunit can go on to switch on phosphodiesterase. Gustducin does the same kind of job in taste receptor cells for bitter, sweet, and umami. Golf serves olfactory receptor neurons. Calmodulin is a calcium binding protein, not a G protein at all.
questions.answerText: Transducin

questions.q: What does the phosphodiesterase activated during phototransduction do?
options: It synthesizes cyclic GMP from GTP
It breaks down cyclic GMP
It phosphorylates the cation channel
It converts all-trans retinal back to 11-cis retinal
questions.why: Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cyclic GMP to 5 prime GMP, which drops the concentration of the messenger that was holding the cation channels open. Building cyclic GMP from GTP is the job of guanylyl cyclase, the opposing enzyme that restores the resting state. The channel is gated by cyclic GMP binding directly, not by phosphorylation, and regeneration of 11-cis retinal happens in the pigment epithelium through separate enzymes.
questions.answerText: It breaks down cyclic GMP

questions.q: When light strikes a photoreceptor, which way does the cyclic GMP concentration go?
options: It falls
It rises
It rises briefly and then returns to the dark level
It does not change, because cyclic AMP carries the signal instead
questions.why: Light activates phosphodiesterase, so cyclic GMP is destroyed faster than it is made and its concentration drops. That fall is the core of the whole cascade, because the cation channels only stay open while cyclic GMP is bound to them.
