A rise in cyclic GMP is what happens in the dark and during recovery after the light goes off. Cyclic AMP is the messenger in olfactory receptor neurons, not in photoreceptors.
questions.answerText: It falls

questions.q: How does the membrane potential of a photoreceptor respond to light?
options: It depolarizes to threshold and fires an action potential
It stays constant while the firing rate rises
It depolarizes without firing an action potential
It hyperpolarizes
questions.why: Light closes the cyclic GMP gated cation channels, which removes a steady inward positive current, so the inside of the cell becomes more negative. This is the single most counterintuitive fact in the visual system, because every other sensory receptor you have studied depolarizes to its stimulus. Photoreceptors also do not fire action potentials at all, so any answer built on threshold or firing rate misdescribes how they signal.
questions.answerText: It hyperpolarizes

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter do photoreceptors release onto bipolar cells?
options: GABA
Glutamate
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
questions.why: Photoreceptors release glutamate continuously in the dark and release less of it in the light, so the message the retina sends inward is written in changes to a steady glutamate stream. GABA and dopamine are used by amacrine and horizontal cells for lateral processing within the retina, not by photoreceptors. Acetylcholine appears at neuromuscular junctions and in autonomic ganglia rather than at the photoreceptor terminal.
questions.answerText: Glutamate

questions.q: In complete darkness, what is happening at the cyclic GMP gated channels of a rod?
options: Cyclic GMP is high, the channels are open, and Na+ and Ca2+ flow in
Cyclic GMP is low, the channels are closed, and no current flows
Cyclic GMP is high, the channels are open, and K+ flows out
Cyclic GMP is low, the channels are open, and Cl- flows in
questions.why: With no light there is nothing to activate phosphodiesterase, so cyclic GMP stays high, holds the channels open, and lets a steady inward flow of Na+ and Ca2+ called the dark current keep the cell near minus 40 mV. That is a depolarized resting state compared with most neurons. Low cyclic GMP with closed channels describes the illuminated cell instead. The channels are cation channels, so they do not carry outward K+ or inward Cl- as their main current.
questions.answerText: Cyclic GMP is high, the channels are open, and Na+ and Ca2+ flow in

questions.q: Cyclic GMP falls inside a cone. What happens to the cation channels in its outer segment?
options: They open wider, because cyclic GMP normally blocks them
They close, because cyclic GMP must stay bound to hold them open
They stay open, because the channels are voltage gated rather than ligand gated
They close, but only after the cell has fired an action potential
questions.why: These channels are ligand gated from the inside, and cyclic GMP is the ligand that props them open, so losing the ligand lets them shut. Treating cyclic GMP as a blocker reverses the logic and would predict depolarization to light. The channels are not voltage gated, which is why the response is graded with light intensity. Photoreceptors never fire action potentials, so nothing about channel closure waits on a spike.
questions.answerText: They close, because cyclic GMP must stay bound to hold them open

questions.q: A steady light is turned on over a rod. What happens to the amount of glutamate released from its terminal?
options: It increases, because the cell is more strongly stimulated
It increases, because closing cation channels traps Ca2+ inside the terminal
It stays the same, because release is independent of membrane potential
It decreases, because hyperpolarization reduces Ca2+ entry at the terminal
questions.why: Release from the photoreceptor terminal depends on voltage gated Ca2+ channels, and hyperpolarization closes them, so less Ca2+ enters and fewer vesicles fuse. The intuitive answer, that a stimulated cell releases more transmitter, is exactly the trap this system sets, because in vision the stimulus reduces output. Release is strictly voltage dependent through Ca2+, and closing the outer segment channels lowers rather than raises internal Ca2+.
questions.answerText: It decreases, because hyperpolarization reduces Ca2+ entry at the terminal

questions.q: A drug inhibits the phosphodiesterase in rod outer segments. What happens when light then strikes those rods?
options: Cyclic GMP falls faster, so the light response is exaggerated
Cyclic GMP stays high, the channels stay open, and the light response fails
Cyclic GMP stays high, so the rods hyperpolarize even in darkness
Cyclic GMP falls, but glutamate release rises instead of falling in the light
questions.why: Phosphodiesterase is the step that translates photon capture into a drop in cyclic GMP, so blocking it leaves the messenger high, the channels open, and the cell stuck in something close to its dark state no matter what the light does. Blocking an enzyme cannot speed up the reaction it catalyzes. High cyclic GMP holds cells depolarized rather than hyperpolarized. Glutamate release always tracks membrane potential, so it cannot rise while the cell hyperpolarizes.
questions.answerText: Cyclic GMP stays high, the channels stay open, and the light response fails

questions.q: A patient's diet has been low in vitamin A for months. What is the expected effect on rod function?
options: Transducin is not made, so the cascade cannot be switched off
Less 11-cis retinal is available, so rhodopsin is scarce and dim light vision suffers
Cyclic GMP cannot be synthesized, so the rods stay hyperpolarized
The rods lose their cyclic GMP gated channels, so the dark current disappears entirely
questions.why: Retinal is made from vitamin A, so a shortage limits how much functional rhodopsin can be assembled, and rods with too little pigment capture too few photons in dim conditions. This is why night blindness is the earliest sign of vitamin A deficiency. Transducin, guanylyl cyclase, and the cation channels are all proteins whose synthesis does not depend on vitamin A, so none of them is the limiting step here.
questions.answerText: Less 11-cis retinal is available, so rhodopsin is scarce and dim light vision suffers

questions.q: An ON bipolar cell carries metabotropic glutamate receptors that hyperpolarize it when glutamate binds. What does light do to that bipolar cell?
options: It hyperpolarizes it, because the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes too
It hyperpolarizes it, because glutamate release rises in the light
It has no effect, because bipolar cells respond only to direct light
It depolarizes it, because the photoreceptor releases less glutamate
questions.why: The photoreceptor hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate, and because glutamate was inhibiting this bipolar cell, removing it lets the bipolar cell depolarize. Sign inversion at this synapse is how the retina turns a light off signal into a light on signal. Assuming the bipolar cell must follow the photoreceptor in the same direction ignores the receptor type on the postsynaptic side. Bipolar cells sit deeper in the retina and do not absorb light themselves, and glutamate release falls rather than rises in light.
questions.answerText: It depolarizes it, because the photoreceptor releases less glutamate

questions.q: During light exposure, intracellular Ca2+ in a photoreceptor falls. How does that help the cell adapt?
options: Low Ca2+ releases guanylyl cyclase from inhibition, so cyclic GMP is rebuilt
Low Ca2+ activates phosphodiesterase further, deepening the response
Low Ca2+ triggers more glutamate release to warn the bipolar cell
Low Ca2+ converts all-trans retinal back to 11-cis inside the outer segment
questions.why: Ca2+ normally restrains guanylyl cyclase, so when the channels close and Ca2+ entry stops, the cyclase speeds up and pushes cyclic GMP back toward its dark level, which reopens channels and resets sensitivity during a steady light. This negative feedback is why you can still see detail in bright sunlight instead of saturating. Deepening the response would be positive feedback, glutamate release falls rather than rises, and retinal regeneration takes place in the pigment epithelium with its own enzymes.
questions.answerText: Low Ca2+ releases guanylyl cyclase from inhibition, so cyclic GMP is rebuilt

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders the steps of phototransduction after a photon is absorbed?
options: Retinal isomerizes, transducin activates phosphodiesterase, cyclic GMP falls, channels close, the cell hyperpolarizes, glutamate release drops
Retinal isomerizes, cyclic GMP rises, channels open, the cell depolarizes, glutamate release rises
Transducin isomerizes retinal, phosphodiesterase makes cyclic GMP, channels open, the cell hyperpolarizes, glutamate rises
Retinal isomerizes, phosphodiesterase is inhibited, cyclic GMP rises, the channels close, the cell hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release drops
questions.why: Each step follows from the one before it: the shape change activates opsin, opsin activates transducin, transducin frees phosphodiesterase, the messenger is destroyed, the channels that needed it shut, the loss of inward current hyperpolarizes the cell, and less depolarization means less Ca2+ and less glutamate. A sequence in which cyclic GMP rises and the cell depolarizes reverses every direction and describes the dark state instead. A sequence in which transducin isomerizes retinal scrambles which molecule acts on which. Any sequence pairing a rise in cyclic GMP with channel closure is impossible, which cannot happen because cyclic GMP is what holds those channels open.
questions.answerText: Retinal isomerizes, transducin activates phosphodiesterase, cyclic GMP falls, channels close, the cell hyperpolarizes, glutamate release drops

questions.q: A mutation leaves the cyclic GMP gated cation channels of a rod permanently open regardless of cyclic GMP. Predict the rod's behavior in light.
options: It hyperpolarizes more strongly than normal, so light signals are exaggerated
It stays depolarized and keeps releasing glutamate, so light produces no signal
It hyperpolarizes normally, because glutamate release does not depend on the channels
It depolarizes further in light, so the bipolar cell receives a reversed signal
questions.why: The only way light changes the membrane potential is by closing those channels, so a channel that ignores cyclic GMP leaves the dark current running and the cell locked near minus 40 mV with tonic glutamate output. The upstream cascade still runs, but its output has nowhere to act. Exaggerated hyperpolarization would require more channel closure, not less. Glutamate release depends on membrane potential through Ca2+ channels, so it cannot change while the potential is fixed, and nothing in this mutation drives the cell further positive during light.
questions.answerText: It stays depolarized and keeps releasing glutamate, so light produces no signal

questions.q: A toxin locks transducin in its active state in a group of cones. Predict cyclic GMP, the channels, the membrane potential, and glutamate release in complete darkness.
options: Cyclic GMP high, channels open, cell depolarized, glutamate release high
Cyclic GMP low, channels closed, cell depolarized, glutamate release high
Cyclic GMP low, channels closed, cell hyperpolarized, glutamate release reduced
Cyclic GMP high, channels closed, cell hyperpolarized, glutamate release reduced
questions.why: Active transducin keeps phosphodiesterase running, so cyclic GMP is destroyed even with no photons, and the cell behaves as though a bright light were shining on it: channels shut, membrane hyperpolarized, transmitter output down. High cyclic GMP with open channels and heavy glutamate release is the true dark state, which this cell can no longer reach. Pairing closed channels with depolarization contradicts the loss of inward current. Pairing high cyclic GMP with closed channels is impossible, because cyclic GMP is the ligand holding those channels open.
questions.answerText: Cyclic GMP low, channels closed, cell hyperpolarized, glutamate release reduced

questions.q: A student objects that hyperpolarizing to light means the rod is sending less information when the stimulus arrives. What is the best answer?
options: The rod switches to action potentials in bright light, which carry the information instead
The rod releases glutamate tonically in darkness, so the retina reads the drop in release as the light signal
The rod releases a second transmitter during hyperpolarization, so the message still gets through to the bipolar cell
Hyperpolarization is too small to matter, and the real signal comes from the pigment epithelium
questions.why: Information sits in the change, not in the absolute direction, and because the rod is depolarized and releasing glutamate steadily in the dark, any reduction in that stream is a clear message to bipolar cells. Sign inverting ON bipolar cells then turn the decrease into a depolarization, so the pathway reaches the ganglion cells as an increase in firing. Photoreceptors never fire action potentials and release only glutamate, and the pigment epithelium supports the photoreceptors metabolically rather than signaling to the retina.
questions.answerText: The rod releases glutamate tonically in darkness, so the retina reads the drop in release as the light signal

questions.q: Which photoreceptor type operates in dim light?
options: Cones
Bipolar cells
Rods
Ganglion cells
questions.why: Rods carry far more pigment per cell and pool their signals, so they respond to very few photons and are the only photoreceptors working under starlight. Cones need much brighter light and go silent in dim conditions, which is why color drains out of a dark room. Bipolar and ganglion cells are second and third order neurons in the retina and do not absorb light at all.
questions.answerText: Rods

questions.q: Which photoreceptor type provides color vision?
options: Cones, which come in three types with different pigments
Rods, which come in three types with different pigments
Rods, which change pigment with wavelength
Cones, which all share one pigment and code color by firing rate
questions.why: Color comes from comparing the outputs of three cone classes whose photopsins peak at short, medium, and long wavelengths, so the brain reads a ratio rather than a single value. Rods all carry the same pigment, rhodopsin, which is why rod vision is monochrome no matter what wavelength arrives. A single pigment cannot signal wavelength through firing rate either, because a dim light of the best wavelength and a bright light of a poor one give the same response.
questions.answerText: Cones, which come in three types with different pigments

questions.q: Which region of the retina gives the sharpest vision?
options: The optic disc
The peripheral retina
The fovea centralis
The ora serrata
questions.why: The fovea is packed with cones, has almost no convergence onto bipolar cells, and the overlying retinal layers are pushed aside, so it resolves the finest detail. The optic disc is where the axons leave and has no photoreceptors at all, making it the blind spot. The peripheral retina is rod dominated and pools heavily, which trades acuity for sensitivity, and the ora serrata is simply the front edge of the retina.
questions.answerText: The fovea centralis

questions.q: Whose axons form the optic nerve?
options: Photoreceptors
Retinal ganglion cells
Amacrine cells
Bipolar cells
questions.why: Ganglion cells are the only retinal neurons that fire action potentials and send axons out of the eye, and those axons converge at the optic disc to become the optic nerve. Photoreceptors and bipolar cells signal with graded potentials over very short distances inside the retina. Amacrine cells modify signals laterally at the bipolar to ganglion cell layer and stay within the retina.
questions.answerText: Retinal ganglion cells

questions.q: Which fibers cross to the other side at the optic chiasm?
options: Fibers from the temporal half of each retina
Fibers from the nasal half of each retina
All fibers from the left eye only
Every fiber from both eyes
questions.why: Nasal retinal fibers, which carry the temporal visual field of each eye, cross at the chiasm, while temporal retinal fibers stay on their own side. That partial crossing is what puts the entire left visual field of both eyes into the right optic tract. If every fiber crossed, each hemisphere would receive one whole eye rather than one half of the world, and a lesion anywhere behind the chiasm would blind one eye instead of one field.
questions.answerText: Fibers from the nasal half of each retina

questions.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays visual information to the cortex?
options: The lateral geniculate nucleus
The ventral posterolateral nucleus
The medial geniculate nucleus
The ventral posteromedial nucleus
questions.why: Optic tract fibers synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus, and its neurons project through the optic radiations to the occipital cortex. The medial geniculate nucleus is the matching relay for hearing. The ventral posterolateral nucleus handles body somatosensation and the ventral posteromedial nucleus handles the face and taste, so neither carries vision.
questions.answerText: The lateral geniculate nucleus

questions.q: Where is the primary visual cortex located?
options: In the temporal lobe
In the frontal lobe
In the parietal lobe
In the occipital lobe
questions.why: The optic radiations end in the cortex around the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe, at the back of the brain. The temporal lobe holds primary auditory cortex, and parts of it handle later object recognition rather than the first cortical step. The parietal lobe holds somatosensory cortex, and the frontal lobe holds motor areas.
questions.answerText: In the occipital lobe

questions.q: What causes the blind spot in each eye?
options: The optic disc contains no photoreceptors
The fovea contains no rods
The lens casts a shadow on the central retina
Blood vessels block light over the macula
questions.why: At the optic disc the ganglion cell axons gather and exit the eye, so there is no room for rods or cones, and any image landing there is not detected. The fovea does lack rods, which affects dim light vision at the center of gaze but leaves plenty of cones, so it is not blind. The lens is transparent and casts no shadow, and although retinal vessels do run in front of the photoreceptors, they are too fine and too stable to create a discrete blind area.
questions.answerText: The optic disc contains no photoreceptors

questions.q: Why is rod vision less sharp than cone vision?
options: Rods are spread evenly across the retina instead of clustering near the center
Rods respond more slowly to a change in light intensity
Many rods converge onto one bipolar cell, so fine detail is pooled away
Rods lack the pigment needed to absorb photons efficiently
questions.why: Convergence sums the output of a wide patch of retina onto a single output neuron, which raises sensitivity but destroys information about which rod in the patch was hit. Foveal cones approach a one to one line to the brain, which preserves position. Rods are actually more sensitive and carry more pigment than cones, so the explanation cannot be a shortage of pigment, and their slower response affects motion blur rather than spatial resolution.
questions.answerText: Many rods converge onto one bipolar cell, so fine detail is pooled away

questions.q: On a clear night a faint star disappears when you look straight at it and reappears when you look slightly to one side. Why?
options: Cones adapt within a second or two and stop responding to a steady point of light
The blind spot sits at the center of gaze and swallows the image
The lens cannot focus a point source onto the fovea
The fovea has no rods, so a very dim point is detected only by peripheral retina
questions.why: Looking straight at something places its image on the fovea, which is all cones, and cones are too insensitive for starlight, so the star vanishes. Shifting your gaze a few degrees moves the image onto rod rich retina, where convergence pools enough photons to register. The blind spot lies about 15 degrees to the nasal side of the fovea, not at the center of gaze, and normal optics focus a distant point perfectly well on the fovea.
questions.answerText: The fovea has no rods, so a very dim point is detected only by peripheral retina

questions.q: A lesion completely destroys the left optic nerve. What visual deficit results?
options: Loss of the left half of the field in both eyes
Loss of the temporal field of both eyes
Total blindness of the left eye
Loss of the right half of the field in both eyes
questions.why: In front of the chiasm every fiber in the nerve comes from one eye, so cutting it removes all input from that eye and nothing from the other, and the patient is blind in the left eye alone. Losing one half of the field in both eyes requires a lesion behind the chiasm, where fibers from the two eyes have already been sorted by field rather than by eye. Loss of both temporal fields is the signature of a lesion at the chiasm itself.
questions.answerText: Total blindness of the left eye

questions.q: A pituitary tumor grows upward and compresses the center of the optic chiasm. What field deficit results?
options: Left homonymous hemianopia, loss of the left field of both eyes
Right homonymous hemianopia, loss of the right field of both eyes
Blindness of the right eye, with the left eye unaffected
Bitemporal hemianopia, loss of the temporal field of each eye
questions.why: The crossing fibers in the middle of the chiasm come from the nasal half of each retina, and the nasal retina views the temporal side of the world, so compressing them cuts out the outer field of both eyes. Patients describe it as tunnel like side vision, sometimes noticed first by bumping into door frames. A homonymous hemianopia requires a lesion of a tract or radiation behind the chiasm, and blindness of a single eye requires a lesion of that eye's optic nerve.
questions.answerText: Bitemporal hemianopia, loss of the temporal field of each eye

questions.q: The right optic tract is severed just behind the chiasm. What field deficit results?
options: Right homonymous hemianopia, loss of the right half of the field in both eyes
Bitemporal hemianopia
Blindness of the right eye
Left homonymous hemianopia, loss of the left half of the field in both eyes
questions.why: The right optic tract carries fibers from the right half of each retina, and the right retina looks at the left half of the world, so the deficit is contralateral and the same half of the field is lost in both eyes. Naming the right field reverses the retina to world relationship, which is the most common error on this competency. Bitemporal loss is the chiasm pattern, and monocular blindness is the optic nerve pattern.
questions.answerText: Left homonymous hemianopia, loss of the left half of the field in both eyes

questions.q: A disease selectively destroys cones in the fovea while sparing rods. What is the expected pattern of vision loss?
options: Loss of central detail and color vision, with dim peripheral vision preserved
Loss of peripheral vision at night, with sharp central vision preserved
Total blindness, because all visual input passes through the fovea
Loss of the temporal half of the field in the affected eye
questions.why: Foveal cones supply reading acuity and color, so losing them takes out the center of the visual world and leaves a functional but coarse rod driven surround. Patients often keep enough peripheral vision to walk around while being unable to read a page. Losing night and peripheral vision while keeping central acuity is the opposite pattern and points to rod loss. Nothing about photoreceptor loss respects a vertical field boundary, so a hemianopia is not expected.
questions.answerText: Loss of central detail and color vision, with dim peripheral vision preserved

questions.q: A patient has lost the left half of the visual field in both eyes, with normal pupillary light reflexes. Where is the lesion?
options: In the left optic nerve
In the optic chiasm
In the right optic tract
In the left optic tract
questions.why: A deficit in the same half of the field in both eyes must be behind the chiasm, because only there are fibers grouped by field rather than by eye, and losing the left field means losing the pathway on the right. The left optic tract would remove the right half of both fields instead. A chiasm lesion would produce bitemporal loss, and a left optic nerve lesion would blind that eye alone rather than half of each field.
questions.answerText: In the right optic tract

questions.q: Trace why a tumor at the optic chiasm produces loss of both temporal fields. Which fibers are damaged and what did they view?
options: The uncrossed temporal retinal fibers, which viewed the nasal half of each field
All fibers of the right optic nerve, which viewed the entire right field
The crossing nasal retinal fibers, which viewed the temporal half of each visual field
The crossing temporal retinal fibers, which viewed the temporal half of each field
questions.why: Light from the temporal side of the world crosses the pupil and lands on the nasal retina, and those nasal fibers are exactly the ones that decussate in the middle of the chiasm, so central compression takes out both temporal fields. Temporal retinal fibers run along the outer edges of the chiasm and stay uncrossed, so they survive a central lesion. Calling the crossing fibers temporal confuses the retinal name with the field name, which is the trap in this whole topic.
questions.answerText: The crossing nasal retinal fibers, which viewed the temporal half of each visual field

questions.q: You walk from bright sunlight into a dark theater. Vision is poor at first and improves over the next 20 to 30 minutes. What accounts for the slow phase of this adaptation?
options: The pupil dilates fully, which takes about half an hour
New rod cells are produced to replace the ones that were bleached by bright sunlight
Cones gradually take over from rods as the eye cools
Rhodopsin is regenerated in rods, which slowly restores their high sensitivity
questions.why: Bright light bleaches rhodopsin faster than it can be rebuilt, so on entering the dark the rods are nearly pigment free and must regenerate 11-cis retinal, a chemical process that takes tens of minutes. Cone adaptation is largely finished within a few minutes, which is why you can see something almost immediately but not the dim details. Pupillary dilation is complete in seconds, and photoreceptors are not replaced on this timescale.
questions.answerText: Rhodopsin is regenerated in rods, which slowly restores their high sensitivity

questions.q: A patient reads the smallest line of an eye chart in a bright room but bumps into furniture in dim hallways. Testing shows rod function is nearly absent while cones are normal. Predict daytime acuity, night peripheral vision, and color vision.
options: Daytime acuity poor, night peripheral vision normal, color vision poor
Daytime acuity poor, night peripheral vision poor, color vision normal
Daytime acuity normal, night peripheral vision normal, color vision poor
Daytime acuity normal, night peripheral vision poor, color vision normal
questions.why: Cones supply high acuity and color under bright light, so both stay intact when only rods are lost. Rods supply the sensitive, rod dominated periphery, so dim conditions and side vision are where the deficit shows up. Predicting poor color or poor daytime acuity would require cone loss, and predicting preserved night vision ignores that cones cannot respond at low light levels.
questions.answerText: Daytime acuity normal, night peripheral vision poor, color vision normal

questions.q: In myopia, where do parallel rays from a distant object come to a focus?
options: In front of the retina
Exactly on the retina
Behind the retina
On the optic disc
questions.why: A myopic eye has too much refractive power for its length, usually because the eyeball is too long or the cornea too steep, so distant rays converge early and are already spreading again by the time they reach the retina. Focus behind the retina is the hyperopic pattern. Focus exactly on the retina defines the normal eye, and the optic disc is a location on the retina rather than a focal plane.
questions.answerText: In front of the retina

questions.q: In hyperopia, where do parallel rays from a distant object come to a focus?
options: In front of the retina
Behind the retina
On the lens surface
Exactly on the retina
questions.why: A hyperopic eye is optically too weak for its length, usually because the eyeball is short, so the rays are still converging when they pass the photoreceptor layer and the theoretical focal point lies behind it. Focus in front of the retina is myopia, the opposite error. Light never focuses on the lens surface, since the lens is part of the focusing system rather than a screen.
questions.answerText: Behind the retina

questions.q: Which type of corrective lens is used for myopia?
options: A convex, converging lens
A cylindrical lens
A prism
A concave, diverging lens
questions.why: The myopic eye has too much power, so the correction must subtract power by spreading the rays slightly before they enter the eye, which pushes the focal point back onto the retina. A convex lens adds power and would make myopia worse, although it is exactly what hyperopia needs. Cylindrical lenses correct unequal curvature in astigmatism, and prisms shift image position for alignment problems rather than fixing focus.
questions.answerText: A concave, diverging lens

questions.q: Which type of corrective lens is used for hyperopia?
options: A concave, diverging lens
A flat lens with a tinted coating
A cylindrical lens
A convex, converging lens
questions.why: The hyperopic eye needs more refractive power, so a converging lens starts the rays inward before they reach the cornea and brings the focal point forward onto the retina. A concave lens removes power and would drive the focus even farther back. Cylindrical lenses address astigmatism, and a tint changes light intensity without changing where the image forms.
questions.answerText: A convex, converging lens

questions.q: What is the underlying cause of presbyopia?
options: The lens loses elasticity with age and can no longer round up
The eyeball elongates with age
The cornea becomes irregular in curvature with age
The pupil dilates more widely with age
questions.why: Lens proteins accumulate and cross link over decades, so the lens stiffens and stops springing into a rounder shape when the zonules slacken, which is why the near point recedes after roughly age 40. The ciliary muscle still contracts, so the failure is in the lens rather than the motor supply. Elongation of the eyeball is myopia, irregular corneal curvature is astigmatism, and the aging pupil in fact becomes smaller rather than larger.
questions.answerText: The lens loses elasticity with age and can no longer round up

questions.q: What is the usual cause of astigmatism?
options: The eyeball is too long from front to back
The lens has hardened and cannot change shape
The cornea is more curved in one meridian than another
The retina is detached at its outer edge
questions.why: A normal cornea is close to spherical, and when one meridian is steeper than the one at right angles to it, light in the two planes focuses at different distances, so no single plane is sharp. That is why patients see lines in one orientation more clearly than lines in another. Excess axial length is myopia, a hardened lens is presbyopia, and retinal detachment causes field loss rather than a refractive error.
questions.answerText: The cornea is more curved in one meridian than another

questions.q: Which type of lens corrects astigmatism?
options: A cylindrical lens
A spherical convex lens
A spherical concave lens
A bifocal lens
questions.why: A cylindrical lens has power in only one meridian, so it can add or subtract power along the axis that is out of step and leave the other axis alone. Spherical lenses change power equally in every meridian, so they can move both focal planes but cannot bring them together. A bifocal simply puts two spherical powers in one frame, usually for presbyopia.
questions.answerText: A cylindrical lens

questions.q: What does emmetropia describe?
options: An eye whose near point has receded past 40 cm
An eye that must accommodate constantly to see distant objects
An eye with equal curvature in every corneal meridian but a short axis
An eye that focuses distant objects on the retina with the lens relaxed
questions.why: Emmetropia is the normal state, where axial length and refractive power match, so no effort and no correction are needed for distance vision. An eye that must accommodate to see far away is hyperopic and is compensating rather than normal. A short axis is hyperopia even if the cornea is perfectly regular, and a receded near point is presbyopia.
questions.answerText: An eye that focuses distant objects on the retina with the lens relaxed

questions.q: A patient's eyeball is longer than average from cornea to retina, and the cornea and lens are normal. Which condition is this and which vision is blurred?
options: Hyperopia, with distance vision blurred
Myopia, with distance vision blurred
Myopia, with near vision blurred
Hyperopia, with near vision blurred
questions.why: A long eye puts the retina behind the focal point of parallel rays, so distant objects blur while near objects, whose rays arrive diverging and focus farther back, can still land correctly. That is why nearsighted people can often read without glasses. Hyperopia comes from an eye that is too short, and blurred near vision with clear distance vision is the hyperopic or presbyopic pattern.
questions.answerText: Myopia, with distance vision blurred

questions.q: A 50-year-old with previously excellent vision now holds the newspaper at arm's length to read it. What has happened and what correction helps?
options: Myopia, corrected with a concave lens
Astigmatism, corrected with a cylindrical lens
Presbyopia, corrected with a convex reading lens
Hyperopia from a shortened eyeball, corrected with a prism
questions.why: Holding print farther away is the classic sign that the near point has receded, which happens as the aging lens stiffens and can no longer add power for close work. A convex lens supplies the extra convergence the lens can no longer produce. Myopia would blur distance rather than near vision, astigmatism blurs one orientation at every distance, and the eyeball does not shorten in adulthood.
questions.answerText: Presbyopia, corrected with a convex reading lens

questions.q: A concave spectacle lens is placed in front of a myopic eye. What does it do to the incoming rays and to the focal point?
options: It converges the rays, moving the focal point forward onto the retina
It diverges the rays slightly, moving the focal point back onto the retina
It converges the rays, increasing total refractive power
It bends rays in only one meridian, evening out the two focal planes
questions.why: The myopic eye already focuses too early, so the correction must reduce net power, and diverging the rays before they hit the cornea delays convergence until the retinal plane. Converging the rays would add power and worsen the error. Bending light in only one meridian describes a cylindrical lens, which is the fix for astigmatism rather than for excess spherical power.
questions.answerText: It diverges the rays slightly, moving the focal point back onto the retina

questions.q: A patient's cornea is steeper along the vertical meridian than the horizontal one. What visual complaint does this predict?
options: Lines in one orientation look sharp while lines at right angles look blurred
Distance vision is uniformly blurred while near vision remains sharp and clear
Vision is sharp in bright light and blurred in dim light
Central vision is lost while peripheral vision remains
questions.why: With two different curvatures the eye has two focal planes, so whichever plane lands on the retina gives a sharp image while the other stays out of focus, and the effect follows the orientation of the detail being viewed. Uniform blur at distance with sharp near vision is myopia, where power is excessive in every meridian equally. Light dependent blur points to pupil size and photoreceptor issues, and central field loss is a retinal problem rather than a refractive one.
questions.answerText: Lines in one orientation look sharp while lines at right angles look blurred

questions.q: A young adult with mild hyperopia sees clearly at distance but reports headaches and eye fatigue after reading. Why?
options: The lens is already fully rounded at rest, so no reserve remains
Accommodation is needed even for distance, so near work demands sustained extra effort
The pupil cannot constrict during near work, so glare from the page tires the eyes quickly
The eyeball lengthens during reading and then rebounds
questions.why: A hyperopic eye is underpowered, so the ciliary muscle must contract just to bring distant objects onto the retina, and reading requires piling more accommodation on top of that, which the muscle cannot sustain comfortably. Young patients can do it, which is why the acuity looks normal, but the effort shows up as strain. The lens at rest is flat, not fully rounded, the pupil constricts normally in these patients, and the eyeball does not change length during reading.
questions.answerText: Accommodation is needed even for distance, so near work demands sustained extra effort

questions.q: A myopic student takes off her glasses and finds she can still read a book held 20 cm from her face without any blur. Explain.
options: Her ciliary muscle relaxes fully, which adds power for near work
Removing the glasses lets the pupil dilate, which sharpens the retinal image
Her excess refractive power suits the diverging rays from a near object
Her eyeball shortens when she looks at something close
questions.why: Myopia means too much power for parallel rays, but rays from a close object are diverging when they arrive, and they need exactly that extra power, so at some near distance the image lands on the retina with no correction at all. This is why myopia is called nearsightedness. A relaxed ciliary muscle reduces lens power rather than adding it, pupil dilation reduces depth of focus, and the eyeball length is fixed.
questions.answerText: Her excess refractive power suits the diverging rays from a near object

questions.q: A healthy 20-year-old sees distant objects clearly but says print blurs unless it is held far away. Testing shows the ciliary muscle and lens elasticity are normal for age. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Presbyopia, because the lens has already stiffened
Myopia, because the eyeball is longer than normal
Hyperopia, where the eye is optically too weak and accommodation is used up on distance
Astigmatism, because two corneal meridians bring light to a focus at different distances
questions.why: Blurred near vision with clear distance vision in someone whose lens is still elastic points to an underpowered eye rather than a failing accommodative mechanism, and hyperopia does exactly that by consuming accommodative reserve on far targets. Presbyopia produces the same symptom but requires a stiffened lens, which the testing has ruled out at this age. Myopia would blur distance first, and astigmatism blurs particular orientations at all distances rather than sparing distance vision entirely.
questions.answerText: Hyperopia, where the eye is optically too weak and accommodation is used up on distance

questions.q: A refractive surgeon removes too much corneal tissue while treating a myopic patient. What is the expected new refractive state and its correction?
options: Myopia that is worse than before, corrected with a stronger concave lens
Emmetropia, needing no correction
Astigmatism, corrected with a cylindrical lens
Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens
questions.why: Flattening the cornea subtracts refractive power, so removing more tissue than needed pushes the focal point past the retina and turns an overpowered eye into an underpowered one. The fix is then a converging lens, the same correction a naturally short eye needs. More myopia would require added power rather than less. Astigmatism would follow only if the tissue removal were uneven between meridians, and hitting the retina exactly is the intended outcome that did not happen here.
questions.answerText: Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens

questions.q: A patient reports blurred vision at every distance. A spherical lens sharpens vertical letter strokes but leaves horizontal strokes soft no matter what power is tried. What is going on?
options: Myopia, because a stronger concave lens has not yet been tried
Astigmatism, because the two meridians focus at different distances
Presbyopia, because accommodation fails only at near
Optic nerve damage, because the retina is receiving a degraded signal
questions.why: The telling detail is that changing spherical power trades one orientation for the other instead of sharpening both, which means the eye holds two focal planes at once and needs power added in only one meridian. Any purely spherical error, myopic or presbyopic, sharpens all orientations together once the right power is found. Optic nerve damage would not improve with any lens, since the image on the retina is already fine.
questions.answerText: Astigmatism, because the two meridians focus at different distances

questions.q: A 60-year-old with lifelong myopia now finds she needs one prescription for driving and a different one for reading. Explain why a single lens no longer works.
options: Her myopia has reversed, so she now needs a converging lens for distance work
Her cornea has become irregular, so each distance needs its own cylinder
Presbyopia has removed her accommodative range, so near objects blur
Her pupil no longer constricts, so depth of focus has collapsed at near
questions.why: A younger myope wearing full distance correction can still accommodate for near, so one lens covers both, but once the lens stiffens that reserve is gone and the distance correction becomes too weak for reading. The result is two prescriptions or a bifocal that adds plus power for near. Myopia does not reverse with age, an irregular cornea would blur both distances rather than separating them, and pupil changes alter depth of focus only slightly and would not create two separate prescriptions.
questions.answerText: Presbyopia has removed her accommodative range, so near objects blur

questions.q: In what order does vibration pass through the auditory ossicles?
options: Stapes, then incus, then malleus
Malleus, then incus, then stapes
Incus, then malleus, then stapes
Malleus, then stapes, then incus
questions.why: The malleus is attached to the tympanic membrane and receives the vibration first, passes it to the incus, and the incus drives the stapes against the oval window. Reversing the order would send energy from the inner ear outward, which is not how airborne sound is collected. Any order that puts the stapes before the incus breaks the physical chain, since the stapes is the only ossicle that contacts the cochlea.
questions.answerText: Malleus, then incus, then stapes

questions.q: Which ossicle presses against the oval window?
options: The malleus
The incus
The stapes
The tympanic membrane
questions.why: The footplate of the stapes sits in the oval window and pushes on the perilymph of the scala vestibuli, converting airborne vibration into a fluid pressure wave. The malleus is at the other end of the chain, on the eardrum, and the incus bridges the two. The tympanic membrane is not an ossicle at all but the membrane that starts the chain moving.
questions.answerText: The stapes

questions.q: Against which structure do the stereocilia of cochlear hair cells bend?
options: The basilar membrane
The oval window membrane
The round window membrane
The tectorial membrane
questions.why: Hair cells sit on the basilar membrane with their stereocilia projecting up into the overlying tectorial membrane, so when the basilar membrane moves the two shear against each other and the stereocilia are deflected. The basilar membrane carries the cells rather than bending them. The oval and round windows are the entry and pressure relief points for the fluid and are nowhere near the stereocilia.
questions.answerText: The tectorial membrane

questions.q: Which ion enters cochlear hair cells through the mechanically gated channels at the tips of the stereocilia?
options: Na+
Ca2+
Cl-
K+
questions.why: Endolymph bathing the stereocilia is unusually rich in K+, so when the tip link channels open, K+ flows down its gradient into the cell and depolarizes it. This is the one place in the body where K+ entry, rather than exit, is the depolarizing step. Na+ would be the answer for most other receptor cells, Ca2+ enters later at the base to trigger transmitter release, and Cl- is not the gating ion here.
questions.answerText: K+

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries auditory information from the cochlea to the brainstem?
options: The facial nerve, CN VII
The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX
The trigeminal nerve, CN V
The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII
questions.why: The cochlear branch of CN VIII carries the spiral ganglion axons that synapse on the hair cells. CN VII runs alongside it through the temporal bone and moves the facial muscles, including the stapedius, but it does not carry hearing. CN V supplies facial sensation and the tensor tympani, and CN IX carries taste and sensation from the posterior tongue and pharynx.
questions.answerText: The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII

questions.q: What is coded by the position along the basilar membrane where vibration peaks?
options: The pitch, or frequency, of the sound
The loudness of the sound
The direction the sound came from
The duration of the sound
questions.why: The basilar membrane varies in width and stiffness along its length, so each frequency sets up a traveling wave that peaks at a particular place, and the brain reads that place as pitch. Loudness is carried by how large the displacement is and how fast the afferents fire, not by where the peak sits. Direction is computed centrally by comparing the two ears, and duration is simply how long the response lasts.
questions.answerText: The pitch, or frequency, of the sound

questions.q: Which part of the basilar membrane responds best to high frequency sounds?
options: The base, near the oval window
The apex, at the far tip of the cochlear spiral
The middle turn, halfway along the spiral
Every part equally, since frequency is coded by firing rate
questions.why: At the base the membrane is narrow and stiff, which suits rapid vibration, so high frequencies peak there and never travel far into the cochlea. The apex is wide and floppy and resonates with low frequencies. A uniform response would make a place code impossible, and firing rate alone cannot carry pitch because axons cannot fire fast enough to track high frequencies.
questions.answerText: The base, near the oval window

questions.q: Which cells are the main sensory receptors for hearing?
options: The outer hair cells of the organ of Corti
The supporting cells of the organ of Corti
The inner hair cells of the organ of Corti
The cells of the stria vascularis
questions.why: A single row of inner hair cells makes the great majority of synapses onto afferent fibers of the cochlear nerve, so they are the cells that report sound to the brain. The three rows of outer hair cells act mostly as an amplifier, changing length to sharpen the traveling wave rather than reporting it. Supporting cells hold the structure together, and the stria vascularis secretes endolymph and maintains its high K+.
questions.answerText: The inner hair cells of the organ of Corti

questions.q: Why is the ossicular chain necessary rather than letting sound strike the oval window directly?
options: It concentrates force from a large membrane onto a small window to move the fluid
It slows the vibration so hair cells have time to respond
It converts sound waves into electrical signals before they reach the cochlear fluid
It filters out high frequencies that would damage the hair cells
questions.why: Fluid is much harder to move than air, so most airborne energy would simply reflect off the oval window, and the ossicles solve this by funneling the force collected over the wide tympanic membrane onto the much smaller stapes footplate, with the lever action of the bones adding a little more. The result is a pressure gain of roughly twenty fold. The ossicles do not slow, transduce, or filter the signal, since transduction happens at the hair cells.
questions.answerText: It concentrates force from a large membrane onto a small window to move the fluid

questions.q: When the stapes pushes inward at the oval window, what must the round window do?
options: Open a channel that lets perilymph drain into the middle ear
Push inward at the same time, to double the pressure wave
Stay rigid, so that pressure builds inside the cochlea
Bulge outward, because cochlear fluid cannot be compressed
questions.why: Perilymph is essentially incompressible in a bony tube, so unless something yields, the stapes cannot move and no traveling wave forms, and the flexible round window membrane is that release point. This is why scarring of the round window impairs hearing. Both windows moving inward together, or a rigid round window, would lock the fluid in place, and the window is a membrane rather than a drainage route.
questions.answerText: Bulge outward, because cochlear fluid cannot be compressed

questions.q: A pure low frequency tone is played. Where along the cochlea will the basilar membrane displacement be greatest?
options: Near the base, where the membrane is narrow and stiff
Near the apex, where the membrane is wide and floppy
Uniformly along the entire length of the membrane
At the round window, where the wave is reflected
questions.why: Low frequencies travel farthest before their traveling wave peaks, because the apex has the mechanical properties that resonate slowly. The stiff base is tuned to high frequencies and passes low ones along without peaking. A uniform response would erase the place code, and the round window is a pressure release membrane rather than a tuned resonator.
questions.answerText: Near the apex, where the membrane is wide and floppy

questions.q: The same tone is played louder. What changes in the cochlea and in the auditory nerve?
options: The peak of the traveling wave shifts toward the base and firing stays constant
Hair cells hyperpolarize more deeply, which the brain reads as loudness
The basilar membrane moves further, hair cells depolarize more, and afferents fire faster
The stapes vibrates at a higher frequency and more hair cells hyperpolarize
questions.why: Loudness is amplitude, so a louder tone deflects the basilar membrane further at the same place, opens more transduction channels, produces a bigger receptor potential, and drives a higher firing rate in the afferent while also recruiting neighboring hair cells. The place of the peak marks pitch, so it does not move when only intensity changes. Hair cells signal sound by depolarizing when bent toward the tallest stereocilia, and frequency does not change with volume.
questions.answerText: The basilar membrane moves further, hair cells depolarize more, and afferents fire faster

questions.q: Stereocilia are deflected away from the tallest one. What happens to the hair cell?
options: Transduction channels close and the cell hyperpolarizes below its resting level
Transduction channels open more widely and the cell depolarizes
Nothing changes, because only bending toward the tallest one is detected
The cell fires an action potential in the opposite direction
questions.why: A fraction of the tip link channels are open at rest, so bending in one direction pulls them further open and bending the other way lets them shut, which drops K+ entry and hyperpolarizes the cell below baseline. That two way swing is how a hair cell follows the back and forth of a sound wave with graded changes in transmitter release. Nothing here opens channels, deflection in both directions is detected, and hair cells do not fire action potentials.
questions.answerText: Transduction channels close and the cell hyperpolarizes below its resting level

questions.q: Years of loud noise exposure destroy hair cells near the base of the cochlea. What hearing loss is expected?
options: Loss of high frequency hearing, with low frequencies relatively spared
Loss of low frequency hearing, with high frequencies relatively spared
Equal loss across all frequencies
Loss of the ability to judge loudness, with pitch intact
questions.why: The base of the cochlea is tuned to high frequencies, so damage there takes those frequencies out first while the apex, which handles low tones, keeps working. This is why noise damage and age related loss both show up first as trouble with consonants and high voices. Low frequency loss would require apical damage, and losing loudness perception while keeping pitch would require a coding failure rather than a loss of a tuned region.
questions.answerText: Loss of high frequency hearing, with low frequencies relatively spared

questions.q: Endolymph has an unusually high K+ concentration. Why does that make K+ entry depolarizing in hair cells?
options: High external K+ makes the channels close instead of open
K+ carries negative charge, so its entry lowers the internal charge
The K+ gradient favors inward movement into the cell, carrying positive charge in
K+ entry drags Cl- into the cell along with it, and Cl- is the actual depolarizing ion
questions.why: In most cells the outside is K+ poor, so open K+ channels let K+ leave and the cell hyperpolarizes, but the stria vascularis pumps K+ into endolymph until the gradient reverses at the tips of the stereocilia, so opening a channel there brings K+ in. Positive charge entering makes the interior less negative, which is depolarization. K+ is a cation, mechanically gated channels respond to tension rather than to external K+ concentration, and Cl- is not involved.
questions.answerText: The K+ gradient favors inward movement into the cell, carrying positive charge in

questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces a sound from the eardrum to the auditory nerve?
options: Tympanic membrane, ossicles, oval window, perilymph wave, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing
Tympanic membrane, ossicles, round window, endolymph wave, tectorial membrane, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing
Tympanic membrane, oval window, ossicles, perilymph wave, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell hyperpolarization, cochlear nerve firing
Ossicles, tympanic membrane, oval window, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing
questions.why: Each step drives the next: air moves the membrane, the membrane moves the bones, the stapes moves the fluid, the fluid moves the basilar membrane, that movement shears the stereocilia against the tectorial membrane, K+ entry depolarizes the hair cell, and glutamate release drives the cochlear nerve. Putting the oval window before the ossicles, or the ossicles before the eardrum, breaks the mechanical chain. Entry through the round window reverses the pressure relief point, and hair cell hyperpolarization would reduce rather than increase nerve firing.
questions.answerText: Tympanic membrane, ossicles, oval window, perilymph wave, basilar membrane, stereocilia bending, hair cell depolarization, cochlear nerve firing

questions.q: In otosclerosis the stapes becomes fixed to the oval window and can no longer move freely. Predict what happens to the traveling wave and to hearing.
options: The traveling wave shifts toward the apex, so only the high frequencies are still audible
Little energy reaches the perilymph, so the wave is weak although hair cells are healthy
Hair cells are destroyed by the extra pressure, causing permanent loss
The round window compensates fully, so hearing stays normal
questions.why: A fixed stapes cannot transfer vibration into the cochlear fluid, so the problem is delivery of energy rather than detection, and the cochlea and nerve remain intact. That is the definition of a conductive loss, and it is why bone conduction, which bypasses the ossicles entirely, still works well in these patients. Nothing here shifts the tuning of the membrane, the fixation reduces pressure transfer instead of raising it, and the round window cannot push fluid on its own.
questions.answerText: Little energy reaches the perilymph, so the wave is weak although hair cells are healthy

questions.q: A drug selectively destroys outer hair cells while leaving inner hair cells and the cochlear nerve intact. Predict the effect on hearing.
options: Hearing is lost completely, since outer hair cells make most of the afferent synapses
Hearing is unchanged, since outer hair cells serve balance rather than hearing
Only loudness coding fails, while faint sounds are heard normally
Loud sounds are still heard, but sensitivity and frequency sharpness are reduced
questions.why: Outer hair cells change length in step with the traveling wave and amplify it, so losing them costs roughly 40 to 50 decibels of sensitivity and blurs the sharp tuning at each place, but the inner hair cells that actually report sound are still connected. Patients hear loud speech but struggle with faint sound and with separating similar frequencies. Inner hair cells, not outer, carry most afferent synapses, and outer hair cells belong to the cochlea rather than the vestibular apparatus.
questions.answerText: Loud sounds are still heard, but sensitivity and frequency sharpness are reduced

questions.q: Two pure tones have the same frequency but one is much louder. Compare where the basilar membrane peaks and what the auditory nerve does.
options: The peak is at the same place for both, and the louder tone produces a higher firing rate
The peak moves toward the base for the louder tone, and firing rate is unchanged
The peak moves toward the apex for the louder tone, and firing rate falls
The peaks are at different places and the firing rates are identical
questions.why: Place codes pitch and firing rate codes loudness, so two tones of the same frequency excite the same region and differ only in how strongly they drive it. The louder tone deflects the membrane further, opens more channels, and adds recruitment of nearby fibers. Any answer that moves the peak with intensity confuses the two codes, and identical firing rates would leave the brain no way to tell the two tones apart.
questions.answerText: The peak is at the same place for both, and the louder tone produces a higher firing rate

questions.q: Where is the lesion in a conductive hearing loss?
options: In the cochlear hair cells
In the outer or middle ear
In the cochlear nerve
In the auditory cortex
questions.why: Conductive loss means sound energy is not reaching the cochlea, so the fault lies in the ear canal, the tympanic membrane, or the ossicular chain. The cochlea and nerve are working normally, which is why bone conduction still delivers sound well. Hair cell and nerve lesions define sensorineural loss, and a cortical lesion causes trouble interpreting sound rather than a simple threshold shift.
questions.answerText: In the outer or middle ear

questions.q: Where is the lesion in a sensorineural hearing loss?
options: In the ear canal
In the cochlea or the cochlear nerve
In the ossicular chain of the middle ear
In the tympanic membrane
questions.why: Sensorineural loss means the sound arrives but cannot be transduced or transmitted, so the problem is at the hair cells, the spiral ganglion, or CN VIII. Because the delivery system is intact, no route of delivery helps, and both air and bone conduction are reduced. The canal, eardrum, and ossicles are all parts of the conducting apparatus, so lesions there produce conductive loss instead.
questions.answerText: In the cochlea or the cochlear nerve

questions.q: In a person with normal hearing, how do air conduction and bone conduction compare on the Rinne test?
options: Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction
Neither is heard once the fork stops touching the skull
The two are heard for exactly the same duration
Air conduction is heard longer and louder than bone conduction
questions.why: The middle ear amplifies airborne sound, so an intact conducting system makes air conduction the more efficient route, usually about twice as long. Bone conduction exceeding air conduction is the abnormal pattern that flags a conductive block. Equal durations would mean the middle ear is adding nothing, and sound presented at the ear canal is clearly heard without any skull contact.
questions.answerText: Air conduction is heard longer and louder than bone conduction

questions.q: In the Weber test, a patient with a conductive loss in one ear hears the tone where?
options: Equally in both ears
Louder in the normal ear
Louder in the affected ear
Only when the fork touches the affected mastoid
questions.why: The bone conducted tone reaches both cochleas, and in the blocked ear the sound is not lost back out through the middle ear and is not competing with room noise, so it seems louder on that side. Lateralization to the better ear is the sensorineural pattern instead. Equal loudness is the normal result, and the Weber fork is placed on the midline of the skull rather than on one mastoid.
questions.answerText: Louder in the affected ear

questions.q: In the Weber test, a patient with a sensorineural loss in one ear hears the tone where?
options: Louder in the affected ear
Equally in both ears
Not at all, in either ear
Louder in the unaffected ear
questions.why: Bone conduction delivers the tone equally to both inner ears, but the damaged cochlea cannot report it well, so the sound is perceived on the healthy side. Lateralizing to the bad ear would mean the inner ear is working and something is blocking delivery, which is the conductive pattern. Equal loudness is normal, and one damaged cochlea does not stop the other from hearing.
questions.answerText: Louder in the unaffected ear

questions.q: Which of these is a typical cause of conductive hearing loss?
options: Fluid in the middle ear from otitis media
Prolonged exposure to loud machinery
An ototoxic antibiotic that kills hair cells
A tumor pressing on the cochlear nerve
questions.why: Middle ear fluid damps the ossicles and keeps the tympanic membrane from vibrating freely, so less energy reaches the oval window while the cochlea remains healthy. Noise exposure and ototoxic drugs destroy hair cells, and a nerve tumor interrupts transmission, so all three of those produce sensorineural loss. The distinguishing question is always whether the trouble is delivery or detection.
questions.answerText: Fluid in the middle ear from otitis media

questions.q: Which of these is a typical cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
options: Loss of cochlear hair cells after years of loud noise
Perforation of the tympanic membrane
A plug of cerumen filling the ear canal
Fixation of the stapes against the oval window by new bone growth
questions.why: Hair cells do not regenerate in humans, so noise damage is permanent and lies inside the cochlea, which makes it sensorineural. Cerumen, a perforated eardrum, and a fixed stapes all interfere with getting vibration to the cochlea while leaving the sensory cells intact, so each of those is conductive. Sorting causes by anatomical location is the fastest way to keep the two categories straight.
questions.answerText: Loss of cochlear hair cells after years of loud noise

questions.q: What Rinne result is expected in the affected ear of a patient with a conductive loss?
options: Air conduction is heard longer than bone conduction
Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction
Neither air nor bone conduction is heard
Both are heard, and both are longer than normal
questions.why: A blocked middle ear removes the amplification that normally makes air conduction superior, while bone conduction goes straight to a healthy cochlea and is unaffected, so the usual relationship reverses. That reversal is the single most useful sign that a loss is conductive. Preserved air over bone conduction with both reduced is the sensorineural pattern, and a conductive loss rarely abolishes hearing altogether.
questions.answerText: Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction

questions.q: A child has had persistent middle ear fluid for weeks and now fails a hearing screen. How is this loss classified and why?
options: Sensorineural, because fluid pressure damages the hair cells
Conductive, because the fluid blocks transfer of vibration to the oval window
Sensorineural, because inflammation reaches the cochlear nerve
Mixed, because the tympanic membrane and cochlea are both involved
questions.why: Fluid loads the eardrum and ossicles so they cannot vibrate freely, which is a delivery problem in the middle ear and therefore conductive by definition. The cochlea is untouched, which is why hearing usually returns fully when the fluid clears. Calling it sensorineural would require damage to hair cells or nerve, and nothing in a simple effusion involves the cochlea.
questions.answerText: Conductive, because the fluid blocks transfer of vibration to the oval window

questions.q: A patient develops hearing loss after several weeks of an aminoglycoside antibiotic known to kill cochlear hair cells. How is this loss classified?
options: Conductive, because the drug thickens middle ear secretions
Sensorineural, because the transducing cells themselves are lost
Conductive, because hair cell loss stiffens the basilar membrane
Neither, because drug effects on hearing are always temporary
questions.why: The sound still reaches the cochlea normally, but with hair cells destroyed there is nothing left to convert the traveling wave into a receptor potential, which places the lesion in the sensory apparatus. Because human hair cells do not regenerate, this loss is usually permanent. Neither the middle ear nor basilar membrane stiffness is affected by the drug, so no part of this is conductive.
questions.answerText: Sensorineural, because the transducing cells themselves are lost

questions.q: A patient has a conductive loss in the right ear only. Predict the Weber result.
options: The tone lateralizes to the left ear
The tone is not heard on either side
The tone is heard equally in both ears
The tone lateralizes to the right ear
questions.why: With a healthy cochlea on both sides, the bone conducted tone is detected equally well, but the blocked right middle ear keeps the sound from leaking back out and shields that ear from background noise, so the tone seems louder on the blocked side. Lateralizing away from the affected ear would mean that cochlea was damaged, which is the sensorineural pattern. A one sided problem of either type rarely gives a midline result.
questions.answerText: The tone lateralizes to the right ear

questions.q: A patient has a sensorineural loss in the left ear only. Predict the Rinne result on that side.
options: Air conduction still outlasts bone conduction, but both are reduced
Bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction on the affected side
Air and bone conduction are both normal in duration
Only bone conduction is heard at all
questions.why: The middle ear is intact, so it still amplifies airborne sound better than the skull transmits it, and the normal air over bone relationship survives even though the damaged cochlea raises the threshold for both routes. That is why the Rinne alone can look deceptively normal in a sensorineural loss and must be read alongside the Weber. Bone conduction beating air conduction requires a conductive block, and truly normal durations would mean no loss at all.
questions.answerText: Air conduction still outlasts bone conduction, but both are reduced

questions.q: Why does bone conduction remain normal in a purely conductive hearing loss?
options: The skull amplifies sound more than the ossicles do
Vibration passes through the skull straight to the cochlea, bypassing the blocked pathway
Bone conducted sound enters through the round window instead of the oval window
The cochlea becomes more sensitive when air conduction is reduced
questions.why: Bone conduction sets the whole temporal bone and the cochlear fluid in motion directly, so whatever is wrong in the canal, eardrum, or ossicles is simply skipped, and a healthy cochlea responds normally. This is the physical basis of every tuning fork test. The skull is actually a less efficient route than the middle ear in a normal ear, and the cochlea does not raise its own sensitivity to compensate.
questions.answerText: Vibration passes through the skull straight to the cochlea, bypassing the blocked pathway

questions.q: Which single finding best separates a conductive loss from a sensorineural loss in the same ear?
options: Whether the loss is worse for high frequencies than for low
Whether the loss came on suddenly or gradually
Whether the patient also reports ringing in the ear
Whether bone conduction exceeds air conduction in that ear
questions.why: Comparing the two delivery routes isolates the question of whether sound is getting in, which is exactly the difference between the two categories, and only a conductive block reverses the normal air over bone relationship. High frequency predominance, tinnitus, and speed of onset are all common in sensorineural loss but occur in conductive cases too, so none of them decides the question on its own.
questions.answerText: Whether bone conduction exceeds air conduction in that ear

questions.q: On testing, the Weber tone lateralizes to the right ear, the right Rinne shows bone conduction longer than air conduction, and the left Rinne is normal. What is the diagnosis?
options: A sensorineural loss in the right ear
A sensorineural loss in the left ear
A conductive loss in the right ear
A conductive loss in the left ear
questions.why: Two findings point the same way: the reversed Rinne on the right says sound is not getting through that middle ear, and the Weber lateralizing toward that same ear says the cochlea underneath is healthy. Taken together only a right sided conductive block fits. A right sensorineural loss would send the Weber to the left and leave the right Rinne in its normal order. Nothing in the results implicates the left ear, whose Rinne is normal.
questions.answerText: A conductive loss in the right ear

questions.q: On testing, the Weber tone lateralizes to the left ear while both ears show air conduction longer than bone conduction. What is the diagnosis?
options: A conductive loss in the left ear
A sensorineural loss in the left ear
A conductive loss in the right ear
A sensorineural loss in the right ear
questions.why: Normal Rinne results on both sides rule out a conductive block, so any hearing loss present must be sensorineural, and lateralization to the left means the left cochlea is the better one, placing the damage on the right. Reading the Weber without the Rinne is what leads students to name the wrong side here. A left sided lesion of either type would send the tone away from the left, and a conductive loss would have reversed a Rinne.
questions.answerText: A sensorineural loss in the right ear

questions.q: A machinist with 25 years of unprotected noise exposure reports gradual hearing loss, worst for high pitched sounds. Predict both tuning fork results and name the type.
options: Weber lateralizes to the worse ear, Rinne is reversed there, and the loss is conductive
Weber lateralizes to the worse ear, Rinne stays air over bone in both ears, and the loss is sensorineural
Weber is midline, Rinne is reversed in both ears, and the loss is conductive
Weber lateralizes to the better ear, Rinne stays air over bone in both ears, and the loss is sensorineural
questions.why: Noise destroys hair cells at the base of the cochlea, which is a sensory lesion, so the middle ear still amplifies normally and the Rinne keeps its usual air over bone order in both ears. Because the damaged cochlea reports bone conducted sound poorly, the Weber goes to the healthier side. Any reversed Rinne would signal a conductive block that noise exposure does not cause, and lateralization toward a damaged cochlea contradicts how the Weber works.
questions.answerText: Weber lateralizes to the better ear, Rinne stays air over bone in both ears, and the loss is sensorineural

questions.q: A patient perforated the right tympanic membrane during a diving accident. Predict the site of the problem, the loss type, and the Weber result.
options: The cochlea is damaged, the loss is sensorineural, and the Weber lateralizes to the left
The cochlear nerve is stretched, the loss is sensorineural, and the Weber lateralizes to the right
Middle ear delivery is impaired, the loss is conductive, and the Weber lateralizes to the left
Middle ear delivery is impaired, the loss is conductive, and the Weber lateralizes to the right
questions.why: A hole in the eardrum means less of the sound pressure is collected and transferred to the ossicles, so this is a delivery failure in the conducting apparatus with an intact cochlea underneath. Since that cochlea works, the bone conducted Weber tone is heard best in the blocked ear, which is the right. Sending the Weber to the left would require the right cochlea to be the damaged one, and pressure injury to the eardrum does not by itself injure the nerve.
questions.answerText: Middle ear delivery is impaired, the loss is conductive, and the Weber lateralizes to the right

questions.q: Which vestibular structures detect rotational, or angular, acceleration of the head?
options: The tympanic cavity
The utricle and saccule
The cochlear duct
The semicircular canals
questions.why: The three semicircular canals are fluid filled loops, and rotating the head sets up relative motion of that fluid, which is only produced by a change in rotational speed. The utricle and saccule instead carry weighted membranes that respond to linear acceleration and to gravity. The cochlear duct handles hearing, and the tympanic cavity is the air filled middle ear.
questions.answerText: The semicircular canals

questions.q: What is the cupula?
options: The calcium carbonate crystal layer of the macula
The gelatinous cap in the ampulla that the hair cell stereocilia project into
The bony wall of the semicircular canal
The membrane that separates perilymph from endolymph within the cochlear duct
questions.why: The cupula sits like a swinging door across the ampulla, and endolymph pushing on it bends the stereocilia embedded in its base. It has the same density as endolymph, which is why it responds to fluid motion but not to gravity. Calcium carbonate crystals belong to the otolithic membrane of the maculae, and the bony canal and cochlear membranes are structural rather than sensory elements.
questions.answerText: The gelatinous cap in the ampulla that the hair cell stereocilia project into

questions.q: Where is the crista ampullaris located?
options: In the wall of the utricle near the macula
In the ampulla of each semicircular canal
At the apex of the cochlear spiral
In the roof of the saccule near the macula
questions.why: Each canal widens into an ampulla, and the crista ampullaris is the ridge of hair cells and supporting cells inside it, topped by the cupula. Putting it in the utricle or saccule confuses it with the macula, the sensory patch of those two chambers. The cochlear apex belongs to hearing and contains no vestibular receptors.
questions.answerText: In the ampulla of each semicircular canal

questions.q: What sits on top of the hair cells in the macula of the utricle and saccule?
options: A cupula of the same density as endolymph
A thin sheet of stiff collagen with no added weight
A gel layer studded with calcium carbonate otoliths
A layer of endolymph secreting cells
questions.why: The otoliths make the overlying membrane denser than the fluid around it, so it lags behind during linear acceleration and slides downhill when the head tilts, dragging the stereocilia with it. Without that extra mass the structure could not sense gravity at all, which is exactly why the cupula, matched in density to endolymph, cannot. Secretory cells maintain endolymph composition but do not form the sensory covering.
questions.answerText: A gel layer studded with calcium carbonate otoliths

questions.q: Which vestibular organ is best positioned to detect horizontal linear acceleration, such as a car pulling away from a stoplight?
options: The utricle, whose macula lies roughly horizontally
The saccule, whose macula lies roughly vertically
The lateral semicircular canal
The cochlear duct
questions.why: A horizontal macula puts the otolithic membrane free to slide forward and back across the hair cells, so forward acceleration shears it in the plane that the utricle monitors. The saccular macula stands vertically and is better suited to up and down acceleration, such as an elevator start. Semicircular canals respond to rotation, not straight line motion, and the cochlear duct serves hearing.
questions.answerText: The utricle, whose macula lies roughly horizontally

questions.q: Which vestibular organ responds best to vertical acceleration, as when an elevator starts upward?
options: The utricle
The posterior semicircular canal
The anterior semicircular canal
The saccule
questions.why: The saccular macula is oriented vertically, so up and down motion shears its otolithic membrane across the hair cells. The utricle, lying horizontally, is tuned to forward, backward, and sideways acceleration and to head tilt. The semicircular canals detect angular acceleration, so a straight ride up in an elevator barely stimulates them.
questions.answerText: The saccule

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries equilibrium information from the vestibular apparatus?
options: The trigeminal nerve, CN V
The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII
The facial nerve, CN VII
The vagus nerve, CN X
questions.why: The vestibular branch of CN VIII carries afferents from the cristae and maculae to the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem and to the cerebellum. CN VII travels beside it in the temporal bone but is motor to facial muscles. CN V carries facial sensation, and CN X supplies thoracic and abdominal viscera, so neither is involved in balance.
questions.answerText: The vestibulocochlear nerve, CN VIII

questions.q: In a vestibular hair cell, what does bending of the stereocilia toward the tall kinocilium do?
options: It depolarizes the cell and increases afferent firing
It hyperpolarizes the cell and decreases afferent firing
It has no effect until the head stops moving
It closes all transduction channels at once
questions.why: Vestibular hair cells fire at a steady baseline rate, and deflection toward the kinocilium opens more transduction channels, depolarizes the cell, and raises that rate above baseline.
