Deflection away from the kinocilium does the opposite and drops firing below baseline, which is how one hair cell reports both directions of motion. Waiting until motion stops would make the system useless during movement, and total channel closure describes the opposite deflection.
questions.answerText: It depolarizes the cell and increases afferent firing

questions.q: A person in a chair is spun rapidly to the right. What happens to the endolymph in the horizontal canals at the start of the spin?
options: It moves ahead of the canal wall and pulls the cupula forward
It stays perfectly still relative to the canal, so the cupula is not deflected
It lags behind the moving canal, so it pushes the cupula opposite to the turn
It drains toward the ampulla and increases pressure there
questions.why: The bony canal turns immediately with the head, but the fluid inside has inertia and is left behind, so relative to the canal wall it flows backward and deflects the cupula. That deflection bends the stereocilia and changes afferent firing, which is what signals the start of the turn. Fluid cannot lead the wall that is driving it, and if it moved perfectly with the canal there would be no stimulus at all. Endolymph is enclosed and does not drain.
questions.answerText: It lags behind the moving canal, so it pushes the cupula opposite to the turn

questions.q: A person is spun at a constant speed for a full minute. What happens to the sensation of turning?
options: It reverses, because the otoliths override the canal signal
It grows stronger, because hair cell firing accumulates over time
It stays constant, because the canals report the speed of rotation rather than acceleration
It fades, because the endolymph catches up to the canal and the cupula returns to center
questions.why: Friction brings the endolymph up to the same speed as the canal within about 20 seconds, and once nothing is shearing the cupula it springs back to its resting position and firing returns to baseline. This is why the semicircular canals report changes in rotation rather than steady rotation. Firing does not accumulate, the canals are acceleration detectors by design, and the otoliths respond to linear motion and cannot reverse a rotational signal.
questions.answerText: It fades, because the endolymph catches up to the canal and the cupula returns to center

questions.q: A person tilts the head to the right and holds it there. What happens in the utricle?
options: The endolymph in the utricle circulates and bends the cupula
Firing returns to baseline within seconds, because the tilt is not accelerating
Gravity pulls the heavy otolithic membrane sideways, shifting hair cell firing
The saccule alone responds, since the utricle detects only rotation
questions.why: Because the otolithic membrane is denser than its surroundings, gravity keeps pulling it downhill for as long as the tilt is held, so the shear on the stereocilia and the change in firing persist and report static head position. The canals, by contrast, adapt within seconds and cannot report a maintained position. The utricle has a macula rather than a cupula, and it responds to linear force and tilt, not rotation.
questions.answerText: Gravity pulls the heavy otolithic membrane sideways, shifting hair cell firing

questions.q: Why are there three semicircular canals on each side rather than one?
options: Each one is tuned to a different speed of rotation
They lie in three perpendicular planes, so rotation about any axis is detected
Two of them detect rotation while the third detects linear acceleration and head tilt
Each one drains endolymph from a different part of the labyrinth
questions.why: Any rotation can be broken into components about three axes, so a set of canals in three perpendicular planes can encode a head turn in any direction by how strongly each is stimulated. Nodding, shaking, and tilting the head each favor a different canal. They are not speed tuned, none of them detects linear motion, and the labyrinth is a closed system rather than a drainage network.
questions.answerText: They lie in three perpendicular planes, so rotation about any axis is detected

questions.q: An astronaut in orbit experiences apparent weightlessness. What happens to the vestibular signals?
options: Both the maculae and the canals stop working entirely
The canals stop reporting rotation, while the maculae still report head tilt normally
The maculae stop reporting tilt, while the canals still report head rotation
Both systems work normally, since neither depends on gravity
questions.why: The maculae work by letting a dense otolithic membrane be pulled by gravity or by linear acceleration, and in free fall there is no such pull, so tilt information disappears. The canals depend on fluid inertia during angular acceleration, which does not require gravity, so turning the head still produces a normal signal. The mismatch between a working canal signal and a silent otolith signal is a major source of space motion sickness.
questions.answerText: The maculae stop reporting tilt, while the canals still report head rotation

questions.q: A patient has lost hair cell function in both maculae but has intact semicircular canals. Which task will be hardest?
options: Detecting the start of a head turn to the left
Hearing a conversation in a quiet room
Sensing which way is up with the eyes closed
Judging the pitch of a musical note
questions.why: Static head orientation relative to gravity is reported by the otolith organs, so losing them removes the internal sense of upright, and without vision to substitute the patient becomes disoriented. The onset of a head turn is a job for the canals, which are intact here. Hearing and pitch discrimination belong to the cochlea, a separate part of the inner ear that this lesion does not touch.
questions.answerText: Sensing which way is up with the eyes closed

questions.q: A dancer spins to the right and then stops abruptly. Immediately after stopping, what does she sense and why?
options: Nothing, because the cupula returns to center as soon as motion stops
A sensation of falling, because the otoliths are displaced by the stop
A stronger sensation of spinning to the right, because hair cell firing rebounds above baseline
A sensation of spinning to the left, because the endolymph keeps moving past the cupula
questions.why: By the end of the spin the endolymph had matched the head's rotation, so when the head stops the fluid keeps going by inertia and deflects the cupula in the direction opposite to the original deflection. The brain reads that as rotation the other way, which is the dizziness felt after spinning. The cupula cannot recenter instantly while fluid is still moving, and the sensation is reversed rather than intensified. The otoliths report linear force and are not the source of this illusion.
questions.answerText: A sensation of spinning to the left, because the endolymph keeps moving past the cupula

questions.q: A passenger sits facing forward in a train that accelerates smoothly ahead on straight, level track with the head held still. Trace which receptors respond.
options: The horizontal semicircular canals respond, while the maculae stay near baseline
The saccular macula responds, while the utricle stays near baseline
Both the canals and both maculae respond equally
The utricular macula responds, while the semicircular canals stay near baseline
questions.why: Forward acceleration is linear and horizontal, so the dense otolithic membrane of the horizontally oriented utricle lags and shears the hair cells beneath it. There is no change in rotation, so the endolymph in the canals stays with its walls and the cupulae are not deflected. The saccule is oriented for vertical motion, so it contributes little on level track.
questions.answerText: The utricular macula responds, while the semicircular canals stay near baseline

questions.q: A patient reports that turning the head produces violent spinning sensations, while standing still with the eyes closed feels normal. Which part of the vestibular apparatus is most likely at fault?
options: The semicircular canals, which report angular acceleration
The saccule, which reports vertical linear acceleration
The utricle, which reports horizontal linear acceleration
The cochlear duct, which reports sound
questions.why: The symptom appears only during rotation and disappears when the head is still, which matches the stimulus the canals are built to detect and rules out an organ that would misreport gravity even at rest. Otolith disease tends to produce a persistent sense of tilt or unsteadiness while standing, which this patient does not have. The cochlear duct handles hearing and would produce hearing loss or tinnitus instead of vertigo.
questions.answerText: The semicircular canals, which report angular acceleration

questions.q: A person leans backward in a reclining chair and holds the position, then quickly nods the head forward and back. Which receptors are active at each stage?
options: The canals signal the maintained lean, and the maculae fire during the nodding
The maculae signal the maintained lean, and the canals fire during the nodding
The maculae handle both stages, since the canals respond only to spinning
The canals handle both stages, since the maculae respond only to sound
questions.why: A held lean is a static orientation to gravity, exactly what the weighted otolithic membranes of the utricle and saccule report and continue to report as long as the position lasts. Nodding is angular acceleration in the vertical plane, so it deflects the cupula in the canals aligned with that plane and the response fades if the motion becomes steady. Swapping the two organs misses that one adapts quickly and the other does not, and the maculae play no role in hearing.
questions.answerText: The maculae signal the maintained lean, and the canals fire during the nodding

questions.q: What are the five basic taste qualities?
options: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and spicy
Sweet, salty, bitter, umami, and fatty
Sweet, sour, salty, metallic, and umami
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami
questions.why: Each of the five has its own receptor mechanism on the taste cell, and umami, the savory taste of glutamate, was the last to be confirmed. Spiciness is not a taste at all but activation of pain and temperature endings by capsaicin through the trigeminal nerve. Metallic and fatty sensations are studied but are not among the established five.
questions.answerText: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami

questions.q: Which second messenger carries the olfactory signal inside an olfactory receptor neuron?
options: Cyclic AMP
Cyclic GMP
Inositol trisphosphate
Diacylglycerol
questions.why: An odorant binds a G protein coupled receptor, Golf activates adenylyl cyclase, and the cyclic AMP produced opens cation channels directly. Cyclic GMP is the messenger in photoreceptors, where the light response closes channels instead of opening them. Inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol are messengers in other G protein pathways, including some taste transduction, but not in the main olfactory cascade.
questions.answerText: Cyclic AMP

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue?
options: The facial nerve, CN VII
The glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX
The trigeminal nerve, CN V
The vagus nerve, CN X
questions.why: Taste from the front of the tongue travels with CN VII, while CN IX carries taste from the posterior third and CN X picks up the few taste buds on the epiglottis and upper esophagus. CN V supplies general touch, temperature, and pain to the anterior tongue, which is why it carries the burn of chili but not the taste.
questions.answerText: The facial nerve, CN VII

questions.q: Through which bony structure do olfactory receptor neuron axons pass on their way to the brain?
options: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
The optic canal of the sphenoid bone
The foramen magnum of the occipital bone
The internal acoustic meatus of the temporal bone
questions.why: The cribriform plate is perforated by many small holes, and bundles of unmyelinated olfactory axons thread through them to reach the olfactory bulb sitting just above. That thin, perforated bone is also why a blow to the head can shear the axons and abolish smell. The optic canal transmits CN II, the internal acoustic meatus transmits CN VII and CN VIII, and the foramen magnum transmits the spinal cord.
questions.answerText: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone

questions.q: Where do olfactory receptor neurons first synapse?
options: In the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb
In the solitary nucleus of the medulla
In the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus
In the piriform cortex of the temporal lobe
questions.why: Receptor neurons expressing the same odorant receptor converge on the same glomerulus, where they synapse on mitral cells, and that sorting is the first step in coding which odorant is present. The solitary nucleus is the first relay for taste, not smell. The ventral posteromedial nucleus is the thalamic taste relay, and the piriform cortex receives olfactory information only after the bulb has processed it.
questions.answerText: In the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb

questions.q: What is unusual about the olfactory pathway compared with the other special senses?
options: Its receptors are modified muscle cells rather than neurons
It has no receptor cells and senses chemicals directly through the mucosa
It sends all of its output to the opposite side of the brain
It reaches cortex and limbic areas without a thalamic relay first
questions.why: Vision, hearing, taste, and body sensation all pass through a thalamic nucleus before reaching cortex, but the olfactory tract runs directly to piriform cortex, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex, with the thalamic route to orbitofrontal cortex added afterward. Olfactory receptor neurons are true bipolar neurons and are the receptor cells themselves, and most olfactory projections stay on the same side.
questions.answerText: It reaches cortex and limbic areas without a thalamic relay first

questions.q: A salty solution and a bitter compound both reach the tongue. How do their transduction mechanisms differ?
options: Salt enters taste cells directly through ion channels, while bitter acts through a G protein coupled receptor
Both act through G protein coupled receptors, but on different cell types
Bitter enters taste cells directly through ion channels, while salt acts through a G protein coupled receptor
Both enter directly through ion channels, but salt uses Na+ and bitter uses K+
questions.why: Na+ from a salty solution flows straight into the taste cell through membrane channels and depolarizes it, which is the simplest transduction mechanism in the body, and sour works similarly through H+. Sweet, bitter, and umami all bind receptors on the cell surface and work through gustducin and a second messenger cascade. Swapping the two mechanisms is the common error here, and no taste is transduced by K+ entry.
questions.answerText: Salt enters taste cells directly through ion channels, while bitter acts through a G protein coupled receptor

questions.q: An odorant binds its receptor and cyclic AMP rises inside the olfactory receptor neuron. What happens next to the membrane?
options: Cation channels close, positive current stops, and the neuron hyperpolarizes
Cl- channels open and the neuron is inhibited
Cation channels open, positive charge flows in, and the neuron depolarizes
The neuron releases transmitter without any change in membrane potential
questions.why: The cyclic AMP gated channels of olfactory neurons open when the messenger rises, so the stimulus produces an inward cation current, a depolarizing receptor potential, and if it is large enough, action potentials along the axon into the bulb. That is the ordinary pattern for a sensory receptor. Channel closure with hyperpolarization describes photoreceptors, which are the exception, and nothing in the cascade opens Cl- channels or releases transmitter independent of voltage.
questions.answerText: Cation channels open, positive charge flows in, and the neuron depolarizes

questions.q: Why does a familiar smell so often trigger an emotional memory before you can name the odor?
options: Olfactory receptors are located within the limbic system itself
Odor molecules cross into the blood and act on the hippocampus as hormones
Olfactory axons reach the amygdala and entorhinal cortex directly, ahead of any naming pathway
Smell signals travel faster than other sensory signals because the axons are heavily myelinated
questions.why: The olfactory tract projects into limbic structures involved in emotion and memory without waiting for a thalamic relay, so the affective response can arrive before the slower route to areas that identify and name the odor. Receptor neurons sit in the nasal epithelium, not in the limbic system, and odorants act on receptors rather than circulating as hormones. Olfactory axons are in fact unmyelinated and slow, so speed is not the explanation.
questions.answerText: Olfactory axons reach the amygdala and entorhinal cortex directly, ahead of any naming pathway

questions.q: A patient with a heavy head cold says food tastes like nothing. Taste testing with salt and sugar solutions is normal. What explains the complaint?
options: The taste buds have been destroyed by the infection
Mucus changes the pH of saliva enough to silence the taste receptors
Flavor depends heavily on smell, and congestion blocks odorants from the epithelium
The facial nerve is inflamed, which abolishes taste from the whole surface of the tongue
questions.why: What we call the taste of food is mostly the odorant portion, sensed retronasally as we chew and swallow, so blocking airflow to the olfactory epithelium flattens flavor while the five basic tastes stay intact. That is exactly the pattern shown by normal salt and sugar testing. Destroyed taste buds or an inflamed CN VII would have made those test solutions abnormal too, and saliva pH shifts in a cold are far too small to silence receptors.
questions.answerText: Flavor depends heavily on smell, and congestion blocks odorants from the epithelium

questions.q: Olfactory receptor neurons are unusual among neurons because they are replaced throughout life. Why is this necessary?
options: They must change their receptor type as the diet changes
They use up their odorant receptors permanently with each binding event
They are directly exposed to the outside air and are regularly damaged
They are destroyed by every action potential they fire
questions.why: These neurons place their cilia in the mucus of the nasal cavity, where dust, pathogens, and dry air reach them, so a basal stem cell population replaces them every month or two, and each new neuron must grow an axon back to the correct glomerulus. Receptors are proteins that release the odorant and are reused, cells do not switch receptor types with diet, and firing an action potential does not destroy a neuron.
questions.answerText: They are directly exposed to the outside air and are regularly damaged

questions.q: Compare the effect of the stimulus on the ion channels of an olfactory receptor neuron and a photoreceptor.
options: Both stimuli open cyclic nucleotide gated channels and both cells depolarize
Odorant closes cyclic AMP gated channels and hyperpolarizes, while light opens cyclic GMP gated channels and depolarizes
Odorant opens cyclic AMP gated channels and depolarizes, while light closes cyclic GMP gated channels and hyperpolarizes
Both stimuli close cyclic nucleotide gated channels, but only the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes
questions.why: Both cells use a cyclic nucleotide gated cation channel, but the cascades push the messenger in opposite directions: odorant binding raises cyclic AMP and opens channels, while light activates a phosphodiesterase that destroys cyclic GMP and lets channels shut. The result is a depolarizing receptor potential in the nose and a hyperpolarizing one in the retina. Treating the two the same misses the point that vision is the exception among the senses, and reversing them assigns each cell the other one's behavior.
questions.answerText: Odorant opens cyclic AMP gated channels and depolarizes, while light closes cyclic GMP gated channels and hyperpolarizes

questions.q: Trace an odorant molecule from the nasal cavity to conscious perception. Which sequence is correct?
options: Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon passes the cribriform plate to a glomerulus, mitral cells project through the olfactory tract to piriform cortex and amygdala
Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon synapses first in the thalamus, and thalamic neurons then project to the olfactory bulb and on to the piriform cortex
Odorant binds a supporting cell, which excites a receptor neuron, whose axon runs to the solitary nucleus and then to the insula
Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon runs to the olfactory bulb, and bulb neurons project first to the occipital cortex
questions.why: The receptor neuron itself sends its axon through the cribriform plate into the bulb, where it synapses in a glomerulus on mitral cells, and the mitral cell axons form the tract that reaches cortex and limbic targets directly. Routing the signal through the thalamus first, or through the solitary nucleus and insula, describes the taste pathway rather than smell. Supporting cells maintain the epithelium and do not transduce, and the occipital cortex is visual.
questions.answerText: Odorant binds cilia of a receptor neuron, the axon passes the cribriform plate to a glomerulus, mitral cells project through the olfactory tract to piriform cortex and amygdala

questions.q: After a fall, a patient can taste salt and sugar normally but cannot smell coffee or identify foods by flavor. Imaging shows an injury at the base of the frontal region. What was most likely damaged and why does flavor suffer?
options: The facial nerve, and flavor suffers because taste buds have lost their innervation
The thalamic taste relay, and flavor suffers because all chemical senses pass through the thalamus
The solitary nucleus, and flavor suffers because taste and smell are relayed together there
The olfactory axons crossing the cribriform plate, and flavor depends largely on the olfactory component
questions.why: Preserved responses to salt and sugar show the taste pathway is intact, so the deficit must be olfactory, and unmyelinated axons crossing a thin perforated bone are the part of that pathway most easily sheared by head trauma. Because most of what people call flavor is the smell of food sensed while chewing, losing smell alone flattens meals. A CN VII, solitary nucleus, or thalamic taste lesion would each have degraded the salt and sugar testing, which was normal here.
questions.answerText: The olfactory axons crossing the cribriform plate, and flavor depends largely on the olfactory component

questions.q: At what distance is a standard Snellen chart read during acuity testing?
options: 10 feet, or about 3 meters
14 inches, or about 35 centimeters
20 feet, or about 6 meters
At whatever distance the letters first become clear
questions.why: Twenty feet is treated as optical infinity, so the rays arriving at the eye are essentially parallel and no accommodation is needed, which is what makes the measurement a clean test of distance vision. Fourteen inches is the standard distance for a handheld near card, which tests a different thing. Ten feet is used only with a mirror system that doubles the path, and letting the subject choose the distance would make results impossible to compare.
questions.answerText: 20 feet, or about 6 meters

questions.q: What does a Snellen result of 20/20 mean?
options: The subject read 20 letters correctly out of the 20 that were tried
The subject sees 20 percent better than average
At 20 feet the subject reads what a normal eye reads at 20 feet
The subject's near point is 20 centimeters
questions.why: The top number is the subject's testing distance and the bottom number is the distance at which a normal eye could read that same line, so matching numbers means normal acuity. Counting letters correct is not how the fraction is built. The fraction is not a percentage of normal, and the near point is measured by a separate accommodation test.
questions.answerText: At 20 feet the subject reads what a normal eye reads at 20 feet

questions.q: What do Ishihara plates test?
options: Visual acuity at near
The size and position of the blind spot in each eye
Color vision, especially red and green discrimination
The near point of accommodation for each eye separately
questions.why: Each plate hides a number in dots that differ from the background only in hue, so a subject who cannot distinguish those hues reads no figure or a different one. The plates are designed mainly around the red and green confusions produced by the common cone pigment deficiencies. Acuity, blind spot mapping, and near point each have their own test in the lab.
questions.answerText: Color vision, especially red and green discrimination

questions.q: What is the approximate near point of accommodation for a healthy young adult?
options: About 1 centimeter
About 1 meter
About 50 centimeters
About 10 centimeters
questions.why: A young elastic lens can add enough power to keep an object sharp until it is roughly a hand's width from the eye, so about 10 cm is the expected result in the lab. One centimeter is far closer than any human lens can manage. Values near 50 cm or a meter are what you record in older subjects whose lenses have stiffened, so finding one in a 20 year old should prompt a repeat measurement.
questions.answerText: About 10 centimeters

questions.q: The blind spot found during the mapping exercise corresponds to which structure?
options: The optic disc, where axons leave the eye
The fovea centralis, at the center of the macula
The macula lutea, around the fovea
The ora serrata, at the retinal edge
questions.why: No rods or cones can sit where the ganglion cell axons gather to form the optic nerve, so any image falling on that patch is not detected and the subject reports the target disappearing. The fovea and the surrounding macula are the region of best vision rather than a gap. The ora serrata is the peripheral edge of the retina and does not create a discrete spot in the field.
questions.answerText: The optic disc, where axons leave the eye

questions.q: Why is each eye tested separately during acuity and blind spot testing?
options: Because binocular testing overstimulates the retina and blurs the chart
Because the chart is only visible from one angle
Because the two eyes cannot accommodate at the same time
Because the other eye would cover the deficit and hide the problem
questions.why: Visual fields overlap heavily, so a defect in one eye is filled in by the other and a subject with a real deficit can score normally with both eyes open, which is exactly why the blind spot goes unnoticed in daily life. Covering one eye removes that compensation. Binocular viewing does not overstimulate anything, both eyes accommodate together, and the chart is meant to be read from straight ahead.
questions.answerText: Because the other eye would cover the deficit and hide the problem

questions.q: An astigmatism chart shows lines radiating from a center point. What does a positive finding look like?
options: Every line looks equally blurred
Lines at some orientations look sharp while others look blurred
The center point disappears entirely
The lines appear to bow outward, as though the chart were curved
questions.why: Astigmatism gives the eye two focal planes at right angles, so only the lines aligned with the plane that lands on the retina are crisp, and the rest are out of focus, which makes the pattern look uneven around the clock. Uniform blur points to a spherical error such as myopia. A vanishing center suggests a central field defect, and bowing of lines suggests distortion at the macula rather than a refractive problem.
questions.answerText: Lines at some orientations look sharp while others look blurred

questions.q: How is the common form of red and green color deficiency inherited?
options: As an autosomal dominant trait affecting both sexes equally
As an X linked recessive trait, so it is far more common in males
As a mitochondrial trait passed only from the mother to all children
It is not inherited and results from retinal injury
questions.why: The genes for the long and medium wavelength cone pigments sit on the X chromosome, so a male with one affected X has no second copy to compensate, which is why roughly 8 percent of males and under 1 percent of females are affected. An autosomal dominant pattern would give equal rates in both sexes. Mitochondrial inheritance would affect all children of an affected mother, and while injury can damage color vision, the common deficiencies are genetic.
questions.answerText: As an X linked recessive trait, so it is far more common in males

questions.q: A subject reads only the line marked 20/50 on the chart. How is this interpreted?
options: Acuity is better than normal, since more letters were read than expected
The result cannot be interpreted without knowing the subject's age
Acuity is normal, since the subject was 20 feet from the chart
Acuity is worse than normal, since a normal eye could read that line from 50 feet
questions.why: The subject must come in to 20 feet to see what an ordinary eye resolves from 50 feet away, so detail is lost and acuity is reduced. A larger bottom number always means worse acuity, which is the reverse of most scoring systems and is the usual source of confusion. Standing at 20 feet is simply the protocol, and the fraction is interpreted the same way at any age.
questions.answerText: Acuity is worse than normal, since a normal eye could read that line from 50 feet

questions.q: A subject reads the 20/15 line correctly. What does this indicate?
options: Acuity is worse than average, because the smaller number means less detail
Acuity is better than average, since a normal eye must come to 15 feet
The subject stood 15 feet from the chart instead of 20
The result is invalid, because 20/20 is the best possible score
questions.why: The subject is resolving from 20 feet what an average eye needs to approach to 15 feet to see, so the eye is doing better than the reference standard, and results down to about 20/10 are seen in healthy young subjects. The bottom number describes the reference eye, not the subject's position. Because 20/20 is an average rather than a ceiling, better scores are perfectly valid.
questions.answerText: Acuity is better than average, since a normal eye must come to 15 feet

questions.q: A 48-year-old subject has a measured near point of 33 centimeters. How should this be interpreted?
options: It is normal for any adult, since the near point does not change with age
It indicates myopia, since the eye focuses too strongly at near
It is consistent with presbyopia, since the near point recedes as the lens stiffens
It indicates a paralyzed ciliary muscle, since accommodation has failed completely
questions.why: The near point moves steadily outward from about 10 cm in youth to a third of a meter or more by the late forties, so this value fits the expected age related change in lens elasticity rather than any disease. Myopia would move the near point closer, not farther away. Complete ciliary paralysis would push the near point out to optical infinity and would also blur near vision through any correction.
questions.answerText: It is consistent with presbyopia, since the near point recedes as the lens stiffens

questions.q: A subject misreads several Ishihara plates but has 20/20 acuity in both eyes. Where does the problem most likely lie?
options: In the cornea, which is scattering light of certain wavelengths
In the cone photopigments, which affects hue discrimination but not resolution
In the lens, which has lost the elasticity needed to focus fine detail
In the optic tract, which is carrying only half of each visual field
questions.why: Sharp acuity proves that the optics and the foveal cone mosaic are resolving fine detail normally, so the failure has to be in which pigments those cones carry rather than in focus. A missing or shifted pigment collapses two hues into one, which is exactly what the plates are designed to expose. Corneal and lens problems would blur the letters as well, and an optic tract lesion would remove half of the visual field rather than confuse colors.
questions.answerText: In the cone photopigments, which affects hue discrimination but not resolution

questions.q: During blind spot mapping the right eye fixates on a central mark and the target disappears when it is moved to the right. Why does the blind spot appear on that side of the field?
options: The optic disc lies temporal to the fovea, and the temporal retina views the temporal field
The blind spot can appear on either side depending on which hand holds the card
The optic disc lies directly behind the fovea, so the spot appears at the center
The optic disc lies nasal to the fovea, and the nasal retina views the temporal field
questions.why: Light crosses through the pupil, so a target in the temporal field lands on the nasal retina, and because the optic disc sits nasal to the fovea, the gap shows up out toward the temple, roughly 15 degrees from center. Placing the disc on the temporal side reverses the anatomy and would predict the spot on the wrong side. The disc is offset from the fovea rather than behind it, and the geometry does not depend on the examiner.
questions.answerText: The optic disc lies nasal to the fovea, and the nasal retina views the temporal field

questions.q: Why does a subject never notice the blind spot while walking around, even though the lab test finds it easily?
options: The other eye covers that part of the field, and the brain fills the gap
The blind spot closes when both eyes are open
Constant eye movement keeps images off the optic disc at all times of day
The blind spot only exists under the bright light used in the lab
questions.why: The two blind spots fall on opposite sides of the field, so each eye supplies what the other misses, and even with one eye closed the visual system continues the surrounding texture across the gap so no hole is perceived. That is why the test requires covering one eye and fixating steadily. The optic disc is a permanent structural gap that does not close, and although the eyes do move, images still cross the disc constantly.
questions.answerText: The other eye covers that part of the field, and the brain fills the gap

questions.q: A subject with glasses is asked to keep them on during acuity testing. What does the recorded result then describe?
options: Uncorrected acuity, which reflects the true optical state of the eye itself
The near point of accommodation for that subject
The strength of the prescription in diopters
Corrected acuity, meaning how the eye performs with its error compensated
questions.why: Testing through the usual correction answers the practical question of how well the person sees in daily life and separates retinal and neural function from a lens problem the glasses already solve. Removing the glasses would measure uncorrected acuity, which is a different and equally legitimate measurement as long as the record says which one was taken. A chart cannot report diopters, and the near point requires the accommodation test.
questions.answerText: Corrected acuity, meaning how the eye performs with its error compensated

questions.q: A 50-year-old reads 20/20 at distance in each eye, passes every Ishihara plate, and has a near point of 45 centimeters. What is the interpretation?
options: Distance acuity and color vision are normal, and the receded near point indicates presbyopia
All results are within normal limits for any adult
The normal chart result rules out any need for correction
The color plates and the receded near point together suggest cone loss in the central fovea
questions.why: Each test isolates a different function, and here two are normal while the third is not, so the deficit is specifically in accommodation rather than in the optics for distance or in the retina. A near point of 45 cm at this age is the expected consequence of a stiffened lens and predicts the need for a reading add. Calling everything normal ignores the near point, and normal color plates argue against foveal cone loss rather than for it.
questions.answerText: Distance acuity and color vision are normal, and the receded near point indicates presbyopia

questions.q: A subject reads only the 20/100 line without glasses but reads 20/20 with them. What does the pair of results establish?
options: The retina is damaged, since acuity was clearly poor on the first test without glasses
The retina and visual pathway are working, and the deficit is a refractive error
The subject has a color vision deficiency that the glasses mask
The near point must also be abnormal, since acuity was reduced
questions.why: A lens in front of the eye can only change where light focuses, so if a lens restores acuity to normal the photoreceptors and the pathway behind them must be intact and the original problem was optical. This comparison is the fastest way in the lab to separate a refractive error from retinal or neural disease. Glasses cannot compensate for missing cone pigments, and the near point is a separate measurement that may well be normal.
questions.answerText: The retina and visual pathway are working, and the deficit is a refractive error

questions.q: A student maps the blind spot, then repeats the test holding the card twice as far from the eye. What happens to the measured gap on the card and why?
options: The gap disappears, because the target no longer falls on the optic disc
The gap measures smaller, because the optic disc always subtends a fixed number of centimeters
The gap is unchanged, because the blind spot is a fixed size on the card
The gap measures larger, because the same angle of field covers more distance farther away
questions.why: The blind spot is a fixed patch of retina, so it always blocks the same angle of the visual field, and an angle spreads over more centimeters the farther away the card is held. Doubling the distance therefore roughly doubles the measured width while the underlying anatomy is unchanged. Treating the spot as a fixed number of centimeters reverses the geometry, and moving the card farther away does not stop light from that direction landing on the disc.
questions.answerText: The gap measures larger, because the same angle of field covers more distance farther away

questions.q: A 19-year-old has 20/20 acuity, a near point of 9 centimeters, and misses eight Ishihara plates. Where in the visual system does the fault lie, and what does the near point add?
options: In the lens, and the near point confirms that it has already stiffened unusually early
At the cone pigments in the retina, and the normal near point shows the optics work
In the optic chiasm, and the near point is irrelevant to that lesion
In the ciliary muscle, and the color plates were probably misread
questions.why: Normal acuity and a normal near point together show that the cornea, lens, and ciliary muscle are delivering a sharp image at every distance, so nothing optical explains the color result, which leaves the pigments in the cones themselves. That combination is the expected profile of an inherited red and green deficiency in a young man. A stiffened lens would have pushed the near point out, and a chiasm lesion would have produced a field defect rather than color confusion.
questions.answerText: At the cone pigments in the retina, and the normal near point shows the optics work

questions.q: Where is the vibrating tuning fork placed to perform the Weber test?
options: On the mastoid process behind one ear
On the midline of the forehead or the top of the skull
Just outside one ear canal without touching the head
On the angle of the jaw on the affected side
questions.why: A midline placement delivers the same bone conducted stimulus to both inner ears, which is the only way a difference in perceived loudness can be attributed to the ears rather than to the placement. Putting the fork on one mastoid tests bone conduction on that side and is the first half of the Rinne. Holding it beside the ear tests air conduction, and the jaw is not a standard site.
questions.answerText: On the midline of the forehead or the top of the skull

questions.q: What is the correct order of steps in the Rinne test?
options: Hold the fork beside the ear canal, and then press its base against the middle of the forehead
Hold the fork beside each ear in turn and compare left with right
Place the fork on both mastoids at once and compare the two sides
Place the fork on the mastoid until the tone fades, then hold it beside the ear canal
questions.why: The test compares bone conduction with air conduction in one ear, so the mastoid placement is timed first and the fork is then moved to the air route to see whether the tone returns. A normal ear still hears it, because the middle ear amplifies airborne sound. Comparing the two sides to each other is what the Weber does, and a forehead placement is the Weber technique rather than the Rinne.
questions.answerText: Place the fork on the mastoid until the tone fades, then hold it beside the ear canal

questions.q: In tuning fork testing, what does lateralization mean?
options: Air conduction outlasts bone conduction in the same ear
The fork is moved from one side of the head to the other
The tone changes pitch as the fork slows down
The tone is heard louder in one ear than the other
questions.why: During the Weber test the sound reaches both cochleas equally, so if the subject reports it as louder on one side the result is said to lateralize to that side, and the direction is what identifies the type of loss. Moving the fork is a step in the procedure rather than a finding. A fading fork loses loudness but not pitch, and comparing air with bone conduction is the Rinne comparison.
questions.answerText: The tone is heard louder in one ear than the other

questions.q: Which tuning fork frequency is standard for the Weber and Rinne tests?
options: 128 Hz
256 Hz
512 Hz
questions.why: A 512 Hz fork sits in the speech range and gives a tone that lasts long enough to time while still being carried well by air, which is why it is the clinical standard. Lower frequency forks such as 128 Hz are felt as vibration as much as heard, so subjects confuse touch with sound. Very high frequency forks fade too quickly for a reliable comparison.
questions.answerText: 512 Hz

questions.q: How should the tuning fork be set vibrating before testing?
options: Struck sharply against the hard edge of the lab bench or a metal table
Struck gently against the heel of the hand or another soft surface
Squeezed between the fingers and released
Tapped against the subject's mastoid process
questions.why: A soft strike produces a clean fundamental tone at a moderate intensity, which is what the comparison depends on. Striking a hard surface adds overtones and can start the tone so loud that a mild difference between the two routes is missed. Squeezing the tines produces almost no vibration, and striking the fork against the subject is uncomfortable and starts the test before the timing begins.
questions.answerText: Struck gently against the heel of the hand or another soft surface

questions.q: How is the Romberg test performed?
options: The subject sits in a rotating chair and is spun ten times
The subject walks heel to toe along a straight line with eyes open
The subject stands with feet together, eyes open and then closed
The subject stands on one leg while counting backward
questions.why: Narrowing the base of support and then removing vision isolates how much the subject depends on sight to stay upright, which is the point of the test. Tandem walking and single leg stance are other balance tasks but do not make the eyes open versus eyes closed comparison. The rotating chair is used to test the semicircular canals by producing nystagmus, which is a different procedure.
questions.answerText: The subject stands with feet together, eyes open and then closed

questions.q: What does closing the eyes remove during the Romberg test?
options: Vestibular input, leaving vision and proprioception
Visual information about body position, leaving vestibular and proprioceptive input
Proprioceptive input from the legs, leaving vision and the vestibular system
Cerebellar control of posture, leaving reflex balance only
questions.why: Balance normally draws on three streams, vision, the vestibular apparatus, and proprioception, and closing the eyes removes only the first, so any remaining steadiness depends on the other two. That is why a subject with a vestibular or proprioceptive deficit can look normal until the eyes close. Closing the eyes has no effect on the inner ear, on joint and muscle receptors, or on the cerebellum.
questions.answerText: Visual information about body position, leaving vestibular and proprioceptive input

questions.q: What is nystagmus?
options: A sustained deviation of both eyes toward one side of the visual field
A loss of the pupillary light reflex in one eye
A rhythmic eye movement with a slow drift and a quick jerk back
An inability to move the eyes past the midline
questions.why: The slow phase is driven by the vestibular signal and the quick phase is the brainstem resetting gaze, and their alternation makes the eyes appear to beat in one direction. Observing it after rotation shows that the canals and their brainstem connections are working. A fixed deviation, a lost pupillary reflex, and restricted eye movement each point to other problems, none of which involve the rhythmic pattern that defines nystagmus.
questions.answerText: A rhythmic eye movement with a slow drift and a quick jerk back

questions.q: During a Weber test a student plugs one ear tightly with a finger. What does the subject report and why?
options: The tone sounds louder in the open ear, because that side is receiving more sound
The tone sounds louder in the plugged ear, because the plug mimics a conductive block
The tone becomes inaudible on both sides
The tone stays exactly midline, because a finger cannot change bone conduction
questions.why: Plugging the canal blocks the air route while leaving the cochlea untouched, which is precisely what a conductive loss does, so the bone conducted tone is not lost back out through the middle ear and is not competing with room noise on that side. Demonstrating this on yourself is the quickest way to remember which way the Weber lateralizes. Nothing about the plug reduces cochlear function or eliminates bone conduction, so the tone is neither shifted to the open ear nor lost.
questions.answerText: The tone sounds louder in the plugged ear, because the plug mimics a conductive block

questions.q: A subject's Weber tone lateralizes to the right ear and the right Rinne shows bone conduction outlasting air conduction. How is this recorded?
options: A sensorineural loss on the right
A conductive loss on the right
A conductive loss on the left
Normal hearing with a technique error
questions.why: Bone beating air on the right says the sound is not getting through that middle ear, and the Weber pointing to the same ear says the cochlea underneath is healthy, so the two findings agree on a right sided conductive block. A right sensorineural loss would send the Weber to the left and leave the Rinne in normal order. Nothing in the findings implicates the left ear, and consistent results across two tests argue against a technique error.
questions.answerText: A conductive loss on the right

questions.q: A subject's Weber tone lateralizes to the left ear while both ears show air conduction outlasting bone conduction. How is this recorded?
options: A sensorineural loss on the right
A conductive loss on the left
A conductive loss on the right
A sensorineural loss on the left
questions.why: Normal Rinne results on both sides mean no middle ear block anywhere, so a lateralizing Weber must reflect a difference between the two cochleas, and the tone is heard on the better side. Hearing it on the left therefore places the damage on the right. Naming the side the tone is heard in is the most common recording error on this test. Either conductive answer would require a reversed Rinne, which was not found.
questions.answerText: A sensorineural loss on the right

questions.q: A subject stands steadily with the eyes open but sways markedly and has to step out when the eyes close. How is this Romberg result interpreted?
options: Negative, since the subject was steady with the eyes open
Positive, indicating that vision was compensating for a balance deficit
Positive, indicating weakness of the leg muscles
Invalid, because the arms were at the sides rather than held outstretched
questions.why: The whole design of the test rests on the comparison between the two conditions, so steadiness with vision followed by instability without it is the positive finding and points to the non visual balance channels. Calling it negative uses only half of the observation. Muscle weakness would show up with the eyes open as well, and arms at the sides is the standard position rather than a protocol violation.
questions.answerText: Positive, indicating that vision was compensating for a balance deficit

questions.q: On the Rinne test the tone fades at the mastoid and the subject then hears it again when the fork is moved beside the ear canal. How is this recorded and what does it mean?
options: Bone conduction greater than air conduction, indicating a conductive loss
Air conduction greater than bone conduction, indicating a sensorineural loss
Air conduction greater than bone conduction, which is the normal pattern
An inconclusive result requiring a different fork
questions.why: Hearing the tone return by the air route after it has faded through bone shows the middle ear is amplifying as it should, which is the expected finding in a healthy ear. The reverse pattern, where nothing is heard at the ear canal after the mastoid tone fades, is what flags a conductive block. A normal Rinne does not by itself prove hearing is normal, because a sensorineural loss preserves this ordering while raising both thresholds, so it must be read with the Weber.
questions.answerText: Air conduction greater than bone conduction, which is the normal pattern

questions.q: A student is spun ten times to the right in a rotating chair and then stopped. What is observed immediately afterward?
options: A sensation of turning to the left, with nystagmus whose quick phase beats to the left
A sensation of turning to the right, with nystagmus whose quick phase beats to the right
No sensation and no eye movement, since the rotation has stopped
A sensation of falling backward, with the eyes fixed straight ahead
questions.why: During the spin the endolymph came up to speed with the canal, so when the head stops the fluid keeps moving and deflects the cupula the opposite way, which the brain reads as rotation in the reverse direction and which drives the eyes accordingly. That is why the post rotatory response reverses instead of matching the original spin. Stopping does not switch the system off, and the illusion is rotational rather than a sense of falling.
questions.answerText: A sensation of turning to the left, with nystagmus whose quick phase beats to the left

questions.q: A subject has cerumen fully occluding the left ear canal. Predict both tuning fork results before the wax is removed.
options: Weber lateralizes to the right, and the left Rinne shows bone outlasting air conduction
Weber lateralizes to the left, and both ears show air outlasting bone conduction
Weber lateralizes to the left, and the left Rinne shows bone conduction outlasting air conduction
Weber stays midline, and the left Rinne shows air outlasting bone conduction
questions.why: A blocked canal stops airborne sound from reaching an otherwise healthy ear, so this is a conductive loss and both tests should say so: the Rinne reverses on the blocked side because bone conduction bypasses the plug, and the Weber goes toward the blocked ear because that cochlea is intact and shielded from room noise. Sending the Weber to the right would indicate a damaged left cochlea instead. A preserved Rinne on the left would mean the canal was not truly blocked.
questions.answerText: Weber lateralizes to the left, and the left Rinne shows bone conduction outlasting air conduction

questions.q: A subject is steady on the Romberg with eyes open and closed but shows no nystagmus at all after ten rotations in the chair. What do these two results together suggest?
options: Both the vestibular system and proprioception have failed, since the chair test was negative
Canal function is impaired, while vision and proprioception keep the subject upright
The cochlea is damaged bilaterally, which explains the absent nystagmus
The results are normal, since a steady Romberg rules out any vestibular problem
questions.why: Post rotatory nystagmus is a direct readout of the canals, so its absence points to a vestibular problem, while quiet standing can be maintained on proprioception alone, which is why the Romberg can look normal in the same person. Reading the two tests together is what makes the pattern interpretable. A failure of proprioception as well would have produced swaying with the eyes closed, and the cochlea handles hearing rather than eye movements.
questions.answerText: Canal function is impaired, while vision and proprioception keep the subject upright

questions.q: A subject reports the Weber tone as louder on the right. Before recording a diagnosis, which single follow up best distinguishes the two possible causes?
options: Repeat the Weber with the fork on the left mastoid instead
Ask the subject to plug the right ear and repeat the Weber test on the forehead
Perform the Rinne on the right ear and compare bone with air conduction
Test the left ear with a lower frequency fork
questions.why: Lateralization to the right is ambiguous on its own, because it fits either a right conductive block or a left sensorineural loss, and only a comparison of the two delivery routes settles which. A reversed Rinne on the right confirms the conductive explanation, and a normal one shifts the diagnosis to the opposite ear. Moving the fork off the midline abandons the equal stimulus the Weber depends on, plugging an ear adds an artificial block on top of the finding, and changing the fork frequency does not address the question.
questions.answerText: Perform the Rinne on the right ear and compare bone with air conduction

questions.q: A classmate insists that a normal Rinne in both ears proves a subject hears normally. Using the logic of the two tests, what is the best response?
options: A conductive loss also preserves the air over bone ordering, so the Rinne misses it
The Rinne is unreliable at 512 Hz, so it should be repeated at a lower frequency
A sensorineural loss keeps air over bone, so the Rinne can be normal despite loss
The Rinne measures loudness rather than conduction, so it says nothing about hearing
questions.why: The Rinne asks only whether the middle ear is doing its amplifying job, so when the cochlea is damaged the two routes are both reduced and their normal ordering survives, which is exactly why the Weber is done alongside it. Tuning fork tests screen for the type of loss rather than measure thresholds, and an audiogram is what quantifies hearing. Conductive loss is the one thing the Rinne detects well, and the standard 512 Hz fork is appropriate for the test.
questions.answerText: A sensorineural loss keeps air over bone, so the Rinne can be normal despite loss

questions.q: Which cell is the final common pathway, the last neuron every motor command must pass through on its way to skeletal muscle?
options: The alpha motor neuron in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
The pyramidal cell in the primary motor cortex
The reticulospinal neuron in the brainstem reticular formation
The interneuron in the intermediate spinal gray matter
questions.why: Every command, whether it comes from the cortex, the brainstem, or a spinal reflex, converges on the alpha motor neuron, which is why it is called the final common pathway. The cortical pyramidal cell and the reticulospinal neuron are upper levels of the hierarchy and reach muscle only by driving that alpha motor neuron. Spinal interneurons shape the command but still hand it off to the alpha motor neuron rather than reaching the muscle themselves.
questions.answerText: The alpha motor neuron in the ventral horn of the spinal cord

questions.q: Which level of the motor hierarchy selects the goal of a voluntary movement and plans the strategy for reaching it?
options: The spinal cord interneuron pools
The association and premotor areas of the cortex
The brainstem reticular formation
The alpha motor neurons of the ventral horn
questions.why: The highest level of the hierarchy decides what to do and roughly how to do it, and that planning work belongs to the prefrontal association cortex together with the premotor and supplementary motor areas. The brainstem sets postural background rather than choosing the goal. Spinal interneurons and alpha motor neurons execute whatever command arrives; they carry out the plan and do not form it.
questions.answerText: The association and premotor areas of the cortex

questions.q: What is the main contribution of the brainstem level to a voluntary movement?
options: It generates the action potential in the muscle fiber itself
It chooses which object the movement will be aimed at
It sets postural tone and balance so the movement has a stable base
It stores the memory of how the movement felt last time
questions.why: Brainstem centers act mostly through the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts on axial and proximal muscles, holding the trunk and limb girdles steady so the hand can be moved accurately. Choosing the target is cortical planning. The muscle action potential is generated at the neuromuscular junction by the lower motor neuron. Motor memory is built in cortical and cerebellar circuits, not in the postural brainstem pathways.
questions.answerText: It sets postural tone and balance so the movement has a stable base

questions.q: Which level of the motor hierarchy carries out the monosynaptic stretch reflex?
options: The primary motor cortex
The cerebellum
The midbrain
The spinal cord
questions.why: The stretch reflex is a single synapse between the Ia afferent from the muscle spindle and the alpha motor neuron supplying the same muscle, and both cells are in the spinal cord, so no higher level is required for the response to occur. The primary motor cortex and midbrain modulate the gain of that reflex but are not part of the loop. The cerebellum monitors the movement and adjusts later commands rather than producing the reflex contraction.
questions.answerText: The spinal cord

questions.q: Where do the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts originate?
options: In the brainstem
In the primary motor cortex
In the dorsal root ganglia
In the basal ganglia
questions.why: Both are brainstem pathways: the vestibulospinal tract arises from the vestibular nuclei and the reticulospinal tracts from the reticular formation, and together they form the middle level of the hierarchy for posture and gross proximal control. Corticospinal fibers, not these tracts, arise in the primary motor cortex. The dorsal root ganglia hold sensory cell bodies and send nothing down the cord. The basal ganglia have no direct descending projection to the spinal cord at all.
questions.answerText: In the brainstem

questions.q: What does the primary motor cortex specify when it issues a command for a voluntary movement?
options: Whether the movement is worth making at all
The force and direction of the movement to be executed
The resting length of the muscle spindle
The concentration of acetylcholine stored in the axon terminal
questions.why: Primary motor cortex output encodes execution parameters, chiefly how much force to produce and in what direction to move, and it distributes those parameters to the correct motor neuron pools. Deciding whether a movement is worth making is a higher planning and motivational function. Spindle resting length is set by gamma motor neurons at the spinal level. Transmitter stores in the terminal are a property of the lower motor neuron, not something the cortex specifies.
questions.answerText: The force and direction of the movement to be executed

questions.q: Where are the central pattern generators that produce the basic rhythm of walking?
options: In the primary motor cortex
In the thalamus
In circuits of the spinal cord
In the muscle spindle itself
questions.why: Central pattern generators are networks of spinal interneurons that alternate flexor and extensor activity on their own, which is why the basic stepping rhythm does not have to be composed step by step by the brain. The cortex starts, stops, and steers walking but does not generate the rhythm. The thalamus is a relay to cortex with no rhythm-generating role for locomotion. The spindle is a sensory receptor and can modulate the pattern but cannot create it.
questions.answerText: In circuits of the spinal cord

questions.q: What is a motor unit?
options: One muscle fiber and all the motor neurons that reach it
One upper motor neuron and the lower motor neuron it drives
One whole muscle and the tendon that attaches it to bone
One alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates
questions.why: A motor unit is one lower motor neuron plus its entire family of muscle fibers, so when that neuron fires, every fiber in the unit contracts together. The reverse arrangement is not how skeletal muscle is wired, since each mature fiber is innervated by only one motor neuron. A whole muscle contains many motor units drawn from many motor neurons. The upper and lower motor neuron pair describes the descending pathway, not the unit of muscle output.
questions.answerText: One alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates

questions.q: A patient has a complete spinal cord transection at T10. Several months later, what happens to the patellar tendon reflex, which is organized at L2 to L4?
options: It is still present, because the reflex arc below the lesion is intact
It is permanently abolished, because the cord below the lesion is disconnected from the brain
It is still present, but only if the patient concentrates on the leg
It is abolished, because the sensory neuron dies once descending input is lost
questions.why: The reflex is a spinal loop from the Ia afferent to the alpha motor neuron at L2 to L4, and none of those elements are damaged by a lesion three segments higher, so tapping the tendon still produces a knee jerk once spinal shock has resolved. Losing the connection to the brain removes voluntary control and descending modulation, not the loop itself. Attention cannot substitute for a pathway that has been cut. The sensory neuron has its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion and survives the cord lesion.
questions.answerText: It is still present, because the reflex arc below the lesion is intact

questions.q: Damage limited to the brainstem reticulospinal and vestibulospinal pathways would be expected to impair which movements the most?
options: Buttoning a shirt with the fingertips
Holding the trunk upright and keeping balance while standing
Detecting a light touch on the sole of the foot while standing
Deciding which of two objects to pick up
questions.why: These brainstem pathways run to axial and proximal muscle pools, so losing them costs postural tone and balance while leaving distal dexterity comparatively intact. Fine finger movement depends on the lateral corticospinal tract, which is a separate pathway. Light touch is a sensory function carried by ascending tracts. Choosing between objects is a cortical planning function above the brainstem level.
questions.answerText: Holding the trunk upright and keeping balance while standing

questions.q: A person reaches for a coffee cup. Which sequence follows the motor hierarchy from planning to contraction?
options: Primary motor cortex, then association cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then muscle
Alpha motor neuron, then primary motor cortex, then association cortex, then muscle
Association cortex, then primary motor cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then muscle
Association cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then primary motor cortex, then muscle
questions.why: The hierarchy runs from the level that sets the goal down to the level that produces force: association and premotor cortex plan the reach, the primary motor cortex specifies the execution parameters, the alpha motor neuron delivers the command, and the muscle contracts. Putting the primary motor cortex before the association cortex reverses planning and execution. The sequences that place the alpha motor neuron in the middle or at the start invert the hierarchy, since the final common pathway cannot precede the levels that command it.
questions.answerText: Association cortex, then primary motor cortex, then alpha motor neuron, then muscle

questions.q: Recording from a person about to make a self-initiated movement, which area shows activity earliest, before the movement begins?
options: The muscle spindles of the antagonist muscle
The ventral horn alpha motor neurons
The neuromuscular junctions of the muscle involved
The supplementary motor and premotor areas
questions.why: Planning precedes execution, so the supplementary motor and premotor areas become active first, well before the command reaches the cord. Alpha motor neurons and neuromuscular junctions fire only once the descending command arrives, so they are late in the sequence, not early. Spindles in the antagonist respond to stretch that occurs after the movement has already started, making them the last of these to change.
questions.answerText: The supplementary motor and premotor areas

questions.q: A small stroke destroys only the hand region of the left primary motor cortex. What is the expected pattern of loss?
options: Loss of independent finger movements on the right, with sitting posture preserved
Loss of all movement and all sensation on the right side of the body
Loss of postural tone in the trunk, with finger movements preserved
Loss of the ability to feel the position of the right hand, with movement preserved
questions.why: The primary motor cortex hand area supplies the corticospinal drive for fractionated finger movement, and the lesion is small and confined, so the deficit is a contralateral hand deficit while brainstem pathways keep trunk posture normal. A loss of everything on one side would require a much larger lesion involving sensory pathways as well. Losing trunk tone while sparing the fingers is the pattern of a brainstem pathway lesion, not a cortical hand area lesion. Position sense travels in ascending sensory tracts and is not lost from a purely motor cortical lesion.
questions.answerText: Loss of independent finger movements on the right, with sitting posture preserved

questions.q: Why can a spinal reflex correct a stumble faster than a cortical response can?
options: Sensory axons conduct faster on the way to the cord than on the way to the brain
The reflex loop is short and uses very few synapses
The spinal cord uses a faster neurotransmitter than the cortex does
Reflex signals travel through gap junctions rather than chemical synapses
questions.why: Latency comes mostly from distance and from synaptic delay, and a spinal loop keeps both small, so the correction begins tens of milliseconds before a cortical route could deliver a command. The same afferent fiber carries the signal in both cases, so conduction velocity in the afferent is not the difference. Transmitter identity does not differ in a way that explains the timing, and glutamate is used at both levels. Spinal reflex synapses are chemical, not electrical.
questions.answerText: The reflex loop is short and uses very few synapses

questions.q: In an experimental preparation, the brainstem is separated from the cortex but left connected to the spinal cord. Extensor tone in the limbs increases markedly. What does this tell you about the normal role of the higher level?
options: The brainstem normally has no influence on muscle tone in the limbs
Cortical input normally supplies all of the excitation reaching extensor motor neurons
Cortical input normally restrains brainstem excitatory drive to extensor motor neurons
The spinal cord normally generates extensor tone without any descending input
questions.why: If tone rises when the higher level is removed, the higher level must have been holding the lower level in check, so cortical influence normally damps the excitatory reticulospinal and vestibulospinal drive to extensors. If the cortex supplied the excitation, removing it would lower tone rather than raise it. The result also shows directly that the brainstem does influence limb tone. The isolated cord immediately after separation is flaccid, so the cord alone does not generate this tone.
questions.answerText: Cortical input normally restrains brainstem excitatory drive to extensor motor neurons

questions.q: Weeks after a complete thoracic cord transection, an animal supported on a moving treadmill produces alternating stepping in the hindlimbs but never begins walking on its own. What does this pattern show about the two levels involved?
options: Spinal circuits have taken over the planning functions normally performed by the cortex
The stepping rhythm is generated in the brainstem and still reaches the hindlimbs through the few fibers that survived
The stepping is a single stretch reflex repeated over and over by the moving belt
Spinal circuits still generate the stepping rhythm, but the descending command that starts and steers walking is gone
questions.why: Two facts have to be reconciled: the rhythm is present, so its generator lies below the cut in the spinal cord, and initiation is absent, so the command to start comes from above the cut. That is the definition of a spinal central pattern generator driven by descending initiation. Nothing crosses a complete transection, so a brainstem rhythm could not reach the hindlimbs. A repeated stretch reflex could not produce the correct flexor and extensor alternation with proper timing. Isolated spinal circuits gain no planning ability; they lost their access to the plan.
questions.answerText: Spinal circuits still generate the stepping rhythm, but the descending command that starts and steers walking is gone

questions.q: A stroke destroys the leg area of the right primary motor cortex. Six weeks later, what is the expected combination of voluntary dorsiflexion and ankle stretch reflex on the left?
options: Voluntary dorsiflexion is lost or very weak, and the ankle reflex is exaggerated
Voluntary dorsiflexion is lost or very weak, and the ankle reflex is absent
Voluntary dorsiflexion is preserved, and the ankle reflex is exaggerated
Both voluntary dorsiflexion and the ankle reflex are normal by six weeks
questions.why: Two separate consequences follow from one lesion. The descending command for voluntary movement is gone, so dorsiflexion to command fails on the opposite side, and the spinal reflex arc is intact but no longer damped by descending input, so the stretch reflex is released and becomes brisk. Preserved voluntary movement would require the descending pathway to be working. An absent reflex would mean the spinal arc itself was damaged, which a cortical lesion does not do. Recovery to fully normal in six weeks is not expected after destruction of the cortical leg area.
questions.answerText: Voluntary dorsiflexion is lost or very weak, and the ankle reflex is exaggerated

questions.q: A person walking on a path sees a low branch and lifts the leg higher to step over it. Which description best captures how the levels of the hierarchy share this task?
options: The spinal cord detects the branch and raises the leg without involving the brain
Cortex modifies the timing and size of the step while spinal circuits keep producing the walking rhythm
The cortex takes over completely and generates each individual muscle contraction of the step cycle
The brainstem detects the branch visually and issues the command to lift the leg
questions.why: Visual information about the obstacle reaches cortex, which adjusts the ongoing pattern by increasing flexion at the right moment, while the spinal pattern generator continues to supply the underlying alternation. The cord has no access to vision, so it cannot detect the branch. If cortex generated every contraction, walking would not survive loss of cortical input, which it partly does. The brainstem contributes postural adjustment during the step but is not the visual processor issuing the modification.
questions.answerText: Cortex modifies the timing and size of the step while spinal circuits keep producing the walking rhythm

questions.q: A patient sits with normal posture, has normal tendon reflexes in both arms, and withdraws the hand promptly from a hot surface, yet cannot lift that arm when asked to. Which level of the hierarchy is most likely damaged?
options: The muscle itself
The alpha motor neurons supplying the arm
The cortical level that issues voluntary commands
The sensory afferents entering the cord from the arm
questions.why: Work backward from what still functions. Reflex withdrawal and normal tendon reflexes prove that the afferents, the spinal circuitry, the alpha motor neurons, and the muscle can all produce contraction, so the failure is specific to movement on command, which points to the level that generates voluntary commands. Damaged muscle or damaged alpha motor neurons would weaken the reflex contraction as well. Damaged afferents would blunt the withdrawal and the tendon reflexes rather than sparing them.
questions.answerText: The cortical level that issues voluntary commands

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of the neurons that begin the corticospinal pathway?
options: In the vestibular nuclei of the brainstem
In the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
In the primary motor cortex of the precentral gyrus
questions.why: Most corticospinal axons arise from large pyramidal cells in layer V of the precentral gyrus, with contributions from nearby premotor and parietal areas. The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex and sends no corticospinal motor output. The ventral horn holds the lower motor neurons where this pathway ends, not where it starts. The vestibular nuclei give rise to the vestibulospinal tract, a separate brainstem pathway.
questions.answerText: In the primary motor cortex of the precentral gyrus

questions.q: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract cross the midline?
options: In the pyramids of the medulla
In the internal capsule
In the cerebral peduncle of the midbrain
At the level of the spinal segment where it ends
questions.why: The pyramidal decussation sits at the junction of the medulla and the spinal cord, and it is the reason a cortical lesion produces weakness on the opposite side of the body. The internal capsule and cerebral peduncle both carry these fibers, but on their original side, before any crossing. Crossing at the segment of termination describes the smaller anterior corticospinal tract, not the lateral tract.
questions.answerText: In the pyramids of the medulla

questions.q: About what fraction of corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation?
options: About 50 percent
About 90 percent
About 10 percent
All of them
questions.why: Roughly 90 percent of the fibers cross in the medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract, and the remaining tenth continue uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract. Ten percent is the size of the uncrossed group, not the crossed one. A half and half split would not produce the strongly contralateral weakness seen after a cortical lesion. Saying all fibers cross ignores the anterior tract entirely.
questions.answerText: About 90 percent

questions.q: Which muscles does the anterior corticospinal tract mainly serve?
options: The small muscles of the hand and foot
The muscles that move the eyes
Axial and proximal muscles of the trunk and shoulder girdle
The smooth muscle in the walls of blood vessels in the limbs
questions.why: The uncrossed anterior tract stays near the midline of the cord and ends on motor pools for axial and proximal muscles, contributing to posture and gross positioning. Fine control of the hand and foot is the job of the crossed lateral tract. Eye muscles are driven by cranial nerve nuclei through corticobulbar and brainstem gaze pathways. Vascular smooth muscle is under autonomic control and receives no corticospinal input.
questions.answerText: Axial and proximal muscles of the trunk and shoulder girdle

questions.q: Through which part of the internal capsule do corticospinal fibers descend?
options: The anterior limb
They bypass the internal capsule entirely
The genu only
The posterior limb
questions.why: Corticospinal fibers are packed into the posterior limb of the internal capsule, which is why a small infarct there can weaken an entire half of the body. The anterior limb carries frontopontine and thalamic connections rather than the limb motor fibers. The genu carries corticobulbar fibers heading for cranial nerve nuclei. Every corticospinal axon passes through the capsule on its way from the corona radiata to the brainstem.
questions.answerText: The posterior limb

questions.q: Which midbrain structure carries corticospinal fibers on their way toward the spinal cord?
options: The cerebral peduncle
The red nucleus
The substantia nigra
The superior colliculus
questions.why: The cerebral peduncle is the massive fiber bundle on the ventral surface of the midbrain, and the corticospinal fibers occupy its middle portion as they pass through. The superior colliculus handles visual orienting reflexes. The red nucleus gives rise to the rubrospinal tract, which is a separate descending pathway. The substantia nigra belongs to the basal ganglia circuitry and sends its output to the striatum, not to the cord.
questions.answerText: The cerebral peduncle

questions.q: Where do lateral corticospinal tract axons end?
options: On sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglion
On alpha motor neurons and interneurons in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
Directly on the motor end plate of the skeletal muscle fiber itself
On second order sensory neurons in the dorsal column nuclei of the medulla
questions.why: The descending axon ends in the spinal gray matter, contacting the alpha motor neuron directly in the case of hand muscles and contacting interneurons for many other pools. It never reaches muscle itself, since the lower motor neuron axon covers that last stretch to the end plate. Dorsal root ganglion cells are sensory and receive no corticospinal ending. The dorsal column nuclei are relay stations on the ascending sensory route.
questions.answerText: On alpha motor neurons and interneurons in the ventral horn of the spinal cord
