questions.q: How many neurons are in series between the primary motor cortex and a skeletal muscle fiber in the corticospinal pathway?
options: Four
One
Two
Three
questions.why: The pathway uses an upper motor neuron running from cortex to the spinal gray matter and a lower motor neuron running from the ventral horn to the muscle, so two cells span the whole distance. One neuron would mean a cortical cell reaching the muscle directly, which does not occur. Three or four would suit a sensory pathway with several relays, but the motor route is deliberately short to keep conduction fast.
questions.answerText: Two

questions.q: A lesion destroys the hand region of the left primary motor cortex. Which hand becomes weak?
options: Neither hand, because brainstem pathways take over hand control
The left hand, because the tract has already crossed above the lesion
Both hands equally, because the tract supplies both sides
The right hand, because the tract crosses below the lesion
questions.why: The decussation is in the medulla, well below the cortex, so fibers leaving the left cortex have not yet crossed and will end up serving the right side of the body. The left hand would be weak only if the lesion sat below the crossing. Bilateral weakness would require the tract to supply both sides equally, which the small uncrossed anterior tract does only for axial muscles. Brainstem pathways cannot substitute for fine hand control.
questions.answerText: The right hand, because the tract crosses below the lesion

questions.q: A lesion damages the right medullary pyramid, just above the pyramidal decussation. Where is the resulting weakness?
options: On the left side of the body
On the right side of the body
On both sides of the body below the neck
In the right arm and the left leg
questions.why: Fibers in the right pyramid have not crossed yet, and they are destined to cross a few millimeters lower and supply the left side, so the weakness appears contralateral to the lesion. Weakness on the same side would require a lesion below the decussation, in the lateral corticospinal tract of the cord. A one-sided pyramid lesion cannot weaken both sides. A split pattern with one arm and the opposite leg does not match a tract that crosses all at one point.
questions.answerText: On the left side of the body

questions.q: A lesion damages the right lateral corticospinal tract at spinal level C5. Where is the weakness?
options: In the left arm and left leg, on the side opposite the lesion
In the right arm and right leg, on the same side as the lesion
In both arms but neither leg
In the right arm only, with the right leg spared
questions.why: By C5 these fibers have already crossed in the medulla, so the tract on the right side of the cord is serving right sided muscles and a lesion there produces ipsilateral weakness below the level. Contralateral weakness is the pattern for a lesion above the decussation. One-sided cord damage does not affect both arms. Fibers for the leg travel in the same tract and are cut too, so the leg is not spared.
questions.answerText: In the right arm and right leg, on the same side as the lesion

questions.q: A small infarct in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule interrupts a dense bundle of corticospinal fibers. What deficit is expected?
options: Weakness of the right hand alone
Weakness of the left arm and left leg together
Weakness of the right arm and right leg together
Weakness confined to the muscles of the trunk
questions.why: Fibers from the whole body map are squeezed into a small volume in the capsule, so a small lesion there strikes arm and leg fibers at once and produces contralateral weakness of the whole side. Weakness of the hand alone is the signature of a small lesion up in the cortex, where the body map is spread out. Left sided weakness would require a lesion below the decussation or on the right. Trunk muscles receive substantial uncrossed input and are the least affected.
questions.answerText: Weakness of the right arm and right leg together

questions.q: If the lateral corticospinal tract alone were selectively interrupted, which task would suffer the most?
options: Standing still with the eyes open
Breathing quietly at rest
Holding the head upright while seated
Picking up a small coin with the fingertips
questions.why: The lateral tract carries the fractionated commands that let individual fingers move independently, so precision grip is what fails first and most completely. Standing still and holding the head up rely on axial and proximal pools driven by brainstem pathways and the anterior corticospinal tract. Quiet breathing is generated by brainstem respiratory centers and does not need the corticospinal tract at all.
questions.answerText: Picking up a small coin with the fingertips

questions.q: The leg region of the primary motor cortex sits on the medial surface of the hemisphere. A stroke that damages only that medial strip on the right would produce what?
options: Weakness of the left leg with relative sparing of the left hand
Weakness of the right leg with relative sparing of the right hand
Weakness of the left hand with relative sparing of the left leg
Equal weakness of the left arm, leg, and face
questions.why: The motor homunculus places the leg at the medial edge and the hand on the lateral convexity, so a medial lesion takes out leg fibers and largely spares hand fibers, and the decussation then places the deficit on the opposite side. Hand weakness with a spared leg would follow a lateral convexity lesion instead. Right sided weakness would require the lesion to be on the left. Equal involvement of arm, leg, and face fits a capsular lesion where all the fibers are packed together.
questions.answerText: Weakness of the left leg with relative sparing of the left hand

questions.q: Which structure would a corticospinal axon reach first after leaving the internal capsule?
options: The pyramid of the medulla
The cerebral peduncle of the midbrain
The lateral corticospinal tract of the cord
The ventral horn of the cervical cord
questions.why: The route runs downward through the brainstem in order, so the midbrain peduncle comes next, then the basilar pons, then the medullary pyramid, then the cord. The pyramid is two brainstem levels further along. The lateral corticospinal tract exists only after the fibers have crossed in the medulla. The ventral horn is the destination at the far end of the pathway.
questions.answerText: The cerebral peduncle of the midbrain

questions.q: A patient has weakness of the right arm and leg, and the tongue deviates toward the left when protruded, indicating a left hypoglossal nerve problem. Where must the single lesion sit relative to the pyramidal decussation?
options: In the left spinal cord, below the decussation
In the right medulla, above the decussation
In the left medulla, above the decussation
In the right cerebral peduncle, above the decussation
questions.why: Two findings have to be satisfied at once. The hypoglossal nerve does not cross, so a left tongue sign places the lesion on the left, and the body weakness on the right then requires the corticospinal fibers to still be uncrossed, which puts the lesion above the decussation on the left. A right sided lesion would weaken the left body and the right tongue. A lesion below the decussation would give left sided weakness on the left. The peduncle is far above the hypoglossal nucleus, so it cannot explain the tongue finding.
questions.answerText: In the left medulla, above the decussation

questions.q: A cord injury damages the right half of the spinal cord at T6. Trace the corticospinal fibers to predict which leg is weak and why.
options: The left leg, because corticospinal fibers cross the midline at the spinal segment where they end
Neither leg, because the anterior corticospinal tract takes over leg control
Both legs, because each lateral tract sends branches to both sides of the cord
The right leg, because those fibers crossed in the medulla and now run on the right side of the cord
questions.why: Follow the fibers: axons from the left cortex crossed in the medulla, descended in the right lateral corticospinal tract, and are heading for right sided motor neurons, so cutting the right half of the cord at T6 weakens the right leg. Crossing at the segment of termination applies only to the small anterior tract, and it serves axial muscles. The lateral tract does not send branches across the midline of the cord. The anterior tract is too small and too axial to preserve leg strength.
questions.answerText: The right leg, because those fibers crossed in the medulla and now run on the right side of the cord

questions.q: Two patients each have a right sided lesion: one in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the other in the lateral corticospinal tract at C7. Which statement about the side of weakness is correct?
options: The capsular lesion weakens the left side, and the C7 lesion weakens the right side
The capsular lesion weakens the right side, and the C7 lesion weakens the left side
Both lesions weaken the right side, since both are on the right
Both lesions weaken the left side, since corticospinal fibers always cross
questions.why: The side of weakness depends entirely on whether the lesion sits above or below the pyramidal decussation. The capsule is above it, so those fibers have not crossed and the deficit appears on the left, while C7 is below it, so those fibers already crossed and the deficit stays on the right. Assuming the fibers have always crossed ignores the capsule, and assuming the deficit always matches the side of the lesion ignores the decussation altogether. The reversed pairing gets both levels backward.
questions.answerText: The capsular lesion weakens the left side, and the C7 lesion weakens the right side

questions.q: After a lesion confined to the left medullary pyramid, which combination of findings on the right side is expected?
options: Sitting posture and trunk control collapse completely while fine finger movements remain entirely accurate
Fine finger movements are severely impaired while sitting posture and trunk control are largely preserved
All voluntary and reflex movement is permanently abolished
Muscle sensation is lost while all movement remains normal
questions.why: The pyramid carries the corticospinal fibers destined for the lateral tract, so the loss falls hardest on fractionated distal movement, and because the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal pathways run outside the pyramid, they survive and continue to support axial posture. Losing posture while sparing the fingers reverses which pathway was cut. Reflexes are spinal and remain, indeed they become brisk, so nothing is permanently abolished. Sensory pathways lie outside the pyramid and are untouched.
questions.answerText: Fine finger movements are severely impaired while sitting posture and trunk control are largely preserved

questions.q: What is the cerebellum's main contribution to movement?
options: It supplies the final excitatory drive that reaches the alpha motor neuron
It decides whether a movement should be started at all
It compares the intended movement with the actual movement and corrects the error
It transduces muscle stretch into trains of sensory action potentials
questions.why: The cerebellum receives a copy of the descending command and sensory feedback about what the limb actually did, and it uses the mismatch to adjust timing and force, which is why its lesions produce clumsy rather than weak movement. Deciding whether to start a movement is the work of the basal ganglia. Excitatory drive to the alpha motor neuron comes from descending tracts and spinal circuits. Stretch transduction is the job of the muscle spindle.
questions.answerText: It compares the intended movement with the actual movement and corrects the error

questions.q: What is the main contribution of the basal ganglia to movement?
options: They generate the walking rhythm used during locomotion
They carry the motor command from the cortex directly down to the spinal cord
They set the sensitivity of the muscle spindle during contraction
They help select and initiate wanted movements while suppressing unwanted ones
questions.why: Basal ganglia circuits gate cortical motor output, releasing the movement that was chosen and holding back the competing ones, which is why their disorders show up as too little movement or too much rather than as weakness. The walking rhythm comes from spinal pattern generators. Spindle sensitivity is set by gamma motor neurons. The basal ganglia have no descending spinal projection and act only by way of the thalamus back to cortex.
questions.answerText: They help select and initiate wanted movements while suppressing unwanted ones

questions.q: Damage to one cerebellar hemisphere produces motor signs on which side of the body?
options: The same side as the damage
The side opposite the damage
Both sides equally
Neither side, since cerebellar damage causes only sensory loss
questions.why: Cerebellar output crosses on its way to the thalamus and the corticospinal tract crosses again in the medulla, and two crossings return the influence to the side it started on, so signs are ipsilateral. Contralateral signs are the pattern for lesions of the motor cortex or the corticospinal tract above the decussation. A unilateral lesion does not affect both sides. Cerebellar damage produces incoordination, which is a motor sign, not a loss of sensation.
questions.answerText: The same side as the damage

questions.q: A tremor that is absent at rest and grows worse as the hand approaches a target points to which structure?
options: The basal ganglia
The cerebellum
The neuromuscular junction
The dorsal columns
questions.why: An intention tremor reflects failed online error correction, the cerebellum's specific job, so the oscillation appears only when the movement demands accuracy. Basal ganglia disease classically gives the opposite timing, a tremor present at rest that quiets during movement. Neuromuscular junction disease produces fatigable weakness, not tremor. Dorsal column loss causes clumsiness from lost position sense, which worsens with the eyes closed rather than near a target.
questions.answerText: The cerebellum

questions.q: Which triad of signs is characteristic of basal ganglia disease of the Parkinson type?
options: Flaccid weakness, absent reflexes, and fasciculations
Intention tremor, dysmetria, and a wide based gait
Resting tremor, rigidity, and slowness of movement
Loss of pain sensation, loss of vibration sense, and numbness
questions.why: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine reduces the release of selected movements, producing bradykinesia with increased tone and a tremor that appears when the limb is at rest. Intention tremor with dysmetria and a wide based gait is the cerebellar picture. Flaccid weakness with areflexia and fasciculations is a lower motor neuron picture. The sensory list describes a peripheral or spinal sensory lesion and involves no motor system at all.
questions.answerText: Resting tremor, rigidity, and slowness of movement

questions.q: What does dysmetria mean?
options: Being unable to start a movement at all unless an external cue is given
Losing muscle bulk in the limb over several weeks
Producing involuntary writhing movements at rest
Misjudging the distance of a movement so the limb overshoots or falls short
questions.why: Dysmetria is an error in the amplitude of a movement, the finger stopping past the nose or short of it, and it is one of the most reliable cerebellar signs. Trouble starting a movement without a cue is akinesia, a basal ganglia feature. Involuntary writhing at rest describes athetosis, also a basal ganglia sign. Wasting of the limb is a lower motor neuron finding and has nothing to do with coordination.
questions.answerText: Misjudging the distance of a movement so the limb overshoots or falls short

questions.q: Which pathway supplies dopamine to the striatum?
options: The projection from the substantia nigra pars compacta
The projection from the cerebellar dentate nucleus
The projection from the subthalamic nucleus
The projection from the globus pallidus interna
questions.why: Dopaminergic cells of the substantia nigra pars compacta send axons to the caudate and putamen, and the death of those cells is what produces Parkinson disease. The subthalamic nucleus is glutamatergic and drives the internal pallidum. The dentate nucleus is cerebellar output and projects to the thalamus. The internal pallidum is the inhibitory output of the basal ganglia and uses GABA, not dopamine.
questions.answerText: The projection from the substantia nigra pars compacta

questions.q: In the basal ganglia, what do the direct and indirect pathways do to movement?
options: The direct pathway suppresses movement and the indirect pathway facilitates it
The direct pathway facilitates movement and the indirect pathway suppresses it
Both pathways facilitate movement, differing only in speed
Both pathways suppress movement, differing only in which muscles they reach
questions.why: Activity in the direct pathway reduces inhibitory output from the internal pallidum, freeing the thalamus to drive cortex and letting the chosen movement go forward, while the indirect pathway increases that inhibitory output and holds competing movements back. Reversing the two would make dopamine loss cause excess movement rather than bradykinesia. The two pathways are opposed in sign, so describing them as both excitatory or both inhibitory removes the selection function entirely.
questions.answerText: The direct pathway facilitates movement and the indirect pathway suppresses it

questions.q: A stroke damages the right cerebellar hemisphere. On which side would you expect the finger to nose test to be inaccurate?
options: On both sides equally
On the left
On the right
On neither side, since accuracy does not depend on the cerebellum
questions.why: Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the cerebellar output crossing and the corticospinal crossing cancel each other, so a right hemisphere lesion disturbs the right arm. A left sided deficit would follow damage to the right motor cortex instead. Damage on one side does not disturb both arms. Finger to nose accuracy is a direct test of cerebellar error correction, so it is very much affected.
questions.answerText: On the right

questions.q: A patient's hand is steady while resting in the lap, but it begins to oscillate as she reaches for a cup and the shaking is worst just before she grasps it. Which structure is implicated?
options: The basal ganglia
The primary motor cortex
The lower motor neuron pool of the forearm
The cerebellum
questions.why: The timing is the clue. A tremor that appears only during a goal directed movement and peaks near the target is an intention tremor and reflects failed cerebellar correction of ongoing error. A basal ganglia tremor behaves in the opposite way, present at rest and damped by voluntary movement. A motor cortex lesion produces weakness rather than oscillation. Lower motor neuron damage gives wasting and twitching at rest, not a tremor tied to reaching.
questions.answerText: The cerebellum

questions.q: A patient's fingers show a slow rhythmic tremor while the hands rest on the knees, and the tremor stops when he picks up a glass. Which structure is implicated?
options: The basal ganglia
The cerebellum
The muscle spindle
The dorsal root ganglion
questions.why: A tremor that is present at rest and quiets with voluntary movement is the classic basal ganglia pattern seen with nigrostriatal dopamine loss. The cerebellar tremor is the mirror image, absent at rest and worst as the hand nears the target. Spindle malfunction alters reflex gain rather than producing a rhythmic resting tremor. Dorsal root ganglion damage causes sensory loss and sensory clumsiness, not tremor.
questions.answerText: The basal ganglia

questions.q: A patient walks with a wide based, staggering gait and sways badly when standing with the feet together, yet strength and reflexes in the legs are normal. Which structure is most likely involved?
options: The internal capsule
The midline cerebellum
The lateral corticospinal tract
The globus pallidus
questions.why: Normal strength and normal reflexes rule out the descending motor pathways, and a wide base with truncal instability points to the midline cerebellum, which coordinates balance and gait. A capsular or corticospinal lesion would leave the leg weak with brisk reflexes. Pallidal disease produces rigidity and slowness or involuntary movements rather than this pattern of unsteadiness with a wide base.
questions.answerText: The midline cerebellum

questions.q: If dopamine input to the striatum falls, what happens to the inhibitory output of the internal globus pallidus and to movement?
options: Pallidal inhibitory output falls and movement becomes excessive
Pallidal inhibitory output rises and movement becomes excessive
Pallidal inhibitory output rises and movement becomes slow and sparse
Pallidal output is unchanged because dopamine acts only on the cerebellum
questions.why: Dopamine normally pushes the direct pathway on and the indirect pathway off, so losing it swings the balance toward the indirect pathway, the internal pallidum fires more, the thalamus is inhibited more, and the cortex receives less drive, which is bradykinesia. Falling pallidal output would release movement, the pattern seen in hyperkinetic disorders. High pallidal output cannot produce excess movement, since more inhibition means less. Dopamine of this system acts on the striatum, not on the cerebellum.
questions.answerText: Pallidal inhibitory output rises and movement becomes slow and sparse

questions.q: A patient has continuous, irregular, dance like movements of the limbs that he cannot suppress. How is this best classified?
options: A lower motor neuron disorder
A hypokinetic basal ganglia disorder
A cerebellar coordination disorder
A hyperkinetic basal ganglia disorder
questions.why: Chorea is an excess of unwanted movement, which means the gate that normally suppresses competing movements has been weakened, and that gating belongs to the basal ganglia. A hypokinetic disorder shows the opposite problem, too little movement. Cerebellar disease makes voluntary movement inaccurate but does not generate involuntary movements at rest. Lower motor neuron disease produces weakness and wasting, and its fasciculations are small twitches within a muscle rather than movements of a whole limb.
questions.answerText: A hyperkinetic basal ganglia disorder

questions.q: Trace the consequences of losing substantia nigra pars compacta neurons through the basal ganglia circuit to the cortex. Which sequence is correct?
options: Less direct pathway activity and more indirect pathway activity, so more pallidal inhibition of thalamus and less cortical drive
More direct pathway activity and less indirect pathway activity, so less pallidal inhibition of thalamus and more cortical drive
Less direct pathway activity and less indirect pathway activity, so no net change in thalamic firing
More pallidal inhibition of thalamus, so the corticospinal tract can no longer cross in the medulla
questions.why: Dopamine excites the direct pathway through D1 receptors and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2 receptors, so removing it does both harms at once, and the two converge on the same endpoint of a more active internal pallidum. Heavier pallidal inhibition quiets the thalamus, cortex receives less drive, and movement becomes slow and hard to start. The first option describes what a dopamine agonist would do. The third ignores the opposite signs at D1 and D2. The last confuses circuit gain with the anatomical decussation, which is unaffected.
questions.answerText: Less direct pathway activity and more indirect pathway activity, so more pallidal inhibition of thalamus and less cortical drive

questions.q: After a stroke, a patient overshoots when reaching with the left hand and cannot perform rapid alternating movements with it, but left arm strength and reflexes are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: In the right cerebellar hemisphere
In the left cerebellar hemisphere
In the right primary motor cortex
In the left lateral corticospinal tract at C5
questions.why: Two inferences are needed. Overshooting and clumsy alternating movements with preserved strength and reflexes identify the problem as cerebellar rather than a descending pathway lesion, and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral, so a left sided deficit means a left sided cerebellum. The right cerebellum would disturb the right hand. A right motor cortex lesion or a cervical corticospinal lesion would both produce weakness with brisk reflexes, which is not what the examination shows.
questions.answerText: In the left cerebellar hemisphere

questions.q: Why do cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion even though the cerebellum influences movement through the cerebral cortex?
options: Cerebellar output never crosses the midline at any point
The cerebellum sends its axons straight down the cord to spinal motor neurons on the same side of the body, so no crossing occurs anywhere
Cerebellar output crosses on the way to the thalamus and the corticospinal tract crosses again, so the influence returns to the starting side
The corticospinal tract does not cross in patients who have cerebellar disease
questions.why: Count the crossings. Deep cerebellar output leaves through the superior cerebellar peduncle and crosses to reach the opposite thalamus and motor cortex, and that cortex then sends corticospinal fibers that cross back in the medulla, so two crossings return the effect to the original side. A pathway with no crossing at all would also give ipsilateral signs, but it is not how the anatomy is built. The cerebellum has no direct projection to spinal motor neurons. The pyramidal decussation is fixed anatomy and does not change with disease.
questions.answerText: Cerebellar output crosses on the way to the thalamus and the corticospinal tract crosses again, so the influence returns to the starting side

questions.q: A lesion destroys the subthalamic nucleus on one side, and the patient develops violent involuntary flinging movements of the opposite limbs. Why does losing this nucleus increase movement?
options: The subthalamic nucleus inhibits the motor cortex directly, so losing it leaves cortical output entirely unopposed
The subthalamic nucleus generates the walking rhythm, so losing it makes the limbs move continuously
The subthalamic nucleus supplies dopamine to the striatum, so losing it mimics Parkinson disease
The subthalamic nucleus drives the internal pallidum, so losing it reduces pallidal inhibition and releases the thalamus
questions.why: The subthalamic nucleus is the excitatory relay of the indirect pathway onto the internal pallidum, so removing it weakens the brake: pallidal firing falls, the thalamus is disinhibited, and cortex drives far more movement than intended. The nucleus does not project to cortex directly, so an unopposed cortex is the wrong mechanism. Dopamine comes from the substantia nigra pars compacta, and losing dopamine would slow movement rather than release it. Locomotor rhythm is generated in the spinal cord.
questions.answerText: The subthalamic nucleus drives the internal pallidum, so losing it reduces pallidal inhibition and releases the thalamus

questions.q: Which neuron is the lower motor neuron?
options: The ventral horn cell whose axon leaves the cord and reaches the muscle
The cortical cell whose axon descends to the spinal cord
The dorsal root ganglion cell that carries stretch information inward
The spinal interneuron that connects one side of the cord to the other
questions.why: The lower motor neuron is the cell that actually contacts skeletal muscle, so its cell body sits in the ventral horn of the cord or in a cranial nerve motor nucleus and its axon runs out in a peripheral nerve. The cortical cell that descends to the cord is the upper motor neuron and stops in the spinal gray matter. Dorsal root ganglion cells are sensory. Interneurons stay inside the central nervous system and never reach muscle.
questions.answerText: The ventral horn cell whose axon leaves the cord and reaches the muscle

questions.q: What happens to muscle tone after an upper motor neuron lesion?
options: Tone falls, producing flaccidity
Tone increases, producing spasticity
Tone is unchanged from normal
Tone rises for a day and then falls permanently
questions.why: Descending pathways normally restrain the spinal stretch reflex, so removing them leaves the reflex circuitry overactive and the limb resists passive stretch, which is spasticity. Flaccidity is the tone change of a lower motor neuron lesion, where the reflex arc itself is broken. Tone does change, and durably, so unchanged tone does not fit. The time course given in the last option is backwards: tone is low at first after an acute lesion and rises over the following weeks.
questions.answerText: Tone increases, producing spasticity

questions.q: What happens to muscle tone after a lower motor neuron lesion?
options: Tone increases, and the muscle becomes spastic
Tone is normal, but only during voluntary effort
Tone falls, and the muscle becomes flaccid
Tone alternates between high and low from minute to minute
questions.why: Cutting the final common pathway removes the only route by which any excitation, voluntary or reflex, can reach the muscle, so the muscle goes limp. Spasticity requires an intact spinal reflex arc released from descending control, which is the upper motor neuron picture. Tone is a resting property and does not become normal only during effort. Fluctuating tone is not a feature of a denervated muscle.
questions.answerText: Tone falls, and the muscle becomes flaccid

questions.q: What happens to deep tendon reflexes after an upper motor neuron lesion has been present for several weeks?
options: They disappear completely
They can be elicited only with the eyes closed
They stay exactly normal
They become exaggerated
questions.why: The spinal reflex arc survives an upper motor neuron lesion and loses the descending inhibition that normally damps it, so tendon taps produce brisk responses and sometimes clonus. Reflexes disappear when the arc itself is interrupted, which is the lower motor neuron pattern. Normal reflexes would mean descending control was still intact. Eye closure is a maneuver used to reinforce a reflex, not a requirement created by the lesion.
questions.answerText: They become exaggerated

questions.q: What happens to deep tendon reflexes after a lower motor neuron lesion?
options: They are reduced or absent
They are exaggerated, with clonus
They are normal, since the reflex needs no motor neuron
They are replaced by an extensor plantar response
questions.why: The lower motor neuron is the efferent limb of the tendon reflex, so damaging it breaks the arc and the tap produces little or no contraction. Brisk reflexes with clonus are the upper motor neuron picture, where the arc is intact but unrestrained. The reflex certainly needs a motor neuron, since without one nothing can reach the muscle. An extensor plantar response is a separate upper motor neuron sign, not a substitute reflex.
questions.answerText: They are reduced or absent

questions.q: What is a Babinski sign?
options: Rapid rhythmic beating of the foot when the ankle is dorsiflexed
Extension of the great toe when the sole of the foot is stroked
Small twitches visible under the skin of a resting muscle
Loss of the ability to feel the sole of the foot being touched
questions.why: Stroking the sole normally makes the toes curl downward, and an upgoing great toe instead indicates loss of corticospinal control, which makes the Babinski sign an upper motor neuron sign. Rhythmic beating at the ankle is clonus, which is also an upper motor neuron sign but a different one. Twitches in a resting muscle are fasciculations and point to the lower motor neuron. Loss of sensation on the sole is a sensory finding and says nothing about motor level.
questions.answerText: Extension of the great toe when the sole of the foot is stroked

questions.q: Fasciculations, the small visible twitches in a muscle at rest, indicate damage at which level?
options: The upper motor neuron
The cerebellum
The lower motor neuron
The sensory afferent fiber
questions.why: A fasciculation is the spontaneous discharge of a single injured motor unit, so it requires a sick or dying lower motor neuron and its muscle fibers. Upper motor neuron lesions leave the motor unit intact and produce spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign instead. Cerebellar disease affects coordination and produces no spontaneous twitching. Sensory fiber damage causes numbness or tingling and cannot make a muscle fiber contract.
questions.answerText: The lower motor neuron

questions.q: How does muscle bulk differ between upper and lower motor neuron lesions?
options: Atrophy is marked in an upper motor neuron lesion and slight in a lower motor neuron lesion
Muscle bulk is preserved in both, since neither affects the muscle itself
Atrophy is equally severe in both, since both cause weakness
Atrophy is marked in a lower motor neuron lesion and slight in an upper motor neuron lesion
questions.why: Denervation strips the muscle of both its activity and the trophic support of its motor neuron, so a lower motor neuron lesion wastes the muscle quickly and severely. After an upper motor neuron lesion the muscle keeps its innervation and its reflex activity, so any wasting is mild, late, and mostly from disuse. Reversing the two contradicts that mechanism. Weakness alone does not determine bulk, which is why the two lesions differ despite both causing weakness.
questions.answerText: Atrophy is marked in a lower motor neuron lesion and slight in an upper motor neuron lesion

questions.q: A limb is flaccid and markedly wasted, the tendon reflexes are absent, and twitches are visible in the muscle at rest. Which level is damaged?
options: The lower motor neuron
The upper motor neuron
The cerebellum
The basal ganglia
questions.why: All four findings point the same way: low tone, absent reflexes, severe wasting, and fasciculations are exactly what happens when the final common pathway to the muscle is destroyed. An upper motor neuron lesion would give the opposite tone and reflexes, spasticity and hyperreflexia, along with a Babinski sign and little wasting. Cerebellar disease causes incoordination with normal strength and bulk. Basal ganglia disease alters the amount of movement rather than abolishing reflexes or wasting the muscle.
questions.answerText: The lower motor neuron

questions.q: A limb is weak and stiff, the tendon reflexes are brisk, the great toe goes up when the sole is stroked, and muscle bulk is nearly normal. Which level is damaged?
options: The lower motor neuron
The upper motor neuron
The neuromuscular junction
The muscle fibers themselves
questions.why: Increased tone, hyperreflexia, an extensor plantar response, and preserved bulk are the four features of an upper motor neuron lesion, and they occur together because the spinal reflex machinery survives and is released from descending control. A lower motor neuron lesion would show flaccidity, lost reflexes, fasciculations, and obvious wasting. Neuromuscular junction disease causes fatigable weakness with normal or reduced reflexes and no Babinski sign. Primary muscle disease weakens and wastes muscle without making reflexes brisk.
questions.answerText: The upper motor neuron

questions.q: A herniated disc compresses the L5 ventral root. Which set of findings is expected in the muscles that root supplies?
options: Spastic weakness with brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response on that side
Normal strength with loss of coordination and an intention tremor
Flaccid weakness with reduced reflexes, fasciculations, and wasting over time
Weakness that worsens through the day and recovers fully with rest
questions.why: The ventral root carries the axons of lower motor neurons, so compressing it is a lower motor neuron lesion and produces the flaccid, areflexic, wasting picture with fasciculations in the affected myotome. Spasticity with brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe requires a lesion of descending pathways in the brain or cord, not of a root. Coordination problems with intention tremor point to the cerebellum. Fatigable weakness that recovers with rest is the pattern of neuromuscular junction disease.
questions.answerText: Flaccid weakness with reduced reflexes, fasciculations, and wasting over time

questions.q: A patient has an infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Two months later, which pattern is expected in the affected arm?
options: Increased tone, absent reflexes, and severe wasting
Decreased tone, absent reflexes, visible fasciculations, and severe wasting
Normal tone and reflexes with inaccurate reaching
Increased tone, brisk reflexes, an extensor plantar response, and little wasting
questions.why: The capsule carries upper motor neuron axons, so interrupting them leaves the spinal arc intact but unrestrained, and after the acute phase the arm shows spasticity, hyperreflexia, a Babinski sign, and preserved bulk. The flaccid areflexic set with fasciculations belongs to a lower motor neuron lesion. Normal tone and reflexes with inaccurate reaching is the cerebellar pattern. High tone with absent reflexes is internally inconsistent, since spasticity is produced by the very reflex arc that would have to be broken for reflexes to vanish.
questions.answerText: Increased tone, brisk reflexes, an extensor plantar response, and little wasting

questions.q: Why is muscle wasting so much more severe after a lower motor neuron lesion than after an upper motor neuron lesion?
options: The muscle loses its innervation entirely, along with the activity and trophic support the motor neuron provides
The muscle loses its blood supply, because the artery feeding it runs alongside the motor axon in the nerve
Upper motor neuron lesions cause the muscle to grow rather than shrink
Lower motor neuron lesions dissolve the tendon that anchors the muscle
questions.why: Denervated fibers receive no activation at all and also lose the trophic influence of their motor neuron, so protein breakdown outpaces synthesis and the muscle wastes rapidly. After an upper motor neuron lesion the motor neuron still fires in reflexes and still supports its fibers, so bulk is largely maintained. Blood supply travels with vessels and is not lost with the motor axon. Upper motor neuron lesions do not cause muscle growth, and tendons are not dissolved by denervation.
questions.answerText: The muscle loses its innervation entirely, along with the activity and trophic support the motor neuron provides

questions.q: A healthy four month old infant shows an upgoing great toe when the sole is stroked. What is the best interpretation?
options: It shows that a lower motor neuron lesion is present in the nerves supplying the leg
It is a normal finding at this age, because corticospinal myelination is incomplete
It proves a cerebellar lesion is present
It means the infant has lost sensation in the sole of the foot
questions.why: The downgoing plantar response depends on mature corticospinal control, and that control develops over the first year or two, so an extensor response in an infant is expected and not a sign of disease. In an adult the same response is an upper motor neuron sign, which is a good example of the same finding meaning different things at different ages. It is never a lower motor neuron sign, since those are flaccidity, lost reflexes, fasciculations, and wasting. It is a motor reflex response and does not indicate cerebellar damage or sensory loss.
questions.answerText: It is a normal finding at this age, because corticospinal myelination is incomplete

questions.q: A patient has visible tongue fasciculations and wasted hand muscles, and at the same time the knee reflexes are very brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. What does this combination indicate?
options: Only the lower motor neuron is affected, and the brisk reflexes are a normal variant
Only the upper motor neuron is affected, and the wasting is from disuse alone
Both upper and lower motor neurons are affected
Neither motor level is affected, since the findings contradict each other
questions.why: Sort the findings by level. Fasciculations and marked wasting can only come from lower motor neuron damage, while brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses can only come from upper motor neuron damage, so both levels must be involved. Calling the brisk reflexes a normal variant ignores the extensor plantars, which are not normal in an adult. Disuse atrophy does not produce fasciculations. The findings do not contradict each other; they are in different regions and simply point to disease at two levels at once.
questions.answerText: Both upper and lower motor neurons are affected

questions.q: A cord lesion destroys the ventral horn at C6 on the left and also cuts the descending tracts at that level. Months later, what is expected in the left biceps at C6 and in the left leg?
options: The biceps is spastic with brisk reflexes, while the leg is flaccid and wasted
Both the biceps and the leg are wasted and flaccid, with reflexes lost in the arm and the leg alike
Both the biceps and the leg are spastic with brisk reflexes
The biceps is wasted and flaccid with a lost reflex, while the leg is spastic with brisk reflexes
questions.why: Two mechanisms operate at once. At the level of the lesion the lower motor neurons themselves are gone, so those muscles show the flaccid, wasted, areflexic picture, while below the level the lower motor neurons survive but lose descending control, so those segments show spasticity and hyperreflexia. Flaccidity everywhere would require destruction of motor neurons at every segment. Spasticity everywhere ignores the destroyed C6 ventral horn. The last option reverses the two zones and puts the lower motor neuron signs below rather than at the lesion.
questions.answerText: The biceps is wasted and flaccid with a lost reflex, while the leg is spastic with brisk reflexes

questions.q: Immediately after an acute spinal cord injury, the limbs below the lesion are flaccid and all reflexes are absent, yet weeks later the same limbs are spastic and hyperreflexic. How is this explained?
options: Spinal circuits are temporarily depressed after the injury and later recover, revealing the release from descending control
The lower motor neurons below the injury died at first and then regenerated over the following weeks, restoring the reflexes
The lesion moved from the lower motor neuron level to the upper motor neuron level
The descending tracts regrew across the injury and restored excess tone
questions.why: The lesion was an upper motor neuron lesion the whole time. Acutely, the sudden loss of descending drive leaves spinal neurons below the injury profoundly unexcitable, a state called spinal shock, so the limbs look flaccid and areflexic and can be mistaken for a lower motor neuron problem. As those circuits regain excitability over days to weeks, the intact reflex arcs are unmasked without their descending restraint and the expected spasticity and hyperreflexia appear. Lower motor neurons neither died nor regenerated, the lesion did not move, and severed descending tracts do not regrow across the injury.
questions.answerText: Spinal circuits are temporarily depressed after the injury and later recover, revealing the release from descending control

questions.q: A patient has a wasted calf with visible fasciculations, an absent ankle reflex, reduced tone in the foot, and a downgoing plantar response. Which single site of damage fits all of these findings?
options: The lateral corticospinal tract at T10
The S1 ventral root
The posterior limb of the internal capsule
The primary motor cortex leg area
questions.why: Every finding here is a lower motor neuron finding: wasting, fasciculations, an absent reflex, and low tone, and the downgoing plantar response actively argues against upper motor neuron involvement. Only a lesion of the motor axons leaving the cord fits, and the S1 root supplies the calf and carries the ankle reflex. The corticospinal tract at T10, the internal capsule, and the motor cortex leg area are all upper motor neuron sites, and each would produce spasticity, brisk reflexes, an upgoing toe, and preserved bulk instead.
questions.answerText: The S1 ventral root

questions.q: How many neurons carry the signal from the central nervous system to the effector in a somatic motor pathway?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.why: A single somatic motor neuron runs the whole way, from its cell body in the CNS out to the skeletal muscle fiber, with no synapse in between. Two is the autonomic arrangement, where a preganglionic and a postganglionic neuron are linked at a ganglion. Three and four do not describe any motor output pathway, although a sensory pathway climbing to the cortex does use three neurons in series.
questions.answerText: One

questions.q: How many neurons in series make up an autonomic motor pathway from the central nervous system to the effector?
options: One
Four
Two
Three
questions.why: Every autonomic pathway uses a preganglionic neuron whose cell body sits in the CNS and a postganglionic neuron whose cell body sits in a ganglion outside the CNS. One neuron is the somatic pattern that runs straight to skeletal muscle. Three and four overcount, since only one peripheral synapse exists between the CNS and the target organ.
questions.answerText: Two

questions.q: Where do the two neurons of an autonomic pathway synapse with each other?
options: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
In an autonomic ganglion outside the central nervous system
In the dorsal root ganglion
Within the wall of the effector cell itself
questions.why: The peripheral synapse happens in an autonomic ganglion, a cluster of postganglionic cell bodies sitting outside the CNS, which is exactly the relay the somatic system lacks. The ventral horn holds the cell bodies of preganglionic and somatic motor neurons, not the relay itself. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies and has no synapse in it at all, and no synapse occurs inside the effector cell.
questions.answerText: In an autonomic ganglion outside the central nervous system

questions.q: Which tissue is the only effector of the somatic motor system?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Glandular epithelium
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: Somatic motor neurons end on skeletal muscle fibers and on nothing else, which is why the division is often called the voluntary motor system. Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glandular epithelium are the three autonomic effectors and receive no somatic innervation at all.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle

questions.q: Which set of tissues does the autonomic nervous system innervate?
options: Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands
Skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle only
Smooth muscle and skeletal muscle only
Glands and skeletal muscle only
questions.why: The autonomic output reaches cardiac muscle, smooth muscle everywhere in the body, and secretory glands, which is the full list of involuntary effectors. Every wrong option smuggles skeletal muscle into the autonomic list, and skeletal muscle is somatic territory. Skeletal muscle blood vessels are autonomic, but the vessel wall is smooth muscle, not the muscle fibers themselves.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands

questions.q: Where is the cell body of an autonomic preganglionic neuron located?
options: In a paravertebral ganglion
In a ganglion near the target organ
In the brainstem or spinal cord
In the wall of the innervated organ
questions.why: The preganglionic cell body is inside the CNS, in a brainstem nucleus or the lateral horn of the spinal cord, and its axon leaves to find a ganglion. Paravertebral ganglia and ganglia near the target organ hold postganglionic cell bodies, which are the second neuron. Cell bodies in the organ wall belong to enteric neurons or terminal ganglia, again postganglionic.
questions.answerText: In the brainstem or spinal cord

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter does a somatic motor neuron release onto skeletal muscle, and at which receptor does it act?
options: Norepinephrine at a beta-1 receptor
Acetylcholine at a muscarinic receptor
Norepinephrine at an alpha-1 receptor
Acetylcholine at a nicotinic receptor
questions.why: The neuromuscular junction uses acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors, which are ligand gated cation channels that depolarize the muscle fiber quickly and reliably. Muscarinic receptors also bind acetylcholine but they sit on parasympathetic target organs, never on skeletal muscle. Norepinephrine at beta-1 or alpha-1 receptors is a sympathetic postganglionic arrangement and has no role at the neuromuscular junction.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine at a nicotinic receptor

questions.q: What effect can a somatic motor neuron have on the skeletal muscle fiber it innervates?
options: Excitation only
Inhibition only
Excitation or inhibition depending on the receptor
Neither, since it only sets resting tone
questions.why: Somatic motor neurons are always excitatory, so the only way to relax a skeletal muscle is to stop firing on it. Autonomic output is the branch that can either excite or inhibit, because the receptor on the target decides the response. Inhibition only is never true of a motor neuron, and setting resting tone without excitation misdescribes what the neuromuscular junction does.
questions.answerText: Excitation only

questions.q: A fiber leaves the spinal cord, synapses on a second neuron in a ganglion, and that second neuron ends on a salivary gland. How is this pathway classified?
options: Somatic, because the fiber originates in the spinal cord
Autonomic, because it uses two neurons and ends on a gland
Somatic, because it includes a peripheral ganglion
Autonomic, because the first neuron is myelinated
questions.why: Two features settle it at once: a peripheral synapse in a ganglion and an effector that is a gland rather than skeletal muscle. Originating in the spinal cord does not distinguish the systems, since both preganglionic and somatic motor cell bodies live there. A peripheral ganglion is the opposite of a somatic feature, and myelination of the first neuron is true but is not the defining criterion asked for.
questions.answerText: Autonomic, because it uses two neurons and ends on a gland

questions.q: A drug blocks nicotinic receptors only in autonomic ganglia and does not reach the neuromuscular junction. What happens to voluntary movement of the biceps?
options: It becomes weak, because the relay through the ganglion has been lost
It becomes uncoordinated, because resting tone in the muscle is lost
It is unaffected, because the somatic pathway has no ganglion
It stops entirely, because acetylcholine can no longer act anywhere
questions.why: The somatic motor neuron runs from the cord to the muscle with no intervening synapse, so a drug confined to ganglia has nothing to block in that pathway. Weakness from a lost relay assumes a ganglion that does not exist in the somatic route. Loss of tone and complete arrest both assume the drug reached the neuromuscular junction, which the question rules out.
questions.answerText: It is unaffected, because the somatic pathway has no ganglion

questions.q: A toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction only. What happens to intestinal smooth muscle?
options: It becomes flaccid along with skeletal muscle
It contracts continuously without relaxing
It loses all spontaneous activity
It continues to contract normally
questions.why: Intestinal smooth muscle is an autonomic effector, so a toxin restricted to the neuromuscular junction never touches it and gut motility carries on. Flaccidity along with skeletal muscle mistakes smooth muscle for a somatic target. Continuous contraction and loss of spontaneous activity both assume the toxin altered autonomic or enteric input, which it did not.
questions.answerText: It continues to contract normally

questions.q: A somatic motor nerve to a limb muscle is cut. What is the immediate consequence for that muscle?
options: Complete flaccid paralysis, because it has no other motor input
Reduced but continuing contraction driven by the opposing autonomic division
Continuous contraction produced by unopposed excitatory input
Normal contraction maintained by pacemaker cells inside the muscle itself
questions.why: Skeletal muscle is innervated by one excitatory neuron and nothing else, so cutting that neuron leaves the fiber with no way to be activated. There is no opposing division for skeletal muscle, which is what makes it different from a dually innervated organ. Skeletal muscle fibers also have no pacemaker activity of their own, unlike cardiac and much smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: Complete flaccid paralysis, because it has no other motor input

questions.q: Which structure would you find in a pathway to the stomach but never in a pathway to the quadriceps?
options: A myelinated axon leaving the spinal cord
A peripheral ganglion containing a synapse
A terminal that releases acetylcholine
A neuronal cell body located inside the central nervous system
questions.why: The peripheral ganglion is the structural signature of the autonomic route, since the somatic neuron reaches its muscle without relaying anywhere. Myelinated axons leaving the cord, acetylcholine release, and CNS cell bodies all occur in both systems, so none of them can separate the two. Acetylcholine in particular is used by every preganglionic fiber and by every somatic motor neuron.
questions.answerText: A peripheral ganglion containing a synapse

questions.q: Why does a signal leaving the spinal cord reach the heart with more synaptic delay than a signal leaving the cord reaches a leg muscle?
options: Cardiac muscle responds more slowly to depolarization than skeletal muscle does
The autonomic route includes an extra synapse at the ganglion
The heart is a greater distance from the spinal cord than the muscles of the leg
Autonomic axons carry an action potential of smaller amplitude
questions.why: Each chemical synapse costs about half a millisecond, and the autonomic pathway pays that cost twice, once in the ganglion and once at the target, while the somatic pathway pays it once. Distance is not the explanation, and the heart is in fact closer to the thoracic cord than the foot is. Action potential size does not vary with the pathway, since action potentials are all or none, and the properties of the effector do not change the delay in the nerve.
questions.answerText: The autonomic route includes an extra synapse at the ganglion

questions.q: Autonomic input to an organ is removed surgically. Why does the organ usually keep working at some level while a denervated skeletal muscle does not?
options: Autonomic axons regrow across the cut within a few minutes
The organ on the opposite side takes over the lost function
Cardiac and smooth muscle generate their own activity, while skeletal muscle cannot
Glands and smooth muscle are not truly innervated in the first place
questions.why: Autonomic effectors modulate an activity they already have, since pacemaker cells in the heart and gut fire on their own, so removing the nerve changes the rate rather than abolishing the function. Skeletal muscle has no intrinsic activity and is silent without its motor neuron. Axons do not regrow in minutes, no contralateral takeover exists for visceral organs, and glands are genuinely innervated.
questions.answerText: Cardiac and smooth muscle generate their own activity, while skeletal muscle cannot

questions.q: A toxin prevents acetylcholine release from every cholinergic terminal in the body. Predict the effect on skeletal muscle contraction and on transmission through autonomic ganglia.
options: Skeletal muscle is paralyzed and ganglionic transmission fails in both autonomic divisions
Skeletal muscle is paralyzed but transmission through both sets of autonomic ganglia continues normally
Skeletal muscle is spared but ganglionic transmission fails
Only parasympathetic ganglia fail, since sympathetic ganglia use norepinephrine
questions.why: Acetylcholine is the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction and at every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic alike, so blocking its release takes out both. Sparing the ganglia forgets that all preganglionic fibers are cholinergic. Sparing skeletal muscle forgets the neuromuscular junction, and the claim that sympathetic ganglia run on norepinephrine confuses the preganglionic transmitter with the postganglionic one, since norepinephrine is released at the sympathetic target rather than in the ganglion.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle is paralyzed and ganglionic transmission fails in both autonomic divisions

questions.q: A researcher traces a nerve to the bladder and finds the first cell body in the sacral spinal cord, a synapse in a ganglion in the bladder wall, and a short second fiber ending on smooth muscle. Which conclusion is supported?
options: This is a somatic motor pathway, since the first cell body sits inside the spinal cord
This is a sensory pathway, since the ganglion lies outside the central nervous system
This is an autonomic pathway, since it has two neurons and a smooth muscle effector
This is a somatic pathway, since the second fiber is short
questions.why: Two neurons in series, a peripheral ganglion, and smooth muscle as the target are together decisive for an autonomic motor pathway. A spinal cord cell body is common to both motor systems and proves nothing on its own. A peripheral ganglion is also present in sensory pathways, but a dorsal root ganglion contains no synapse and does not end on smooth muscle, and the length of the second fiber is a divisional clue rather than a somatic one.
questions.answerText: This is an autonomic pathway, since it has two neurons and a smooth muscle effector

questions.q: After a complete spinal cord transection at T6, a patient has no voluntary leg movement, yet the heart continues to beat and the intestines still move contents along. What best explains the difference between the two effectors?
options: The heart and gut are innervated by somatic motor nerves that were spared below the level of the injury, while the leg nerves were not
The legs receive dual autonomic innervation, and the transection interrupted both of those inputs at the same time
Skeletal muscle depends entirely on descending somatic drive, while cardiac and smooth muscle have intrinsic pacemaker activity that autonomic nerves only modulate
Autonomic axons conduct faster than somatic axons and can carry their signals across the damaged segment of the cord
questions.why: The heart and gut set their own baseline rhythm, so losing part of their autonomic input alters how fast they work rather than whether they work, while a skeletal muscle with no command from above simply does not contract. The heart and gut have no somatic innervation to spare. Skeletal muscle is never dually innervated, and autonomic axons are in fact slower, being thinly myelinated or unmyelinated, and no axon crosses a complete transection.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle depends entirely on descending somatic drive, while cardiac and smooth muscle have intrinsic pacemaker activity that autonomic nerves only modulate

questions.q: Two nerves are recorded during a reflex. Nerve A shows one action potential from cord to effector with a single synaptic delay at the end. Nerve B shows a delay partway along the route and a second delay at the effector. Which effectors are the most likely targets of A and B?
options: A ends on cardiac muscle and B ends on skeletal muscle
A ends on a gland and B ends on skeletal muscle
A ends on smooth muscle and B ends on cardiac muscle
A ends on skeletal muscle and B ends on a gland
questions.why: A single terminal delay marks a one neuron somatic route, whose only possible target is skeletal muscle, while a mid route delay marks the ganglionic synapse of a two neuron autonomic route, whose targets are cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands. The options that put cardiac or smooth muscle on the single delay route forget that no visceral effector is reached without a ganglion. The option placing skeletal muscle on the two delay route makes the same error in reverse.
questions.answerText: A ends on skeletal muscle and B ends on a gland

questions.q: From which spinal segments do sympathetic preganglionic fibers leave the central nervous system?
options: T1 through L2
C1 through C8
S2 through S4
L3 through S1
questions.why: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral horn from the first thoracic through the second lumbar segment, which is why the division is called thoracolumbar. S2 through S4 is the sacral half of the parasympathetic outflow. The cervical and lower lumbar segments contain no autonomic preganglionic cell bodies, although sympathetic fibers do travel up the chain to reach the head.
questions.answerText: T1 through L2

questions.q: Where does parasympathetic output leave the central nervous system?
options: From the thoracic and upper lumbar segments of the spinal cord only
From the brainstem by cranial nerves and from spinal segments S2 to S4
From the cervical segments of the spinal cord and from the brainstem
From every spinal segment along the whole length of the cord
questions.why: The parasympathetic division is craniosacral, leaving in cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X and in the sacral roots from S2 to S4. Thoracic and lumbar outflow is the sympathetic pattern. The cervical cord carries no preganglionic cell bodies of either division, and no division leaves at every level.
questions.answerText: From the brainstem by cranial nerves and from spinal segments S2 to S4

questions.q: Where are most sympathetic ganglia located?
options: Inside the wall of each individual target organ
Within the brainstem, next to the nuclei of the cranial nerves
In a chain alongside the vertebral column, close to the spinal cord
Scattered through the mesentery, just outside the wall of each organ
questions.why: Sympathetic ganglia lie in the paravertebral chain flanking the vertebral column, with a few prevertebral ganglia in front of the aorta, so the relay happens near the cord rather than near the target. Ganglia inside the organ wall are the parasympathetic pattern. Ganglia are by definition outside the CNS, so the brainstem option cannot be right.
questions.answerText: In a chain alongside the vertebral column, close to the spinal cord

questions.q: Where are parasympathetic ganglia located?
options: In a chain beside the vertebral column
In the lateral horn of the spinal cord
In front of the abdominal aorta
In or very near the wall of the target organ
questions.why: Parasympathetic ganglia sit on or in the organ they supply, which is why the postganglionic fiber is so short. The paravertebral chain and the prevertebral ganglia in front of the aorta are both sympathetic locations. The lateral horn is inside the spinal cord and holds preganglionic cell bodies, not a ganglion.
questions.answerText: In or very near the wall of the target organ

questions.q: In the sympathetic division, how do the lengths of the preganglionic and postganglionic fibers compare?
options: The preganglionic fiber is short and the postganglionic fiber is long
The preganglionic fiber is long and the postganglionic fiber is short
Both fibers are about the same length
Both fibers are short, since the ganglion sits midway
questions.why: Because the sympathetic ganglion is near the cord, the first fiber has only a short distance to travel and the second must cover the rest of the way to the organ. The long preganglionic and short postganglionic pattern is parasympathetic, and it follows directly from where that division puts its ganglia. Equal lengths would require a ganglion halfway to every organ, which neither division uses.
questions.answerText: The preganglionic fiber is short and the postganglionic fiber is long

questions.q: Which nerve carries most of the parasympathetic supply to the thoracic and abdominal organs?
options: The phrenic nerve
The vagus nerve
The greater splanchnic nerve
The pelvic splanchnic nerve
questions.why: The vagus, cranial nerve X, supplies the heart, lungs, stomach, and most of the intestine, carrying the great majority of parasympathetic traffic below the neck. The greater splanchnic nerve is sympathetic preganglionic fiber heading for prevertebral ganglia. The pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic but serve only the distal colon and pelvic organs, and the phrenic nerve is somatic motor to the diaphragm.
questions.answerText: The vagus nerve

questions.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic activity on heart rate?
options: It raises heart rate
It slows heart rate
It leaves heart rate unchanged but raises contractility
It raises heart rate only during inspiration
questions.why: Vagal activity slows depolarization of the sinoatrial node, so the firing rate and therefore the heart rate falls. Raising heart rate is the sympathetic effect. The parasympathetic division has little influence on ventricular contractility, so holding rate steady while raising contractility reverses the true pattern, and the inspiratory rise in rate is caused by reduced vagal activity rather than increased vagal activity.
questions.answerText: It slows heart rate

questions.q: What is the effect of sympathetic activity on gastrointestinal motility and secretion?
options: Motility increases and secretion decreases
Both increase
Both decrease
Motility decreases and secretion increases
questions.why: Sympathetic output turns digestion down as a unit, slowing smooth muscle in the gut wall and reducing glandular secretion while blood is directed elsewhere. Increases in both are the parasympathetic pattern of rest and digest. The two split options describe a mismatch that does not occur, since the division acts on motility and secretion in the same direction.
questions.answerText: Both decrease

questions.q: A student begins to sprint and sympathetic output to the heart rises sharply. Predict the change in heart rate.
options: Heart rate falls
Heart rate rises
Heart rate is unchanged while stroke volume falls
Heart rate rises only after the sprint ends
questions.why: Sympathetic fibers to the sinoatrial node speed its pacemaker depolarization, so more sympathetic traffic means a faster rate, and the change begins within a few beats. A fall in rate would require increased vagal activity instead. Stroke volume rises rather than falls under sympathetic drive, and the response happens during the effort, not after it.
questions.answerText: Heart rate rises

questions.q: After a large meal, parasympathetic outflow to the gut increases. Predict what happens to intestinal motility and glandular secretion.
options: Both decrease
Motility increases while secretion falls
Both increase
Motility falls while secretion rises
questions.why: Parasympathetic activity is the digestive setting, raising smooth muscle activity in the gut wall and stimulating secretion so food is moved and broken down. Decreases in both would follow sympathetic activation instead. The mixed options split two responses that this division always drives in the same direction.
questions.answerText: Both increase

questions.q: In an anesthetized animal the vagus nerve is stimulated electrically. Predict the effect on the sinoatrial node.
options: It depolarizes more slowly, so the heart rate falls
It depolarizes faster, so the heart rate rises
It stops responding to any input at all
It is unaffected, since the vagus supplies only the lungs
questions.why: Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine on the sinoatrial node, slowing its pacemaker drift toward threshold and lowering the rate. Faster depolarization is what sympathetic stimulation produces. The node keeps responding to other inputs during vagal stimulation, and the vagus supplies the heart as well as the lungs and abdominal viscera.
questions.answerText: It depolarizes more slowly, so the heart rate falls

questions.q: A lesion destroys the lateral horn neurons from T1 to L2 while leaving the brainstem and sacral cord intact. Which division is lost?
options: The parasympathetic division
Both divisions equally
The sympathetic division
Neither, since these neurons are somatic
questions.why: T1 to L2 is exactly the thoracolumbar outflow, so destroying those lateral horn cell bodies removes the sympathetic preganglionic supply. The parasympathetic division survives because its cell bodies are craniosacral and the lesion spares both the brainstem and S2 to S4. Lateral horn neurons are autonomic preganglionic, not somatic, which is why voluntary movement would be relatively preserved.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: A dissection shows a very long preganglionic fiber that finally synapses in a small ganglion sitting on the wall of the bladder. Which division is this?
options: Sympathetic, because the first fiber travels a long distance
Parasympathetic, because the ganglion is at the target organ
Sympathetic, because the bladder sits among the pelvic organs
Parasympathetic, because every long autonomic fiber is cholinergic
questions.why: Ganglion position is the reliable clue: a relay in the organ wall means a parasympathetic pathway, and the long first fiber follows from that geometry. A long fiber alone does not identify a division, since sympathetic postganglionic fibers are long too. The bladder receives both divisions, so its location settles nothing, and being cholinergic does not track fiber length, since every preganglionic fiber in both divisions releases acetylcholine.
questions.answerText: Parasympathetic, because the ganglion is at the target organ

questions.q: Why does a burst of sympathetic activity usually affect many organs at once while a burst of parasympathetic activity is more targeted?
options: Sympathetic axons conduct much faster than parasympathetic axons do, so more organs respond
Parasympathetic fibers release a weaker neurotransmitter with a smaller effect on the target
Each sympathetic preganglionic fiber diverges onto many postganglionic neurons in the chain
Sympathetic ganglia contain no synapses at all, so incoming signals pass straight through them
questions.why: A single sympathetic preganglionic fiber can synapse on dozens of postganglionic neurons spread up and down the paravertebral chain, so one input fans out to many targets, while a parasympathetic fiber ends in a ganglion serving one organ. Conduction speed does not determine how many organs respond. Acetylcholine is not a weaker transmitter, and sympathetic ganglia certainly contain synapses, which is where the divergence happens.
questions.answerText: Each sympathetic preganglionic fiber diverges onto many postganglionic neurons in the chain

questions.q: A person is startled by a loud noise. Predict the simultaneous change in heart rate and in gastrointestinal motility.
options: Heart rate falls and gastrointestinal motility rises
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility rise
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility fall
Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls
questions.why: A startle recruits the sympathetic division, which speeds the sinoatrial node while inhibiting gut smooth muscle, shifting resources from digestion to circulation. Falling rate with rising motility is the parasympathetic pattern seen after a meal. The two options that move both variables the same way miss the point that this division pushes the heart and the gut in opposite directions.
questions.answerText: Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls

questions.q: A drug blocks synaptic transmission only in ganglia located within organ walls and does not reach the paravertebral chain. Predict the effect on resting heart rate and on gastric motility.
options: Heart rate rises and gastric motility falls
Heart rate falls and gastric motility rises
Both are unchanged, since the chain is intact
Heart rate falls and gastric motility is unchanged
questions.why: Ganglia in organ walls are parasympathetic, so the drug removes vagal influence while leaving sympathetic transmission through the chain untouched. Losing the brake on the sinoatrial node lets the rate climb, and losing the parasympathetic drive to the stomach lowers motility. A slower heart with a more active stomach would describe losing sympathetic input instead. Nothing is unchanged, because the intact chain is now unopposed.
questions.answerText: Heart rate rises and gastric motility falls

questions.q: Both vagus nerves are cut in an experimental animal. Predict the resting heart rate and the gastric secretion rate compared with before the cut.
options: Heart rate is lower and gastric secretion is higher
Heart rate is higher and gastric secretion is higher
Heart rate is higher and gastric secretion is lower
Both are unchanged, since sympathetic input compensates
questions.why: The vagus carries parasympathetic fibers to both organs, so cutting it removes a slowing influence at the heart and a stimulating influence at the stomach, and the two effects therefore go in opposite directions. A lower rate would follow from losing sympathetic rather than vagal input. Higher secretion contradicts the loss of the main stimulus to gastric glands, and no compensation restores a signal the stomach no longer receives.
questions.answerText: Heart rate is higher and gastric secretion is lower

questions.q: A patient has a lesion confined to spinal segments S2 to S4. Which organ is most likely to show impaired autonomic control, and why is the heart spared?
options: The stomach is impaired, and the heart is spared because it receives sympathetic fibers only
The distal colon is impaired, and the heart is spared because its parasympathetic supply is vagal
The heart is impaired as well, since every parasympathetic fiber in the body leaves at sacral levels
The bronchi are impaired, and the heart is spared because it contains no autonomic ganglia
questions.why: Sacral preganglionic fibers in the pelvic splanchnic nerves supply the distal colon and pelvic organs, while the heart, stomach, and bronchi get their parasympathetic supply from the vagus, which leaves the brainstem well above the lesion. The stomach and bronchi are therefore spared for the same reason the heart is. The heart is not sympathetic only, since vagal fibers reach the sinoatrial node, and parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral rather than purely sacral.
questions.answerText: The distal colon is impaired, and the heart is spared because its parasympathetic supply is vagal

questions.q: During a frightening event, preganglionic fibers from the upper thoracic cord fire into the paravertebral chain. Trace the consequence for the heart and explain why the effect outlasts the moment of fright.
options: Postganglionic fibers slow the sinoatrial node, and a vagal rebound afterward prolongs that slowing for minutes
Postganglionic fibers speed the sinoatrial node, and circulating catecholamines from the adrenal medulla prolong the effect
Preganglionic fibers reach the sinoatrial node directly, so the whole effect ends the moment the firing stops
The chain relays into the vagus nerve, which then speeds the sinoatrial node for several minutes afterward
questions.why: Thoracic preganglionic fibers synapse in the chain, postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine on the sinoatrial node and raise the rate, and the same preganglionic outflow drives the adrenal medulla to release catecholamines into the blood, which are cleared slowly and keep the rate up after the alarm passes. Slowing the node is the vagal response. No preganglionic fiber reaches the heart directly, and the sympathetic chain does not relay into the vagus, which is a separate cranial nerve carrying the opposing division.
questions.answerText: Postganglionic fibers speed the sinoatrial node, and circulating catecholamines from the adrenal medulla prolong the effect

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter binds to nicotinic receptors?
options: Acetylcholine
Norepinephrine
Epinephrine
Dopamine
questions.why: Nicotinic receptors are cholinergic, so acetylcholine is their ligand, and the name comes from nicotine mimicking acetylcholine at this site. Norepinephrine and epinephrine bind adrenergic receptors, the alpha and beta family. Dopamine has its own receptors and is not the transmitter at ganglia or at the neuromuscular junction.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine

questions.q: Where are nicotinic receptors found in the autonomic nervous system?
options: On sympathetic ganglion neurons only
On parasympathetic ganglion neurons only
On the postganglionic neurons of every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic
On the smooth muscle and gland cells at the end of every autonomic pathway, in both divisions
questions.why: Both divisions use acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors for the ganglionic synapse, which is the one step the two divisions share, and the same receptor appears at the skeletal neuromuscular junction. Restricting nicotinic receptors to one division misses that shared step. Target organ smooth muscle carries muscarinic or adrenergic receptors instead, so the nicotinic receptor is a relay receptor rather than an effector receptor.
questions.answerText: On the postganglionic neurons of every autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic

questions.q: Which receptor does acetylcholine act on at a parasympathetic target organ?
options: A nicotinic receptor
A muscarinic receptor
A beta-1 receptor
An alpha-1 receptor
questions.why: Parasympathetic postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors on cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands. Nicotinic receptors do bind acetylcholine, but in the autonomic system they sit in the ganglion, one synapse earlier. Beta-1 and alpha-1 are adrenergic and bind norepinephrine, so they belong to sympathetic targets.
questions.answerText: A muscarinic receptor

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter do sympathetic postganglionic fibers release onto alpha and beta receptors?
options: Acetylcholine
Serotonin
Glutamate
Norepinephrine
questions.why: Sympathetic postganglionic terminals are adrenergic and release norepinephrine, which binds alpha and beta receptors on the target tissue. Acetylcholine is the transmitter one step earlier, in the ganglion, and also at parasympathetic targets. Serotonin and glutamate are central nervous system transmitters and are not used at autonomic effectors.
questions.answerText: Norepinephrine

questions.q: Which adrenergic receptor subtype is the dominant one on cardiac muscle?
options: Alpha-1
Beta-1
Beta-2
Alpha-2
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors dominate on the sinoatrial node and the ventricular myocardium, so norepinephrine there raises rate and force of contraction. Beta-2 receptors are the ones on bronchiolar smooth muscle and on the vascular smooth muscle of skeletal muscle. Alpha-1 receptors are on most vascular smooth muscle, and alpha-2 receptors act mainly as presynaptic autoreceptors.
questions.answerText: Beta-1

questions.q: Which receptor on bronchiolar smooth muscle produces relaxation when it is activated?
options: Alpha-1
