Muscarinic
Beta-2
Nicotinic
questions.why: Beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle relax the bronchioles and widen the airway, which is why circulating epinephrine eases breathing. Muscarinic receptors are also on airway smooth muscle but do the opposite, constricting the bronchioles. Alpha-1 receptors are found on most vascular smooth muscle rather than on airways, and nicotinic receptors are on ganglion neurons and skeletal muscle, not on smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: Beta-2

questions.q: Which receptor on most vascular smooth muscle produces vasoconstriction?
options: Beta-1
Beta-2
Muscarinic
Alpha-1
questions.why: Alpha-1 receptors dominate on the smooth muscle of most arterioles, so norepinephrine narrows them and raises resistance. Beta-2 receptors on the vessels of skeletal muscle produce the opposite response, dilation, which is why blood is redistributed toward working muscle. Beta-1 receptors are the cardiac subtype, and vascular smooth muscle in general receives no parasympathetic muscarinic innervation.
questions.answerText: Alpha-1

questions.q: How does a nicotinic receptor produce its effect on the cell?
options: It is a ligand gated ion channel that opens and lets cations enter
It is a G protein coupled receptor that changes cyclic AMP
It is an enzyme linked receptor that phosphorylates a target protein
It enters the cell and binds DNA to change transcription
questions.why: The nicotinic receptor is the channel itself, so binding acetylcholine opens a pore, cations flow in, and the cell depolarizes within milliseconds. Muscarinic and adrenergic receptors are the G protein coupled ones, which act through second messengers and are therefore slower. Enzyme linked receptors and intracellular DNA binding receptors belong to hormones such as insulin and cortisol, not to fast synaptic transmission.
questions.answerText: It is a ligand gated ion channel that opens and lets cations enter

questions.q: Acetylcholine is released onto muscarinic receptors on the sinoatrial node. Predict the change in heart rate.
options: Heart rate rises
Heart rate falls
Heart rate is unchanged but contractility rises
Heart rate rises and then falls below baseline
questions.why: Muscarinic activation on the node slows its pacemaker depolarization, so threshold is reached less often and the rate drops. A rise in rate would require beta-1 activation by norepinephrine instead. Contractility is a beta-1 effect on the ventricles, and there is no biphasic rise before the fall.
questions.answerText: Heart rate falls

questions.q: Norepinephrine binds beta-1 receptors in the heart. Predict the effect on rate and on force of contraction.
options: Rate increases and force decreases
Both rate and force decrease
Both rate and force increase
Rate is unchanged and force increases
questions.why: Beta-1 activation raises cyclic AMP in cardiac cells, which speeds the pacemaker current in the node and increases calcium entry in working myocardium, so the heart beats both faster and harder. Falling rate and force would follow muscarinic activation. Rate and force move together under beta-1 stimulation, so the split options describe a dissociation that does not occur here.
questions.answerText: Both rate and force increase

questions.q: Epinephrine activates beta-2 receptors on the arterioles supplying skeletal muscle. Predict the change in vessel diameter and in flow to that muscle.
options: The vessels dilate and flow increases
The vessels constrict and flow decreases
The vessels constrict and flow increases
Diameter is unchanged and flow falls
questions.why: Beta-2 receptors relax vascular smooth muscle in skeletal muscle beds, so the arterioles widen, resistance falls, and more blood reaches the working muscle. Constriction is what alpha-1 activation would do, and alpha-1 is the dominant receptor in most other vascular beds. Constriction with increased flow is internally contradictory, since narrowing a vessel raises resistance and lowers flow at a given pressure.
questions.answerText: The vessels dilate and flow increases

questions.q: Norepinephrine reaches alpha-1 receptors on arterioles in the skin. Predict the change in vessel radius and in resistance in that bed.
options: Radius rises and resistance falls
Radius falls and resistance falls
Radius rises and resistance rises
Radius falls and resistance rises
questions.why: Alpha-1 activation contracts vascular smooth muscle, narrowing the arteriole, and resistance climbs steeply as radius falls. Widening with falling resistance is the beta-2 response, which occurs in skeletal muscle vessels rather than skin. The two mismatched options break the inverse relationship between radius and resistance that holds in every vascular bed.
questions.answerText: Radius falls and resistance rises

questions.q: Acetylcholine acts on muscarinic receptors on bronchiolar smooth muscle. Predict the effect on airway diameter.
options: The airway widens
The airway narrows
Diameter does not change, since airways lack muscarinic receptors
The airway widens only during expiration
questions.why: Muscarinic activation contracts airway smooth muscle, so the bronchioles narrow and resistance to airflow rises, which is the parasympathetic setting for the lungs. Widening is the beta-2 response to epinephrine on the same muscle, and holding those two opposite responses apart is the point of this pair. Airways do carry muscarinic receptors, and the response does not depend on the phase of breathing.
questions.answerText: The airway narrows

questions.q: A receptor on a postganglionic neuron responds to acetylcholine within a few milliseconds by opening a cation channel. Which receptor is it?
options: A muscarinic receptor
A beta-2 receptor
A nicotinic receptor
An alpha-1 receptor
questions.why: Speed plus a directly gated cation channel identifies the nicotinic receptor, which is why ganglionic transmission is fast and reliable. Muscarinic receptors also bind acetylcholine but work through G proteins, so their responses take longer and can be inhibitory. Beta-2 and alpha-1 receptors bind norepinephrine rather than acetylcholine and are also G protein coupled.
questions.answerText: A nicotinic receptor

questions.q: A cell responds to norepinephrine with contraction of its smooth muscle. The response is blocked by an agent selective for alpha-1 receptors. Where is this cell most likely located?
options: In the sinoatrial node
In the wall of an arteriole
In a bronchiole
In an autonomic ganglion
questions.why: Alpha-1 receptors driving contraction of smooth muscle is the signature of most vascular beds, where norepinephrine causes vasoconstriction. The sinoatrial node responds to norepinephrine through beta-1 receptors, and it is cardiac muscle rather than smooth muscle. Bronchiolar smooth muscle is dominated by beta-2 receptors that relax it, and ganglion neurons carry nicotinic receptors and are not muscle at all.
questions.answerText: In the wall of an arteriole

questions.q: An agent activates nicotinic receptors everywhere they occur. Predict what happens at autonomic ganglia and at skeletal muscle.
options: Only the sympathetic ganglia are driven, and skeletal muscle is left completely unaffected
Both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia are stimulated, and skeletal muscle is depolarized
Only the parasympathetic ganglia are driven, and skeletal muscle relaxes instead of contracting
Both sets of ganglia are unaffected, while skeletal muscle is strongly depolarized throughout the body
questions.why: Nicotinic receptors sit at every autonomic ganglion in both divisions and at the neuromuscular junction, so a nonselective activator drives all three sites at once and the visceral result is a confusing mixture of sympathetic and parasympathetic signs. Limiting the effect to one division ignores that both use the same ganglionic receptor. Sparing the ganglia or the muscle each ignores one of the two locations where this receptor is found.
questions.answerText: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia are stimulated, and skeletal muscle is depolarized

questions.q: Circulating epinephrine reaches both the skin, where alpha-1 receptors dominate, and skeletal muscle vessels, where beta-2 receptors dominate. Predict how blood flow is distributed between the two beds.
options: Both beds receive more flow, since epinephrine dilates all vessels
Skin flow rises and skeletal muscle flow falls
Both beds receive less flow, since epinephrine constricts all vessels
Skin flow falls and skeletal muscle flow rises
questions.why: The same hormone produces opposite responses because the receptor on the tissue decides the outcome, so alpha-1 constriction in skin and beta-2 dilation in muscle together shunt blood toward the muscle that needs it. Treating epinephrine as a universal dilator or a universal constrictor misses that its effect is receptor dependent. Reversing the two beds inverts which receptor sits where.
questions.answerText: Skin flow falls and skeletal muscle flow rises

questions.q: A substance raises heart rate and relaxes bronchiolar smooth muscle but produces no constriction of skin arterioles. Which receptor family is it acting on?
options: Beta receptors
Alpha receptors
Muscarinic receptors
Nicotinic receptors
questions.why: Working back from the results, a faster heart points to beta-1 and relaxed airways to beta-2, while the absence of skin vasoconstriction rules out alpha-1 activity, so the agent is beta selective. Alpha activation would have constricted the skin vessels. Muscarinic activation would have slowed the heart and narrowed the airways, the reverse of both findings, and nicotinic activation would have driven both divisions at the ganglia rather than producing this clean pattern.
questions.answerText: Beta receptors

questions.q: Parasympathetic terminals release acetylcholine onto both the sinoatrial node and intestinal smooth muscle, yet the node slows while the intestine becomes more active. What accounts for the opposite outcomes?
options: The intestine receives its acetylcholine from sympathetic rather than parasympathetic fibers
The two tissues carry different muscarinic receptor subtypes coupled to different intracellular pathways
Acetylcholine is broken down much faster at the sinoatrial node than it is in the intestinal wall
The sinoatrial node receives nicotinic input while the intestine receives muscarinic input instead
questions.why: The transmitter does not carry the instruction, the receptor does, and the muscarinic subtypes on cardiac and intestinal tissue couple to different G protein pathways, one that slows pacemaker depolarization and one that promotes contraction. Speed of breakdown changes how long a response lasts, not its direction. Sympathetic fibers to the gut release norepinephrine, and the sinoatrial node is not a ganglion, so it carries muscarinic rather than nicotinic receptors.
questions.answerText: The two tissues carry different muscarinic receptor subtypes coupled to different intracellular pathways

questions.q: What does it mean to say an organ is dually innervated?
options: It receives input from both the sympathetic and the parasympathetic division
It receives input from somatic motor neurons as well as autonomic neurons
It receives two separate preganglionic fibers that converge on a single ganglion
It is supplied by nerves arising from both the left and the right side of the cord
questions.why: Dual innervation means both autonomic divisions reach the same target, which usually lets the organ be pushed in either direction. Somatic plus autonomic input does not occur on the same effector, since skeletal muscle is somatic only. Convergence in a ganglion and bilateral supply are real features of nerve anatomy but neither one is what the term describes.
questions.answerText: It receives input from both the sympathetic and the parasympathetic division

questions.q: What is autonomic tone?
options: The maximum firing rate a division is able to reach
The steady background firing rate a division maintains at rest
The stiffness a muscle develops when it is stretched continuously
The delay between a stimulus arriving and the organ responding to it
questions.why: Autonomic fibers fire continuously at a low baseline rate, so the nervous system can raise or lower an organ activity simply by changing that ongoing rate. The maximum firing rate describes a ceiling, not the resting baseline. Stiffness from stretch is muscle tone in a mechanical sense, a different use of the word, and the delay to a response is latency.
questions.answerText: The steady background firing rate a division maintains at rest

questions.q: Which division exerts the greater tone on the heart in a resting person?
options: The sympathetic division
Neither, since tone is absent at rest
The parasympathetic division
Both equally, so the rate sits at the intrinsic value
questions.why: Vagal tone dominates at rest, which is why the resting heart rate sits well below the pace the sinoatrial node would set on its own. Sympathetic tone to the heart is present but weaker at rest and rises with activity. Tone is not absent at rest, and if the two were balanced the rate would sit near the intrinsic value of about 100 beats per minute rather than near 70.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: What rate does the sinoatrial node set when all autonomic input to it is removed?
options: About 40 beats per minute
About 70 beats per minute
About 140 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
questions.why: Stripped of both divisions, the sinoatrial node depolarizes on its own at roughly 100 beats per minute, and that intrinsic rate is the reference point for judging tone. About 70 is the usual resting rate, which is lower precisely because vagal tone is holding the node back. About 40 is closer to what a ventricular pacemaker would produce, and 140 is a rate reached only with strong sympathetic drive.
questions.answerText: About 100 beats per minute

questions.q: Which division maintains the resting tone of most arterioles?
options: The sympathetic division
The parasympathetic division
Both divisions in balance
Neither, since arteriolar diameter is set only locally
questions.why: Most arterioles receive sympathetic fibers only, and their continuous low level firing holds the vessels partly constricted, a baseline called vasomotor tone. The parasympathetic division does not supply the great majority of blood vessels, so a balance between divisions is not available there. Local metabolic factors also influence diameter, but they act on top of that sympathetic baseline rather than replacing it.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: Which of these structures receives sympathetic innervation only?
options: The stomach
Sweat glands of the skin
The sinoatrial node
The bronchioles
questions.why: Sweat glands, piloerector muscles, most blood vessels, and the adrenal medulla are supplied by the sympathetic division alone, so they cannot be controlled by opposing inputs. The stomach, the sinoatrial node, and the bronchioles are all dually innervated and receive vagal fibers as well. Recognizing which targets are singly innervated tells you which ones must be regulated by changing one firing rate up and down.
questions.answerText: Sweat glands of the skin

questions.q: In a vessel supplied only by sympathetic fibers, how is vasodilation produced?
options: By recruiting parasympathetic fibers that also supply the vessel
By switching which transmitter is released from that same sympathetic fiber
By decreasing the sympathetic firing rate below its resting tone
By blocking the local metabolic signals that keep the vessel constricted
questions.why: Because the baseline is a partly constricted vessel, simply firing less allows the smooth muscle to relax, so one division achieves two directions by moving above and below its tone. There are no parasympathetic fibers to recruit in these beds. Neurons do not switch their transmitter from moment to moment, and local metabolites such as carbon dioxide dilate rather than constrict these vessels.
questions.answerText: By decreasing the sympathetic firing rate below its resting tone

questions.q: In most dually innervated organs, how do the effects of the two divisions relate to each other?
options: They are identical, so the effects add together
They are unrelated, since each targets a different tissue layer
They alternate, so only one division is active at a time
They are antagonistic, pushing the organ in opposite directions
questions.why: The usual arrangement is opposition, as at the heart where one division speeds the node and the other slows it, which gives fine control from two continuously active inputs. Identical effects occur in a few places such as the salivary glands, but that is the exception rather than the rule. Both divisions reach the same effector cells, and both are active at once rather than taking turns.
questions.answerText: They are antagonistic, pushing the organ in opposite directions

questions.q: A resting person has a heart rate of 72 beats per minute while the intrinsic rate of the sinoatrial node is about 100. What does this difference indicate?
options: Sympathetic tone is holding the rate down
Parasympathetic tone is holding the rate down
The sinoatrial node is damaged
Both divisions are silent at rest
questions.why: A resting rate below the intrinsic rate can only mean an active brake, and vagal tone is that brake. Sympathetic tone pushes the rate up, so more of it would move the heart above 100 rather than below. A node that is damaged would not still be pacing normally, and if both divisions were silent the rate would sit at the intrinsic value.
questions.answerText: Parasympathetic tone is holding the rate down

questions.q: Both vagus nerves to the heart are blocked in a resting person while sympathetic fibers are left intact. Predict the heart rate.
options: It falls toward 40 beats per minute
It stays at the previous resting rate
It rises above the previous resting rate
It becomes irregular but averages the same
questions.why: Removing the dominant resting brake unmasks the intrinsic pacemaker rate plus whatever sympathetic tone remains, so the rate climbs. A fall would require losing sympathetic rather than vagal input. Staying the same would only happen if vagal tone had been absent, and while beat to beat variability does drop after vagal block, the average rate clearly increases.
questions.answerText: It rises above the previous resting rate

questions.q: Sympathetic fibers to the heart are blocked in a resting person while vagal fibers stay intact. Predict the change in heart rate.
options: It falls to about half the resting value
It rises toward the intrinsic rate
It is unchanged, since only exercise uses sympathetic fibers
It falls modestly, because sympathetic tone at rest is small
questions.why: At rest the sympathetic contribution to heart rate is the smaller of the two, so removing it lowers the rate somewhat but leaves the vagally braked pace largely intact. Halving the rate overstates a tone that is minor at rest. A rise would follow vagal block, not sympathetic block, and sympathetic fibers do fire at rest rather than only during exercise.
questions.answerText: It falls modestly, because sympathetic tone at rest is small

questions.q: Sympathetic firing to the arterioles of the skin decreases. Predict what happens to those vessels.
options: They dilate, because the constricting tone is reduced
They constrict, because parasympathetic input takes over
They stay the same, since tone is fixed
They dilate, because parasympathetic fibers are activated
questions.why: The resting vessel is held partly closed by sympathetic tone, so a fall in firing releases that grip and the vessel widens, which is exactly how skin flow rises when the body needs to lose heat. No parasympathetic supply exists in these vessels, so both options invoking it are wrong regardless of the direction they predict. Tone is a variable firing rate, not a fixed setting.
questions.answerText: They dilate, because the constricting tone is reduced

questions.q: A drug blocks both autonomic divisions at the heart completely. Predict the resulting heart rate.
options: About 40 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
About 70 beats per minute
Zero, since the heart needs neural input
questions.why: With both inputs gone the sinoatrial node runs at its own intrinsic rate of roughly 100 beats per minute, so the rate rises rather than falls. About 70 is the rate with normal tone present, mostly vagal. About 40 would suggest a slower pacemaker taking over, and the heart does not stop, since the node depolarizes spontaneously without any nerve supply.
questions.answerText: About 100 beats per minute

questions.q: Parasympathetic input to the small intestine is removed while sympathetic input remains. Predict the change in motility.
options: Motility rises, because the input that normally inhibits the gut has been removed
Motility is unchanged, since the enteric nervous system runs the gut on its own
Motility falls, because the stimulating input is gone and the inhibitory input is unopposed
Motility rises briefly and then stops entirely a few minutes later
questions.why: The parasympathetic division stimulates the gut, so removing it takes away the accelerator and leaves the sympathetic brake acting alone, which lowers motility. Calling the parasympathetic input inhibitory reverses the roles of the two divisions at this organ. The enteric system does keep some activity going, so motility falls rather than stopping, and there is no initial surge.
questions.answerText: Motility falls, because the stimulating input is gone and the inhibitory input is unopposed

questions.q: Why does losing one division change a dually innervated organ less dramatically than losing the only division supplying a singly innervated organ?
options: Singly innervated organs have no intrinsic or local activity of their own to fall back on
The remaining division still acts on the organ and can be adjusted up or down
Dually innervated organs regenerate their lost nerve supply much faster than other organs
Singly innervated organs are controlled by hormones rather than by nerves at all
questions.why: In a dually innervated organ the surviving division still delivers a graded, adjustable signal, so control is reduced rather than lost. Singly innervated targets such as arterioles do have intrinsic and local control, so an absence of intrinsic activity is not the reason. Nerve regeneration speed does not differ by innervation pattern, and hormones supplement rather than replace innervation.
questions.answerText: The remaining division still acts on the organ and can be adjusted up or down

questions.q: A resting subject with a heart rate of 72 is given a drug that blocks vagal input to the heart, and the rate rises to 96. A second subject is given a drug that blocks sympathetic input, and the rate falls from 72 to 64. What do these results show about resting autonomic tone at the heart?
options: Sympathetic tone is much greater than parasympathetic tone at rest
Parasympathetic tone is much greater than sympathetic tone at rest
The two tones are equal, since both drugs changed the rate
Neither tone exists at rest, since the node sets its own rate
questions.why: The size of the change after each block measures the tone that was removed, and losing the vagus moved the rate by 24 beats while losing sympathetic input moved it by only 8, so the vagal brake was doing most of the work. Equal tones would produce equal shifts in opposite directions. Both tones clearly exist at rest, since blocking either one moved the rate away from 72.
questions.answerText: Parasympathetic tone is much greater than sympathetic tone at rest

questions.q: A person whose vagal supply to the heart has been interrupted begins moderate exercise. Predict the resting rate before exercise and the ability to raise rate during exercise.
options: Resting rate is elevated, and rate can still rise because sympathetic fibers are intact
Resting rate is normal, but the heart is unable to raise its rate at all during exercise
Resting rate is lower than usual, and the rate still rises normally during exercise
Resting rate is elevated, and the heart is already at its ceiling and cannot rise further
questions.why: Without vagal tone the baseline sits near the intrinsic rate, which is higher than normal, and because the sympathetic supply is untouched the usual exercise increase still occurs, although the total range from rest to peak is narrower. A normal or low resting rate would require vagal tone that is no longer present. The heart is not at its ceiling at rest, so further increase remains possible.
questions.answerText: Resting rate is elevated, and rate can still rise because sympathetic fibers are intact

questions.q: All sympathetic fibers to one arm are cut. Predict the blood flow and skin temperature in that arm compared with the other arm shortly afterward.
options: Flow is lower and the skin is cooler, because the vessels lost their nerve supply
Flow is higher and the skin is warmer, because vasomotor tone was removed
Flow and temperature are unchanged, since parasympathetic fibers take over
Flow is higher but the skin is cooler, because sweating increases
questions.why: Sympathetic fibers hold these vessels partly constricted, so cutting them removes the constricting tone, the arterioles widen, and warm blood flows more freely into the skin. Expecting cooling treats the sympathetic input as a dilator, which reverses its role in most vascular beds. There are no parasympathetic fibers to compensate, and sweating decreases rather than increases after sympathetic denervation, since sweat glands are sympathetic targets.
questions.answerText: Flow is higher and the skin is warmer, because vasomotor tone was removed

questions.q: Salivary glands are unusual in that both divisions increase secretion, the parasympathetic producing copious watery saliva and the sympathetic a small thick volume. Predict what happens to salivary output if parasympathetic input alone is removed.
options: Output rises, since the opposing division is now unopposed
Output is unchanged, since the sympathetic supply is equivalent
Output falls sharply and what remains is scant and thick
Output stops completely, since the gland has only one supply
questions.why: Here the two divisions cooperate rather than oppose, so losing the parasympathetic side removes the main source of watery secretion and leaves only the small thick sympathetic contribution. Expecting a rise applies the antagonistic model that does not hold at this gland. The two supplies are not equivalent in volume, and secretion does not stop because the sympathetic supply survives.
questions.answerText: Output falls sharply and what remains is scant and thick

questions.q: The secretory cells of the adrenal medulla are best described as modified versions of which cell?
options: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons
Preganglionic sympathetic neurons
Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons
Skeletal muscle fibers
questions.why: Chromaffin cells develop from the same neural crest tissue as postganglionic sympathetic neurons and sit in the same position in the pathway, one synapse downstream of the CNS. Preganglionic neurons are the cells that innervate them, not the cells themselves. There is no parasympathetic component to the medulla, and chromaffin cells are secretory rather than contractile.
questions.answerText: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons

questions.q: Which fibers innervate the cells of the adrenal medulla?
options: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers
Sympathetic preganglionic fibers
Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers
Somatic motor fibers
questions.why: Preganglionic sympathetic axons run through the chain without synapsing and end directly on the chromaffin cells, which is exactly the arrangement seen at any sympathetic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers would imply a synapse had already happened somewhere else. The medulla receives no parasympathetic or somatic supply.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers

questions.q: Which transmitter and receptor are used where the nerve meets the adrenal medullary cells?
options: Norepinephrine acting on beta-1 receptors
Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors
Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors
Epinephrine acting on alpha-1 receptors
questions.why: This synapse follows the ganglionic rule exactly, acetylcholine released by a preganglionic fiber onto nicotinic receptors, which is the strongest evidence that the medulla is a modified ganglion. Muscarinic receptors would place the synapse at a parasympathetic target instead. Norepinephrine and epinephrine act on adrenergic receptors at the far end of the pathway, not at the ganglionic step.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors

questions.q: Which catecholamine makes up the majority of adrenal medullary secretion?
options: Norepinephrine
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
Epinephrine
questions.why: About eighty percent of the output is epinephrine and most of the rest is norepinephrine, so the medulla is the body main source of circulating epinephrine. Norepinephrine is the minority product here even though it is the transmitter at ordinary sympathetic nerve endings. Dopamine is released in trace amounts, and acetylcholine is the input to these cells rather than their product.
questions.answerText: Epinephrine

questions.q: Where does the adrenal medulla release its secretions?
options: Into the bloodstream
Into a synaptic cleft at the target organ
Into the interstitial fluid of the kidney only
Into the lumen of a duct
questions.why: Chromaffin cells secrete into capillaries, so their catecholamines act as hormones and reach every tissue with the appropriate receptors. Release into a synaptic cleft is what an ordinary postganglionic neuron does, and it is the difference that makes the medullary response broader and longer. The medulla is not a duct gland and its secretion is not confined to the kidney, despite the location of the adrenal glands.
questions.answerText: Into the bloodstream

questions.q: What structural feature do adrenal medullary cells lack that ordinary postganglionic sympathetic neurons have?
options: A cell body
An axon
Nicotinic receptors
Secretory vesicles
questions.why: Chromaffin cells kept the secretory machinery of a sympathetic neuron but never grew an axon, so instead of delivering transmitter to one target they dump it into the blood. They certainly have cell bodies, and they carry nicotinic receptors just as any postganglionic neuron does. They are full of secretory vesicles, which is how the catecholamines are stored before release.
questions.answerText: An axon

questions.q: How long do the effects of circulating catecholamines from the adrenal medulla last compared with the effects of direct sympathetic nerve stimulation?
options: Considerably shorter, ending within a few milliseconds of the stimulus
Exactly the same, since the transmitter molecules involved are identical
Considerably longer, lasting seconds to minutes after the stimulus ends
Longer only in those tissues that also receive direct sympathetic innervation
questions.why: Hormonal catecholamines linger in the blood for a period measured in minutes, so the response outlasts the nerve traffic that triggered it, while a nerve released transmitter is cleared from the cleft almost at once. Identical transmitters do not mean identical time courses, because how the molecule is removed differs completely. The prolonged effect appears in every responsive tissue, innervated or not.
questions.answerText: Considerably longer, lasting seconds to minutes after the stimulus ends

questions.q: Why is norepinephrine removed from a sympathetic synapse so much faster than circulating epinephrine is removed from the blood?
options: It is destroyed by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft
It diffuses into bone and is stored there
It is filtered by the kidney within milliseconds
The nerve terminal takes it back up almost immediately
questions.why: Reuptake into the presynaptic terminal clears the cleft within a fraction of a second, while a hormone in the blood must wait for enzymes in the liver and other tissues to break it down. Acetylcholinesterase acts on acetylcholine and has no effect on catecholamines. Bone storage is not a route of removal, and renal handling takes far longer than milliseconds.
questions.answerText: The nerve terminal takes it back up almost immediately

questions.q: A gland is found in which a preganglionic fiber ends directly on secretory cells that carry nicotinic receptors and release catecholamines. How should this gland be classified?
options: As a modified sympathetic ganglion
As a terminal ganglion of the parasympathetic division
As an ordinary endocrine gland with no neural connection at all
As an effector organ of the somatic motor system
questions.why: The pattern of a preganglionic fiber, a nicotinic synapse, and cells that release catecholamines is the sympathetic ganglion pattern, with the single change that the output goes into the blood instead of down an axon. A parasympathetic terminal ganglion would release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors nearby. An ordinary endocrine gland is controlled hormonally rather than by a preganglionic nerve, and a somatic effector would be skeletal muscle.
questions.answerText: As a modified sympathetic ganglion

questions.q: A drug blocks nicotinic receptors throughout the body. Predict its effect on adrenal medullary secretion.
options: Secretion rises, since the inhibitory input is removed
Secretion falls, because the synapse onto chromaffin cells is nicotinic
Secretion is unchanged, since the medulla is hormonally controlled
Secretion is unchanged, since chromaffin cells use muscarinic receptors
questions.why: The only drive to the chromaffin cells arrives through a nicotinic synapse, so blocking that receptor silences the gland. The input is excitatory rather than inhibitory, so removing it cannot raise output. The medulla is not under hormonal control from the pituitary the way the adrenal cortex is, and its receptors are nicotinic, not muscarinic.
questions.answerText: Secretion falls, because the synapse onto chromaffin cells is nicotinic

questions.q: A stimulus activates both the sympathetic nerves to the heart and the adrenal medulla, then stops. Which influence on the heart fades first?
options: The hormonal effect, because the hormone is quickly diluted in the circulating blood
Both fade together, since the two act on the same cardiac receptors
The direct nerve effect, because transmitter is cleared from the synapse rapidly
Neither fades, since the effects of catecholamines are permanent
questions.why: Reuptake ends the synaptic signal in under a second, while circulating catecholamines keep acting for minutes until they are metabolized, so the nerve effect disappears first. Dilution does lower hormone concentration but does not clear it faster than reuptake clears a cleft. Acting on the same beta-1 receptors does not equalize the two time courses, since duration is set by removal, and no catecholamine effect is permanent.
questions.answerText: The direct nerve effect, because transmitter is cleared from the synapse rapidly

questions.q: The adrenal medulla is removed while all sympathetic nerves are left intact. Predict the response to a sudden fright.
options: No sympathetic response occurs anywhere in the body
The response is normal in size but takes much longer to begin
A sympathetic response still occurs but is smaller and shorter lived
The response is larger than normal, since a hormonal brake has been removed
questions.why: Direct innervation still reaches the heart, vessels, and other targets, so the immediate response happens, but without the circulating catecholamines it is less widespread and fades as soon as nerve traffic stops. A complete absence of response would require losing the sympathetic nerves themselves. Onset actually depends on the nerves, which are the faster route, and the medullary output is excitatory, so its loss cannot enlarge the response.
questions.answerText: A sympathetic response still occurs but is smaller and shorter lived

questions.q: Circulating epinephrine reaches a bronchiole that receives little or no direct sympathetic innervation. Predict the effect on that airway.
options: It dilates, because beta-2 receptors are reached through the blood
It is unaffected, because a hormone cannot act on a tissue that lacks innervation
It constricts, because epinephrine acts on alpha-1 receptors in the airway wall
It is unaffected, because epinephrine is unable to leave the capillary bed
questions.why: A hormone only needs a receptor, not a nerve ending, so beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle respond to blood borne epinephrine and the bronchiole widens. Requiring innervation confuses a hormonal signal with a synaptic one. Alpha-1 receptors dominate on most vascular smooth muscle rather than on airways, and catecholamines cross capillary walls readily.
questions.answerText: It dilates, because beta-2 receptors are reached through the blood

questions.q: Which route delivers its effect to the heart sooner after the central nervous system commands a sympathetic response?
options: The adrenal medulla, since its hormones reach a larger number of receptors
The direct sympathetic nerve, since it does not depend on circulation time
Both arrive at the same instant, since a single central command triggers both routes
The adrenal medulla, since epinephrine binds the beta-1 receptor more tightly
questions.why: The nerve delivers transmitter directly onto the node in milliseconds, while the hormone must be secreted, enter the blood, and be carried to the heart, which takes several seconds. Acting on more receptors changes how widespread the effect is, not how quickly it starts. A single central command does trigger both routes, but they arrive on very different timescales, and receptor affinity does not shorten circulation time.
questions.answerText: The direct sympathetic nerve, since it does not depend on circulation time

questions.q: A person is startled, and the fright passes in a second, yet the heart is still racing two minutes later. Trace the reason.
options: Sympathetic nerves to the heart continue firing at a high rate for minutes after the startling stimulus ends
Catecholamines released into the blood from the adrenal medulla are still circulating and acting on cardiac beta-1 receptors
Acetylcholine accumulated at the sinoatrial node during the startle and keeps those pacemaker cells depolarized
The vagus nerve was inactivated by the startle and needs several minutes to recover its resting activity
questions.why: The same preganglionic burst that drove the cardiac nerves also drove the chromaffin cells, and hormonal catecholamines are cleared over minutes rather than milliseconds, so the beta-1 effect on the node outlasts the nerve traffic. Nerve firing tracks the stimulus and stops with it. Acetylcholine slows the node rather than speeding it, and the vagus is not switched off for minutes by a single startle.
questions.answerText: Catecholamines released into the blood from the adrenal medulla are still circulating and acting on cardiac beta-1 receptors

questions.q: In an experiment, brief stimulation of the cardiac sympathetic nerve and brief stimulation of the nerve to the adrenal medulla are compared. How do the two heart rate responses differ in onset and in duration?
options: The nerve response starts later than the medullary response and also lasts considerably longer than it does
Both responses start and end at the same time, since both of them act on the same cardiac beta-1 receptors
The nerve response starts sooner and ends sooner, while the medullary response starts later and lasts longer
The medullary response starts sooner, because hormones are carried in fast moving arterial blood
questions.why: Direct innervation wins on speed because there is no transport step, and hormonal release wins on duration because clearance from blood is slow compared with synaptic reuptake, so the two routes trade off against each other. Reversing the pattern ignores both the circulation delay and the difference in clearance. Sharing a receptor does not equalize the timing, since timing depends on delivery and removal rather than on the receptor.
questions.answerText: The nerve response starts sooner and ends sooner, while the medullary response starts later and lasts longer

questions.q: A ganglionic blocking agent prevents transmission at nicotinic receptors in all autonomic ganglia. Predict its effect on direct sympathetic output to blood vessels and on adrenal catecholamine release.
options: Both are lost, because both depend on the same nicotinic synapse
Direct output is lost but medullary release continues
Direct output continues but medullary release is lost
Neither is affected, since sympathetic targets use adrenergic receptors
questions.why: The chromaffin cell synapse is a ganglionic synapse in everything but name, so an agent that blocks nicotinic transmission silences the medulla at the same time it silences ordinary sympathetic ganglia, and both branches of sympathetic output fail together. Sparing either one treats the medulla as if it sat outside the sympathetic pathway. The adrenergic receptors on the targets are downstream and are never reached, because nothing gets past the blocked relay.
questions.answerText: Both are lost, because both depend on the same nicotinic synapse

questions.q: During prolonged exercise, blood epinephrine rises and remains elevated while a subject sustains a high heart rate. If the same subject had only direct sympathetic innervation and no adrenal medulla, what would change about the cardiovascular response?
options: The response would begin noticeably later than normal but would still climb to the same peak
The response would still begin promptly but would depend entirely on ongoing nerve traffic and would reach fewer poorly innervated tissues
The heart rate could not rise at all, because a sustained rise depends on circulating epinephrine rather than on nerves
The response would be identical in size and in duration, since the nerve and the hormone do the same job
questions.why: Nerves supply the fast, targeted component and the medulla supplies a slower, broader, longer lasting component, so removing the hormone leaves onset intact but makes the response narrower in reach and immediately reversible when firing stops. Onset would not be delayed, since the nerves are the faster route. The heart is directly innervated and its rate would still rise, and the two routes are complementary rather than identical.
questions.answerText: The response would still begin promptly but would depend entirely on ongoing nerve traffic and would reach fewer poorly innervated tissues

questions.q: A beta blocker occupies which receptor?
options: The beta adrenergic receptor
The muscarinic cholinergic receptor
The nicotinic cholinergic receptor
The alpha adrenergic receptor
questions.why: A beta blocker sits on beta adrenergic receptors, the sites where norepinephrine and epinephrine normally act on the heart and on certain smooth muscle. Muscarinic and nicotinic receptors bind acetylcholine and belong to a different transmitter system entirely. Alpha receptors are adrenergic but are a separate subtype, dominant on most vascular smooth muscle rather than on the heart.
questions.answerText: The beta adrenergic receptor

questions.q: What does a receptor antagonist do at the receptor it occupies?
options: It activates the receptor even more strongly than the natural ligand does
It binds without activating and prevents the normal ligand from acting
It destroys the receptor protein permanently and irreversibly
It increases the amount of transmitter that is released onto the receptor
questions.why: An antagonist occupies the binding site but produces no signal, so the natural transmitter can no longer reach the receptor and its usual effect on the organ is lost. Producing a stronger effect describes an agonist. Antagonists do not destroy receptors, and they act on the receiving side rather than changing how much transmitter is released.
questions.answerText: It binds without activating and prevents the normal ligand from acting

questions.q: A muscarinic antagonist prevents which transmitter from acting at parasympathetic target organs?
options: Norepinephrine
Epinephrine
Acetylcholine
Dopamine
questions.why: Muscarinic receptors are the acetylcholine receptors on parasympathetic targets, so blocking them removes the effect of acetylcholine released by postganglionic parasympathetic fibers. Norepinephrine and epinephrine act on alpha and beta receptors and are unaffected by this block. Dopamine is not the transmitter at autonomic effector organs.
questions.answerText: Acetylcholine

questions.q: Does a muscarinic antagonist interfere with transmission at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?
options: Yes, because both of these sites use acetylcholine
Yes, but only at high doses and only in cardiac muscle
No, because the neuromuscular junction uses norepinephrine instead
No, because that junction uses nicotinic receptors
questions.why: Sharing a transmitter is not the same as sharing a receptor, and the neuromuscular junction carries nicotinic receptors that a muscarinic blocker does not fit. Answering yes because both sites use acetylcholine makes exactly the mistake this card is designed to catch. The neuromuscular junction does not use norepinephrine, and cardiac muscle is not a skeletal neuromuscular junction.
questions.answerText: No, because that junction uses nicotinic receptors

questions.q: Which receptor subtype on the heart is the main target of a beta-1 selective blocker?
options: Beta-2
Muscarinic
Alpha-1
Beta-1
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors dominate on cardiac tissue, so a blocker selective for that subtype has its main effect on the heart. Beta-2 receptors are found on bronchiolar smooth muscle and on skeletal muscle vessels, which is why a selective agent leaves airways relatively alone. Alpha-1 receptors are on most vascular smooth muscle, and muscarinic receptors on the heart are cholinergic and unaffected by a beta blocker.
questions.answerText: Beta-1

questions.q: Which division's influence on the heart is reduced by a beta blocker?
options: The parasympathetic division
Both divisions equally
The sympathetic division
Neither, since the heart is not innervated
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors are the sympathetic receptors on the heart, so blocking them removes sympathetic influence and leaves vagal influence intact and relatively unopposed. The parasympathetic effect on the heart runs through muscarinic receptors and would need a different blocker. The heart is dually innervated, so both statements denying innervation or claiming equal effect are wrong.
questions.answerText: The sympathetic division

questions.q: Which division's influence on the gut is reduced by a muscarinic antagonist?
options: The sympathetic division
The somatic motor system
Both divisions equally
The parasympathetic division
questions.why: The gut receives parasympathetic acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, so blocking those receptors removes the main stimulating input to intestinal smooth muscle. Sympathetic influence on the gut works through adrenergic receptors and is left in place. The gut has no somatic motor supply to its smooth muscle, so no somatic effect is possible.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: A nonselective beta blocker acts at which receptors?
options: Both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors
Beta-1 receptors on the heart and alpha-1 receptors on vessels
Beta-2 receptors and muscarinic receptors together
Beta-1 receptors on the heart only
questions.why: Nonselective means the agent does not distinguish between the beta subtypes, so it occupies beta-1 receptors on the heart and beta-2 receptors on airway and skeletal muscle vessels alike. Adding alpha-1 or muscarinic receptors to the list crosses into different receptor families that a beta blocker does not fit. Beta-1 only would describe a selective agent instead.
questions.answerText: Both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors

questions.q: A beta blocker reaches the heart of a resting person. Predict the effect on heart rate.
options: Heart rate rises
Heart rate becomes irregular but averages the same
Heart rate is unchanged
Heart rate falls
questions.why: Blocking beta-1 receptors removes the sympathetic push on the sinoatrial node, so the node depolarizes more slowly and the rate drops toward or below the value set by vagal tone alone. A rise would follow removal of the vagal brake, which a beta blocker does not touch. Some sympathetic tone is present even at rest, so the rate does change.
questions.answerText: Heart rate falls

questions.q: A muscarinic antagonist reaches the heart of a resting person. Predict the effect on heart rate.
options: Heart rate falls
Heart rate is unchanged
Heart rate rises
Heart rate falls, then returns to baseline
questions.why: Muscarinic receptors carry the vagal signal to the sinoatrial node, so blocking them removes the resting brake and the rate climbs toward the intrinsic pacemaker rate. A fall would follow blockade of beta-1 receptors instead. Because vagal tone dominates the resting heart, this change is substantial rather than absent.
questions.answerText: Heart rate rises

questions.q: A muscarinic antagonist reaches the small intestine. Predict the effect on motility.
options: Motility increases
Motility increases then stops abruptly
Motility is unchanged
Motility decreases
questions.why: Parasympathetic acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors is the main stimulus to intestinal smooth muscle, so blocking those receptors slows the gut. An increase would require blocking the sympathetic input instead, which is the inhibitory one here. Enteric activity persists, so motility is reduced rather than abolished, but it is clearly changed.
questions.answerText: Motility decreases

questions.q: A nonselective beta blocker reaches the bronchioles. Predict the effect on airway diameter.
options: The airways widen, because beta-2 receptors normally constrict them
The airways widen, because this blocker occupies muscarinic receptors as well
The airways are unaffected, since airway smooth muscle carries only muscarinic receptors
The airways narrow somewhat, because beta-2 mediated relaxation is lost
questions.why: Beta-2 receptors normally relax airway smooth muscle in response to circulating epinephrine, so blocking them removes a dilating influence and leaves the airway narrower than it would otherwise be. Calling beta-2 a constrictor reverses its action. Airways carry both muscarinic and beta-2 receptors, and a beta blocker has no effect at muscarinic sites.
questions.answerText: The airways narrow somewhat, because beta-2 mediated relaxation is lost

questions.q: A muscarinic antagonist reaches the salivary glands. Predict the effect on saliva production.
options: It rises, because sympathetic secretion is now completely unopposed
It is unchanged, since the salivary glands receive sympathetic fibers only
It falls markedly, producing a dry mouth
It rises, because blocking a receptor increases secretion from the gland
questions.why: Watery salivary secretion is driven by parasympathetic acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, so removing that signal leaves only the small thick sympathetic contribution and the mouth feels dry. The sympathetic supply cannot compensate in volume. Salivary glands do receive parasympathetic fibers, and blocking a receptor removes an effect rather than creating one.
questions.answerText: It falls markedly, producing a dry mouth

questions.q: A beta blocker reaches the ventricular myocardium. Predict the effect on the force of contraction.
options: Force increases
Force is unchanged, since beta receptors affect heart rate only
Force decreases
Force increases at rest but decreases once exercise begins
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors on working myocardium increase calcium entry and therefore contractile force, so blocking them lowers the force of each beat as well as the rate. Restricting beta effects to rate alone misses the contractility half of the cardiac response. Blocking an excitatory receptor cannot raise force under any condition.
questions.answerText: Force decreases

questions.q: A person takes a nonselective beta blocker. Predict the combined effect on the heart and on the bronchioles.
options: The heart slows and contracts less forcefully, and the bronchioles narrow
The heart slows and contracts less forcefully, while the bronchioles widen at the same time
The heart speeds up, while the bronchioles narrow at the same time
The heart is left unaffected, and only the bronchioles narrow in response
questions.why: The same agent hits beta-1 receptors on the heart, lowering rate and force, and beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle, removing the relaxing influence so the airways narrow, which is why airway effects matter with nonselective agents. Widening airways would require the beta-2 receptor to be constrictor, which it is not. A faster heart would follow muscarinic blockade instead, and the heart cannot be spared by an agent that occupies beta-1 receptors.
questions.answerText: The heart slows and contracts less forcefully, and the bronchioles narrow

questions.q: A person receives a muscarinic antagonist. Predict the effect on heart rate and on gastrointestinal motility.
options: Heart rate falls and gastrointestinal motility rises
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility fall
Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls
Both heart rate and gastrointestinal motility rise
questions.why: Removing parasympathetic influence produces opposite changes in the two organs, because that division normally slows the heart and speeds the gut, so blocking it releases the heart and quiets the gut. Falling rate with rising motility describes adding parasympathetic activity rather than blocking it. The two options that move both in the same direction miss the fact that the same division has opposite effects on these targets.
questions.answerText: Heart rate rises and gastrointestinal motility falls

questions.q: A person taking a beta-1 selective blocker begins moderate exercise. Predict the heart rate response compared with the same exercise without the drug.
options: Heart rate is unable to rise at all during the exercise
Heart rate falls even further as the exercise continues
Heart rate rises to the same peak value but does so more slowly
Heart rate still rises but reaches a lower peak
questions.why: Blockade is competitive and partial, and withdrawal of vagal tone still contributes to the early rise, so the rate increases but the sympathetic beta-1 contribution is blunted and the ceiling is lower. Complete inability to rise overstates the block and ignores vagal withdrawal. The peak is reduced rather than merely delayed, and a further fall during exercise contradicts the normal direction of the exercise response.
questions.answerText: Heart rate still rises but reaches a lower peak

questions.q: After a drug is given, a subject shows a faster heart rate, reduced gastric secretion, and slowed intestinal motility, while arteriolar resistance is unchanged. Which receptor was blocked?
options: The beta-1 receptor
The alpha-1 receptor
The muscarinic receptor
The nicotinic receptor
questions.why: Every finding points to loss of parasympathetic effect at target organs, and unchanged arteriolar resistance fits because most vessels have no parasympathetic supply, so a muscarinic block leaves them alone. Blocking beta-1 receptors would have slowed the heart rather than speeding it. Blocking alpha-1 receptors would have lowered arteriolar resistance, and blocking nicotinic receptors would have shut down both divisions and dropped vascular resistance as well.
questions.answerText: The muscarinic receptor

questions.q: What does heart rate variability measure?
options: The beat to beat variation in the interval between successive heartbeats
The difference between the highest and the lowest heart rate reached during exercise
The variation in the size of the R wave recorded from one beat to the next
The change in heart rate measured between sitting and standing
questions.why: Heart rate variability is calculated from the intervals between successive R waves, so it describes how much the timing of the heartbeat fluctuates from one beat to the next. The exercise range and the sitting to standing change are separate measures of cardiovascular reserve and of the orthostatic response. Variation in R wave amplitude reflects electrode position and body movement rather than autonomic control.
questions.answerText: The beat to beat variation in the interval between successive heartbeats

questions.q: Which autonomic division is chiefly responsible for the rapid beat to beat component of heart rate variability?
options: The sympathetic division
Neither, since variability comes from the sinoatrial node alone
Both contribute equally to fast changes
The parasympathetic division
questions.why: Vagal effects on the sinoatrial node begin and end within a single beat, so only the parasympathetic division can make heart rate fluctuate that quickly. Sympathetic effects work through a slower second messenger pathway and take seconds to build and decay, so they shape slower trends rather than beat to beat swings. The node alone would produce a very regular rhythm, which is why a denervated heart shows little variability.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic division

questions.q: In respiratory sinus arrhythmia, what happens to heart rate during inspiration?
options: It decreases
It stays constant
It becomes irregular without a consistent direction
It increases
questions.why: Vagal traffic to the heart falls during inspiration, so the brake is briefly lifted and the rate rises, then falls again on expiration as vagal activity returns. A slowing during inspiration reverses the pattern. A constant rate would mean the vagal modulation is absent, which is itself a finding in people with reduced parasympathetic control, and the pattern is consistent enough to be timed against the breathing cycle.
questions.answerText: It increases

questions.q: How is a cold pressor test performed?
options: The subject breathes chilled air for several minutes while heart rate is recorded continuously
The whole body is cooled with a fan until the subject begins to shiver visibly
Ice is applied to the skin of the neck over the carotid sinus for a full minute
The hand is immersed in ice water for one to two minutes while blood pressure is recorded
questions.why: Immersing a hand in ice water delivers a strong painful cold stimulus, and blood pressure is measured during the immersion to gauge the sympathetic response. Cooling the whole body or breathing cold air produces slower thermoregulatory changes rather than the sharp pressor response being tested. Pressure on the carotid sinus is a different maneuver that tests the baroreceptor reflex.
questions.answerText: The hand is immersed in ice water for one to two minutes while blood pressure is recorded

questions.q: What is the expected blood pressure response during a cold pressor test?
options: Blood pressure falls
Blood pressure is unchanged
Blood pressure falls then rises above baseline
Blood pressure rises
questions.why: The painful cold stimulus drives a sympathetic discharge that constricts arterioles and raises peripheral resistance, so systolic and diastolic pressure both climb within a minute. A fall would indicate the sympathetic response is not occurring. There is no initial drop, since the reflex is a direct pressor response rather than a baroreceptor mediated one.
questions.answerText: Blood pressure rises

questions.q: What does an orthostatic challenge consist of?
options: Moving from lying down to standing while heart rate and blood pressure are recorded
Holding a forced expiration against a closed airway for fifteen seconds
Exercising on a stationary cycle at a fixed workload for several minutes
Breathing deeply and slowly at a paced six breaths per minute
questions.why: The orthostatic test uses the change in posture itself as the stimulus, since standing shifts blood into the legs and challenges the reflexes that defend blood pressure. Forced expiration against a closed airway is the Valsalva maneuver, and paced deep breathing is used to test respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Fixed workload exercise measures cardiovascular fitness rather than the postural reflex.
questions.answerText: Moving from lying down to standing while heart rate and blood pressure are recorded

questions.q: Which recording is used to obtain the intervals from which heart rate variability is calculated?
options: The electrocardiogram, using the time between successive R waves
A spirometer trace, using the time between successive breaths
A blood pressure cuff, using the systolic value from each beat
A pulse oximeter, using the oxygen saturation value from each beat
questions.why: The R wave is sharp and easy to time precisely, so the R to R interval on the electrocardiogram is the standard measurement for variability. A spirometer records breathing, which is a driver of variability but not the measurement itself. Cuff pressures and oxygen saturation do not resolve individual beats with the precision needed.
questions.answerText: The electrocardiogram, using the time between successive R waves

questions.q: What blood pressure change within three minutes of standing defines orthostatic hypotension?
options: A fall of at least 5 mmHg systolic or at least 5 mmHg diastolic
A rise of at least 20 mmHg in the systolic pressure
Any measurable fall in the mean arterial pressure at all
A fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or at least 10 mmHg diastolic
questions.why: The accepted threshold is a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing, large enough to exceed the small transient dip that healthy people show. A 5 mmHg change is within the normal transient response and would label almost everyone. A rise describes the opposite finding, and any fall at all is too loose a criterion to be useful.
questions.answerText: A fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or at least 10 mmHg diastolic

questions.q: A resting subject shows large beat to beat variation in R to R interval. How should this be interpreted?
options: As parasympathetic dominance at the heart
As sympathetic dominance at the heart
As loss of all autonomic input to the heart
As a faulty electrode connection
questions.why: High variability at rest reflects strong, rapidly changing vagal influence on the sinoatrial node, which is the hallmark of parasympathetic dominance. Sympathetic dominance produces a faster and more regular rhythm because its effects change slowly. A heart stripped of autonomic input beats with very little variability, which is the opposite finding, and a genuine variability pattern tracks the breathing cycle rather than appearing as random noise.
questions.answerText: As parasympathetic dominance at the heart

questions.q: During a cold pressor test, blood pressure rises. Which mechanism accounts for most of the rise?
options: Alpha-1 mediated arteriolar constriction raising peripheral resistance
Beta-2 mediated dilation of the vessels supplying skeletal muscle
Withdrawal of resting vagal tone from the arterioles
Increased compliance of the veins in the legs
questions.why: Sympathetic outflow triggered by the painful stimulus reaches alpha-1 receptors on arterioles throughout the body, and the resulting rise in total peripheral resistance is the main driver of the pressure increase. Beta-2 dilation lowers resistance and would work against the response. Arterioles have essentially no vagal supply, so there is no vagal tone there to withdraw, and greater venous compliance would reduce venous return rather than raise pressure.
questions.answerText: Alpha-1 mediated arteriolar constriction raising peripheral resistance

questions.q: A subject stands up from lying down and heart rate rises by 15 beats per minute within 15 seconds. How is this interpreted?
options: As an abnormal parasympathetic surge
As a complete failure of the baroreceptor reflex
As clear evidence of orthostatic hypotension
As a normal sympathetic response with vagal withdrawal
questions.why: Standing unloads the baroreceptors, and the reflex answer is less vagal traffic and more sympathetic traffic to the heart, so a prompt rise of this size is the expected healthy result. A parasympathetic surge would slow the heart. Orthostatic hypotension is defined by a fall in blood pressure rather than by a rise in rate, and a working reflex is exactly what this response demonstrates.
questions.answerText: As a normal sympathetic response with vagal withdrawal

questions.q: An electrocardiogram shows a steady R to R interval of 800 ms. What is the heart rate?
options: 60 beats per minute
80 beats per minute
48 beats per minute
75 beats per minute
questions.why: There are 60000 ms in a minute, so dividing 60000 by an 800 ms interval gives 75 beats per minute. Choosing 80 comes from dividing 800 into a rounded number of seconds incorrectly, and 60 would be the rate if the interval were a full 1000 ms. A rate of 48 corresponds to an interval of about 1250 ms, much longer than the one recorded.
questions.answerText: 75 beats per minute

questions.q: A subject is asked to breathe slowly and deeply, and the record shows heart rate falling during each expiration. What causes the slowing?
options: An increase in vagal activity to the sinoatrial node
An increase in the sympathetic activity reaching the ventricles
A decrease in the vagal activity reaching the sinoatrial node
A fall in arterial pressure that briefly unloads the baroreceptors
questions.why: Vagal traffic to the node rises during expiration and falls during inspiration, so the expiratory phase is when the brake is applied most strongly and the rate drops. Reduced vagal activity is what produces the inspiratory speeding, the other half of the same cycle. Sympathetic effects are too slow to shape single breaths, and unloading the baroreceptors would raise the rate rather than lower it.
questions.answerText: An increase in vagal activity to the sinoatrial node

questions.q: A resting subject shows a fast heart rate with almost no beat to beat variation. How should this be interpreted?
options: As parasympathetic dominance with strong vagal influence
As an entirely normal finding during quiet breathing
As the sign of an unusually fit cardiovascular system
As sympathetic dominance with reduced vagal influence
questions.why: Losing the fast fluctuations means losing the vagal modulation that creates them, and a fast baseline rate points the same way, toward sympathetic dominance. Strong vagal influence produces the opposite pattern, a slower rate with wide variation. Trained endurance athletes typically show high variability with a low resting rate, and quiet breathing normally produces visible respiratory variation rather than none.
questions.answerText: As sympathetic dominance with reduced vagal influence

questions.q: A subject stands up. Trace the sequence from the mechanical effect of standing to the change in heart rate.
options: Blood pools in the legs, venous return and stroke volume fall, baroreceptor firing drops, and sympathetic outflow rises to speed the heart
Blood shifts into the chest, stroke volume rises, baroreceptor firing rises, and vagal outflow then speeds the heart up
Blood pools in the legs, stroke volume falls, baroreceptor firing rises, and vagal outflow then slows the heart further
Blood pools in the legs, arterial pressure rises directly as a result, and the heart then slows down to compensate
questions.why: Gravity moves blood into the leg veins, so less returns to the heart, stroke volume falls, arterial pressure dips, the baroreceptors fire less, and the reflex answer is more sympathetic and less vagal drive, which raises the rate. The option that has blood shifting to the chest describes lying down rather than standing. The two options with rising baroreceptor firing get the direction backward, since a falling pressure means less stretch and less firing.
questions.answerText: Blood pools in the legs, venous return and stroke volume fall, baroreceptor firing drops, and sympathetic outflow rises to speed the heart

questions.q: On standing, a subject blood pressure falls 30 mmHg systolic and stays low, while heart rate rises by only 3 beats per minute. What does this pattern suggest?
options: An exaggerated sympathetic response to the orthostatic challenge
A normal response that requires no explanation
Excessive vagal withdrawal on standing
An inadequate sympathetic response to the orthostatic challenge
questions.why: A pressure drop of that size should trigger a brisk rise in heart rate and vasoconstriction, so the missing tachycardia points to a sympathetic limb that is not responding as it should. An exaggerated sympathetic response would show a large rise in rate and a defended pressure. Excessive vagal withdrawal would also speed the heart, again the opposite of what was recorded, and a sustained 30 mmHg fall meets the definition of orthostatic hypotension rather than a normal response.
questions.answerText: An inadequate sympathetic response to the orthostatic challenge

questions.q: Two subjects are compared at rest. Subject A has a heart rate of 52 with wide beat to beat variation, and subject B has a heart rate of 88 with narrow variation. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: Subject A is parasympathetically dominant and subject B is sympathetically dominant
Subject A is sympathetically dominant and subject B is parasympathetically dominant
Both subjects are parasympathetically dominant, since both are at rest
Neither interpretation is possible without a cold pressor test
questions.why: A low rate with wide variability means strong vagal influence on the node, while a high rate with little variability means that vagal influence is reduced and sympathetic influence is relatively greater, so the two records sit at opposite ends of the same scale. Reversing the two assignments contradicts both the rate and the variability. Being at rest does not guarantee vagal dominance, and the resting record itself carries enough information to interpret, although a challenge test would add more.
questions.answerText: Subject A is parasympathetically dominant and subject B is sympathetically dominant

questions.q: During a cold pressor test on a subject whose cardiac beta-1 receptors are blocked, blood pressure still rises substantially while heart rate barely changes. What explains the result?
options: The pressure rise came from a much larger stroke volume driven by cardiac beta-1 receptors
The pressure rise comes from a large increase in vagal tone to the arterioles
The block prevented the sympathetic discharge from occurring anywhere at all
The pressure rise comes mainly from alpha-1 vasoconstriction, which the block does not affect
questions.why: The cold pressor response raises pressure chiefly by narrowing arterioles through alpha-1 receptors, and those receptors are untouched by a beta-1 block, so resistance still climbs while the cardiac contribution is blunted and the rate stays flat. Arterioles have essentially no vagal supply, so increased vagal tone cannot be the source. A receptor block acts on the target rather than on the outflow itself, and a beta-1 driven stroke volume increase is precisely what the block prevented.
questions.answerText: The pressure rise comes mainly from alpha-1 vasoconstriction, which the block does not affect
